The Bhagavad Gita, in which the god Krishna counsels the warrior Arjuna before battle, describes several paths to it: selfless action, knowledge, and loving devotion, bhakti. Yoga began as a discipline for this spiritual path, set out in the Yoga Sutras around the early centuries AD. Dharma, one's duty according to stage of life and place in society, is the moral core of everyday life.

From the early centuries AD, Indian traders and priests carried Hindu and Buddhist ideas across the Bay of Bengal. Kings in Cambodia, Champa in today's Vietnam, and Java in Indonesia adopted Sanskrit, Indian gods and temple building. At home, dynasties like the Cholas of south India built vast temples to Shiva, and devotional bhakti poetry spread. Bali remains Hinduism's outpost in Southeast Asia.

Temple Hinduism under many dynasties

Kingdoms such as the Cholas built great temples, and poet-saints sang devotion to Shiva and Vishnu. From the 1200s the Delhi Sultanate ruled much of the north, but Hindu Vijayanagara, founded in 1336, held the south.

The kingdoms of the Kathmandu valley blended Hindu and Buddhist worship. Pashupatinath, a temple of Shiva, is one of Hinduism's holiest sites.

dd-hinduism.q: Why could Hinduism adapt to so many different rulers and ideas?
a: A single church enforced one creed everywhere
It had no single church or creed and absorbed rather than replaced
Its rulers forbade all other religions
It stayed confined to one small region
dd-hinduism.why: Hinduism wove Vedic ritual, local gods, philosophy and devotion together, and with no single church or creed it could adapt and outlast empires.

dd-hinduism.p:
Southeast Asian states shaped by Indian religion

From 802 the Khmer kings of Angkor linked their rule to Shiva or Vishnu and built huge temple-mountains. Later kings turned to Buddhism, which most Cambodians follow today.

Khmer temples to Shiva, such as Phanom Rung, stand in north-east Thailand. Thai kings still use court rituals performed by Brahmin priests.

Ancient texts describe four varnas: priests (Brahmins), warriors and rulers, merchants, and labourers. In practice society was divided into thousands of birth-based groups, jatis, which governed marriage and work, while those outside the system, now known as Dalits, faced 'untouchability'. Historians debate how rigid caste was before British rule, when censuses helped fix and rank categories. Reformers from the Buddha to Gandhi and B. R. Ambedkar, a Dalit who chaired the committee that drafted India's constitution, challenged it. The constitution abolished untouchability in 1950 and reserved places in education and government for disadvantaged castes, though discrimination persists.

dd-hinduism.q: How does caste still matter in India today?
a: It is required by India's constitution
It is outlawed as grounds for discrimination but still shapes lives
dd-hinduism.why: India's constitution abolished untouchability in 1950 and reserved places for disadvantaged castes, yet caste still shapes many lives and discrimination persists.

dd-hinduism.p: About 1.2 billion people were Hindu in 2020, by Pew Research Center estimates, about 15% of the world. About 95% of them live in India, and Nepal is the only other Hindu-majority country. From 1834 to 1917 over a million Indians went as indentured labourers to colonies like Mauritius, Fiji and Guyana. Large communities now also live in the United States, Britain and the Gulf.

India has about 1.1 billion Hindus, 79% of its people. Hindu nationalism, championed by the Bharatiya Janata Party, which has led India's government since 2014, has become a powerful political force.

About 81% of Nepalis are Hindu. Nepal was the world's last Hindu kingdom until it declared itself secular in 2006 and abolished the monarchy in 2008.

Descendants of indentured and plantation workers, 1800s–1900s

Mauritius is about 48% Hindu, the only country besides India and Nepal where Hindus are the largest group. It was the first colony to receive indentured Indian workers, in 1834.

Indentured workers arrived from 1879 to 1916. About a quarter of Fijians are Hindu, a share that has fallen as many Indo-Fijians emigrated after the coups that began in 1987.

dd-hinduism.q: What helped hold together Hindu belief across a vast land of many languages?
a: Temples, pilgrimages and festivals, with priests preserving the texts
dd-hinduism.why: Brahmin priests preserved the sacred texts, while temples, pilgrimages and festivals bound together a vast land with many languages.

dd-hinduism.p:
Hindus were about 22% of East Bengal's people in 1951 but about 8% in Bangladesh's 2022 census, some 13 million, after waves of emigration to India.

About 12–13% of Sri Lankans are Hindu, mostly Tamils in the north and east and on the hill-country tea estates.

Hindu life is marked by festivals. Diwali, the festival of lights, celebrates the victory of light over darkness with lamps, sweets and fireworks; Holi welcomes spring with clouds of coloured powder. Pilgrimage takes Hindus to holy rivers, mountains and cities, above all Varanasi on the Ganges, where many hope to be cremated. The Kumbh Mela, held in rotation at four riverside cities, is among the largest gatherings on Earth. Uttar Pradesh's government claimed about 660 million visits during the 2025 Maha Kumbh at Prayagraj, a figure some analysts doubt, but even sceptics count tens of millions.

Hindu ideas such as karma, rebirth, yoga and meditation, which shaped Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism, have spread worldwide. In 2020, by Pew Research Center estimates, about 1.2 billion people were Hindu, about 95% of them in India. Caste, though outlawed as a basis for discrimination by India's constitution, still shapes many lives, and the rise of Hindu nationalism has made the faith central to Indian politics.

About 1.2 billion Hindus, mostly in India and Nepal, make it the third-largest religion. Festivals such as Diwali, the festival of lights, and Holi, the festival of colours, are celebrated worldwide, and yoga and meditation, rooted in Hindu traditions, have spread across the globe.

dd-hinduism.s: Most Hindus worship many forms of one divine reality.

dd-judaism.p: Judaism grew from the religion of the Israelites, who lived in the hills of Canaan from about 1200 BC. By 900 BC they had two kingdoms, Israel and Judah, and came to worship one God. Assyria destroyed Israel in 722 BC, and in 586 BC Babylon destroyed Jerusalem's Temple and exiled Judah's leaders, but the exiles kept their faith.

items: "Hear O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one" (the Shema).
Made with Abraham and renewed at Sinai with Moses.
Five books of Moses; 613 commandments guide life.
Justice and good deeds matter as much as belief.

steps: Leaves Mesopotamia for Canaan; father of the Jewish people.
Leads the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt; receives the Torah at Sinai.
Jerusalem becomes the capital; the First Temple is built.
Babylon destroys the Temple in 586 BC; exiles return and rebuild.

a: The five books of Moses, the core of Jewish law

dd-judaism.p: Rome destroyed the rebuilt Temple in AD 70, and rabbis rebuilt Judaism around prayer, study and law. Scattered from Iraq to Spain, Jews lived as minorities, often protected but repeatedly expelled and massacred. The Holocaust murdered about 6 million Jews, and in 1948 the State of Israel was founded.

Judaism took shape among a small people caught between great empires. Defeat and exile could have ended their faith; instead, many scholars argue, it sharpened the belief that one God ruled all nations and that history had a purpose. After AD 70 Judaism centred on a portable book, the Torah, and on law kept at home and in the synagogue, so it could survive anywhere without a temple, a state or a king.

dd-judaism.q: What happened to Judaism after Rome destroyed the Second Temple in AD 70?
a: It died out within a generation
Rabbis rebuilt it around prayer, study and law
Jews immediately founded a new kingdom
dd-judaism.why: With sacrifice ended, rabbis rebuilt Judaism around the Torah, prayer, study and law kept at home and in the synagogue.

dd-judaism.h: Ancient Israel and the exile, c. 900–538 BC
dd-judaism.p: According to the Bible, the Israelites escaped slavery in Egypt and settled in Canaan. By about 900 BC there were two kingdoms, Israel and Judah, in today's Israel and Palestinian territories. Assyria destroyed Israel in 722 BC. In 586 BC Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple and took many Judeans into exile in Iraq, until the Persian king Cyrus let them return in 538 BC.

Two kingdoms of the Israelites, c. 900–586 BC

Judah's heartland lay in the hills around Jerusalem, Bethlehem and Hebron. Its kings claimed descent from David, and its name gave us the words 'Jew' and 'Judaism'.

The northern kingdom, Israel, was the larger and richer of the two. Assyria conquered it in 722 BC and deported many of its people, the origin of the tradition of the 'ten lost tribes'.

The empires that conquered them

Babylon deported Judeans in 597 and 586 BC. Many stayed after the return, and Jews lived in Iraq for about 2,500 years, until most left in 1950–52.

dd-judaism.q: What did the Holocaust do to Europe's Jewish communities?
a: It murdered about two-thirds of Europe's Jews
It moved them peacefully to new homes
It affected only Jews in Germany
dd-judaism.why: Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered about 6 million Jews; centuries-old communities in Poland, Lithuania and Ukraine vanished, and Yiddish culture almost disappeared.

dd-judaism.p:
Conquered Babylon in 539 BC and freed the exiles

Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC and let the exiles go home. The rebuilt Second Temple in Jerusalem was finished around 515 BC.

Jews believe in one God who made a covenant with Abraham and gave the Torah, the five books of Moses, to Moses at Mount Sinai. By rabbinic count the Torah holds 613 commandments, from the Ten Commandments to the food laws known as kashrut. Every week Shabbat, from Friday sunset to Saturday night, is kept for rest, prayer and family meals. Festivals retell the people's story: Passover recalls the Exodus from Egypt, and Yom Kippur is a day of fasting and atonement. Judaism puts more weight on deeds than on creed, and Jewish identity passes down through families as well as through faith.

When Rome destroyed the Temple in AD 70, sacrifice ended, and Judaism was rebuilt by rabbis, teachers of the law. Around AD 200 they wrote down the oral law as the Mishnah. Centuries of debate on it became the Talmud; the Babylonian Talmud, finished around 500–600 in today's Iraq, is still studied line by line. Synagogues, where a quorum of ten could pray, could be built anywhere. Study itself became a form of worship, and communities from Yemen to Poland kept schools so boys could read Hebrew. This portable faith let Judaism survive almost 1,900 years without a state of its own.

After Rome destroyed the Second Temple in AD 70, Jews lived as minorities across the Middle East, North Africa and Europe. Medieval Europe expelled them again and again: from England in 1290, France in 1394, Spain in 1492 and Portugal in 1496–97. Sephardi exiles found refuge in the Ottoman Empire, while Ashkenazi Jews moved east to Poland and Lithuania.

Edward I expelled England's Jews in 1290. They were allowed back only in 1656, under Oliver Cromwell.

The French crown expelled its Jews several times, finally in 1394. Small communities survived in papal Avignon and in Alsace, which was not yet French.

dd-judaism.q: According to many scholars, how did defeat and exile in Babylon affect the Judeans' faith?
a: They abandoned it for Babylonian gods
It sharpened their belief that one God ruled all nations
It made them adopt Persian beliefs
dd-judaism.why: Defeat and exile could have ended the faith; instead, many scholars argue, it sharpened the belief that one God ruled all nations and that history had a purpose.

dd-judaism.p:
Yiddish-speaking Jews of central and eastern Europe

Polish rulers protected Jews by charter from 1264. By the 1600s Poland-Lithuania had the largest Jewish community in the world, with its own council of self-government.

Grand Duke Vytautas granted Lithuania's Jews privileges in 1388. Vilnius later became so famous for learning it was called the 'Jerusalem of Lithuania'.

Where many exiles from Spain and Portugal settled

Sultan Bayezid II welcomed Jews expelled from Spain. Istanbul and other Ottoman cities gained large Sephardi communities speaking Ladino, a form of Spanish.

Thessaloniki, then Ottoman, became one of the great Sephardi cities, where Jews were the largest group for about 400 years.

dd-judaism.q: Which ideas from Judaism were carried further by Christianity and Islam?
a: Worship centred on a living king
A single God who demands justice, and a weekly day of rest
dd-judaism.why: Judaism gave the world the Hebrew Bible, a weekly day of rest and the idea of one God demanding justice; Christianity and Islam both look back to Abraham.

dd-judaism.p: Centuries of dispersal created distinct Jewish cultures. Ashkenazi Jews, from medieval Germany and later Eastern Europe, spoke Yiddish. Sephardi Jews, expelled from Spain and Portugal, spoke Ladino and settled around the Mediterranean. Mizrahi Jews had lived for millennia in Iraq, Iran, Yemen and North Africa. Modern times added religious branches. Reform Judaism, born in 19th-century Germany, adapted practice to modern life; Orthodox Jews kept traditional law, and Hasidism, begun by the Baal Shem Tov in 18th-century Ukraine, stressed joyful devotion. Conservative Judaism took a middle path, and many Israeli Jews describe themselves as secular.

About 15.8 million Jews lived worldwide in 2025, by demographer Sergio DellaPergola's estimates, slightly fewer than before the Holocaust. Nearly half live in Israel, founded in 1948, and about 6.3 million in the United States. France, Canada and Britain follow. The old heartlands of Poland and the Middle East now have very few Jews.

Home to about 46% of the world's Jews

Israel was declared in 1948 after a UN plan to partition British Palestine. War followed, and by most estimates about 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled. Its conflict with the Palestinians remains unresolved.

Estimates by demographer Sergio DellaPergola

About 6.3 million Jews, by Jewish Agency estimates. Most descend from about 2 million Jews who arrived from Eastern Europe between 1881 and 1924, fleeing poverty and pogroms.

France has Europe's largest Jewish community, roughly 440,000. Most French Jews descend from North African Jews who arrived in the 1950s and 60s.

dd-judaism.q: Why could Judaism survive almost 1,900 years without a state of its own?
a: It depended on a single great temple
It centred on a portable book and law kept anywhere
Jews never left the Land of Israel
dd-judaism.why: Centred on the Torah, synagogues that could be built anywhere, and study as worship, Judaism could survive without a temple, a state or a king.

dd-judaism.p:
Destroyed in the Holocaust or emptied by emigration after 1948

About 3.3 million Jews lived in Poland in 1939, a tenth of its people. About 90% were murdered in the Holocaust, and most survivors left.

About 95% of Lithuania's Jews were murdered in 1941–44, one of the highest shares in Europe. Most were shot near their homes.

Between 1941 and 1945 Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered about 6 million Jews, two-thirds of Europe's Jews. In the occupied Soviet Union victims were shot beside mass graves; from across Europe others were deported in freight trains to death camps in occupied Poland, such as Auschwitz-Birkenau and Treblinka, and gassed. Over a million Jewish children were killed. Centuries-old communities in Poland, Lithuania and Ukraine vanished, and Yiddish culture almost disappeared with them. The Holocaust, called the Shoah in Hebrew, greatly strengthened support for a Jewish state, and Israel was founded three years after the war ended.

Judaism gave the world the Hebrew Bible, a weekly day of rest and the idea of a single God who demands justice, ideas carried further by Christianity and Islam, which both look back to Abraham. Christian hostility and later racial antisemitism culminated in the Holocaust. Today about 15.8 million Jews live mainly in Israel and the United States, and Israel's conflict with the Palestinians remains unresolved.

About 15 million Jews live today, mainly in Israel and the United States. The Sabbath, from Friday sunset to Saturday, and festivals such as Passover, which remembers the Exodus, and Yom Kippur, the day of atonement, shape Jewish life. Judaism is the parent faith of both Christianity and Islam.

dd-judaism.s: Christianity and Islam both grew out of Judaism.

dd-buddhism.p: In the 5th century BC Siddhartha Gautama, by tradition a prince of the Shakya clan, left his comfortable life to seek an end to suffering. Buddhists believe he found enlightenment at Bodh Gaya and became the Buddha, the 'awakened one', and he taught for about 45 years across the Ganges plain. Around 250 BC the emperor Ashoka backed his teaching and sent missions abroad.

steps: Suffering comes from craving and attachment.
dd-buddhism.p: The Buddha's first teaching, given near Varanasi.

dd-buddhism.h: The Eightfold Path, in three parts

l: Focus on monks and personal liberation

dd-buddhism.p: Monks then carried it along the Silk Road to China, Korea and Japan, by sea to South-East Asia, and over the Himalaya to Tibet. In India itself it faded, and after about 1200 it almost disappeared there.

dd-buddhism.q: What do Buddhists believe Siddhartha Gautama achieved at Bodh Gaya?
a: He was crowned emperor of India
He found enlightenment and became the Buddha
He founded the city of Pataliputra
dd-buddhism.why: Buddhists believe Siddhartha found enlightenment under the Bodhi tree and became the Buddha, the 'awakened one', then taught for about 45 years.

dd-buddhism.p: The Buddha offered a path open to anyone, whatever their caste, and he founded an order of monks and nuns, the sangha, that could spread and preserve his teaching. Kings found it a useful source of moral authority, and merchants supported monasteries along their routes. It adapted readily, absorbing local gods and customs wherever it went.

dd-buddhism.h: The Buddha's homeland and Ashoka's empire, c. 250 BC
dd-buddhism.p: Siddhartha Gautama was born, according to tradition, at Lumbini in today's Nepal, and taught in the Ganges plain of northern India in the 5th century BC. Two centuries later the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, ruling from Afghanistan to Bangladesh, turned to Buddhism after a bloody war, carved its values on rocks and pillars, and sent monks abroad. Sri Lankan tradition says his son Mahinda brought the teaching to Sri Lanka.

dd-buddhism.q: Why did Buddhism almost disappear from India after about 1200?
a: Its monks all moved to Japan
Hindu devotion revived, and its royally backed monasteries were sacked
dd-buddhism.why: Buddhism came to depend on royally supported monasteries; as Hindu devotion revived and Turkish armies sacked monasteries around 1200, monks fled to Tibet and Nepal.

dd-buddhism.p:
c. 268–232 BC, capital Pataliputra

The Buddha lived and taught in today's Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. Ashoka ruled nearly all of India except the far south, and his edicts survive on rocks and pillars across it.

The north-west, Gandhara, was part of Ashoka's empire. It later became a great centre of Buddhist learning and art.

Buddhist since c. 250 BC, by tradition

Sri Lanka claims an unbroken Buddhist tradition from about 250 BC. Its monks wrote down the Pali scriptures in the 1st century BC, among the earliest Buddhist texts put in writing.

According to legend, the young prince Siddhartha had been shielded from all suffering until, outside his palace, he saw an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering holy man. At 29 he left home; years of harsh fasting nearly killed him, so he sought a 'Middle Way' between luxury and self-denial. His first sermon set out the Four Noble Truths: life involves suffering; suffering comes from craving; it can end; and the Noble Eightfold Path of right views, conduct and meditation leads there. Buddhists believe beings are reborn again and again according to their karma, their deeds, until they reach nirvana, the ending of craving and of rebirth. There is no creator god at the centre of the teaching.

dd-buddhism.h: Along the trade routes, c. AD 1–800
dd-buddhism.p: Monks travelled with merchants. Overland, Buddhism went from Gandhara in Pakistan through Central Asia to China by the 1st century AD, then on to Korea in 372 and Japan in the 6th century. By sea, it reached Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Indonesia, often alongside Hindu cults. Tibet adopted it in the 7th–8th centuries. Chinese pilgrims walked the other way to India to collect scriptures.

Silk Road monasteries; later Muslim

Afghanistan was a crossroads of Buddhist monasteries for centuries, until Islam spread from the 7th century onwards.

Gandhara, around Peshawar and Taxila, blended Greek and Indian art and gave the Buddha one of his first portraits in human form, in the 1st–2nd centuries AD.

dd-buddhism.q: Why could the Buddha's teaching appeal to so many people?
a: It was open to anyone, whatever their caste
It was reserved for Brahmin priests
dd-buddhism.why: The Buddha offered a path open to anyone regardless of caste, and his order of monks and nuns, the sangha, spread and preserved the teaching.

dd-buddhism.p:
Mahayana Buddhism, in Chinese translation

Buddhism reached China around the 1st century AD. Monks translated thousands of texts, and the pilgrim Xuanzang walked to India and back in 629–645.

The kingdom of Goguryeo, in the north, received Buddhism from China in 372; Baekje followed in 384 and Silla in the early 6th century.

Reached largely by sea

Sri Lanka became the stronghold of Theravada, the 'teaching of the elders', and later sent monks to renew it in Myanmar and Thailand.

The kingdom of Bagan adopted Theravada Buddhism in the 11th century and covered its plain with thousands of temples.

dd-buddhism.q: Where is Buddhism mainly practised today?
a: Almost entirely in Asia, though meditation has spread worldwide
dd-buddhism.why: About 324 million Buddhists live almost all in Asia, from Sri Lanka to Mongolia, while in India Buddhists are under 1%; meditation has spread around the world.

dd-buddhism.p: Theravada, the 'teaching of the elders', follows the Pali scriptures and stresses monks and their discipline; it is the main tradition of Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia. Mahayana, the 'great vehicle', arose around the 1st century BC with new scriptures praising bodhisattvas, beings who delay their own release to help others. It spread to China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam, where it gave rise to schools such as Zen and Pure Land. Vajrayana, or Tibetan Buddhism, adds rituals, mantras and the guidance of lamas, some recognised as reborn teachers. Its best-known figure is the 14th Dalai Lama, who fled to India after a failed Tibetan uprising against Chinese rule in 1959.

The Pew Research Center counted about 324 million Buddhists in 2020, about 4% of humanity, almost all in Asia. Buddhists are the majority in seven countries, from Sri Lanka to Mongolia; Thailand has the most, about 68 million. In China and Japan, Buddhist practice mixes with other traditions and many people do not call themselves Buddhist. In India, its birthplace, Buddhists are under 1% of the population.

Mostly Theravada in the south, Tibetan in the Himalaya and Mongolia

About 70% of Sri Lankans are Buddhist, by Pew's estimate. The Temple of the Tooth in Kandy holds what Buddhists revere as a tooth of the Buddha.

About 89% of Myanmar's people are Buddhist, by Pew's estimate, and monks have long played a big part in its politics.

Mostly Mahayana, mixed with local traditions

China has tens of millions of Buddhists, including Tibetans. Pew counted about 53 million self-identified Buddhists in 2020, though far more worship at Buddhist temples.

Most Japanese have Buddhist funerals and visit Shinto shrines too, but many do not call themselves members of any religion.

dd-buddhism.q: What turning point around 260 BC helped Buddhism spread beyond India?
a: The emperor Ashoka turned to it and sent missions abroad
dd-buddhism.why: After the bloody Kalinga war, Ashoka backed Buddhism, carved its values on rocks and pillars, and sent monks abroad, by tradition his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka.

dd-buddhism.p:
Now mostly Hindu or Muslim

India had about 8.4 million Buddhists in its 2011 census, many of them followers of B. R. Ambedkar, who converted with hundreds of thousands of Dalits in 1956.

Lumbini is a pilgrimage site, but about 8% of Nepal's people are Buddhist; most are Hindu.

Buddhism did not fall in one blow. From about the 5th century, Hindu devotional movements won back royal patrons and ordinary believers, and some Hindus came to honour the Buddha as an incarnation of the god Vishnu. Buddhism came to depend on great monasteries supported by kings, so it was vulnerable when that support ended. Around 1200 Turkish armies from the north-west sacked the monasteries of Bihar, according to most accounts including Nalanda, and monks fled to Tibet and Nepal. A modern revival began in 1956, when the Dalit leader B. R. Ambedkar, chief architect of India's constitution, converted with hundreds of thousands of followers to reject the caste system.

Buddhism became one of the world's great religions, with about 324 million followers in 2020 by Pew's count, and it shaped the art, writing, architecture and ethics of much of Asia. It split into broad traditions: Theravada in Sri Lanka and mainland South-East Asia, Mahayana in East Asia and Vietnam, and Vajrayana in Tibet, Bhutan and Mongolia. Meditation, often stripped of religion, has spread around the world.

About 500 million people follow Buddhism, mostly in East and South-East Asia. Meditation and mindfulness practices drawn from it have spread worldwide, and the Dalai Lama, exiled from Tibet, is one of the best-known religious leaders on Earth.

dd-buddhism.q: According to the Buddha, what causes suffering?

dd-chinafaiths.p: Confucius, a minor official and teacher in the state of Lu, taught in the 6th and 5th centuries BC that society would be orderly if rulers were virtuous and everyone did their duty within the family. Around the same era, Daoist sages taught people to live simply and in harmony with the Dao, the way of nature. After the harsh Qin dynasty burned books, the Han made Confucianism the official learning in 136 BC, while Daoism grew into an organised religion with priests, temples and gods.

a: Respect and care for one’s parents

dd-chinafaiths.p: From about 605, officials were chosen by exams on the Confucian classics, a system copied in Korea and Vietnam. Buddhism, Confucianism and Daoism came to be called the 'three teachings'.

dd-chinafaiths.q: What did Confucius teach would make society orderly?
a: Virtuous rulers and everyone doing their duty within the family
Withdrawing from society to live in the mountains
Worship of a single creator god
dd-chinafaiths.why: Confucius taught that society would be orderly if rulers were virtuous and everyone did their duty within the family, with filial piety the root of virtue.

dd-chinafaiths.p: These ideas were answers to chaos. The Zhou kingdom had collapsed into centuries of war, and thinkers competed to tell rulers how to restore peace. Confucianism suited emperors because it taught loyalty and gave them a trained, educated class of officials. Daoism offered what Confucianism lacked: a relationship with nature, a route to inner calm and, for its religious followers, hopes of long life and immortality.

dd-chinafaiths.h: The age of the philosophers, c. 500–100 BC
dd-chinafaiths.p: As the old Zhou kingdom of China broke into warring states, thinkers argued over how to bring back order: the 'Hundred Schools'. Confucius taught that order begins with virtuous rulers and loyal families. Daoists, inspired by the book credited to Laozi, urged people to follow the Dao, the natural 'way', and not to force things. The Qin, who united China in 221 BC, favoured harsh Legalist laws instead, but the Han made Confucianism the state's official learning.

dd-chinafaiths.q: How did Confucian ideas shape government beyond China?
a: They were rejected everywhere outside China
Korea and Vietnam copied China's exams on the Confucian classics
dd-chinafaiths.why: Korea's Joseon kings built a strictly Confucian state and Vietnam held similar exams for centuries; Japan used Confucian ethics too, though rank stayed hereditary.

dd-chinafaiths.p:
Split into rival states, 770–221 BC

Confucius, Mencius, Laozi and Zhuangzi all lived in north and central China between about 550 and 280 BC. In 213 BC the Qin burned many books, Confucian classics among them; the Han revived them.

Confucius did not write the Analects: his followers collected his sayings after his death in 479 BC. He taught ren, humaneness or goodness, and li, proper ritual and manners, which he believed shaped character. Later Confucians taught that society rested on five relationships: ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger brother, and friend and friend. Each side owed the other duties, though superiors were owed obedience. Filial piety, honouring and caring for parents and ancestors, was the root of all virtue. He also gave a version of the golden rule: 'Do not impose on others what you yourself do not desire.' His ideal was the junzi, the gentleman, whose nobility came from learning and conduct, not birth.

By 1700 Confucian ideas ran the governments of East Asia. China had chosen officials by exams on the Confucian classics since the 600s. Korea's Joseon kings, from 1392, built one of the most strictly Confucian states ever, and Vietnam's rulers held similar exams from 1075 to 1919. In Japan the Tokugawa shoguns used Confucian ethics to teach loyalty to samurai, though rank there stayed hereditary rather than won by exams.

Officials chosen by exams on the classics

The exams, begun under the Sui around 605, were based from the 1310s on Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucian readings of the classics. They were abolished in 1905. Tibet and Xinjiang were not yet under Qing rule.

The Qing conquered western Taiwan in 1683 and built Confucian schools there; the mountainous east stayed outside their control.

dd-chinafaiths.q: What problem were Confucius and the other early Chinese thinkers trying to solve?
a: How to restore peace after the Zhou kingdom collapsed into war
dd-chinafaiths.why: These ideas were answers to chaos: the Zhou kingdom had broken into warring states, and the 'Hundred Schools' competed to tell rulers how to restore order.

dd-chinafaiths.p:
A Neo-Confucian state, 1392–1897

Korea held state exams on the classics from 958 until 1894. Joseon scholars followed Zhu Xi so strictly that they cut back Buddhist temples and influence.

The north was part of Joseon Korea, which shaped family rites, ancestor worship and respect for elders across the peninsula.

Confucian exams, 1075–1919

Though Vietnam fought hard to stay independent of China, its kings borrowed China's Confucian state model, its exams and classical Chinese writing.

dd-chinafaiths.q: How do these traditions live on in China and East Asia today?
a: They have vanished since the Cultural Revolution
China has revived Confucius, and Daoist ideas like tai chi spread worldwide
Confucianism is now China's only official religion
dd-chinafaiths.why: After Mao's attacks, China has revived Confucius as a symbol of national culture since the 1980s, while Daoist ideas from yin and yang to tai chi have spread worldwide.

dd-chinafaiths.p: The Daodejing, a short book of about 5,000 Chinese characters, opens by saying that 'the Dao that can be told is not the eternal Dao'. Tradition credits it to Laozi, an older contemporary of Confucius, but many scholars think it was compiled later, around the 4th century BC, and some doubt Laozi existed. It praises wu wei, acting without forcing, like water that yields yet wears away rock. The playful Zhuangzi told of dreaming he was a butterfly and waking unsure whether he was a man who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming of being a man. Later Daoist alchemists hunting for elixirs of immortality, by the 9th century AD, stumbled on gunpowder.

Confucianism has no churches or members, but its values of family, education and respect for elders run deep across East Asia. Under Mao, China attacked Confucius as feudal; since the 1980s it has embraced him again. Daoism survives in temples, festivals, tai chi and Chinese medicine, mixed with Buddhism and folk worship of gods and ancestors, from China to Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore.

Daoist and folk temples, Confucian revival

Daoism is one of China's five officially recognised religions; Confucianism is not counted as one. From 2004 China opened Confucius Institutes abroad, which critics in some countries saw as tools of state influence.

Taiwan celebrates Teachers' Day on 28 September, Confucius's traditional birthday, with dawn ceremonies at Confucian temples.

Temples brought by migrants

About half of Chinese Singaporeans called themselves Buddhist or Taoist in the 2020 census. In the 1980s schools briefly offered Confucian ethics as a subject.

Chinese Malaysians, nearly a quarter of the population, keep Daoist and Buddhist temples and festivals such as the Hungry Ghost Festival.

dd-chinafaiths.q: Why did the Han and later emperors favour Confucianism?
a: It taught loyalty and supplied a trained class of officials
It rejected all ritual and hierarchy
It came from a foreign conqueror
dd-chinafaiths.why: Confucianism suited emperors because it taught loyalty and gave them educated officials; from about 605 officials were chosen by exams on the Confucian classics.

dd-chinafaiths.p:
Values and rites more than religion

South Korea's exam-driven schooling, respect for seniority and ancestral rites at Chuseok and Lunar New Year reflect a deep Confucian heritage.

Few Japanese call themselves Confucian, but ideas of loyalty, hierarchy and duty to family helped shape its schools and companies.

Few people in traditional China chose just one teaching. A scholar-official might follow Confucian duty at work, seek Daoist calm in retirement and call Buddhist monks to his parents' funerals, while villagers prayed to local gods and honoured their ancestors at home altars. A popular saying held that the three teachings were one. In the 12th century the philosopher Zhu Xi, answering Buddhist and Daoist ideas about the mind and the universe, shaped Neo-Confucianism, which became the basis of the state exams. That mix explains why surveys struggle to count Chinese religion: many people who say they have no religion still burn incense for their ancestors at the Qingming festival every spring.

For over 2,000 years Confucian values shaped East Asian government, schooling and family life, and the habit of selecting officials by written exam is often said to have influenced civil services as far away as Britain. Reformers blamed Confucianism for China's weakness after 1900, and Mao's Cultural Revolution attacked it. Since the 1980s China has revived Confucius as a symbol of national culture, and Daoist ideas, from yin and yang to tai chi, have spread worldwide.

Confucian ideals of education, family and hierarchy still shape China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam: the imperial exams, ancestor worship and the prestige of teachers come from them. Daoist ideas live on in tai chi, feng shui and traditional medicine.

dd-chinafaiths.s: Yin and yang is a Daoist idea of balancing opposites.
dd-chinafaiths.why: Light and dark, active and passive.

Zhang Daoling founds the Daoist Way of the Celestial Masters, by tradition
China abolishes the Confucian civil service exams

dd-christianity.p: Christianity began around AD 30 among the Jewish followers of Jesus of Nazareth, whom the Romans crucified in Jerusalem. Believing he had risen from the dead, apostles such as Paul spread the faith through the cities of the Roman Empire, despite waves of persecution. The emperor Constantine backed it from 312, and in 380 it became Rome's official religion.

items: Born a Jew, crucified around AD 30, believed to have risen from the dead.
Jesus’s death and resurrection offer forgiveness of sins.

steps: Luther breaks with Rome; Protestant churches form.
About half of Christians are Catholic, a third Protestant, the rest mostly Orthodox.

a: Father, Son and Holy Spirit as one God

dd-christianity.p: In 1054 the Latin West and Greek East split into the Catholic and Orthodox churches, and from 1517 the Reformation divided western Europe into Catholic and Protestant. European empires and missionaries then carried Christianity to the Americas, Africa and Asia, and it became the world's largest religion.

a: As a Greek philosophy school in Athens
As the official faith of Constantine's army
Among Jewish followers of Jesus, who believed he had risen
As a reform movement within Roman paganism
dd-christianity.why: Christianity began around AD 30 among the Jewish followers of Jesus of Nazareth; believing he had risen, apostles like Paul spread it through Roman cities.

dd-christianity.p: Christianity offered a personal God, forgiveness and eternal life to anyone, slave or free, Jew or Gentile, and its churches cared for widows, orphans and the sick, which won converts in crowded Roman cities. Imperial backing after Constantine made it the faith of rulers, and later of empires. Its splits came from disputes over authority as much as belief: whether the pope ruled the whole church, and, for Luther, whether scripture outweighed church tradition.

dd-christianity.h: Christianity in the Roman world, AD 30–400
dd-christianity.p: Jesus, a Jewish teacher, was crucified by the Romans in Jerusalem around AD 30. His followers believed he had risen from the dead, and missionaries such as Paul carried the faith through the cities of the Roman Empire, from Turkey and Greece to Italy. After waves of persecution, Constantine backed Christianity from 312, and in 380 it became the empire's official religion. Armenia and Ethiopia adopted it too.

dd-christianity.q: What were Christianity's great splits mainly about, as well as belief?
a: Authority: the pope's power, and scripture against church tradition
Whether to accept non-Jews at all
dd-christianity.why: The 1054 split turned on the pope's authority, and Luther's Reformation on whether scripture outweighed church tradition, dividing Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant.

dd-christianity.p:
Christian state religion from 380; borders of 395

Constantine won power in Rome in 312 and granted Christians freedom of worship in 313. The bishops of Rome, later called popes, claimed Peter's authority.

Christians were martyred at Lyon in 177. By 400 Gaul had bishops in most of its cities.

Converted in the 300s

According to tradition, King Tiridates III made Armenia the first Christian state in 301; some historians prefer a date around 314.

The kingdom of Iberia, in eastern Georgia, adopted Christianity in the 330s, by tradition through a woman missionary, Saint Nino.

Jesus was a Jewish preacher from Nazareth in Galilee. Most historians agree that he lived, was baptised by John the Baptist and was crucified on the orders of Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, around AD 30–33. According to the Gospels, written a few decades later, he healed the sick, taught in parables, preached the coming kingdom of God and rose from the dead three days after his death. Christians believe he is the Son of God and that his death and resurrection offer salvation. Most Christians also believe in the Trinity, one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, as defined by councils in the 300s.

The first Christians were Jews, but Paul argued that non-Jews could join without keeping Jewish law, and churches spread through the Greek-speaking cities of the empire. Romans saw Christians' refusal to sacrifice to the gods as dangerous, and persecution came in waves, the worst under Diocletian from 303. In 312 Constantine won a battle at Rome's Milvian Bridge, after a vision of the cross according to his biographer Eusebius, and in 313 he granted Christians freedom of worship. He called the Council of Nicaea in 325. In 380 Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the state religion, and pagan sacrifice was banned soon after.

In 1054 the Latin church of Rome and the Greek church of Constantinople excommunicated each other's leaders, a split never healed. From 1517 Martin Luther's protest in Germany launched the Reformation, and by 1600 much of northern Europe was Protestant. Catholic Spain and Portugal carried their faith to the Americas and the Philippines, while Russia became the leading Orthodox power.

Including Spanish and Portuguese colonies

Spain was the champion of the Counter-Reformation. Its Inquisition suppressed Protestants, and its empire spread Catholicism across the Americas.

Portugal took Catholic missions to Brazil, Africa and Asia, from Goa in India to Macau and Japan.

dd-christianity.q: Why did Christianity win converts in crowded Roman cities?
a: It offered forgiveness to anyone, and its churches cared for the needy
It was required by Roman law from the start
It allowed only wealthy citizens to join
It promised military victories over Persia
dd-christianity.why: Christianity offered a personal God, forgiveness and eternal life to anyone, slave or free, and its churches cared for widows, orphans and the sick.

dd-christianity.p:
Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican

Sweden's kings broke with Rome from the 1520s and made the Lutheran church the state church, as Denmark and Norway also did.

Luther's protest split the German lands. The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 let each prince choose Lutheran or Catholic for his territory, roughly north and south.

Most under Ottoman or Russian rule

Greece's Orthodox Christians lived under Ottoman rule, which allowed them to keep their church under the patriarch in Constantinople.

After Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453, Russia was the only great independent Orthodox state, and from 1589 Moscow had its own patriarch.

dd-christianity.q: How has Christianity's centre of gravity shifted in modern times?
a: Towards Western Europe, where attendance is rising
Southwards: sub-Saharan Africa now has more Christians than any other region
It has stayed in Europe as in 1910
dd-christianity.why: In 1910 about two-thirds of Christians lived in Europe; Europe has grown more secular, while by 2020 sub-Saharan Africa had more Christians than any other region.

dd-christianity.p: Christianity's big families grew from splits. Western and Eastern churches drifted apart over language, the pope's authority and a word added to the creed, and in 1054 papal envoys and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other. The Catholic Church, led by the pope, is the largest, with about 1.4 billion members. The Orthodox churches are a family of self-governing national churches, the biggest in Russia. Protestants, born of Luther's 1517 protest against indulgences, stress the Bible and faith over church authority; they include Lutherans, Anglicans, Baptists, Methodists and fast-growing Pentecostals. Older Oriental churches, such as Ethiopia's and Armenia's, separated after a dispute in 451.

About 2.3 billion people were Christian in 2020, by Pew Research Center estimates, nearly three in ten people on Earth. The United States has the most Christians, mostly Protestant, and Brazil the most Catholics. Russia leads the Orthodox world. As Europe has grown more secular, sub-Saharan Africa, with countries like Kenya and DR Congo, has become home to more Christians than any other region.

Largest church among Christians

Brazil has more Catholics than any other country, but evangelical Protestants have grown fast, to over a quarter of Brazilians in the 2022 census.

Vatican City, inside Rome, is the seat of the pope, head of about 1.4 billion Catholics. Leo XIV, elected in May 2025, is the first pope from the United States.

Including Anglican, Pentecostal and African-initiated churches

The US has more Christians than any other country, about 217 million in 2020, though their share fell from 78% to 64% in a decade. Most are Protestant, and about a fifth of Americans are Catholic.

Kenya is over 80% Christian, mostly Protestant of many kinds, with a large Catholic minority. Most Kenyans became Christian during the 1900s.

dd-christianity.q: What turned Christianity from a persecuted sect into the faith of rulers?
a: Constantine's backing from 312 and official status in 380
dd-christianity.why: Constantine backed Christianity from 312 and granted freedom of worship in 313; in 380 Theodosius made it Rome's official religion, the faith of rulers and later of empires.

dd-christianity.p:
Eastern and Oriental Orthodox

The Russian Orthodox Church was persecuted under Soviet rule and revived after 1991. It is the largest Orthodox church, closely tied to the state.

Most Ukrainians are Orthodox. In 2019 the Orthodox Church of Ukraine became independent of Moscow, and Russia's invasion in 2022 pushed many more believers away from the Moscow-linked church.

In 1910 about two-thirds of the world's Christians lived in Europe, by Pew Research Center estimates. Mission schools and hospitals in the colonial era, and then African-led churches after independence, made Africa a Christian heartland, and Pew estimates that by 2020 sub-Saharan Africa had more Christians than any other region. Pentecostal and charismatic churches, with lively worship, healing and prophecy, have spread fast across Africa, Latin America and Asia. Meanwhile church attendance and Christian identity have fallen across Western Europe and, more recently, in the United States, where the Christian share fell from 78% to 64% between 2010 and 2020.

Christianity shaped Western law, art, universities, the calendar and ideas of human dignity, and it was also used to justify crusades, colonial conquest and persecution. In 2020, by Pew Research Center estimates, about 2.3 billion people were Christian, roughly half of them Catholic. Its centre of gravity has moved south: Europe is growing more secular, while sub-Saharan Africa now has more Christians than any other region.

With about 2.3 billion followers it is the world's largest religion. Its centre of gravity has moved south: more Christians now live in Africa and Latin America than in Europe. Christmas and Easter are celebrated worldwide.

dd-christianity.s: More Christians now live in Africa and Latin America than in Europe.

The Great Schism splits the Catholic West and Orthodox East

dd-islam.p: Around 610 Muhammad, a merchant of Mecca, began preaching that God had sent him revelations, which Muslims believe were recorded in the Quran. Persecuted, his community moved to Medina in 622, and by his death in 632 most of Arabia had accepted Islam. Within a century the caliphs' armies built an empire from Spain to Pakistan.

items: "There is no god but God, and Muhammad is his messenger."
Five times a day, facing Mecca.
Giving a share of wealth to the poor.
From dawn to sunset in Ramadan.
To Mecca once in a lifetime, if able.

dd-islam.q: Which direction do Muslims face when they pray?

dd-islam.p: A quarrel over who should lead Muslims divided Sunni from Shia. Later, Turkish dynasties carried Islam into India and the Balkans, while traders and Sufi mystics spread it to West Africa and Southeast Asia. After centuries of power under empires like the Ottomans, most Muslim lands fell under European rule before winning independence in the 20th century.

dd-islam.q: How did Islam begin, according to Muslim belief?
a: Muhammad received revelations from God, recorded in the Quran
A caliph in Baghdad wrote down a new law code
Persian priests reformed their old religion
Ottoman sultans founded it in Constantinople
dd-islam.why: Muslims believe that from about 610 God's revelations came to Muhammad, a merchant of Mecca, and were recorded in the Quran.

dd-islam.p: Islam united Arabia's feuding tribes under one faith and one leader, and conquest spread Muslim rule while the Byzantine and Persian empires were exhausted by war with each other. Conversion was slower than conquest: over centuries people joined the religion of their rulers, drawn by its simple creed, its law and the advantages of belonging. Beyond the empires, Islam travelled with merchants, whose shared faith, law and Arabic letters linked ports from East Africa to Indonesia.

dd-islam.h: The Prophet and the first conquests, 610–750
dd-islam.p: Muslims believe that from about 610 God's revelations, later written down as the Quran, came to Muhammad, a merchant of Mecca in today's Saudi Arabia, through the angel Gabriel. By his death in 632 most of Arabia had accepted Islam. His successors, the caliphs, took Syria and Egypt and overthrew Persia, in today's Iran. By 750 their rule ran from Spain to Pakistan.

dd-islam.q: How did Islam reach West Africa and Southeast Asia, where most Muslims now live?
a: Mainly through Arab armies conquering them
With traders and Sufi mystics along trade routes
dd-islam.why: Most Muslims live in lands Arab armies never conquered: Islam travelled with merchants across the Sahara and Indian Ocean, and Sufis helped it take root locally.

dd-islam.p:
622–632

Muhammad preached in Mecca from around 610, moved to Medina in 622 and returned to take Mecca in 630. By his death in 632 most Arabian tribes had accepted Islam.

Yemen's leaders accepted Islam in Muhammad's lifetime, and Yemeni tribesmen fought in the conquests that followed.

632–750, under the first caliphs and the Umayyads

Iraq was the scene of the struggles over who should lead Muslims after Muhammad. Ali, the fourth caliph, ruled from Kufa and was murdered there in 661.

Arab armies beat the Byzantines at the Yarmuk river in 636. From 661 Damascus was the capital of the Umayyad caliphs.

Islam means 'submission' to God, in Arabic Allah, the same God worshipped by Jews and Christians. Muslims believe Muhammad was the last of a line of prophets that includes Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and that the Quran is God's word. Practice rests on five pillars: declaring that there is no god but God and Muhammad is his messenger; praying five times a day facing Mecca; giving alms to the poor; fasting from dawn to sunset in the month of Ramadan; and making the hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, once in a lifetime if able. In May 2026 about 1.7 million pilgrims made the hajj, by Saudi official count.

When Muhammad died in 632, Muslims disagreed over who should lead them. Most accepted Abu Bakr, his close companion, as the first caliph; they became the Sunnis, 'people of the tradition'. Others believed Muhammad had chosen his cousin and son-in-law Ali, and that leadership belonged to his family; they became the Shia, from 'shiat Ali', the party of Ali. Ali became the fourth caliph but was murdered in 661, and in 680 his son Husayn was killed at Karbala, a martyrdom Shia Muslims mourn every year at Ashura. Today about 85–90% of Muslims are Sunni. The two share the Quran and the five pillars.

By 1500 Islam had spread far beyond the lands the Arabs conquered. Turkish dynasties carried it into north India, and the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453 and much of the Balkans. Merchants, scholars and Sufi mystics carried it along trade routes to West Africa, as in Mali, and to Indonesia and Malaysia. In the west, Christian Spain took Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain, in 1492.

The rising Sunni power

The Ottomans, a Turkish dynasty from Anatolia, took Constantinople in 1453 and made it their capital; eastern Anatolia was still ruled by rivals. In 1516–17 they conquered the Mamluk lands, including Mecca and Medina.

The Ottomans took most of Bosnia in 1463, and over the following century many Bosnians converted to Islam.

dd-islam.q: Why could the early Muslim conquests spread so fast?
a: Rome had already converted to Islam
The Byzantine and Persian empires were exhausted by war with each other
Arabia had always been one united kingdom
dd-islam.why: Islam united Arabia's feuding tribes, and the caliphs' armies struck while the Byzantine and Persian empires were worn out by fighting each other.

dd-islam.p:
From Morocco to Central Asia

The Mamluk sultans ruled Egypt and Syria from Cairo, then one of the world's largest cities, until the Ottomans conquered them in 1516–17.

The Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate. Najaf and Karbala remained the holiest places of Shia Islam after Mecca and Medina.

Muslim rulers over mostly Hindu subjects

Bengal had Muslim rulers from about 1204. According to historian Richard Eaton, mass conversion in its eastern delta, today's mainly Muslim Bangladesh, came mostly from the late 1500s, as forests were cleared for rice farming.

From 1206 the Delhi Sultanate ruled much of north India, and other sultanates ruled Gujarat, Bengal and the Deccan. Most Indians stayed Hindu, and the south was ruled by Hindu Vijayanagara.

dd-islam.q: Which legacy of Islamic civilisation still shows in everyday words today?
a: Words like 'algebra' and 'algorithm' from its mathematicians
dd-islam.why: Scholars built on Greek, Persian and Indian learning; al-Khwarizmi's book gave us 'algebra' and his name 'algorithm', and Arabic numerals reached Europe through the Islamic world.

dd-islam.p: Under the Abbasid caliphs, Baghdad, founded in 762, became one of the world's greatest cities. Scholars translated Greek works of philosophy, medicine and science into Arabic, and built on them. Al-Khwarizmi wrote the book on equations that gave us the word 'algebra', and his name gave us 'algorithm'. Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was used in European universities for centuries. Indian numerals, including zero, passed through the Islamic world to Europe, where they became known as Arabic numerals. Cities such as Córdoba, Cairo and Samarkand had libraries, observatories and hospitals. Many of these works later reached Europe through Spain and Sicily.

About 2 billion people were Muslim in 2020, a quarter of humanity, by Pew Research Center estimates, and Muslims were the fastest-growing major religious group. Most are Sunni. Shia Muslims, about 10–13%, are the majority in Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Bahrain. Most Muslims live in Asia: Indonesia has the most, followed by Pakistan, India and Bangladesh.

Over half Muslim, mostly Sunni (Pew estimates, 2020)

Bangladesh, about nine-tenths Muslim, has the world's fourth-largest Muslim population. It split from Pakistan in 1971.

Egypt is the most populous Arab country and about nine-tenths Muslim, almost all Sunni. Most of its Christians belong to the Coptic Orthodox Church.

Iran is the largest Shia-majority country, about nine-tenths Shia. Since the 1979 revolution it has been an Islamic republic led by a senior Shia cleric.

Most Iraqis are Shia, though Sunni rulers held power until 2003. Its shrines at Najaf and Karbala draw millions of Shia pilgrims.

dd-islam.q: What first divided Sunni and Shia Muslims?
a: Whether to keep the five pillars
A dispute over who should lead Muslims after Muhammad
dd-islam.why: Most accepted Abu Bakr as caliph and became Sunnis; others believed leadership belonged to Muhammad's family through Ali and became the Shia. Both share the Quran and five pillars.

dd-islam.p:
Muslim-majority, split between branches

Lebanon's Muslims are split almost evenly between Sunni and Shia, and over a quarter of its people are Christian. Top offices are shared out among religious communities.

Oman's ruling family follows Ibadi Islam, a third branch older than the Sunni-Shia split. Estimates of the Ibadi and Sunni shares vary, but they are of similar size.

Today most Muslims live in lands Arab armies never conquered. Islam reached West Africa with traders crossing the Sahara by camel, and rulers in Ghana, Mali and Songhay adopted it; Mali's Mansa Musa dazzled Cairo with his gold on his pilgrimage in 1324. Along the Indian Ocean, Arab, Persian and Indian merchants settled in ports from Kilwa to Malacca and married locally. Sufi mystics, who sought a personal experience of God, often blended Islam with local customs, which helped it take root. By about 1600 Islam had become the main religion of Java and Sumatra, laying the foundations of Indonesia, today the largest Muslim country.

Islamic civilisation preserved and extended Greek, Persian and Indian learning, giving the world advances in medicine, astronomy and mathematics, and words like algebra. Today about 2 billion Muslims, a quarter of humanity by Pew Research Center estimates, live mainly in Asia and Africa, with Indonesia the largest Muslim country. Debates over the role of Islamic law in the state, and the Sunni-Shia rivalry between Saudi Arabia and Iran, shape the politics of the Middle East.
About 2 billion Muslims make Islam the second-largest and fastest-growing religion. The country with the most Muslims is Indonesia, not an Arab country; only about a fifth of Muslims are Arabs.

dd-islam.why: Only about a fifth are; Indonesia has the most Muslims.

dd-mesopotamia.p: From about 3500 BC the Sumerians of southern Iraq built walled cities such as Uruk and Ur, and invented writing to keep temple accounts. Around 2300 BC Sargon of Akkad united the cities into the first known empire. Around 1750 BC Hammurabi of Babylon conquered his neighbours and set up his famous law code.

steps: The Tigris and Euphrates flooded and left fertile soil.
Extra grain fed priests, scribes and soldiers.
Uruk and Ur grew; cuneiform kept the accounts.

items: 60 minutes in an hour, 360 degrees in a circle.

dd-mesopotamia.q: Why do we have 60 minutes in an hour?
a: From the Mesopotamian base-60 number system

dd-mesopotamia.p: In the first millennium BC Assyria, from Nineveh, conquered lands from Iran to Egypt with a ruthless professional army, until Babylonians and Medes destroyed it in 612 BC. Babylon then ruled the region under Nebuchadnezzar II, who took Jerusalem, until Cyrus of Persia captured the city in 539 BC.

dd-mesopotamia.q: What did the Sumerians of southern Iraq first invent writing for?
a: Keeping temple accounts of goods and rations
dd-mesopotamia.why: Writing began at Uruk around 3300 BC as accounting: officials pressed signs into clay to track barley, beer, sheep and workers' rations.

dd-mesopotamia.p: The rivers brought water and rich silt to a flat, dry land with almost no stone, timber or metal. Farming there needed canals and teamwork, and trade was needed for everything else, so temples and kings that could organise labour, store grain and keep records grew powerful. Open plains with no natural borders meant constant war between cities, and later between empires that tried to control the rivers and trade routes.

dd-mesopotamia.h: Sumer and the Akkadian Empire, c. 2250 BC
dd-mesopotamia.p: Southern Iraq was Sumer, a land of a dozen rival city-states such as Uruk, Ur and Lagash, each with its own god, temple and ruler. Around 2300 BC Sargon of Akkad conquered them all and built the first known empire, reaching into Syria and Iran. Ships from Bahrain, Oman and the Indus valley in Pakistan brought copper, timber, carnelian and pearls up the Gulf.

dd-mesopotamia.q: What new idea did Hammurabi's code help establish?
a: That all people were equal before the law
That only priests could judge crimes
That laws were secret and unwritten
That a king rules under written law
dd-mesopotamia.why: Hammurabi's laws, carved on a stele around 1750 BC, set punishments, wages and rules for divorce; the idea of a king ruling under written law goes back to Mesopotamia.

dd-mesopotamia.p:
c. 2330–2150 BC, at its height under Sargon and Naram-Sin

Sumer filled the far south, among marshes and irrigated fields; Akkad lay just north, near today's Baghdad. Sargon made Akkadian, a Semitic language, the language of power, though Sumerian lived on in temples.

The head of the Gulf was the gateway for Mesopotamia's sea trade. In the third millennium BC the coastline lay further north than today.

Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha in Mesopotamian texts

Bahrain was Dilmun, a trading hub the Sumerians also saw as a paradise. Thousands of burial mounds there are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Oman was probably Magan, the land of copper and diorite. Naram-Sin claimed to have conquered it and brought back black stone for his statues.

Writing was not invented to record poems or prayers, but to count. Temple officials at Uruk tracked barley, beer, sheep and workers' rations by pressing signs into wet clay with a reed, from about 3300 BC. The early signs were pictures, but they turned into wedge-shaped strokes, which is why we call the script cuneiform, from the Latin for 'wedge'. Scribes trained for years in schools they called 'tablet houses', copying lists and proverbs. Cuneiform was used for some 3,000 years, for over a dozen languages, and hundreds of thousands of tablets survive, because clay lasts; many were baked hard when the libraries holding them burned.

Around 1750 BC King Hammurabi of Babylon had about 282 laws carved on a black stone stele over two metres tall, topped by an image of him before the sun god of justice. Some sound harsh: if a builder's house collapsed and killed its owner, the builder was to be put to death. Punishments depended on rank. 'An eye for an eye' applied between equals, but a noble who blinded a commoner paid silver. The code also set wages, fixed rules for divorce and protected widows. It was not the first: Ur-Nammu of Ur issued laws about 350 years earlier. The stele was found at Susa, in Iran, in 1901 and is now in the Louvre.

dd-mesopotamia.h: The Assyrian Empire at its height, c. 670 BC
dd-mesopotamia.p: From Ashur and Nineveh in northern Iraq, Assyrian kings built the largest empire yet seen. They took Syria, Phoenicia in Lebanon and the kingdom of Israel, and in 671 BC King Esarhaddon conquered Egypt. Assyria ruled by terror and deportation, moving whole peoples across the empire. Yet it fell fast: in 612 BC Babylonians and Medes destroyed Nineveh.

Ruled by governors appointed by the king

Northern Iraq was Assyria's heartland. From about 900 BC its kings campaigned every year, and Babylonia, in the south, was ruled by Assyria or its puppets, though it often rebelled.

The Aramaean kingdoms of Syria, including Damascus in 732 BC, were turned into provinces. Aramaic, their language, became the shared language of the empire.

dd-mesopotamia.q: Why did powerful temples and kings grow up in Mesopotamia?
a: Farming needed canals and teamwork, organised labour and stored grain
Mountains protected them from all invaders
The land was rich in stone, timber and metal
dd-mesopotamia.why: In a flat, dry land, farming depended on canals and teamwork, so temples and kings that could organise labour, store grain and keep records grew powerful.

dd-mesopotamia.p:
Kept their kings, paid tribute

An inscription of Esarhaddon lists ten kings of Cyprus who sent him tribute.

The kingdoms of Ammon, Moab and Edom kept their own kings but paid tribute to Assyria.

Conquered 671 BC, lost c. 655 BC

Esarhaddon took Memphis in 671 BC. Egypt was ruled through local princes, and one of them, Psamtik I, threw off Assyrian control by about 655 BC.

dd-mesopotamia.q: Which Mesopotamian legacy do we still use every day?
a: Counting in 60s, giving 60 minutes and 360 degrees
dd-mesopotamia.why: Mesopotamians counted in base 60; passed on through Greek astronomers, it still gives us 60 seconds, 60 minutes and 360 degrees in a circle.

dd-mesopotamia.p: The Epic of Gilgamesh, one of the oldest known works of literature, tells of a proud king of Uruk who loses his friend Enkidu and searches for eternal life. He meets Utnapishtim, who tells how the gods sent a flood to destroy mankind and how he survived by building a great boat, loading it with animals and sending out birds to find land. In 1872 George Smith, a self-taught scholar at the British Museum, recognised this story on a tablet from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh. Its likeness to the Bible's story of Noah caused a sensation. Most scholars think both drew on older Mesopotamian flood traditions.

After Assyria fell, Babylon in Iraq took its western lands. Its king Nebuchadnezzar II beat Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC, then twice took Jerusalem, destroying it in 587 or 586 BC and deporting many people of Judah to Babylon. He rebuilt Babylon on a grand scale, with the blue-glazed Ishtar Gate. Medes held Iran, Lydia ruled western Turkey, and Egypt stayed a rival. In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia took Babylon.

Neo-Babylonian or Chaldean dynasty, 626–539 BC

Babylon was rebuilt with millions of baked bricks, many stamped with Nebuchadnezzar's name. The famous Hanging Gardens appear in no Babylonian text, and some scholars think they were at Nineveh.

Babylon took Syria from Egypt after Carchemish in 605 BC, and Aramaic remained the everyday language of the region.

Its size and power are debated

The Medes, from western Iran, helped destroy Assyria in 612 BC. Their capital was Ecbatana, today's Hamadan. Cyrus of Persia overthrew them around 550 BC.

dd-mesopotamia.q: Why was Mesopotamia a land of almost constant war?
a: Its people worshipped gods of war only
Open plains with no natural borders left cities and empires exposed
Its deserts were full of nomad raiders alone
dd-mesopotamia.why: Open plains with no natural borders meant constant war between cities, and later between empires that tried to control the rivers and trade routes.

dd-mesopotamia.p: Egypt under the Saite kings fought Babylon for the Levant, lost at Carchemish, but kept its independence until Persia conquered it in 525 BC.

Mesopotamians counted in base 60 as well as base 10, perhaps because 60 divides evenly in so many ways. That system, passed down through Greek astronomers, still gives us 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle. Babylonian astronomers recorded the movements of the moon and planets for centuries, predicted eclipses, and divided the sky into the twelve signs of the zodiac. Mesopotamians brewed beer, used the potter's wheel and some of the earliest wheeled vehicles, and wrote contracts, receipts and loan documents. Even the idea that a king rules under a written law goes back to them.

Mesopotamia gave the world writing, written law, the first literature, and the 60-based counting that still gives us 60 minutes and 360 degrees. Its astronomy, maths and stories passed to the Persians, Greeks and Hebrews, and Babylon became a byword in the Bible. Cuneiform faded after Alexander's time and was forgotten until scholars deciphered it in the 1850s, using inscriptions from Iran.

dd-mesopotamia.s: Hammurabi wrote one of the first law codes.

dd-egypt.p: Around 3100 BC the towns of the Nile valley were united into one kingdom under a single king. In the Old Kingdom (c. 2686–2181 BC) kings built ever-larger pyramids, culminating in the Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza around 2560 BC. After a time of division, the Middle Kingdom reunited the land from Thebes and pushed forts south into Nubia.

items: Kept ma’at, cosmic order, for the land.
Weighed against a feather of truth.
So the soul could return to it.

steps: Aligned precisely with the stars and compass points.
Millions of limestone blocks cut with copper tools.
Dragged on sledges, possibly up ramps, by paid workers, not slaves.
The Great Pyramid: 146 m tall, tallest building for nearly 4,000 years.

dd-egypt.q: Who built the pyramids, according to recent evidence?
dd-egypt.why: Their villages and tombs have been found.

dd-egypt.p: Foreign Hyksos kings then ruled the north until the New Kingdom (c. 1550–1069 BC) drove them out and built an empire from Sudan to Syria under pharaohs such as Hatshepsut, Thutmose III and Ramesses II. Libyan, Nubian and Persian rulers followed, then Alexander the Great in 332 BC and the Greek Ptolemies, whose last queen, Cleopatra VII, died in 30 BC.

dd-egypt.q: What happened in Egypt around 3100 BC?
a: The towns of the Nile valley were united under one king
dd-egypt.why: Around 3100 BC the Nile valley's towns were united into one kingdom, beginning about 3,000 years of rule by pharaohs.

dd-egypt.p: The Nile made it possible. Its yearly flood left a strip of black, fertile soil in the desert, so farmers grew large grain surpluses that fed priests, scribes, soldiers and builders. The river was also a highway that let one king control the whole valley, while deserts on both sides kept most invaders away. Kings ruled as the gods' representatives on earth, keepers of maat, the order of the world, which gave the state great authority for millennia.

dd-egypt.h: The Old and Middle Kingdoms, c. 2600–1800 BC
dd-egypt.p: Egypt was a ribbon of green along the Nile, with desert on both sides. Old Kingdom pharaohs ruled from Memphis to the First Cataract at Aswan and built the pyramids of Giza around 2500 BC. Middle Kingdom kings, ruling from Thebes and later near Memphis, pushed south into Nubia in today's Sudan and guarded the Second Cataract with mudbrick forts.

dd-egypt.q: What happened to Egypt's old religion and writing after Roman and Arab rule?
a: Christianity and Islam replaced them; hieroglyphs went unread until 1822
They were unchanged until modern times
Romans made hieroglyphs their official script
dd-egypt.why: Christianity, then Islam and Arabic, replaced the old religion and language; the last hieroglyphs were carved in AD 394, and Champollion cracked the script in 1822.

dd-egypt.p:
The Nile valley and delta, united around 3100 BC

Nearly all Egyptians lived on the narrow strip watered by the Nile flood, while the deserts were left to miners and caravans. The Old Kingdom lasted c. 2686–2181 BC, the Middle Kingdom c. 2055–1650 BC.

Conquered to the Second Cataract, c. 1850 BC

Nubia, the Nile valley south of Egypt, had gold and trade routes into Africa. The Middle Kingdom conquered Lower Nubia and built a chain of forts against the kingdom of Kerma further south.

Egypt's kings built pyramids for about a thousand years, starting with Djoser's step pyramid at Saqqara around 2650 BC. The Great Pyramid of Khufu, finished around 2560 BC, used about 2.3 million stone blocks and stood about 146 metres tall, the tallest human-made structure on Earth for over 3,800 years. It was not built by slaves. Archaeologists digging the workers' town at Giza found bakeries, breweries, cattle bones and the tombs of workers buried with honour near their king. They estimate a workforce of perhaps 20,000–30,000 at its peak, far fewer than the 100,000 the Greek writer Herodotus claimed. The workers used copper tools, ramps, sledges and Nile boats to move the stone.

Egyptians worshipped hundreds of gods: Ra the sun god, Osiris, ruler of the dead, his wife Isis, their son Horus, with whom each living king was identified, and jackal-headed Anubis, guardian of embalming. They believed the dead could live on if the body was preserved, so the wealthy were mummified: the organs were removed and stored, the body dried with natron salt and wrapped in linen, a process that took about 70 days. In the Hall of Judgement, they believed, the dead person's heart was weighed against the feather of Maat, goddess of truth. A heart heavy with wrongdoing was eaten by the monster Ammit. Spells in the Book of the Dead helped souls pass the test.

dd-egypt.h: The New Kingdom empire, c. 1450–1250 BC
dd-egypt.p: After driving out the Hyksos around 1550 BC, New Kingdom pharaohs built an empire. Thutmose III campaigned as far as the Euphrates, and Nubia in today's Sudan was ruled as a colony as far as the Fourth Cataract. City-states in today's Israel, Lebanon and Syria paid tribute. Ramesses II fought the Hittites of Turkey at Kadesh in 1274 BC, and both sides later made peace.
Egypt was at its richest and strongest. Pharaohs such as Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II ruled from about 1550 to 1069 BC.

dd-egypt.q: Why could Egypt feed priests, scribes, soldiers and builders?
a: The Nile's yearly flood left fertile soil for big grain surpluses
Rain fell all year in the desert
dd-egypt.why: The Nile's flood left a strip of black, fertile soil in the desert, so farmers grew large grain surpluses that fed priests, scribes, soldiers and builders.

dd-egypt.p:
Ruled by an Egyptian viceroy

Egypt conquered the kingdom of Kerma and ruled Nubia to the Fourth Cataract, taking its gold. Boundary inscriptions at Kurgus, further upstream, mark how far its armies went. Later, in the 700s BC, Nubian kings from Napata conquered Egypt.

Local kings who paid tribute to the pharaoh

Canaanite city-states such as Megiddo, Hazor and Gaza were ruled by local kings under Egyptian governors and garrisons.

Gaza was the main Egyptian base in Canaan and the starting point for campaigns north.

dd-egypt.q: How does ancient Egypt still shape the world today?
a: Its law code is used in modern courts
Its language is spoken across North Africa
Its monuments draw millions of visitors and gave rise to Egyptology
Its calendar is still Egypt's official one
dd-egypt.why: Egypt's monuments still shape how the world imagines the ancient past: its temples and tombs draw millions of visitors and gave rise to the science of Egyptology.

dd-egypt.p: Hieroglyphs appeared by about 3200 BC, among the world's earliest writing. The script mixed signs for sounds with signs for whole words, and scribes used faster joined-up scripts, hieratic and later demotic, for everyday writing. As Christianity spread, the knowledge faded: the last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved at Philae in AD 394. The key came in 1799, when French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone, a decree of 196 BC written in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek. The British took it in 1801, and it has been in the British Museum since 1802. Building on work by Thomas Young, Jean-François Champollion used royal names in oval cartouches to crack the script in 1822.

In 332 BC Alexander the Great took Egypt from the Persians and founded Alexandria. His general Ptolemy made himself king, and his family ruled for almost 300 years, at times holding Cyprus, eastern Libya and the southern Levant. The last of them, Cleopatra VII, allied with Rome's Julius Caesar and Mark Antony, but lost to Octavian. In 30 BC Rome took Egypt.

Also Aegean islands and coasts of Anatolia, not shown

The Ptolemies ruled as pharaohs, building temples in Egyptian style, but their court in Alexandria spoke Greek. Egypt's grain made them rich.

Cyprus was a Ptolemaic possession for most of the dynasty. Mark Antony returned it to Cleopatra in the 30s BC.

dd-egypt.q: What helped one king hold the whole country for so long?
a: A huge navy in the Mediterranean
The Nile highway, desert barriers, and kings as gods' representatives
dd-egypt.why: The river let one king control the valley, deserts kept most invaders away, and kings ruled as the gods' representatives, keepers of maat, giving the state great authority.

dd-egypt.p: Cleopatra VII (69–30 BC) was not Egyptian by descent: her family, the Ptolemies, were Macedonian Greeks who had ruled Egypt since Alexander's death. According to the Greek biographer Plutarch, she spoke many languages and was the first of her dynasty to learn Egyptian. She allied with Julius Caesar, with whom she had a son, Caesarion, and then with Mark Antony, with whom she had three children. Octavian defeated them at Actium in 31 BC, and both took their own lives in Alexandria in 30 BC; the famous asp bite comes from ancient accounts that historians cannot confirm. Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.

Egypt became a Roman province and fed Rome with its grain. Christianity, and after the Arab conquest of 639–642 Islam and Arabic, replaced the old religion and language, and the ability to read hieroglyphs was lost until 1822. Greek visitors admired Egypt's learning, and its monuments still shape how the world imagines the ancient past: its temples and tombs draw millions of visitors and gave rise to the science of Egyptology.

dd-egypt.s: Hieroglyphs were deciphered thanks to the Rosetta Stone.
