dd-greece.p: After a dark age following the collapse of the Mycenaean palaces, Greek city-states revived from about 800 BC, adopted an alphabet from the Phoenicians and founded colonies from Spain to the Black Sea. Athens and Sparta led them against Persian invasions, winning at Marathon in 490 BC and at Salamis and Plataea in 480–479 BC. Athens then enjoyed a golden age of democracy, drama, philosophy and building, crowned by the Parthenon.

items: Questioned everything; executed for "corrupting the youth".
Logic, science and ethics; tutor of Alexander.

dd-greece.p: Rivalry with Sparta led to the Peloponnesian War of 431–404 BC, which Athens lost. Weakened by constant wars, the cities fell under Philip II of Macedon in 338 BC, and under Rome by 146 BC.

Greece's mountains and islands divided it into hundreds of small, fiercely independent cities, so no single kingdom formed. Citizens who fought side by side as armoured infantry, the hoplites, demanded a say in government. Sea trade and colonies brought wealth and contact with Egypt and the Near East, whose ideas Greeks borrowed and reworked. The same independence made the cities unable to stay united once Persia was beaten.

dd-greece.q: What did Athens and Sparta lead the Greek city-states to achieve in 490–479 BC?
dd-greece.why: The Greeks beat Persia at Marathon in 490 BC and at Salamis and Plataea in 480–479 BC, opening Athens' golden age.

dd-greece.h: The Greek world spreads, c. 550 BC
dd-greece.p: Ancient Greece was never one country but hundreds of independent city-states, or poleis. From about 750 BC, short of good farmland, they sent out settlers who founded new cities around the Mediterranean and Black Sea: in southern Italy and Sicily, France, Spain, Libya and Ukraine, joining older Greek cities on the Aegean coast of Turkey. Plato said the Greeks lived around the sea 'like frogs around a pond'.

Mainland Greece, the islands and Ionia

Mountains and sea split Greece into small city-states, each with its own laws, army and gods' festivals. They shared a language, Homer's epics and games such as the Olympics.

The Aegean coast, called Ionia, held some of the richest Greek cities, such as Miletus and Ephesus. Byzantium guarded the Bosporus.

Southern Italy, Sicily, Gaul and Spain

So many Greeks settled in southern Italy and Sicily that Romans called it Magna Graecia, 'Great Greece'. Naples began as the Greek Neapolis, 'new city'.

Massalia traded wine and pottery up the Rhône into Gaul and founded colonies of its own, such as Nikaia, today's Nice, and Antipolis, today's Antibes.

dd-greece.q: What did the rivalry between Athens and Sparta finally lead to?
a: A lasting union of all Greeks
War that left the cities weak enough for Macedon and then Rome
dd-greece.why: Athens lost the Peloponnesian War in 404 BC; weakened by constant wars, the cities fell to Philip II of Macedon in 338 BC and to Rome by 146 BC.

dd-greece.p:
Grain, fish and slaves for the Aegean

Greek cities such as Olbia and Panticapaeum, in Crimea, shipped grain to Athens, which came to depend on Black Sea wheat.

On the Taman peninsula, Greek cities such as Phanagoria traded with the Scythians of the steppe.

Sparta was unlike any other Greek city. Its citizens, the Spartiates, were full-time soldiers who did not farm or trade. Their land was worked by helots, a conquered people who greatly outnumbered them and were kept down by fear: according to Plutarch, each year Sparta's officials formally declared war on them, so they could be killed without guilt. From about the age of seven, Spartan boys were trained in the agoge, a harsh state upbringing of hunger, beatings and drill. Spartan women were unusually free by Greek standards, exercised outdoors and, by Aristotle's time, owned perhaps two-fifths of the land. Yet citizen numbers kept falling, from about 8,000 in 480 BC to fewer than 1,000 in Aristotle's day.

In 480 BC the Persian king Xerxes invaded Greece with a vast army. Herodotus put it at over 2.6 million fighting men, which is impossible; modern estimates are mostly between 100,000 and 300,000. At the narrow pass of Thermopylae, about 7,000 Greeks, not just 300 Spartans, held them for two days. When a local man showed the Persians a mountain path around the pass, King Leonidas sent most of the army away. He stayed with his 300 Spartans, about 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans, and they were killed or captured. The stand became a legend of sacrifice, but the battle that saved Greece was the naval victory at Salamis weeks later.

After beating Persia, Greece split into two camps: Athens, with its navy and an empire of Aegean allies, and Sparta, with the best army and the Peloponnesian League. Their war lasted 27 years. Athens' great expedition against Syracuse in Sicily, in Italy, ended in disaster in 413 BC. Then Persia, ruled from Iran, paid for a Spartan fleet, which destroyed Athens' navy in 405 BC.

Athens and its allies against Sparta and its allies

Athens led the Delian League, founded in 478 BC to fight Persia, and turned it into an empire paying tribute. Sparta led the Peloponnesian League. Athens surrendered in 404 BC, and Sparta tore down its Long Walls.

dd-greece.q: Why did ancient Greece never form a single kingdom?
a: Mountains and islands split it into many small, independent cities
Its people spoke many unrelated languages
dd-greece.why: Greece's mountains and islands divided it into hundreds of fiercely independent city-states that shared a language, Homer's epics and games, but no single ruler.

dd-greece.p:
Target of Athens' great expedition

Syracuse, Sicily's greatest Greek city, defeated the Athenian invasion of 415–413 BC. Athens lost tens of thousands of men and about 200 ships.

Sparta's paymaster from 412 BC

Persia's kings had lost the Persian Wars, but by funding Sparta's fleet they won back the Greek cities of Ionia in 387 BC.

Ionian Greek cities on the coast paid tribute to Athens. When the war turned, many revolted, and they returned to Persian rule after the war.

dd-greece.q: Where can Greek influence still be seen today?
a: In democracy, philosophy, theatre, English words and temple-style buildings
dd-greece.why: Greek ideas, from democracy and philosophy to theatre and the Olympics, became a foundation of the West, and buildings like the US Capitol copy Greek temples.

dd-greece.p: According to tradition, the Olympics began in 776 BC at Olympia, a sanctuary of Zeus, and were held every four years for over a thousand years. A sacred truce let athletes and spectators travel safely. Events grew from a single footrace to boxing, wrestling, the brutal pankration, chariot racing and the pentathlon. Athletes competed naked, and only free Greek men could take part; married women were barred from watching. Winners got only an olive wreath, but their home cities might reward them with statues, cash and free meals for life. The games probably ended under Christian Roman emperors around AD 393–435 and were revived in Athens in 1896.

Greek thinkers looked for natural explanations of the world. It began in Ionia, on the coast of Turkey, where Thales of Miletus asked what everything is made of. Athens, in Greece, became the centre of philosophy with Socrates, Plato and Aristotle. In southern Italy Pythagoras' followers studied numbers, and later Alexandria, in Egypt, drew mathematicians such as Euclid.

Athens drew thinkers from across the Greek world. Socrates questioned everything, Plato wrote his dialogues, and Aristotle, from Stagira in the north, studied everything from logic to marine life. Democritus of Abdera taught that all things are made of atoms.

Where Greek philosophy and science began

Ionian thinkers such as Thales, Anaximander and Heraclitus tried to explain nature without myths. Herodotus, the 'father of history', was born at Halicarnassus, today's Bodrum.

dd-greece.q: Why did ordinary citizens in Greek cities demand a say in government?
a: Their kings asked them to vote
They fought side by side as armoured hoplite infantry
dd-greece.why: Citizens who fought side by side as armoured infantry, the hoplites, demanded a say in government, which helped give rise to Athens' democracy.

dd-greece.p:
Greek southern Italy and Sicily

Southern Italy and Sicily were full of thinkers: Pythagoras at Croton, Parmenides at Elea, Empedocles at Acragas, who proposed four elements, and Archimedes at Syracuse.

Socrates wrote nothing. He spent his days in the Athenian marketplace asking people what justice, courage or piety really were, and showing that they did not know. His pupil Plato made him the hero of his dialogues. In 399 BC, after Athens' defeat by Sparta and a brief, bloody rule by pro-Spartan oligarchs, some of them Socrates' former associates, he was tried for impiety and corrupting the young. A jury of about 500 citizens convicted him, and he died by drinking hemlock, refusing a chance to escape. Plato's account of his trial and death made Socrates a symbol of free thought.

Greek ideas became a foundation of Western civilisation: philosophy, democracy, history writing, theatre, geometry, medicine and the Olympic Games. Rome adopted Greek art, gods and learning, and Greek remained the common language of the eastern Mediterranean for centuries. Countless English words, from 'politics' to 'theatre', are Greek, and buildings from the US Capitol to the British Museum copy Greek temples.
Democracy, philosophy, theatre, the Olympics, history writing and much of science and medicine began in ancient Greece. Words such as 'politics', 'democracy' and 'theatre' are Greek.

dd-persia.p: In 550 BC Cyrus the Great united the Medes and Persians, then conquered Anatolia, Babylon and Central Asia. Under Darius I the Achaemenid Empire reached from Egypt and Thrace to the Indus, but its invasions of Greece failed in 490 and 480 BC. Alexander the Great conquered it in 334–330 BC, and his Greek successors, the Seleucids, ruled Iran until the Parthians, from the north-east, took over in the 2nd century BC.

items: Cyrus and Darius: from Egypt to India; ended by Alexander.
Horse archers who held off Rome.
Rival of Rome and Byzantium; ended by the Arabs.

steps: 2,700 km with relay riders: the first postal system.
Conquered peoples kept their gods and laws.

dd-persia.q: Which Persian king let the Jews return from exile?

dd-persia.p: In AD 224 the Sasanians replaced them. Parthians and Sasanians fought Rome and Byzantium for about 700 years, until both sides were exhausted and Arab Muslim armies conquered Persia between 633 and 651.

dd-persia.q: What did Cyrus the Great and Darius I build?
a: A Persian empire stretching from Egypt and Thrace to the Indus
A kingdom confined to southern Iran
dd-persia.why: Cyrus united Medes and Persians in 550 BC and conquered Anatolia, Babylon and Central Asia; under Darius I the empire reached from Egypt and Thrace to the Indus.

dd-persia.p: The Iranian plateau sat at the crossroads between Mesopotamia, India and the Central Asian steppe, so whoever held it controlled great trade routes and rich farmland. Persian kings ruled a huge, varied empire by leaving local customs, religions and elites largely in place in return for tribute and soldiers. Their rivalry with Greece and Rome came from competition for the same rich borderlands: Anatolia, Syria, Mesopotamia and Armenia.

In 550 BC Cyrus, king of the Persians of south-west Iran, overthrew his Median overlords and went on to take Anatolia, Iraq and Central Asia. His son added Egypt, and Darius I reached the Indus in Pakistan and Thrace in Bulgaria. About 20 provinces, or satrapies, paid tribute, linked by the Royal Road. Two invasions of Greece failed, at Marathon in 490 BC and Salamis in 480 BC.

dd-persia.q: What made the Arab Muslim conquest of Persia possible in 633–651?
a: Persia had already converted to Islam
Alexander's heirs invited the Arabs in
A great flood ruined Persia's farms
Persia and Byzantium had exhausted each other in centuries of war
dd-persia.why: Parthians and Sasanians fought Rome and Byzantium for about 700 years; after the ruinous war of 602–628, Arab armies struck both exhausted empires.

dd-persia.p:
Media, Lydia, Babylon and Central Asia

The Persians came from Parsa, today's Fars province. Persian kings called themselves 'King of Kings' and ruled through local elites, not by imposing one religion or language.

Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC, probably with little fighting. Mesopotamia became one of the richest provinces, and Aramaic the common language of government.
Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525 BC. Darius finished a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, linking Egypt to Persia by ship.

The Indus valley and Thrace

Darius took the Indus valley around 518 BC. According to Herodotus, it paid the largest tribute of any province, in gold dust.

Darius crossed into Europe around 513 BC and made Thrace a province, and Macedon accepted Persian overlordship for a time.

Darius I divided the empire into about 20 provinces, called satrapies, each under a governor, or satrap, with royal officials and garrison commanders reporting separately to the king. Provinces paid set tribute in silver, gold, horses or grain. A network of roads, above all the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa, more than 2,400 kilometres long, had stations where relay riders changed horses. Herodotus wrote that nothing stopped these couriers, not snow, rain, heat or darkness, a line now carved on New York's main post office. Thousands of clay tablets found at Persepolis record rations paid to the workers who built it, including extra rations for women who had just given birth.

After Alexander's conquest and Greek Seleucid rule, the Parthians, horse-riding warriors from the north-east of Iran, built a new Persian empire from the 240s BC. By 141 BC they held Mesopotamia, in Iraq. Their mounted archers crushed a Roman army at Carrhae in 53 BC, and for nearly three centuries Rome and Parthia faced each other across the Euphrates, fighting above all over Armenia. Parthia grew rich from Silk Road trade passing between China and Rome.

Arsacid dynasty, c. 247 BC–AD 224

The Parthians began as the Parni, nomads who settled in Parthia, in north-east Iran. They ruled loosely, through great noble families and vassal kings.

Mesopotamia was the economic heart of Parthia, and Ctesiphon its capital. The emperor Trajan conquered it in 116, but Rome gave it up the next year.

dd-persia.q: How did Persian kings hold together such a huge, varied empire?
a: They forced everyone to adopt one religion and language
They left local customs and elites in place in return for tribute
dd-persia.why: Persian kings ruled through local elites, leaving customs and religions largely in place; satrapies paid set tribute and were linked by roads like the Royal Road.

dd-persia.p:
Ruled by Parthian princes, crowned with Rome's approval

Armenia was the great prize between the two empires. A compromise in AD 63 let a Parthian prince rule Armenia if he was crowned by Rome's emperor.

Eastern Anatolia was the Roman side of the frontier, and Roman legions were based along the upper Euphrates.

The Euphrates, across eastern Syria, was the usual frontier. Rome held the west, governed from Antioch, now in Turkey.

dd-persia.q: How did Iran differ from Egypt and Syria after the Arab conquest?
a: It stayed Zoroastrian to this day
It adopted Islam but kept its own Persian language
It became Arabic-speaking within a generation
dd-persia.why: Most Iranians adopted Islam over centuries, but Iran kept Persian, helped by Ferdowsi's Shahnameh; Iranians still celebrate Nowruz and look back on Cyrus with pride.

dd-persia.p: Ancient Persians followed the teachings of the prophet Zarathustra, or Zoroaster, whose dates are uncertain; estimates range from about 1500 to 500 BC. Zoroastrians believe the wise lord Ahura Mazda is opposed by a destructive spirit, and that each person must choose good thoughts, good words and good deeds. Fire, a symbol of purity, burns in their temples. Darius I credited his victories to Ahura Mazda in his inscriptions, and the Sasanians made Zoroastrianism a state religion with a powerful priesthood. Many scholars think its ideas of a final judgement, heaven and hell influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Perhaps 100,000–200,000 Zoroastrians remain, many of them Parsis in India.

dd-persia.h: Sasanian Persia and Byzantium, c. AD 600
dd-persia.p: In 224 Ardashir, a Persian noble from Fars in Iran, overthrew the Parthians and founded the Sasanian dynasty, which made Zoroastrianism its state religion. His son Shapur I captured a Roman emperor in 260. From 602 to 628 Persia and the Byzantine Empire, ruled from Turkey, fought a ruinous war. Arab Muslim armies then struck both: they took Ctesiphon, in Iraq, in 637 and Iran by 651, and the last Sasanian king was killed at Merv.

AD 224–651

The Sasanians saw themselves as heirs of the Achaemenids and revived Persian kingship, art and Zoroastrian religion. After 651 Iran became Muslim slowly, over centuries.

The Sasanian capital Ctesiphon, near today's Baghdad, lay in Iraq. It fell to the Arabs in 637.

dd-persia.q: Why did Persia fight Greece and Rome for so long?
a: They competed for the same rich borderlands like Anatolia, Syria and Armenia
Rome tried to impose Christianity on Persia
They disagreed about the Olympic Games
dd-persia.why: Their rivalry came from competition for the same rich borderlands: Anatolia, Syria, Mesopotamia and Armenia, with Armenia the great prize between Rome and Parthia.

dd-persia.p:
The Eastern Roman Empire

Byzantium, ruled from Constantinople, was Persia's great rival. In 626 Persian and Avar forces besieged Constantinople, but failed.

Under Khosrow II, Persia overran Byzantine Syria, Palestine and Egypt in 611–619, but Emperor Heraclius won the war by 628 and the lands were handed back.

After the Arab conquest, Iran slowly became Muslim, but it did not become Arab. Around 1010 the poet Ferdowsi finished the Shahnameh, the 'Book of Kings', an epic of about 50,000 couplets retelling Iran's history and legends from the first kings to the Arab conquest. He wrote it in Persian with few Arabic words, and it helped keep the language and its memory alive. Persian scholars and officials shaped Islamic science, literature and government. Many Iranians later followed Shia Islam, which became the state religion under the Safavids from 1501. Today the spring festival of Nowruz, with roots in pre-Islamic Persia, is celebrated by about 300 million people, by UN estimates.

Arab conquest brought Islam, which most Iranians adopted over the next few centuries, but unlike Egypt or Syria, Iran kept its own language. Persian, written in Arabic script, became the language of poetry and government from the Ottoman court to Mughal India, and Persian officials helped run the Abbasid caliphate. Iranians today still celebrate Nowruz, the Persian new year, and look back on Cyrus and the ancient empires with pride.

dd-rome.p: According to Roman tradition, Rome threw out its last king around 509 BC and became a republic run by elected magistrates and a Senate. It conquered Italy, then fought three wars with Carthage, surviving Hannibal's invasion and destroying the city in 146 BC. Conquest brought riches and slaves but also civil wars between generals.

r: Pax Romana: two centuries of peace

items: Roots of most European legal systems.

dd-rome.q: Who was the first Roman emperor?

dd-rome.p: Julius Caesar won one and was murdered in 44 BC; his heir Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC. The empire peaked in the 100s AD, survived a near-collapse in the 200s and became Christian under Constantine. From 376 Germanic peoples moved in, Rome was sacked in 410, and the last western emperor was deposed in 476.

dd-rome.q: How did Rome's government change between 509 BC and 27 BC?
a: From a republic of elected magistrates and a Senate to emperors
From a democracy to a monarchy ruled by Carthage
From an empire to a group of city-states
dd-rome.why: Rome expelled its last king around 509 BC and became a republic; after civil wars between generals, Caesar's heir Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC.

dd-rome.p: Rome turned beaten enemies into allies who supplied soldiers, and later into citizens, so its manpower seemed endless. Its legions were disciplined and its roads moved them quickly. But the Republic's institutions, built for a city-state, could not control generals with private armies and huge provinces. Centuries later the West fell to a mix of civil wars, money troubles, pressure on a long frontier and the loss of rich provinces such as Africa.

By 264 BC Rome ruled peninsular Italy, and it then fought three wars with Carthage, a Phoenician sea power based in Tunisia. Rome won the first and took Sicily. In 218 BC Carthage's general Hannibal marched from Spain over the Pyrenees and through France, then crossed the Alps with war elephants and crushed Roman armies in Italy. Rome refused to give in, and beat him at Zama, in Africa, in 202 BC.

dd-rome.q: What do most historians now say caused the fall of the Western Empire?
a: A chain of problems: civil wars, invasions, lost rich provinces
Lead poisoning from water pipes alone
dd-rome.why: Most historians stress civil wars, the Huns driving Goths into the empire, pressure on a long frontier and the loss of Africa's taxes in 439.

dd-rome.p:
Italy with Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica

Rome ruled the peninsula through alliances, and after 241 BC also held Sicily. Celtic Gauls still held the Po valley in the north and joined Hannibal.

North Africa, southern Spain and Malta

Carthage was founded by Phoenicians from Tyre, by tradition in 814 BC. It grew rich on trade and ruled the coast of North Africa with a powerful navy.

Malta was Carthaginian until Rome took it in 218 BC, at the start of the war.

Romans hated the idea of kings, so the Republic split power. Two consuls, elected each year, led the state and its armies, and each could block the other. The Senate, a council of former officials who served for life, had no formal power to make laws but in practice guided policy, finance and war. Citizens voted in assemblies, but in some of them votes were grouped so the rich counted far more. Tribunes of the plebs, the common people, could veto acts that harmed them. In an emergency, a dictator could rule for up to six months. The letters SPQR, 'the Senate and People of Rome', summed up the ideal.

By the time of Augustus, Rome may have had about a million people, a size no city in Europe clearly matched again until London around 1800. Most lived in crowded apartment blocks, insulae, several storeys high, which often burned or collapsed. Under Augustus about 200,000 citizen men received free grain each month, and eleven aqueducts eventually brought fresh water to fountains, homes and huge public baths. Crowds of perhaps 50,000 watched gladiators and wild beast hunts in the Colosseum, opened in AD 80, while the Circus Maximus held far more for chariot races. The poet Juvenal mocked a people who cared only for 'bread and circuses'.

By the 1st century BC Rome ruled most of the Mediterranean, but rival generals fought for power. Julius Caesar conquered Gaul, today's France and Belgium, in 58–50 BC, then crossed the Rubicon into Italy with his army in 49 BC, starting a civil war. He won, backed Cleopatra in Egypt, and was named dictator for life. On 15 March 44 BC senators stabbed him to death in Rome.

Italy was the heart of the Republic. After the Social War of 91–88 BC, Rome granted citizenship to its Italian allies.

Caesar beat Pompey's supporters at Thapsus in 46 BC and annexed the Numidian kingdom next door as Africa Nova.

dd-rome.q: Why did Rome's manpower seem endless?
a: Every Roman family had ten sons
It turned beaten enemies into allies, and later into citizens
dd-rome.why: Rome made defeated enemies into allies who supplied soldiers, and later into citizens; in AD 212 Caracalla made almost all free people Roman citizens.

dd-rome.p:
58–50 BC, plus the older southern province

Southern France had been the Roman province of Narbonensis since the 120s BC. Caesar's war conquered the rest; ancient writers claimed a million Gauls died, a figure that cannot be checked.

Caesar called the Belgae the bravest of the Gauls. He defeated them in 57 BC and crushed their revolts in 54–53 BC.

Cleopatra's kingdom, dependent on Rome

Egypt was still independent under the Ptolemies, but its rulers depended on Roman support. Cleopatra had a son, Caesarion, she said was Caesar's.

dd-rome.q: Which part of Rome's legacy shapes much of Europe and Latin America today?
a: Roman law and the Latin-based Romance languages
The Senate's power to name kings
dd-rome.why: Latin became the Romance languages, and Roman law shaped legal codes across Europe and Latin America; words like senate, republic and citizen come from Rome.

dd-rome.p: Conquest flooded Italy with captives. By one modern estimate, there were perhaps 1–1.5 million slaves in Italy under Augustus, out of 6–7.5 million people. They worked in mines, on great estates, in homes and as teachers, doctors and secretaries. Some were freed, and their children could become full citizens. In 73 BC the Thracian gladiator Spartacus broke out of a training school at Capua with about 70 others. Tens of thousands of slaves joined him, and they beat several Roman armies before Crassus crushed them in 71 BC. According to the historian Appian, 6,000 captives were crucified along the Appian Way between Capua and Rome.

dd-rome.h: The Western Empire breaks up, AD 476
dd-rome.p: In 376 the Goths, fleeing the Huns, crossed the Danube into the empire, and two years later they killed the emperor Valens at Adrianople. In 410 the Visigoths sacked Rome. Vandals took Carthage, in Tunisia, in 439. By 476, when the general Odoacer deposed the last western emperor in Italy, Germanic kings ruled Spain and France. The Eastern Empire, in Greece and Turkey, survived.

The Greek-speaking East was richer and more populous, and paid or diverted invaders westward. It lasted until 1453.

Constantinople, founded in 330, was the Eastern capital. Its emperor Zeno received Odoacer's embassy in 476.

King of Italy from 476, nominally under the East

Odoacer, a Germanic officer, deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476 and ruled as king, keeping the Senate and Roman officials. In 493 Theodoric the Ostrogoth killed him and took Italy.

dd-rome.q: Why did the Roman Republic collapse into civil wars?
a: City-state institutions could not control generals with private armies
dd-rome.why: The Republic's institutions, built for a city-state, could not control generals with private armies and huge provinces, so rivals like Caesar fought for power.

dd-rome.p:
Kingdom of Toulouse

By 476 the Visigoths ruled most of Spain, while the Suebi held the north-west, around Galicia.

The Visigoths ruled the south-west from Toulouse, Burgundians the Rhône valley, and Franks the north. A Roman general, Syagrius, held out around Soissons until 486.

Few questions have produced more answers: the German historian Alexander Demandt once collected 210 suggested causes. Edward Gibbon, writing in the 1770s and 1780s, blamed Christianity and barbarism. Popular theories such as lead poisoning from water pipes have little support. Most historians now stress a chain of problems: civil wars between rival emperors, the arrival of the Huns, which drove Goths and others into the empire, and the loss of the tax-rich provinces of Africa in 439. Some scholars prefer to speak of a 'transformation' of the Roman world rather than a fall, while others point to archaeology showing a sharp drop in living standards in the West.

The Eastern Empire went on until 1453, and the idea of Rome lived on in the Holy Roman Empire, the tsars and the papacy. Latin became the Romance languages and the language of science and the Church, and Roman law shaped the legal codes of much of Europe and Latin America. Words such as senate, republic, dictator and citizen, and the Latin alphabet, all come from Rome.

dd-rome.s: Roman law is the basis of many legal systems today.
dd-rome.why: Especially in continental Europe and Latin America.

dd-alexander.p: Alexander became king of Macedon at 20, in 336 BC, after his father Philip II was murdered. In 334 BC he invaded the Persian Empire with about 35,000 men, won battles at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela, and took Egypt, Babylon and Persepolis. He spent three hard years subduing Bactria and Sogdiana, then crossed into India, until his army refused to go further in 326 BC.

steps: His father built the Macedonian phalanx with 6 m spears.
Darius III could not stop him at Issus or Gaugamela.
He kept Persian officials and married a Bactrian princess.

dd-alexander.h: Alexander’s age at his death in 323 BC
dd-alexander.p: In 11 years he built an empire from Greece to India, then died in Babylon, probably of fever.

He died in Babylon in 323 BC, aged 32. His generals tore the empire apart, and Greek kingdoms ruled Egypt and western Asia until Rome and Parthia absorbed them; the last, Ptolemaic Egypt, fell in 30 BC.

dd-alexander.q: What did Alexander the Great achieve between 334 and 326 BC?
a: He conquered the Persian Empire and reached India
He defended Macedon against Persian invasion
dd-alexander.why: Alexander invaded Persia in 334 BC, won at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela, took Egypt and Persepolis, and pushed into India until his army refused to go on.

dd-alexander.p: Philip II had built the best army of its day, with long-speared infantry and heavy cavalry, and had already planned the attack on Persia. The Persian Empire was vast but loosely held, and many subjects had little loyalty to Darius III. Alexander added bold, personal leadership and tactical skill, and he kept local officials and customs in place to win over conquered peoples.

In 334 BC Alexander crossed from Macedon, in northern Greece, into Asia. He beat the Persians at the Granicus and at Issus, took Egypt without a fight, and crushed King Darius III at Gaugamela, in Iraq. He then fought for three years in Afghanistan and Uzbekistan and pushed into the Punjab, in Pakistan and India, where his exhausted army refused to go on. He died in Babylon in 323 BC, aged 32.

dd-alexander.q: What happened to Alexander's empire after he died in 323 BC?
a: His son ruled it for fifty years
It became a single Greek republic
Persia immediately took it all back
His generals divided it into rival Greek kingdoms
dd-alexander.why: With no adult heir, his generals fought for forty years; the Ptolemies, Seleucids and Antigonids ruled until Rome and Parthia absorbed them, ending with Egypt in 30 BC.

dd-alexander.p:
Under Macedonian control from 338 BC

Alexander's father Philip II made Macedon the master of Greece at Chaeronea in 338 BC. Alexander razed rebellious Thebes in 335 BC before leaving for Asia.

Part of ancient Macedon lay in today's North Macedonia, though its heartland and capital, Pella, lay in today's Greece.

The Persian governor surrendered Egypt in 332 BC. At the desert oracle of Siwa, priests reportedly greeted Alexander as son of the god Amun.

After Gaugamela, Babylon opened its gates. Alexander planned to make it his capital and died there.

Alexander was tutored by the philosopher Aristotle, and as a boy, according to Plutarch, he tamed the wild horse Bucephalus, which carried him to India. Many famous stories cannot be checked: ancient writers disagreed over whether he cut the Gordian knot with his sword or simply pulled out its pin. The surviving histories were written centuries later, using lost eyewitness accounts. They show a brilliant, reckless general who led from the front and was badly wounded several times. They also show his cruelty: he razed Thebes, and after the siege of Tyre, ancient historians say, thousands were killed or enslaved. In a drunken quarrel in 328 BC he killed his friend Cleitus, who had saved his life.

Alexander left no adult heir, and his generals fought over his empire for forty years. Three dynasties emerged: the Ptolemies in Egypt, the Seleucids in Syria, Iraq and Iran, and the Antigonids in Macedon. Greek settlers in Bactria, in Afghanistan, broke away around 250 BC. Seleucus had already handed the far east to India's Mauryan Empire in exchange for 500 war elephants. Greek-speaking kings now ruled millions of Egyptians, Syrians and Persians.

Capital Alexandria

The Ptolemies ruled as pharaohs and Greek kings at once. Greek was the language of government, and Alexandria drew scholars from across the Mediterranean.

dd-alexander.q: What had Alexander's father, Philip II, already given him?
a: The best army of its day and a plan to attack Persia
A navy that controlled the Indian Ocean
dd-alexander.why: Philip II built the best army of its day, with long-speared infantry and heavy cavalry, and had already planned the attack on Persia.

dd-alexander.p:
Capitals Antioch and Seleucia

The Seleucids ruled from Antioch, in today's Turkey near the Syrian border, and fought six wars with the Ptolemies over southern Syria and Palestine.

Mesopotamia was the Seleucids' richest region. Babylon's priests kept up their temples and astronomical records under Greek rule.

Dominating mainland Greece

Macedon dominated Greece, but leagues of cities, the Achaeans and Aetolians, and proud Athens and Sparta kept some independence.

dd-alexander.q: What lasting legacy did Alexander's conquests leave?
a: Latin became the language of Asia
Greek became a shared language of the eastern Mediterranean and Middle East
dd-alexander.why: The Hellenistic age made Greek a shared language for nearly a thousand years, which is why the New Testament was written in Greek; Greek art even influenced Buddhist sculpture.

dd-alexander.p: Alexander wanted to rule as king of Asia, not just as a Greek conqueror. He adopted Persian court dress and ceremony, married the Bactrian noblewoman Roxana, and at Susa in 324 BC held a mass wedding where some 80–90 of his officers married Persian and other Iranian noblewomen. He trained 30,000 Persian youths to fight in the Macedonian style. Many Macedonians resented this, especially the demand that they bow before him as Persians bowed to their kings. After his death most officers abandoned their Persian wives, but the mixing he began went on in the cities he founded, many named Alexandria.

dd-alexander.h: Rome and Parthia take over, 168–30 BC
dd-alexander.p: The Greek kingdoms were swallowed one by one. Rome defeated Macedon in 168 BC and took Greece by 146 BC. Parthia seized Iran and, by 141 BC, Iraq. Pergamon passed to Rome in 133 BC, and Pompey ended the Seleucids in Syria in 64 BC. Last came Egypt: after Cleopatra and Mark Antony lost at Actium, Rome took it in 30 BC. Yet the Greek language and culture lived on, in the Roman East for centuries.

Macedon and Greece

Rome turned Macedon into a province in 148 BC and crushed a Greek revolt in 146 BC. Rome then absorbed Greek art, philosophy and literature.

The kingdom of Pergamon

Pergamon became the Roman province of Asia, one of Rome's richest. Its Greek cities flourished under Roman rule.

dd-alexander.q: Why was the Persian Empire open to conquest?
a: It had no army at all
It had already been conquered by Rome
It was vast but loosely held, and many subjects felt little loyalty
dd-alexander.why: The Persian Empire was vast but loosely held, and many subjects had little loyalty to Darius III; Alexander won others over by keeping local officials and customs.

dd-alexander.p:
Seleucid Syria and Judea

The Jewish Maccabees revolted against the Seleucids from 167 BC, an event marked by Hanukkah, and won independence; Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC.

Weakened by civil wars, the Seleucid kingdom shrank to a rump around Antioch, which Pompey made the Roman province of Syria in 64 BC.

In Ptolemaic Alexandria, the Library and Museum drew scholars from across the Greek world. There Euclid wrote his Elements of geometry, and Eratosthenes estimated the size of the Earth around 240 BC with remarkable accuracy. Jewish scholars in the city translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek, the Septuagint. Far to the east, at Ai-Khanoum in Afghanistan, archaeologists found a Greek theatre and gymnasium. In Gandhara, artists blending Greek and Indian styles made some of the first statues of the Buddha in human form. Alexander's own body was seized by Ptolemy and entombed in Alexandria, where the Roman emperor Augustus visited it; the tomb's location has since been lost.

Alexander's conquests began the Hellenistic age. Greek became the shared language of the eastern Mediterranean and Middle East for nearly a thousand years, which is why the New Testament was written in Greek. Greek cities, art and science spread as far as Afghanistan and northern India, influencing early Buddhist sculpture. His career became the model of the world conqueror, admired by Julius Caesar and Napoleon, and he lives on in legend from Europe to Iran, where he is remembered as both hero and destroyer.
His generals split the empire, but Greek became the shared language from Egypt to Afghanistan for centuries. Alexandria’s library and lighthouse became wonders of the world.

dd-maya.p: By about 300 BC Maya farmers in the forests of Central America were building large cities such as El Mirador, with pyramids and causeways, and carving the first Maya writing. In the Classic period, about 250–900, dozens of kingdoms ruled by divine kings flourished, among them Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copán, and they waged constant wars on one another. In the 800s the southern lowland cities stopped raising monuments, and most were abandoned.

items: The only full writing system of the ancient Americas.
They used zero centuries before Europe.

dd-maya.h: Why the southern cities emptied, c. 900
steps: Cities grew to tens of thousands.
Forests cut for farms and lime plaster.
Kings lost authority; people left for the north and the countryside.

a: No: millions of Maya live today

dd-maya.p: Life went on in northern Yucatán at Chichén Itzá and later Mayapán, and in the highland kingdoms. Spanish invaders arrived from 1524, but the last independent Maya kingdom, at Nojpetén, fell only in 1697.

dd-maya.q: How was the Classic Maya world organised politically?
a: As one empire ruled from a single capital
As dozens of rival kingdoms, each with a divine king
As a republic of elected councils
As a province of the Aztec Empire
dd-maya.why: The Maya never formed one empire: dozens of kingdoms such as Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copán shared one culture but waged constant wars on one another.

dd-maya.p: Maize, beans and squash, grown on terraces, raised fields and forest plots, fed millions of people, and rulers turned that surplus into temples, palaces and armies. Kings claimed descent from gods and held power through ritual, alliances and war. The collapse had several causes, and historians weigh them differently: severe droughts in the 800s and 900s, endless warfare, crowded land and exhausted soils, and a loss of faith in kings who could not bring rain.

The Maya never formed one empire. Dozens of kingdoms, each with a divine king, shared one culture across Guatemala, Belize, southern Mexico and western Honduras. In the 500s–600s two great powers, Tikal and the Snake kingdom of Calakmul, fought for supremacy through webs of allies. In the 800s most southern lowland cities stopped building, and by about 950 many lay empty.

dd-maya.q: Why did the Spanish conquest of the Maya take so long, until 1697?
a: Spain was not interested in the region
With no single capital, kingdoms had to be conquered one by one
dd-maya.why: With no single capital to capture, Spain conquered kingdom by kingdom; the Itza at Nojpetén stayed free until 1697, over 170 years after the Aztecs fell.

dd-maya.p:
Lowland and highland kingdoms sharing one writing system

The Petén lowlands of northern Guatemala held the densest cluster of Classic cities, including Tikal. A 2018 laser (lidar) survey found over 60,000 structures hidden under the forest there.

Belize held Caracol, an ally of Calakmul, and Lamanai, one of the few cities lived in without a break from early times to the Spanish arrival.

Maya writing is the most complete script of the ancient Americas: about 800 signs, some standing for whole words and others for syllables. Scribes painted books on bark paper, but in 1562 the friar Diego de Landa burned many at Maní, and only four codices survive. For centuries no one could read the inscriptions. In 1952 the Soviet scholar Yuri Knorozov showed that the script recorded sounds, and in 1960 Tatiana Proskouriakoff proved that monuments told the life stories of real kings. Since the 1970s scholars have learned to read most texts. They tell of births, coronations, marriages, alliances, wars and captives, a history of rival kingdoms rather than a peaceful land of priests.

dd-maya.h: The Spanish conquest of the Maya, 1524–1697
dd-maya.p: With no single capital to capture, the Spanish had to conquer the Maya kingdom by kingdom. Pedro de Alvarado invaded the highlands of Guatemala in 1524. In Yucatán, in Mexico, the Montejo family needed about twenty years and founded Mérida in 1542. The Itza kingdom in the Petén forest stayed free until March 1697, over 170 years after the fall of the Aztecs.

Invaded by Pedro de Alvarado

Alvarado took the highlands from 1524, helped by thousands of Nahua allies from Mexico. The Itza of the Petén lowlands held out until 1697.

Alvarado's forces pushed into Cuscatlán, the land of the Pipil, a Nahua people living beside the Maya, from 1524.

dd-maya.q: What allowed Maya rulers to build temples, palaces and armies?
a: Maize, beans and squash that fed millions
Trade with China across the Pacific
dd-maya.why: Maize, beans and squash, grown on terraces, raised fields and forest plots, fed millions, and rulers turned that surplus into temples, palaces and armies.

dd-maya.p:
Conquered by the Montejos

Yucatán's divided Maya states fought off the Montejos twice before falling by 1546. A great revolt that year in the east was crushed. Chiapas was conquered from 1524.

The Maya used several calendars at once. A 260-day ritual count meshed with a 365-day year, so the same combination came round only every 52 years. For history they used the Long Count, which numbered days from a starting point equal to 11 August 3114 BC in our calendar. Their counting system used a symbol for zero, one of the earliest in the world. One great cycle of the Long Count ended on 21 December 2012, which led to worldwide talk of a Maya prophecy of doom. Maya inscriptions predict no such thing: one at Palenque refers to a date thousands of years later, and scholars see 2012 as a completion, like a calendar rolling over.

dd-maya.q: What is true of the Maya people today?
a: They vanished when the cities emptied
Over 6 million people still speak Maya languages
They live mainly in South America
dd-maya.why: The cities emptied but the Maya did not vanish: over 6 million people speak about 30 Maya languages, mostly in Guatemala and south-eastern Mexico.

dd-maya.p: The Maya did not vanish. Over 6 million people speak about 30 Maya languages, most of them in Guatemala, where Maya people are about two-fifths of the population, and in south-eastern Mexico. Smaller communities live in Belize and Honduras. Maya farmers still grow maize, beans and squash, and some communities keep the old 260-day calendar for rituals.

Over 20 Maya languages, including K'iche', Q'eqchi', Kaqchikel and Mam

In the 2018 census about 42% of Guatemalans identified as Maya. A UN-backed truth commission found that 83% of identified victims of the 1960–96 civil war were Maya, and that state agents committed acts of genocide.

dd-maya.q: What do many scholars think caused the southern lowland cities to empty in the 800s?
a: Severe drought striking a society already strained by war and crowding
An epidemic brought by Aztec traders
dd-maya.why: Lake sediments show severe droughts; many scholars think they hit a society already strained by warfare, deforestation and dense populations, and kings lost authority when rains failed.

dd-maya.p:
Yucatec, Tsotsil, Tseltal, Ch'ol, Mopan, Ch'orti' and others

About a tenth of Belizeans are Maya, mostly Mopan, Q'eqchi' and Yucatec. In 2015 Belize's top court upheld Maya customary land rights in the south.

The 2020 census counted over 2 million speakers of Maya languages in Mexico, above all Yucatec Maya, Tseltal, Tsotsil and Ch'ol, in Yucatán, Quintana Roo, Campeche and Chiapas.

Between about 800 and 950 kings across the southern lowlands stopped erecting dated monuments; the last known Long Count date, at Toniná, records the year 909. Populations fell sharply as people left for the north and the highlands. Lake sediments in Yucatán show severe droughts in this period, with rainfall falling by about half at their worst, according to a 2018 study. Many scholars think drought struck a society already strained by warfare, deforestation and dense populations: lidar surveys suggest the lowlands held millions of people at their peak. When rains failed and kings could no longer deliver, cities lost their reason to exist. The collapse was a slow decline over generations, not a sudden disappearance.

The Maya cities emptied, but the Maya people did not disappear. Spanish conquest brought disease, forced labour and Catholicism, which many Maya blended with older beliefs. Their descendants rose against outside rule, in the Caste War of Yucatán from 1847 and in Chiapas in 1994, and suffered terribly in Guatemala's civil war. Today over 6 million people speak Maya languages, and ruins such as Tikal and Chichén Itzá draw millions of visitors.

dd-africa.p: From about the 100s, the Kingdom of Aksum in the Ethiopian highlands traded across the Red Sea, minted gold coins and, around 330, adopted Christianity. In West Africa, Ghana grew rich by the 800s on gold sent north across the Sahara. Mali replaced it in the 1200s, and in 1324 its ruler Mansa Musa crossed Egypt on pilgrimage with so much gold that he became famous in Europe.

items: Nubian kings ruled Egypt; more pyramids than Egypt.
Ethiopian trading power; early Christian kingdom.
Stone city that traded gold to the Indian Ocean.

steps: Arrive around AD 300 and make desert crossings possible.
West African gold for Saharan salt, weight for weight.
Merchants bring Islam, writing and scholarship.
Ghana, Mali and Songhai tax the trade.

a: Ruler of Mali, perhaps the richest person ever
dd-africa.why: His 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca crashed the price of gold in Cairo.

dd-africa.p: Songhai, based at Gao, became the largest West African empire in the 1500s. On the east coast, Swahili city-states such as Kilwa grew wealthy on Indian Ocean trade, while inland the rulers of Great Zimbabwe built a city of stone.

dd-africa.q: What made Ghana, Mali and Songhai rich and powerful?
a: Silver mines worked by Roman engineers
Control of West African gold traded across the Sahara
Spice plantations on the Atlantic coast
dd-africa.why: West Africa had gold and the Sahara had salt; rulers who controlled gold fields and caravan routes could tax them, raise armies and build cities.

dd-africa.p: Trade made these states. West Africa had gold, the Sahara had salt, and from the early centuries AD camels made regular desert crossings possible. Islam later linked West African rulers and merchants to North Africa and the Middle East. On the east coast the monsoon winds carried ships to Arabia and India and back each year. Rulers who controlled gold fields, ports or caravan routes could tax them, raise armies and build cities.

From highlands in today's Ethiopia and Eritrea, Aksum grew rich on Red Sea trade, exporting ivory and gold through its port, Adulis. It minted its own gold coins from about 270. Around 330 King Ezana became a Christian, making Aksum one of the first Christian states. A Persian prophet of the 200s, Mani, listed it among the world's four great powers, with Rome, Persia and China.

dd-africa.q: How did Portuguese arrival from the 1400s change these trading states?
a: It made Saharan routes busier than ever
It had no effect on African trade
It led Mali to conquer Portugal
Atlantic trade, including in enslaved people, drew wealth from older routes
dd-africa.why: From the 1400s Atlantic trade, including a vast trade in enslaved people, drew wealth away from the Saharan and Swahili routes.

dd-africa.p:
Northern Ethiopian and Eritrean highlands, with the Red Sea coast

Northern Ethiopia, especially Tigray, was Aksum's heartland. Ethiopia's Orthodox Church traces its roots to Ezana's conversion around 330.

The Eritrean highlands and coast were part of Aksum, and its port of Adulis lay on the Gulf of Zula.

Kush (Meroë) in the 300s; Yemen in the 520s

Northern Sudan was home to the kingdom of Kush, centred on Meroë. Ezana's inscriptions describe a campaign there in the mid-300s.

Around 525 Aksum's King Kaleb invaded Himyar in Yemen. Aksumite rule soon gave way to a general, Abraha, who ruled largely on his own.

Aksum's main Mediterranean trading partner

Roman Egypt traded with Aksum through Red Sea ports such as Berenice. Christianity reached Aksum through these links.

In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, set out for Mecca with a huge following and many camel-loads of gold. When he stopped in Cairo he spent and gave away so much that, according to the Arab writer al-Umari, the value of gold there was still depressed twelve years later. The visit put Mali on the map, literally: the Catalan Atlas of 1375, made in Majorca, shows him on a throne holding a gold nugget. Modern claims that he was 'the richest person who ever lived' make good headlines but cannot be measured. On his way home he brought scholars and an architect, and Mali built mosques in Timbuktu and Gao.

dd-africa.h: West Africa's gold empires: Mali, c. 1350
dd-africa.p: West Africa's gold paid for an empire three times over. Ghana, in today's Mauritania and Mali, ruled the gold trade by the 800s. Mali followed from about 1235 and was at its height around 1350, when camel caravans carried its gold north across the Sahara to Morocco and Egypt in exchange for salt and goods. Songhai, ruling from Gao, became the largest of the three in the 1500s.

From the Atlantic coast to beyond the Niger bend

The Gambia River valley was Mali's western edge. Portuguese ships sailed up the river in the 1450s, seeking a route to Mali's gold.

Today's Mali was the heart of all three empires: Ghana in the west, Mali along the upper Niger, and Songhai at Gao and Timbuktu. It took its name from the Mali Empire at independence in 1960.

dd-africa.q: What made regular trade across the Sahara possible?
a: Camels, from the early centuries AD
dd-africa.why: From the early centuries AD camels made regular desert crossings possible, linking West African gold to North Africa and the Mediterranean world.

dd-africa.p:
North African trading partners

Moroccan merchants ran much of the caravan trade. In 1591 a Moroccan army with firearms crossed the desert and defeated Songhai at Tondibi.

Oasis towns in the Algerian Sahara, such as those of Tuat, were stops for caravans between the Niger and North Africa.

Timbuktu began as a seasonal camp near the Niger and became a meeting point for camel caravans and river boats. By the 1400s and 1500s it was a centre of Islamic learning, with scholars teaching law, astronomy, medicine and grammar around mosques such as Sankore and Djinguereber. Families copied and collected manuscripts for centuries, and hundreds of thousands survive. When armed groups occupied the city in 2012–13, librarians and residents smuggled most of them south to Bamako in boxes and sacks, though some were burned. In Europe the name came to mean somewhere impossibly remote, but for West Africans it was a crossroads.

dd-africa.q: Why did modern Ghana, Mali and Zimbabwe take names from these old states?
a: They were their exact colonial borders
Europeans chose the names for them
To claim a proud African past that colonial writers had denied
They were ruled by the same dynasties
dd-africa.why: Colonial writers denied Africans had built such states, a claim archaeology disproved; at independence Ghana, Mali and Zimbabwe took their names.

dd-africa.h: The Swahili coast and Great Zimbabwe, c. 1400
dd-africa.p: Along the coast of Kenya, Tanzania and Mozambique, Muslim city-states such as Kilwa, Mombasa and Mogadishu traded with Arabia, India and China on the monsoon winds. Their language, Swahili, mixed Bantu roots with Arabic words. Inland, the rulers of Great Zimbabwe in Zimbabwe controlled gold that reached the coast at Sofala. Their stone city, built without mortar, was the largest in southern Africa.

Trading towns along the coast and islands

The Comoros were part of the Swahili world, with Muslim towns and trading links to Kilwa and Madagascar.

Mombasa, Malindi and Lamu were among the leading Swahili towns. In 1505 a Portuguese fleet sacked Mombasa.

dd-africa.q: What drove the wealth of the Swahili city-states such as Kilwa?
a: Indian Ocean trade carried by the monsoon winds
dd-africa.why: On the east coast the monsoon winds carried ships to Arabia and India and back each year, and towns like Kilwa grew rich on gold reaching the coast at Sofala.

dd-africa.p:
A gold-rich state on the Zimbabwe plateau

Great Zimbabwe was built from about the 1000s by ancestors of the Shona people. Chinese porcelain and Persian goods found there show its trading reach.

Great Zimbabwe's walls, some 11 metres high, were built from granite blocks fitted without mortar between about the 1000s and 1400s. When Europeans saw them in the 1870s, the explorer Karl Mauch claimed they were the work of the Queen of Sheba, and others credited Phoenicians or Arabs. Archaeologists disagreed: David Randall-MacIver in 1905 and Gertrude Caton-Thompson in 1929 showed the city was medieval and African, built by ancestors of the Shona. Rhodesia's white-minority government still pressed for the old myths in the 1960s and 1970s. At independence in 1980 the country took the city's name, and a carved soapstone bird from the site is on its flag.

From the 1400s Portuguese ships reached Africa's coasts, and Atlantic trade, including a vast trade in enslaved people, drew wealth away from the Saharan and Swahili routes. Colonial writers later denied that Africans had built states like these, a claim archaeology disproved. Independent nations took their names: Ghana in 1957, Mali in 1960, Zimbabwe in 1980. Swahili is now spoken by over 100 million people, and Ethiopia's Orthodox Church still traces its roots to Aksum.

Africa’s pre-colonial kingdoms show a long history of states, trade and learning, contrary to the colonial myth of a continent 'without history'. Many modern nations take their names from them: Ghana, Mali, Benin, Zimbabwe.

dd-africa.s: Modern Ghana lies where the old Ghana Empire was.
dd-africa.why: The old empire was further north-west, in Mali and Mauritania; the name was borrowed.

Sundiata Keita founds the Mali Empire, according to tradition
Mansa Musa passes through Cairo on pilgrimage to Mecca
Great Zimbabwe and Kilwa at their height
Songhai's Sonni Ali takes Timbuktu

dd-byzantium.p: In 330 Emperor Constantine refounded the Greek city of Byzantium as Constantinople, a new Christian capital for the Roman Empire. When the western half fell in 476, the eastern empire carried on. Justinian (527–565) reconquered Italy, North Africa and southern Spain, codified Roman law and built Hagia Sophia, but plague and war drained his empire.

dd-byzantium.h: Rome in the West and East

items: Triple land walls held for 1,000 years.
A chain blocked the Golden Horn.
Burning liquid that floated on water.
Between Europe, Asia and the Black Sea.

dd-byzantium.why: Under Mehmed II, using huge cannons.

dd-byzantium.p: In the 600s Arab armies took Syria, Egypt and North Africa, though Constantinople's walls and Greek fire held. The empire revived around 1000, then lost most of Anatolia after the Seljuk Turks defeated it at Manzikert in 1071. Crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204; the Byzantines retook it in 1261, but the Ottomans captured it on 29 May 1453.

a: A Greek kingdom founded by Alexander
An Ottoman province in the Balkans
The eastern Roman Empire, which carried on after the West fell
dd-byzantium.why: The eastern empire, ruled from Constantinople, carried on after 476; its people called themselves Romans, and 'Byzantine' was a later name popularised by Western scholars.

dd-byzantium.p: It lasted so long thanks to Constantinople's near-impregnable site, protected by sea on three sides and huge land walls, along with a trained bureaucracy, a trusted gold coin, the solidus, and skilled diplomacy that played enemies against each other. It declined because it faced enemies on every side, from Persians and Arabs to Bulgars, Normans and Turks, and because the Venetian-backed Fourth Crusade of 1204 broke it into rival states that never fully recovered.

Emperor Justinian (527–565) set out to win back the lost western half of the Roman Empire. His generals took North Africa from the Vandals in 533–534, Italy from the Ostrogoths after a war lasting until 554, and a strip of southern Spain in 552. From Constantinople, today's Istanbul in Turkey, the empire again ruled most of the Mediterranean, but plague and war left it exhausted.

dd-byzantium.q: How did Byzantium help shape the Renaissance and European law?
a: Justinian's law code and Greek texts brought to Italy by fleeing scholars
It founded Europe's first universities in Spain
dd-byzantium.why: Justinian's law code became the basis of civil law in much of Europe, and Byzantine scholars fleeing to Italy brought ancient Greek texts that fed the Renaissance.

dd-byzantium.p:
Lands held in 527

Anatolia and Constantinople were the heart of the empire. Its people called themselves Romans and mostly spoke Greek.

Greece was an old and largely Greek-speaking part of the eastern empire, with great cities such as Thessaloniki and Corinth.

533–554

The war against the Ostrogoths lasted from 535 to 554 and ruined much of Italy. In 568 the Lombards invaded and took most of the north.

The Vandal kingdom of North Africa fell in 533–534. Carthage stayed Byzantine until the Arabs took it in 698.

After riots in 532 burned the old cathedral, Justinian had a new one built in under six years. His designers, the mathematicians Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, raised a dome about 31 metres across that seemed to float on a ring of 40 windows. Earthquakes brought it partly down in 558, and it was rebuilt higher. A later legend has Justinian exclaim on entering, 'Solomon, I have surpassed you!' It was the world's largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years. After 1453 the Ottomans made it a mosque and added minarets; it became a museum in 1934 and a mosque again in 2020, with many of its gold mosaics still visible.

Around 672, according to Byzantine chroniclers, an engineer named Kallinikos, a refugee from Syria, brought the empire a terrifying new weapon. Greek fire was a liquid sprayed through bronze tubes from the bows of warships; it burst into flame, kept burning on water and was very hard to put out. It helped beat off the great Arab sieges of Constantinople in 674–678 and 717–718. The recipe was a state secret, known only to a few families, and it was guarded so well that it was eventually lost. Historians think it was probably based on crude oil, perhaps mixed with resin, but nobody knows exactly how it was made or fired.

Between 634 and 718 Arab armies took Syria, Egypt and North Africa, and twice besieged Constantinople. The empire held on to Anatolia and Greece, and under Basil II, who conquered Bulgaria by 1018, it recovered much of the Balkans. Then defeat by the Seljuk Turks at Manzikert in 1071 opened Anatolia to the Turks. Crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204, and the Ottomans took it in 1453.

After the Battle of Yarmuk in 636 Syria became the heart of the Umayyad Caliphate, ruled from Damascus.

Egypt, the empire's richest province, fell to the Arabs in 639–642. Its loss cost Constantinople its main grain supply.

dd-byzantium.q: Why did Constantinople hold out for over a thousand years?
a: Sea on three sides, huge land walls, and skilled diplomacy
dd-byzantium.why: Its near-impregnable site, a trained bureaucracy, a trusted gold coin and diplomacy that played enemies against each other kept it going; Greek fire helped beat Arab sieges.

dd-byzantium.p:
At the death of Basil II

Anatolia was the core that survived the Arab attacks. After Manzikert in 1071 the Turks settled most of it, and the empire kept only the west and the coasts.

Greece stayed Byzantine. Crete was retaken from the Arabs in 961, and the empire's last foothold, the Morea, fell in 1460.

No one in the empire called themselves 'Byzantine'. They were Romaioi, Romans, and their state was the Roman Empire, ruled without a break from Augustus to its last emperor, Constantine XI, who died defending the walls in 1453. The name 'Byzantine' was popularised by Western scholars after the empire fell, from the old name of the city. Greek was the everyday language and the language of church and government, while Latin faded after the 600s. Western Europeans, especially after Charlemagne was crowned emperor in 800, preferred to call it 'the empire of the Greeks', a quarrel over who were the real Romans that lasted centuries.

dd-byzantium.q: Which Byzantine legacy is still alive among many Slavic peoples?
a: Orthodox Christianity and the Cyrillic alphabet
dd-byzantium.why: Missionaries spread Orthodox Christianity and the forerunner of Cyrillic to the Slavs; today over 200 million Orthodox Christians live from Greece and Serbia to Russia.

dd-byzantium.p: Byzantine missionaries took Christianity, its liturgy and an alphabet to the Slavs. Bulgaria was baptised in 864, and in 988 Prince Vladimir of Kyiv, in today's Ukraine, made Orthodoxy the faith of the Rus. After 1453 Russia saw itself as Byzantium's heir. Today the Orthodox Church is the largest faith from Greece and Serbia to Russia.

Greek-speaking Orthodox lands

The Church of Greece and the Greek language are Byzantium's most direct heirs. Modern Greeks long called themselves Romioi, 'Romans'.

Cyprus has its own Orthodox church, independent since the 400s.

Slavic and Balkan lands that took Orthodoxy from Constantinople

Khan Boris I was baptised in 864. Disciples of Cyril and Methodius developed the Cyrillic alphabet in Bulgaria around 900.

The Serbs became Christian under Byzantine influence. In 1219 Saint Sava won the Serbian church its independence.

dd-byzantium.q: Which event broke the empire into rival states that never fully recovered?
a: The Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople in 1204
The baptism of Vladimir of Kyiv
dd-byzantium.why: After losing most of Anatolia at Manzikert in 1071, the empire was broken apart by the Venetian-backed Fourth Crusade of 1204; the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453.

dd-byzantium.p:
Christian since the 300s

Georgia became Christian in the 300s. It shared Byzantium's Orthodox faith, while keeping its own church and alphabet.

Byzantium's longest-lasting export was its faith. In 863 the brothers Cyril and Methodius of Thessaloniki went to the Slavs of Moravia with an alphabet they had made for Slavonic; their followers in Bulgaria developed Cyrillic from it. According to the Primary Chronicle, envoys of Vladimir of Kyiv said of a service in Hagia Sophia that they 'knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth', and in 988 Vladimir was baptised. The split with Rome, dated to 1054, made the Eastern churches a separate tradition. Today there are over 200 million Orthodox Christians, from Greece and Serbia to Ukraine and Russia, many still using liturgies written in Byzantine times.

Justinian's law code became the basis of civil law in much of Europe, and Byzantine scholars who fled to Italy brought ancient Greek texts that fed the Renaissance. Byzantine missionaries spread Orthodox Christianity and the forerunner of the Cyrillic alphabet to the Slavs, and Moscow later claimed to be the 'Third Rome'. The Ottomans made Constantinople, today's Istanbul, the capital of their own empire.

It preserved Greek and Roman learning, which reached Italy and helped spark the Renaissance. Justinian's law code shaped European law, and Orthodox Christianity spread from it to Russia and the Balkans.

dd-byzantium.s: The Hagia Sophia was built as a church.
dd-byzantium.why: In 537; later a mosque, then a museum, now a mosque again.

Justinian's Hagia Sophia is dedicated
The Great Schism splits the Orthodox and Catholic churches
Seljuk Turks defeat the Byzantines at Manzikert
The Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople
The Ottomans capture Constantinople

dd-vikings.p: On 8 June 793 raiders from Scandinavia sacked the monastery of Lindisfarne, and for two centuries Vikings raided coasts and rivers across Europe. Raiding grew into conquest: a Danish Great Army landed in England in 865 and settled the north and east, the Danelaw, and in 911 the Frankish king granted the lower Seine to the chief Rollo, founding Normandy. Norse settlers founded Dublin, settled Iceland from about 870 and Greenland around 985, and briefly reached Newfoundland around 1000.

steps: Fast, shallow boats that could cross oceans and row up rivers.
Little farmland in Norway and a growing population.
Rich, undefended monasteries and trading towns.
Raiding brought silver, status and stories.

items: Scotland, Ireland, Iceland, Greenland, North America.
Russian rivers to Constantinople and Baghdad.

dd-vikings.p: In the east, Swedes called the Rus traded down the rivers of Russia to Constantinople and the Caspian, and their princes ruled Kyiv. The age is often said to end in 1066, when the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada was killed at Stamford Bridge.

dd-vikings.q: How did Viking activity change between the sack of Lindisfarne in 793 and about 1000?
a: Raiding grew into conquest and settlement across Europe and the Atlantic
Vikings stopped raiding and turned only to farming at home
Vikings were driven out of every land they had raided
Raids stayed small and never went beyond Britain
dd-vikings.why: Raids grew into conquest: the Danelaw in England, Normandy in France, Dublin, Iceland, Greenland and, briefly, Newfoundland.

dd-vikings.p: Historians still debate the causes. Ambitious chiefs needed silver and land to reward their followers, and Scandinavia had little good farmland to spare. Fast, shallow ships let them cross open sea and row far up rivers, and rich, poorly defended monasteries and trading towns made easy targets. Booming trade with the Islamic world, and quarrels among the Frankish and English kingdoms, drew them further in.

dd-vikings.h: Raids and settlements in the west, 793–c. 1000
dd-vikings.p: Viking raids began with the sack of Lindisfarne in 793. Danes later settled the north and east of England, the Danelaw, and in 911 a Frankish king granted Normandy in France to the chief Rollo. Norwegians founded Dublin in Ireland and sailed on to Iceland and Greenland, and around 1000 they reached Newfoundland in Canada, five centuries before Columbus.

dd-vikings.q: What gave the Vikings their great advantage in reaching so many places?
a: Horse archers who could ride across the steppe
Light, shallow longships that crossed open sea and rowed up rivers
dd-vikings.why: Longships drew only about a metre of water, so crews could land on any beach, cross open sea and row far up rivers like the Seine.

dd-vikings.p:
Norway, Denmark and Sweden

Norwegians raided Scotland and Ireland and settled the Atlantic islands, Iceland and Greenland. Norway became one kingdom under Harald Fairhair and his successors in the late 800s and 900s.

Danes led the great armies that raided the Frankish lands and conquered much of England. Danish king Cnut ruled England, Denmark and Norway in the 1020s.

Lands where Norse settlers took over or founded towns

Settlers arrived from about 870, many from Norway and the British Isles. In 930 they founded the Althing, one of the world's oldest assemblies.

Norse farmers settled the Faroe Islands in the 800s, and their language became today's Faroese.

dd-vikings.q: Why does Kyivan Rus still matter to several countries today?
a: It is a common root of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus
It was the first kingdom of Sweden
It founded the city of Constantinople
It is where the English language began
dd-vikings.why: Rus princes of Norse origin ruled Kyiv, and after Kyivan Rus became Orthodox in 988 it became a common root of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus.

dd-vikings.p:
A small base used for a few years around 1000

Leif Erikson's voyages reached a land the sagas called Vinland. The base at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland, was used only briefly.

The longship was the Vikings' great advantage. Built of overlapping oak planks, it was light, flexible and shallow, drawing only about a metre of water, so crews could land on any beach and row far up rivers like the Seine. A big square woollen sail drove it at sea, and oars took over in calm water or on rivers. The warship Skuldelev 2, built near Dublin around 1042 and sunk in Roskilde Fjord in Denmark, was about 30 metres long and carried around 60–70 men; a replica sailed from Roskilde to Dublin in 2007. Grand ships were also buried with the dead, as at Oseberg in Norway in 834. Sailors navigated by coastlines, sun, stars, birds and whales.

'Viking' meant going raiding, not a people: most Norse were farmers, fishers and craftspeople who never went 'a-viking'. They wore no horned helmets. The only fairly complete Viking helmet, found at Gjermundbu in Norway, is a plain iron cap; the horns come from 19th-century painters and the costumes for Wagner's operas in 1876. Combs are among the commonest finds, and free women could own property and divorce. Communities settled disputes at assemblies called things, the root of Iceland's Althing. But the raids were brutal, and slaving was central to the economy: captives from Ireland, Britain and eastern Europe were sold in markets from Dublin to the Volga.

dd-vikings.h: The Rus and the river roads, c. 860–1000
dd-vikings.p: Swedish Vikings, called the Rus, rowed and dragged their boats along the rivers of eastern Europe. On the Dnieper they reached Kyiv and the Black Sea, then Constantinople, the 'great city' they called Miklagard. On the Volga they traded furs and slaves for Arab silver. Their leaders founded Kyivan Rus, a state spanning today's Ukraine, Belarus and western Russia.

Sweden, home of most eastern Vikings

Tens of thousands of Arab silver coins have been found on the Swedish island of Gotland alone, brought back by trade along the eastern rivers.

dd-vikings.q: What drove ambitious Scandinavian chiefs to go raiding, according to the chapter?
a: They were fleeing a Christian invasion of Scandinavia
They needed silver and land to reward their followers
Their kings ordered them to spread the Norse religion
The Frankish king paid them to attack England
dd-vikings.why: Chiefs needed silver and land to reward followers, and Scandinavia had little good farmland to spare, though historians still debate the causes.

dd-vikings.p:
Ruled by Norse-descended princes who soon spoke Slavic

Polotsk, in today's Belarus, was one of the oldest towns of the Rus, ruled by its own princes.

Kyiv became the Rus capital around 882. The state's princes made treaties with the Byzantine Empire in 911 and 944.

dd-vikings.h: The Rus: Vikings in the east
dd-vikings.p: Swedish traders, known to their neighbours as the Rus, rowed across the Baltic and up the rivers of eastern Europe, dragging their boats overland between rivers. The Byzantine emperor Constantine VII recorded the names of the Dnieper rapids in both Norse and Slavic. According to the Primary Chronicle, written around 1113, the Varangian Rurik was invited to rule Novgorod in 862; how much of this is legend is debated. The Rus raided Constantinople in 860, and Rurik's successors ruled from Kyiv and made trade treaties with the Byzantines. Norsemen served the emperor in the Varangian Guard, and one carved runes into a balustrade in Hagia Sophia. Within a few generations the Rus princes spoke Slavic and, from 988, worshipped as Orthodox Christians.

dd-vikings.q: What did Rollo's settlers in Normandy go on to do?
a: They founded Dublin and the first Irish towns
They settled Iceland and founded the Althing
They ruled Kyiv and traded with Constantinople
Their Norman descendants conquered England, southern Italy and Sicily
dd-vikings.why: Normandy grew from lands granted to Rollo in 911, and the Normans descended from his settlers conquered England in 1066 and southern Italy and Sicily.

dd-vikings.p: Denmark, Norway and Sweden became Christian kingdoms, taking shape around 1000. Norse settlers peopled Iceland and the Faroes, founded Dublin, and left English with words such as 'sky', 'egg' and 'they'. The Normans, descended from Rollo's settlers, conquered England in 1066 and southern Italy and Sicily. In the east, Kyivan Rus became Orthodox in 988, a common root of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus.
Vikings founded Dublin, settled Iceland and Normandy, and helped found the first Russian state. English took hundreds of Norse words such as 'sky', 'egg', 'knife' and 'Thursday' (Thor’s day).

pts: Raiders sack the monastery of Lindisfarne
The Danish Great Army lands in England
Rollo is granted the land that becomes Normandy
Iceland's settlers found the Althing assembly
Norse reach Newfoundland, at L'Anse aux Meadows
Harald Hardrada is killed at Stamford Bridge
