dd-napoleon.p: Napoleon Bonaparte, a Corsican artillery officer, made his name retaking Toulon in 1793 and won fame with his Italian campaign of 1796–97. After a failed expedition to Egypt, he seized power in 1799 as First Consul, made peace with the Church and issued his Civil Code. In 1804 he crowned himself emperor.

items: Each could fight alone until others arrived.
Concentrated guns at the decisive point.

steps: Banned trade with Britain; Europe suffered.
A guerrilla war drained his armies.
Wellington and Blücher defeat him; exile to St Helena.

dd-napoleon.q: Which law code did Napoleon create?
dd-napoleon.why: Still the basis of law in France and many other countries.

dd-napoleon.p: He crushed Austria and Russia at Austerlitz in 1805 and Prussia at Jena in 1806, but Britain's navy stayed unbeaten after Trafalgar. Spain's guerrilla war from 1808 drained him, and the invasion of Russia in 1812 destroyed his army. Beaten at Leipzig in 1813, he abdicated in 1814, returned for the Hundred Days, and lost for good at Waterloo in 1815.

dd-napoleon.q: What was Napoleon's path from 1799 to 1815?
a: He seized power, became emperor and dominated Europe, then fell after Russia and Waterloo
He served loyally as a general under a restored king
He led France to conquer Britain and Russia permanently
He ruled Italy only and never governed France
dd-napoleon.why: He seized power in 1799, crowned himself emperor in 1804, crushed Austria, Russia and Prussia, then lost his army in Russia and was beaten at Waterloo.

dd-napoleon.p: The revolution had swept away the old elites and opened careers to talent, and its wars made generals powerful. Bonaparte combined military genius, speed and ruthless self-promotion, and the French, worn out by a decade of upheaval, welcomed order. His victories rested on large conscript armies and flexible corps. But his ambition knew no limit, and his attempt to strangle Britain's trade drew him into Spain and Russia. Europe's rulers finally united against him.

Born on Corsica in 1769, Napoleon Bonaparte was 26 when France gave him its army in Italy. In 1796–97 he beat the Austrians again and again and dictated the peace. In 1798 he sailed for Egypt, taking Malta on the way, to strike at Britain's route to India. He won on land, but Nelson destroyed his fleet, and his march into Ottoman Palestine stalled at Acre, in today's Israel. In 1799 he slipped home and seized power.

dd-napoleon.q: Which of Napoleon's changes outlasted his defeat?
a: His family's rule over France and Spain
French control of Russia's Baltic coast
His Civil Code, which shaped law across Europe and beyond
dd-napoleon.why: Kings were restored in 1815, but his Civil Code shaped the law of much of Europe, Latin America and beyond, and remains French law today.

dd-napoleon.p: Bonaparte returned in October 1799 to a country tired of the Directory. On 9–10 November he led a coup and became First Consul.

Against Austria and its Italian allies

Bonaparte drove the Austrians out of Lombardy, and in 1797 created the Cisalpine Republic around Milan. At Campo Formio he handed the ancient Republic of Venice to Austria.

Malta, Egypt and the march into Palestine

The French took Malta from the Knights of St John in June 1798. Britain, helped by Maltese rebels, captured it in 1800 and kept it until 1964.

Egypt was an Ottoman province run by Mamluk beys. The French were defeated and evacuated in 1801, but over 150 scholars who came with them produced the vast 'Description de l'Égypte', founding modern Egyptology.

Napoleon chaired many of the meetings that drafted the Civil Code, issued in March 1804 with 2,281 articles. It swept away France's patchwork of hundreds of local laws and made all male citizens equal before one law. It protected property, ended feudal privileges and allowed civil marriage and divorce. It also put wives and children firmly under the authority of husbands and fathers. French armies carried it to Belgium, the Netherlands, western Germany and Italy, and many countries later copied it, from Latin America to Egypt. On Saint Helena Napoleon is reported to have said that his Code, not his forty battles, would live forever. Its core is still French law today.

In June 1812 about 450,000 men crossed the Neman into the Russian Empire, today's Lithuania, and more followed. Only about half were French: Germans, Poles, Italians and Austrians marched too. The Russians fell back, fought at Borodino and abandoned Moscow, which burned. Napoleon waited a month for a peace offer that never came, then retreated in October. Hunger, cold, disease and Cossack raids destroyed his army.

Including the annexed Low Countries

Napoleon's quarrel with the tsar, who had left the Continental System blockading Britain, led to the war. He left the army in December and raced back to Paris.

dd-napoleon.q: Why were the French willing to accept Napoleon's seizure of power?
a: He promised to restore the old nobility
He was the rightful heir of Louis XVI
Worn out by a decade of upheaval, they welcomed order
Britain demanded that France choose him
dd-napoleon.why: The revolution had opened careers to talent and made generals powerful, and a France tired of upheaval welcomed the order he offered.

dd-napoleon.p:
Confederation of the Rhine and a Prussian corps

German states sent more troops than any nation but France. Prussia's corps of about 20,000 changed sides at Tauroggen on 30 December 1812, starting Germany's war of liberation.

Napoleon's Polish state

About 90,000 Poles and Lithuanians served, hoping Napoleon would restore Poland. Prince Józef Poniatowski commanded the Polish corps.

dd-napoleon.q: How did Napoleon's era help shape modern Europe?
a: By stirring national feeling that helped bring about nation-states
By ending all wars in Europe for a century
By making French the only language of Germany and Italy
By turning Europe into one federal republic
dd-napoleon.why: He ended the Holy Roman Empire, simplified Germany's map and stirred national feeling in Germany, Italy and Spain, feeding the nation-states of the 1800s.

dd-napoleon.p: The idea of a tiny, touchy Napoleon is mostly myth. His height at death was recorded as 5 feet 2 inches in old French units, which is about 1.69 metres, or 5 feet 6 or 7 inches in English measures. That was average or a little above for a Frenchman of his time. The confusion came partly from the different inches, partly from his nickname, 'the little corporal', which was a term of affection from his soldiers, and partly from British cartoonists such as James Gillray, who drew him as a tantrum-throwing dwarf. He was also often seen beside his tall Imperial Guard.

Beaten by a coalition in 1813–14, Napoleon gave up his throne and was sent to the island of Elba, off Italy. In February 1815 he escaped, landed in France and reached Paris without a shot fired. These Hundred Days ended at Waterloo in Belgium, where a British-led army and the Prussians beat him. The British shipped him to Saint Helena, a remote island in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821.
Louis XVIII, brother of the guillotined king, fled when Napoleon returned, then came back after Waterloo. In 1840 Napoleon's body was brought home to Les Invalides in Paris.

British, Dutch, Belgian, German and Prussian troops

The Duke of Wellington's army was only about one-third British; the rest were Dutch, Belgian and German. Napoleon surrendered to a British warship in July 1815.

Dutch and Belgian troops under the Prince of Orange held the crossroads at Quatre Bras on 16 June, and fought at Waterloo two days later.

dd-napoleon.q: What drew Napoleon into his ruinous wars in Spain and Russia?
a: A plan to restore the Holy Roman Empire
His attempt to strangle Britain's trade
His wish to free Spain's American colonies
dd-napoleon.why: His bid to choke Britain's trade drew him into Spain and Russia; the tsar's leaving the Continental System led to the 1812 invasion.

dd-napoleon.p: Saint Helena lies nearly 2,000 km from Africa. Most historians think Napoleon died of stomach cancer; theories of arsenic poisoning are disputed.

The revolution had abolished slavery in 1794, but in 1802 Napoleon brought it back in Guadeloupe and French Guiana, and kept it in Martinique. He sent a large army under his brother-in-law Leclerc to retake Saint-Domingue. Its leader Toussaint Louverture was seized and died in a French prison in 1803. The French army was destroyed by yellow fever and by the resistance led by Jean-Jacques Dessalines, and Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804. The failing campaign helped persuade Napoleon to sell Louisiana to the United States in 1803 for 15 million dollars, doubling the young country's size. France finally abolished slavery in 1848.

The Congress of Vienna restored kings, but much of Napoleon's work lasted. His Civil Code shaped the law of much of Europe, Latin America and beyond, and his prefects, lycées and Bank of France still structure French life. He ended the Holy Roman Empire and simplified Germany's map from hundreds of states to a few dozen, and by stirring national feeling in Germany, Italy and Spain he helped bring about the nation-states of the 1800s.

dd-greatgame.p: In the 1800s the Russian Empire conquered the steppe and the khanates of Central Asia, while Britain expanded across India, and each feared the other would reach Afghanistan first. Britain invaded in 1839 to install a friendly ruler, but a revolt in Kabul forced its army to retreat in January 1842, and almost all were lost. A second war in 1878–80 gave Britain control of Afghan foreign policy.

l: Feared Russia reaching the Indian Ocean

dd-greatgame.q: Why did Afghanistan matter in the Great Game?
a: It was a buffer between British India and Russia
dd-greatgame.why: Its borders were drawn by the rivals.

dd-greatgame.p: The two empires then drew Afghanistan's borders, including the Durand Line, agreed between Britain and the emir in 1893, and the Wakhan Corridor, and in 1907 settled their rivalry. In the 20th century the Soviet Union invaded in 1979 and the US-led coalition in 2001; both eventually left.

dd-greatgame.q: What was the 'Great Game' of the 1800s?
a: A trade war between Britain and China over tea
The rivalry between Russia and Britain over Central Asia and Afghanistan
A contest between France and Britain for Egypt
Afghanistan's war to conquer British India
dd-greatgame.why: Russia conquered Central Asia while Britain expanded across India, and each feared the other would reach Afghanistan first.

dd-greatgame.p: Britain saw India as the jewel of its empire and feared a Russian advance through the mountain passes, while Russia pushed south for security, trade and prestige, and to gain leverage over Britain. Afghanistan, a mountainous kingdom of many peoples, sat between them. Later invaders came for new reasons: the Soviets to save a failing communist ally, the Americans to destroy al-Qaeda and the Taliban regime that sheltered it after 9/11.

dd-greatgame.h: Russia, Britain and the buffer between, c. 1885–1907
dd-greatgame.p: Through the 1800s the Russian Empire pushed south into Central Asia, taking Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan, while Britain ruled India and feared a Russian march on it. Neither side wanted the other on its border, so Afghanistan became the buffer. Britain and the Afghan emir agreed the Durand Line in 1893, the thin Wakhan Corridor kept the two empires apart, and in 1907 they settled their rivalry by treaty.

dd-greatgame.q: How did Afghanistan's place between the two empires shape it?
a: It was split in half between Russia and Britain
It was annexed into British India in 1893
It became a buffer state whose borders the empires drew
It became a Russian protectorate in 1907
dd-greatgame.why: Neither empire wanted the other on its border, so Afghanistan became a buffer, with the Durand Line and Wakhan Corridor drawn between them.

dd-greatgame.p:
Including the protectorates of Bukhara and Khiva

Russia conquered the Kazakh steppe and then the khanates of Central Asia between the 1840s and 1880s, bringing its border to Afghanistan.

Russia took Tashkent in 1865 and Samarkand in 1868, and made Bukhara and Khiva protectorates.

Ruled by Britain directly or through princes

British strategists feared Russia might invade India through Afghanistan, though historians doubt Russia ever seriously planned it.

The Durand Line of 1893 split the Pashtun lands between Afghanistan and British India. Afghanistan has never formally accepted it as an international border.

dd-greatgame.q: Which Great Game legacy still causes tension today?
a: The Durand Line, which divides the Pashtun people between Afghanistan and Pakistan
British control of Afghan foreign policy
dd-greatgame.why: The Durand Line of 1893 split the Pashtun lands; Afghanistan has never formally accepted it, and it still strains relations with Pakistan.

dd-greatgame.p:
Buffer state; Britain controlled its foreign affairs

Britain fought wars here in 1839–42 and 1878–80, then left the emir to rule at home while it controlled his foreign policy. Afghanistan's borders were drawn by the two empires.

In 1839 a British-Indian army marched into Afghanistan and put Shah Shuja on the throne in place of Dost Mohammad. Afghans saw him as a foreign puppet, and in November 1841 Kabul rose in revolt; in December the British envoy, William Macnaghten, was killed at a meeting with Dost Mohammad's son Akbar Khan. On 6 January 1842 about 4,500 soldiers, most of them Indian sepoys, and some 12,000 camp followers set out in deep snow for Jalalabad, about 140 km away. Harassed through the passes, almost all were killed, captured or froze. Dr William Brydon reached Jalalabad on 13 January, famous as the sole survivor, though a few sepoys and one other European straggled in later and about 100 hostages were later freed.

By 1900 both empires had new worries. Russia had been shaken by defeat against Japan and revolution in 1905, and Britain was more alarmed by Germany's rising navy. In August 1907 they signed a convention that divided Persia into a Russian sphere in the north, a British sphere in the south-east and a neutral zone between, without consulting the Persians. Russia accepted that Afghanistan lay in Britain's sphere, and both agreed to leave Tibet alone. The deal ended the Great Game, a phrase made famous by Rudyard Kipling's novel Kim, and helped bring Britain, France and Russia together before World War I.

Three great powers sent armies into Afghanistan. Britain invaded in 1839 and lost almost a whole army retreating from Kabul in 1842. The Soviet Union invaded in 1979 to prop up a communist government and left in 1989. The United States and its allies invaded in 2001 after the 9/11 attacks and left in 2021, as the Taliban took back power. Each won the first battles easily and then struggled to hold the country.
Afghans fought each other as well as the invaders in every war. The Soviet war and the civil wars after it killed perhaps a million or more people and drove millions into exile.

dd-greatgame.q: Why did Britain worry so much about Russia's advance south?
a: It feared a Russian march through the passes on India
Russia threatened to invade Britain itself
dd-greatgame.why: Britain saw India as the jewel of its empire and feared a Russian advance through the mountain passes, though historians doubt Russia seriously planned it.

dd-greatgame.p:
Invaded 1839–42 and 1878–80; also part of the 2001 coalition

In January 1842 about 4,500 British and Indian soldiers and some 12,000 camp followers left Kabul in winter; almost all were killed, captured or died of cold. Britain fought again in 1878–80 and 1919.

Invaded 1979–89

The Soviet Union sent about 100,000 troops at its peak. About 15,000 Soviet soldiers died, and the last troops left on 15 February 1989.

Soviet columns entered Afghanistan from Termez, in Soviet Uzbekistan, in December 1979 and left the same way in 1989.

dd-greatgame.q: What has usually defeated invaders of Afghanistan, according to the chapter?
a: Losing the first battles on entering the country
Lack of roads into the country
Holding the country, not entering it
dd-greatgame.why: Each invader won the first battles easily; mountains, local loyalties, cross-border refuges and foreign-backed governments made holding the country the hard part.

dd-greatgame.p: Afghanistan is often called the 'graveyard of empires', but the cliché needs care. Many empires did rule it: Alexander the Great, the Mauryans, Persians and Mughals, and it was itself the base of great empires. Britain suffered disasters in 1842 and at Maiwand in 1880, yet gained what it wanted, control of Afghan foreign policy, until 1919. What has defeated invaders is holding the country, not entering it: high mountains, a society of strong local and tribal loyalties, fighters with refuges and suppliers across the borders, especially in Pakistan, and governments that depended on foreign money and looked foreign-backed. The Soviet Union and the US were not destroyed by Afghanistan, but their wars there were long, costly failures.

The Great Game fixed the borders of Afghanistan and Central Asia, and the Durand Line still divides the Pashtun people and strains relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan. The Soviet war fed the Cold War's end and produced the jihadist networks behind al-Qaeda. Twenty years of US-led war ended in 2021 with the Taliban back in power. Afghanistan has also given the world the much-debated label 'graveyard of empires'.

dd-greatgame.s: Afghanistan’s narrow Wakhan Corridor was created so that Russia and British India would not touch.

dd-israel.p: Britain ruled Palestine from 1917 to 1948, as Jewish immigration and Arab resistance grew. In 1947 the UN proposed partition; Israel declared independence in 1948 and won the war that followed, while about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled. In 1967 Israel captured the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza, and settlements followed.

steps: Zionism (from the 1890s) and Arab nationalism both claim the land.
The Balfour Declaration (1917) backs a Jewish homeland; Arabs were also promised independence.
Israel is founded; about 700,000 Palestinians flee or are expelled (the Nakba).
Israel takes the West Bank, Gaza, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights.

dd-israel.q: What did the Oslo Accords (1993) create?
dd-israel.why: Limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank and Gaza.

dd-israel.p: Palestinian uprisings began in 1987 and 2000, and the 1993 Oslo Accords created limited Palestinian self-rule but no state. Hamas took over Gaza in 2007. Its attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 began a war that devastated Gaza; a ceasefire began in October 2025, but killing continued into 2026.

Two national movements claim the same land. Zionism, born in Europe in the 1880s amid antisemitism, sought a Jewish homeland in the land of the Bible, and the Holocaust made the case urgent for many. Palestinian Arabs, whose families had lived there for generations, sought independence and saw Jewish immigration as a threat. Since 1967 the core disputes have been borders, Israeli settlements, security, Jerusalem and the fate of the refugees.

dd-israel.q: What happened in 1948 in the former British mandate of Palestine?
a: Britain annexed Palestine into its empire
Israel was founded and won the war; about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled
A single Arab-Jewish state was founded under UN rule
Jordan and Egypt divided the whole territory between them
dd-israel.why: Israel declared independence in May 1948 and defeated its neighbours' armies; Israelis call it the War of Independence, Palestinians the Nakba.

dd-israel.p: Britain took Palestine from the Ottoman Empire in 1917–18 and ruled it under a League of Nations mandate. In the 1917 Balfour Declaration it had promised to support a 'national home for the Jewish people' there, without prejudicing the 'civil and religious rights' of the Arab majority. Jewish immigration grew, especially after the Nazis came to power in Germany, and Arab opposition grew with it. Land east of the Jordan River became Transjordan, and Syria and Lebanon went to France.

Ruled by Britain, today Israel and the Palestinian territories

The 1922 census counted about 757,000 people, about 11% of them Jewish. By 1947 there were about 1.9 million, roughly a third Jewish.

Palestinian Arabs, Muslim and Christian, were the large majority. Their leaders rejected the Balfour Declaration and demanded independence and an end to Jewish immigration.

A British-backed emirate under Abdullah, set apart in 1921

Transjordan was part of the Palestine mandate but closed to Jewish settlement. It became independent as Jordan in 1946.

dd-israel.q: What did the 1993 Oslo Accords achieve?
a: Mutual recognition and limited Palestinian self-rule, but no state
A full peace treaty settling Jerusalem
dd-israel.why: Israel and the PLO recognised each other and agreed on interim self-rule, leaving borders, Jerusalem, refugees and settlements for talks that never succeeded.

dd-israel.p:
Syria and Lebanon

France ruled Syria as a mandate after crushing King Faisal's Arab kingdom in 1920. It became independent in 1946.

France created Greater Lebanon in 1920 with a Christian majority at the time. It became independent in 1943.

For Israelis, 1948 is the War of Independence: a state for a people just emerging from the Holocaust, defended against five Arab armies, at the cost of about 6,000 lives, around 1% of its Jewish population. For Palestinians it is the Nakba, the 'catastrophe': about 700,000 people, over half the Arab population, fled or were driven out, and Israel did not let them return. Historians, including Israeli 'new historians' using army archives from the 1980s, have shown that both flight from fear and deliberate expulsions occurred. In the decades after 1948, most of the roughly 800,000 Jews of the Arab world also left or were forced out, many to Israel. Today UNRWA registers about 6 million Palestinian refugees and their descendants.

At Oslo in 1993 Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization recognised each other and agreed on interim self-rule, leaving borders, Jerusalem, refugees and settlements for later. Those talks never succeeded. Each side blames the other. Many Israelis point to Palestinian rejection of offers in 2000 and 2008 and to suicide bombings in the 1990s and 2000s, which killed hundreds of Israelis. Many Palestinians point to the continued growth of settlements, checkpoints and military rule, which they say made a viable state impossible. Rabin's assassination in 1995, the bloody second intifada of 2000–05 and the split between Fatah in the West Bank and Hamas in Gaza after 2007 deepened mutual distrust.

In 1947 the UN proposed splitting Palestine into Jewish and Arab states. Jewish leaders accepted and Arab leaders rejected the plan, and civil war began. Israel declared independence in May 1948 and defeated the armies of its neighbours. About 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled. Jordan took the West Bank and Egypt ran Gaza. In June 1967 Israel captured both, now the Palestinian territories (Palestine), plus Sinai and the Golan Heights from Syria.

About 78% of the old mandate

Israel calls 1948 its War of Independence. About 6,000 Israelis, around 1% of the Jewish population, were killed. Israel took in Holocaust survivors and, over the next decades, most Jews from Arab countries.

dd-israel.q: What lies at the root of the conflict, as the chapter describes it?
a: A dispute between Britain and France over trade routes
Two national movements claiming the same land
A quarrel over oil fields in the Negev
dd-israel.why: Zionism sought a Jewish homeland in the land of the Bible, while Palestinian Arabs, long rooted there, sought independence and saw Jewish immigration as a threat.

dd-israel.p:
Held by Jordan and Egypt 1948–67; occupied by Israel since 1967

Palestinians call 1948 the Nakba, the 'catastrophe': hundreds of villages emptied and refugees were not allowed back. After 1967 Israel occupied the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza, and about 300,000 more Palestinians fled.

Sinai (returned to Egypt by 1982) and the Golan Heights

Egypt ran the Gaza Strip from 1948 to 1967 without annexing it. Israel took Sinai in 1967; Egypt won it back through the 1979 peace treaty.

Israel took the Golan Heights in 1967 and applied its law there in 1981. Most countries regard it as occupied Syrian land; the US recognised Israeli sovereignty in 2019.

dd-israel.q: Where did the core disputes stand in 2026?
a: They had been settled by a two-state treaty
They remained unresolved, with the West Bank still occupied and doubts about two states
Israel had withdrawn from all the territories it took in 1967
No country recognised a State of Palestine
dd-israel.why: Israel still occupied the West Bank, Gaza lay largely in ruins after the 2023 war, and polls showed many on both sides doubting a two-state solution.

dd-israel.p: On 7 October 2023 Hamas-led fighters broke into southern Israel, killing about 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and taking 251 hostages: the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. Israel answered with a bombing campaign and invasion aimed at destroying Hamas. By October 2026 more than 74,000 people had been killed in Gaza, by the count of its Hamas-run health ministry, and most of its 2 million people had been displaced, many repeatedly. In 2025 UN-backed experts declared famine in parts of Gaza, a finding Israel disputed. South Africa accused Israel of genocide at the International Court of Justice, and in 2024 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Prime Minister Netanyahu, his former defence minister and a Hamas military commander. Israel rejects the accusations as baseless.

Egypt made peace with Israel in 1979 and Jordan in 1994. The 1993 Oslo Accords set up a Palestinian Authority, but no Palestinian state followed. In 2020 the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Morocco established ties with Israel. On 7 October 2023 Hamas attacked Israel from Gaza, starting a devastating war that spread to Lebanon and, in 2024–2026, to direct fighting with Iran. A Gaza ceasefire began in October 2025, but violence continued.

About 10 million people live in Israel, a fifth of them Arab citizens. Israel says its Gaza war aimed to destroy Hamas and free the hostages, all of whom were returned, alive or dead, by January 2026.

West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza

More than 74,000 people were killed in Gaza by October 2026, by the count of its Hamas-run health ministry, which the UN has found broadly reliable; Israel says many were fighters. Israel still held over half the Strip.

dd-israel.q: Why was the 1967 war a turning point?
a: It ended with a Palestinian state on the 1947 borders
It returned Gaza and the West Bank to Britain
It led Egypt and Jordan to annex Israel
Israel captured the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza, and settlements followed
dd-israel.why: Since 1967 the core disputes have been borders, settlements, security, Jerusalem and the refugees, all tied to the territories Israel captured.

dd-israel.p:
Egypt 1979, Jordan 1994

Egypt became the first Arab state to make peace with Israel, at Camp David in 1978–79, and regained Sinai. President Anwar Sadat was assassinated in 1981, partly over the treaty.

Jordan signed a peace treaty in 1994. Many of its citizens are of Palestinian origin, and it is the custodian of Muslim holy sites in Jerusalem.

A US-brokered ceasefire began on 10 October 2025. All living hostages were freed within days in exchange for about 2,000 Palestinian prisoners and detainees, and the remains of the last hostage, Ran Gvili, were recovered in January 2026. But the plan's second stage stalled: Hamas had not disarmed despite talks on a phased handover of weapons, an international stabilisation force was only beginning to form, and Israel kept control of over half of Gaza. Gaza's health ministry counted over 1,500 more deaths after the truce by October 2026. In the West Bank, settlement building and settler violence rose sharply, according to the UN. Polls showed many Israelis and Palestinians doubting that a two-state solution could still work.

In October 2026 Israel still occupied the West Bank, where over 500,000 settlers lived, plus over 200,000 in East Jerusalem; most of the world regards the settlements as illegal under international law, which Israel disputes. About 157 of 193 UN members recognise a State of Palestine. Gaza lay largely in ruins, Hamas had not disarmed, and Israel held over half the Strip. In Israel's 27 October 2026 election, neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition won a majority.

Oslo Accords: Israel and the PLO recognise each other

A Gaza ceasefire begins on 10 October

dd-holocaust.p: After taking power in 1933, the Nazis stripped Germany's Jews of their rights, property and citizenship, and in the Kristallnacht pogrom of 1938 burned hundreds of synagogues. When Germany conquered Poland in 1939, it forced Jews into sealed ghettos. From June 1941 German units and local collaborators shot Jews across the occupied Soviet lands.

dd-holocaust.h: How it happened, step by step
steps: Nazis blamed Jews for Germany’s problems.
The Nuremberg Laws (1935) stripped Jews of citizenship.
From 1939 Jews were confined; from 1941 mass shootings in the East.
From 1942 industrial killing at Auschwitz, Treblinka and others.

dd-holocaust.h: Jews murdered, two-thirds of Europe’s Jews
dd-holocaust.p: Millions of others were also killed: Roma, disabled people, Poles, Soviet prisoners and gay men.

a: Laws that removed Jews’ citizenship and rights
dd-holocaust.why: Passed in 1935; the trials came in 1945–46.

dd-holocaust.p: From 1942 trains carried Jews from all over Europe to death camps in occupied Poland, such as Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau, where most were gassed on arrival. By 1945 about six million Jews had been murdered, two in every three in Europe. Roma, disabled people, Polish civilians, Soviet prisoners of war and others were also persecuted and killed.

Hatred of Jews had deep roots in European history, and in the 19th century it took a new, racial form. Nazi ideology made it central: Hitler saw Jews as a racial enemy to blame for Germany's defeat and for communism. Persecution grew step by step, and war, conquest and the invasion of the Soviet Union turned it into mass murder. Historians debate how far it followed a plan, but it needed the work of many thousands of officials, soldiers and collaborators, and the indifference of many more.

a: The wartime bombing of German cities by the Allies
The forced expulsion of Germans from eastern Europe after 1945
Nazi Germany's murder of about six million Jews, two in every three in Europe
A famine in occupied Poland caused by crop failure
dd-holocaust.why: By 1945 about six million Jews had been murdered; Roma, disabled people, Polish civilians, Soviet prisoners of war and others were also persecuted and killed.

dd-holocaust.p: When Hitler took power in 1933, about 523,000 Jews lived in Germany. The Nazis drove them out of jobs, schools and public life, and the 1935 Nuremberg Laws took away their citizenship. After the Kristallnacht pogrom of November 1938, Jews in Germany and annexed Austria tried desperately to leave. About 400,000 escaped by 1939, many to the United States, Palestine and Britain, but most countries limited how many they would admit.

Including annexed Austria and the occupied Czech lands

In 1933 Jews were less than 1% of Germany's people. By the end of 1939 about 202,000 remained, and in October 1941 the Nazis banned emigration.

After the Anschluss of March 1938, Vienna's Jews were humiliated in the streets and robbed. About 117,000 left Austria by September 1939.

Main destinations, though all set strict limits

About 95,000 Jewish refugees from the German Reich reached the US by 1939. Strict quotas held numbers down: by June 1939, 309,000 had applied for 27,000 places.

About 40,000 refugees reached Britain by 1939. After Kristallnacht the Kindertransport brought about 10,000 Jewish children, most of whom never saw their parents again.

dd-holocaust.q: How did the world respond legally after the war?
a: It declared that no individual could be held responsible
It handed all cases to German courts alone
It agreed that wartime crimes could not be tried
Nazi leaders were tried at Nuremberg, and genocide was banned by UN convention
dd-holocaust.why: Leading Nazis were tried at Nuremberg, and the word 'genocide' was coined and banned by a UN convention in 1948, though many perpetrators were never punished.

dd-holocaust.p:
Needed no visa

Shanghai, partly under Japanese control, required no entry visa, and more than 18,000 Jews from the German Reich found refuge there.

The Nazis aimed to murder every Jew within their reach, and about six million were killed, including about 1.5 million children. They also persecuted others they saw as racially or politically undesirable. According to the US Holocaust Memorial Museum, they and their allies killed at least 250,000, and possibly up to 500,000, Roma and Sinti; 250,000–300,000 disabled people; about 3.3 million Soviet prisoners of war, mostly through starvation; and about 1.8 million non-Jewish Polish civilians. Croatia's Ustaša regime murdered over 310,000 Serbs. Tens of thousands of German political opponents and people labelled 'asocial' or 'criminal' died, as did about 1,700 Jehovah's Witnesses, hundreds or possibly thousands of gay men, and Black Germans.

The murder grew out of earlier crimes. From 1939 the Nazi 'euthanasia' programme killed disabled patients in gas chambers, and its staff later ran the death camps. About 2 million Jews were shot near their homes, often at pits dug at the edge of town. Gassing was then industrialised: at Treblinka, Sobibor and Bełżec, staffed by a few dozen SS men and around 100 auxiliary guards each, almost everyone was killed within hours of arrival. Railways, police, civil servants and companies all played a part. The Nazis tried to hide the crime, using code words such as 'resettlement' and later digging up and burning bodies, but they left enormous written evidence.

After invading Poland in 1939, Germany forced its Jews into sealed ghettos, where hunger and disease killed hundreds of thousands. When Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, mobile killing units, the Einsatzgruppen, with police battalions and local collaborators, shot Jews town by town across Lithuania, Belarus and Ukraine. About 2 million Jews were murdered in mass shootings. In January 1942 officials met at Wannsee to coordinate the murder of all Europe's Jews.

Hundreds of ghettos; from 1941–42 the death camps

Poland had Europe's largest Jewish community, about 3.3 million. In the ghettos people were crammed in, starved and used for forced labour, and about nine in ten Polish Jews were eventually murdered.

dd-holocaust.q: What role did antisemitism play in Nazi ideology?
a: It was central: Hitler saw Jews as a racial enemy
It was a minor issue the Nazis rarely mentioned
It was introduced only after the war began
It applied only to Jews outside Germany
dd-holocaust.why: Hatred of Jews had deep roots and took a racial form in the 1800s; Nazi ideology made it central, blaming Jews for Germany's defeat and for communism.

dd-holocaust.p:
Soviet lands invaded in 1941

About nine in ten of Lithuania's Jews were murdered, most shot in 1941 by German units and Lithuanian collaborators, many at Ponary outside Vilnius.

Most of Riga's Jews were shot in the Rumbula forest in late 1941, along with Jews deported there from Germany.

From October 1941 its Jews were deported east

From October 1941 Jews from Germany, Austria and Prague were deported to ghettos in Łódź, Riga, Minsk and Kaunas. Many were shot soon after arrival.

dd-holocaust.q: How is the Holocaust remembered and reflected today?
a: It shaped human rights law and Germany's identity, and is remembered each 27 January
It is remembered only in Israel
It is no longer taught or commemorated
Remembrance is limited to a single museum in Berlin
dd-holocaust.why: It shaped human rights law and Germany's postwar identity, and the UN marks 27 January, the day Auschwitz was liberated, as Holocaust Remembrance Day.

dd-holocaust.p: Jews resisted in many ways. In the Warsaw ghetto, historian Emanuel Ringelblum's secret team buried an archive in milk cans so the world would know, and in April 1943 young fighters held off German troops for nearly a month. Prisoners revolted at Treblinka, Sobibor and Auschwitz, and thousands of Jews fought as partisans in the forests of Belarus and Lithuania. Some non-Jews risked death to help. Danes ferried Jews to Sweden, the Japanese diplomat Chiune Sugihara issued over 2,000 transit visas, and Oskar Schindler protected about 1,200 workers. Yad Vashem has honoured more than 28,000 such rescuers as 'Righteous Among the Nations', while noting that most people did nothing.

From 1942 trains carried Jews from across Europe to death camps that Germany built in occupied Poland. At Treblinka, Sobibor and Bełżec almost everyone was gassed on arrival. At Auschwitz-Birkenau, the largest, SS doctors chose some for forced labour and sent the rest to the gas chambers. Jews were deported from France, the Netherlands, Greece, Italy and, in 1944, Hungary. In Denmark and Bulgaria, most Jews were saved.
The six death camps, Chełmno, Bełżec, Sobibor, Treblinka, Majdanek and Auschwitz-Birkenau, were all built by Germany in occupied Poland. About 2.7 million Jews were murdered in them.

Most sent east by train

About 165,000 German Jews were murdered. Many were sent first to the Theresienstadt ghetto, near Prague, or straight to the ghettos and camps of the east.

In 1942 the Slovak state handed about 58,000 of its Jews to Germany for deportation, and paid for each one.

dd-holocaust.q: How did persecution in the 1930s become mass murder?
a: It was ordered all at once on the day Hitler took power
It grew step by step, and war and conquest turned it into mass murder
It was carried out by a handful of officials acting alone
It began only after Germany's surrender in 1945
dd-holocaust.why: From laws stripping rights to ghettos, then shootings from 1941 and death camps from 1942; it needed many thousands of officials, soldiers and collaborators.

dd-holocaust.p:
In October 1943 Danes ferried about 7,200 Jews across the sea to neutral Sweden, saving almost all of Denmark's Jews.

Protests in March 1943 stopped the deportation of Bulgaria's own 48,000 Jews, and they survived. Bulgaria did deport over 11,000 Jews from the lands it occupied.

Soviet troops reached Majdanek in July 1944 and Auschwitz on 27 January 1945. British and American soldiers who entered Bergen-Belsen, Buchenwald and Dachau in April 1945 found thousands of starving prisoners and unburied dead, and filmed them as evidence. The Nuremberg trials of 1945–46 judged leading Nazis, and Israel tried Adolf Eichmann, an organiser of the deportations, in 1961. Many perpetrators were never punished. Israel's Yad Vashem, founded in 1953, collects the names of the murdered, and the UN made 27 January International Holocaust Remembrance Day in 2005. Many European countries now ban Holocaust denial, and many Roma mark 2 August, when in 1944 the SS murdered almost 2,900 Roma and Sinti left in the 'Gypsy family camp' at Auschwitz-Birkenau.

Survivors faced a destroyed world; many could not go home, and hundreds of thousands moved to Israel, the United States and elsewhere. Nazi leaders were tried at Nuremberg, and the word 'genocide' was coined to name the crime, banned by a UN convention in 1948. The Holocaust shaped human rights law and Germany's postwar identity, and it is remembered every 27 January, the day Auschwitz was liberated.

The Holocaust led to the Genocide Convention and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), and strengthened the case for the State of Israel. 'Never again' remains a guiding principle of international law.

dd-pacific.p: Japan, which had seized Manchuria in 1931, went to full-scale war with China in July 1937, took the capital Nanjing and massacred many of its people. In December 1941 it attacked the US fleet at Pearl Harbor and, within six months, conquered the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore, Burma and the Dutch East Indies. At Midway in June 1942 the US Navy sank four Japanese carriers.

steps: Japan wanted Asian resources, conquering Manchuria and invading China.
In 1941 the US cut off oil; Japan had 18 months of reserves.
Attack Pearl Harbor, seize South-East Asia’s oil, and negotiate.
It united America for total war.
Four Japanese carriers sunk; the turning point.
Skip strongholds; take islands for airfields.
Bloody battles within bomber range of Japan.

dd-pacific.p: From Guadalcanal onwards, American forces fought island by island towards Japan, while bombers burned its cities. After the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet attack on Manchuria, Japan surrendered in August 1945.

dd-pacific.q: What was the course of Japan's war in Asia and the Pacific?
a: Japan defended its home islands but never attacked abroad
Japan conquered vast lands by 1942, was driven back, and surrendered in 1945
Japan and the US fought briefly in 1941, then made peace
China invaded and occupied Japan in 1937
dd-pacific.why: After war with China and Pearl Harbor, Japan conquered much of Southeast Asia, but was driven back from Midway on and surrendered in August 1945.

dd-pacific.p: Japan's military-dominated government sought an empire in Asia for raw materials, markets and security, and the war in China became a costly stalemate. When Japan moved into French Indochina in 1941, the US, Britain and the Netherlands froze its assets and cut off its oil, most of which came from the US. Rather than give up China, Japan's leaders gambled on seizing Southeast Asia's oil and crippling the US Navy, hoping America would accept a negotiated peace.

Japan invaded China in 1937. After striking Pearl Harbor in December 1941 it conquered the Philippines, Malaya, Indonesia and Burma in six months. The tide turned at Midway in June 1942. US forces then fought island by island towards Japan, from Guadalcanal to Okinawa, and the war ended after the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.

dd-pacific.q: What pushed Japan to attack the US in December 1941?
a: An oil embargo after it moved into Indochina, and a refusal to leave China
A Soviet alliance with the United States against Japan
dd-pacific.why: The US, Britain and the Netherlands cut off its oil; rather than give up China, Japan gambled on seizing Southeast Asia's oil and crippling the US fleet.

dd-pacific.p: About 2.5–3 million Japanese died. US firebombing burned most big cities, and a single raid on Tokyo in March 1945 killed perhaps 100,000 people.

Taiwan, Korea and the League of Nations mandate islands

A Japanese colony since 1895 and a base for the 1941–42 invasions to the south.

A Japanese colony since 1910. Koreans were drafted as labourers and soldiers, and many women were forced into military brothels as so-called 'comfort women'.

dd-pacific.q: How did the Pacific War reshape Asia beyond Japan?
a: European colonial rule was restored for good
Korea was divided, and independence movements in Southeast Asia gained pace
The atomic bomb was never used again or developed further
dd-pacific.why: Korea was split at the 38th parallel, China's civil war resumed, and Japan's defeat of European rulers speeded independence across Southeast Asia.

dd-pacific.p:
Including the puppet state of Manchukuo and French Indochina

Japan drove the British out of Burma in 1942. Allied prisoners and Asian labourers built the Burma Railway, where many tens of thousands died.

British Malaya fell in ten weeks. Singapore surrendered on 15 February 1942, with about 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops taken prisoner.

Japan's leaders believed their country needed an empire to survive as a great power, and the army increasingly controlled policy. After seizing Manchuria in 1931 and invading China in 1937, Japan found itself bogged down in a war it could not finish. When it occupied southern French Indochina in July 1941, the US, Britain and the Netherlands answered with an oil embargo, and Japan had reserves of oil for perhaps 18 months to two years. The US demanded withdrawal from China. Japan's leaders chose war, planning to seize the oil of the Dutch East Indies and knock out the US fleet, though some, including Admiral Yamamoto, warned that Japan could not win a long war.

Six months after Pearl Harbor, Yamamoto tried to lure the remaining US carriers into a trap near Midway Atoll. But American codebreakers had read enough of Japan's naval code to learn the plan, and Admiral Nimitz placed three carriers in ambush. On 4 June, after waves of US attacks failed, dive bombers caught the Japanese carriers while they were refuelling and rearming their planes in the hangars below, and set three ablaze in minutes; a fourth was hit later that day and sank the next morning. The US lost the carrier Yorktown. Japan lost four fleet carriers and many skilled aircrew, and never again took the offensive in the central Pacific.

Japan surrendered on 15 August 1945 and signed on 2 September. The US occupied Japan until 1952. Korea was split at the 38th parallel between Soviet and US zones, and Taiwan came under the Republic of China. In Southeast Asia, nationalists who had seen European rulers beaten declared independence in Indonesia and Vietnam, and colonial empires there broke up within a few years.
Under General MacArthur, Japan got a new constitution in 1947 that kept the emperor as a symbol and renounced war. The occupation ended in 1952.

dd-pacific.q: Why did Japan seek an empire in Asia?
a: To spread democracy across the region
To free European colonies at the request of their peoples
To gain raw materials, markets and security for a great power
To protect China from a Soviet invasion
dd-pacific.why: Japan's military-dominated government sought an empire for raw materials, markets and security, and the war in China became a costly stalemate.

dd-pacific.p:
Became North Korea in 1948

Soviet troops took the surrender north of the 38th parallel and backed Kim Il Sung, who led North Korea from 1948.

Became South Korea in 1948

US troops took the surrender south of the 38th parallel. Rival states formed in 1948, and the Korean War followed in 1950.

dd-pacific.q: What happened to Japan after its defeat?
a: It kept its empire but lost its emperor
It was divided between the US and the Soviet Union
It became a communist state allied to China
It was occupied by the US and rebuilt as a pacifist democracy
dd-pacific.why: Japan lost its empire, was occupied by the US until 1952 and, under a new constitution renouncing war, became a democracy and US ally.

dd-pacific.p: In 1945 US leaders faced a planned invasion of Japan, with casualty estimates that varied widely and remain debated. President Truman and his advisers argued that the bombs saved lives by ending the war quickly. Since the 1960s some historians have argued that Japan was close to surrender, that alternatives such as letting it keep its emperor or waiting for the Soviet attack might have worked, and that impressing the Soviet Union was a motive. Others reply that Japan's leaders were still divided after both bombs, and the emperor himself had to break the deadlock. Many scholars now see the bombs and the Soviet declaration of war together as forcing the surrender.

The war killed perhaps 20 million or more people across Asia and the Pacific, most of them Chinese; estimates vary widely. Japan lost its empire, was occupied by the US and rebuilt as a pacifist democracy and US ally. Korea was divided, China's civil war resumed, and the defeat of European colonial rulers by Japan speeded independence across Southeast Asia. The atomic bombs opened the nuclear age.

dd-vietnam.p: In 1945 Ho Chi Minh declared Vietnam independent, and his communist-led Viet Minh fought France until its defeat at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. The Geneva Accords split the country at the 17th parallel, and the promised elections never came. In the South, communist guerrillas, the Viet Cong, rose against the US-backed government, supplied from the North along the Ho Chi Minh Trail.

l: North Vietnam and the Viet Cong
Communist, led by Ho Chi Minh
Supplied by the USSR and China
Guerrilla war; Ho Chi Minh Trail

hl: The trail ran through Laos and Cambodia

a: If one country fell to communism, its neighbours would follow

dd-vietnam.p: From 1965 the United States sent combat troops and bombed the North, peaking at over 540,000 soldiers. The 1968 Tet Offensive turned American opinion against the war. US forces left after the 1973 Paris Peace Accords, and in April 1975 Saigon fell to the North.

dd-vietnam.q: How did the Vietnam War end?
a: South Vietnam conquered the North in 1973
The country stayed divided under a UN peace force
US forces left in 1973, and Saigon fell to the North in 1975
dd-vietnam.why: After the 1973 Paris Peace Accords US forces left, and in April 1975 Saigon fell; Vietnam was reunited under communist rule in 1976.

dd-vietnam.p: For Vietnamese communists this was a war for independence and unification, first against France and then against the US-backed South. For the United States it was a front in the Cold War: leaders believed that if South Vietnam fell, communism would spread across Southeast Asia like falling dominoes. Each president feared being blamed for 'losing' Vietnam, so commitment grew step by step.

France ruled Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia as French Indochina from the 1880s. In 1946 Ho Chi Minh's communist-led Viet Minh began a war for independence, and in May 1954 it defeated the French at Dien Bien Phu. The Geneva Accords then split Vietnam at the 17th parallel: a communist North and a Western-backed South. Nationwide elections promised for 1956 never took place.

dd-vietnam.q: What happened in the region after 1975?
a: Laos and Cambodia also became communist, and many 'boat people' fled Vietnam
Vietnam was split again at the 17th parallel
dd-vietnam.why: Laos and Cambodia became communist in 1975, the Khmer Rouge killed a vast share of Cambodians, and hundreds of thousands fled Vietnam by sea.

dd-vietnam.p:
Ruled by France from the 1880s to 1954

Vietnam fought France from 1946 to 1954. The Geneva Accords split it at the 17th parallel, and about 800,000–1 million people, mostly Catholics, moved south.

Laos became fully independent in 1953–54. Its civil war between royalists and the communist Pathet Lao became bound up with Vietnam's.

In 1954 President Eisenhower compared Southeast Asia to a row of dominoes: if one country fell to communism, the rest would follow. That 'domino theory' guided four presidents. The US funded France's war, then backed the South Vietnamese leader Ngo Dinh Diem and sent military advisers, about 16,000 by 1963. In August 1964 North Vietnamese boats attacked the destroyer USS Maddox in the Gulf of Tonkin. A second attack reported two days later almost certainly never happened, as a later US National Security Agency study concluded. Even so, Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution almost unanimously, letting President Johnson wage war without a declaration. Marines landed at Da Nang in March 1965.

Communist guerrillas, the Viet Cong, fought to topple South Vietnam, supplied by North Vietnam down the Ho Chi Minh Trail through Laos and Cambodia. From 1965 the United States sent combat troops and bombed the North, with over 500,000 soldiers there by 1968. American forces left in 1973, and on 30 April 1975 North Vietnamese tanks rolled into Saigon.

North and South, divided at the 17th parallel until 1975

About 58,000 Americans died. Estimates of Vietnamese dead, soldiers and civilians, range from under 1 million to over 3 million; Vietnam's government gave about 3 million in 1995.

dd-vietnam.q: Why did the United States commit troops to Vietnam?
a: It feared communism would spread across Southeast Asia like falling dominoes
France asked it to take over Indochina as a colony
North Vietnam had invaded the United States
dd-vietnam.why: US leaders saw Vietnam as a Cold War front; the 'domino theory' guided four presidents, and each feared being blamed for 'losing' Vietnam.

dd-vietnam.p:
Neutral on paper, drawn into the war

The Trail ran mainly through eastern Laos. The US dropped over 2 million tons of bombs on Laos in 1964–73, and unexploded bombs still kill and injure people.

The US secretly bombed Trail bases in Cambodia from 1969 and invaded briefly in 1970. The war helped the Khmer Rouge take power in April 1975.

On 30–31 January 1968, during the Tet lunar new year truce, communist forces attacked more than 100 towns and cities across South Vietnam at once. Commandos even got inside the US embassy compound in Saigon. In Hue the fighting lasted nearly a month, and communist forces killed thousands of civilians there. Militarily the offensive failed: the Viet Cong lost tens of thousands of fighters and did not spark the uprising they hoped for. Politically it was a turning point. American leaders had said the war was being won, and viewers now saw it on television. On 31 March President Johnson announced he would not seek re-election and began moves towards peace talks.

dd-vietnam.q: How do Vietnam and the US relate today?
a: They restored relations in 1995 and are now trading partners
They have had no contact since 1975
dd-vietnam.why: Vietnam opened its economy from 1986, restored relations with the US in 1995, and is now a fast-growing trading partner.

dd-vietnam.h: Who sent troops, and who backed Hanoi, 1965–1973
dd-vietnam.p: The United States persuaded allies to send troops: South Korea sent the most, with up to 50,000 at a time, followed by Thailand, Australia, the Philippines and New Zealand. North Vietnam fought with weapons, aid and advisers from the Soviet Union and China, though the two communist giants were bitter rivals by then.
About 2.7 million Americans served in Vietnam and about 58,000 died. At the peak, in 1969, over 540,000 were there at once.

Fighting alongside South Vietnam and the US

South Korea sent about 320,000 troops in all, up to 50,000 at a time, and about 5,000 died. The US paid generously, which helped South Korea's economy.

About 60,000 Australians served, many of them conscripts, and about 520 died. The war divided Australia as it did America.

dd-vietnam.q: Why was the 1968 Tet Offensive a turning point?
a: It won the war for the Viet Cong outright
It led China to send troops to fight the US
It ended the bombing of Laos
Though a military failure, it turned American opinion against the war
dd-vietnam.why: The Viet Cong lost heavily, but leaders had said the war was being won; after Tet, Johnson stood down and moved towards peace talks.

dd-vietnam.p:
Split into North and South until 1975

South Vietnam's own army lost an estimated 200,000–250,000 dead. After 1975 the country was reunited as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam.

Vietnam was the first 'television war', and it split America. Young men were drafted, and many saw the system as unfair, because student deferments shielded the better off. Protests grew from campus teach-ins in 1965 to marches of hundreds of thousands. News of the My Lai massacre broke in 1969; only one officer, Lieutenant William Calley, was convicted. In May 1970 National Guard troops shot dead four students at Kent State University in Ohio. The 1971 Pentagon Papers showed that officials had long doubted the war could be won. The draft ended in 1973, and Congress passed the War Powers Resolution to limit presidents' power to make war.

Vietnam was reunited under communist rule in 1976, and Laos and Cambodia also became communist in 1975, where the Khmer Rouge then killed a vast share of Cambodia's people. Hundreds of thousands of 'boat people' fled Vietnam. In the US the defeat bred distrust of government and caution about foreign wars. Vietnam opened its economy from 1986, restored relations with the US in 1995, and is now a fast-growing trading partner.
Vietnam was the first war the US clearly lost. It made Americans wary of foreign wars for decades, and Vietnam, still communist, is now a fast-growing economy and a US partner against China.

dd-berlin.p: In 1945 the victors split Germany and its capital, Berlin, into four zones. In June 1948 the Soviet Union blockaded West Berlin, and for eleven months American and British planes kept its two million people alive. In 1949 Germany became two states, and over the next twelve years well over 2.5 million East Germans fled west, most through Berlin's open sector border.

steps: Berlin sat inside East Germany but was split four ways.
About 3.5 million East Germans fled West through Berlin by 1961.
Overnight, barbed wire, then concrete, sealed West Berlin.
About 140 people died trying to cross.

dd-berlin.q: Why did East Germany build the Berlin Wall?
a: To stop its people fleeing to the West
To mark a new border with Poland
dd-berlin.why: It called it an "anti-fascist protection wall".

dd-berlin.p: On 13 August 1961 East Germany sealed it, and the Berlin Wall split the city for 28 years. In 1989, as communism weakened across Eastern Europe, East Germans fled through Hungary and protested in the streets. On 9 November the Wall opened, and on 3 October 1990 Germany reunited.

dd-berlin.q: What happened to Berlin on 13 August 1961?
a: The Soviet Union began blockading West Berlin
East Germany sealed the border, and the Wall went up
Germany was divided into four occupation zones
The Western allies flew coal into the city
dd-berlin.why: East Germany sealed West Berlin's border with barbed wire, soon replaced by concrete, and the Wall split the city for 28 years.

dd-berlin.p: Berlin was split because the wartime allies could not agree on Germany's future, and it sat deep inside the Soviet zone. The blockade was Stalin's attempt to push the West out. The Wall was built because East Germany was losing its young and skilled workers to the richer West. It fell because Mikhail Gorbachev would no longer use Soviet troops to prop up communist rulers, and East Germans, by fleeing and protesting, forced the issue.

After Germany's surrender in May 1945, the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union each occupied a zone of Germany. Berlin lay about 160 km inside the Soviet zone, but it too was split into four sectors. Germany's lands east of the Oder and Neisse rivers went to Poland. In 1949 the western zones became West Germany and the Soviet zone East Germany.

dd-berlin.q: What did reunification in 1990 mean for eastern Germany?
a: West Germany adopted the East's economic system
Berlin stayed divided as a free city
Eastern wages and jobs caught up within a year
It joined the West's democracy and economy, at great cost
dd-berlin.why: The East was merged into West Germany's democracy and economy; it cost a great deal, and eastern wages and jobs took decades to catch up.

dd-berlin.p:
Four zones, and four sectors in Berlin

The four powers ran Germany jointly through the Allied Control Council in Berlin, but they soon split. West Germany was founded in May 1949 and communist East Germany in October.
The Soviet Union held the largest zone in the east and the eastern sector of Berlin. It took heavy reparations, dismantling factories and shipping them east.
The US held the south, including Bavaria, and the south-western sector of Berlin. From 1947 its Marshall Plan aid helped rebuild western Germany.

The first barrier, on 13 August 1961, was barbed wire, soon replaced by concrete. By the 1980s the border around West Berlin, about 155 km long, had two walls with a 'death strip' between them, lit at night and watched from about 300 towers, with dogs, trip wires and anti-vehicle trenches. East German guards had orders to stop escapes, if necessary by shooting. In October 1961 American and Soviet tanks faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie for about a day. In 1962 eighteen-year-old Peter Fechter was shot and bled to death in the strip in full view of West Berliners. According to the Berlin Wall Memorial, at least 140 people were killed at the Wall or died in connection with it.

In June 1948, after the western powers launched a new currency, the Soviet Union cut road, rail and canal links to West Berlin, hoping to force them out. Instead the United States and Britain supplied the city's two million people by air. Over eleven months planes flew in food, medicine and, above all, coal along three air corridors. In May 1949 Stalin gave up the blockade.

West Berlin was an island inside the Soviet zone

West Berlin's 2 million people lived on rations. On Easter 1949 crews delivered nearly 13,000 tons in 24 hours, and the Soviets lifted the blockade on 12 May.

dd-berlin.q: Why did East Germany build the Berlin Wall?
a: To keep out Western armies after the airlift
To protect Berlin from a NATO invasion
It was losing young and skilled workers who fled west
The four occupying powers agreed it would end the blockade
dd-berlin.why: Well over 2.5 million East Germans had fled west by 1961, most through Berlin's open border, draining the East of its young and skilled people.

dd-berlin.p:
The US and Britain, with crews from the Commonwealth

The US Air Force flew about three quarters of the cargo. About 278,000 flights in all brought about 2.3 million tons, nearly two thirds of it coal.

The RAF and British civil airlines flew about a quarter of the cargo, much of it from bases around Hamburg and Hanover.

Supplied its own garrison and built Tegel airport

France had few transport planes, but its engineers built Tegel airport in its sector, then blew up a Soviet-controlled radio mast that stood in the way.

dd-berlin.q: What marked the milestone Berlin passed in February 2018?
a: The Wall was finally demolished completely
The Wall had been gone longer than it stood
Parliament moved back into the Reichstag
The Stasi files were opened to the public
dd-berlin.why: The Wall stood for 28 years; by February 2018 it had been gone for longer, and only short stretches survive as memorials.

dd-berlin.p: Over 5,000 people escaped across the Wall, by many accounts. Two days after the border closed, the young guard Conrad Schumann jumped over the barbed wire, a moment caught in a famous photograph. In the first months people leapt from windows of houses on Bernauer Strasse, whose fronts stood on the border line, until they were bricked up. Students dug tunnels from the West: in October 1964, 57 people crawled to freedom through 'Tunnel 57'. Others hid in car boots, used forged passports or crashed through checkpoints. In February 1989 Chris Gueffroy became the last person shot dead trying to cross; weeks later, Winfried Freudenberg died when his gas balloon crashed in West Berlin.

By 1961 over 2.5 million people had fled East Germany, most through Berlin. On 13 August its government sealed the border with barbed wire, then a wall. The Wall stood for 28 years. In 1989, with Mikhail Gorbachev's Soviet Union no longer willing to use force, Hungary opened its border to Austria, East Germans crowded embassies in Czechoslovakia and mass protests swept East Germany. On 9 November the Wall opened.

West and East Germany, 1949–1990

The Wall ran about 155 km around West Berlin. At least 140 people were killed at it or died in connection with it, according to the Berlin Wall Memorial. Germany reunited on 3 October 1990.

Where East Germans fled that summer and autumn

Hungary's reformers began removing the fence on the Austrian border in May 1989 and, on 11 September, let East Germans leave freely. Tens of thousands did.

East Germans climbed into the West German embassy in Prague. Sealed trains took them west through East Germany, a humiliation for its rulers.

dd-berlin.q: Why did the Wall fall in 1989 rather than earlier?
a: Gorbachev would not use Soviet troops, and East Germans fled and protested
West Germany invaded and forced the border open
East Germany's leaders voted to reunite with the West
The United States paid the Soviet Union to remove it
dd-berlin.why: Gorbachev's Soviet Union no longer propped up communist rulers by force, and East Germans fleeing through Hungary and protesting at home forced the issue.

dd-berlin.p: Neutral Austria was the gateway west. East Germans who crossed from Hungary travelled on to West Germany, which treated them as its own citizens.

On 9 November 1989 the East German politburo member Günter Schabowski announced new travel rules at a live press conference. Asked when they took effect, he looked at his notes and said 'immediately, without delay', though they were meant for the next day. Thousands of East Berliners went to the crossings. At Bornholmer Strasse, the officer in charge, Harald Jäger, faced a growing crowd and no clear orders, and at about 11.30 pm he opened the gate. Others followed. That night Berliners climbed onto the Wall at the Brandenburg Gate, and soon people were chipping at it with hammers. Nobody had decided to end the Wall; a mistake and the crowds did it.

Reunification merged the East into West Germany's democracy and economy, at great cost; eastern wages and jobs took decades to catch up. Berlin became the capital again, and parliament moved into the rebuilt Reichstag in 1999. The Stasi's secret police files were opened to the people they had watched. Since February 2018 the Wall has been gone for longer than it stood, and only short stretches remain as memorials.

dd-partition.p: By 1946 Britain wanted to leave India quickly, but the Congress party, which sought one united India, and the Muslim League, which demanded Pakistan, could not agree. Communal riots spread from Calcutta in August 1946. The last viceroy, Lord Mountbatten, brought the handover forward to August 1947, and British India was split: Pakistan became independent on 14 August, India on 15 August.

steps: Congress wanted one India; the Muslim League feared Hindu-majority rule.
Britain, broke after WW2, left in 1947, a year early.
Drawn in five weeks by a lawyer who had never been to India.
15 million moved; up to 1 million were killed.

dd-partition.q: What happened to East Pakistan in 1971?

dd-partition.p: The new borders through Punjab and Bengal were announced two days later. Hindus and Sikhs fled east and Muslims west, and both sides carried out massacres. In October fighting began over Kashmir, and in January 1948 Gandhi was assassinated by a Hindu nationalist.

dd-partition.q: What happened to British India in August 1947?
a: It became one united, independent India
It was split into two independent states, India and Pakistan
Britain handed Punjab and Bengal to Pakistan alone
It became independent as three states, including Bangladesh
dd-partition.why: Pakistan became independent on 14 August and India on 15 August, with Punjab and Bengal cut in two by new borders.

dd-partition.p: Under British rule, Hindu and Muslim politics drifted apart; separate electorates for Muslims from 1909 hardened the divide, and historians debate how far Britain encouraged it. The Muslim League under Muhammad Ali Jinnah argued that Muslims were a separate nation who would be dominated in a Hindu-majority India, and from 1940 demanded Pakistan. Congress leaders rejected this. Weakened by the Second World War, Britain chose a fast exit over a negotiated settlement.

dd-partition.h: The partition of British India, August 1947
dd-partition.p: At midnight on 14–15 August 1947 British India became two countries: Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan, whose eastern wing is today's Bangladesh. The provinces of Punjab and Bengal were cut in two by lines drawn in five weeks by a British lawyer, Cyril Radcliffe, and published only after independence. Somewhere between 10 and 20 million people crossed the new borders, and hundreds of thousands were killed.

dd-partition.q: Why did Britain bring the handover forward to August 1947?
a: Congress and the League had agreed a detailed settlement
Weakened by war, it chose a fast exit over a negotiated settlement
The United Nations ordered it to leave at once
Radcliffe needed more time to finish the border
dd-partition.why: Exhausted by the Second World War, Britain chose speed; Mountbatten argued it would limit bloodshed, while critics say the haste made it worse.

dd-partition.p:
Independent on 15 August 1947

India received most of British India and about 330 million people, including some 35 million Muslims who stayed. It took over most of the 560-odd princely states, by persuasion or, in Hyderabad in 1948, by force.

Independent on 14 August 1947, in two wings 1,600 km apart

West Pakistan included western Punjab, Sindh, the North-West Frontier and Baluchistan. Millions of Muslim refugees from India arrived, and most Hindus and Sikhs left.

Eastern Bengal became East Pakistan, separated from West Pakistan by India. It had more people than the west but less power, which led to its breakaway in 1971.

dd-partition.q: How does partition still shape the region today?
a: India and Pakistan remain rivals, both claiming divided Kashmir
Pakistan and India have since reunited as one federation
Kashmir became an independent state after a UN plebiscite
The border is open, so split families visit freely
dd-partition.why: The two nuclear-armed rivals have fought several wars, clashed again in 2025, and both still claim Kashmir, divided along the Line of Control.

dd-partition.h: A line drawn in five weeks
dd-partition.p: Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer who had never been to India, arrived in July 1947 to chair the commissions that would divide Punjab and Bengal. He had about five weeks, out-of-date maps and census figures, and orders to follow Muslim and non-Muslim majorities while weighing 'other factors' such as rivers, railways and canals. Many villages, farms and holy places ended up on the wrong side for their people. To avoid blame falling on the British at the handover, the award was published only on 17 August, two days after independence. Radcliffe refused his fee and, it is said, burned his papers.

The partition was one of the largest migrations in history: somewhere between 10 and 20 million people moved, on foot in columns stretching for miles, by bullock cart and by crowded train. Hindu, Sikh and Muslim mobs and militias attacked one another; trains sometimes arrived carrying only the dead. Estimates of deaths range from about 200,000 to 2 million, and a figure of about 1 million is often cited. Women suffered especially: an estimated 75,000 to 100,000 were abducted, and many were raped, and some families killed their own women to 'save their honour'. Many survivors never spoke of what they saw, and oral history projects began recording them only decades later.

dd-partition.h: Kashmir and the wars that followed, 1947–2025
dd-partition.p: Kashmir, a Muslim-majority princely state with a Hindu ruler, joined India in October 1947 as tribal fighters from Pakistan invaded. The two fought wars over it in 1947–48 and 1965, and the 1971 war created Bangladesh. Today India holds about 55% of the old state, Pakistan about 30% and China about 15%. Both India and Pakistan claim all of it, and in 1998 both tested nuclear weapons.

Holds Jammu, the Kashmir Valley and Ladakh

India sees all of Kashmir as Indian by the 1947 accession. It has fought an insurgency in the valley since 1989, and in 2019 ended the region's special autonomy and split it into two union territories.

dd-partition.q: What did the Muslim League under Jinnah argue?
a: That Britain should stay to protect minorities
That Kashmir should become fully independent
That Muslims were a separate nation, at risk in a Hindu-majority India
That India should be split along its rivers and railways
dd-partition.why: Jinnah's Muslim League argued Muslims were a separate nation and, from 1940, demanded Pakistan; Congress leaders, seeking a united India, rejected this.

dd-partition.p:
Holds Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan

Pakistan argues that Muslim-majority Kashmir should have been Pakistani and calls for the UN-backed plebiscite promised in 1948–49, which has never been held. India accuses it of backing militants.

Former East Pakistan, independent since 1971

In 1971 Pakistan's army cracked down on Bengali nationalists. Death estimates range from 26,000, by a Pakistani inquiry, to 3 million, Bangladesh's official figure; about 10 million fled to India before India intervened.

dd-partition.q: What happened to people when the new borders were announced?
a: Most stayed put, as the borders followed old provinces
Only soldiers and officials were moved
Between 10 and 20 million people fled, amid massacres on both sides
Britain organised a peaceful exchange of populations
dd-partition.why: Hindus and Sikhs fled east and Muslims west, in one of history's largest migrations, while mobs and militias on all sides killed hundreds of thousands.

dd-partition.p: Princely states could choose India or Pakistan. Kashmir's Hindu Maharaja, Hari Singh, ruling a Muslim majority, hesitated. In October 1947 Pashtun tribal fighters from Pakistan invaded, and he signed accession to India in return for troops. The war ended with a UN ceasefire in 1949 along a line that, renamed the Line of Control in 1972, still divides the region. A promised plebiscite never took place. An insurgency in the Indian-held valley since 1989 has killed tens of thousands, and drove most Kashmiri Hindus, the Pandits, from their homes in 1990. In 2019 India ended the region's autonomy; in 2026 its elected government, in office since 2024, was still demanding that statehood be restored.

The two countries remember the same year differently. In India, 15 August is a day of freedom, and partition is often remembered as a tragedy and a wound to the nation; since 2021 India has also marked 14 August as 'Partition Horrors Remembrance Day'. In Pakistan, 14 August celebrates the birth of a homeland for South Asia's Muslims, achieved at great cost. For Bangladeshis, 1971 matters more. Novels such as Khushwant Singh's 'Train to Pakistan' and Saadat Hasan Manto's stories, written by people who lived through it, remain some of the most powerful records of the violence.

Partition left India and Pakistan bitter rivals. They have fought wars in 1947–48, 1965, 1971 and 1999, and clashed again in May 2025; both tested nuclear weapons in 1998. In 1971 East Pakistan broke away as Bangladesh. Kashmir remains divided and claimed by both. Families split by the border still cannot easily visit, and the memory of 1947 shapes Hindu–Muslim relations in the region today.
India and Pakistan have fought four wars, mostly over Kashmir, and both now have nuclear weapons. Partition still shapes family histories for hundreds of millions.
