dd-nuclear.p: In December 1938 scientists in Berlin discovered that uranium atoms could be split, releasing huge energy. The United States, fearing a Nazi bomb, built the first atomic weapons, and in August 1945 destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The Soviet Union tested its own bomb in 1949, and an arms race followed: hydrogen bombs, intercontinental missiles and, by the mid-1980s, about 70,000 warheads worldwide.

items: France, UK, India, Pakistan, Israel, North Korea

steps: Enough to destroy each other many times.
No one can win, so no one starts.

dd-nuclear.p: In 1962 the Cuban Missile Crisis brought the world close to nuclear war. Treaties then banned most tests, limited the spread of weapons and, after the Cold War, cut arsenals by over 80%, though nine countries still have them.

dd-nuclear.q: What followed the Soviet Union's first atomic bomb test in 1949?
a: A treaty banning all nuclear weapons
The US gave up its bombs
An arms race reaching about 70,000 warheads by the mid-1980s
Nuclear weapons were used in Korea
dd-nuclear.why: The superpowers raced to build hydrogen bombs and intercontinental missiles, and by the mid-1980s about 70,000 warheads existed worldwide.

dd-nuclear.p: Physics made the bomb possible, and World War II made it urgent: scientists feared Hitler would build one first. After 1945 the Cold War rivals each believed only their own arsenal could deter the other, which led to 'mutually assured destruction'. Other countries built bombs for security against rivals, such as China against the superpowers, India against China and Pakistan against India, or for prestige and independence, as Britain and France did.

In December 1938 chemists in Berlin split uranium atoms, and scientists soon realised this could release enormous energy. Fearing a Nazi bomb, the United States, with Britain and Canada, built one in the secret Manhattan Project. The first was tested in New Mexico in July 1945, and in August two bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki in Japan. The Soviet Union tested its own in 1949.

dd-nuclear.q: What has the 1968 Non-Proliferation Treaty achieved?
a: It made Japan a nuclear power
It has kept nuclear-armed states to nine
dd-nuclear.why: Joined by almost every country, the treaty has limited the spread of the bomb, and South Africa and Ukraine even gave up weapons they held.

dd-nuclear.p:
The US-led wartime bomb project

The Manhattan Project employed about 130,000 people at its peak and cost about $2 billion, at secret sites from Tennessee to Washington state.

British scientists showed in 1940–41 that a bomb was feasible. Britain merged its project into the American one in 1943 and tested its own bomb in 1952.
Germany discovered fission, but its wartime nuclear programme never came close to a bomb. Many of the scientists who built the American bomb were refugees from Nazi Europe.
Japan is the only country attacked with nuclear weapons. Survivors, the hibakusha, suffered burns, radiation sickness and higher cancer rates for decades.

When a neutron hits the nucleus of a uranium-235 or plutonium-239 atom, the nucleus can split, releasing energy and two or three more neutrons. Those split more atoms, a chain reaction that, in a bomb, runs away in less than a millionth of a second. The Hiroshima bomb released energy equal to about 15,000 tonnes of TNT. Hydrogen bombs, first tested by the US in 1952, use a fission explosion to fuse hydrogen atoms, and can be hundreds or thousands of times stronger. The largest ever, the Soviet 'Tsar Bomba' of 1961, released about 50 million tonnes. The hard part is making the fuel: enriching uranium or producing plutonium takes huge industrial plants.

By 1962 the superpowers had thousands of nuclear weapons. In October an American spy plane photographed Soviet missile sites being built in Cuba, 145 km from Florida. President Kennedy ordered a naval 'quarantine' of the island. After 13 tense days, Soviet leader Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in return for a US pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret promise to withdraw US missiles from Turkey.
The US had far more long-range nuclear weapons than the Soviet Union in 1962. Its Strategic Air Command went to DEFCON 2, the highest alert level ever publicly confirmed.

dd-nuclear.q: Why did the United States build the first atomic bombs?
a: It feared Nazi Germany would build one first
The Soviet Union threatened to attack
dd-nuclear.why: Fission was discovered in Berlin in 1938, and fearing a Nazi bomb, the US, with Britain and Canada, built one in the secret Manhattan Project.

dd-nuclear.p: Khrushchev sent missiles to Cuba to protect his ally and to offset American missiles near Soviet borders. Backing down hurt his standing, and he was ousted in 1964.

Soviet missiles secretly installed

After a failed US-backed invasion at the Bay of Pigs in 1961, Fidel Castro accepted Soviet missiles. About 40,000 Soviet troops were sent to the island.

dd-nuclear.q: Why are nuclear dangers growing again today?
a: Arsenals are growing, led by China, and the last US–Russian limits expired
Every country now has nuclear weapons
dd-nuclear.why: No nuclear weapon has been used in war since 1945, but China is expanding fast and New START expired in February 2026, leaving no US–Russian limits.

dd-nuclear.p: The Cuban Missile Crisis was more dangerous than people knew at the time. Kennedy's advisers did not know that Soviet forces in Cuba also had about 100 short-range nuclear weapons. On 27 October 1962, the worst day, a U-2 was shot down over Cuba, killing its pilot. The same day US ships dropped practice depth charges to force a Soviet submarine to surface. Its crew had lost contact with Moscow, and the submarine carried a nuclear torpedo; according to later accounts, officer Vasily Arkhipov refused to agree to launch it. Afterwards the two sides set up a direct hotline, and in 1963 signed a treaty banning tests in the air, sea and space.

Nine countries have nuclear weapons, with about 12,200 warheads in January 2026 by SIPRI's estimate; Russia and the United States hold about 85% of them. The 1968 Non-Proliferation Treaty recognises five nuclear powers. India, Pakistan and North Korea built bombs outside it, and Israel is believed to have them. South Africa and Ukraine gave theirs up. The last US–Russian arms limits expired in February 2026.

Tested before 1967

SIPRI estimated about 5,000 US warheads in January 2026, including over 1,300 retired and awaiting dismantlement. New START, which capped deployed strategic warheads at 1,550, expired in February 2026.

Russia has the largest arsenal, about 5,400 warheads by SIPRI's estimate. It suspended its participation in New START in 2023 and said it would keep the limits only if the US did.

India tested a device in 1974 and weapons in 1998, and has about 190 warheads by SIPRI's estimate. It never joined the NPT.

Pakistan tested weapons in 1998, weeks after India, and has about 170 warheads by SIPRI's estimate.

dd-nuclear.q: Why did the Cold War rivals keep building ever larger arsenals?
a: Each believed only its own arsenal could deter the other
They planned to test them all in space
They wanted to sell them to allies
dd-nuclear.why: Each side believed its weapons deterred the other, leading to 'mutually assured destruction', with forces ready to strike within minutes.

dd-nuclear.p: During the Cold War, schoolchildren in the United States practised 'duck and cover' drills, and some families built fallout shelters. Both superpowers kept bombers and missiles ready to strike within minutes. That brought close calls: in September 1983 a Soviet early-warning system reported US missiles heading for the Soviet Union, and the duty officer, Stanislav Petrov, judged it a false alarm, which it was. Over 2,000 nuclear tests have been carried out since 1945, many in the open air before 1963, spreading fallout and harming people near test sites from Nevada to Kazakhstan and the Pacific islands.

No nuclear weapon has been used in war since 1945, which many credit to deterrence and luck. The 1968 Non-Proliferation Treaty, joined by almost every country, has kept the number of nuclear-armed states to nine. But arsenals are growing again, China is expanding fast, and the last US–Russian arms control treaty expired in February 2026. Nuclear power, born of the same science, still supplies about a tenth of the world's electricity.

dd-globalization.p: After World War II the United States and its allies built new institutions, the IMF, the World Bank and the GATT, to keep trade open and currencies stable. Tariffs fell round after round, Western Europe formed a common market, and from 1956 the shipping container slashed the cost of moving goods. Japan, then South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore grew rich by exporting.

l: Over a billion people out of extreme poverty
r: Factory jobs lost in rich countries

dd-globalization.p: After the Cold War almost the whole world joined in: China opened from 1978 and entered the World Trade Organization in 2001, becoming the world's factory. From 2008, and especially after 2016, a backlash grew, and in 2025 the United States raised tariffs to their highest level since the 1930s.

The Allies blamed the tariff wars of the 1930s for deepening the Depression and helping cause war, so they wanted rules for open trade. Cheaper shipping, jet travel, computers and the internet made it easy to split production across continents. Companies chased lower costs, consumers wanted cheaper goods, and poorer countries saw exports as the fastest route out of poverty. The end of communism opened huge new markets and workforces.

dd-globalization.q: What happened to world trade after World War II?
a: It shrank as countries raised tariffs
Tariffs fell round after round and trade grew hugely
It was run only by the Soviet Union
dd-globalization.why: Under the GATT and later the WTO, tariffs fell step by step, and trade grew from about a quarter of world output in 1960 to around 60% by 2008.

dd-globalization.p: Blaming the trade wars of the 1930s for the Depression and war, the United States and Britain led the building of a new system. In 1947, 23 countries signed the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) to cut tariffs step by step. In 1957 six countries, including France and West Germany, founded a common market. The Soviet Union and its allies traded mostly among themselves.

The 23 original members, apart from the EEC six and Czechoslovakia

The US, by far the largest economy after 1945, pushed for open trade and stable currencies, and the dollar became the system's anchor.

Britain helped design the post-war system at Bretton Woods, where the economist John Maynard Keynes led its delegation.

The EEC six; all but Italy and West Germany were also GATT founders

France and West Germany joined their coal and steel industries in 1951, then founded the European Economic Community in 1957 with Italy and the Benelux countries.

Italy joined the GATT in 1950 and was a founder of the EEC in 1957. Its north boomed in the 1950s and 1960s.

dd-globalization.q: Who lost out from globalisation, fuelling a backlash?
a: Consumers, who paid more for goods
Factory towns in rich countries that lost jobs
dd-globalization.why: Gains were uneven: consumers got cheaper goods and hundreds of millions escaped poverty, but factory towns in the US and Europe lost jobs and inequality rose.

dd-globalization.p:
Comecon, founded 1949

The Soviet Union set up Comecon in 1949 to link the planned economies of Eastern Europe, largely cut off from Western trade.

Czechoslovakia signed the GATT in 1947, just before the Communist takeover in 1948, and then joined Comecon in 1949.

dd-globalization.h: The box that changed the world
dd-globalization.p: Until the 1950s ships were loaded by gangs of dockworkers carrying sacks, barrels and crates, and a ship could spend as long in port as at sea. In 1956 the American trucking owner Malcom McLean sent a converted tanker, the Ideal X, from Newark to Houston with 58 metal boxes on deck. Standard containers could be lifted straight from ship to truck or train, cutting the cost of loading, by one estimate, from almost $6 a ton to about 16 cents. Theft and breakage fell, and ports moved to vast new terminals. Today ships carrying over 20,000 containers link Asia, Europe and the Americas, and shipping a T-shirt across the world costs only a few cents.

In 1978 China was poor and largely closed. Deng Xiaoping's reforms let farmers sell surplus crops, and from 1980 special economic zones such as Shenzhen welcomed foreign factories. Cheap labour, good ports and huge investment in roads and power made China the place to make almost anything. After it joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 its exports grew about sevenfold in a decade. The World Bank estimates that around 800 million Chinese people escaped extreme poverty over four decades. By 2025 China made nearly a third of the world's manufactured goods and ran a record trade surplus of nearly $1.2 trillion.

First Japan, then South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore grew rich by exporting to Western markets. From 1978 China opened to foreign investment, starting in special economic zones, and joined the World Trade Organization in 2001. Container ships carried its goods west through Singapore and the Suez Canal, and Southeast Asian countries such as Vietnam built export factories too.

Export boom from the 1950s

Japan rebuilt after 1945 and by the 1970s exported cars, ships and electronics worldwide. By 1968 it was the world's second-largest economy.

dd-globalization.q: Why did the Allies want rules for open trade after 1945?
a: They blamed 1930s tariff wars for the Depression and war
They wanted to stop Japan exporting
They hoped to end the use of the dollar
dd-globalization.why: Believing tariff wars had deepened the Depression and helped cause war, the US and Britain led the building of the IMF, World Bank and GATT.

dd-globalization.p:
Rapid export-led growth, 1960s–1990s

South Korea, as poor as many African countries in 1960, built firms such as Samsung and Hyundai and became a rich industrial nation.

Taiwan moved from textiles to electronics. TSMC, founded in 1987, now makes most of the world's most advanced computer chips.

Opening from 1978; WTO member from 2001

Deng Xiaoping's reforms from 1978 opened China to foreign investment. After it joined the WTO in December 2001 its exports grew about sevenfold in a decade.

dd-globalization.q: Which describes the direction of world trade today?
a: Tariffs are at record lows everywhere
Governments use tariffs and subsidies, and trade is splitting into rival blocs
All countries have left the WTO
dd-globalization.why: After the 2025 US tariffs, the highest since the 1930s, governments protect industries and security, while others sign new deals such as RCEP and EU–Mercosur.

dd-globalization.p: Economists broadly agree that trade made the world richer overall, but the gains were uneven. Consumers got cheaper goods and exporters boomed, while factory towns in the US and Europe lost jobs: one well-known study estimated that Chinese import competition cost the US about 2–2.4 million jobs in 1999–2011. Protesters disrupted the WTO's 1999 meeting in Seattle, and after the 2008 financial crisis anger grew. Britain voted to leave the EU in 2016, and the US began a trade war with China in 2018. Supporters of tariffs argue they protect jobs and security; critics say they raise prices and invite retaliation.

In 2025 the United States raised tariffs to their highest level since the 1930s, hitting China hardest. In February 2026 the US Supreme Court struck down the main tariffs, and the government replaced them with others. China still ran a record trade surplus of about $1.2 trillion. Elsewhere trade deals grew: Asia's RCEP, the world's largest bloc, and an EU deal with Brazil and its Mercosur partners.

North American free-trade area, NAFTA's successor from 2020

The US imposed tariffs on most countries in 2025. After the Supreme Court ruling it used other laws: a 10% global tariff from February 2026, then, from July, tariffs of 10–12.5% on 60 economies, plus higher duties on steel, aluminium and cars.

Canada, the largest market for US exports, was hit by US tariffs from 2025. In July 2026 the US declined to renew the North American agreement, which now faces yearly reviews, and put 50% tariffs on some Canadian goods.

Single market of 27 countries

Germany, Europe's biggest exporter, was hit by US tariffs on cars and machinery. In July 2025 the EU agreed a deal with a 15% US tariff ceiling on most goods.

dd-globalization.q: How did the shipping container change trade?
a: It made ships slower but safer
It was used only for oil
It slashed the cost of moving goods worldwide
dd-globalization.why: Standard boxes lifted straight from ship to truck or train cut loading costs from almost $6 a ton to about 16 cents, making long supply chains cheap.

dd-globalization.p:
15 Asia-Pacific signatories, in force from 2022

US tariffs on Chinese goods briefly reached 145% in April 2025 before a truce. China's exports still grew in 2025 as it sold more to Southeast Asia, Africa, Latin America and Europe.

Japan agreed a trade deal with the US in 2025, pledging large investments in return for lower tariffs. It is also a member of RCEP and the CPTPP, another Asia-Pacific trade pact.

In April 2025 President Trump announced tariffs on imports from almost every country, calling the day 'Liberation Day'. Tariffs between the US and China briefly passed 100% before truces in Geneva and Busan. Many partners, including the EU, Japan and Britain, agreed deals accepting US tariffs of about 10–15%. In February 2026 the US Supreme Court ruled that the emergency law used for most of these tariffs did not allow them, and companies began claiming refunds. The administration replaced them with tariffs under other laws, while other countries signed new deals with each other, such as the EU's agreement with Mercosur.

Trade grew from about a quarter of world output in 1960 to around 60% by 2008. Hundreds of millions escaped extreme poverty, above all in China and the rest of East Asia, and goods became cheaper everywhere. But factory towns in rich countries lost jobs, inequality rose, and long supply chains proved fragile in the pandemic. Governments now use tariffs and subsidies to protect industries and national security, and trade is splitting into rival blocs.

The first container ship sails from Newark to Houston
Deng Xiaoping begins opening China to foreign trade and investment
The World Trade Organization is founded
China joins the WTO
The US imposes tariffs on almost every country

dd-humanrights.p: Human rights are the basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person, whatever their nationality, sex, religion or race. The idea had roots in religious teachings and the Enlightenment, but it became a global standard only after World War II and the Holocaust.

steps: The king is under the law.
The UN sets out rights for everyone, led by Eleanor Roosevelt.

dd-humanrights.q: When was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted?
dd-humanrights.why: In response to the horrors of WW2.

dd-humanrights.p: In 1945, 51 countries founded the United Nations to keep the peace, and in 1948 its General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt. Later treaties banned genocide, torture and racial discrimination, and courts such as the European Court of Human Rights and the International Criminal Court tried to enforce them.

dd-humanrights.q: Why was the United Nations founded in 1945?
a: To keep the peace after World War II
To run a single world government
dd-humanrights.why: After the devastation of World War II, 51 countries founded the UN to prevent another world war and give countries a forum to settle disputes.

dd-humanrights.p: The horrors of World War II, including the Holocaust and the deaths of tens of millions, convinced world leaders that how a state treats its own people is everyone's concern. They hoped that agreed rules, and a forum where countries could talk, would prevent another world war.

dd-humanrights.h: The founding members of the United Nations, 1945
dd-humanrights.p: Fifty-one countries signed up to the UN Charter in 1945. Most of Africa and much of Asia were still colonies with no seat, so the founders came mostly from Europe and the Americas, along with India, then still British, and China, Egypt, Ethiopia and Liberia. The Soviet Union won two extra seats, for Ukraine and Belarus. Today the UN has 193 members.

dd-humanrights.q: Why was the Universal Declaration not enough to protect rights on its own?
a: It was not a binding law
dd-humanrights.why: The Declaration set standards but did not bind states, so later treaties and courts tried to make rights enforceable.

dd-humanrights.p:
In today's borders

Ethiopia, invaded by Italy in 1935, had seen the old League of Nations fail to protect it.

British India signed the Charter in 1945, two years before independence.
One seat for the USSR, plus separate seats for Ukraine and Belarus

The United Nations replaced the failed League of Nations. Its Charter was signed in San Francisco in June 1945 and took effect on 24 October, now celebrated as UN Day. Every member has a vote in the General Assembly, but real power lies with the Security Council, where five victors of World War II, the United States, the Soviet Union (now Russia), Britain, France and China, hold permanent seats and a veto. The UN's headquarters in New York opened in the early 1950s, and agencies such as UNICEF and the World Health Organization were set up alongside it.

Drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, widow of President Franklin Roosevelt, with Lebanon's Charles Malik, China's P. C. Chang and France's René Cassin among its authors, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in Paris on 10 December 1948. Its 30 articles begin: 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.' They include freedom from torture and slavery, freedom of speech and religion, the right to a fair trial, and rights to education and work. Forty-eight countries voted in favour, none against, and eight abstained.

dd-humanrights.h: Voting for the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 1948
dd-humanrights.p: On 10 December 1948 the UN General Assembly, meeting in Paris, adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Forty-eight countries voted yes and none voted against. Eight abstained: the Soviet Union and its allies objected to parts of it, Saudi Arabia disliked the freedom to change religion, and South Africa was building apartheid. Two members, Honduras and Yemen, did not vote.

48 countries, in today's borders

Eleanor Roosevelt, the US delegate, chaired the committee that drafted the Declaration.

The French jurist René Cassin wrote much of the first full draft. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1968.

dd-humanrights.q: Who chaired the committee that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
dd-humanrights.why: Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the drafting committee, working with authors such as Charles Malik, P. C. Chang and René Cassin.

dd-humanrights.p:
The Soviet bloc, Saudi Arabia and South Africa

The Soviet bloc said the text did not go far enough on economic rights and abstained.

Saudi Arabia objected to the articles on freedom to change religion and on equal rights in marriage.

The Declaration was not a binding law, so later treaties tried to make rights enforceable. The Genocide Convention of 1948 made genocide an international crime, using a word coined by the lawyer Raphael Lemkin. In 1950 members of the Council of Europe signed the European Convention on Human Rights, whose court in Strasbourg can rule against governments. After the wars in Yugoslavia and the Rwandan genocide, UN tribunals tried those responsible, and in 2002 a permanent International Criminal Court opened in The Hague, though the United States, Russia, China and India have not joined it.

dd-humanrights.q: Where does the International Criminal Court sit?
dd-humanrights.why: The ICC opened in The Hague in 2002 to try individuals for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.

dd-humanrights.h: The European Convention on Human Rights today
dd-humanrights.p: Europe went furthest in turning rights into law. Members of the Council of Europe, founded in 1949, sign the European Convention on Human Rights, and people in them can take a case to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France, once courts at home have ruled. Its 46 members stretch from Iceland to Azerbaijan. Russia was expelled in 2022 after invading Ukraine, and Belarus has never joined.

46 countries

Turkey has had more judgments against it at the Strasbourg court than any other country.

British lawyers helped draft the Convention, and since 2000 the UK's Human Rights Act has let its courts apply it directly.

dd-humanrights.q: Which countries hold a veto on the UN Security Council?
a: Germany, Japan, India, Brazil and Italy
The US, Russia, Britain, France and China
dd-humanrights.why: Five victors of World War II hold permanent seats and can veto any Security Council resolution.

dd-humanrights.p: Russia joined in 1996 and was expelled in March 2022, weeks after it invaded Ukraine.

Human rights often collide with power politics. During the Cold War each side accused the other of abuses while backing friendly dictators, and the Security Council veto has blocked action in crises from Syria to Ukraine. Yet the idea of universal rights has also brought real change: international pressure helped end apartheid in South Africa, and courts have held some leaders to account, such as Liberia's Charles Taylor, convicted of war crimes in 2012. Some governments argue that 'universal' rights reflect Western values; supporters reply that they were drafted by people from many cultures and traditions.

The UN has grown to 193 members and runs peacekeeping, refugee and food agencies around the world. Human rights became a shared language for activists, from the anti-apartheid movement to campaigns for women's and gay rights. But enforcement is weak: the Security Council's five permanent members can veto action, and many governments sign treaties they then ignore.

The UN adopts the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
The European Convention on Human Rights is signed in Rome
The UN adopts covenants on civil, political, economic and social rights
The International Criminal Court opens in The Hague

dd-space.p: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a beeping metal ball, into orbit. Americans were stunned, and the US answered with Explorer 1 in 1958 and a new agency, NASA. The Soviets kept winning firsts: Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space on 12 April 1961, Valentina Tereshkova the first woman in 1963, and Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk in 1965.

steps: Armstrong and Aldrin walk on the Moon.
Former rivals build a space station together.

dd-space.q: Who was the first person in space?

dd-space.p: President Kennedy set the US the goal of reaching the Moon. Apollo 8 circled it at Christmas 1968, and on 20 July 1969 Apollo 11 landed. By 1972 twelve Americans had walked on the Moon, and in 1975 an Apollo and a Soyuz docked in orbit.

dd-space.q: What was the Space Race's most famous result?
a: Apollo 11 landing people on the Moon in 1969
The first satellite launched by Britain
dd-space.why: After early Soviet firsts like Sputnik and Gagarin, Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969, and twelve Americans walked on the Moon by 1972.

dd-space.p: The race grew out of the Cold War. Both superpowers were building long-range missiles to carry nuclear warheads, and a rocket that can put a satellite in orbit can also hit a city across the world. Firsts in space were also propaganda: each side wanted to show the world that its system, communist or capitalist, was the more advanced.

The Soviet Union launched the first satellite, Sputnik, in October 1957 and put Yuri Gagarin into orbit in April 1961, both from a secret base in today's Kazakhstan. The United States answered with the Apollo programme, and in July 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon. In 1975 the rivals met in orbit, when an Apollo and a Soyuz docked.

dd-space.q: Why did each side race to win 'firsts' in space?
a: To show the world its system was more advanced
To find new places to live
To share technology with each other
dd-space.why: Space firsts were propaganda, meant to prove that communism or capitalism was the more advanced system; Sputnik's shock led the US to found NASA.

dd-space.p:
Launched from Baikonur; trained cosmonauts at Star City

Moscow ran the Soviet programme, led in secret by the engineer Sergei Korolev. It won the early firsts: satellite, animal, man, woman and spacewalk in orbit.

Korolev was born in Zhytomyr, in today's Ukraine. Soviet rockets and missiles were also designed and built in Dnipro.

Launched from Cape Canaveral; ran missions from Houston

Shocked by Sputnik, the US founded NASA in 1958. Its Apollo programme landed 12 astronauts on the Moon between 1969 and 1972.

dd-space.q: How does the 1975 Apollo–Soyuz docking connect to space today?
a: It led decades later to the International Space Station
It gave the Moon to the United Nations
It made China the leading space power
dd-space.why: The handshake in orbit eased the rivalry and led to the International Space Station, built from 1998 by Russia, the US and partners.

dd-space.p: Both sides' rockets descended from Nazi Germany's V-2, the first long-range ballistic missile, fired at London and Antwerp from 1944. It was built partly by concentration camp prisoners, and more people died making it than were killed by it. After the war its chief designer, Wernher von Braun, surrendered to the Americans and later led the team that built the Saturn V Moon rocket. The Soviets took German engineers and V-2 parts too, but their programme was led by Sergei Korolev, a designer who had survived years in Stalin's prison camps. His R-7, the world's first intercontinental missile, launched Sputnik and Gagarin. Korolev's name was kept secret until he died in 1966.

Apollo 11 lifted off from Florida on 16 July 1969 on a Saturn V, still among the most powerful rockets ever flown. Four days later Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin flew the lunar module Eagle down to the Sea of Tranquillity while Michael Collins stayed in orbit. Computer alarms flashed during the descent, and Armstrong steered past a boulder field by hand, landing with little fuel left. Hundreds of millions of people watched him step out and say, 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.' The two men spent about two and a half hours outside, collected about 22 kg of rock and splashed down in the Pacific on 24 July.

dd-space.h: Countries that reached orbit on their own rockets, 2026
dd-space.p: After the Soviet Union and the United States, countries such as France, Japan, China and India built their own launchers. North Korea and South Korea both made it by 2013. Today private companies are joining: Rocket Lab from New Zealand since 2018, and Germany's Isar Aerospace in 2026. European countries also launch together through the European Space Agency.

Soviet Union 1957, United States 1958

The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 in 1957. Russia inherited its rockets, including the Soyuz, still flying after more than 50 years.

Explorer 1 reached orbit in January 1958. Today US companies such as SpaceX carry out most of the world's launches.

dd-space.q: Why were space rockets so closely tied to the Cold War?
a: They were built to carry tourists
They were invented by NASA for science
A rocket that reaches orbit can also carry a nuclear warhead
Both sides wanted to mine the Moon
dd-space.why: Both superpowers were building long-range nuclear missiles; Korolev's R-7, the first intercontinental missile, launched Sputnik and Gagarin.

dd-space.p:
France, Japan, China, Britain, India

France became the third space power in 1965, launching its Diamant rocket from Algeria. It later led Europe's Ariane rockets, launched from French Guiana.

Japan reached orbit in February 1970 with a small rocket called Lambda, launching the satellite Ohsumi.

Israel, Iran, North Korea, South Korea

Israel launched its first satellite, Ofeq 1, in 1988. Its rockets fire west over the Mediterranean to avoid flying over its neighbours.

Iran put a satellite into orbit in 2009 with its Safir rocket. Western governments say the programme also helps its missile work.

dd-space.q: How did the Space Race change everyday life?
a: It ended the use of rockets
Satellites brought weather forecasts, global television and later GPS
dd-space.why: Weather, communication and navigation satellites grew out of the race, and it poured money into science and computing.

dd-space.p: The biggest gifts are in orbit. Weather satellites, starting with TIROS-1 in 1960, transformed forecasting. Communication satellites such as Telstar in 1962 carried live television across oceans. The US military's GPS, opened to civilians and fully working by 1995, now guides phones, planes, farm machines and bank timing, alongside Russia's GLONASS, Europe's Galileo and China's BeiDou. Space also changed how people saw Earth: the 1968 'Earthrise' photo from Apollo 8 became an emblem of the environmental movement. Some famous 'spin-offs' are myths, though: NASA did not invent Tang, Velcro or Teflon, it only made them famous.

The race made satellites part of daily life: weather forecasts, global television and phone links, spy satellites and, later, GPS. It poured money into science and computing. After the Moon landings both sides turned to space stations, and the 1975 handshake in orbit led, decades later, to the International Space Station, built from 1998 by Russia, the US and partners. Today China, India and private companies are the new players.

dd-polynesia.p: The ancestors of the Polynesians spoke Austronesian languages that spread from Taiwan through Island South-East Asia. By about 1350 BC their descendants, makers of stamped Lapita pottery, lived in the Bismarck Archipelago off New Guinea. Sailing east into islands no one had ever reached, they settled Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji, and by about 850 BC Tonga and Samoa, where Polynesian culture took shape.

items: Rising and setting points of stars.
Fly out to fish and return to land at dusk.
Clouds pile up and turn green over lagoons.

steps: Tahiti and the Marquesas, c. AD 900.
Hawaii, Rapa Nui (Easter Island) and Aotearoa (NZ), c. 1000–1300.

dd-polynesia.p: Then came a long pause. Around 1000 AD voyagers reached the Society Islands, and within about three centuries they found Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and finally New Zealand, around 1250–1300, completing the last great human migration to empty lands.

dd-polynesia.q: What did the voyages of the Polynesians' ancestors achieve?
a: They conquered the coasts of Asia
They settled a vast triangle of empty islands, ending with New Zealand
They settled Australia for the first time
dd-polynesia.why: From Lapita times to about 1250–1300, voyagers settled islands no one had reached, from Tonga and Samoa to Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and finally New Zealand.

dd-polynesia.p: The voyagers had superb double-hulled and outrigger canoes and a deep knowledge of stars, swells, winds and birds, passed down by trained navigators. They sailed deliberately, often against the prevailing easterly winds so they could ride home if they found nothing. Why they set out is debated: growing populations, quarrels between chiefs, younger sons seeking land, and shifts in wind patterns that opened eastward routes may all have played a part.

dd-polynesia.h: Out of Asia: the Lapita voyagers, c. 1350–800 BC
dd-polynesia.p: Polynesians' ancestors spoke Austronesian languages, which spread from Taiwan through the Philippines and Indonesia. By about 1350 BC a seafaring people known for their stamped Lapita pottery lived off Papua New Guinea. Within a few centuries they sailed into the empty islands beyond, Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji, and by about 850 BC reached Tonga and then Samoa, the cradle of Polynesian culture.

dd-polynesia.q: What happened to Polynesian societies after European contact from the 1760s?
a: Disease, missionaries and colonial rule arrived
dd-polynesia.why: Contact brought disease, missionaries and colonial rule; Hawaiʻi's monarchy was overthrown, and Rapa Nui and other islands came under foreign powers.

dd-polynesia.p:
Where the language family began, over 5,000 years ago

Most linguists trace the Austronesian languages, spoken from Madagascar to Rapa Nui, back to Taiwan, where Indigenous peoples still speak the oldest branches.

Austronesian speakers spread south from about 2000 BC

Austronesian farmers and seafarers moved from Taiwan into the Philippines around 2000 BC, carrying pottery, rice and outrigger canoes.

The Bismarck Archipelago

The Lapita culture first appears in the Bismarck Archipelago, off northern New Guinea, where newcomers mixed with peoples who had lived there for tens of thousands of years.

Polynesian navigators carried a map of the sky in their heads. They knew where dozens of stars rose and set on the horizon, and steered by them through the night, holding the canoe's angle to the ocean swells by feel when clouds hid the sky. Islands could be sensed long before they were seen: a fixed cloud over a peak, a green tint on clouds above a lagoon, swells bent and reflected by land. Birds such as terns and noddies fly out to fish by day and return to land at dusk, pointing the way. In 1769 the Raiatean navigator Tupaia, sailing with Captain Cook, drew a chart showing dozens of islands across the Pacific.

dd-polynesia.h: The settlement of East Polynesia, c. 1000–1300
dd-polynesia.p: After a pause of nearly 2,000 years in Western Polynesia, voyagers pushed east. By radiocarbon dating they reached the Society Islands, in French Polynesia, around 1025–1120. Within a few generations they found nearly every habitable island in a vast triangle of ocean: Hawaiʻi in the United States, Rapa Nui (Easter Island) in Chile, and last, around 1250–1300, Aotearoa, New Zealand.

Tonga and Samoa had been settled for about 2,000 years when East Polynesia was first reached.

Samoan tradition calls Savaiʻi, its largest island, the ancestral homeland; many East Polynesians remembered a homeland called Hawaiki or Savaiki.

dd-polynesia.q: How did Polynesian navigators find islands without instruments?
a: They drifted wherever the currents took them
They used stars, swells, clouds and birds
They sailed only within sight of land
dd-polynesia.why: Trained navigators steered by rising and setting stars and ocean swells, and read clouds, reflected swells and homing birds to sense land beyond sight.

dd-polynesia.p:
The first East Polynesian homeland, which Māori remember as Hawaiki

The Society Islands, with Tahiti and Raiatea, were the first part of East Polynesia settled. The Marquesas, Tuamotus and Australs followed soon after.

The great burst to the corners of the triangle

The Cook Islands lay on the route between the Society Islands and New Zealand, and Rarotonga became a hub for voyagers.

Pitcairn and nearby Henderson were settled, then abandoned, Henderson by about 1500 and Pitcairn later, perhaps when trade links to Mangareva broke down.

dd-polynesia.q: What did Hōkūleʻa's 1976 voyage to Tahiti help spark?
a: A revival of wayfinding, languages and Polynesian culture
Proof that Polynesia was settled from America
dd-polynesia.why: Sailing by stars, swells and birds alone, Hōkūleʻa showed the old skills worked and helped inspire a revival of voyaging and Māori and Hawaiian languages.

dd-polynesia.p: Voyaging canoes were usually double-hulled, two hulls lashed together under a deck, with sails woven from pandanus leaves, and could be 15–20 metres long or more. A settling party carried everything it needed to start life on an empty island: taro, breadfruit, bananas, yams and coconuts as plants or cuttings, paper mulberry for making bark cloth, and pigs, dogs and chickens. The Pacific rat came too, perhaps as a stowaway, perhaps as food, and its DNA now helps scientists trace the voyages. Not every island got everything: New Zealand's settlers arrived without pigs or chickens, and its colder climate could not grow most tropical crops, so they turned to sweet potato, birds and seafood.

Polynesians live in three independent states, Tonga, Samoa and Tuvalu, in self-governing islands tied to New Zealand, and in French, American and British territories. Others are peoples within larger countries: Māori in New Zealand, Native Hawaiians in the United States and Rapa Nui in Chile. In 1976 the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti without instruments, sparking a revival of wayfinding.

Tonga is the Pacific's only kingdom and was never formally colonised; it was a British protected state from 1900 to 1970.

Samoa, ruled by New Zealand from 1914, became independent in 1962, the first Pacific island nation to do so in the 20th century.

Self-governing; their people are New Zealand citizens

The Cook Islands have governed themselves in free association with New Zealand since 1965.

Niue, a single raised coral island, has been self-governing in free association with New Zealand since 1974.

dd-polynesia.q: Why did voyagers often sail against the prevailing easterly winds?
a: So they could ride home if they found nothing
Because their canoes could not sail downwind
dd-polynesia.why: Sailing deliberately into the wind meant a safe return was possible, showing these were planned voyages of discovery, not accidental drifts.

dd-polynesia.p:
French, American and British

French Polynesia is a self-governing overseas country of France. It hosted France's nuclear tests from 1966 to 1996.

The sweet potato, a South American plant, was growing in Polynesia before Columbus; burnt remains from the Cook Islands date to around 1200–1400, and Polynesian kumara resembles the Quechua word kumar. Most scholars think Polynesians, or less likely South Americans, made the crossing, though some botanists have argued the plant drifted on its own. In 2020 a genetic study of modern Polynesians found traces of Native American ancestry, pointing to a contact around 1200 with people most closely related to Indigenous groups of today's Colombia. In 1947 Thor Heyerdahl's raft Kon-Tiki drifted from Peru to the Tuamotus to argue that Polynesia was settled from America; language, archaeology and DNA show it was settled from Asia.

Polynesians spread one family of closely related languages, gods and customs across a triangle of ocean from Hawaiʻi to New Zealand to Rapa Nui. On isolated islands they built distinct societies, from the moai of Rapa Nui to Hawaiʻi's kingdoms. From the 1760s European contact brought disease, missionaries and colonial rule. Since the 1970s a revival of voyaging, languages and culture, led by Hōkūleʻa and Māori and Hawaiian schools, has restored pride in that heritage.

dd-brazil.p: Portugal claimed Brazil in 1500 and built a colony of sugar plantations and, from the 1690s, gold mines, worked by millions of enslaved Africans. In 1808 the Portuguese royal family fled Napoleon to Rio, and in 1822 Prince Pedro declared independence and made Brazil an empire. It stayed united, fought Paraguay in 1864–70, and in 1888 became the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery.

items: The only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas.
60% of the Amazon is in Brazil.
More people of African descent than any country but Nigeria.
Borders every South American country but Chile and Ecuador.

a: The Treaty of Tordesillas gave it to Portugal
dd-brazil.why: The 1494 line split the New World.

dd-brazil.p: A coup made it a republic in 1889. Getúlio Vargas dominated the mid-1900s, the capital moved to Brasília in 1960, and the military ruled from 1964 to 1985. Since then Brazil has been a democracy, led by figures as different as Lula and Jair Bolsonaro.

Portugal's monarchy, which ruled from Rio and then through its own heir, held Brazil's regions together while Spanish America split into many republics. Sugar, gold, coffee and slavery shaped a deeply unequal society, with land and power concentrated among a small elite. That inequality, and the Cold War fear of communism, helped bring the 1964 coup. Since 1985 Brazilians have argued over how to share the wealth of a resource-rich country and how to fight corruption and crime.

dd-brazil.q: How did Brazil become independent from Portugal?
a: After a long war led by enslaved Africans
Prince Pedro declared independence in 1822 and became emperor
Spain conquered it and set it free
A military coup created a republic in 1822
dd-brazil.why: The Portuguese court had fled Napoleon to Rio in 1808, and in 1822 Prince Pedro, the king's heir, declared Brazil independent as an empire.

dd-brazil.p: Pedro Álvares Cabral claimed Brazil for Portugal in 1500. The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas gave Portugal only the eastern bulge, but slave raiders, cattle ranchers and gold seekers pushed far west, and in 1750 Spain accepted most of their gains. Sugar plantations and then gold mines were worked by enslaved Africans, shipped largely from Angola: nearly 5 million in all, more than to any other country.

Borders largely fixed by the 1750 Treaty of Madrid

Brazil was Portugal's richest colony. Sugar dominated in the 1500s–1600s and gold in the 1700s. Enslaved Africans and their descendants made up much of the population.

The mother country and its main slave-trading colony

Portugal, a small kingdom, came to depend on Brazilian sugar and gold, much of which flowed on to Britain to pay for imports.

Portugal held Luanda from 1576. Angola was the largest single source of the Africans taken to Brazil, and Brazilian merchants ran much of the trade.

dd-brazil.q: What helped bring the military coup of 1964?
a: Inequality and Cold War fear of communism
dd-brazil.why: President Goulart's land reform plans alarmed landowners, business and Washington, and the generals then ruled for 21 years until 1985.

dd-brazil.p:
Gold finds in Mato Grosso in the 1720s drew Portuguese settlers right up to Spain's lands in today's Bolivia.

Jesuits built missions for the Guaraní in Spanish Paraguay. In the 1620s–30s slave raiders from São Paulo, the bandeirantes, destroyed those in Guairá, now in Brazil, and enslaved thousands.

Brazil took in more enslaved Africans than any other country: nearly 5 million, by the SlaveVoyages database's estimate, against about 400,000 brought to North America. On sugar estates in Bahia and Pernambuco, and later in gold mines and coffee farms, many died within a few years, so planters kept buying new captives. People resisted by escaping to free settlements called quilombos; the largest, Palmares, held out for most of the 1600s, and its last leader, Zumbi, is honoured on 20 November, now a national holiday. Slavery was abolished only in 1888, with no land or compensation for the freed. Today over half of Brazilians identify as Black or mixed race.

In 1964 the army overthrew President João Goulart, whose land reform plans alarmed landowners, business and Washington, which backed the coup. The generals ruled for 21 years, picking presidents, censoring the press and banning most opposition. From 1968 they tortured and killed opponents: a National Truth Commission in 2014 named 434 people killed or disappeared. The years 1968–73 brought a growth 'miracle', with roads, dams and factories, but also huge foreign debts and widening inequality. Mass protests demanding direct elections in 1984 helped end military rule in 1985, and a new constitution followed in 1988. A 1979 amnesty law has shielded officers from prosecution for these crimes.

In 1808 the Portuguese court fled Napoleon to Rio, and in 1822 Prince Pedro declared Brazil independent and became its emperor. Unlike Spanish America, it stayed in one piece. It lost Uruguay in 1828, and with Argentina and Uruguay crushed Paraguay in the bloodiest war in South American history, 1864–1870. Brazil ended slavery in 1888, became a republic in 1889 and bought Acre from Bolivia in 1903.

An independent monarchy, 1822–1889

Pedro I and his son Pedro II ruled until 1889. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

dd-brazil.q: Why did Brazil stay united while Spanish America split into many republics?
a: Portugal's monarchy, ruling from Rio and then via its heir
It had no regions to divide
dd-brazil.why: A shared monarchy gave Brazil's regions a single centre of loyalty, so it stayed in one piece as Spanish America broke apart.

dd-brazil.p:
The Triple Alliance with Brazil

Argentina fought with Brazil against Paraguay and gained land in the north-east, including today's Misiones and Formosa provinces.

Brazil annexed the land as its Cisplatine Province in 1821. After a war with Argentina, Britain helped broker its independence as Uruguay in 1828.

Lost the war and much of its population

Paraguay attacked first, in 1864. Estimates vary widely, but many historians believe it lost around half its people to battle, hunger and disease, and it ceded land to Brazil and Argentina.

a: Sharply split, with Lula narrowly beating Flávio Bolsonaro in a runoff
dd-brazil.why: Brazil has been a democracy since 1985, but after Jair Bolsonaro's 2025 coup conviction, Lula narrowly beat his son Flávio in an October 2026 runoff.

dd-brazil.p: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a former metalworker and union leader, was president from 2003 to 2010, when a commodity boom and cash transfers such as Bolsa Família lifted millions out of poverty. A huge corruption scandal, Car Wash, later engulfed his party, and he spent 580 days in prison from 2018 before the Supreme Court annulled his convictions in 2021. The far-right former army captain Jair Bolsonaro won in 2018. Lula beat him narrowly in 2022, and on 8 January 2023 Bolsonaro supporters stormed Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential palace. In 2025 Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years for plotting a coup, and in October 2026 Lula narrowly beat his son Flávio to win a fourth term.

Brazil has about 213 million people and covers nearly half of South America. It holds about 60% of the Amazon rainforest, which it shares with seven other countries and French Guiana, and is the world's biggest exporter of soybeans, coffee and beef, much of it to China. With Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay it founded the Mercosur trade bloc in 1991. On 25 October 2026 President Lula narrowly beat Flávio Bolsonaro in a runoff to win a fourth term.

Lula, president in 2003–2010 and again since 2023, won a fourth term in the 25 October runoff with about 52% of the vote. Flávio, son of ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, had led the first round and did not formally concede.

Founded 1991; Bolivia became a full member in 2024

Argentina is Brazil's main partner and old rival in South America, and its third-largest trading partner after China and the US.

Paraguay and Brazil share the Itaipu dam on the Paraná River, one of the world's largest hydroelectric plants.

dd-brazil.q: What shaped Brazil into a deeply unequal society?
a: Sugar, gold, coffee and slavery, with land held by a small elite
dd-brazil.why: Nearly 5 million enslaved Africans worked plantations and mines, and abolition in 1888 brought no land or compensation, leaving power with a small elite.

dd-brazil.p:
Members with Brazil and Bolivia of the Amazon Cooperation Treaty

The Amazon River rises in the Peruvian Andes. The Amazon Cooperation Treaty of 1978 links the eight countries that share the basin.

Colombia and Brazil share a long border deep in the rainforest, where illegal mining and drug routes cross.

The Amazon is the world's largest rainforest, and about 60% of it lies in Brazil. Since the 1970s highways, cattle ranches, soy farms and illegal mining have cleared roughly a fifth of Brazil's share. Scientists warn that if too much is lost, parts of the forest could dry out and turn into savanna, releasing vast amounts of carbon. Clearing rose under Bolsonaro and fell sharply after Lula returned in 2023, dropping for a fourth year in a row in 2025, according to the space agency INPE. The forest is also home to hundreds of Indigenous peoples, and in 2025 Brazil hosted the COP30 climate summit at Belém.

Brazil has about 213 million people, Latin America's largest economy and the largest share of the Amazon rainforest. It is a farming superpower and a voice for the Global South in the BRICS group. Its politics are sharply split: in 2025 its Supreme Court sentenced former president Jair Bolsonaro to 27 years for plotting a coup, and in October 2026 Lula narrowly beat his son Flávio in a presidential runoff to win a fourth term.

Military dictatorship

dd-japan.p: In 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu won the battle of Sekigahara, and from 1603 his family ruled Japan as shoguns from Edo for over 250 years, while the emperor stayed in Kyoto with little power. Fearing Christian missionaries and foreign meddling, the shoguns banned Christianity, expelled the Portuguese in 1639 and confined Dutch traders to the island of Dejima. Japan enjoyed long peace, growing cities and a rich urban culture.

items: Followed bushido, the way of the warrior.

dd-japan.why: Shoguns ruled in the emperor’s name.

dd-japan.p: In 1853 Commodore Perry's American warships arrived at Uraga and forced treaties on the shogun. Rebel samurai overthrew him in 1868 in the name of Emperor Meiji, and the new government rebuilt Japan on Western lines so fast that by 1905 it had defeated Russia.

dd-japan.q: What did the Meiji Restoration of 1868 do?
a: Restored the shogun's power over the emperor
Toppled the shogun and rebuilt Japan rapidly on Western lines
Closed Japan to all foreign trade
Made Japan a colony of the United States
dd-japan.why: Rebel samurai overthrew the shogun in the emperor's name, and the new government modernised so fast that Japan defeated Russia by 1905.

dd-japan.p: Seclusion grew from the shoguns' fear that Christianity and European powers could split the country, as rival lords had done in the century of civil war before 1600. Japan opened because it had no answer to steam-powered warships, and China's defeat in the Opium War showed what resisting could cost. The shogun's surrender to foreign demands discredited him, and samurai from Satsuma and Choshu concluded that only a strong, modern state under the emperor could keep Japan independent.

dd-japan.h: Tokugawa Japan and its few windows, c. 1700
dd-japan.p: After 1639 the Tokugawa shoguns, ruling from Edo, kept most foreigners out of Japan and banned Japanese from going abroad. Trade did not stop, it was channelled: Dutch merchants were confined to the tiny island of Dejima in Nagasaki harbour, Chinese traders lived in a walled quarter of the same city, and Korea traded through the island of Tsushima.

dd-japan.q: What did Japan become after the Meiji reforms?
a: A neutral country with no army
The first non-Western industrial nation and an Asian great power
dd-japan.why: Japan industrialised, won Taiwan in 1895, beat Russia in 1905 and annexed Korea in 1910, ruling its colonies harshly.

dd-japan.p:
The shogun in Edo, about 260 lords in their domains

The shoguns ruled Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu. Hokkaido was mostly Ainu land, reached through the Matsumae domain in the far south, and the Ryukyu kingdom (Okinawa) was under Satsuma's control from 1609.

The only Europeans allowed to trade

The Dutch East India Company won the trade because it did not try to spread Christianity. Its men were moved to Dejima in 1641 and rarely allowed to leave.

Came to Nagasaki on their own junks

Chinese merchants were Japan's biggest trading partners, bringing silk, sugar and books, and from 1689 they had to live in a walled quarter of Nagasaki.

Under the Tokugawa, the emperor reigned in Kyoto while the shogun ruled from Edo. About 260 lords, the daimyo, governed their own domains but were tightly watched: under the system of 'alternate attendance' they had to spend every other year in Edo and leave their wives and heirs there as virtual hostages. The samurai were a hereditary warrior class who alone could wear two swords, but with no wars to fight for over two centuries most became salaried officials and clerks. Society was ranked into samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants, yet merchants often grew rich while many samurai fell into debt.

dd-japan.h: Perry's black ships force Japan open, 1853–1858
dd-japan.p: In July 1853 Commodore Matthew Perry steamed into the bay at Uraga with four warships, carrying a letter demanding that Japan open its ports to the United States. He returned in 1854 with more ships and got a treaty. By 1858 Japan had signed unequal treaties with the US, Britain, France, Russia and the Netherlands, and the shogun's weakness in giving way set off his fall.
Japan's leaders had watched Britain defeat China in the Opium War (1839–42). Facing modern warships with no modern navy of their own, they chose to sign rather than fight.

dd-japan.q: Why did the Tokugawa shoguns close Japan to most foreigners?
a: They feared Christianity and European powers could split the country
dd-japan.why: Remembering the civil wars before 1600, the shoguns banned Christianity, expelled the Portuguese and confined Dutch traders to Dejima.

dd-japan.p:
The 'Ansei treaties' with five Western powers

The US wanted coal and supplies for its ships in the Pacific and safe treatment for shipwrecked sailors. The 1858 Harris Treaty opened more ports and set low tariffs.

Britain signed a treaty in 1858 on terms like America's: foreigners in Japan were tried in their own consular courts, not Japanese ones.

The word sakoku, 'closed country', was only coined in 1801, and Japan was never fully sealed. It traded through four gateways: Nagasaki, where the Dutch lived on Dejima, a fan-shaped artificial island about 120 metres long, and Chinese merchants in their own quarter; Tsushima for Korea; Satsuma for the Ryukyu kingdom; and Matsumae for the Ainu of Hokkaido. What was banned was Christianity, Portuguese and Spanish ships, and Japanese travel abroad, on pain of death. Through Dutch books, Japanese scholars studied European medicine and astronomy, a field called 'Dutch learning' (rangaku).

dd-japan.q: Why does the Meiji model still matter to Asia today?
a: Its state-led catch-up influenced later Asian economies
It ended all empires in Asia
It made Japan Asia's only democracy
It kept Japan out of every later war
dd-japan.why: Meiji Japan showed a state could deliberately drive rapid modernisation, a model of state-led catch-up that influenced later Asian economies.

dd-japan.p: In 1868 rebel samurai from Satsuma and Choshu toppled the shogun and restored power to the young Emperor Meiji. The new government copied Western industry, schools and armed forces at great speed. Japan then built an empire: it won Taiwan from China in 1895, beat Russia in 1905 and gained southern Sakhalin, and annexed Korea in 1910.

Including Hokkaido (from 1869) and Okinawa (from 1879)

The Meiji government abolished the domains in 1871, ended the samurai class, brought in conscription in 1873 and a constitution in 1889. Hokkaido and Okinawa were absorbed as Japanese land.

dd-japan.q: Why did Japan give way to Perry's black ships in 1853–54?
a: Perry offered to make the shogun emperor
It had no answer to steam warships and feared China's fate
dd-japan.why: Without a modern navy, and having watched Britain defeat China in the Opium War, Japan's leaders chose to sign treaties rather than fight.

dd-japan.p:
Taiwan 1895, Korea 1910

China ceded Taiwan after losing the 1894–95 war over Korea. Japan crushed local resistance and ruled the island as a colony until 1945.

Japan made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in August 1910, ruling it harshly until 1945.

The Meiji leaders worked under the slogan 'rich country, strong army'. In 1871 they abolished the domains and replaced them with prefectures, and in 1871–73 the Iwakura Mission toured the US and Europe to study how modern states worked. The government ended samurai privileges, created a conscript army, built the first railway from Tokyo to Yokohama in 1872, set up state factories and made schooling compulsory. Not everyone agreed: in 1877 discontented samurai under Saigo Takamori rose in the Satsuma Rebellion and were crushed by the new army. The 1889 constitution created a parliament but left great power with the emperor and the military.

Japan became the first non-Western country to industrialise and the first Asian great power of modern times. It won Taiwan in 1895, defeated Russia in 1905 and annexed Korea in 1910, and its victory inspired nationalists across Asia even as its own colonial rule was harsh. The same drive for empire later carried Japan into China and the Pacific War. The Meiji model of state-led catch-up influenced later Asian economies.

Portuguese expelled; Dutch moved to Dejima in 1641
Perry's black ships arrive at Uraga

Japan adopts its first constitution
Japan defeats Russia; Korea annexed in 1910

dd-australia.p: In January 1788 the First Fleet landed convicts and marines at Sydney Cove, founding a British penal colony on land Aboriginal peoples had lived on for at least 50,000 years. Over the next century Britain set up six colonies around the continent and sent about 160,000 convicts until 1868. Free settlers, sheep farming and the gold rushes of the 1850s drew far more people, as frontier violence and disease devastated Aboriginal communities.

steps: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples: the oldest living cultures.
The First Fleet founds a British convict colony at Sydney.
Immigrants pour in; colonies grow rich.

dd-australia.s: Indigenous Australians were counted in the national census from 1967.

dd-australia.p: In New Zealand, Māori chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi with Britain in 1840, but wars and land confiscations followed. Australia federated in 1901 and New Zealand became a dominion in 1907. Both fought at Gallipoli in 1915 and grew into prosperous, independent democracies.

dd-australia.q: What did the First Fleet found at Sydney Cove in 1788?
a: A British penal colony on Aboriginal land
dd-australia.why: Convicts and marines landed on land Aboriginal peoples had lived on for at least 50,000 years; Britain sent about 160,000 convicts until 1868.

dd-australia.p: Britain needed a new dumping ground for convicts after losing America, and wanted a foothold in the Pacific. Its law treated Australia as terra nullius, land belonging to no one, so no treaty was made there, while in New Zealand the strength of Māori and missionary pressure led to a treaty. Cheap land, wool and gold then pulled in settlers, whose demand for land drove conflict with Indigenous peoples.

After losing its American colonies, which had taken about 50,000 of its convicts, Britain needed a new place to send them. In May 1787 eleven ships, the First Fleet, sailed for Australia with about 1,400 people, over 750 of them convicts. On 26 January 1788 they raised the British flag at Sydney Cove, on land where Aboriginal people had lived for at least 50,000 years.

dd-australia.q: What did settlers' demand for land bring to Indigenous peoples?
a: Protection under the Treaty of Waitangi in Australia
Frontier violence, disease, wars and land confiscations
dd-australia.why: In Australia frontier violence and disease devastated Aboriginal communities, while in New Zealand wars from 1845 to 1872 brought huge confiscations of Māori land.

dd-australia.p:
Sent about 160,000 convicts to Australia, 1788–1868

Britain's prisons and old prison ships were overflowing, and transportation was the usual sentence for many crimes, including theft.

Tens of thousands of the convicts were Irish, some of them rebels against British rule.

Took British convicts until the American Revolution

Britain had sent convicts to its American colonies until the War of Independence began in 1775.

New South Wales, claimed by Britain from 1788

James Cook had claimed the east coast for Britain in 1770. Britain treated the land as terra nullius, belonging to no one, though hundreds of Aboriginal nations lived there.

Most convicts were transported for theft, often petty, usually for seven or fourteen years. The first years at Sydney were hungry: crops failed and the colony waited anxiously for supply ships. Convicts were assigned to work for the government or free settlers, building roads and clearing land, and harsh punishments, from flogging to remote prisons such as Port Arthur in Tasmania, awaited those who broke the rules. Many who served their time, called emancipists, stayed on, farmed and prospered. Transportation to New South Wales ended in 1840 and to Western Australia in 1868. For the Eora people of Sydney, the colony's arrival brought a smallpox epidemic in 1789 that killed many.

Britain founded colonies around Australia's coast, from Tasmania in 1803 to Western Australia in 1829. Settlers and their sheep pushed inland, and frontier violence and new diseases devastated Aboriginal peoples. In New Zealand the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi led to British rule, then to wars over Māori land. Gold rushes from 1851 brought waves of migrants, and in 1901 the six colonies federated as the Commonwealth of Australia.

Six British colonies, federated in 1901

Historians estimate that frontier violence killed tens of thousands of Aboriginal people, and that disease killed far more. Federation came in 1901, and one of the first laws began the White Australia policy.

dd-australia.q: Why did Britain send convicts to Australia?
a: It had lost America and needed a new place for them
Gold had already been found there
France had offered to share the land
dd-australia.why: America had taken about 50,000 British convicts before independence, so overflowing prisons needed a new destination, and Britain also wanted a Pacific foothold.

dd-australia.p:
British colony from 1840, a dominion from 1907

The English and Māori texts of the Treaty of Waitangi differ on what chiefs gave up. Wars from 1845 to 1872 and land confiscations followed. In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote.

On 6 February 1840 dozens of Māori chiefs signed a treaty with the British Crown at Waitangi, and over 500 signed in the months that followed. The English text says the chiefs ceded sovereignty. The Māori text uses 'kāwanatanga', governance, and promises chiefs 'tino rangatiratanga', full authority over their lands and treasures. That gap has shaped New Zealand ever since. Disputes over land led to the New Zealand Wars of 1845–1872 and huge confiscations. Since 1975 the Waitangi Tribunal has investigated breaches, leading to settlements with many iwi. In April 2025 Parliament voted down a bill to redefine the treaty's principles, by 112 votes to 11, after large Māori-led protests.

dd-australia.q: How have both countries tried to reckon with their colonial past?
a: Through land rights, the Waitangi Tribunal and official apologies
By returning all land to Indigenous owners
dd-australia.why: The Mabo case, the 2008 apology and the Waitangi Tribunal marked change, though debates continue, as in Australia's 2023 vote against an Indigenous Voice.

dd-australia.p: Once overwhelmingly British, Australia opened to Asian migrants after the White Australia policy ended in the 1970s. In the 2021 census over a quarter of Australians had been born overseas, most often in England, India, China, New Zealand and the Philippines. New Zealand has close family ties with Pacific islands such as Samoa and the Cook Islands, and Māori make up about one in six of its people.

About 27.6% of Australians were born overseas in 2021. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were 3.2% of those counted.

In the 2023 census about 17.8% of New Zealanders identified as Māori. Te reo Māori has been an official language since 1987.

With India, the largest birthplace of migrants to Australia

England was the top overseas birthplace in Australia's 2021 census, with over 900,000 people. King Charles III is still head of state of both countries.

dd-australia.q: Why was a treaty made in New Zealand but not in Australia?
a: Māori asked to be ruled by Britain
Britain treated Australia as terra nullius, while Māori strength forced a treaty
dd-australia.why: British law called Australia land belonging to no one, but in New Zealand Māori strength and missionary pressure led to the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi.

dd-australia.p:
Among the top birthplaces of Australians born abroad

India passed China and New Zealand to become the second-largest overseas birthplace in Australia in 2021, with about 670,000 people.

Chinese miners came in the 1850s gold rushes. In 2021 about 550,000 Australians had been born in China.

In a 1967 referendum about 91% of Australians voted to let the federal government make laws for Aboriginal people and count them in the census. In 1992 the High Court's Mabo decision rejected terra nullius and recognised native title. A 1997 inquiry found that between one in three and one in ten Indigenous children had been taken from their families between about 1910 and 1970, the Stolen Generations, and in 2008 Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologised in Parliament. In October 2023 about 60% of voters rejected a proposal to give Indigenous Australians a constitutional Voice to Parliament. Supporters saw a lost chance at recognition; many opponents said it would divide Australians by race.

Both countries became stable democracies and early pioneers of votes for women. For decades Australia kept a White Australia immigration policy, removed many Aboriginal children from their families and denied Indigenous land rights. Since the 1960s both have tried to reckon with that past, through land rights, the Waitangi Tribunal and official apologies, and today both are diverse countries drawing many migrants from Asia and the Pacific.

dd-frenchrev.p: In May 1789 a bankrupt Louis XVI called the Estates-General for the first time since 1614. The commoners' deputies proclaimed a National Assembly, Parisians stormed the Bastille on 14 July, and in August the Assembly abolished noble privileges and declared the Rights of Man. In 1791 the king tried to flee, and in 1792, with Austria and Prussia invading, crowds overthrew the monarchy and a republic was declared.

steps: Wars, including helping America, bankrupted the crown.
Clergy and nobles paid little; the Third Estate paid most.
Bad harvests in 1788 doubled the price of bread.
Enlightenment talk of rights and consent.

items: About 0.5% of people; paid almost no tax.

dd-frenchrev.q: What was the motto of the Revolution?

dd-frenchrev.p: Louis was guillotined in January 1793. Under Robespierre's Committee of Public Safety, the Terror executed thousands of suspected enemies until his own fall in July 1794. A weak Directory followed, until General Bonaparte seized power in November 1799.

dd-frenchrev.q: What did the French Revolution do to France's monarchy between 1789 and 1793?
a: It made the king share power with Austria
It overthrew the monarchy, declared a republic and executed Louis XVI
It restored the king's absolute power after a short revolt
It replaced Louis XVI with his brother
dd-frenchrev.why: Crowds overthrew the monarchy in 1792, a republic was declared, and Louis XVI was guillotined in January 1793.

dd-frenchrev.p: France's crown was deep in debt after costly wars, including its help for the American revolutionaries, and the nobles and clergy were largely exempt from tax. Bad harvests in 1788 sent bread prices soaring. Enlightenment writers had taught educated people to question privilege and divine-right monarchy. Once the old order cracked, war, fear of counter-revolution and hunger pushed politics to extremes. Historians still debate how far the revolution was driven by class, ideas or chance.

In 1789 France, western Europe's most populous kingdom with about 28 million people, was bankrupt. Louis XVI called the Estates-General to Versailles, its commoners declared themselves a National Assembly, and Paris crowds stormed the Bastille. By 1793 the king was dead, and the republic was fighting rebels in the west and south. In the richest colony, Saint-Domingue, today's Haiti, enslaved people rose in 1791, and France abolished slavery in 1794.

dd-frenchrev.q: How did the revolution's ideas spread beyond France?
a: Through the Catholic Church's support for the republic
Through Britain, which adopted the revolution's constitution
Through its wars, continued by Napoleon, and French-style sister republics
dd-frenchrev.why: France's armies conquered Belgium, the Rhineland and more, and set up sister republics such as the Batavian and Helvetic, spreading equal citizenship and written constitutions.

dd-frenchrev.p:
Kingdom until 1792, then the First Republic

France was split into three estates: clergy, nobles and everyone else, about 97% of the people. In August 1789 the Assembly abolished noble privileges and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.

France's richest colony

Saint-Domingue produced much of the world's sugar and coffee, worked by about half a million enslaved people. Their revolt from 1791 led France's commissioners to free them in 1793, and Paris abolished slavery in all French colonies in 1794.

In September 1793, with France invaded and in revolt, the Convention passed the Law of Suspects, allowing the arrest of anyone thought hostile to the revolution. According to Britannica, at least 300,000 people were arrested, about 17,000 were officially executed, and perhaps 10,000 more died in prison or without trial. Most victims were not nobles but peasants and townspeople, many from rebel regions such as the Vendée. The guillotine, adopted in 1792 as a humane and equal method, became its symbol. The revolution's leaders turned on each other: Danton was executed in April 1794, and Robespierre himself on 28 July, the day after his arrest.

In April 1792 France declared war on Austria, which held today's Belgium, and Prussia joined in. After Louis XVI's execution in 1793, Britain, the Dutch Republic, Spain and others joined the First Coalition. Facing invasion and revolt, the republic conscripted all unmarried men aged 18 to 25 and fielded the largest armies Europe had seen. By 1795 it had won Belgium, the Netherlands and the Rhineland.
The levée en masse of August 1793 put the whole nation on a war footing. France's armies grew to several hundred thousand men, led by officers promoted for talent rather than birth.

dd-frenchrev.q: Why did Louis XVI call the Estates-General in 1789?
a: He wanted to declare war on Britain
Paris crowds had already stormed the Bastille
His crown was bankrupt, and nobles and clergy paid little tax
The pope ordered him to reform the Church
dd-frenchrev.why: Wars, including France's help for the American revolutionaries, left the crown deep in debt, while the nobles and clergy were largely exempt from tax.

dd-frenchrev.p:
Habsburg lands, Prussia and the Holy Roman Empire

Austria was the main enemy on land. It lost the Austrian Netherlands and, after Napoleon's Italian campaign, made peace at Campo Formio in 1797.

The Austrian Netherlands changed hands twice before France won them in 1794. They were annexed to France in 1795.

Britain joined the war in February 1793. Its navy blockaded France and seized French colonies, and it paid allies to fight on land.

French armies crossed the frozen rivers in the winter of 1794–95. The Dutch Republic became the Batavian Republic, a French ally.

dd-frenchrev.q: Which of these is a lasting legacy of the French Revolution?
a: The metric system and the political words 'left' and 'right'
dd-frenchrev.why: The revolutionary calendar and decimal time did not last, but the metric system is used almost everywhere and 'left' and 'right' still describe politics.

dd-frenchrev.p: The revolutionaries set out to rebuild daily life on reason. A new calendar started at Year I, from the republic's founding in September 1792. It had twelve months of 30 days with names drawn from nature, such as Thermidor, the month of heat, and ten-day weeks with only one day of rest. It was used until the end of 1805. Decimal clocks, with ten-hour days, were tried for only about 17 months. The metric system was a lasting success: the metre was defined in 1791 as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, and it is now used almost everywhere.

Victories let France annex Belgium, the Rhineland, Savoy and Nice, and surround itself with 'sister republics' modelled on its own: the Batavian in the Netherlands, the Helvetic in Switzerland, and several in Italy. A Second Coalition, of Britain, Austria, Russia and the Ottomans, struck back in 1799. That November, General Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in a coup.

Including the Rhineland, held from 1794

After the Terror ended in 1794, a five-man Directory ruled from 1795. It was weak and corrupt, depended on the army, and was toppled by Bonaparte in 1799.

Belgium was annexed in 1795 and divided into French departments, with French law, conscription and the closing of monasteries.

Batavian, Helvetic, Cisalpine, Ligurian, Roman and Parthenopean

The Batavian Republic, proclaimed in 1795, abolished the old provinces' privileges and gave the Netherlands its first national constitution in 1798.

France invaded the old Swiss Confederation in 1798 and set up the centralised Helvetic Republic. Geneva was annexed to France.

dd-frenchrev.q: What pushed the revolution towards the Terror after 1792?
a: War, fear of counter-revolution and hunger
A peace treaty with Austria and Prussia
The return of the king from Varennes as a popular hero
dd-frenchrev.why: With France invaded and in revolt, the Law of Suspects of 1793 allowed mass arrests; about 17,000 people were officially executed.

dd-frenchrev.p:
At war with France from 1798–99

Britain's navy destroyed the French fleet at the Nile in August 1798. In Ireland the United Irishmen rose with French help in 1798, and were crushed.

The 1798 rising of the United Irishmen, inspired by the French Revolution, was put down with great loss of life. The Act of Union of 1800 then merged Ireland into the United Kingdom.

Women were central to the revolution's great days. In October 1789 thousands of Parisian market women marched to Versailles over the price of bread and brought the royal family back to Paris. In 1791 the playwright Olympe de Gouges published a 'Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen', arguing that women should share every right men had won. The republic legalised divorce in 1792, but it never gave women the vote. In 1793 it closed women's political clubs, and de Gouges was guillotined that November. French women won the vote only in 1944.

The revolution ended absolute monarchy and feudal privilege in France and made equal citizenship, written constitutions and national sovereignty central to modern politics. Its wars, continued by Napoleon, spread these ideas across Europe. It gave the world the words 'left' and 'right', the metric system and the model of the nation in arms. Its motto, 'Liberty, Equality, Fraternity', is still France's, and the storming of the Bastille is celebrated every 14 July.
