Latin alphabet replaces Arabic script
Turkey joins NATO
Military coups in 1960 and 1980
A coup attempt fails; mass purges follow
İmamoğlu is jailed; the PKK announces it will disband

items: Treaty of Lausanne; the Republic of Turkey is declared
A coup attempt fails; mass purges follow

dd-japanmodern.p: Japan surrendered in August 1945 after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet attack on Manchuria. US-led forces occupied it until 1952, writing a new constitution that made the emperor a symbol and renounced war. Allied to the United States, Japan rebuilt at astonishing speed: bullet trains ran from 1964, and by 1968 its economy was the world's second largest.

steps: Lost decades and an ageing society.

dd-japanmodern.p: The oldest population on Earth; it shrinks by about half a million a year.

In the 1980s Japanese cars and electronics dominated world markets, until a giant stock and property bubble burst in 1990–91. Decades of slow growth followed, along with the 2011 tsunami and nuclear disaster and a shrinking, ageing population.

Japan had an educated workforce, a strong state and industrial know-how left from before the war. The Cold War made the US want a strong Japanese ally, so it opened its markets, bought supplies for the Korean War and paid for most of Japan's defence. High savings, close cooperation between officials and big companies, and a cheap yen powered exports. Easy credit in the late 1980s inflated the bubble, and slow clean-up of bad debts after it burst prolonged the slump.

dd-japanmodern.q: What did the US-led occupation change about Japan after 1945?
a: It annexed Japan to the United States
A new constitution made the emperor a symbol and renounced war
It restored the emperor's full powers
It divided Japan into US and Soviet zones
dd-japanmodern.why: The 1947 constitution, drafted by MacArthur's staff, made the emperor a symbol, gave women the vote, and its Article 9 renounces war.

dd-japanmodern.p: In August 1945 US atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the Soviet Union attacked, and Japan surrendered. It lost everything it had gained since 1895: Taiwan, Korea, Manchuria and its other conquests in China, and its Pacific islands. American forces under General Douglas MacArthur occupied Japan until 1952, disarmed it and gave it a democratic constitution that renounced war.

Occupied by Allied, mainly US, forces, 1945–1952

About 3 million Japanese died in the war. The occupation broke up big business groups, gave women the vote and land to tenant farmers, and kept the emperor as a symbol without power.

Taiwan from 1895, Korea from 1910

Taiwan passed to the Republic of China in 1945. Its government fled there in 1949 after losing China's civil war.

Korea was freed from Japanese rule in August 1945 but split at the 38th parallel between US and Soviet forces.

dd-japanmodern.q: What long-term problem has Japan faced since 2008?
a: Losing its alliance with the United States
dd-japanmodern.why: Japan's population has fallen since 2008; nearly 3 in 10 people are 65 or over, and births in 2025 were the lowest on record.

dd-japanmodern.p:
Manchuria from 1931 and much of eastern China from 1937

China suffered more than any other country from Japan's war, with estimates of 10–20 million or more dead. Japanese troops there surrendered in September 1945.

On 15 August 1945 most Japanese heard their emperor's voice for the first time, on the radio, telling them to 'endure the unendurable'. The occupation that followed, under General Douglas MacArthur, aimed to make Japan peaceful and democratic. Women won the vote, unions were legalised, the big family-owned business groups were broken up, and landlords had to sell land to their tenants. Emperor Hirohito was not put on trial; in 1946 he denied that he was divine. A Tokyo tribunal sentenced seven wartime leaders, including Prime Minister Hideki Tojo, to death. The constitution of 1947, drafted by MacArthur's staff, has never been amended, and its Article 9 still renounces war.

Between the mid-1950s and early 1970s Japan's economy grew about 10% a year. Millions moved from farms to cities, and families bought the 'three sacred treasures' of the 1950s: a television, a washing machine and a fridge. Big companies offered lifetime jobs to male workers in return for long hours and loyalty, and the trade ministry, MITI, steered investment into steel, ships, cars and electronics. Toyota's lean production and Sony's transistor radios and Walkman became famous worldwide. Growth had costs too: pollution scandals such as Minamata disease, caused by factory mercury, poisoned thousands. By the 1980s many Americans feared that Japan would overtake the US.

Independent again from 1952, Japan relied on the United States for defence and poured its energy into growth. Bullet trains opened for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and by 1968 Japan had the world's second-largest economy. It restored ties with South Korea in 1965 and China in 1972. Toyota, Sony and Honda conquered world markets, and by 1989 a stock and property bubble made Japan seem unstoppable.

World's second-largest economy, 1968–2010

Japan's economy grew about 10% a year in the 1950s and 1960s. One party, the Liberal Democratic Party, governed without a break from 1955 to 1993.

dd-japanmodern.q: Why did the Cold War help Japan's economy recover so quickly?
a: The Soviet Union paid reparations to Japan
Japan sold weapons to both sides
The US wanted a strong ally, so opened markets and defended it
dd-japanmodern.why: The US bought supplies for the Korean War, opened its markets to Japanese goods and covered most of Japan's defence, freeing it to focus on growth.

dd-japanmodern.p:
Security treaty since 1951, revised in 1960

The US kept bases in Japan, opened its market to Japanese goods and bought supplies there for the Korean War. By the 1980s, trade deficits with Japan caused anger in Washington.

South Korea in 1965, China in 1972

The 1965 treaty restored relations and gave South Korea $800 million in grants and loans, which helped fund its growth. Disputes over colonial-era wrongs continued.

Japan and China restored relations in September 1972. Japanese aid and investment later helped China's opening-up after 1978.

dd-japanmodern.q: How is Japan responding to China's rise and North Korea's missiles today?
a: By stretching its pacifist constitution and spending more on defence
By ending its alliance with the US
dd-japanmodern.why: Under Sanae Takaichi, its first woman prime minister, Japan is raising defence spending while remaining a close US ally.

dd-japanmodern.p: In the late 1980s cheap credit drove share and land prices to absurd heights: at the peak, the land under Tokyo's Imperial Palace was said to be worth more than all of California. The Nikkei stock index hit 38,916 on 29 December 1989, then lost most of its value, and did not pass that peak again until February 2024. Banks sat on bad loans, prices fell for years, and growth stalled; China overtook Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010. Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's 'Abenomics' from 2012 used cheap money and spending to fight deflation. Abe was assassinated in 2022, and inflation has finally returned, though wages have struggled to keep up.

Japan remains a close ally of the United States and the world's fourth-largest economy, but its population is shrinking and ageing. It disputes islands with Russia, China and South Korea, and North Korean missiles have flown over it. Sanae Takaichi, Japan's first woman prime minister, won a landslide in February 2026, and is raising defence spending amid a deep chill with China.

Japan had about 122 million people in 2026, with a record 29.6% aged 65 or over and only about 671,000 Japanese births in 2025. In 2025 it raised defence spending to about 2% of GDP, ahead of schedule.

About 55,000 US troops are based in Japan

Under the 1960 security treaty the US defends Japan, including, it has said, the Senkaku Islands. Japan hosts more US troops than any other country.

a: A stock and property bubble, inflated by easy credit, burst
A US ban on Japanese cars
dd-japanmodern.why: Cheap credit drove share and land prices to absurd heights; when the bubble burst, slow clean-up of bad debts prolonged the slump into the 'lost decades'.

dd-japanmodern.p:
Southern Kurils, Senkaku Islands, Takeshima/Dokdo

Russia holds the four islands Japan claims off Hokkaido. It broke off peace treaty talks in 2022 after Japan backed sanctions over Ukraine.

China is Japan's largest trading partner. After Takaichi said in November 2025 that an attack on Taiwan could threaten Japan's survival, China halted Japanese seafood imports and urged its citizens not to travel there.

Japan has one of the world's oldest populations. Its people peaked at about 128 million in 2008, and in 2025 only about 671,000 Japanese babies were born there, the lowest since records began in 1899. The 2025 census found 29% of people aged 65 or over, and millions of homes in the countryside stand empty. Japan has turned to robots and to older workers, and, more cautiously, to immigrants: a record of almost 4.3 million foreign residents lived there in mid-2026, though immigration is a growing political issue. With few children and high costs, many young people delay marriage, and the government has repeatedly expanded child benefits with little effect on birth rates so far.

Japan is still the world's fourth-largest economy, a technology leader and a cultural power, from anime to sushi. But its population has fallen since 2008, and nearly 3 in 10 people are 65 or over. Facing China's rise and North Korea's missiles, it has stretched its pacifist constitution, and under Sanae Takaichi, its first woman prime minister, who won a landslide in February 2026, it is spending more on defence.

pts: Atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki; Japan surrenders
The new constitution renounces war
Tokyo hosts the Olympics; the first bullet train opens
The bubble bursts, starting the 'lost decades'
Earthquake, tsunami and the Fukushima nuclear disaster
Sanae Takaichi becomes Japan's first woman prime minister

items: Atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki; Japan surrenders
Tokyo hosts the Olympics; the first bullet train opens
The bubble bursts, starting the 'lost decades'
Earthquake, tsunami and the Fukushima nuclear disaster

dd-india.p: India became independent in 1947 and a republic in 1950, with a constitution guaranteeing votes for all adults. Jawaharlal Nehru's Congress governments built a secular, state-planned economy and steered clear of Cold War blocs. His daughter Indira Gandhi helped Bangladesh break away in 1971, suspended democracy during the 1975–77 Emergency, and was assassinated in 1984.

items: Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu and more.

dd-india.q: Which is the most populous country?

dd-india.p: A debt crisis in 1991 forced market reforms that unleashed faster growth. From the 1990s the Hindu nationalist BJP rose, and since 2014 Narendra Modi has led India, winning a third term in 2024. By 2023 India was the world's most populous country.

India's founders inherited a poor, mostly rural and illiterate country of hundreds of languages, castes and faiths, and chose federal democracy to hold it together. The state-led economy brought steel, dams and the Green Revolution's food security, but growth stayed slow, which made the 1991 reforms possible. Politics shifted as lower castes, regional parties and Hindu nationalism challenged Congress's dominance, and Modi's mix of welfare, infrastructure and Hindu identity won wide support.

dd-india.q: What kind of state did India's founders build after independence?
a: A military-run state allied to the Soviet Union
A monarchy under the former British viceroy
A secular federal democracy with votes for all adults
dd-india.why: The 1950 constitution gave every adult the vote, and Nehru's Congress governments built a secular, state-planned economy outside the Cold War blocs.

dd-india.p: Jawaharlal Nehru, prime minister from 1947 until his death in 1964, built India as a secular democracy with a state-led economy of dams and steel mills. Abroad he refused to join either Cold War bloc and, with leaders of Yugoslavia, Egypt, Indonesia and Ghana, founded the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961. That year India took Goa from Portugal. In 1962 a border war with China ended in a humiliating defeat.

A republic from 26 January 1950

India's first general election, in 1951–52, had about 173 million voters, most of them unable to read, who chose parties by symbols. Nehru's Congress party won easily.

Belgrade summit, 1961

Yugoslavia's Tito hosted the first Non-Aligned summit in Belgrade in 1961. He, Nehru and Egypt's Nasser were the movement's leading figures.

Gamal Abdel Nasser, Nehru's close partner, gave the movement Arab and African weight after the 1956 Suez Crisis.

dd-india.q: How did Indian politics shift from the 1990s?
a: The Congress party won every election until 2024
India abolished elections for a decade
Lower castes, regional parties and Hindu nationalism challenged Congress
India adopted a one-party communist system
dd-india.why: The Hindu nationalist BJP rose, and since 2014 Narendra Modi has led India with a mix of welfare, infrastructure and Hindu identity.

dd-india.p:
Border war, October–November 1962

China and India disputed borders in the west and the east. China's 1962 attack shocked India, and the long frontier, the Line of Actual Control, is still not agreed.

The constitution, drafted under the Dalit lawyer B. R. Ambedkar, gave every adult the vote in 1950, when most Indians could not read, so parties used symbols such as a hand, a lotus or an elephant. It abolished 'untouchability' and reserved seats, jobs and university places for the lowest castes and tribes. In 2024 nearly 970 million people were eligible to vote over six weeks, using electronic machines, with polling stations within about 2 kilometres of every voter, including one for a single monk in a Gir forest temple. Only once was democracy suspended: during Indira Gandhi's 1975–77 Emergency, after which voters threw her out.

The Congress party was long led by one family, unrelated to Mahatma Gandhi. Nehru governed for 17 years. His daughter Indira won the 1971 war, but in 1975, after a court voided her election, declared an Emergency, jailing opponents and running a forced sterilisation drive. In 1984 she sent the army into the Golden Temple in Amritsar against Sikh militants; months later her Sikh bodyguards shot her, and mobs killed about 3,000 Sikhs in Delhi. Her son Rajiv was killed by a Tamil Tiger bomber in 1991. Rajiv's Italian-born widow Sonia led Congress back to power in 2004, and their son Rahul Gandhi led the opposition after 2024.

Indira Gandhi made India the dominant power in South Asia. In 1971 Indian troops helped Bangladesh win independence from Pakistan, and in 1974 India tested a nuclear device. Later governments sent peacekeepers to Sri Lanka and foiled a coup in the Maldives. Rivalry with China and Pakistan, both nuclear powers, remained the great danger: in 2020 Indian and Chinese soldiers fought with clubs and stones in the Himalayas.
India's wars with Pakistan, from 1947 to the clash of May 2025, are covered in the partition deep dive.

dd-india.q: Why did India's founders choose federal democracy?
a: To hold together a poor country of many languages, castes and faiths
Because Britain required it as a condition of independence
Because most Indians were already literate voters
dd-india.why: They inherited a poor, mostly rural and illiterate country of hundreds of languages, castes and faiths, and saw federal democracy as the way to keep it united.

dd-india.p:
Bangladesh 1971, Sri Lanka 1987–90, Maldives 1988

In 1971 Pakistan's army cracked down on East Pakistan, and about 10 million refugees fled to India. India intervened in December, and Pakistan's forces in Dhaka surrendered after 13 days.

About 1,200 Indian soldiers died fighting the Tamil Tigers in 1987–90. In 1991 a Tamil Tiger suicide bomber killed Rajiv Gandhi, who had sent the troops.

Border disputes and wars

China is India's biggest source of imports and its main strategic rival. After the 2020 clash both sides kept tens of thousands of troops on the border; they agreed on patrolling in 2024.

Pakistan tested nuclear weapons weeks after India in 1998. The two have fought four wars and many clashes, mostly over Kashmir.

dd-india.q: What is India's position in the world today?
a: The most populous country, partnering with both the West and Russia
A small economy cut off from world trade
dd-india.why: India passed China in population in 2023, works with the US, Japan and Australia in the Quad, and still buys Russian oil and arms.

dd-india.p: For decades the 'Licence Raj' required permits to open or expand a business, and growth averaged about 3.5 percent a year, a rate mocked as the 'Hindu rate of growth'. In 1991 India had foreign currency left for only a few weeks of imports and pledged its gold reserves abroad. Finance Minister Manmohan Singh cut tariffs, scrapped licences and welcomed foreign investors. Growth roughly doubled. Software firms in Bengaluru and Hyderabad served the world, and a vast middle class grew. Under Modi, India built highways, airports and a digital payments system, UPI, that handles billions of transactions a month, though manufacturing jobs have lagged.

With over 1.4 billion people, India passed China as the most populous country in 2023, and by IMF estimates it is the sixth-largest economy, forecast to pass Britain and Japan in 2027. It works with the United States, Japan and Australia in the Quad, but also belongs to BRICS with China, Russia and others, and buys Russian oil and arms. Some 35 million people of Indian origin live abroad, many in the Gulf, Britain and North America.
India sent more money home from abroad than any other country, about $130 billion in remittances in 2024. Its income per person was still about a twelfth of Japan's.

US, Japan, Australia: an Indo-Pacific security group

About 5 million people of Indian origin live in the US. In 2025 the US raised tariffs on Indian goods to 50%, partly over Russian oil; an interim deal in February 2026 cut them sharply.

Japan, a Quad partner, has funded India's metro systems and its first high-speed railway, between Mumbai and Ahmedabad.

a: A debt crisis that left India almost out of foreign currency
A demand from the Non-Aligned Movement
dd-india.why: With currency for only a few weeks of imports, India cut tariffs and scrapped the 'Licence Raj', and growth roughly doubled.

dd-india.p:
With India: Brazil, Russia, China, South Africa

India kept buying Russian arms and, after 2022, became one of the largest buyers of Russian oil, declining to join Western sanctions.

India passed China in population in 2023, by UN estimates. China's economy was still more than four times larger.

Narendra Modi, who says he sold tea as a boy, was an organiser for the Hindu nationalist RSS, then chief minister of Gujarat during the 2002 riots, in which over 1,000 people, mostly Muslims, were killed; a Supreme Court-appointed inquiry found no case against him. As prime minister he cut red tape, cancelled most banknotes overnight in 2016, and expanded toilets, gas and bank accounts for the poor. In 2024 he opened a Ram temple in Ayodhya, on the site of a mosque demolished by Hindu activists in 1992. Supporters see a confident Hindu-majority nation. Critics point to a 2019 law offering fast-track citizenship to refugees from three neighbouring countries, except Muslims, pressure on the press and rising sectarian tension.

India is now a major economy, a nuclear power, a space power and a sought-after partner of both the West and Russia. Extreme poverty has fallen sharply, by World Bank estimates, though jobs for its young population remain a challenge. Critics, including rights groups, say democracy and minority rights, especially for Muslims, have weakened under Modi; his government rejects this. In 2026 the BJP won West Bengal for the first time, while youth-led protests over jobs and exam leaks challenged the government.

dd-apartheid.p: In 1948 the National Party won an election in which almost all voters were white and began building apartheid, Afrikaans for 'separateness'. Laws classified every person by race, decided where they could live and work, and banned mixed marriages. Black South Africans were assigned to ethnic 'homelands' and needed passes to be in white areas. Resistance grew. In 1960 police killed 69 protesters at Sharpeville, and the ANC was banned and turned to armed struggle.

items: Everyone was labelled White, Black, Coloured or Indian.
Separate areas, schools, beaches and buses.
Black people made citizens of poor "Bantustans".
Black people needed passes to enter white areas.

steps: First free election; Mandela becomes president.

dd-apartheid.p: Nelson Mandela was jailed for life in 1964. Students rose in Soweto in 1976, and the 1980s brought township revolts, states of emergency and world sanctions. In 1990 President F. W. de Klerk freed Mandela, and in 1994 Mandela was elected president.

a: A policy of gradual votes for all South Africans
A legal system classifying people by race to keep white power
A trade pact between South Africa and its neighbours
dd-apartheid.why: From 1948 laws classified every person by race, decided where they could live and work, banned mixed marriages and assigned Black people to 'homelands'.

dd-apartheid.p: Racial segregation and white rule went back to colonial times, but after 1948 Afrikaner nationalists turned it into a total legal system to keep political power and cheap Black labour in white hands. It finally ended because resistance at home made the country hard to govern, sanctions and debt crises squeezed the economy, and the end of the Cold War removed the government's claim to be fighting communism.

dd-apartheid.h: Apartheid South Africa and its neighbours, 1980s
dd-apartheid.p: From 1948 South Africa classified everyone by race and gave power only to the white minority. It also ruled Namibia, in defiance of the UN. Black South Africans were assigned to ten 'homelands', scattered patches inside South Africa too small to show here. Neighbours such as Zambia and Mozambique, the Frontline States, sheltered exiled resistance movements and suffered South African raids in return.

dd-apartheid.q: Which pressures together brought apartheid to an end?
a: A vote by white South Africans in 1960
Resistance at home, sanctions and debt, and the Cold War's end
dd-apartheid.why: Township revolts made the country hard to govern, sanctions and refused loans squeezed the economy, and the Cold War's end removed the anti-communist excuse.

dd-apartheid.p:
Including its ten 'homelands' (Bantustans)

The homelands covered about 13% of the land for about three-quarters of the people. Four were declared 'independent', and about 3.5 million people were forcibly moved under apartheid.

South West Africa, today's Namibia, 1915–1990

South Africa took German South West Africa in 1915 and imposed apartheid there. The UN ended its mandate in 1966, but SWAPO fought until independence in 1990.

dd-apartheid.q: What legacy of apartheid remains in South Africa today?
a: Deep inequality, with wealth, land and jobs largely following old racial lines
dd-apartheid.why: Democracy and an admired constitution replaced apartheid, but South Africa remains one of the most unequal countries on Earth.

dd-apartheid.p:
Neighbours working to end white minority rule

Zambia hosted the ANC's headquarters in exile, in Lusaka, through the 1970s and 1980s.

Under Julius Nyerere, Tanzania was a founder of the Frontline States and hosted ANC training camps.

Apartheid rested on a stack of laws. The Population Registration Act of 1950 put every person in a racial category: White, Native (later Bantu or Black), Coloured or Asian (Indian). The Group Areas Act decided which race could live in each part of a town, and whole communities, such as Sophiatown in Johannesburg and District Six in Cape Town, were bulldozed. Mixed marriages were banned in 1949. Black men and women had to carry passes, and hundreds of thousands were arrested every year for pass offences. Bantu Education gave Black children deliberately inferior schooling. Separate amenities laws reserved beaches, buses and benches by race. The homelands policy aimed to strip Black South Africans of their citizenship altogether.

The African National Congress, founded in 1912, led peaceful campaigns against apartheid in the 1950s, including the 1955 Freedom Charter declaring that 'South Africa belongs to all who live in it'. After Sharpeville it was banned, and Nelson Mandela, a young lawyer, helped found its armed wing, Umkhonto we Sizwe, which began sabotage attacks in 1961. Arrested in 1962, he told the Rivonia Trial court in 1964 that a democratic, free society was an ideal for which he was prepared to die. He spent 27 years in prison, 18 of them on Robben Island, breaking rocks in a lime quarry. Released in 1990, he negotiated the transition and shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with de Klerk.

dd-apartheid.h: The end of white rule in southern Africa, 1961–1994
dd-apartheid.p: Majority rule spread south across Africa. British territories such as Zambia and Botswana became independent in the 1960s, and Portugal left Angola and Mozambique in 1975. White-ruled Rhodesia became Zimbabwe in 1980, and Namibia won independence in 1990. South Africa came last, with its first election open to all in April 1994.

British territories become independent

Tanganyika became independent from Britain in 1961 and joined Zanzibar in 1964 to form Tanzania.

Northern Rhodesia became independent as Zambia in 1964.

dd-apartheid.q: Why did Afrikaner nationalists build apartheid after 1948?
a: To defend South Africa against a Soviet invasion
Because the UN required separate development
To keep political power and cheap Black labour in white hands
To give each ethnic group its own vote
dd-apartheid.why: Segregation dated from colonial times, but the National Party turned it into a total legal system to protect white power and cheap labour.

dd-apartheid.p:
Portugal's colonies, after long wars

Angola became independent from Portugal in 1975, after a 1974 coup in Lisbon ended the colonial wars. A civil war followed at once.

Mozambique became independent from Portugal in June 1975 under FRELIMO, which had fought for independence since 1964.

Rhodesia becomes Zimbabwe

Rhodesia's white minority declared independence from Britain in 1965. After a guerrilla war, elections in 1980 created Zimbabwe.

dd-apartheid.q: How did South Africa deal with apartheid-era crimes after 1994?
a: Through a Truth and Reconciliation Commission offering amnesty for full confession
Through Nuremberg-style trials of all officials
Through a blanket amnesty with no hearings
dd-apartheid.why: Chaired by Desmond Tutu, the commission heard victims in public and granted amnesty to perpetrators who fully confessed politically motivated crimes.

dd-apartheid.p: From the 1960s South Africa was excluded from the Olympics and most international sport, and in 1977 the UN made an arms embargo mandatory. In the 1980s campaigns pushed foreign companies and universities to disinvest, and in 1986 the US Congress passed sanctions over President Reagan's veto. Banks refused new loans in 1985. On 2 February 1990 de Klerk unbanned the ANC, and Mandela walked free nine days later. Negotiations were tense and violent: thousands died in political fighting, and the assassination of the ANC and Communist Party leader Chris Hani in April 1993 nearly derailed the talks. On 27 April 1994 voters queued for hours to cast their first ballots.

Instead of Nuremberg-style trials or a blanket amnesty, South Africa chose a Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, which held hearings from 1996. Victims told their stories in public, many on live television. Perpetrators could apply for amnesty if they fully confessed politically motivated crimes; about 7,000 applied and fewer than 900 were granted it. The commission's 1998 report found the apartheid state responsible for most gross human rights violations, but also criticised abuses by the ANC. Supporters praise it as a model copied around the world; critics say few who were refused amnesty were ever prosecuted, and victims received little compensation.

South Africa became a democracy with one of the world's most admired constitutions, and Mandela came to symbolise reconciliation. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission heard the stories of victims and perpetrators. But apartheid's legacy endures: South Africa remains one of the most unequal countries on Earth, and wealth, land and jobs still largely follow the old racial lines.

dd-eu.p: In 1950 France proposed pooling French and German coal and steel, and in 1951 six countries formed the European Coal and Steel Community. The 1957 Treaties of Rome created a common market with shared institutions in Brussels. Britain, Ireland and Denmark joined in 1973, then Greece, Spain and Portugal as they left dictatorship behind.

steps: Six countries pool coal and steel so war is impossible.
Treaty of Rome: a common market.

items: Goods, people, money and services move freely.
No passport checks at most borders.
Common rules on trade, environment and rights.

dd-eu.p: The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 created the European Union, a single market let goods, money and people move freely, and euro notes and coins arrived in 2002. In 2004 ten countries joined, most of them from the old Soviet bloc. A debt crisis shook the euro from 2010, and in 2020 Britain became the first member to leave.

dd-eu.q: How did the European Union begin?
a: As a military alliance against the Soviet Union
As a single currency for France and Britain
As six countries pooling their coal and steel in 1951
As a trade club founded by Britain in 1960
dd-eu.why: The Schuman Declaration of 1950 led six countries to form the European Coal and Steel Community, and the 1957 Treaties of Rome created a common market.

dd-eu.p: After two world wars, leaders such as Jean Monnet, Robert Schuman and Konrad Adenauer wanted to bind France and Germany so tightly that war between them became impossible. The Cold War gave Western Europe a further reason to unite, with US encouragement, and a larger market promised growth. Later, joining offered newer democracies in the south and east security, prosperity and a way back into Europe.

On 9 May 1950 the French foreign minister, Robert Schuman, proposed putting French and German coal and steel, the stuff of war, under one shared authority. France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg signed up in 1951, and the 1957 Treaties of Rome created a common market. Britain stayed out and in 1960 set up a looser free trade club instead.

dd-eu.q: What did the single market and the euro change for Europeans?
a: Each country had to print its own new currency
Goods, money and people could move freely, and many share one currency
Citizens lost the right to work abroad
dd-eu.why: Citizens can live, work and study in any member, and 21 of the 27 members use the euro.

dd-eu.p:
Coal and Steel Community 1951, Economic Community 1957

France feared a revived Germany. Sharing control of German coal and steel offered security without occupation.

Italy, a new democracy after Mussolini, saw European integration as a path to recovery and respectability.

European Free Trade Association, led by Britain

Britain, with its empire and Commonwealth trade, refused to give up sovereignty. It applied to join in 1961, but France's President de Gaulle vetoed it twice.

Norway helped found the free trade group, and its voters later rejected EU membership twice, in 1972 and 1994.

The EU is neither a country nor an ordinary alliance. The European Commission, with one commissioner per country, proposes laws and enforces the rules. Those laws must be passed by both the Council, where national ministers vote, and the European Parliament, elected by citizens every five years. Leaders of the member states meet as the European Council to set direction, and the Court of Justice in Luxembourg settles disputes. Foreign policy and taxes still need unanimity, so one country can block a decision. The EU's budget is only about 1% of its members' combined national income; most public spending stays national.

Britain, Ireland and Denmark joined in 1973. Greece, Spain and Portugal followed in the 1980s, after shedding dictatorships. After the Cold War, Austria, Finland and Sweden joined in 1995, and in 2004 ten countries came in at once, most of them formerly communist, including Poland. Croatia was the last to join, in 2013, and in 2020 Britain became the first member to leave.

Denmark, Ireland, Greece, Spain, Portugal, Austria, Finland, Sweden

Denmark joined with Britain and Ireland, but it keeps its own currency, the krone.

Ireland was one of the poorest members when it joined in 1973. EU funds and the single market helped make it one of the richest.

dd-eu.q: Why did leaders such as Schuman and Adenauer want to pool coal and steel?
a: To bind France and Germany so tightly that war became impossible
dd-eu.why: Coal and steel were the stuff of war; sharing control of them gave France security without occupation and Germany a way back to trust.

dd-eu.p:
Mostly former communist countries

Poland, the largest of the 2004 entrants, has become one of the EU's fastest-growing economies.

Cyprus joined in 2004 while divided. EU law is suspended in the Turkish Cypriot north.

Citizens of any member can live, work and study in any other. In most of the EU and four neighbours, the Schengen area, people cross borders without passport checks. Since 2017, using a mobile phone in another member country costs the same as at home. Over 15 million people have studied or trained abroad through the Erasmus programme, begun in 1987. EU rules require new phones to use the same USB-C charging port, entitle air passengers to compensation for long delays, and give people rights over their personal data under the GDPR, rules that many global firms now apply worldwide.

dd-eu.q: What pushed the EU towards common defence and new enlargement?
dd-eu.why: After Russia invaded, Ukraine applied within days and became a candidate, and the EU moved towards common defence.

dd-eu.h: The EU, the euro and who wants in, October 2026
dd-eu.p: The EU has 27 members and about 450 million people. 21 of them share the euro, most recently Bulgaria from January 2026. Norway, Iceland and Switzerland stay outside but trade in its single market. Nine countries are official candidates: Montenegro is closest and could join around 2028, while Ukraine applied days after Russia's 2022 invasion. In August 2026 Icelanders voted against restarting membership talks.

21 countries

Bulgaria joined the EU in 2007 and on 1 January 2026 became the 21st country to use the euro.

Denmark has a legal opt-out from the euro, though it pegs its krone to it.

Poland, like most newer members, is committed to adopting the euro one day but has set no date.

dd-eu.q: Why did countries like Spain, Portugal and Poland want to join?
a: Membership let them keep their dictatorships
They were forced in by NATO
They wanted to adopt the krone
It offered new democracies security, prosperity and a way back into Europe
dd-eu.why: Greece, Spain and Portugal joined after shedding dictatorships, and in 2004 most new members were formerly communist states.

dd-eu.p:
Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein in the EEA; Switzerland by treaties

Norway voted against joining in 1972 and 1994, but follows most single market rules through the European Economic Area.

Iceland applied in 2009 and froze talks in 2013. In August 2026 about 53% voted against restarting them, with fishing rights a key worry.

Some famous stories are false. The EU never banned curved bananas: a 1994 rule set quality grades for green bananas, which had to be free of 'abnormal curvature', while lower grades allowed defects of shape. Real crises have been serious, though. After 2010 Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Cyprus needed rescue loans, and harsh austerity in Greece led to anger and fears it would leave the euro, until the European Central Bank promised in 2012 to do 'whatever it takes'. The 2015 refugee arrivals divided members, and in 2016 British voters chose to leave by 52% to 48%. In 2020 the EU agreed for the first time to borrow jointly on a large scale to recover from Covid.

The EU has 27 members and about 450 million people, and 21 of them use the euro. Its rules on trade, competition, data and product safety shape business far beyond its borders, and it won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2012. Critics argue it is remote and undemocratic, and Brexit showed the pull of national sovereignty. Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine pushed it towards common defence and new enlargement.

cradles.what: Around 9500 BC people in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East began to farm wheat and barley and herd sheep and goats. Villages such as Jericho grew, and by about 3500 BC Sumer, in southern Iraq, had true cities like Uruk, with temples, kings and scribes. Writing appeared there and in Egypt around 3200 BC, and Egypt was united under one king about 3100 BC; its Great Pyramid rose around 2560 BC. The Indus cities of Pakistan and north-west India, with grid streets and drains, peaked about 2600–1900 BC, and the Shang ruled the Yellow River valley from about 1600 BC. In the Americas, Caral in Peru and the Olmecs in Mexico began their own civilisations independently.
cradles.why: Farming produced surplus food, so some people could become priests, soldiers, craftsmen and rulers instead of farmers. Great rivers gave fertile silt and water, but irrigation needed organising, and rulers who controlled water and grain stores gained power. In Mesopotamia, writing began as bookkeeping for temples and palaces. Similar steps happened separately in several places, which suggests they followed naturally from farming and dense populations.
cradles.after: These societies invented the basic tools of civilisation: writing, law codes such as Hammurabi's of about 1750 BC, the wheel, bronze, calendars and the state with its taxes and armies. The Indus cities declined after about 1900 BC, probably partly from drought and shifting rivers. Around 1200 BC many eastern Mediterranean kingdoms collapsed, but the Phoenician alphabet that spread afterwards is the ancestor of Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic scripts.

religions.what: In northern India the hymns of the Rigveda were composed from about 1500 BC, and over centuries this Vedic religion grew into Hinduism. Around 500 BC the Buddha taught there that suffering ends by ending craving, and about 250 BC the emperor Ashoka helped spread his teaching. The Israelites came to worship a single God, and exile in Babylon after 586 BC helped shape the Hebrew Bible. Around AD 30 Rome crucified Jesus in Jerusalem; his followers, including missionaries like Paul, spread Christianity across the empire, which made it the state religion in 380. From 610 Muhammad preached Islam in Mecca and Medina, and by his death in 632 most of Arabia followed it.
religions.why: Many historians call about 800–200 BC the Axial Age, when thinkers from Greece to India and China, including Confucius, asked new questions about ethics and salvation as cities and states grew. Religions spread when rulers adopted them, as Ashoka did Buddhism and Constantine Christianity, and along trade routes. Many scholars think Jewish monotheism took its final shape through conquest and exile.
religions.after: These faiths still shape how most people live, eat, marry and mark time. In 2020, by Pew Research Center estimates, about 2.3 billion people were Christian, 2 billion Muslim and 1.2 billion Hindu. Buddhism faded in India but became central in East and South-East Asia. Judaism, Christianity and Islam share Abraham and Jerusalem, a bond that has also fuelled rivalry and conflict over holy places.

ancient.what: In the 550s BC Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire, and under Darius I it ran from Egypt to the Indus. When Persia invaded Greece, the city-states beat it at Marathon in 490 BC and Salamis in 480 BC. Athens, which had begun democracy in 508–507 BC, then had a golden age of theatre, philosophy and building, before losing a long war with Sparta. In 334 BC Alexander of Macedon invaded Persia, conquered it and reached India, dying in 323 BC aged 32. In the east, Qin united China in 221 BC, and the Han dynasty ruled it from 202 BC to AD 220.
ancient.why: Persia grew through a strong army and a light touch: it let conquered peoples keep their gods and customs, and governed through provinces linked by roads. Greece's mountains and islands split it into rival cities, where citizens argued and experimented. Philip II of Macedon built a professional army that his son Alexander used against a weakened Persia. In China, centuries of war between rival states ended when Qin, organised for war by harsh Legalist laws, defeated the rest.
ancient.after: Alexander's conquests spread Greek language and culture from Egypt to Afghanistan, and Rome later inherited it. Greek philosophy, science, democracy and drama, from Plato and Aristotle on, became a foundation of Western thought. Persia left a model of tolerant imperial rule. Qin and Han created the idea of one unified China ruled by an emperor and officials, and most Chinese still call themselves Han.

silk.what: In 138 BC the Han emperor sent the envoy Zhang Qian west, and caravan routes soon linked China, through Central Asian oases such as Kashgar and Samarkand, to Persia and the Mediterranean. Few merchants made the whole journey: Sogdian, Persian and other middlemen passed goods from city to city. Silk and later paper went west; horses, glass, silver and Buddhism went east. At sea, ships rode the monsoon winds between China, India, Arabia and East Africa. In the 1200s the Mongol Empire made the land routes safer than ever, but in the 1340s they also carried the Black Death west. From 1405 to 1433 Zheng He's huge Chinese fleets sailed the Indian Ocean.
silk.why: Different regions made things others wanted and could not produce: China long kept the secret of making silk, which reached Byzantium only in the AD 550s, while the Han needed strong horses from Central Asia. Rulers grew rich taxing the trade, so empires such as the Han, Tang, Persians and Mongols protected the routes. Predictable monsoon winds made long sea voyages possible and cheaper than camel caravans.
silk.after: The routes spread more than goods. Buddhism reached China, Islam spread into Central Asia, and paper, the compass and gunpowder travelled from China westward. The Black Death killed perhaps a third or more of Europe's people. To bypass the Venetian and Muslim middlemen who controlled the spice trade, the Portuguese sought their own sea route to Asia, which led to Vasco da Gama's voyage to India in 1498 and the age of European exploration.

rome.what: Rome began as a small Italian city that became a republic around 509 BC. It conquered Italy, destroyed its rival Carthage in 146 BC and took the eastern Mediterranean. After civil wars and Julius Caesar's murder in 44 BC, his heir Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC, and two centuries of relative peace followed. Under Trajan, in AD 117, the empire stretched from northern Britain to Egypt and Mesopotamia. After a crisis of civil wars in the 200s, Constantine backed Christianity and founded Constantinople in 330. From 395 the empire was split for good; Germanic peoples sacked Rome in 410 and deposed the last western emperor in 476, but the East lasted until 1453.
rome.why: Rome won through disciplined legions, alliances that turned defeated Italians into allies and citizens, and roads that moved troops and trade. Later, the West fell from many causes that historians weigh differently: repeated civil wars, heavy taxes and a weakening economy, a long frontier, and Germanic peoples pushed west by the Huns, settling inside the empire. The richer, better-defended East, with its walled capital, survived.
rome.after: Rome shaped Europe and the lands it settled. Latin grew into Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian, and the Latin alphabet is now the world's most used. Roman law underlies the legal systems of most of continental Europe and Latin America. The Catholic Church kept Rome's language and organisation, and the Byzantine East spread Orthodox Christianity to Russia and the Balkans.

americas.what: From about 250 to 900 the Maya built rival city-states such as Tikal in Central America, with stone pyramids, astronomy and the Americas' fullest writing system, before many lowland cities were abandoned. In the 1400s the Aztecs, from their island capital Tenochtitlan, ruled much of Mexico through tribute, while the Inca, from Cusco, conquered the Andes from Ecuador to Chile and linked it by roads. Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492, and in 1519 Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico; with native allies he destroyed Tenochtitlan in 1521. In 1532 Francisco Pizarro seized the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca, executed him in 1533 and took Cusco.
americas.why: Maize, beans and potatoes fed dense populations and supported states, as wheat and rice did elsewhere. The conquests were swift because smallpox and other European diseases, against which native peoples had no immunity, killed huge numbers before and during the fighting. Thousands of native allies, such as the Tlaxcalans, who resented Aztec rule, fought beside the Spanish, and the Inca had just been torn by a civil war. Steel, horses and guns helped too.
americas.after: Within a century epidemics, war and forced labour had killed most of the native population; estimates vary widely, but many regions lost over 80 per cent. Spain built a vast empire, and Spanish and Catholicism became dominant from Mexico to Chile. Silver from Potosí and Mexico flowed to Europe and China. Maize, potatoes, tomatoes and chocolate spread worldwide, and millions still speak Maya languages and Quechua.

islam.what: Around 610 Muhammad, a merchant of Mecca, began preaching that he had received revelations from God. Persecuted, he and his followers moved to Medina in 622, and by his death in 632 most of Arabia had accepted his rule. His successors, the caliphs, sent Arab armies against the two great empires: they took Syria and Egypt from the Byzantines and destroyed Persia's Sasanian Empire by 651. A dispute over who should lead turned to civil war, and from 661 the Umayyads ruled from Damascus. In the 710s their armies conquered most of Spain, Sindh and much of Central Asia. In 750 the Abbasids overthrew them and moved the capital to Baghdad.
islam.why: Islam united Arabia's feuding tribes under one faith and leader, and religious zeal, the hope of booty and the needs of the new state drove them outward. The Byzantine and Persian empires had just exhausted each other in a war from 602 to 628 and been weakened by plague. Many subjects, tired of heavy taxes and religious persecution, did not fight hard for their old rulers. The conquerors let Christians and Jews keep their faith in return for a special tax.
islam.after: Most people in the conquered lands became Muslim only gradually, over centuries, but Arabic largely replaced older languages from Iraq to Morocco, creating today's Arab world, while Iran kept Persian. The quarrel over succession became the lasting split between Sunni and Shia Muslims. Under the Abbasids, Baghdad became a centre of science and learning that preserved and extended Greek, Persian and Indian knowledge.

crusades.what: In 1095 the Byzantine emperor asked the West for help against the Seljuk Turks, and Pope Urban II called on Western Christians to take Jerusalem. On the way, some crusaders massacred Jews in the Rhineland. The First Crusade took Antioch, then in 1099 stormed Jerusalem, killing many of its people, and founded four crusader states, mostly along the Levant coast. Muslim rulers began to fight back: Zengi took Edessa in 1144, and Saladin, who united Egypt and Syria, crushed the crusaders at Hattin and retook Jerusalem in 1187. The Third Crusade regained a coastal strip, but not Jerusalem. In 1204 the Fourth Crusade sacked Christian Constantinople, and in 1291 the Mamluks of Egypt took Acre, the last major crusader city.
crusades.why: Most historians now think crusaders were driven mainly by piety: the pope promised forgiveness of sins to those who fought, and Jerusalem was Christianity's holiest place. Popes also saw a chance to lead Western Christendom and reach out to Byzantium. Land, loot and adventure attracted some, and Italian cities sought trade. The First Crusade succeeded largely because the Muslim world was divided between rival Seljuk princes and the Fatimids of Egypt.
crusades.after: The crusades left the Middle East's map largely as it was, but the sack of 1204 crippled Byzantium and eased the later Ottoman advance into Europe. Venice and Genoa grew rich on eastern trade. Relations between Western and Eastern Christians, and between Christians and Jews, grew more bitter. The crusades are still remembered, and invoked, in politics and rhetoric on all sides today.

mongol.what: In 1206 a chieftain named Temüjin united the feuding tribes of the Mongolian steppe and was proclaimed Genghis Khan. His horse archers overran northern China and, after the murder of his envoys, destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia, sacking Bukhara and Samarkand. His sons and grandsons pushed on: they crushed Russia's principalities in 1237–40, raided Poland and Hungary, sacked Baghdad in 1258 and, under Kublai Khan, finished conquering Song China in 1279. Cities that resisted were often massacred. By then the empire had split into four khanates: the Yuan in China, the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate and the Ilkhanate.
mongol.why: The Mongols were superb mounted archers, and Genghis Khan reorganised the tribes into a disciplined army of units of ten, a hundred and a thousand, promoting men for loyalty and skill rather than birth. He used terror to make cities surrender and borrowed Chinese and Persian engineers for sieges. Their neighbours were divided and weak. The empire split because each branch of Genghis's family ruled its own lands, and a civil war over the succession after 1259 broke their unity.
mongol.after: For a century, Mongol peace made the Silk Road safer than ever, letting goods, ideas and travellers like Marco Polo cross Eurasia, and probably helping the Black Death spread west in the 1340s. Baghdad's fall ended the Abbasid caliphate. China was reunited under the Yuan, overthrown by the Ming in 1368. Moscow rose as the Golden Horde's tax collector and threw off its rule in 1480, becoming the core of the Russian state.

ottoman.what: Around 1300 a Turkish chief named Osman founded a small state in north-west Anatolia. His heirs crossed into Europe in the 1350s, conquered much of the Balkans, and in 1453 Mehmed II took Constantinople with huge cannon, ending the Byzantine Empire. Selim I conquered Syria and Egypt in 1516–17, and Suleiman the Magnificent took Hungary and Baghdad and besieged Vienna in 1529. The second siege of Vienna failed in 1683, and from then on the empire shrank: Hungary went to the Habsburgs, Crimea to Russia, and the Balkan nations broke away in the 1800s. The Ottomans joined World War I on Germany's side and lost.
ottoman.why: The Ottomans rose on the frontier of a weak Byzantium and a divided Balkans. A strong central state, a paid standing army of Janissaries, early use of gunpowder and fairly tolerant rule over Christians and Jews helped them hold a vast, mixed empire. Its later decline is debated: historians now stress adaptation as much as decay, but Europe's growing military and economic power, Russian expansion, debt and nationalism among its peoples steadily wore it down.
ottoman.after: In 1915 the Ottoman government deported and killed huge numbers of Armenians, which most historians call genocide, a term Turkey rejects. After the war Britain and France divided the Arab lands, and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923, abolishing the caliphate in 1924. Many of today's borders, conflicts and mixed populations from Bosnia to Iraq go back to Ottoman rule and its breakup.

old.what: A few states on today's map are far older than their neighbours. In Europe, San Marino traces its founding to 301, a treaty of 1278 gave Andorra its two co-princes, the Grimaldis took Monaco in 1297, and Liechtenstein became a principality in 1719. The Vatican is all that remains of the Papal States, which once ruled central Italy. Beyond Europe, a handful of countries were never ruled as European colonies: Japan, Thailand, Iran, Nepal and Ethiopia, which crushed an Italian army at Adwa in 1896 and suffered only a brief Italian occupation in 1936–41. Most of them still lost land or bowed to pressure from the great empires.
old.why: The microstates survived because they were too small to be worth a war, useful to bigger neighbours, or protected by treaties and old feudal rights. The uncolonised countries had strong states, hard terrain or skilled leaders. Thailand, Iran and Afghanistan were kept as buffers between rival empires, Ethiopia fought off invasion with modern rifles, and Japan modernised fast enough to become a great power itself.
old.after: These states give the map its oldest borders. The microstates thrive today on tourism, finance and low taxes, and the Pope rules a sovereign state at the head of the world's largest church. Ethiopia's victory at Adwa became a symbol of African independence, and its capital now hosts the African Union. Japan, never colonised, became an empire that later colonised its neighbours.

explore.what: In 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing west for Spain to reach Asia, landed in the Caribbean instead. Six years later Vasco da Gama sailed round Africa to India, and in 1519–22 Magellan's expedition went round the world. Spanish conquistadors toppled the Aztec Empire in 1521 and the Inca in the 1530s, and silver from Mexico and Potosí flowed to Europe and China. Portugal built a chain of trading forts from Africa to Asia and took Brazil. In the 1600s the Dutch, English and French followed with colonies and trading companies. To work sugar plantations and mines, Europeans shipped about 12.5 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic.
explore.why: Europeans wanted direct access to Asia's spices and silk without Venetian and Muslim middlemen, and gold to pay for them. Portugal and Spain, on the Atlantic edge, had ocean-going ships, compasses and guns, and crusading zeal fresh from the reconquest of Iberia. In the Americas, smallpox and other European diseases, against which Native peoples had no immunity, did more to make conquest possible than guns or horses. Rivalry between Europe's states kept the race going.
explore.after: The voyages joined the world's continents for good. Native American populations collapsed, by most estimates by as much as 90 per cent in many places, and crops like maize and potatoes spread worldwide. Spanish and Portuguese became the languages of Latin America, and Catholicism its main faith. The slave trade created the African diaspora of the Americas and racial hierarchies whose effects still last. Europe began its rise to global dominance.

reformation.what: In 1517 the monk Martin Luther attacked the Church's sale of indulgences, and printed pamphlets spread his ideas across Germany within weeks. He refused to recant at the Diet of Worms in 1521, and German princes protected him. Other reformers followed: Zwingli in Zurich and Calvin in Geneva. Henry VIII broke with Rome in 1534 to end his marriage. The Catholic Church struck back with the Council of Trent and the Jesuits. Religious wars followed: in Germany, in France between Catholics and Huguenots, and in the Netherlands against Spain. The Thirty Years' War of 1618–48 devastated Germany before the Peace of Westphalia ended it.
reformation.why: Many Christians resented a Church they saw as corrupt, rich and run from Rome, and humanist scholars were reading the Bible afresh in its original languages. The printing press let Luther reach a mass audience the Church could not silence. Above all, princes and kings had political reasons to back reform: it gave them control of church lands and freed them from pope and emperor. Wars mixed faith with dynastic and great-power rivalry.
reformation.after: Western Christianity split for good: a Protestant north, a Catholic south, and a line through Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands that still shows on maps of belief. The Thirty Years' War killed perhaps 4.5 to 8 million people. Westphalia extended the Augsburg settlement to Calvinists and is often seen as the birth of sovereign states, though historians debate this. Bible reading boosted literacy, and toleration slowly became a European ideal.

asiaemp.what: In 1526 Babur, a Central Asian prince descended from Timur and Genghis Khan, won at Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire. His grandson Akbar ruled a mostly Hindu India with tolerance, Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal, and Aurangzeb pushed the empire to its greatest size before his death in 1707. In 1644 the Manchus took Beijing and founded the Qing dynasty, which by 1760 had conquered Taiwan, Mongolia and Xinjiang and brought Tibet under its control. Meanwhile Russia's Cossacks crossed Siberia and reached the Pacific in 1639, and the tsars kept expanding. Safavid Persia ruled Iran in between.
asiaemp.why: These states combined cavalry, gunpowder armies and large bureaucracies that could tax rich farming populations. India and China were among the world's largest economies: by economist Angus Maddison's estimates, each produced around a quarter of world output in 1700. The Qing pushed into Inner Asia to destroy the rival Dzungar Mongols and secure their frontier, and Russia was drawn east by furs and weak opponents.
asiaemp.after: Their borders still shape the map. India, Pakistan and Bangladesh grew from the Mughal lands, which the British East India Company took over after the empire broke up. Today's China rests on the Qing frontiers, the basis of its claims to Tibet, Xinjiang and Taiwan. Many Tibetans and Uyghurs dispute Chinese rule, and Taiwan has been governed separately since 1949. Russia became and remains the largest country on earth.

industry.what: From the 1760s, inventors in Britain mechanised cotton spinning, and James Watt's improved steam engine, sold from 1776 and adapted to drive machinery in the 1780s, freed factories from rivers. Coal and iron output soared, and in 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened the age of steam trains. Belgium, France, the German states and the United States followed in the mid-1800s. A second wave after 1870 brought steel, electricity, chemicals and oil, and spread industry to Japan, Russia, Sweden and northern Italy. Millions moved into crowded factory towns, working long hours, children included. By 1900 the United States was the largest industrial economy and Germany made more steel than Britain.
industry.why: Britain had cheap coal close to its towns, high wages that made machines worth buying, capital and markets from overseas trade and colonies, and secure property rights and patents. Its farms fed a growing population. Why Europe and not China or India industrialised first is one of history's big debates, sometimes called the Great Divergence: some historians stress coal and colonies, others institutions and science.
industry.after: For the first time, living standards could rise year after year, and world population rose from about 1 billion in 1800 to nearly 1.8 billion by 1914. Industrial nations used steamships, railways and machine guns to dominate the rest of the world. Factory work gave rise to trade unions, socialism and the welfare state. Burning coal and then oil began the rise in carbon dioxide behind today's climate change.

revolutions.what: Britain's American colonies rebelled in 1775, declared independence in 1776 and, with French help, won it in 1783. In 1789 a bankrupt France erupted: crowds stormed the Bastille, the monarchy fell, Louis XVI was guillotined in 1793, and the Terror followed. In Saint-Domingue, enslaved people rose in 1791 and founded Haiti in 1804. Napoleon seized power in 1799 and conquered much of Europe, but his invasion of Russia in 1812 cost him around half a million men, and he fell at Waterloo in 1815. His occupation of Spain in 1808 set off the wars in which Bolívar, San Martín and others freed Spanish America.
revolutions.why: Enlightenment ideas of natural rights and government by consent gave rebels a cause. Britain's new taxes after the Seven Years' War angered its colonists. France's debts, partly from aiding the Americans, high bread prices and anger at noble privilege broke the old regime. Haiti's revolt grew from the brutality of slavery and the French Revolution's talk of equality. When Napoleon toppled Spain's king, colonial elites took power themselves.
revolutions.after: The revolutions made popular sovereignty, written constitutions and rights of citizens central to politics, and even gave us 'left' and 'right'. Napoleon's law code and the nationalism he stirred reshaped Europe. Haiti abolished slavery but was forced in 1825 to pay France a huge indemnity. Latin America gained independence but often saw instability and rule by strongmen, while slavery lasted in the US until 1865 and Brazil until 1888.

nations.what: After 1815 nationalism, the idea that each people should have its own state, kept redrawing the map. Greece, Belgium, Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria broke away from larger states, most from the shrinking Ottoman Empire. Piedmont united Italy in 1861, helped by Garibaldi's conquest of the south, and Bismarck's Prussia beat Denmark, Austria and France to found the German Empire in 1871. Across the Atlantic the United States bought Louisiana, took the south-west in its war with Mexico in 1846–48 and reached the Pacific. Latin American wars fixed borders that still stand: Chile's victory in the War of the Pacific left Bolivia landlocked. Britain's settler colonies united as Canada in 1867, Australia in 1901 and South Africa in 1910.
nations.why: The French Revolution, newspapers and schools taught people to see themselves as Italians, Germans or Greeks rather than subjects of a dynasty. Railways and industry made bigger states possible and profitable, but armies settled the borders: Bismarck said the great questions would be decided by 'iron and blood'. In the Americas, cheap land, mass immigration and a belief in 'Manifest Destiny' drove settlers west, at the expense of Mexico and Indigenous nations.
nations.after: Europe and the Americas took much of their modern shape. A united Germany became the strongest power in Europe, and France longed to win back Alsace-Lorraine, while rival nationalisms made the Balkans a powder keg; both fed into 1914. The United States, now spanning a continent, became the world's largest economy by about 1890. Indigenous peoples in North America and Australia lost most of their land.

scramble.what: In 1870 Europeans held only about a tenth of Africa, mostly on the coasts. Then the race began. At the Berlin Conference of 1884–85, hosted by Bismarck, European powers agreed rules for claiming land, with no Africans present. By 1914 they ruled about nine-tenths of the continent, often with straight-line borders. Conquest was often brutal: forced labour for rubber in King Leopold's Congo caused an international outcry, and Germany crushed the Herero and Nama in Namibia. Only Ethiopia, which beat Italy at Adwa in 1896, and Liberia stayed independent. In Asia France took Indochina, the US took the Philippines and Japan took Taiwan and Korea, while Britain's empire grew to rule nearly a quarter of the world's people.
scramble.why: Industrial Europe wanted raw materials such as rubber, cotton and copper, new markets, and safe sea routes, above all Britain's route to India through the Suez Canal. Rivalry fed on itself: each power grabbed land to keep others out, and colonies became a badge of national prestige. Machine guns, steamships and quinine against malaria made conquest cheap, and racist ideas of a 'civilising mission' were used to justify it.
scramble.after: Colonial lines became the borders of most African states at independence, often splitting peoples or joining rivals. Colonial economies were built to export raw materials, a pattern many countries still struggle to escape. Imperial rivalry added to the tensions behind World War I, and resentment of foreign rule fed the independence movements that brought these empires down after 1945.

ww1.what: In June 1914 a Bosnian Serb nationalist shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary, backed by Germany, declared war on Serbia. Russia mobilised to defend Serbia, Germany declared war on Russia and France, and its march through neutral Belgium brought in Britain. In the west the armies dug trenches from the North Sea to Switzerland, and battles such as Verdun and the Somme killed hundreds of thousands for a few miles of mud. The war spread to the Ottoman Empire, Italy and the colonies. Russia collapsed into revolution in 1917, but the United States joined the Allies, and an exhausted Germany signed an armistice on 11 November 1918.
ww1.why: Europe's great powers were locked into rival alliances: Germany and Austria-Hungary against France and Russia, with Britain tied to both. Decades of imperial rivalry, an arms race and nationalism, above all in the Balkans, turned a local crisis into a general war. Military plans built for speed, like Germany's scheme to defeat France first by going through Belgium, left little room for diplomacy in July 1914. Historians still debate how much of the blame lies with Germany.
ww1.after: About 9 million soldiers and millions of civilians died. Four empires fell, the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman, and new countries such as Poland and Czechoslovakia appeared, while Britain and France divided the Arab Middle East between them. The Russian Revolution produced the Soviet Union, and the harsh Treaty of Versailles left Germany bitter, helping set the stage for World War II. The United States emerged as a world power.

interwar.what: In 1917 Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in Russia, won a civil war and founded the Soviet Union in 1922. Under Stalin, forced collective farming brought a famine that killed millions, above all in Ukraine, and the Great Terror of 1937–38 shot about 700,000 people. In Italy Mussolini's Fascists took power in 1922. The Wall Street Crash of 1929 began the Great Depression: world trade collapsed, and about a quarter of American workers lost their jobs. With six million Germans unemployed, Hitler became chancellor in 1933 and built a dictatorship. Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and invaded China in 1937, Italy conquered Ethiopia, and Hitler took Austria and the Czech lands. After a pact with Stalin, he invaded Poland in 1939.
interwar.why: World War I toppled empires, left millions of bitter veterans and spread fear of communist revolution, which fascists exploited by promising order and national glory. Germans resented the Treaty of Versailles, and the Depression's mass unemployment drove voters to extremes. The League of Nations had no army, the US stayed out, and Britain and France, dreading another war, chose appeasement. Historians still debate whether standing firm earlier, say over the Rhineland in 1936, would have stopped Hitler.
interwar.after: The decade ended in the deadliest war in history. Its lessons shaped the world after 1945: the belief that appeasing aggressors invites war, welfare states and government economic management meant to prevent another depression, and institutions such as the UN and the IMF built to protect peace and trade. The Soviet one-party state built in these years lasted until 1991.

ww2.what: Germany invaded Poland in September 1939 and by mid-1940 had overrun western Europe, leaving Britain fighting alone. In June 1941 Hitler invaded the Soviet Union, and in December Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and overran South-East Asia. In occupied Europe the Nazis carried out the Holocaust, murdering about six million Jews in mass shootings and in death camps such as Auschwitz. The tide turned in 1942–43 at Midway, El Alamein and Stalingrad. The Red Army drove west, the Allies landed in Normandy in 1944, and Germany surrendered in May 1945. In the Pacific, US forces fought island by island towards Japan; after atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August, killing an estimated 150,000–200,000 by the end of 1945, Japan surrendered.
ww2.why: The war grew out of the failures of the 1919 peace: German resentment of Versailles, the Depression, and regimes that glorified conquest. Hitler wanted 'living space' in the east and a Europe without Jews; Japan wanted an Asian empire and the oil it lacked, which the US cut off in 1941. Appeasement, and then the Nazi–Soviet Pact, let Hitler attack Poland without fearing a war on two fronts.
ww2.after: Over 60 million people died, most of them civilians, including about 27 million Soviet citizens. Europe was split between US and Soviet camps, Germany and Korea were divided, and Poland was moved west as millions were expelled. The United Nations was founded, and the Holocaust led to the Genocide Convention and strengthened the case for a Jewish state. Weakened Britain and France began losing their empires, and nuclear weapons changed war for ever.

asia.what: Japan's defeat in 1945 left Europe's Asian empires shaken, and nationalists moved fast. The US granted the Philippines independence in 1946. In 1947 Britain left India, splitting it into India and Muslim-majority Pakistan; over 10 million people fled across the new borders, and estimates of the dead range from 200,000 to 2 million. Burma and Ceylon followed in 1948. Indonesia fought the Dutch until 1949, and Vietnam defeated France at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. In the Middle East, Britain and France gave up their mandates: Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, and Palestine, where Israel was founded in 1948. Malaya became independent in 1957, and Britain's withdrawal from the Gulf in 1971 created the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Bahrain.
asia.why: The war shattered the myth of European invincibility: Japan took Singapore and the Dutch East Indies within three months. Nationalist movements, some decades old like Gandhi's Indian National Congress, were ready to take over, and Britain, nearly bankrupted by the war, could no longer afford to hold India by force. The US and the new United Nations opposed old-style empires, while France and the Netherlands, which fought to stay, lost costly wars.
asia.after: The new states, from India to Indonesia, held a large share of humanity, and several grew into major powers. Hasty borders left lasting conflicts: India and Pakistan both claim Kashmir and have fought over it repeatedly, and both now have nuclear weapons, while Bangladesh broke from Pakistan in 1971. Vietnam's struggle merged into the Cold War. Many new states joined the Non-Aligned Movement, refusing to take sides between the superpowers.

coldwar.what: After 1945 the United States and the Soviet Union, allies against Hitler, became rivals. Soviet-backed communists took over Eastern Europe, an 'Iron Curtain' fell across the continent, and the US answered with Marshall Plan aid and the NATO alliance. Germany and Korea were split; the Soviets blockaded West Berlin in 1948–49, and in 1961 East Germany built the Berlin Wall. Both sides raced to build nuclear weapons, and in 1962 Soviet missiles in Cuba brought the world close to nuclear war. Instead the superpowers fought through others, in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Angola and Central America. Under Gorbachev the Soviet grip loosened: the Berlin Wall opened in 1989, and the Soviet Union broke up in 1991.
coldwar.why: The two powers had opposite systems, one-party communism with a planned economy against democracy and markets, and each believed the other wanted to spread its own. Stalin wanted friendly governments as a buffer after two German invasions; the US, resolved not to repeat the appeasement of the 1930s, set out to 'contain' communism. Nuclear weapons made direct war suicidal, so the rivalry ran through arms races, spies, aid and proxy wars. Historians still argue over which side bore more blame.
coldwar.after: The United States was left as the only superpower, and NATO and the European Union expanded east, which Russia's leaders came to oppose. Fifteen countries emerged from the Soviet Union. Korea remains divided, communist parties still rule China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and North Korea, and thousands of nuclear warheads built in these years still exist. Proxy wars left long civil conflicts, as in Afghanistan and Angola.

mideast.what: In 1948, as British rule ended, Israel declared independence and neighbouring Arab states attacked. Israel won, about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, and Jordan and Egypt held the West Bank and Gaza. In 1967 Israel took those lands, East Jerusalem, the Golan Heights and Sinai. After Egypt and Syria attacked in 1973, Arab producers cut off oil to the US and others and prices quadrupled. Egypt made peace in 1979 and regained Sinai. That year Iran's revolution created an Islamic republic; Iraq attacked it in 1980, starting an eight-year war, then invaded Kuwait in 1990. The 1993 Oslo Accords brought limited Palestinian self-rule but no state, and wars followed, including in Gaza after Hamas's attack of 7 October 2023.
mideast.why: Two national movements, Zionism and Palestinian Arab nationalism, claimed the same land, and in World War I Britain made promises to both Arabs and Zionists that were hard to reconcile. After the Holocaust, support for a Jewish state grew; the UN's 1947 partition plan was accepted by Jewish leaders and rejected by Arab leaders, and war followed. Meanwhile the region holds nearly half the world's proven oil, so outside powers competed for influence there.
mideast.after: The Israeli–Palestinian conflict is unresolved: Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967 and settlements there have grown, while Jerusalem and the refugees' future remain disputed. Most UN members recognise a State of Palestine; Israel and the US do not. Most Jews of the Arab world left or were driven out after 1948, many to Israel. Oil made the Gulf states rich and central to US strategy, and the US fought repeated wars there, from Kuwait in 1991 to Iraq in 2003.

china.what: On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China, and the defeated Nationalists withdrew to Taiwan. Mao's Great Leap Forward of 1958–62 forced peasants into communes and caused a famine that killed tens of millions; scholars' estimates range from 15 to over 40 million. His Cultural Revolution of 1966–76 brought a decade of purges and chaos. After Mao died, Deng Xiaoping from 1978 let farmers sell their crops, opened special economic zones such as Shenzhen and welcomed foreign investment. Growth near 10% a year followed for three decades. The party crushed the Tiananmen Square protests in 1989, joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and passed Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010.
china.why: The Communists won the civil war because the Nationalist government was weakened by corruption, runaway inflation and eight years of war with Japan, while Mao's party won over the peasants. Mao's disasters came from forcing utopian plans on the country with no one able to object. Deng's reforms worked because China had a vast, cheap, disciplined workforce, and it opened just as world trade boomed and Western firms looked for low-cost factories.
china.after: About 800 million people left extreme poverty, the largest fall in poverty in history, and China became the world's biggest manufacturer and goods exporter. One-party rule stayed and tightened under Xi Jinping from 2012: after the 2019 protests Beijing imposed a security law on Hong Kong that critics say ended many freedoms, and Western governments and UN experts condemned mass detention in Xinjiang, which Beijing calls counter-terrorism. Rivalry with the US over trade, technology, Taiwan and the South China Sea now shapes world politics.

europe.what: In 1950 France proposed pooling its coal and steel, the industries of war, with West Germany's, and in 1951 six countries signed up. The Treaty of Rome created a common market from 1958. Britain, Ireland and Denmark joined in 1973, then Greece, Spain and Portugal after their dictatorships ended. The 1992 Maastricht Treaty founded the European Union, and the euro was launched in 1999, with notes and coins in 2002. In 2004 ten countries joined, most of them former communist states. The euro crisis from 2010 nearly forced Greece out, and in 2016 Britain voted to leave, departing in 2020.
europe.why: Two world wars had wrecked Europe, and its leaders wanted to bind France and Germany so tightly that another war between them would be impossible. A bigger shared market promised prosperity, and unity, encouraged by the United States, gave strength against the Soviet threat. Later, joining became the way for former dictatorships and communist states to lock in democracy and catch up economically.
europe.after: The old rivals of Western Europe have not fought each other since 1945, their longest peace in centuries. The EU is a single market of about 450 million people, 21 of its 27 members use the euro, and its rules on trade, competition and data are followed far beyond its borders. Arguments over national sovereignty, migration and debt continue. Russia's invasion of Ukraine pushed the EU towards closer defence ties and a new wave of candidates, Ukraine among them.

africa.what: In March 1957 Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became the first black African colony south of the Sahara to win independence. In 1960, the "Year of Africa", 17 countries followed, most of them French colonies freed by negotiation. Elsewhere freedom came through war: Algeria fought France from 1954 to 1962, and Portugal fought guerrillas in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau until its own army overthrew the dictatorship in Lisbon in 1974. The Congo fell into crisis within days of its sudden independence from Belgium in 1960. White-minority Rhodesia broke from Britain in 1965 to avoid majority rule and held out until 1980, when it became Zimbabwe.
africa.why: The Second World War weakened Britain and France, and Africans who had fought for them came home demanding rights. Nationalist leaders built mass parties, the new United Nations backed self-determination, and both superpowers opposed old-style empires, while colonies grew costly to hold. Where many white settlers lived, as in Algeria, Kenya and Rhodesia, or where the colonial power was a dictatorship, as in Portugal, the end came through war.
africa.after: Almost every new state kept the colonial borders, which African leaders agreed in 1964 to respect, so many countries joined rival peoples and divided others.
