Debates over the role of Islamic law in the state, and the Sunni-Shia rivalry between Saudi Arabia and Iran, shape the politics of the Middle East.

sections.t: Islam means 'submission' to God, in Arabic Allah, the same God worshipped by Jews and Christians. Muslims believe Muhammad was the last of a line of prophets that includes Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and that the Quran is God's word. Practice rests on five pillars: declaring that there is no god but God and Muhammad is his messenger; praying five times a day facing Mecca; giving alms to the poor; fasting from dawn to sunset in the month of Ramadan; and making the hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, once in a lifetime if able. In May 2026 about 1.7 million pilgrims made the hajj, by Saudi official count.

When Muhammad died in 632, Muslims disagreed over who should lead them. Most accepted Abu Bakr, his close companion, as the first caliph; they became the Sunnis, 'people of the tradition'. Others believed Muhammad had chosen his cousin and son-in-law Ali, and that leadership belonged to his family; they became the Shia, from 'shiat Ali', the party of Ali. Ali became the fourth caliph but was murdered in 661, and in 680 his son Husayn was killed at Karbala, a martyrdom Shia Muslims mourn every year at Ashura. Today about 85–90% of Muslims are Sunni. The two share the Quran and the five pillars.

Under the Abbasid caliphs, Baghdad, founded in 762, became one of the world's greatest cities. Scholars translated Greek works of philosophy, medicine and science into Arabic, and built on them. Al-Khwarizmi wrote the book on equations that gave us the word 'algebra', and his name gave us 'algorithm'. Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was used in European universities for centuries. Indian numerals, including zero, passed through the Islamic world to Europe, where they became known as Arabic numerals. Cities such as Córdoba, Cairo and Samarkand had libraries, observatories and hospitals. Many of these works later reached Europe through Spain and Sicily.

Today most Muslims live in lands Arab armies never conquered. Islam reached West Africa with traders crossing the Sahara by camel, and rulers in Ghana, Mali and Songhay adopted it; Mali's Mansa Musa dazzled Cairo with his gold on his pilgrimage in 1324. Along the Indian Ocean, Arab, Persian and Indian merchants settled in ports from Kilwa to Malacca and married locally. Sufi mystics, who sought a personal experience of God, often blended Islam with local customs, which helped it take root. By about 1600 Islam had become the main religion of Java and Sumatra, laying the foundations of Indonesia, today the largest Muslim country.

dd-mesopotamia.what: From about 3500 BC the Sumerians of southern Iraq built walled cities such as Uruk and Ur, and invented writing to keep temple accounts. Around 2300 BC Sargon of Akkad united the cities into the first known empire. Around 1750 BC Hammurabi of Babylon conquered his neighbours and set up his famous law code. In the first millennium BC Assyria, from Nineveh, conquered lands from Iran to Egypt with a ruthless professional army, until Babylonians and Medes destroyed it in 612 BC. Babylon then ruled the region under Nebuchadnezzar II, who took Jerusalem, until Cyrus of Persia captured the city in 539 BC.
dd-mesopotamia.why: The rivers brought water and rich silt to a flat, dry land with almost no stone, timber or metal. Farming there needed canals and teamwork, and trade was needed for everything else, so temples and kings that could organise labour, store grain and keep records grew powerful. Open plains with no natural borders meant constant war between cities, and later between empires that tried to control the rivers and trade routes.
dd-mesopotamia.after: Mesopotamia gave the world writing, written law, the first literature, and the 60-based counting that still gives us 60 minutes and 360 degrees. Its astronomy, maths and stories passed to the Persians, Greeks and Hebrews, and Babylon became a byword in the Bible. Cuneiform faded after Alexander's time and was forgotten until scholars deciphered it in the 1850s, using inscriptions from Iran.

sections.t: Writing was not invented to record poems or prayers, but to count. Temple officials at Uruk tracked barley, beer, sheep and workers' rations by pressing signs into wet clay with a reed, from about 3300 BC. The early signs were pictures, but they turned into wedge-shaped strokes, which is why we call the script cuneiform, from the Latin for 'wedge'. Scribes trained for years in schools they called 'tablet houses', copying lists and proverbs. Cuneiform was used for some 3,000 years, for over a dozen languages, and hundreds of thousands of tablets survive, because clay lasts; many were baked hard when the libraries holding them burned.

Around 1750 BC King Hammurabi of Babylon had about 282 laws carved on a black stone stele over two metres tall, topped by an image of him before the sun god of justice. Some sound harsh: if a builder's house collapsed and killed its owner, the builder was to be put to death. Punishments depended on rank. 'An eye for an eye' applied between equals, but a noble who blinded a commoner paid silver. The code also set wages, fixed rules for divorce and protected widows. It was not the first: Ur-Nammu of Ur issued laws about 350 years earlier. The stele was found at Susa, in Iran, in 1901 and is now in the Louvre.

The Epic of Gilgamesh, one of the oldest known works of literature, tells of a proud king of Uruk who loses his friend Enkidu and searches for eternal life. He meets Utnapishtim, who tells how the gods sent a flood to destroy mankind and how he survived by building a great boat, loading it with animals and sending out birds to find land. In 1872 George Smith, a self-taught scholar at the British Museum, recognised this story on a tablet from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh. Its likeness to the Bible's story of Noah caused a sensation. Most scholars think both drew on older Mesopotamian flood traditions.

Mesopotamians counted in base 60 as well as base 10, perhaps because 60 divides evenly in so many ways. That system, passed down through Greek astronomers, still gives us 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle. Babylonian astronomers recorded the movements of the moon and planets for centuries, predicted eclipses, and divided the sky into the twelve signs of the zodiac. Mesopotamians brewed beer, used the potter's wheel and some of the earliest wheeled vehicles, and wrote contracts, receipts and loan documents. Even the idea that a king rules under a written law goes back to them.

dd-egypt.what: Around 3100 BC the towns of the Nile valley were united into one kingdom under a single king. In the Old Kingdom (c. 2686–2181 BC) kings built ever-larger pyramids, culminating in the Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza around 2560 BC. After a time of division, the Middle Kingdom reunited the land from Thebes and pushed forts south into Nubia. Foreign Hyksos kings then ruled the north until the New Kingdom (c. 1550–1069 BC) drove them out and built an empire from Sudan to Syria under pharaohs such as Hatshepsut, Thutmose III and Ramesses II. Libyan, Nubian and Persian rulers followed, then Alexander the Great in 332 BC and the Greek Ptolemies, whose last queen, Cleopatra VII, died in 30 BC.
dd-egypt.why: The Nile made it possible. Its yearly flood left a strip of black, fertile soil in the desert, so farmers grew large grain surpluses that fed priests, scribes, soldiers and builders. The river was also a highway that let one king control the whole valley, while deserts on both sides kept most invaders away. Kings ruled as the gods' representatives on earth, keepers of maat, the order of the world, which gave the state great authority for millennia.
dd-egypt.after: Egypt became a Roman province and fed Rome with its grain. Christianity, and after the Arab conquest of 639–642 Islam and Arabic, replaced the old religion and language, and the ability to read hieroglyphs was lost until 1822. Greek visitors admired Egypt's learning, and its monuments still shape how the world imagines the ancient past: its temples and tombs draw millions of visitors and gave rise to the science of Egyptology.

sections.t: Egypt's kings built pyramids for about a thousand years, starting with Djoser's step pyramid at Saqqara around 2650 BC. The Great Pyramid of Khufu, finished around 2560 BC, used about 2.3 million stone blocks and stood about 146 metres tall, the tallest human-made structure on Earth for over 3,800 years. It was not built by slaves. Archaeologists digging the workers' town at Giza found bakeries, breweries, cattle bones and the tombs of workers buried with honour near their king. They estimate a workforce of perhaps 20,000–30,000 at its peak, far fewer than the 100,000 the Greek writer Herodotus claimed. The workers used copper tools, ramps, sledges and Nile boats to move the stone.

Egyptians worshipped hundreds of gods: Ra the sun god, Osiris, ruler of the dead, his wife Isis, their son Horus, with whom each living king was identified, and jackal-headed Anubis, guardian of embalming. They believed the dead could live on if the body was preserved, so the wealthy were mummified: the organs were removed and stored, the body dried with natron salt and wrapped in linen, a process that took about 70 days. In the Hall of Judgement, they believed, the dead person's heart was weighed against the feather of Maat, goddess of truth. A heart heavy with wrongdoing was eaten by the monster Ammit. Spells in the Book of the Dead helped souls pass the test.

Hieroglyphs appeared by about 3200 BC, among the world's earliest writing. The script mixed signs for sounds with signs for whole words, and scribes used faster joined-up scripts, hieratic and later demotic, for everyday writing. As Christianity spread, the knowledge faded: the last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved at Philae in AD 394. The key came in 1799, when French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone, a decree of 196 BC written in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek. The British took it in 1801, and it has been in the British Museum since 1802. Building on work by Thomas Young, Jean-François Champollion used royal names in oval cartouches to crack the script in 1822.

Cleopatra VII (69–30 BC) was not Egyptian by descent: her family, the Ptolemies, were Macedonian Greeks who had ruled Egypt since Alexander's death. According to the Greek biographer Plutarch, she spoke many languages and was the first of her dynasty to learn Egyptian. She allied with Julius Caesar, with whom she had a son, Caesarion, and then with Mark Antony, with whom she had three children. Octavian defeated them at Actium in 31 BC, and both took their own lives in Alexandria in 30 BC; the famous asp bite comes from ancient accounts that historians cannot confirm. Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.

dd-greece.what: After a dark age following the collapse of the Mycenaean palaces, Greek city-states revived from about 800 BC, adopted an alphabet from the Phoenicians and founded colonies from Spain to the Black Sea. Athens and Sparta led them against Persian invasions, winning at Marathon in 490 BC and at Salamis and Plataea in 480–479 BC. Athens then enjoyed a golden age of democracy, drama, philosophy and building, crowned by the Parthenon. Rivalry with Sparta led to the Peloponnesian War of 431–404 BC, which Athens lost. Weakened by constant wars, the cities fell under Philip II of Macedon in 338 BC, and under Rome by 146 BC.
dd-greece.why: Greece's mountains and islands divided it into hundreds of small, fiercely independent cities, so no single kingdom formed. Citizens who fought side by side as armoured infantry, the hoplites, demanded a say in government. Sea trade and colonies brought wealth and contact with Egypt and the Near East, whose ideas Greeks borrowed and reworked. The same independence made the cities unable to stay united once Persia was beaten.
dd-greece.after: Greek ideas became a foundation of Western civilisation: philosophy, democracy, history writing, theatre, geometry, medicine and the Olympic Games. Rome adopted Greek art, gods and learning, and Greek remained the common language of the eastern Mediterranean for centuries. Countless English words, from 'politics' to 'theatre', are Greek, and buildings from the US Capitol to the British Museum copy Greek temples.

sections.t: Sparta was unlike any other Greek city. Its citizens, the Spartiates, were full-time soldiers who did not farm or trade. Their land was worked by helots, a conquered people who greatly outnumbered them and were kept down by fear: according to Plutarch, each year Sparta's officials formally declared war on them, so they could be killed without guilt. From about the age of seven, Spartan boys were trained in the agoge, a harsh state upbringing of hunger, beatings and drill. Spartan women were unusually free by Greek standards, exercised outdoors and, by Aristotle's time, owned perhaps two-fifths of the land. Yet citizen numbers kept falling, from about 8,000 in 480 BC to fewer than 1,000 in Aristotle's day.

In 480 BC the Persian king Xerxes invaded Greece with a vast army. Herodotus put it at over 2.6 million fighting men, which is impossible; modern estimates are mostly between 100,000 and 300,000. At the narrow pass of Thermopylae, about 7,000 Greeks, not just 300 Spartans, held them for two days. When a local man showed the Persians a mountain path around the pass, King Leonidas sent most of the army away. He stayed with his 300 Spartans, about 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans, and they were killed or captured. The stand became a legend of sacrifice, but the battle that saved Greece was the naval victory at Salamis weeks later.

According to tradition, the Olympics began in 776 BC at Olympia, a sanctuary of Zeus, and were held every four years for over a thousand years. A sacred truce let athletes and spectators travel safely. Events grew from a single footrace to boxing, wrestling, the brutal pankration, chariot racing and the pentathlon. Athletes competed naked, and only free Greek men could take part; married women were barred from watching. Winners got only an olive wreath, but their home cities might reward them with statues, cash and free meals for life. The games probably ended under Christian Roman emperors around AD 393–435 and were revived in Athens in 1896.

Socrates wrote nothing. He spent his days in the Athenian marketplace asking people what justice, courage or piety really were, and showing that they did not know. His pupil Plato made him the hero of his dialogues. In 399 BC, after Athens' defeat by Sparta and a brief, bloody rule by pro-Spartan oligarchs, some of them Socrates' former associates, he was tried for impiety and corrupting the young. A jury of about 500 citizens convicted him, and he died by drinking hemlock, refusing a chance to escape. Plato's account of his trial and death made Socrates a symbol of free thought.

dd-persia.what: In 550 BC Cyrus the Great united the Medes and Persians, then conquered Anatolia, Babylon and Central Asia. Under Darius I the Achaemenid Empire reached from Egypt and Thrace to the Indus, but its invasions of Greece failed in 490 and 480 BC. Alexander the Great conquered it in 334–330 BC, and his Greek successors, the Seleucids, ruled Iran until the Parthians, from the north-east, took over in the 2nd century BC. In AD 224 the Sasanians replaced them. Parthians and Sasanians fought Rome and Byzantium for about 700 years, until both sides were exhausted and Arab Muslim armies conquered Persia between 633 and 651.
dd-persia.why: The Iranian plateau sat at the crossroads between Mesopotamia, India and the Central Asian steppe, so whoever held it controlled great trade routes and rich farmland. Persian kings ruled a huge, varied empire by leaving local customs, religions and elites largely in place in return for tribute and soldiers. Their rivalry with Greece and Rome came from competition for the same rich borderlands: Anatolia, Syria, Mesopotamia and Armenia.
dd-persia.after: Arab conquest brought Islam, which most Iranians adopted over the next few centuries, but unlike Egypt or Syria, Iran kept its own language. Persian, written in Arabic script, became the language of poetry and government from the Ottoman court to Mughal India, and Persian officials helped run the Abbasid caliphate. Iranians today still celebrate Nowruz, the Persian new year, and look back on Cyrus and the ancient empires with pride.

sections.t: Darius I divided the empire into about 20 provinces, called satrapies, each under a governor, or satrap, with royal officials and garrison commanders reporting separately to the king. Provinces paid set tribute in silver, gold, horses or grain. A network of roads, above all the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa, more than 2,400 kilometres long, had stations where relay riders changed horses. Herodotus wrote that nothing stopped these couriers, not snow, rain, heat or darkness, a line now carved on New York's main post office. Thousands of clay tablets found at Persepolis record rations paid to the workers who built it, including extra rations for women who had just given birth.

Ancient Persians followed the teachings of the prophet Zarathustra, or Zoroaster, whose dates are uncertain; estimates range from about 1500 to 500 BC. Zoroastrians believe the wise lord Ahura Mazda is opposed by a destructive spirit, and that each person must choose good thoughts, good words and good deeds. Fire, a symbol of purity, burns in their temples. Darius I credited his victories to Ahura Mazda in his inscriptions, and the Sasanians made Zoroastrianism a state religion with a powerful priesthood. Many scholars think its ideas of a final judgement, heaven and hell influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Perhaps 100,000–200,000 Zoroastrians remain, many of them Parsis in India.

After the Arab conquest, Iran slowly became Muslim, but it did not become Arab. Around 1010 the poet Ferdowsi finished the Shahnameh, the 'Book of Kings', an epic of about 50,000 couplets retelling Iran's history and legends from the first kings to the Arab conquest. He wrote it in Persian with few Arabic words, and it helped keep the language and its memory alive. Persian scholars and officials shaped Islamic science, literature and government. Many Iranians later followed Shia Islam, which became the state religion under the Safavids from 1501. Today the spring festival of Nowruz, with roots in pre-Islamic Persia, is celebrated by about 300 million people, by UN estimates.

dd-rome.what: According to Roman tradition, Rome threw out its last king around 509 BC and became a republic run by elected magistrates and a Senate. It conquered Italy, then fought three wars with Carthage, surviving Hannibal's invasion and destroying the city in 146 BC. Conquest brought riches and slaves but also civil wars between generals. Julius Caesar won one and was murdered in 44 BC; his heir Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC. The empire peaked in the 100s AD, survived a near-collapse in the 200s and became Christian under Constantine. From 376 Germanic peoples moved in, Rome was sacked in 410, and the last western emperor was deposed in 476.
dd-rome.why: Rome turned beaten enemies into allies who supplied soldiers, and later into citizens, so its manpower seemed endless. Its legions were disciplined and its roads moved them quickly. But the Republic's institutions, built for a city-state, could not control generals with private armies and huge provinces. Centuries later the West fell to a mix of civil wars, money troubles, pressure on a long frontier and the loss of rich provinces such as Africa.
dd-rome.after: The Eastern Empire went on until 1453, and the idea of Rome lived on in the Holy Roman Empire, the tsars and the papacy. Latin became the Romance languages and the language of science and the Church, and Roman law shaped the legal codes of much of Europe and Latin America. Words such as senate, republic, dictator and citizen, and the Latin alphabet, all come from Rome.

sections.t: Romans hated the idea of kings, so the Republic split power. Two consuls, elected each year, led the state and its armies, and each could block the other. The Senate, a council of former officials who served for life, had no formal power to make laws but in practice guided policy, finance and war. Citizens voted in assemblies, but in some of them votes were grouped so the rich counted far more. Tribunes of the plebs, the common people, could veto acts that harmed them. In an emergency, a dictator could rule for up to six months. The letters SPQR, 'the Senate and People of Rome', summed up the ideal.

By the time of Augustus, Rome may have had about a million people, a size no city in Europe clearly matched again until London around 1800. Most lived in crowded apartment blocks, insulae, several storeys high, which often burned or collapsed. Under Augustus about 200,000 citizen men received free grain each month, and eleven aqueducts eventually brought fresh water to fountains, homes and huge public baths. Crowds of perhaps 50,000 watched gladiators and wild beast hunts in the Colosseum, opened in AD 80, while the Circus Maximus held far more for chariot races. The poet Juvenal mocked a people who cared only for 'bread and circuses'.

Conquest flooded Italy with captives. By one modern estimate, there were perhaps 1–1.5 million slaves in Italy under Augustus, out of 6–7.5 million people. They worked in mines, on great estates, in homes and as teachers, doctors and secretaries. Some were freed, and their children could become full citizens. In 73 BC the Thracian gladiator Spartacus broke out of a training school at Capua with about 70 others. Tens of thousands of slaves joined him, and they beat several Roman armies before Crassus crushed them in 71 BC. According to the historian Appian, 6,000 captives were crucified along the Appian Way between Capua and Rome.

Few questions have produced more answers: the German historian Alexander Demandt once collected 210 suggested causes. Edward Gibbon, writing in the 1770s and 1780s, blamed Christianity and barbarism. Popular theories such as lead poisoning from water pipes have little support. Most historians now stress a chain of problems: civil wars between rival emperors, the arrival of the Huns, which drove Goths and others into the empire, and the loss of the tax-rich provinces of Africa in 439. Some scholars prefer to speak of a 'transformation' of the Roman world rather than a fall, while others point to archaeology showing a sharp drop in living standards in the West.

dd-alexander.what: Alexander became king of Macedon at 20, in 336 BC, after his father Philip II was murdered. In 334 BC he invaded the Persian Empire with about 35,000 men, won battles at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela, and took Egypt, Babylon and Persepolis. He spent three hard years subduing Bactria and Sogdiana, then crossed into India, until his army refused to go further in 326 BC. He died in Babylon in 323 BC, aged 32. His generals tore the empire apart, and Greek kingdoms ruled Egypt and western Asia until Rome and Parthia absorbed them; the last, Ptolemaic Egypt, fell in 30 BC.
dd-alexander.why: Philip II had built the best army of its day, with long-speared infantry and heavy cavalry, and had already planned the attack on Persia. The Persian Empire was vast but loosely held, and many subjects had little loyalty to Darius III. Alexander added bold, personal leadership and tactical skill, and he kept local officials and customs in place to win over conquered peoples.
dd-alexander.after: Alexander's conquests began the Hellenistic age. Greek became the shared language of the eastern Mediterranean and Middle East for nearly a thousand years, which is why the New Testament was written in Greek. Greek cities, art and science spread as far as Afghanistan and northern India, influencing early Buddhist sculpture. His career became the model of the world conqueror, admired by Julius Caesar and Napoleon, and he lives on in legend from Europe to Iran, where he is remembered as both hero and destroyer.

sections.t: Alexander was tutored by the philosopher Aristotle, and as a boy, according to Plutarch, he tamed the wild horse Bucephalus, which carried him to India. Many famous stories cannot be checked: ancient writers disagreed over whether he cut the Gordian knot with his sword or simply pulled out its pin. The surviving histories were written centuries later, using lost eyewitness accounts. They show a brilliant, reckless general who led from the front and was badly wounded several times. They also show his cruelty: he razed Thebes, and after the siege of Tyre, ancient historians say, thousands were killed or enslaved. In a drunken quarrel in 328 BC he killed his friend Cleitus, who had saved his life.

Alexander wanted to rule as king of Asia, not just as a Greek conqueror. He adopted Persian court dress and ceremony, married the Bactrian noblewoman Roxana, and at Susa in 324 BC held a mass wedding where some 80–90 of his officers married Persian and other Iranian noblewomen. He trained 30,000 Persian youths to fight in the Macedonian style. Many Macedonians resented this, especially the demand that they bow before him as Persians bowed to their kings. After his death most officers abandoned their Persian wives, but the mixing he began went on in the cities he founded, many named Alexandria.

In Ptolemaic Alexandria, the Library and Museum drew scholars from across the Greek world. There Euclid wrote his Elements of geometry, and Eratosthenes estimated the size of the Earth around 240 BC with remarkable accuracy. Jewish scholars in the city translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek, the Septuagint. Far to the east, at Ai-Khanoum in Afghanistan, archaeologists found a Greek theatre and gymnasium. In Gandhara, artists blending Greek and Indian styles made some of the first statues of the Buddha in human form. Alexander's own body was seized by Ptolemy and entombed in Alexandria, where the Roman emperor Augustus visited it; the tomb's location has since been lost.

dd-maya.what: By about 300 BC Maya farmers in the forests of Central America were building large cities such as El Mirador, with pyramids and causeways, and carving the first Maya writing. In the Classic period, about 250–900, dozens of kingdoms ruled by divine kings flourished, among them Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copán, and they waged constant wars on one another. In the 800s the southern lowland cities stopped raising monuments, and most were abandoned. Life went on in northern Yucatán at Chichén Itzá and later Mayapán, and in the highland kingdoms. Spanish invaders arrived from 1524, but the last independent Maya kingdom, at Nojpetén, fell only in 1697.
dd-maya.why: Maize, beans and squash, grown on terraces, raised fields and forest plots, fed millions of people, and rulers turned that surplus into temples, palaces and armies. Kings claimed descent from gods and held power through ritual, alliances and war. The collapse had several causes, and historians weigh them differently: severe droughts in the 800s and 900s, endless warfare, crowded land and exhausted soils, and a loss of faith in kings who could not bring rain.
dd-maya.after: The Maya cities emptied, but the Maya people did not disappear. Spanish conquest brought disease, forced labour and Catholicism, which many Maya blended with older beliefs. Their descendants rose against outside rule, in the Caste War of Yucatán from 1847 and in Chiapas in 1994, and suffered terribly in Guatemala's civil war. Today over 6 million people speak Maya languages, and ruins such as Tikal and Chichén Itzá draw millions of visitors.

sections.t: Maya writing is the most complete script of the ancient Americas: about 800 signs, some standing for whole words and others for syllables. Scribes painted books on bark paper, but in 1562 the friar Diego de Landa burned many at Maní, and only four codices survive. For centuries no one could read the inscriptions. In 1952 the Soviet scholar Yuri Knorozov showed that the script recorded sounds, and in 1960 Tatiana Proskouriakoff proved that monuments told the life stories of real kings. Since the 1970s scholars have learned to read most texts. They tell of births, coronations, marriages, alliances, wars and captives, a history of rival kingdoms rather than a peaceful land of priests.

The Maya used several calendars at once. A 260-day ritual count meshed with a 365-day year, so the same combination came round only every 52 years. For history they used the Long Count, which numbered days from a starting point equal to 11 August 3114 BC in our calendar. Their counting system used a symbol for zero, one of the earliest in the world. One great cycle of the Long Count ended on 21 December 2012, which led to worldwide talk of a Maya prophecy of doom. Maya inscriptions predict no such thing: one at Palenque refers to a date thousands of years later, and scholars see 2012 as a completion, like a calendar rolling over.

Between about 800 and 950 kings across the southern lowlands stopped erecting dated monuments; the last known Long Count date, at Toniná, records the year 909. Populations fell sharply as people left for the north and the highlands. Lake sediments in Yucatán show severe droughts in this period, with rainfall falling by about half at their worst, according to a 2018 study. Many scholars think drought struck a society already strained by warfare, deforestation and dense populations: lidar surveys suggest the lowlands held millions of people at their peak. When rains failed and kings could no longer deliver, cities lost their reason to exist. The collapse was a slow decline over generations, not a sudden disappearance.

dd-africa.what: From about the 100s, the Kingdom of Aksum in the Ethiopian highlands traded across the Red Sea, minted gold coins and, around 330, adopted Christianity. In West Africa, Ghana grew rich by the 800s on gold sent north across the Sahara. Mali replaced it in the 1200s, and in 1324 its ruler Mansa Musa crossed Egypt on pilgrimage with so much gold that he became famous in Europe. Songhai, based at Gao, became the largest West African empire in the 1500s. On the east coast, Swahili city-states such as Kilwa grew wealthy on Indian Ocean trade, while inland the rulers of Great Zimbabwe built a city of stone.
dd-africa.why: Trade made these states. West Africa had gold, the Sahara had salt, and from the early centuries AD camels made regular desert crossings possible. Islam later linked West African rulers and merchants to North Africa and the Middle East. On the east coast the monsoon winds carried ships to Arabia and India and back each year. Rulers who controlled gold fields, ports or caravan routes could tax them, raise armies and build cities.
dd-africa.after: From the 1400s Portuguese ships reached Africa's coasts, and Atlantic trade, including a vast trade in enslaved people, drew wealth away from the Saharan and Swahili routes. Colonial writers later denied that Africans had built states like these, a claim archaeology disproved. Independent nations took their names: Ghana in 1957, Mali in 1960, Zimbabwe in 1980. Swahili is now spoken by over 100 million people, and Ethiopia's Orthodox Church still traces its roots to Aksum.

sections.t: In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, set out for Mecca with a huge following and many camel-loads of gold. When he stopped in Cairo he spent and gave away so much that, according to the Arab writer al-Umari, the value of gold there was still depressed twelve years later. The visit put Mali on the map, literally: the Catalan Atlas of 1375, made in Majorca, shows him on a throne holding a gold nugget. Modern claims that he was 'the richest person who ever lived' make good headlines but cannot be measured. On his way home he brought scholars and an architect, and Mali built mosques in Timbuktu and Gao.

Timbuktu began as a seasonal camp near the Niger and became a meeting point for camel caravans and river boats. By the 1400s and 1500s it was a centre of Islamic learning, with scholars teaching law, astronomy, medicine and grammar around mosques such as Sankore and Djinguereber. Families copied and collected manuscripts for centuries, and hundreds of thousands survive. When armed groups occupied the city in 2012–13, librarians and residents smuggled most of them south to Bamako in boxes and sacks, though some were burned. In Europe the name came to mean somewhere impossibly remote, but for West Africans it was a crossroads.

Great Zimbabwe's walls, some 11 metres high, were built from granite blocks fitted without mortar between about the 1000s and 1400s. When Europeans saw them in the 1870s, the explorer Karl Mauch claimed they were the work of the Queen of Sheba, and others credited Phoenicians or Arabs. Archaeologists disagreed: David Randall-MacIver in 1905 and Gertrude Caton-Thompson in 1929 showed the city was medieval and African, built by ancestors of the Shona. Rhodesia's white-minority government still pressed for the old myths in the 1960s and 1970s. At independence in 1980 the country took the city's name, and a carved soapstone bird from the site is on its flag.

dd-byzantium.what: In 330 Emperor Constantine refounded the Greek city of Byzantium as Constantinople, a new Christian capital for the Roman Empire. When the western half fell in 476, the eastern empire carried on. Justinian (527–565) reconquered Italy, North Africa and southern Spain, codified Roman law and built Hagia Sophia, but plague and war drained his empire. In the 600s Arab armies took Syria, Egypt and North Africa, though Constantinople's walls and Greek fire held. The empire revived around 1000, then lost most of Anatolia after the Seljuk Turks defeated it at Manzikert in 1071. Crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204; the Byzantines retook it in 1261, but the Ottomans captured it on 29 May 1453.
dd-byzantium.why: It lasted so long thanks to Constantinople's near-impregnable site, protected by sea on three sides and huge land walls, along with a trained bureaucracy, a trusted gold coin, the solidus, and skilled diplomacy that played enemies against each other. It declined because it faced enemies on every side, from Persians and Arabs to Bulgars, Normans and Turks, and because the Venetian-backed Fourth Crusade of 1204 broke it into rival states that never fully recovered.
dd-byzantium.after: Justinian's law code became the basis of civil law in much of Europe, and Byzantine scholars who fled to Italy brought ancient Greek texts that fed the Renaissance. Byzantine missionaries spread Orthodox Christianity and the forerunner of the Cyrillic alphabet to the Slavs, and Moscow later claimed to be the 'Third Rome'. The Ottomans made Constantinople, today's Istanbul, the capital of their own empire.

sections.t: After riots in 532 burned the old cathedral, Justinian had a new one built in under six years. His designers, the mathematicians Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, raised a dome about 31 metres across that seemed to float on a ring of 40 windows. Earthquakes brought it partly down in 558, and it was rebuilt higher. A later legend has Justinian exclaim on entering, 'Solomon, I have surpassed you!' It was the world's largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years. After 1453 the Ottomans made it a mosque and added minarets; it became a museum in 1934 and a mosque again in 2020, with many of its gold mosaics still visible.

Around 672, according to Byzantine chroniclers, an engineer named Kallinikos, a refugee from Syria, brought the empire a terrifying new weapon. Greek fire was a liquid sprayed through bronze tubes from the bows of warships; it burst into flame, kept burning on water and was very hard to put out. It helped beat off the great Arab sieges of Constantinople in 674–678 and 717–718. The recipe was a state secret, known only to a few families, and it was guarded so well that it was eventually lost. Historians think it was probably based on crude oil, perhaps mixed with resin, but nobody knows exactly how it was made or fired.

No one in the empire called themselves 'Byzantine'. They were Romaioi, Romans, and their state was the Roman Empire, ruled without a break from Augustus to its last emperor, Constantine XI, who died defending the walls in 1453. The name 'Byzantine' was popularised by Western scholars after the empire fell, from the old name of the city. Greek was the everyday language and the language of church and government, while Latin faded after the 600s. Western Europeans, especially after Charlemagne was crowned emperor in 800, preferred to call it 'the empire of the Greeks', a quarrel over who were the real Romans that lasted centuries.

Byzantium's longest-lasting export was its faith. In 863 the brothers Cyril and Methodius of Thessaloniki went to the Slavs of Moravia with an alphabet they had made for Slavonic; their followers in Bulgaria developed Cyrillic from it. According to the Primary Chronicle, envoys of Vladimir of Kyiv said of a service in Hagia Sophia that they 'knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth', and in 988 Vladimir was baptised. The split with Rome, dated to 1054, made the Eastern churches a separate tradition. Today there are over 200 million Orthodox Christians, from Greece and Serbia to Ukraine and Russia, many still using liturgies written in Byzantine times.

dd-vikings.what: On 8 June 793 raiders from Scandinavia sacked the monastery of Lindisfarne, and for two centuries Vikings raided coasts and rivers across Europe. Raiding grew into conquest: a Danish Great Army landed in England in 865 and settled the north and east, the Danelaw, and in 911 the Frankish king granted the lower Seine to the chief Rollo, founding Normandy. Norse settlers founded Dublin, settled Iceland from about 870 and Greenland around 985, and briefly reached Newfoundland around 1000. In the east, Swedes called the Rus traded down the rivers of Russia to Constantinople and the Caspian, and their princes ruled Kyiv. The age is often said to end in 1066, when the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada was killed at Stamford Bridge.
dd-vikings.why: Historians still debate the causes. Ambitious chiefs needed silver and land to reward their followers, and Scandinavia had little good farmland to spare. Fast, shallow ships let them cross open sea and row far up rivers, and rich, poorly defended monasteries and trading towns made easy targets. Booming trade with the Islamic world, and quarrels among the Frankish and English kingdoms, drew them further in.
dd-vikings.after: Denmark, Norway and Sweden became Christian kingdoms, taking shape around 1000. Norse settlers peopled Iceland and the Faroes, founded Dublin, and left English with words such as 'sky', 'egg' and 'they'. The Normans, descended from Rollo's settlers, conquered England in 1066 and southern Italy and Sicily. In the east, Kyivan Rus became Orthodox in 988, a common root of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus.

sections.t: The longship was the Vikings' great advantage. Built of overlapping oak planks, it was light, flexible and shallow, drawing only about a metre of water, so crews could land on any beach and row far up rivers like the Seine. A big square woollen sail drove it at sea, and oars took over in calm water or on rivers. The warship Skuldelev 2, built near Dublin around 1042 and sunk in Roskilde Fjord in Denmark, was about 30 metres long and carried around 60–70 men; a replica sailed from Roskilde to Dublin in 2007. Grand ships were also buried with the dead, as at Oseberg in Norway in 834. Sailors navigated by coastlines, sun, stars, birds and whales.

'Viking' meant going raiding, not a people: most Norse were farmers, fishers and craftspeople who never went 'a-viking'. They wore no horned helmets. The only fairly complete Viking helmet, found at Gjermundbu in Norway, is a plain iron cap; the horns come from 19th-century painters and the costumes for Wagner's operas in 1876. Combs are among the commonest finds, and free women could own property and divorce. Communities settled disputes at assemblies called things, the root of Iceland's Althing. But the raids were brutal, and slaving was central to the economy: captives from Ireland, Britain and eastern Europe were sold in markets from Dublin to the Volga.

sections.h: The Rus: Vikings in the east
sections.t: Swedish traders, known to their neighbours as the Rus, rowed across the Baltic and up the rivers of eastern Europe, dragging their boats overland between rivers. The Byzantine emperor Constantine VII recorded the names of the Dnieper rapids in both Norse and Slavic. According to the Primary Chronicle, written around 1113, the Varangian Rurik was invited to rule Novgorod in 862; how much of this is legend is debated. The Rus raided Constantinople in 860, and Rurik's successors ruled from Kyiv and made trade treaties with the Byzantines. Norsemen served the emperor in the Varangian Guard, and one carved runes into a balustrade in Hagia Sophia. Within a few generations the Rus princes spoke Slavic and, from 988, worshipped as Orthodox Christians.

dd-russia.what: In the 800s Scandinavian-led princes built a state, Rus', along the rivers from Novgorod to Kyiv, and in 988 it adopted Orthodox Christianity from Byzantium. Mongol armies conquered it in 1237–40. Moscow's princes rose as the Mongols' tax collectors, threw off their rule in 1480, and under Ivan IV took the title of tsar. Cossacks crossed Siberia to the Pacific by 1639. Peter the Great made Russia a European great power and an empire in 1721, and Catherine the Great pushed it to the Black Sea. By 1914 the tsars ruled a sixth of the world's land, until war and revolution brought them down in 1917.
dd-russia.why: Russia grew across open plains with few natural barriers, where expansion meant security and new lands to tax, and Siberia's furs drew traders east. Its rulers concentrated power in an autocratic tsar, backed by the Orthodox Church and a service nobility rewarded with land and serfs. Rivals were weakened in turn: the Mongol khanates, Sweden, Poland-Lithuania and the Ottomans. The empire's weaknesses were rigid autocracy, peasant poverty and late industrialisation, which defeat in war exposed.
dd-russia.after: The Bolsheviks who seized power in 1917 rebuilt most of the empire as the Soviet Union, and when it broke up in 1991, its 15 republics became independent along borders largely drawn in Soviet times. Russia remains the world's largest country, stretching across 11 time zones. Ukraine, Belarus and Russia all claim Kyivan Rus' as part of their history, and rival readings of that shared past have featured in the full-scale war Russia launched against Ukraine in 2022.

sections.t: Peter I, who ruled from 1682 to 1725, stood about two metres tall and was determined to modernise Russia on European lines. In 1697–98 he toured Western Europe with a large embassy, working for a time in a Dutch shipyard. Back home he ordered nobles to shave their beards or pay a tax, built a navy, and forced the nobility to serve the state. In 1703, on land taken from Sweden, he founded St Petersburg, built by tens of thousands of conscripted labourers, many of whom died. Victory over Sweden at Poltava in 1709 made Russia the leading power in the Baltic, and in 1721 he took the title of emperor.

For centuries most Russians were peasants, and from the law code of 1649 most were serfs, bound to the land and to their lords. Landowners could sell serfs, send them into the army for 25 years or have them flogged. Serfdom held back farming and industry, and peasant revolts, such as Pugachev's uprising in 1773–75, terrified the nobility. After defeat in the Crimean War, Alexander II freed the serfs in 1861; more than 20 million privately owned serfs gained their freedom, two years before slaves were freed in the United States. But they had to pay for their land over 49 years, and rural poverty fuelled the unrest that followed.

Nicholas II believed he ruled by God's will and resisted sharing power. Defeat by Japan in 1905 brought strikes and revolution, forcing him to allow an elected parliament, the Duma, though he soon limited its power. The First World War was disastrous: millions of soldiers were killed, wounded or captured, and cities ran short of bread. In March 1917, by the Western calendar, strikes and mutinies in Petrograd forced Nicholas to abdicate, ending three centuries of Romanov rule. A Provisional Government kept fighting the war, and in November the Bolsheviks under Lenin seized power. Nicholas and his family were shot at Yekaterinburg in July 1918.

dd-mongols.what: Temüjin, born around 1162, survived exile and feuds to unite the Mongol tribes, and in 1206 he was proclaimed Genghis Khan. He attacked the Western Xia and Jin in northern China, took Beijing in 1215, and in 1219–21 destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire of Central Asia and Iran. After his death in 1227 his sons and grandsons conquered the rest of northern China, the Russian principalities and Iraq, raided Poland and Hungary, and sacked Baghdad in 1258. Kublai Khan completed the conquest of Song China in 1279. But the empire split into four rival khanates, and the Yuan were driven out of China in 1368.
dd-mongols.why: Mongol armies were made up of superb horse archers, each with several horses, who could cover huge distances fast. Genghis Khan broke up old tribal loyalties, organised his men in units of tens, hundreds and thousands, and promoted for loyalty and talent. Spies, feigned retreats, captured engineers and calculated terror made cities surrender. Their enemies were often divided, and some, like the Rus princes, never united against them.
dd-mongols.after: The conquests killed huge numbers of people and wrecked cities and irrigation systems from Iran to Hungary. Yet the empire also linked Eurasia: merchants, missionaries and envoys travelled from Italy to China, spreading paper money, gunpowder, maps and, probably, the Black Death. Moscow rose as the Golden Horde's tax collector. In Mongolia Genghis Khan is revered as the father of the nation, while in Iran, Iraq and Russia he is remembered above all as a destroyer.

sections.t: Every Mongol man was a cavalryman, trained from childhood to ride and shoot a powerful composite bow from the saddle. On campaign each rider brought several spare horses, so armies could move scores of kilometres a day, living on mare's milk, dried meat and whatever they took. Genghis Khan organised them in a decimal system: units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000, the tumen. Their favourite tactic was the feigned retreat, luring enemies into a chase and then surrounding them. Against walled cities they used Chinese and Persian engineers, catapults and captured prisoners pushed in front as shields. Cities that surrendered at once were usually spared; those that resisted were often massacred, and word of it spread ahead of the army.

To hold their empire together the Mongols built the yam, a relay network of post stations with fresh horses, roughly a day's ride apart or less, where messengers could cover hundreds of kilometres in a day. Officials carried a paiza, a metal tablet that served as a passport and ordered locals to give them horses and food. The khans protected merchants and tolerated every religion, taxing trade rather than blocking it. Travellers crossed Asia as never before: the friar William of Rubruck reached Karakorum in 1254, Marco Polo spent about 17 years in Kublai's China, and the Nestorian monk Rabban Bar Sauma travelled from Beijing to Rome and Paris in 1287–88. Historians call this the Pax Mongolica, the Mongol peace.

Medieval chroniclers gave staggering death tolls, such as over a million at Merv in 1221, which historians regard as exaggerated. Even so, the destruction was real: whole cities in Central Asia and Iran were depopulated, and Iraq's ancient irrigation took centuries to recover. A popular claim is that one in 200 men alive today descends from Genghis Khan. It comes from a 2003 genetic study that found one male lineage shared by about 8% of men in a large region of Asia; the authors linked it to Genghis Khan's family, but this link is unproven. Another story says Mongols hurled plague corpses into the besieged Crimean port of Caffa in 1346; it comes from one Italian writer and is debated.

dd-habsburgs.what: In 1273 the German princes elected Rudolf of Habsburg, a minor Swiss count, as their king, and in 1278 he won Austria. From 1438 Habsburgs held the title of Holy Roman Emperor almost without a break until 1806. Well-planned marriages gave Charles V the Netherlands, Spain and its American empire, and his brother Ferdinand Bohemia and Hungary. After 1556 the family split into Spanish and Austrian lines. The Spanish line died out in 1700, but the Austrians drove back the Ottomans after 1683 and ruled a vast Danube empire. Defeated by Prussia in 1866, they shared power with Hungary from 1867. Defeat in World War I broke the empire apart in 1918.
dd-habsburgs.why: The Habsburgs rose through elections, inheritance and alliances more than conquest. Each marriage was a bet that the other line might die out, and several times it did. Their lands had no common language or nation, so the dynasty itself, the Catholic Church, the army and the civil service held them together. That worked in an age of kings but grew weaker as nationalism spread in the 1800s.
dd-habsburgs.after: Austria-Hungary's collapse created or enlarged Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Poland, Yugoslavia, Romania and Italy, and its quarrels over borders and minorities shaped Central Europe for decades. The Habsburgs left Baroque palaces, churches and cafés from Brussels to Lviv, and Vienna as a great capital of music. The family still exists: Otto von Habsburg, son of the last emperor, sat in the European Parliament for 20 years.

sections.t: A Latin saying summed up the family's method: 'Let others wage war; you, happy Austria, marry.' Emperor Maximilian I married Mary of Burgundy in 1477 and gained the rich Netherlands. He then married his son Philip to Joanna, heiress of Castile and Aragon, and in 1515, at a double wedding in Vienna, matched two of his grandchildren with the children of King Vladislaus of Bohemia and Hungary. Within 11 years both bets paid off. Spain's other heirs died young, and in 1526 the young King Louis II of Hungary drowned fleeing the battle of Mohács, so his crowns passed to his Habsburg brother-in-law, Ferdinand. The Habsburgs did fight many wars, but marriage made their empire.

To keep thrones in the family, Habsburgs often married cousins, and King Philip IV of Spain married his own niece. Portraits across two centuries show a jutting lower jaw and heavy lip, often called the 'Habsburg jaw'. A 2019 study by Spanish geneticists and facial surgeons linked the feature to the family's inbreeding. The extreme case was Charles II of Spain, the last of his line: his parents were uncle and niece, and he was sickly, struggled to chew and had no children. His death in 1700 ended Habsburg rule in Spain and set off the War of the Spanish Succession.

Emperor Charles VI had no sons, so in 1713 he issued the Pragmatic Sanction to let his daughter inherit. When Maria Theresa took the throne in 1740, aged 23, Prussia's Frederick II invaded rich Silesia at once, and a European war followed. She lost Silesia but kept the rest, and ruled for 40 years. She centralised taxes and the army, and in 1774 brought in compulsory schooling for children aged six to twelve. She also had 16 children; her daughter Marie Antoinette married the future Louis XVI of France. Her son Joseph II pushed further, easing serfdom and granting religious toleration in 1781.

dd-ottomans.what: Around 1300 Osman, a Turkish chief on the Byzantine frontier, founded a small state in north-west Anatolia. His heirs took Bursa, crossed into Europe in 1354 and conquered much of the Balkans, survived a crushing defeat by Timur in 1402, and in 1453 Mehmed II captured Constantinople. Selim I conquered Syria, Egypt and the holy cities of Arabia in 1516–17, and Suleiman the Magnificent took Hungary and Iraq. After the failed siege of Vienna in 1683 the empire slowly lost land to Austria, Russia and its own peoples. It joined World War I on Germany's side, lost, and was dissolved in 1922; the Republic of Turkey followed in 1923.
dd-ottomans.why: The Ottomans rose on a frontier where Byzantium and the Balkan kingdoms were weak and divided. They built a strong centralised state, an elite slave army of Janissaries and early skill with cannon, and they let Christians and Jews keep their faiths in return for taxes and loyalty. Their decline is debated: historians now stress reform and adaptation as much as decay, but Europe's growing economic and military power, Russian expansion, debt and nationalism wore the empire down.
dd-ottomans.after: More than 30 countries today were once wholly or partly Ottoman, and many of their borders, conflicts and mixed communities, from Bosnia to Iraq and Israel and Palestine, go back to the empire and its breakup. Its end brought the Armenian genocide, which Turkey disputes, and the Greek–Turkish population exchange. Atatürk's republic turned away from the Ottoman past, but Ottoman food, music, architecture and words live on across the Balkans and the Middle East.

sections.t: The sultan's best soldiers were slaves. Under the devshirme, or 'collection', officials visited Christian villages, mostly in the Balkans, every few years and took a share of the boys, roughly aged 8 to 18. They were converted to Islam, taught Turkish and trained. The strongest became Janissaries, a paid standing infantry armed with guns long before most European armies had one; the brightest went to the palace school and could rise to the top. Sokollu Mehmed Pasha, taken from a Serbian Orthodox family in Bosnia, became grand vizier to three sultans. Over time Janissaries married, ran businesses and toppled sultans they disliked, until Mahmud II destroyed the corps in 1826.

From the 1460s sultans lived in Topkapı Palace in Istanbul, which mixed government offices with the harem, the private household of the sultan's mother, wives, concubines, children and servants. The Ottomans had no rule that the eldest son inherited, so princes fought for the throne. Mehmed II's law code allowed a new sultan to execute his brothers for the sake of order, and in 1595 Mehmed III had 19 brothers killed. Later, princes were instead confined in palace apartments. In the 'sultanate of women' from the mid-1500s, mothers and wives such as Hürrem, a captive from today's Ukraine whom Suleiman freed and married, wielded real political power.

The Ottoman Empire was a Muslim state with huge Christian and Jewish populations, and for centuries Christians were a majority in its European provinces. Non-Muslims paid an extra tax and faced legal limits, but they could worship, run their own schools and courts, and were led by their own religious heads, an arrangement later called the millet system. When Spain expelled its Jews in 1492, Sultan Bayezid II welcomed many to Thessaloniki and Istanbul. This was not equality, and there were forced conversions and violence. In the 1800s, reforms called the Tanzimat promised equal rights, but rising nationalism turned communities against one another, with tragic results in the empire's final decades.

dd-aztecinca.what: In 1428 the Mexica of Tenochtitlan and two allied cities overthrew their overlords and built an empire across central Mexico, ruled from an island city in a lake. In the Andes, the Inca ruler Pachacuti began conquests around 1438 that created the largest state in the Americas. In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico; with tens of thousands of native allies and the help of a smallpox epidemic, he took Tenochtitlan in August 1521. In 1532 Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, collected a vast ransom and executed him. Inca resistance held out in the forests of Vilcabamba until 1572.
dd-aztecinca.why: Both empires were young, built by conquest within a century, and many subject peoples resented paying tribute; Tlaxcala and other enemies of the Aztecs joined the Spaniards in large numbers. European diseases, to which Americans had no immunity, killed rulers and armies, and in Peru an epidemic set off a civil war between two royal brothers just before Pizarro arrived. Steel, horses and guns helped too, but the Spaniards were always vastly outnumbered and could not have won alone.
dd-aztecinca.after: Spain built a new empire on the ruins: Mexico City rose over Tenochtitlan, and Lima became the capital of Spanish South America. Silver from Potosí and Zacatecas flowed to Europe and China. Epidemics, war and forced labour caused one of history's worst population collapses. Yet Indigenous peoples endured: millions still speak Nahuatl and Quechua, and Mexico's flag shows the eagle and cactus of Tenochtitlan's founding legend.

sections.t: According to Mexica tradition, their god told them to settle where they saw an eagle on a cactus, and they founded Tenochtitlan on a swampy island around 1325. Two centuries later it was one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps 200,000 people by many estimates. Causeways linked it to the shore, an aqueduct brought fresh water, and farmers grew crops on chinampas, fertile plots built up from the lake bed. A great market at Tlatelolco amazed the Spaniards. At the centre rose the Templo Mayor, a twin pyramid to the rain god Tlaloc and the war god Huitzilopochtli, where captives were sacrificed; the numbers are debated, and some Spanish figures are surely inflated.

sections.h: How so few defeated so many
sections.t: Cortés began with about 600 Spaniards, and Pizarro had 168 at Cajamarca. Their success was not a matter of a few men conquering empires alone. In Mexico, Tlaxcala and other peoples who hated Aztec rule supplied most of the soldiers; the final siege involved tens of thousands of native warriors. Smallpox arrived in 1520 and killed many of the city's defenders and its new emperor, Cuitláhuac. In Peru, epidemic disease and a war of succession between Atahualpa and Huáscar had already shattered the empire. A popular story says Moctezuma took Cortés for the returning god Quetzalcoatl, but many historians think this was invented after the conquest.

The Inca state ran without coins, markets in the European sense or a known writing system. Instead, households owed labour, called mit'a: farming state fields, building roads, weaving cloth or serving in the army. The state stored the produce in thousands of warehouses and redistributed food and cloth in hard times and at feasts. Officials recorded censuses and tribute on quipus, knotted cords whose numbers can be read but whose full meaning is still debated. Relay runners, the chasquis, carried messages along some 30,000–40,000 km of roads, with rope bridges over gorges. The Spaniards later turned the mit'a into forced labour in the silver mines.

dd-spanish.what: In 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella took Granada and sent Columbus west. Spanish settlers seized the Caribbean islands, then Hernán Cortés toppled the Aztecs in 1519–21 and Francisco Pizarro the Incas from 1532, with Indigenous allies and epidemics doing much of the work. Silver strikes at Potosí and Zacatecas in the 1540s paid for a global empire, and from 1565 galleons linked Mexico with Manila. Under Philip II Spain also ruled much of Italy, the Netherlands and, from 1580, Portugal. Wars, debt and the Dutch revolt wore it down, Napoleon's invasion in 1808 set off the independence wars, and in 1898 the United States took Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines.
dd-spanish.why: Spain's crowns emerged from the Reconquista united, militant and Catholic, with nobles hungry for land and glory. Columbus's voyage opened a hemisphere whose peoples had no immunity to Old World diseases. Royal law made conquerors' gains the Crown's, and American silver let Spain's Habsburg kings fight wars across Europe. But it also brought inflation and debt, and Spain's rivals, the Dutch, English and French, grew stronger on trade.
dd-spanish.after: Spanish is now the native language of about 500 million people, and Latin America is home to roughly 40% of the world's Catholics, by Pew Research estimates. The empire also left mixed societies, cities on a grid around a central plaza, and deep inequality rooted in colonial land and labour systems. Its silver dollar, the 'piece of eight', became the first global currency and the model for the US dollar.

sections.t: In 1545 silver was found in the Cerro Rico, a mountain over 4,000 metres up in the Andes. Within decades Potosí was one of the largest cities in the Americas, with churches, gambling houses and a royal mint. In the 1570s Viceroy Francisco de Toledo adapted an Inca labour draft, the mita, forcing thousands of Indigenous men each year to work the mines, where accidents, cold and mercury poisoning killed many. Coins struck there, the famous 'pieces of eight', circulated from Europe to China. 'Vale un Potosí', it is worth a Potosí, entered Spanish as a phrase for great riches, and in Don Quixote even 'the mines of Potosí' are too little to repay Sancho.

Spaniards argued fiercely about whether conquest was just. Bartolomé de las Casas, a settler who became a Dominican friar, spent 50 years denouncing the abuse of Indigenous people, and his 'Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies' was published in 1552. Pressure from him and others helped produce the New Laws of 1542, which banned enslaving Indigenous people and limited the encomienda labour grants, though settlers resisted them. In 1550–51 Las Casas debated the scholar Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda at Valladolid on whether Native peoples could be conquered for their own good. Neither was declared the winner. Spain's enemies later used Las Casas's writings to build the 'Black Legend' of unique Spanish cruelty.

By 1825 Spain had lost the American mainland, but Cuba and Puerto Rico stayed Spanish, kept rich by sugar and by slavery, abolished only in 1873 in Puerto Rico and 1886 in Cuba. Cubans rose in 1868 and again in 1895, when the poet José Martí helped launch the revolt and was killed in battle. In February 1898 the US warship Maine blew up in Havana harbour, and the United States declared war that April. It destroyed one Spanish fleet at Manila Bay and another off Santiago de Cuba. In the Treaty of Paris Spain gave up Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, the last for 20 million dollars. Spaniards called it simply 'the Disaster', and a generation of writers set out to rethink their country.

dd-mughals.what: In 1526 Babur, a Central Asian prince descended from Timur and Genghis Khan, invaded from Kabul and defeated the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat. His son Humayun was driven out by the Afghan Sher Shah Suri but returned in 1555. Akbar, who ruled from 1556 to 1605, built a vast, well-run empire across northern India. Jahangir and Shah Jahan presided over a golden age of painting and architecture, including the Taj Mahal. Aurangzeb pushed the empire to its greatest size, but after his death in 1707 it fragmented. Persians, Afghans, Marathas and finally the British took its lands, and in 1858 Britain exiled the last emperor.
dd-mughals.why: The Mughals won with cavalry, gunpowder and skilled generals, and held power by bringing local elites into the system: Hindu Rajput princes became generals and in-laws, and nobles held ranked offices paid from land revenue. Decline came from long, costly wars in the Deccan, succession struggles, nobles turning governorships into hereditary states, and Maratha, Sikh and Afghan challengers. Historians still debate how much Aurangzeb's religious policies also played a part.
dd-mughals.after: The Mughal collapse opened the way for the British East India Company, which used Bengal's wealth to conquer India. Mughal buildings such as the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort and Lahore's Badshahi Mosque are national symbols; India's prime minister speaks from the Red Fort each Independence Day. Urdu grew from the empire's mix of Persian and local speech, and Mughal food, painting and music still shape South Asian culture. The Mughal past is also argued over in today's Indian politics.

sections.t: Akbar came to the throne at 13 and ruled for almost 50 years. He married Rajput princesses, made Hindu nobles generals and ministers, and in 1564 abolished the jizya, a tax on non-Muslims. At his new city of Fatehpur Sikri he built a House of Worship where Sunni and Shia scholars, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuit priests debated before him. He promoted sulh-i kul, 'peace with all', and late in life founded a small devotional circle around himself, the Din-i Ilahi, which did not outlast him. Though he probably could not read, he built a huge library and had Hindu epics translated into Persian. His finance minister, Todar Mal, surveyed lands to set fair taxes.

sections.h: The Taj Mahal: facts and legends
sections.t: When his wife Mumtaz Mahal died giving birth to their 14th child in 1631, Shah Jahan ordered a tomb for her at Agra. Building went on for about 20 years, with some 20,000 workers according to traditional accounts, and craftsmen inlaid the white marble with semi-precious stones. Some well-known stories are legends. There is no evidence that the emperor cut off the builders' hands so they could never build anything as fine. Nor is there evidence that he planned a black twin across the river. What is recorded is that his son Aurangzeb deposed him in 1658, and he spent his last years confined in Agra Fort, within sight of the tomb, where he was buried beside his wife.

Aurangzeb seized the throne in 1658 and defeated his three brothers, two of whom he had executed. A devout Sunni, he ruled by Islamic law, banned some court music and in 1679 reimposed the jizya; he also destroyed some major temples, though he funded others and still employed many Hindu nobles. Historians argue over how far his religious policies turned subjects against him. Certain is that from 1681 he spent his last 26 years campaigning in the Deccan. He conquered Bijapur and Golconda, but the Marathas, built up by Shivaji, fought on. The wars drained the treasury, and when he died in 1707 aged 88, a rapid break-up followed.

dd-british.what: English traders and settlers founded colonies in North America and the Caribbean from the 1600s, while the East India Company traded in India. Britain lost thirteen American colonies in 1783 but expanded elsewhere: it conquered most of India, settled Australia from 1788 and New Zealand, and voted to abolish slavery in 1833. In the late 1800s it seized large parts of Africa. By 1920 the empire covered about a quarter of the world's land. After the Second World War it unravelled fast: India left in 1947, most of Africa and the Caribbean in the 1950s–60s, and Hong Kong was handed to China in 1997.
dd-british.why: Britain had a powerful navy, early industry, banks that could fund wars and trading companies, and a rivalry with France and Spain that drove expansion. Profits from sugar, slavery, cotton, tea and opium fed growth, and local allies and rivalries helped a few officials rule vast populations. After 1945 Britain was nearly bankrupt, nationalist movements were strong, and both superpowers opposed colonial empires.
dd-british.after: English became the world's common language, and parliamentary government, common law, railways and sports such as cricket spread across former colonies. So did lasting wounds: borders drawn in London, the partitions of India and Palestine, and the legacies of slavery and land seizure. Historians and the public still argue over how to weigh its benefits against its violence. The Commonwealth links 56 countries, and Britain still holds 14 overseas territories.

sections.t: Britain never ruled its empire with British manpower alone. In India a few thousand British officials, backed by tens of thousands of British troops, governed over 300 million people, relying on Indian troops, clerks and around 560 princely states whose rulers accepted British control. In Africa, 'indirect rule' worked through chiefs and emirs. Much early expansion was done not by the state but by companies: the East India Company had its own army, about 200,000 strong by 1803, larger than Britain's. The Royal Navy, steamships, the telegraph and the Suez Canal stitched it together; by 1902 an undersea cable circled the globe on British territory, nicknamed the 'All Red Line'.

British ships carried about 3 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic, more than any nation in the 1700s, and Caribbean sugar made planters and ports such as Liverpool and Bristol rich. Then a campaign by Quakers, evangelicals such as William Wilberforce, freed people such as Olaudah Equiano, and repeated revolts by the enslaved turned opinion. Parliament banned the trade in 1807 and slavery itself in 1833, taking effect in 1834. The government paid £20 million, about 40% of its yearly budget, in compensation to slave owners, not to the roughly 800,000 freed people, who were forced to work for their former owners for years as 'apprentices'. The Royal Navy then patrolled West Africa against slavers.

Britons were long taught that the empire spread peace, trade, law and Christianity. Its defenders point to railways, universities, the rule of law and the fight against slavery. Critics point to conquest and dispossession, from Aboriginal Australia to the Kenyan highlands, to massacres such as Amritsar in 1919, to concentration camps in the Boer War, where over 26,000 Boer women and children and at least 14,000 black Africans died, and to famines. An estimated 2 to 3 million people died in the Bengal famine of 1943, which most historians agree wartime British policy made worse, though they debate how much. Polls show Britons are divided on whether to be proud of the empire.

The empire's legacy is everywhere. English is spoken by over a billion people, and many countries share Westminster-style parliaments, common law, cricket and left-hand driving. Migration ran both ways: Indian workers went to the Caribbean, Fiji and East Africa, and after 1948 people from the colonies, such as the Windrush generation from the Caribbean, helped rebuild Britain. Many of today's conflicts trace back to imperial decisions, including Kashmir, Israel and Palestine, and Northern Ireland. The Commonwealth, led symbolically by King Charles III, is a voluntary club of 56 countries, and he is still head of state of Canada, Australia, New Zealand and several smaller nations.

dd-napoleon.what: Napoleon Bonaparte, a Corsican artillery officer, made his name retaking Toulon in 1793 and won fame with his Italian campaign of 1796–97. After a failed expedition to Egypt, he seized power in 1799 as First Consul, made peace with the Church and issued his Civil Code. In 1804 he crowned himself emperor. He crushed Austria and Russia at Austerlitz in 1805 and Prussia at Jena in 1806, but Britain's navy stayed unbeaten after Trafalgar. Spain's guerrilla war from 1808 drained him, and the invasion of Russia in 1812 destroyed his army. Beaten at Leipzig in 1813, he abdicated in 1814, returned for the Hundred Days, and lost for good at Waterloo in 1815.
dd-napoleon.why: The revolution had swept away the old elites and opened careers to talent, and its wars made generals powerful. Bonaparte combined military genius, speed and ruthless self-promotion, and the French, worn out by a decade of upheaval, welcomed order. His victories rested on large conscript armies and flexible corps. But his ambition knew no limit, and his attempt to strangle Britain's trade drew him into Spain and Russia. Europe's rulers finally united against him.
dd-napoleon.after: The Congress of Vienna restored kings, but much of Napoleon's work lasted. His Civil Code shaped the law of much of Europe, Latin America and beyond, and his prefects, lycées and Bank of France still structure French life. He ended the Holy Roman Empire and simplified Germany's map from hundreds of states to a few dozen, and by stirring national feeling in Germany, Italy and Spain he helped bring about the nation-states of the 1800s.

sections.t: Napoleon chaired many of the meetings that drafted the Civil Code, issued in March 1804 with 2,281 articles. It swept away France's patchwork of hundreds of local laws and made all male citizens equal before one law. It protected property, ended feudal privileges and allowed civil marriage and divorce. It also put wives and children firmly under the authority of husbands and fathers. French armies carried it to Belgium, the Netherlands, western Germany and Italy, and many countries later copied it, from Latin America to Egypt. On Saint Helena Napoleon is reported to have said that his Code, not his forty battles, would live forever. Its core is still French law today.

The idea of a tiny, touchy Napoleon is mostly myth. His height at death was recorded as 5 feet 2 inches in old French units, which is about 1.69 metres, or 5 feet 6 or 7 inches in English measures. That was average or a little above for a Frenchman of his time. The confusion came partly from the different inches, partly from his nickname, 'the little corporal', which was a term of affection from his soldiers, and partly from British cartoonists such as James Gillray, who drew him as a tantrum-throwing dwarf. He was also often seen beside his tall Imperial Guard.

The revolution had abolished slavery in 1794, but in 1802 Napoleon brought it back in Guadeloupe and French Guiana, and kept it in Martinique. He sent a large army under his brother-in-law Leclerc to retake Saint-Domingue. Its leader Toussaint Louverture was seized and died in a French prison in 1803. The French army was destroyed by yellow fever and by the resistance led by Jean-Jacques Dessalines, and Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804. The failing campaign helped persuade Napoleon to sell Louisiana to the United States in 1803 for 15 million dollars, doubling the young country's size. France finally abolished slavery in 1848.

dd-greatgame.what: In the 1800s the Russian Empire conquered the steppe and the khanates of Central Asia, while Britain expanded across India, and each feared the other would reach Afghanistan first. Britain invaded in 1839 to install a friendly ruler, but a revolt in Kabul forced its army to retreat in January 1842, and almost all were lost. A second war in 1878–80 gave Britain control of Afghan foreign policy. The two empires then drew Afghanistan's borders, including the Durand Line, agreed between Britain and the emir in 1893, and the Wakhan Corridor, and in 1907 settled their rivalry. In the 20th century the Soviet Union invaded in 1979 and the US-led coalition in 2001; both eventually left.
dd-greatgame.why: Britain saw India as the jewel of its empire and feared a Russian advance through the mountain passes, while Russia pushed south for security, trade and prestige, and to gain leverage over Britain. Afghanistan, a mountainous kingdom of many peoples, sat between them. Later invaders came for new reasons: the Soviets to save a failing communist ally, the Americans to destroy al-Qaeda and the Taliban regime that sheltered it after 9/11.
dd-greatgame.after: The Great Game fixed the borders of Afghanistan and Central Asia, and the Durand Line still divides the Pashtun people and strains relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan. The Soviet war fed the Cold War's end and produced the jihadist networks behind al-Qaeda. Twenty years of US-led war ended in 2021 with the Taliban back in power. Afghanistan has also given the world the much-debated label 'graveyard of empires'.

sections.t: In 1839 a British-Indian army marched into Afghanistan and put Shah Shuja on the throne in place of Dost Mohammad. Afghans saw him as a foreign puppet, and in November 1841 Kabul rose in revolt; in December the British envoy, William Macnaghten, was killed at a meeting with Dost Mohammad's son Akbar Khan. On 6 January 1842 about 4,500 soldiers, most of them Indian sepoys, and some 12,000 camp followers set out in deep snow for Jalalabad, about 140 km away. Harassed through the passes, almost all were killed, captured or froze. Dr William Brydon reached Jalalabad on 13 January, famous as the sole survivor, though a few sepoys and one other European straggled in later and about 100 hostages were later freed.

By 1900 both empires had new worries. Russia had been shaken by defeat against Japan and revolution in 1905, and Britain was more alarmed by Germany's rising navy. In August 1907 they signed a convention that divided Persia into a Russian sphere in the north, a British sphere in the south-east and a neutral zone between, without consulting the Persians. Russia accepted that Afghanistan lay in Britain's sphere, and both agreed to leave Tibet alone. The deal ended the Great Game, a phrase made famous by Rudyard Kipling's novel Kim, and helped bring Britain, France and Russia together before World War I.

Afghanistan is often called the 'graveyard of empires', but the cliché needs care. Many empires did rule it: Alexander the Great, the Mauryans, Persians and Mughals, and it was itself the base of great empires. Britain suffered disasters in 1842 and at Maiwand in 1880, yet gained what it wanted, control of Afghan foreign policy, until 1919. What has defeated invaders is holding the country, not entering it: high mountains, a society of strong local and tribal loyalties, fighters with refuges and suppliers across the borders, especially in Pakistan, and governments that depended on foreign money and looked foreign-backed. The Soviet Union and the US were not destroyed by Afghanistan, but their wars there were long, costly failures.

dd-israel.what: Britain ruled Palestine from 1917 to 1948, as Jewish immigration and Arab resistance grew. In 1947 the UN proposed partition; Israel declared independence in 1948 and won the war that followed, while about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled. In 1967 Israel captured the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza, and settlements followed. Palestinian uprisings began in 1987 and 2000, and the 1993 Oslo Accords created limited Palestinian self-rule but no state. Hamas took over Gaza in 2007. Its attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 began a war that devastated Gaza; a ceasefire began in October 2025, but killing continued into 2026.
dd-israel.why: Two national movements claim the same land. Zionism, born in Europe in the 1880s amid antisemitism, sought a Jewish homeland in the land of the Bible, and the Holocaust made the case urgent for many. Palestinian Arabs, whose families had lived there for generations, sought independence and saw Jewish immigration as a threat. Since 1967 the core disputes have been borders, Israeli settlements, security, Jerusalem and the fate of the refugees.
dd-israel.after: In October 2026 Israel still occupied the West Bank, where over 500,000 settlers lived, plus over 200,000 in East Jerusalem; most of the world regards the settlements as illegal under international law, which Israel disputes. About 157 of 193 UN members recognise a State of Palestine. Gaza lay largely in ruins, Hamas had not disarmed, and Israel held over half the Strip. In Israel's 27 October 2026 election, neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition won a majority.
