The revolution also had a cultural side: the government paid painters such as Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros to cover public buildings with giant murals of Mexico's Indigenous past and its struggles, art still seen by millions.

Mexican smuggling gangs grew rich in the 1990s, when cocaine routes from Colombia shifted from the Caribbean to Mexico. In December 2006 President Felipe Calderón sent the army against the cartels. Killing their leaders split them into warring factions, and violence soared: official INEGI figures record well over 400,000 homicides since 2007, and more than 130,000 people are listed as missing. Most guns used by the cartels are smuggled from the US, the main market for their drugs, now including fentanyl. The jailed Sinaloa boss Joaquín 'El Chapo' Guzmán is serving life in the US, and in February 2026 troops killed 'El Mencho', head of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

Since NAFTA, car plants and electronics factories have made northern Mexico part of one North American production line, and by 2023 Mexico had overtaken China as the largest source of US imports. That closeness brings pressure. In 2025 and 2026 the US imposed tariffs on Mexican cars, steel and aluminium, linked trade talks to migration and fentanyl, and declined to extend the USMCA unchanged at its 2026 review. President Sheinbaum, who took office in October 2024, sent troops to the border, sent dozens of cartel figures to the US and raised tariffs on Chinese goods, while insisting that any US military action on Mexican soil would violate its sovereignty.

dd-germany.what: In 1871, after wars with Denmark, Austria and France, Prussia's Otto von Bismarck united the German states into an empire, which grew into Europe's industrial powerhouse. Germany lost World War I, and the Weimar Republic that followed was battered by hyperinflation and the Great Depression. In 1933 Adolf Hitler took power, built a dictatorship, launched World War II and murdered about 6 million Jews in the Holocaust. Defeated in 1945, Germany lost its eastern lands and was occupied, and in 1949 it split into a democratic West and a communist East. The Berlin Wall divided the two from 1961 until crowds breached it in 1989, and Germany reunited peacefully in 1990.
dd-germany.why: Germany came late to national unity, and it was made by Prussian arms rather than by a popular revolution. Its rapid rise unsettled its neighbours, and its leaders' gamble in 1914 led to a defeat many Germans refused to accept. The Versailles treaty, economic collapse and fear of communism helped the Nazis win mass support. After 1945 the Cold War decided Germany's fate: the Soviet Union and the Western Allies each built a German state in their own image.
dd-germany.after: West Germany built a stable democracy and, with France, the core of what became the European Union. Since 1990 united Germany has been the EU's largest economy and most populous member, with about 83 million people. Its long reliance on Russian gas and on exports to China was shaken after 2022, and under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, in office since May 2025, it is spending heavily on defence. Gaps in wealth and voting between east and west remain.

sections.t: In 1862 Otto von Bismarck told Prussia's parliament that the great questions of the day would be decided not by speeches and majority votes but by 'iron and blood'. He then fought three short wars in seven years and let France's declaration of war in 1870 unite the southern German states behind Prussia. As chancellor until 1890 he built a web of alliances to keep France isolated, and introduced the world's first national health insurance, accident insurance and old-age pensions, partly to win workers away from the socialists. His successor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, let the alliances lapse and built a navy to rival Britain's, helping create the tensions that led to 1914.

The Weimar Republic, founded in 1919, gave women the vote and fostered a burst of art, science and film, but it was blamed for the hated peace treaty. In 1923 hyperinflation made money almost worthless: a loaf of bread cost billions of marks by November. A few calmer years ended with the Great Depression, which left about 6 million Germans jobless by 1932. The Nazis became the largest party in July 1932 with 37% of the vote, and conservative politicians, believing they could control him, had Hitler appointed chancellor in January 1933. Within months he had banned other parties, crushed the unions and opened the first concentration camps.

East Germany called its border fortifications an 'anti-fascist protection rampart', but their real purpose was to stop people leaving: about 2.7 million had fled west between 1949 and 1961. Behind the Wall, the East offered jobs, cheap rents and childcare, but long waits for goods: ordering a Trabant car could mean waiting over ten years. The Stasi secret police employed about 91,000 staff by 1989 and relied on a large network of informers, often neighbours, colleagues or even spouses. After reunification, citizens could read their own Stasi files, and millions of people have asked to see them.

After 1945 Germany slowly confronted the Nazi era. West Germany agreed in 1952 to pay reparations to Israel and to Holocaust survivors, and its own courts tried Auschwitz guards in the 1960s. In 1970 Chancellor Willy Brandt knelt in silence at the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, an image that came to symbolise German remorse. Today schoolchildren visit former camps, Berlin has a large Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe beside the Brandenburg Gate, and over 100,000 small brass 'Stumbling Stones' set in pavements across Europe name individual victims outside the homes where they lived.

dd-iran.what: In 1906 a constitutional revolution gave Iran a parliament, but Russia and Britain soon split it into zones of influence, and oil struck in 1908 made it a prize. Reza Shah seized power in the 1920s and modernised by force. In 1951 Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh nationalised the British-run oil industry, and in 1953 a coup backed by the CIA and Britain's MI6 removed him. His son Mohammad Reza Shah ruled ever more harshly until a mass uprising in 1978–79 brought Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini to power and created an Islamic republic. Iraq invaded in 1980, starting an eight-year war. Decades of sanctions and nuclear disputes followed, and in 2026 US and Israeli strikes killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.
dd-iran.why: Iran's oil and its position between Russia, the Gulf and India drew outside powers in, and many Iranians came to see foreign meddling, above all the 1953 coup, as the root of their troubles. The Shah's rapid Westernisation, repression by his SAVAK secret police and a widening gap between rich and poor united clerics, leftists, liberals and bazaar merchants against him. After 1979 the new state defined itself against the US and Israel, which in turn saw its nuclear programme, missiles and armed allies as a threat.
dd-iran.after: The Islamic Republic built a network of allied armed groups, such as Lebanon's Hezbollah and Yemen's Houthis, and a nuclear programme it says is peaceful. Sanctions hurt its economy, and protest movements, from 2009 to 2022 and again in January 2026, were put down by force. The 2025 and 2026 wars with Israel and the US killed thousands, disrupted oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and left Iran's future deeply uncertain.

sections.t: In 1951 Iran's parliament nationalised the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, which had paid Iran far less than it paid the British government in taxes. Its champion, the elderly Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh, became a national hero. Britain answered with a boycott of Iranian oil, and after failing to dislodge him it won over the US, which feared a communist takeover. In August 1953 a CIA and MI6 plan, carried out with Iranian officers, paid crowds and royalists, toppled Mosaddegh, who was jailed and then kept under house arrest until his death. The Shah returned stronger, and US firms took a large share of Iran's oil. The CIA formally acknowledged its role in documents released in 2013.

Khomeini's system rests on velayat-e faqih, guardianship by a senior Islamic jurist. The Supreme Leader commands the armed forces, appoints the head of the judiciary and state media, and has the final say on big decisions. Iranians do elect a president and parliament, but the Guardian Council, twelve clerics and lawyers, vets every candidate and can strike down laws it judges un-Islamic. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, created in 1979 to protect the revolution, grew into a military and business empire. An elected Assembly of Experts chooses the leader: Khomeini ruled until 1989, Ali Khamenei until 2026, and in March 2026 the Assembly chose his son Mojtaba.

Iranian women are highly educated, and for years made up about half or more of university students, but since the early 1980s the law has required them to cover their hair in public. In September 2022 Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman, died after being detained by the morality police over her headscarf. Protests spread across the country under the slogan 'Woman, Life, Freedom', with women burning their scarves in the streets. Security forces killed over 500 people, according to the group Iran Human Rights, and several protesters were executed. A new wave of protests over a collapsing currency began in December 2025. Iran's government said over 3,000 died in the January 2026 crackdown; rights groups counted more.

Under the 2015 nuclear deal Iran limited its uranium enrichment in return for sanctions relief, but President Trump pulled the US out in 2018, and Iran then enriched uranium to 60%, close to weapons grade, while saying it did not seek a bomb. After Hamas attacked Israel in October 2023, Israel badly weakened Hezbollah and Iran's other allies, and Iran and Israel struck each other directly for the first time in 2024. In June 2025 Israel and the US bombed Iran's nuclear sites. Their 2026 war, which killed Khamenei, disrupted the world's oil supply. By October 2026 a spring truce had collapsed, and talks through Pakistan and Qatar had not ended the fighting.

dd-koreas.what: Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled it harshly until its defeat in 1945. American and Soviet troops then split the peninsula at the 38th parallel, meant as a temporary line. In 1948 two states appeared: a US-backed South under Syngman Rhee and a Soviet-backed North under Kim Il Sung. In June 1950 the North invaded. A US-led UN force drove it back almost to China, China's armies pushed the UN south again, and the front settled near the old line. An armistice in July 1953 created the Demilitarised Zone, but no peace treaty. The South later grew rich and democratic, while the North became a nuclear-armed family dictatorship.
dd-koreas.why: Korea was divided because the Cold War began just as Japan's empire collapsed. Neither superpower would accept a united Korea run by the other's side, and both Korean leaders wanted to reunite the country on their own terms. The war froze the split, and each state then built its identity in opposition to the other.
dd-koreas.after: The Korean War killed millions and left the peninsula one of the most heavily armed places on Earth, with US troops still in the South. Millions of families were separated. South Korea became a top-15 world economy and a cultural force, from Samsung to K-pop. North Korea, poor and isolated, has built nuclear weapons, and in 2024 it formally gave up the goal of reunification.

sections.t: On 25 June 1950 North Korean tanks crossed the 38th parallel, took Seoul in three days and drove the South's army and the first US troops into a corner around Pusan. In September General Douglas MacArthur landed at Inchon, cut the North's supply lines and pushed north towards the Chinese border. In late 1950 hundreds of thousands of Chinese troops struck back, and in the frozen mountains around the Chosin Reservoir US Marines had to fight their way out. From mid-1951 the war became a bloody stalemate near the 38th parallel while truce talks dragged on for two years. Common estimates put the dead at about 3 million, more than half of them civilians.

In 1960 South Korea was one of the world's poorest countries, with an income of under $200 a person, and most economists believe the more industrialised North was richer into the 1970s. Under the military ruler Park Chung-hee, who seized power in 1961, the state steered cheap loans to family-run conglomerates such as Samsung and Hyundai and pushed exports: first wigs and textiles, then ships, steel, cars and microchips. Growth was rapid but came with repression until mass protests won democracy in 1987. By 2025, according to the Bank of Korea, the South's income per person was about $37,000, roughly 28 times the North's, and its total economy about 56 times larger.

Kim Il Sung ruled from 1948 until his death in 1994, building a personality cult and the ideology of Juche, or self-reliance. His son Kim Jong Il inherited a country whose economy collapsed when Soviet aid ended. In the famine of the mid-1990s, estimates of the dead range from several hundred thousand to over two million. Since 2011 the grandson, Kim Jong Un, has ruled. A 2014 UN inquiry found crimes against humanity, including political prison camps estimated to hold 80,000–120,000 people. Kim had his uncle executed in 2013, and his half-brother was murdered with a nerve agent in Malaysia in 2017. His daughter, Kim Ju Ae, is widely seen as a possible successor.

North Korea announced its withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty in 2003 and tested its first nuclear device in 2006. Five more tests followed, the largest in 2017, which it called a hydrogen bomb. It has also tested missiles that experts believe can reach the whole United States. Years of talks, sanctions and three meetings between Kim Jong Un and President Trump in 2018–19 failed to stop the programme, and in 2023 North Korea wrote its nuclear status into its constitution. SIPRI estimated it had about 60 warheads in January 2026. Its closer ties with Russia since 2024 have brought it money, oil and, many analysts fear, military technology.

dd-turkey.what: After the Ottoman Empire's defeat in World War I, Mustafa Kemal led a war of independence against Greek, Armenian and Allied forces and founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923. As president he abolished the caliphate, replaced Islamic law with European codes and Arabic script with the Latin alphabet, and gave women the vote. Multi-party elections came in 1950, but the army, seeing itself as guardian of his legacy, seized power or forced out governments in 1960, 1971, 1980 and 1997. Turkey joined NATO in 1952 and invaded Cyprus in 1974. From 2002 Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's AK Party dominated politics, and after a failed coup in 2016 he gained sweeping presidential powers.
dd-turkey.why: Kemal and his circle blamed the empire's decline on religious tradition and believed only a secular, Western-style nation-state could survive among the great powers. Their reforms were imposed from above, and many pious Anatolians and Kurds felt left out. That divide, between a secular elite backed by the army and a conservative, religious majority, shaped Turkish politics for decades and helped Erdoğan rise.
dd-turkey.after: Turkey became a large industrial economy of over 85 million people and a regional power, with troops in Syria, Iraq, Libya and beyond. Under Erdoğan religion returned to public life, while critics, journalists and opposition leaders, including Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, were jailed, which his government says is a matter for independent courts. In 2025 the PKK announced it would disband, and in August 2026 parliament passed a law setting out terms for its fighters to disarm and return.

sections.t: Between 1924 and 1935 Mustafa Kemal remade daily life. The caliphate was abolished in 1924 and religious courts and Sufi lodges closed. The fez was banned in 1925, and Swiss, Italian and German law codes replaced Islamic law. In 1928 the Latin alphabet replaced Arabic script within months, and Kemal toured the country with a chalkboard teaching the new letters. Women won the vote in national elections in 1934, before women in France or Italy. A 1934 law required everyone to take a surname, and parliament gave Kemal the name Atatürk, 'Father of the Turks'. He ruled as a one-party leader until his death in 1938, and insulting his memory is still a crime.

Kurds make up perhaps 15–20 percent of Turkey's people, by most estimates. The early republic defined everyone as Turkish, crushed Kurdish revolts in 1925 and 1937–38, and for decades restricted the Kurdish language. In 1984 the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), led by Abdullah Öcalan and listed as a terrorist group by Turkey, the US and the EU, began an armed insurgency. About 40,000 people were killed, and thousands of Kurdish villages were emptied in the 1990s. Öcalan was captured in Kenya in 1999. After a 2013–15 peace process collapsed, Öcalan called in February 2025 for the PKK to disarm, and in May it announced it would dissolve.

A former Istanbul mayor from a pious, working-class background, Erdoğan led the AK Party to victory in 2002 and became prime minister in 2003. Early on he tamed the army, began EU membership talks and presided over fast growth. Over time his rule grew more personal: protests over Istanbul's Gezi Park in 2013 were put down hard, and after the 2016 coup attempt, which he blames on the Gülen movement, over 150,000 people were detained or dismissed. A 2017 referendum created a powerful presidency. High inflation, which peaked above 80 percent in 2022, hurt living standards, and the opposition won major cities in 2019 and 2024. Erdoğan's term runs until 2028.

Turkey straddles two continents, with Istanbul spanning the Bosphorus, and its foreign policy reflects that. It is a NATO member with the alliance's second-largest army and has been an EU candidate since 1999, though membership talks have been frozen since 2018. It also buys Russian air defences and gas, hosts millions of Syrian refugees, and builds influence across the Middle East, Africa and Central Asia. Turkish drones have shaped wars from Libya to Karabakh and Ukraine. Erdoğan has positioned Turkey as a broker, hosting Russian–Ukrainian talks, while condemning Israel over Gaza and staying out of the 2026 war on Iran.

dd-japanmodern.what: Japan surrendered in August 1945 after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet attack on Manchuria. US-led forces occupied it until 1952, writing a new constitution that made the emperor a symbol and renounced war. Allied to the United States, Japan rebuilt at astonishing speed: bullet trains ran from 1964, and by 1968 its economy was the world's second largest. In the 1980s Japanese cars and electronics dominated world markets, until a giant stock and property bubble burst in 1990–91. Decades of slow growth followed, along with the 2011 tsunami and nuclear disaster and a shrinking, ageing population.
dd-japanmodern.why: Japan had an educated workforce, a strong state and industrial know-how left from before the war. The Cold War made the US want a strong Japanese ally, so it opened its markets, bought supplies for the Korean War and paid for most of Japan's defence. High savings, close cooperation between officials and big companies, and a cheap yen powered exports. Easy credit in the late 1980s inflated the bubble, and slow clean-up of bad debts after it burst prolonged the slump.
dd-japanmodern.after: Japan is still the world's fourth-largest economy, a technology leader and a cultural power, from anime to sushi. But its population has fallen since 2008, and nearly 3 in 10 people are 65 or over. Facing China's rise and North Korea's missiles, it has stretched its pacifist constitution, and under Sanae Takaichi, its first woman prime minister, who won a landslide in February 2026, it is spending more on defence.

sections.t: On 15 August 1945 most Japanese heard their emperor's voice for the first time, on the radio, telling them to 'endure the unendurable'. The occupation that followed, under General Douglas MacArthur, aimed to make Japan peaceful and democratic. Women won the vote, unions were legalised, the big family-owned business groups were broken up, and landlords had to sell land to their tenants. Emperor Hirohito was not put on trial; in 1946 he denied that he was divine. A Tokyo tribunal sentenced seven wartime leaders, including Prime Minister Hideki Tojo, to death. The constitution of 1947, drafted by MacArthur's staff, has never been amended, and its Article 9 still renounces war.

Between the mid-1950s and early 1970s Japan's economy grew about 10% a year. Millions moved from farms to cities, and families bought the 'three sacred treasures' of the 1950s: a television, a washing machine and a fridge. Big companies offered lifetime jobs to male workers in return for long hours and loyalty, and the trade ministry, MITI, steered investment into steel, ships, cars and electronics. Toyota's lean production and Sony's transistor radios and Walkman became famous worldwide. Growth had costs too: pollution scandals such as Minamata disease, caused by factory mercury, poisoned thousands. By the 1980s many Americans feared that Japan would overtake the US.

In the late 1980s cheap credit drove share and land prices to absurd heights: at the peak, the land under Tokyo's Imperial Palace was said to be worth more than all of California. The Nikkei stock index hit 38,916 on 29 December 1989, then lost most of its value, and did not pass that peak again until February 2024. Banks sat on bad loans, prices fell for years, and growth stalled; China overtook Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010. Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's 'Abenomics' from 2012 used cheap money and spending to fight deflation. Abe was assassinated in 2022, and inflation has finally returned, though wages have struggled to keep up.

Japan has one of the world's oldest populations. Its people peaked at about 128 million in 2008, and in 2025 only about 671,000 Japanese babies were born there, the lowest since records began in 1899. The 2025 census found 29% of people aged 65 or over, and millions of homes in the countryside stand empty. Japan has turned to robots and to older workers, and, more cautiously, to immigrants: a record of almost 4.3 million foreign residents lived there in mid-2026, though immigration is a growing political issue. With few children and high costs, many young people delay marriage, and the government has repeatedly expanded child benefits with little effect on birth rates so far.

dd-india.what: India became independent in 1947 and a republic in 1950, with a constitution guaranteeing votes for all adults. Jawaharlal Nehru's Congress governments built a secular, state-planned economy and steered clear of Cold War blocs. His daughter Indira Gandhi helped Bangladesh break away in 1971, suspended democracy during the 1975–77 Emergency, and was assassinated in 1984. A debt crisis in 1991 forced market reforms that unleashed faster growth. From the 1990s the Hindu nationalist BJP rose, and since 2014 Narendra Modi has led India, winning a third term in 2024. By 2023 India was the world's most populous country.
dd-india.why: India's founders inherited a poor, mostly rural and illiterate country of hundreds of languages, castes and faiths, and chose federal democracy to hold it together. The state-led economy brought steel, dams and the Green Revolution's food security, but growth stayed slow, which made the 1991 reforms possible. Politics shifted as lower castes, regional parties and Hindu nationalism challenged Congress's dominance, and Modi's mix of welfare, infrastructure and Hindu identity won wide support.
dd-india.after: India is now a major economy, a nuclear power, a space power and a sought-after partner of both the West and Russia. Extreme poverty has fallen sharply, by World Bank estimates, though jobs for its young population remain a challenge. Critics, including rights groups, say democracy and minority rights, especially for Muslims, have weakened under Modi; his government rejects this. In 2026 the BJP won West Bengal for the first time, while youth-led protests over jobs and exam leaks challenged the government.

sections.t: The constitution, drafted under the Dalit lawyer B. R. Ambedkar, gave every adult the vote in 1950, when most Indians could not read, so parties used symbols such as a hand, a lotus or an elephant. It abolished 'untouchability' and reserved seats, jobs and university places for the lowest castes and tribes. In 2024 nearly 970 million people were eligible to vote over six weeks, using electronic machines, with polling stations within about 2 kilometres of every voter, including one for a single monk in a Gir forest temple. Only once was democracy suspended: during Indira Gandhi's 1975–77 Emergency, after which voters threw her out.

The Congress party was long led by one family, unrelated to Mahatma Gandhi. Nehru governed for 17 years. His daughter Indira won the 1971 war, but in 1975, after a court voided her election, declared an Emergency, jailing opponents and running a forced sterilisation drive. In 1984 she sent the army into the Golden Temple in Amritsar against Sikh militants; months later her Sikh bodyguards shot her, and mobs killed about 3,000 Sikhs in Delhi. Her son Rajiv was killed by a Tamil Tiger bomber in 1991. Rajiv's Italian-born widow Sonia led Congress back to power in 2004, and their son Rahul Gandhi led the opposition after 2024.

For decades the 'Licence Raj' required permits to open or expand a business, and growth averaged about 3.5 percent a year, a rate mocked as the 'Hindu rate of growth'. In 1991 India had foreign currency left for only a few weeks of imports and pledged its gold reserves abroad. Finance Minister Manmohan Singh cut tariffs, scrapped licences and welcomed foreign investors. Growth roughly doubled. Software firms in Bengaluru and Hyderabad served the world, and a vast middle class grew. Under Modi, India built highways, airports and a digital payments system, UPI, that handles billions of transactions a month, though manufacturing jobs have lagged.

Narendra Modi, who says he sold tea as a boy, was an organiser for the Hindu nationalist RSS, then chief minister of Gujarat during the 2002 riots, in which over 1,000 people, mostly Muslims, were killed; a Supreme Court-appointed inquiry found no case against him. As prime minister he cut red tape, cancelled most banknotes overnight in 2016, and expanded toilets, gas and bank accounts for the poor. In 2024 he opened a Ram temple in Ayodhya, on the site of a mosque demolished by Hindu activists in 1992. Supporters see a confident Hindu-majority nation. Critics point to a 2019 law offering fast-track citizenship to refugees from three neighbouring countries, except Muslims, pressure on the press and rising sectarian tension.

dd-apartheid.what: In 1948 the National Party won an election in which almost all voters were white and began building apartheid, Afrikaans for 'separateness'. Laws classified every person by race, decided where they could live and work, and banned mixed marriages. Black South Africans were assigned to ethnic 'homelands' and needed passes to be in white areas. Resistance grew. In 1960 police killed 69 protesters at Sharpeville, and the ANC was banned and turned to armed struggle. Nelson Mandela was jailed for life in 1964. Students rose in Soweto in 1976, and the 1980s brought township revolts, states of emergency and world sanctions. In 1990 President F. W. de Klerk freed Mandela, and in 1994 Mandela was elected president.
dd-apartheid.why: Racial segregation and white rule went back to colonial times, but after 1948 Afrikaner nationalists turned it into a total legal system to keep political power and cheap Black labour in white hands. It finally ended because resistance at home made the country hard to govern, sanctions and debt crises squeezed the economy, and the end of the Cold War removed the government's claim to be fighting communism.
dd-apartheid.after: South Africa became a democracy with one of the world's most admired constitutions, and Mandela came to symbolise reconciliation. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission heard the stories of victims and perpetrators. But apartheid's legacy endures: South Africa remains one of the most unequal countries on Earth, and wealth, land and jobs still largely follow the old racial lines.

sections.t: Apartheid rested on a stack of laws. The Population Registration Act of 1950 put every person in a racial category: White, Native (later Bantu or Black), Coloured or Asian (Indian). The Group Areas Act decided which race could live in each part of a town, and whole communities, such as Sophiatown in Johannesburg and District Six in Cape Town, were bulldozed. Mixed marriages were banned in 1949. Black men and women had to carry passes, and hundreds of thousands were arrested every year for pass offences. Bantu Education gave Black children deliberately inferior schooling. Separate amenities laws reserved beaches, buses and benches by race. The homelands policy aimed to strip Black South Africans of their citizenship altogether.

The African National Congress, founded in 1912, led peaceful campaigns against apartheid in the 1950s, including the 1955 Freedom Charter declaring that 'South Africa belongs to all who live in it'. After Sharpeville it was banned, and Nelson Mandela, a young lawyer, helped found its armed wing, Umkhonto we Sizwe, which began sabotage attacks in 1961. Arrested in 1962, he told the Rivonia Trial court in 1964 that a democratic, free society was an ideal for which he was prepared to die. He spent 27 years in prison, 18 of them on Robben Island, breaking rocks in a lime quarry. Released in 1990, he negotiated the transition and shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with de Klerk.

From the 1960s South Africa was excluded from the Olympics and most international sport, and in 1977 the UN made an arms embargo mandatory. In the 1980s campaigns pushed foreign companies and universities to disinvest, and in 1986 the US Congress passed sanctions over President Reagan's veto. Banks refused new loans in 1985. On 2 February 1990 de Klerk unbanned the ANC, and Mandela walked free nine days later. Negotiations were tense and violent: thousands died in political fighting, and the assassination of the ANC and Communist Party leader Chris Hani in April 1993 nearly derailed the talks. On 27 April 1994 voters queued for hours to cast their first ballots.

Instead of Nuremberg-style trials or a blanket amnesty, South Africa chose a Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, which held hearings from 1996. Victims told their stories in public, many on live television. Perpetrators could apply for amnesty if they fully confessed politically motivated crimes; about 7,000 applied and fewer than 900 were granted it. The commission's 1998 report found the apartheid state responsible for most gross human rights violations, but also criticised abuses by the ANC. Supporters praise it as a model copied around the world; critics say few who were refused amnesty were ever prosecuted, and victims received little compensation.

dd-eu.what: In 1950 France proposed pooling French and German coal and steel, and in 1951 six countries formed the European Coal and Steel Community. The 1957 Treaties of Rome created a common market with shared institutions in Brussels. Britain, Ireland and Denmark joined in 1973, then Greece, Spain and Portugal as they left dictatorship behind. The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 created the European Union, a single market let goods, money and people move freely, and euro notes and coins arrived in 2002. In 2004 ten countries joined, most of them from the old Soviet bloc. A debt crisis shook the euro from 2010, and in 2020 Britain became the first member to leave.
dd-eu.why: After two world wars, leaders such as Jean Monnet, Robert Schuman and Konrad Adenauer wanted to bind France and Germany so tightly that war between them became impossible. The Cold War gave Western Europe a further reason to unite, with US encouragement, and a larger market promised growth. Later, joining offered newer democracies in the south and east security, prosperity and a way back into Europe.
dd-eu.after: The EU has 27 members and about 450 million people, and 21 of them use the euro. Its rules on trade, competition, data and product safety shape business far beyond its borders, and it won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2012. Critics argue it is remote and undemocratic, and Brexit showed the pull of national sovereignty. Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine pushed it towards common defence and new enlargement.

sections.t: The EU is neither a country nor an ordinary alliance. The European Commission, with one commissioner per country, proposes laws and enforces the rules. Those laws must be passed by both the Council, where national ministers vote, and the European Parliament, elected by citizens every five years. Leaders of the member states meet as the European Council to set direction, and the Court of Justice in Luxembourg settles disputes. Foreign policy and taxes still need unanimity, so one country can block a decision. The EU's budget is only about 1% of its members' combined national income; most public spending stays national.

Citizens of any member can live, work and study in any other. In most of the EU and four neighbours, the Schengen area, people cross borders without passport checks. Since 2017, using a mobile phone in another member country costs the same as at home. Over 15 million people have studied or trained abroad through the Erasmus programme, begun in 1987. EU rules require new phones to use the same USB-C charging port, entitle air passengers to compensation for long delays, and give people rights over their personal data under the GDPR, rules that many global firms now apply worldwide.

Some famous stories are false. The EU never banned curved bananas: a 1994 rule set quality grades for green bananas, which had to be free of 'abnormal curvature', while lower grades allowed defects of shape. Real crises have been serious, though. After 2010 Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Cyprus needed rescue loans, and harsh austerity in Greece led to anger and fears it would leave the euro, until the European Central Bank promised in 2012 to do 'whatever it takes'. The 2015 refugee arrivals divided members, and in 2016 British voters chose to leave by 52% to 48%. In 2020 the EU agreed for the first time to borrow jointly on a large scale to recover from Covid.

cards.p: Afghanistan is a landlocked, mountainous country where Central Asia, South Asia and the Middle East meet. The Hindu Kush mountains divide it, and passes such as the Khyber linked India to the rest of Asia. Its people include Pashtuns, Tajiks, Hazaras and Uzbeks.

Alexander the Great, the Buddhist Kushans (who carved the giant Bamiyan Buddhas, destroyed by the Taliban in 2001), Arab Muslims, Mongols and Mughals all passed through. Ahmad Shah Durrani founded the modern Afghan state in 1747.

In the 1800s Afghanistan was a buffer between British India and the Russian Empire, the 'Great Game'. Britain invaded twice; in 1842 almost its whole army was destroyed retreating from Kabul. Afghans won full independence in 1919.

cards.q: Why is Afghanistan called the 'graveyard of empires'?
a: Invaders, from Britain to the Soviets and the US, failed to control it
It has the most ancient tombs
cards.why: Its mountains and fierce local resistance.

cards.p: After a communist coup, the Soviet Union invaded in 1979. Mujahideen fighters, armed by the US, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, fought for ten years; about a million Afghans died and millions fled. The Soviets left in 1989, and civil war followed.

cards.h: Taliban, the US and the Taliban again
cards.p: The Taliban took Kabul in 1996 and imposed a harsh Islamic rule, sheltering al-Qaeda. After 9/11 the US invaded and toppled them; 20 years of war followed. When US troops left in August 2021, the Taliban retook the country within weeks. They have banned girls from secondary school and university.
Angola is a large country on Africa's south-west coast, rich in oil and diamonds; Luanda is one of Africa's most expensive cities. Portuguese is the official language.

cards.h: Queen Njinga and the slave trade
cards.p: The Portuguese arrived in 1482 and founded Luanda in 1576. Angola became the largest single source of the Atlantic slave trade: millions were shipped, mostly to Brazil. Queen Njinga of Ndongo and Matamba resisted the Portuguese for decades in the 1600s and is a national heroine.

cards.q: Who was Queen Njinga?
a: A 1600s Angolan ruler who resisted Portugal

cards.p: A war of independence began in 1961. After Portugal's 1974 revolution Angola became independent in 1975, but three movements fought for power. The civil war became a Cold War proxy war: Cuba and the Soviets backed the MPLA government, the US and South Africa the UNITA rebels. It lasted until 2002 and killed about 500,000.
Peace and oil brought rapid growth, but under President dos Santos (1979–2017) wealth went to a small elite; his daughter became Africa's richest woman. Poverty remains widespread.

cards.s: Angola's civil war was a Cold War proxy war.
cards.why: Cuba and the Soviets versus the US and South Africa.

cards.p: Albania, 'Shqipëria', land of eagles, is a small, mountainous Balkan country on the Adriatic. Albanian is a unique branch of the Indo-European family. Albanians are mostly Muslim, with Orthodox and Catholic minorities, and famously relaxed about religion.

Descended in part from the ancient Illyrians, Albanians were ruled by Rome and Byzantium. The hero Skanderbeg resisted the Ottomans for 25 years in the 1400s; after him, the Ottomans ruled for over 400 years and many converted to Islam.

cards.q: Who is Albania’s national hero?
cards.why: He fought the Ottomans in the 1400s.

cards.p: Albania became independent in 1912. Communist dictator Enver Hoxha (1944–85) cut ties with Yugoslavia, the USSR and finally China, banned all religion in 1967, the world's first officially atheist state, and built about 170,000 concrete bunkers.

Communism fell in 1991. A pyramid-scheme collapse caused near civil war in 1997. Albania joined NATO in 2009 and is an EU candidate; tourism is booming. In World War II Albanians sheltered Jews, ending the war with more Jews than they began with.

cards.s: Albania was declared the world’s first atheist state.

cards.p: Andorra is a tiny, mountainous country in the Pyrenees between France and Spain. Catalan is its language.
Since 1278 it has had two co-princes: the Bishop of Urgell in Spain and the ruler of France, now France's president. Isolated for centuries, it was a land of shepherds and smugglers.

cards.q: Who are Andorra’s co-princes?
a: A Spanish bishop and the French president

cards.p: A 1993 constitution made Andorra a parliamentary democracy, still with the two co-princes.
Low taxes, ski resorts and duty-free shopping draw millions of visitors. It has one of the highest life expectancies on Earth.

cards.s: Andorra’s official language is Catalan.
cards.why: The only country where it is.

cards.p: The United Arab Emirates is a federation of seven emirates, including Abu Dhabi and Dubai, on the Persian Gulf. Only about 1 in 9 residents are Emirati citizens; most are foreign workers from South Asia and elsewhere.

For centuries people lived from pearl diving, fishing, trade and herding. Britain signed truces with the sheikhs from 1820 to stop piracy, so the area was called the Trucial States. Japan's cultured pearls ruined the pearling trade in the 1930s.

cards.q: What was the main industry before oil?
cards.why: Ruined by cultured pearls in the 1930s.

cards.p: Oil was found in Abu Dhabi in 1958. When Britain left in 1971, Sheikh Zayed united six emirates (Ras al-Khaimah joined in 1972) into the UAE.

Oil wealth built gleaming cities; Dubai diversified into trade, tourism and finance, with the Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building, and Emirates airline. The UAE normalised relations with Israel in 2020 and sent a probe to Mars. It is an absolute monarchy with no political freedoms.

cards.s: The UAE is a federation of seven emirates.

units.title: From the Andes to the Pampas

cards.p: Argentina stretches 3,700 km from the subtropical north to Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego near Antarctica. Its heart is the Pampas, flat grasslands perfect for cattle and wheat. About a third of its 46 million people live in greater Buenos Aires.

The north was on the edge of the Inca world. Spanish settlers founded Buenos Aires for good in 1580; it was a smuggling port on the edge of the empire until it became capital of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776. Gauchos, cowboys of the Pampas, became a national symbol.

When Napoleon took Spain, Buenos Aires set up its own government on 25 May 1810, and Argentina declared independence on 9 July 1816. General José de San Martín then crossed the Andes to free Chile and Peru.

cards.q: Which general crossed the Andes to free Chile and Peru?

cards.p:
After decades of civil war, a constitution in 1853 brought stability. Railways, refrigerated ships and British investment made the Pampas feed Europe with beef and wheat. Around 1900 Argentina was one of the ten richest countries on Earth.

In the 'Conquest of the Desert' (1878–85) the army seized Patagonia from indigenous peoples.

About 6 million Europeans, mostly Italians and Spaniards, arrived between 1870 and 1930. They shaped the Spanish of Buenos Aires, its food and the tango, born in the port's working-class neighbourhoods.

cards.q: Where did most immigrants to Argentina come from?

cards.p: Juan Perón, elected in 1946, and his wife Eva (Evita) championed workers, unions and the poor, nationalised industry and built a cult of personality. Peronism still dominates Argentine politics. Coups followed: the army overthrew governments six times between 1930 and 1976.

cards.h: The Dirty War and the Falklands
cards.p: The 1976–83 military junta waged a 'Dirty War' against the left: about 30,000 people 'disappeared'. Their mothers marched weekly in the Plaza de Mayo. In 1982 the junta invaded the British-held Falklands (Malvinas); Britain retook them, and the defeat brought democracy back in 1983.

Argentina has suffered repeated debt defaults and inflation, most dramatically in 2001. Since 2023 the libertarian president Javier Milei has slashed spending to tame inflation. Argentines take pride in football (three World Cups, Maradona and Messi), tango, beef and Pope Francis, the first Latin American pope.

Armenia is a small, mountainous, landlocked country in the South Caucasus, a fraction of historic Armenia. Mount Ararat, the national symbol, is visible from Yerevan but lies in Turkey. Armenians have their own alphabet, created in 405.

Yerevan was founded as Erebuni in 782 BC. In 301 Armenia became the first country to adopt Christianity as its state religion. For centuries Armenia was divided between Persia, Byzantium, the Ottomans and Russia.

cards.q: What was Armenia the first to do?
a: Adopt Christianity as a state religion

cards.p: In 1915–16 the Ottoman government deported and massacred its Armenian population; about a million died. Armenians and most historians call it genocide; Turkey rejects the term. Survivors scattered into a large diaspora in Russia, the US, France and the Middle East.
Armenia was Soviet until 1991. It won a war over Nagorno-Karabakh in 1994 but lost it to Azerbaijan in 2020–23, when its Armenians fled. Armenia is now seeking peace and closer ties with the West.

cards.s: Mount Ararat lies in Turkey.
cards.why: Though it is Armenia’s national symbol.

cards.p: Antigua and Barbuda are two low Caribbean islands, said to have 365 beaches.
English settlers arrived in 1632; sugar plantations used enslaved Africans. Nelson's Dockyard was a key Royal Navy base.

cards.q: Which naval hero gave his name to Antigua’s dockyard?

cards.p: The islands became independent in 1981 under Vere Bird, whose family dominated politics for decades.
Tourism is the economy; Hurricane Irma in 2017 left Barbuda almost uninhabitable for a time.

cards.s: Antigua became independent in 1981.

cards.p: Australia is both a country and a continent: mostly flat, very dry outback in the middle, with most of its 27 million people in cities along the east and south-east coasts. It split from other continents so long ago that its animals, such as kangaroos and koalas, are found nowhere else.

cards.h: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
cards.p:
People arrived in Australia at least 50,000 to 65,000 years ago, making Aboriginal cultures among the oldest continuous cultures on Earth. Hundreds of nations, with about 250 languages, lived across the continent, guided by the Dreaming: stories of ancestral beings who shaped the land and laid down law.

Land is sacred, and caring for Country is a duty. Uluru is one of the most sacred places.

cards.q: How long have people lived in Australia?
cards.why: Among the oldest continuous cultures on Earth.

cards.p:
Captain James Cook claimed the east coast for Britain in 1770. After losing America, Britain needed somewhere to send convicts, and on 26 January 1788 the First Fleet landed at Sydney Cove with about 750 convicts. About 160,000 convicts were transported in all.

26 January is Australia Day, and to many Aboriginal people 'Invasion Day'.

Settlers spread across the land, claimed as terra nullius, 'land belonging to no one'. Disease, frontier massacres and dispossession devastated Aboriginal peoples; their population fell by perhaps 90%. From 1910 to the 1970s, many Aboriginal children were taken from their families: the Stolen Generations.

Gold rushes from 1851 brought immigrants and wealth. Six separate British colonies grew up, and on 1 January 1901 they federated into the Commonwealth of Australia. Its first laws included the 'White Australia' policy, restricting non-European immigration until the 1970s.

Australia fought for Britain in World War I. At Gallipoli in 1915, Australian and New Zealand (ANZAC) troops suffered heavy losses; ANZAC Day, 25 April, became a defining national day. In World War II Japan bombed Darwin, and Australia turned to the US as its key ally.

After 1945 mass immigration, first from Europe, then from Asia after White Australia ended, transformed the country; about 30% of Australians were born overseas. In 1967 Aboriginal people were counted in the census; in 1992 the Mabo ruling overturned terra nullius; in 2008 the government apologised to the Stolen Generations. In 2023 voters rejected a proposed Indigenous 'Voice' to Parliament.

items: Reconciliation and recognition are unfinished business.
King Charles III is head of state
China is the largest trading partner; the US the key ally.
And a harsh climate of drought and fire.

cards.p: Austria is a small Alpine country today, but for centuries Vienna was the capital of one of Europe's greatest empires. The Danube flows through it, linking Germany to the Balkans.

From 1278 the Habsburg family ruled Austria, and through clever marriages ('Let others wage war; you, happy Austria, marry') they gained Spain, the Netherlands, Bohemia and Hungary. For centuries they were Holy Roman Emperors. Vienna held off Ottoman sieges in 1529 and 1683.

Empress Maria Theresa (1740–80) reformed the state. Vienna became the music capital of the world: Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert and later Strauss's waltzes. After Napoleon, Chancellor Metternich hosted the Congress of Vienna in 1815 that redrew Europe.

cards.q: How did the Habsburgs gain much of their empire?

units.title: Collapse, Nazism and the Second Republic

cards.p: In 1867 the empire became Austria-Hungary, a dual monarchy of many peoples. In 1914 the heir, Franz Ferdinand, was shot in Sarajevo; Austria-Hungary's war on Serbia began World War I, which destroyed the empire in 1918. Austria became a small German-speaking republic.

In March 1938 Hitler, himself born in Austria, annexed it to Germany, the Anschluss, welcomed by cheering crowds; Vienna's Jews were persecuted and most murdered or driven out. For decades Austria presented itself as Hitler's 'first victim' before acknowledging its role.

Occupied by the four Allies until 1955, Austria regained independence by promising permanent neutrality. It became prosperous, joined the EU in 1995, and hosts UN agencies and OPEC in Vienna, often ranked the world's most liveable city.

items: The second Ottoman siege of Vienna

cards.p: Azerbaijan sits on the Caspian Sea in the South Caucasus. Natural gas seeping from the ground fed 'eternal flames' and Zoroastrian fire temples, giving it the name 'land of fire'. Baku became the world's first great oil city in the late 1800s.

Azerbaijanis are a Turkic, mostly Shia Muslim people. The region was long part of Persia until Russia took it in 1813–28; the border split Azerbaijanis between Russia and Iran, where more Azerbaijanis live today than in Azerbaijan itself.

cards.q: Why is Azerbaijan called the 'land of fire'?
a: Natural gas burns from the ground

cards.p: Azerbaijan was independent in 1918–20, the first secular democratic republic in the Muslim world, then Soviet. Baku's oil fuelled the Soviet war effort.

As the USSR collapsed, Armenians in Nagorno-Karabakh broke away; Armenia won a war in 1994. Azerbaijan, rich from oil and gas, won back much of the region in 2020 and took the rest in 2023, after which nearly all its Armenians fled. The Aliyev family has ruled since 1993.

cards.s: Azerbaijan retook Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023.

cards.p: Burundi is a small, hilly, densely populated country by Lake Tanganyika, one of the poorest in the world. Like Rwanda, its people are Hutu, Tutsi and Twa, sharing one language, Kirundi.
A Tutsi-dominated monarchy ruled for centuries. Germany, then Belgium, ruled it with Rwanda; independence came in 1962.

cards.q: Which lake does Burundi border?
cards.why: One of the deepest lakes on Earth.

cards.p: Hutu–Tutsi violence killed hundreds of thousands: the Tutsi-led army massacred Hutus in 1972, and a civil war (1993–2005) followed the murder of the first Hutu president.
A peace deal shared power between groups. President Nkurunziza's disputed third term in 2015 brought repression; he died in 2020.

cards.s: Burundi became independent in 1962.

cards.p: Belgium is a small country between France, Germany and the Netherlands, divided into Dutch-speaking Flanders in the north and French-speaking Wallonia in the south, with bilingual Brussels, home of the EU and NATO.

Julius Caesar called the Belgae the bravest of the Gauls. In the Middle Ages Bruges and Ghent grew rich on cloth, and Flemish painters such as van Eyck flourished. Ruled in turn by Burgundy, Spain, Austria and France, it was so fought over it was called the 'cockpit of Europe': Napoleon met his end at Waterloo in 1815.

cards.q: Which battle ended Napoleon’s career?

cards.p: Belgium broke from the Netherlands in 1830 and became a kingdom. It industrialised early. King Leopold II's brutal rule of the Congo, then Belgian colonial rule, killed millions.

Germany invaded neutral Belgium in both world wars; Ypres and the 'Flanders fields' saw some of World War I's worst battles. After 1945 Belgium was a founder of the EU and NATO, both headquartered in Brussels. Tension between Flemish and Walloons has repeatedly paralysed government.

cards.s: Brussels hosts the headquarters of the EU and NATO.

cards.p: Benin is a narrow country on West Africa's coast. It is the birthplace of Vodun (voodoo), still officially celebrated, which travelled with enslaved people to Haiti, Brazil and Louisiana.

The kingdom of Dahomey, based at Abomey, grew powerful from the 1600s by selling captives to European slave traders through Ouidah. It was famous for its all-female regiments, the Agojie. France conquered it in 1894.

cards.q: Which religion was born in what is now Benin?

cards.p: Dahomey became independent in 1960 and had many coups; Mathieu Kérékou's Marxist regime renamed it Benin in 1975. In 1990 a national conference peacefully restored democracy, a model for Africa.
Benin is a cotton producer and trading hub; jihadist violence has spread into its north, and democracy has narrowed recently.

cards.s: Benin was formerly called Dahomey.

cards.p: Burkina Faso, 'land of upright people', is a landlocked country in the Sahel of West Africa. Most people farm; cotton and gold are the main exports.

From around the 1100s the Mossi kingdoms, led by the Mogho Naba of Ouagadougou, resisted the great Sahel empires of Mali and Songhai. France conquered the region in the 1890s; it was called Upper Volta.

cards.q: What does 'Burkina Faso' mean?

cards.p: Upper Volta became independent in 1960. In 1983 Captain Thomas Sankara, a charismatic young revolutionary, took power, renamed it Burkina Faso, and launched campaigns for vaccination, literacy, women's rights and tree-planting. He was killed in a 1987 coup by Blaise Compaoré, who ruled until a popular uprising in 2014.

Since 2015 jihadist groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have spread across the country, killing thousands and displacing two million. Soldiers seized power in coups in 2022, turned away from France and towards Russia.

cards.s: Thomas Sankara renamed Upper Volta as Burkina Faso.

cards.p: Bangladesh lies on the world's largest river delta, where the Ganges and Brahmaputra meet the Bay of Bengal. It is one of the most densely populated countries on Earth, about 175 million people in an area smaller than England plus Wales. Floods and cyclones are part of life; so is extraordinarily fertile land.

Bengal was home to Buddhist and Hindu kingdoms, then from 1204 Muslim rulers; under the Mughals it was one of the richest provinces in Asia, famous for fine muslin cloth. Most people in the east became Muslim. The British East India Company's conquest began here, at Plassey in 1757, and the 1770 and 1943 famines killed millions.

cards.q: Which two great rivers form the Bangladesh delta?

cards.p: At Partition in 1947 Muslim-majority East Bengal became East Pakistan, 1,500 km from West Pakistan, which dominated it. In 1952 students died protesting for the Bengali language; 21 February is now International Mother Language Day worldwide.

After Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's party won the 1970 election, Pakistan's army launched a brutal crackdown; hundreds of thousands, perhaps far more, were killed and 10 million fled to India. India intervened, and Bangladesh won independence in December 1971.

Once called a 'basket case', Bangladesh became one of the fastest-growing economies, the world's second-largest clothing exporter, with big gains in health and girls' education; microcredit, pioneered by Muhammad Yunus, spread worldwide. In 2024 student protests toppled Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, and Yunus led an interim government. Rising seas threaten much of the low-lying land.

cards.q: What does International Mother Language Day commemorate?
a: Students killed in 1952 defending the Bengali language

cards.p: Bulgaria lies in the eastern Balkans, on the Black Sea, with the Danube to the north and mountains such as the Balkans and Rila. Some of the world's oldest worked gold, from Varna, is 6,000 years old.

The Thracians lived here in ancient times. The Bulgars founded a state in 681 and adopted Orthodox Christianity in 864; the Cyrillic alphabet, now used by over 250 million people, was developed in Bulgaria. The Ottomans ruled it for nearly 500 years from 1396.

cards.q: Which alphabet was developed in medieval Bulgaria?
cards.why: Now used for Russian and many other languages.

cards.p: With Russia's help Bulgaria won autonomy in 1878. It fought on the losing side in both world wars, but in 1943 it refused to deport its own Jews, saving about 48,000.

Bulgaria was a loyal Soviet ally under Todor Zhivkov (1954–89). After 1989 it became a democracy, joining NATO in 2004 and the EU in 2007, and the euro in 2026. Corruption and political instability remain.

cards.s: Bulgaria saved its own Jews from deportation in World War II.

cards.p: Bahrain is a small island kingdom in the Persian Gulf, linked to Saudi Arabia by a causeway. Most citizens are Shia Muslims, ruled by a Sunni royal family.
Ancient Dilmun was a great trading centre with Mesopotamia. Pearling made Bahrain rich for centuries. The Al Khalifa family has ruled since 1783; it was a British protectorate from 1861.

cards.q: What was ancient Bahrain called?

cards.p: Bahrain was the first Gulf state to find oil, in 1932, and became independent in 1971. As oil ran low it became a banking and tourism hub; it hosts the US Fifth Fleet.
Mainly Shia protests in 2011 were crushed with help from Saudi troops. Bahrain normalised relations with Israel in 2020.

cards.s: Bahrain was the first Gulf state to find oil.

cards.p: The Bahamas are about 700 islands off Florida in the Atlantic, with famous clear blue waters.

Columbus first landed in the Americas here, at San Salvador, in 1492; the native Lucayans were soon wiped out. In the early 1700s Nassau was a pirate republic, home to Blackbeard, until Britain restored control.

cards.q: Where did Columbus first land in the Americas?

cards.p: The Bahamas became independent from Britain in 1973.
Tourism and offshore finance make it one of the richest countries in the Caribbean; hurricanes such as Dorian (2019) are a growing danger.

cards.s: Nassau was once a pirate base.

cards.p: Bosnia and Herzegovina is a mountainous Balkan country with three main peoples: Bosniaks (mostly Muslim), Serbs (Orthodox) and Croats (Catholic). Sarajevo, with mosques, churches and synagogues side by side, was called 'the Jerusalem of Europe'.

Medieval Bosnia was a kingdom with its own church. The Ottomans conquered it in 1463, and many Bosnians became Muslim. Austria-Hungary took it in 1878; in 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in Sarajevo, starting World War I.

cards.q: Which event happened in Sarajevo in 1914?
a: The end of World War I

cards.p: Bosnia was part of Yugoslavia. When it declared independence in 1992, Bosnian Serb forces, backed by Serbia, besieged Sarajevo for almost four years and carried out 'ethnic cleansing'. In July 1995 they murdered about 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica, a genocide. About 100,000 died in the war.

The 1995 Dayton Agreement ended the war but created a complex state of two entities, a Bosniak–Croat federation and the Serb Republic, with a three-member presidency and an international High Representative. Ethnic divisions still paralyse politics. Mostar's Old Bridge, destroyed in 1993, was rebuilt in 2004.

cards.s: The Dayton Agreement ended the Bosnian War.

cards.p: Belarus is a flat, forested, landlocked country between Poland and Russia. Its name means 'White Rus'. Most people speak Russian, though Belarusian is also official.

The principality of Polotsk was part of Kyivan Rus. From the 1300s the region was the heart of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, then the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth; Russia took it in the partitions of 1772–95. Before 1941 Minsk and many towns were largely Jewish.

cards.q: Which state did Belarus belong to for centuries before Russia?

cards.p: Belarus became a Soviet republic. In World War II it suffered perhaps more than anywhere: about a quarter of its people died, including almost all its Jews, and hundreds of villages were burned with their inhabitants, like Khatyn. Chernobyl's fallout in 1986 fell mostly on Belarus.

Belarus became independent in 1991. Alexander Lukashenko has ruled since 1994, 'Europe's last dictator'. Mass protests after the rigged 2020 election were crushed. He lets Russia use Belarus as a base, including for the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

cards.s: About a quarter of Belarus’s people died in World War II.
cards.why: Perhaps the highest share of any country.

cards.p: Belize is the only English-speaking country in Central America, with jungle, Maya ruins and the second-largest barrier reef in the world. Its people are Mestizo, Kriol, Maya and Garifuna.
Maya cities such as Caracol flourished here. British 'Baymen' cut logwood and mahogany using enslaved Africans from the 1600s; it became British Honduras in 1862.

cards.q: Which country claims Belize?

cards.p: Belize became independent in 1981; British troops stayed because Guatemala claimed it. A capital, Belmopan, was built inland after a 1961 hurricane hit Belize City.
Tourism and the reef are vital. The border dispute with Guatemala is before the International Court of Justice.

cards.s: English is the official language of Belize.
cards.why: The only one in Central America.

cards.p: Bolivia is landlocked in the heart of South America, from the high Altiplano, with Lake Titicaca and the Uyuni salt flat (the world's largest), to Amazon lowlands. It has the largest indigenous share of any country in the Americas, mostly Quechua and Aymara.

Tiwanaku, near Lake Titicaca, was a great Andean civilisation around 500–1000. The Inca followed. Spain found a 'mountain of silver' at Potosí in 1545; it became one of the largest cities in the world, and its silver financed the Spanish Empire, mined by indigenous forced labour.

cards.q: Why was Potosí so important to Spain?
a: Its silver mountain financed the empire

cards.p: Bolivia became independent in 1825, named after Bolívar. It lost its coast to Chile (1879–84) and land to Paraguay in the Chaco War (1932–35). A 1952 revolution brought land reform and votes for indigenous people. Coups were frequent.

In 2005 Evo Morales became the first indigenous president, renaming the country a 'Plurinational State'. He was forced out in 2019 amid disputed elections. Bolivia holds huge lithium reserves; an economic crisis hit in 2023–25.

cards.s: Bolivia lost its sea coast to Chile.
cards.why: In the War of the Pacific.

cards.p: Brazil covers half of South America and is the fifth-largest country on Earth, with most of the Amazon rainforest, the largest on the planet. Most of its 210 million people live near the Atlantic coast, in cities like São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. It is the only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas.

Millions of indigenous people, such as the Tupi, lived here when Pedro Álvares Cabral landed in 1500 and claimed it for Portugal under the Treaty of Tordesillas. The land was named after brazilwood, a red dye tree.

Brazil grew rich on sugar plantations in the north-east, and later gold in Minas Gerais. They were worked by enslaved Africans: about 4.9 million were brought to Brazil, more than to any other country, about 40% of the whole Atlantic slave trade. Escaped slaves built free communities, quilombos, such as Palmares.

That history made Brazil one of the most racially mixed societies on Earth, and a deeply unequal one.

When Napoleon invaded Portugal in 1807, the Portuguese royal family fled to Rio, making it the capital of the empire. In 1822 Prince Pedro declared Brazil independent and himself emperor, almost without war.

cards.q: Which country received more enslaved Africans than any other?

cards.p: Brazil was an empire until 1889. It was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888; the next year the army overthrew the emperor and declared a republic. Millions of European and Japanese immigrants came to work on coffee farms around São Paulo.

Getúlio Vargas ruled from 1930 to 1945 and again in the 1950s, building industry and a strong state. In 1960 a new capital, Brasília, was built from scratch in the empty interior to pull development inland.
In 1964 a US-backed military coup ended democracy. The generals ruled until 1985, with an 'economic miracle' in the early 1970s, censorship, torture and a growing debt. Democracy returned in 1985.

items: The royal court moves to Rio

cards.p: The 1994 Real Plan tamed hyperinflation. Under President Lula (2003–10), a commodity boom and welfare programmes lifted tens of millions out of poverty. Then came recession and huge corruption scandals. Jair Bolsonaro, a far-right former officer, governed from 2019 to 2022; Lula won again in 2022, and Bolsonaro was convicted in 2025 for plotting a coup.
The Amazon stores vast carbon and holds a tenth of the world's species. Clearing for cattle and soy has destroyed about a fifth of Brazil's share; how to protect it is a global question.

items: A proud mixed identity, alongside racism.
Evangelicals now a third of Brazilians.

cards.p: Barbados is a coral island, the easternmost in the Caribbean. It is the birthplace of rum and of singer Rihanna.
English settlers arrived in 1627 and Barbados became the first great sugar colony, a model of plantation slavery copied across the Caribbean and the American South.

cards.q: What did Barbados become in 2021?

cards.p: Barbados became independent in 1966 and built one of the Caribbean's best education systems.
In 2021 it removed the British monarch and became a republic. Prime Minister Mia Mottley is a leading global voice on climate finance.

cards.s: Barbados is the birthplace of rum.

cards.p: Brunei is a small, oil-rich sultanate on the island of Borneo, in two parts surrounded by Malaysia.
In the 1500s the Bruneian Empire ruled much of Borneo and the southern Philippines. It shrank, losing land to Sarawak, and became a British protectorate in 1888. Oil was found in 1929.

cards.q: What made Brunei rich?

cards.p: Brunei became fully independent in 1984 and declined to join Malaysia.
The sultan, on the throne since 1967, is one of the world's longest-reigning and richest monarchs. Citizens pay no income tax; strict sharia law was introduced in 2014.

cards.s: Brunei’s citizens pay no income tax.

cards.p: Bhutan is a small Himalayan kingdom between India and China, deeply Buddhist, with dzongs (fortress-monasteries) and Tiger's Nest monastery on a cliff. It is the world's only carbon-negative country.
Buddhism arrived in the 600s–700s. In the 1600s the Tibetan lama Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal unified Bhutan, built dzongs and repelled Tibetan invasions.

cards.q: What did Bhutan put ahead of GDP?

cards.p: The Wangchuck dynasty has ruled since 1907. Bhutan stayed isolated until the 1960s; TV arrived only in 1999.
The fourth king declared 'gross national happiness' more important than GDP and handed power to an elected parliament in 2008. Many young Bhutanese now emigrate.

cards.s: Bhutan only allowed television in 1999.

cards.p: Botswana is a landlocked country of the Kalahari desert and the Okavango Delta, a vast inland wetland full of wildlife. Most people are Tswana.
Tswana chiefs asked Britain for protection from Boer settlers and Rhodes's company, and Bechuanaland became a British protectorate in 1885; Britain largely left it alone.

cards.q: What made Botswana prosperous?

cards.p: At independence in 1966 Botswana was among the poorest countries on Earth. Its first president, Seretse Khama, whose marriage to a white Englishwoman had caused a scandal, built honest institutions.

Diamonds discovered just after independence were managed well, making Botswana one of Africa's richest, most stable and least corrupt democracies. In 2024 the ruling party lost power for the first time, peacefully.

cards.s: Botswana has had peaceful democracy since independence.

cards.p: The Central African Republic is a landlocked country at the very centre of Africa, rich in diamonds, gold and forests but among the poorest countries on Earth.
Slave raids from Sudan and Chad depopulated much of the region in the 1800s. France colonised it as Ubangi-Shari, handing much of it to companies that used forced labour.

cards.q: Where is the Central African Republic?
a: At the centre of Africa, landlocked

cards.p: Independent in 1960, it was seized by Jean-Bédel Bokassa in 1966, who crowned himself emperor in 1977 in a ceremony costing about a third of the national budget. France removed him in 1979.
Coups and civil wars followed; since 2013 fighting between mainly Muslim Séléka and Christian anti-balaka militias has killed thousands. Russian Wagner mercenaries back the government.

cards.s: Bokassa crowned himself emperor in 1977.

cards.p: Switzerland is a small, mountainous country in the Alps, with no coast. It has four national languages, German, French, Italian and Romansh, yet a strong shared identity. Its mountain valleys shaped a tradition of local self-government.

In 1291, by tradition, three mountain cantons, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, swore an alliance against the Habsburgs; the legend of William Tell, who shot an apple off his son's head, comes from this struggle. Other cantons joined, and Swiss pikemen became Europe's most feared mercenaries; the Pope's Swiss Guard remains.

Zwingli in Zurich and Calvin in Geneva led the Reformation, and the cantons split between Catholic and Protestant. After the Congress of Vienna in 1815 recognised its permanent neutrality, Switzerland has not fought a foreign war.

cards.q: Since when has Switzerland’s neutrality been recognised?

cards.p: After a brief civil war, the 1848 constitution created a federal state, with 26 cantons keeping wide powers. Swiss citizens vote in referendums several times a year on everything from taxes to building rules: the world's most direct democracy. Women, however, got the federal vote only in 1971.

cards.h: Banks, watches and the Red Cross
cards.p: Switzerland grew rich on banking (with famous secrecy), watches, chocolate, pharmaceuticals and tourism. Geneva hosts the Red Cross, founded there in 1863, and many UN agencies. In World War II it stayed neutral but traded with Nazi Germany and turned away many refugees, a record later examined. It joined the UN only in 2002 and stays outside the EU.

items: Power stays with the people and cantons.

cards.p: Chile is over 4,000 km long but on average only 177 km wide, squeezed between the Andes and the Pacific. It runs from the Atacama, the driest desert on Earth, through a Mediterranean-like central valley (wine) to the glaciers and fjords of Patagonia.

The Inca reached central Chile, but the Mapuche people in the south resisted both the Inca and then the Spanish for over 300 years. Pedro de Valdivia founded Santiago in 1541. Chile won independence under Bernardo O'Higgins, helped by San Martín's army, in 1818.

cards.q: Which people resisted Spanish rule for over 300 years?

cards.p: Chile became one of Latin America's most stable republics. In the War of the Pacific (1879–83) it took nitrate-rich land from Peru and Bolivia, leaving Bolivia landlocked. Later copper became its main export; Chile is the world's largest producer.

In 1970 Salvador Allende became the first Marxist elected president in Latin America. On 11 September 1973, amid economic chaos and with US backing, General Augusto Pinochet seized power in a coup; Allende died in the presidential palace. Pinochet's dictatorship killed or disappeared over 3,000 and tortured tens of thousands, while free-market reforms reshaped the economy.

In a 1988 referendum Chileans voted Pinochet out, and democracy returned in 1990. Chile became one of Latin America's richest countries, but inequality fuelled huge protests in 2019. Voters then rejected two proposed new constitutions. It also suffers great earthquakes, such as the strongest ever recorded, in 1960.

Côte d'Ivoire (Ivory Coast) is the world's largest cocoa producer, about 40% of global supply. Abidjan is its economic capital; Yamoussoukro, with a basilica modelled on St Peter's, is the official capital.
Akan kingdoms such as the Baoulé and Kong ruled before France made it a colony in 1893, building plantations of coffee and cocoa.

cards.q: What is Côte d’Ivoire the world’s largest producer of?

cards.p: Félix Houphouët-Boigny led independence in 1960 and ruled for 33 years, keeping close ties with France; booming cocoa made it West Africa's success story.
After his death, disputes over 'Ivorian-ness' led to civil wars in 2002–07 and 2010–11. Since then, under Alassane Ouattara, the economy has grown fast.

cards.s: Côte d’Ivoire was a French colony.

cards.p: Cameroon has rainforest, savannah, mountains, desert and coast, and about 250 ethnic groups, earning the name 'Africa in miniature'. Mount Cameroon is an active volcano.

Portuguese sailors named it after the prawns (camarões) in its river. Germany colonised it in 1884; after World War I it was split between France and Britain. That split left a French-speaking majority and an English-speaking minority.

cards.q: Why does Cameroon have English- and French-speaking regions?
a: It was divided between Britain and France after World War I
It was settled by both peoples
It borders both Nigeria and France

cards.p: French Cameroun became independent in 1960 and joined part of British Cameroons in 1961. Paul Biya, president since 1982, is one of the world's longest-serving and oldest leaders.

Since 2017 a separatist conflict in the English-speaking regions has killed thousands, and Boko Haram attacks the far north. Cameroon is football-mad: the 'Indomitable Lions' reached the World Cup quarter-finals in 1990.

cards.s: Cameroon is called 'Africa in miniature'.
cards.why: For its variety of landscapes and peoples.

units.title: Kingdoms and the Congo Free State

cards.p: The Democratic Republic of the Congo is Africa's second-largest country, the size of western Europe, covering most of the Congo River basin and the second-largest rainforest on Earth. Beneath it lie vast deposits of copper, cobalt (used in phone and car batteries), gold, diamonds and coltan.

From the 1300s the Kingdom of Kongo ruled the lower river; its king converted to Christianity in 1491 and exchanged ambassadors with Portugal and the Pope. But the slave trade devastated it, and millions of Congolese were shipped to the Americas.

In 1885 King Leopold II of Belgium took the Congo as his personal property, the 'Congo Free State'. To harvest rubber his agents used forced labour, hostage-taking and mutilation; millions died. International outrage forced Belgium to take it over as a colony in 1908.

cards.q: Who owned the Congo as personal property from 1885?

cards.p: The Congo became independent in 1960 with almost no trained administrators. The first prime minister, Patrice Lumumba, was overthrown and murdered in 1961 with Belgian and US involvement. Joseph Mobutu seized power in 1965, renamed the country Zaire and looted it for 32 years.

After Rwanda's 1994 genocide, the conflict spilled into eastern Congo. Two wars (1996–2003) drew in nine African countries and killed millions, mostly through disease and hunger. Armed groups, including the Rwanda-backed M23, still fight over the minerals of the east.

The Republic of the Congo, often called Congo-Brazzaville, lies on the west bank of the Congo River, opposite Kinshasa; the two capitals are the closest pair in the world. Much is rainforest, and oil is the main export.

The Kongo and Teke kingdoms ruled before the French explorer Savorgnan de Brazza signed treaties in 1880; Brazzaville became the capital of French Equatorial Africa and, in World War II, of Free France in Africa.

cards.q: Which two capital cities face each other across the Congo River?
cards.why: The closest pair of capitals in the world.

cards.p: Independent in 1960, Congo became Africa's first Marxist state in 1970. Civil wars in the 1990s killed thousands.
Denis Sassou Nguesso has ruled for most of the time since 1979. Despite oil wealth, most people remain poor.

cards.s: Brazzaville was a capital of Free France in World War II.

cards.h: Two oceans and three mountain ranges
cards.p: Colombia is the only South American country with coasts on both the Pacific and the Caribbean. Three Andean ranges divide it, with the capital Bogotá high on a plateau. It is one of the most biodiverse countries on Earth, and its name honours Columbus.

The Muisca people of the highlands made exquisite gold work; their ritual of covering a chief in gold dust and throwing offerings into Lake Guatavita gave rise to the legend of El Dorado. The Spanish conquered them in the 1530s and founded Bogotá. Cartagena became a fortified port for treasure fleets and the slave trade.
Simón Bolívar won the decisive Battle of Boyacá in 1819, and Gran Colombia (today Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama) became independent. It broke apart in 1830.

cards.q: Where does the legend of El Dorado come from?
a: A Muisca ritual at Lake Guatavita
cards.why: A chief covered in gold dust.

cards.p: Liberals and Conservatives fought repeated civil wars; Panama broke away with US help in 1903. After a popular leader's assassination in 1948, 'La Violencia' killed about 200,000 people.

From the 1960s Marxist guerrillas such as the FARC, then right-wing paramilitaries, fought a war in the countryside. In the 1980s Pablo Escobar's Medellín cartel made Colombia the centre of the cocaine trade and waged war on the state. The conflict killed about 450,000 people and displaced millions.

In 2016 the government signed a peace deal with the FARC, and President Santos won the Nobel Peace Prize. Medellín transformed itself into a model of urban renewal. Gustavo Petro, a former guerrilla, became the first left-wing president in 2022. Colombia is known for coffee, flowers and the magical realism of Gabriel García Márquez.
The Comoros are volcanic islands between Mozambique and Madagascar, mostly Muslim, mixing African, Arab and Malagasy heritage. They produce much of the world's ylang-ylang perfume oil.
Swahili and Arab sultanates ruled the islands. France took them in the 1800s.

cards.q: Which Comorian island stayed French?

cards.p: Comoros declared independence in 1975, but the island of Mayotte voted to stay French.
It has had about 20 coups or attempts, several led by French mercenary Bob Denard.

cards.s: The Comoros have had about 20 coups or attempts.

cards.p: Cape Verde is a dry, volcanic archipelago 600 km off West Africa. Most people are of mixed African and Portuguese descent and speak Cape Verdean Creole; morna music is famous.
Uninhabited until the Portuguese arrived in 1456, Cidade Velha became the first European colonial town in the tropics and a hub of the Atlantic slave trade. Droughts caused terrible famines.

cards.q: Who led Cape Verde’s struggle for independence?

cards.p: Cape Verde won independence in 1975 after a joint struggle with Guinea-Bissau led by Amílcar Cabral.
It became one of Africa's most stable democracies; more Cape Verdeans live abroad than at home.

cards.s: Cape Verde was uninhabited before the Portuguese came.

cards.p: Costa Rica, 'rich coast', is a small Central American country between two oceans, with volcanoes and rainforests holding about 5% of the world's species. A quarter of its land is protected.

Columbus named it in 1502, but it had little gold and few people, so it stayed a poor, small-farmer colony. Coffee and later bananas made it prosper after independence (1821). A short civil war in 1948 led to a new constitution.

cards.q: What does 'Costa Rica' mean?

cards.p: In 1948 President José Figueres abolished the army and spent the money on schools and health. Costa Rica has been a stable democracy ever since, rare in the region. Óscar Arias won the 1987 Nobel Peace Prize for Central American peace plans.
