Most of it is cold forest and tundra; most Russians live in the west, on the flat European plain, which has no natural barriers. That openness to invasion, from Mongols to Napoleon to Hitler, has shaped Russia's fear of attack and hunger for buffer lands.

In the 800s Viking traders called the Rus ruled the Slavic peoples along the rivers from the Baltic to the Black Sea, with Kyiv as their capital. In 988 Prince Vladimir was baptised into Orthodox Christianity from Byzantium; Orthodoxy, with its icons and onion domes, became the core of Russian culture.

Russia, Ukraine and Belarus all trace their origins to Kyivan Rus, a claim at the heart of today's war.

lines: Route from the Varangians to the Greeks

cards.p: In 1237–40 the Mongols destroyed Kyiv and conquered the Rus lands. For 240 years Russian princes paid tribute to the Golden Horde. Moscow, a small town, rose by collecting tribute for the khans, then led the fight against them; in 1480 it threw off Mongol rule.

cards.q: Which form of Christianity did Russia adopt?

cards.p: Ivan IV, 'the Terrible', crowned himself the first tsar ('caesar') in 1547. He conquered the Volga khanates, opening the way to Siberia, and terrorised his own nobles. Moscow called itself the 'Third Rome', heir to Rome and Constantinople.
Cossacks and fur traders crossed Siberia, reaching the Pacific by 1639. Russia became the largest country in the world.

Peter the Great (1682–1725) forced Russia to modernise on western lines: he built a navy, made nobles shave their beards, and built a new capital, St Petersburg, as a 'window on Europe'. Catherine the Great (1762–96) took Crimea and much of Poland.

In 1812 Napoleon took Moscow, but the city burned and the winter destroyed his army.

Most Russians were serfs, bound to the land, until Alexander II freed them in 1861. Russia remained poor, autocratic and repressive; writers such as Tolstoy and Dostoevsky explored its soul, while revolutionaries killed Alexander II in 1881.

Defeat by Japan in 1905 sparked a revolution; World War I's slaughter and hunger finished the tsars.

In February 1917 Tsar Nicholas II abdicated. In October Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power, promising 'peace, land and bread'. They won a brutal civil war, murdered the tsar's family, and in 1922 founded the Soviet Union, the first communist state.

Joseph Stalin forced peasants into collective farms and drove crash industrialisation. Millions died: in the famine of 1932–33, especially in Ukraine (the Holodomor), and in the Great Terror and the Gulag labour camps.

In World War II the Soviet Union lost about 27 million people but destroyed most of the German army and took Berlin. Victory in the 'Great Patriotic War' is still the core of Russian national pride.

The USSR became a nuclear superpower, put the first satellite and first man, Yuri Gagarin, into space, and ruled eastern Europe. But its economy stagnated. Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms from 1985 loosened control, and in 1991 the Soviet Union broke into 15 countries.

cards.q: Why is World War II so central to Russian identity?
a: The Soviet Union lost about 27 million people and defeated Nazi Germany
It was the first war Russia won
cards.why: Victory Day, 9 May, is the biggest national holiday.

cards.p: Under Boris Yeltsin, prices were freed and state firms sold off; inflation wiped out savings, life expectancy fell, and a few oligarchs grabbed vast wealth. Many Russians remember the 1990s as chaos and humiliation.

Vladimir Putin, a former KGB officer, became president in 2000. High oil prices brought a boom, and he restored order, but also took control of the media, jailed or exiled opponents, and fought wars in Chechnya and Georgia.

He annexed Crimea in 2014 and in 2022 launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Europe's largest war since 1945, bringing sweeping Western sanctions.

items: A long history of attack drives the hunger for buffers.
Order valued over freedom after times of chaos.
A claim to lead the Slavic and Orthodox lands.

cards.p: Rwanda is a small, green, densely populated country of hills in central Africa. Its people share one language, Kinyarwanda, and the same culture; the categories Hutu, Tutsi and Twa were social as much as ethnic.

A Tutsi-led monarchy ruled the kingdom. Germany and then Belgium (from 1916) ruled through it; Belgium hardened the categories, issuing identity cards stating 'Hutu' or 'Tutsi' and favouring Tutsis. A Hutu revolution from 1959 drove many Tutsis into exile; independence came in 1962.

cards.q: What did Belgian colonial rulers introduce that hardened divisions?
a: Identity cards stating Hutu or Tutsi

cards.p: From April to July 1994, after the Hutu president's plane was shot down, Hutu extremists, the army and militias murdered about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi and moderate Hutu, in about 100 days, often with machetes and urged on by radio. The UN and the world failed to stop it. The Tutsi-led RPF rebels ended it.

Under Paul Kagame, Rwanda has rebuilt, banned ethnic labels, held community gacaca courts and become one of Africa's cleanest, safest and fastest-growing countries, with more women in parliament than any other nation. Critics point to tight political control and its role in eastern Congo's wars.

cards.s: About 800,000 people were murdered in Rwanda in about 100 days in 1994.

units.title: Arabia and the birth of Islam

cards.p: Saudi Arabia covers most of the Arabian Peninsula, almost all desert, with no permanent rivers. People lived as Bedouin herders and in oasis towns and trading ports. Beneath the sand lies about a sixth of the world's proven oil.

Islam was born here. Muhammad began preaching in Mecca around 610 and moved to Medina in 622. Mecca, with the Kaaba, is the holiest city of Islam: Muslims everywhere pray facing it, and about 2 million make the Hajj pilgrimage each year. Non-Muslims may not enter the city.

After the early caliphs moved their capitals to Damascus and Baghdad, Arabia became a quieter backwater, though the holy cities stayed central.

cards.q: Which direction do Muslims around the world face to pray?

units.title: The House of Saud and oil

cards.h: An alliance of faith and power
cards.p: In 1744 Muhammad ibn Saud, a local ruler in central Arabia, allied with Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, a preacher of a strict, puritanical form of Sunni Islam (Wahhabism). The alliance between the Saud family and the clerics is still the foundation of the state.

Abdulaziz ibn Saud captured Riyadh in 1902 and over 30 years conquered most of Arabia, including Mecca and Medina in 1924–25. In 1932 he proclaimed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, named after his family. Every king since has been one of his sons.

Oil was found in 1938. American companies, later the state-owned Saudi Aramco, developed the world's largest reserves. Oil money transformed a poor desert into a wealthy state with free health care and education, but also made it dependent on oil. In 1973 Saudi Arabia led the Arab oil embargo that quadrupled prices. A close alliance with the US, oil for security, developed.

cards.q: Why is Saudi Arabia called 'Saudi'?
a: It is named after the ruling Saud family

cards.p: In 1979 extremists seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca; the regime responded by giving clerics more power. Fifteen of the nineteen 9/11 hijackers were Saudi. Rivalry with Shia Iran shapes the region, including a war in Yemen since 2015.

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, de facto ruler since 2017, launched Vision 2030 to end dependence on oil: tourism, cinemas, concerts, giant projects such as NEOM, and from 2018 women allowed to drive. At the same time dissent is crushed; the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018 damaged his reputation.

items: Wealth, and the need to move beyond it.
Absolute rule by the Saud family
A young population and fast social change.

cards.p: Sudan lies on the Nile; at Khartoum the Blue Nile from Ethiopia meets the White Nile. It is mostly desert in the north and savannah in the south and west, including Darfur.

Ancient Nubia's Kingdom of Kush conquered Egypt and ruled it as pharaohs around 750 BC. At Meroë it built more pyramids than Egypt. Christian Nubian kingdoms lasted until the 1400s, and then the Muslim Funj sultanate ruled.

cards.q: Which ancient kingdom in Sudan once ruled Egypt?
cards.why: Its kings ruled as pharaohs around 750 BC.

cards.p: Egypt conquered Sudan in 1821. In 1881 a religious leader, the Mahdi, led a revolt and took Khartoum in 1885, killing the British general Gordon. Britain reconquered it in 1898 and ruled it with Egypt until independence in 1956.

Sudan has known almost constant war. The mostly Christian and animist south fought the Arab-Muslim north for decades, until South Sudan became independent in 2011. In Darfur from 2003 government-backed militias killed perhaps 300,000. Since April 2023 a war between the army and the RSF militia has caused the world's largest displacement and hunger crisis.

cards.s: South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011.

cards.p: Senegal, on Africa's Atlantic bulge, has Dakar on its westernmost point. It is about 95% Muslim, organised around Sufi brotherhoods such as the Mourides, whose holy city is Touba.
Senegal was part of the Ghana, Mali and Jolof empires. Europeans traded slaves from Gorée Island and other posts. France made Saint-Louis and Dakar the capitals of French West Africa.

cards.q: Which city was the capital of French West Africa?
cards.why: Senegal was the heart of French West Africa.

cards.p: Senegal became independent in 1960 under the poet-president Léopold Sédar Senghor, a founder of the Négritude movement. It is one of the few African countries never to have had a coup.
Power has changed hands peacefully several times; in 2024 voters elected the young outsider Bassirou Diomaye Faye. Offshore oil and gas began flowing in 2024.

cards.s: Senegal has never had a military coup.

cards.p: Singapore is a tiny island city-state at the tip of the Malay Peninsula, on the Strait of Malacca, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes. Its people are mostly Chinese, Malay and Indian; English, Mandarin, Malay and Tamil are official.
A port called Temasek existed in the 1300s. In 1819 Stamford Raffles of the British East India Company founded a free-trade port here; it boomed. Japan captured it in 1942 in Britain's worst defeat.

cards.q: Who founded modern Singapore?

units.title: Lee Kuan Yew and the miracle

cards.p: Singapore joined Malaysia in 1963 but was expelled in 1965; Lee Kuan Yew wept on TV. With no resources, it built itself as a hub of trade, finance and manufacturing.

Under Lee and the People's Action Party, ruling since 1959, Singapore became one of the world's richest countries, clean, safe and efficient, with excellent schools and public housing for 80% of people, but strict laws and limits on political freedom.

cards.s: Singapore was expelled from Malaysia in 1965.

cards.p: The Solomon Islands are a Melanesian archipelago of about 900 islands in the South Pacific, with over 70 languages.
People arrived about 30,000 years ago. Britain made it a protectorate in 1893. In 1942–43 the Battle of Guadalcanal, one of World War II's fiercest, turned the Pacific war against Japan.

cards.q: Which World War II battle took place in the Solomon Islands?

cards.p: The Solomon Islands became independent in 1978.
Ethnic conflict (1998–2003) brought an Australian-led peacekeeping mission. In 2019 it switched recognition from Taiwan to China and signed a security pact with Beijing.

cards.s: The Solomon Islands switched recognition from Taiwan to China in 2019.

cards.p: Sierra Leone, 'lion mountains' in Portuguese, is on West Africa's Atlantic coast, with one of the world's largest natural harbours at Freetown. It is rich in diamonds.

In 1787 British abolitionists founded Freetown as a home for freed slaves, including Black Loyalists from America and Africans freed from slave ships by the Royal Navy. Their descendants, the Krio, created a distinct culture and language. Britain made it a colony in 1808.

cards.q: Why was Freetown founded?
a: As a home for freed slaves

cards.p: Independent in 1961, Sierra Leone suffered a brutal civil war (1991–2002), funded by 'blood diamonds', in which rebels became infamous for amputations and child soldiers. About 50,000 died; British troops helped end it.
Peace has held, with democratic elections. The 2014–16 Ebola epidemic killed about 4,000. It remains among the poorest countries.

cards.s: Sierra Leone’s civil war was funded by diamonds.

cards.p: El Salvador is the smallest and most densely populated country in Central America, the only one without a Caribbean coast, full of volcanoes. Its name means 'the Saviour'.

The Pipil, related to the Aztecs, ruled Cuzcatlán before Spain conquered it from 1524. After independence (1821) a few families, the 'Fourteen Families', controlled the coffee plantations. In 1932 the army massacred thousands of mostly indigenous peasants, La Matanza.

cards.q: What does 'El Salvador' mean?

cards.p: A civil war (1980–92) between the US-backed military government and leftist FMLN guerrillas killed about 75,000; Archbishop Óscar Romero was shot while saying Mass in 1980. Peace came in 1992.

Gangs such as MS-13, born in Los Angeles, made El Salvador one of the world's most violent countries. Since 2019 President Nayib Bukele has jailed over 80,000 suspects under emergency rule, making it among the safest in the region, while undermining democratic checks. It made bitcoin legal tender in 2021.

cards.s: Archbishop Óscar Romero was assassinated in 1980.
cards.why: He was later made a saint.

cards.p: San Marino is a tiny republic on Mount Titano, completely surrounded by Italy.

By tradition it was founded in 301 by Marinus, a Christian stonemason, making it the oldest surviving republic in the world. It survived because it was small and poor, and Garibaldi spared it in thanks for sheltering him.

cards.q: Why is San Marino famous?
a: It is the oldest surviving republic

cards.p: Italy recognised it in 1862. It is ruled by two Captains Regent, elected every six months, a system centuries old.
Tourism, banking and stamps support it; it uses the euro.

cards.s: San Marino has two heads of state at once.

units.title: Land of Punt and the coast

cards.p: Somalia has Africa's longest mainland coastline, along the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Almost all Somalis share one language and Sunni Islam, but society is organised by clans. Many are pastoral herders of camels; Somalia has the most camels in the world.
Ancient Egyptians traded with the 'Land of Punt', probably here. Mogadishu was a rich Indian Ocean port in the Middle Ages. In the 1800s Britain took the north (Somaliland) and Italy the south.

cards.q: What organises Somali society?
cards.why: Almost all Somalis share one language and faith.

cards.p: British and Italian Somalia united at independence in 1960. Siad Barre seized power in 1969; his war with Ethiopia over the Ogaden failed. When he fell in 1991, the state collapsed into clan warfare and famine; US troops were killed in Mogadishu in 1993 ('Black Hawk Down').

Piracy boomed off the coast in the 2000s. The jihadist group al-Shabaab still controls parts of the south. Somaliland in the north has run itself peacefully since 1991 but is not internationally recognised. A federal government in Mogadishu is slowly rebuilding.

cards.s: Somaliland has governed itself since 1991.

cards.p: Serbia is a landlocked Balkan country, where the Sava meets the Danube at Belgrade. Most Serbs are Orthodox Christians, and Serbian is written in both Cyrillic and Latin.

The Nemanjić dynasty built a medieval Serbian kingdom, an empire under Stefan Dušan in the 1300s. At the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 the Ottomans defeated the Serbs; the battle became the founding myth of Serbian identity, and Kosovo its sacred heartland. Ottoman rule lasted until uprisings from 1804 won independence by 1878.

cards.q: Why is the 1389 Battle of Kosovo important to Serbs?
a: It became the founding myth of Serbian identity

cards.p: A Bosnian Serb shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914, starting World War I; Serbia lost a large share of its people. Afterwards it led the new Yugoslavia, Tito's communist federation after 1945.

As Yugoslavia broke up, Slobodan Milošević backed Serb forces in wars in Croatia and Bosnia. NATO bombed Serbia in 1999 over Kosovo, which declared independence in 2008; Serbia does not recognise it. Serbia is an EU candidate with close ties to Russia; student-led protests have shaken the government since 2024.

cards.s: Serbia recognises Kosovo’s independence.

cards.p: South Sudan, in east-central Africa, became independent in 2011. The White Nile flows through the Sudd, one of the world's largest wetlands. Its peoples, such as the Dinka and Nuer, are largely cattle herders, mostly Christian or traditional believers.
In the 1800s Egyptian and Arab slave raiders preyed on the region. Under British–Egyptian rule it was governed separately from the Arab-Muslim north and neglected.

cards.q: When did South Sudan become independent?

cards.p: When Sudan became independent in 1956, the south rebelled against northern domination. Two civil wars (1955–72, 1983–2005) killed about 2.5 million. A 2005 peace deal led to a 2011 referendum in which 98.8% voted for independence.

In 2013 a power struggle between President Salva Kiir (a Dinka) and his deputy Riek Machar (a Nuer) became a civil war that killed about 400,000. A fragile peace holds; most people depend on aid despite oil wealth.

cards.s: South Sudan is the world’s newest country.

cards.p: São Tomé and Príncipe are two small volcanic islands in the Gulf of Guinea, on the equator, Africa's second-smallest country.

Uninhabited until the Portuguese arrived in 1470, they became a model for plantation slavery, first for sugar, later for cocoa; in the early 1900s it was the world's largest cocoa producer, using forced labour.

cards.q: What were São Tomé’s plantations famous for in 1900?
cards.why: The world’s largest producer at the time.

cards.p: Independent in 1975 after Portugal's revolution, it was a one-party Marxist state until 1990.
It is now a peaceful democracy dependent on cocoa, tourism and aid.

cards.s: São Tomé was uninhabited before the Portuguese arrived.

cards.p: Suriname, on South America's north coast, is mostly rainforest and the only Dutch-speaking country in the Americas. Its people are remarkably mixed: descendants of Indians, Javanese, Africans, Maroons, Chinese and Indigenous peoples.

In 1667 the Dutch took Suriname from England and kept it in exchange for New Amsterdam (New York). Sugar plantations were worked by enslaved Africans; escaped Maroons built free communities in the forest. After abolition in 1863, workers came from India and Java.

cards.q: What did the Dutch give England in exchange for Suriname?

cards.p: Suriname became independent in 1975; a third of its people moved to the Netherlands. Dési Bouterse seized power in 1980; his soldiers killed 15 critics in 1982.
Gold, bauxite and new offshore oil drive the economy; Jennifer Geerlings-Simons became the first woman president in 2025.

cards.s: Suriname is the only Dutch-speaking country in the Americas.

cards.p: Slovakia is a mountainous country in central Europe, with the Tatra mountains and more castles per person than almost anywhere. It makes more cars per person than any other country.

Slavs formed Great Moravia in the 800s, where Saints Cyril and Methodius brought Christianity in the Slavic language. From the 900s Slovakia was part of the Kingdom of Hungary for a thousand years; Bratislava was Hungary's capital while the Ottomans held Buda.

cards.q: For about how long was Slovakia part of Hungary?

cards.p: Slovakia joined the Czechs in Czechoslovakia in 1918. In World War II a Nazi puppet Slovak state deported Jews. After 1948 it was communist; Alexander Dubček, a Slovak, led the 1968 Prague Spring.
After the 1989 Velvet Revolution, Slovakia became independent peacefully on 1 January 1993. It joined NATO and the EU in 2004 and the euro in 2009.

cards.s: Slovakia became independent in 1993.

cards.p: Slovenia is a small, green country between the Alps and a short Adriatic coast, with Lake Bled and huge caves. Slovenian is a Slavic language.
Slavs settled in the 500s. For most of its history the land was ruled by the Habsburgs as part of Austria, while Slovenians kept their language alive.

cards.q: Which empire ruled Slovenia for most of its history?

cards.p: After 1918 Slovenia was part of Yugoslavia, its richest region.
In 1991 Slovenia declared independence; a Ten-Day War with the Yugoslav army ended quickly. It joined the EU and NATO in 2004 and the euro in 2007, the first ex-communist country to do so.

cards.s: Slovenia’s war of independence lasted ten days.

cards.p: Sweden is long and forested, with thousands of lakes and a Baltic coast; the north lies beyond the Arctic Circle, with midnight sun and polar night. Most of its 10.5 million people live in the south.

Swedish Vikings, the Varangians, traded and raided east down the rivers of Russia to Constantinople and Baghdad. Sweden became Christian around 1000 and a kingdom in the Middle Ages. From 1397 it was in a union with Denmark and Norway, until Gustav Vasa broke away in 1523 and made Sweden Lutheran.

In the 1600s Sweden became a great power. Gustavus Adolphus led Protestant armies in the Thirty Years War, and the Swedish empire ringed the Baltic, from Finland to northern Germany. It ended when Russia's Peter the Great defeated Charles XII at Poltava in 1709.

cards.q: What ended Sweden’s days as a great power?
a: Defeat by Russia at Poltava in 1709
cards.why: Peter the Great beat Charles XII.

cards.p: Sweden lost Finland to Russia in 1809 and has not fought a war since 1814, the longest peace of any country. In the 1800s poverty drove about 1.3 million Swedes, a quarter of the population, to emigrate, mostly to the American Midwest.

Industry (steel, Volvo, Ericsson, IKEA) and the Social Democrats, in power for most of the 1900s, built the 'Swedish model': high taxes, a generous welfare state, strong unions and equality. Sweden stayed neutral in both world wars. Alfred Nobel founded the Nobel Prizes.
Sweden joined the EU in 1995, welcomed many refugees, and, after Russia invaded Ukraine, ended 200 years of military non-alignment by joining NATO in 2024.
Eswatini (formerly Swaziland) is a small, landlocked kingdom between South Africa and Mozambique. Its people, the Swazi, share one language and culture.
King Sobhuza I built the Swazi kingdom in the 1800s. Britain made it a protectorate after the Boer War.

cards.q: What is Eswatini's former name?

cards.p: Independent in 1968, it is Africa's last absolute monarchy. King Sobhuza II reigned 82 years; Mswati III has ruled since 1986.
In 2018 the king renamed it Eswatini. It has one of the world's highest HIV rates, and pro-democracy protests in 2021 were crushed.

cards.s: Eswatini is an absolute monarchy.

cards.p: Seychelles is an archipelago of 115 islands in the Indian Ocean, Africa's smallest country by population, with granite islands and giant tortoises.
Uninhabited until the French settled it in 1770 with enslaved Africans; Britain took it in 1814.

cards.q: Who first settled Seychelles?

cards.p: Seychelles became independent in 1976; a coup in 1977 brought one-party rule until 1993.
Tourism and fishing make it Africa's richest country per person. Half its land is protected.

cards.s: Seychelles is Africa’s richest country per person.

cards.p: Syria lies on the eastern Mediterranean, between Turkey, Iraq and the Arab world. Damascus and Aleppo are among the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth.

Ebla, the Phoenicians, Assyrians, Persians, Greeks and Romans ruled here; Palmyra was a great caravan city. Paul converted on the road to Damascus. Damascus was capital of the Umayyad caliphate (661–750), and the Ottomans ruled from 1516 to 1918.

cards.q: Which city was capital of the Umayyad caliphate?

cards.p: France ruled Syria as a League of Nations mandate until 1946. After coups, Hafez al-Assad seized power in 1970; in 1982 his forces killed thousands at Hama. His son Bashar succeeded him in 2000.

In 2011 peaceful protests were met with force, leading to a civil war that killed about 500,000 and drove 13 million from their homes, many to Turkey, Lebanon and Europe. Russia, Iran, the US, Turkey and the Islamic State all fought there. In December 2024 rebels swept into Damascus and Assad fled to Moscow.

cards.s: Bashar al-Assad's rule ended in December 2024.

cards.p: Chad is a vast landlocked country: Sahara in the north (including the Tibesti mountains), Sahel in the middle and savannah in the south. Lake Chad has shrunk by about 90% since the 1960s. One of the oldest known human-like fossils, 'Toumaï', about 7 million years old, was found here.
The Kanem-Bornu Empire around Lake Chad lasted about a thousand years, controlling trans-Saharan trade. France conquered the region by 1920.

cards.q: What has happened to Lake Chad since the 1960s?

cards.p: Chad became independent in 1960 and has seen decades of civil war between north and south, coups, and a war with Libya over the Aouzou Strip in the 1980s.
Idriss Déby ruled from 1990 until he was killed fighting rebels in 2021; his son Mahamat took over. Chad hosts over a million refugees from Sudan's war.

cards.s: A 7-million-year-old human-like fossil was found in Chad.

cards.p: Togo is a narrow country on West Africa's Gulf of Guinea, between Ghana and Benin. Its coast was part of the 'Slave Coast'; the Ewe and Kabye are major peoples, and many practise Vodun alongside Christianity and Islam.
Germany made Togoland a colony in 1884. After World War I it was split: the west joined British Gold Coast (Ghana) and the east became French Togo.

cards.q: Which European country first colonised Togo?

cards.p: Togo became independent in 1960; its first president was killed in Africa's first post-independence coup in 1963. Gnassingbé Eyadéma ruled from 1967 to 2005, and his son Faure has ruled since, changing the constitution in 2024 to stay in power.
Lomé's deep-water port is one of West Africa's busiest; phosphate and cotton are key exports.

cards.s: One family has ruled Togo since 1967.

cards.h: The heart of mainland South-East Asia
cards.p: Thailand sits in the middle of mainland South-East Asia. Its heartland is the rice-rich plain of the Chao Phraya River, with Bangkok near its mouth. About 93% of Thais are Theravada Buddhists, and Buddhism shapes daily life, from monks' morning alms rounds to the many temples, or wats.

Tai peoples moved south from China. The kingdom of Sukhothai (from 1238) is seen as the first Thai state; the Thai script dates from it. Ayutthaya (1351–1767) became a great trading city, visited by Chinese, Persian and European merchants, until Burmese armies destroyed it in 1767.

cards.q: What is the main religion of Thailand?

cards.p: In 1782 King Rama I founded Bangkok and the Chakri dynasty, which still reigns. The king is revered as protector of the nation and of Buddhism.

Siam, as it was called until 1939, was the only South-East Asian country never colonised. Kings Mongkut (Rama IV) and Chulalongkorn (Rama V) modernised the state, abolished slavery and played Britain (in Burma and Malaya) against France (in Indochina), giving up some territory to keep the core independent as a buffer.
A coup in 1932 ended absolute monarchy. In World War II Thailand allied with Japan, but a Free Thai movement worked with the Allies, which let it escape treatment as a defeated enemy.

cards.q: Why was Thailand never colonised?
a: It modernised and played Britain and France off as a buffer state
It was too small to matter
It joined the British Empire voluntarily
cards.why: It gave up some territory to stay independent.

cards.p: Thailand has had about a dozen successful coups since 1932, most recently in 2006 and 2014; the army sees itself as guardian of 'nation, religion and king'. King Bhumibol reigned for 70 years (1946–2016) and was deeply revered; criticising the monarchy can bring 15 years in prison.

Thailand became a manufacturing hub and one of the world's top tourist destinations, with around 35 million visitors a year before Covid. A long divide between the Bangkok elite and the poorer rural north and north-east drives its politics.

items: Most men once spent time as monks.
Coups are a recurring part of politics.

cards.p: Tajikistan is a small, very mountainous country in Central Asia; over 90% is mountains, including the Pamirs, 'the roof of the world'. Unlike their Turkic neighbours, Tajiks speak a form of Persian.
The region was part of Sogdiana and of Persian empires; Tajiks see the Samanid dynasty (819–999) of Bukhara as their golden age. Russia conquered it in the late 1800s.

cards.q: What language family is Tajik part of?

cards.p: The Soviets created Tajikistan in 1929, leaving the historic Tajik cities of Samarkand and Bukhara in Uzbekistan.

After independence in 1991, a civil war (1992–97) killed up to 100,000. Emomali Rahmon has ruled since 1992. Tajikistan is the poorest former Soviet republic; about a third of its income comes from migrants working in Russia.

cards.s: Tajikistan is mostly mountains.

cards.p: Turkmenistan is mostly the Karakum desert, between the Caspian Sea and the Amu Darya river. It has among the world's largest natural gas reserves. The 'Door to Hell', a gas crater burning since 1971, draws visitors.

Merv was a great Silk Road city, perhaps the largest in the world in the 1100s, before the Mongols destroyed it in 1221. Turkmen tribes, famed horsemen and carpet-weavers, resisted Russia until the battle of Geok Tepe in 1881.

cards.q: What resource does Turkmenistan have huge reserves of?
cards.why: Among the largest in the world.

cards.p: The Soviets created Turkmenistan in 1924 and forced nomads onto collective farms growing cotton.

After independence in 1991, Saparmurat Niyazov, 'Turkmenbashi', ruled with an extreme personality cult, renaming months after himself and building a golden revolving statue. His successors, father and son Berdimuhamedov, keep it one of the world's most closed countries.

cards.s: Turkmenistan is one of the world’s most closed countries.

cards.p: Timor-Leste (East Timor) is the eastern half of Timor island, plus an enclave, Oecusse. It is one of only two mainly Catholic countries in Asia.
Portugal ruled from the 1500s, trading sandalwood; the Dutch held the west.

cards.q: Who occupied Timor-Leste from 1975 to 1999?
cards.why: About a fifth of people died.

cards.p: When Portugal left in 1975, Indonesia invaded. Its occupation killed perhaps 100,000–180,000 people, a fifth of the population.

In a 1999 UN vote 78.5% chose independence; militias then burned the country until peacekeepers arrived. It became independent in 2002, Asia's newest nation; it joined ASEAN in 2025. José Ramos-Horta won the Nobel Peace Prize.

cards.s: Timor-Leste became independent in 2002.

cards.p: Tonga is an archipelago of about 170 islands in the South Pacific. It is the only Pacific nation never formally colonised.

Polynesian navigators, reading stars, waves and birds, settled the remote Pacific in one of humanity's greatest feats of exploration. Lapita people arrived around 800 BC. From about 1200 the Tu'i Tonga kings ruled a maritime empire across the Pacific. Captain Cook called them the 'Friendly Islands' in 1773.

cards.q: What makes Tonga unique in the Pacific?

cards.p: King George Tupou I united Tonga and gave it a constitution in 1875. It was a British protected state from 1900 to 1970 but kept its monarchy and land.
Reforms in 2010 made parliament more democratic. In 2022 an underwater volcano, Hunga Tonga, erupted in one of the largest explosions ever recorded.

cards.s: A huge volcanic eruption struck Tonga in 2022.

cards.p: Trinidad and Tobago lie just off Venezuela, the southernmost Caribbean nation. Trinidad has oil, gas and the Pitch Lake; its Carnival, calypso, soca and the steel pan, invented here, are world-famous.

Columbus named Trinidad in 1498. Spain, then Britain from 1797, ruled; enslaved Africans and, after 1838, Indian indentured workers came, so today people are about equally of African and Indian descent.

cards.q: Which instrument was invented in Trinidad?

cards.p: Independent in 1962 under Eric Williams, a historian of slavery, it became a republic in 1976.
Oil and gas made it one of the richest Caribbean countries; crime is a growing concern.

cards.s: Trinidad and Tobago is rich in oil and gas.

cards.p: Tunisia is the northernmost country in Africa, on the Mediterranean opposite Sicily. Its Sahara south contrasts with fertile northern plains of olives.

Phoenicians founded Carthage in 814 BC; it became a great sea power that fought Rome. Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants to attack Italy, but Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC. Arabs brought Islam in the 600s and founded Kairouan.

cards.q: Which great city, rival of Rome, stood in Tunisia?

cards.p: France made Tunisia a protectorate in 1881. Habib Bourguiba won independence in 1956 and built a secular state with the Arab world's most advanced women's rights.

In December 2010 a street vendor, Mohamed Bouazizi, set himself on fire in protest; demonstrations toppled the dictator Ben Ali in January 2011 and set off the Arab Spring. Tunisia became the region's only lasting democracy, until President Kais Saied seized sweeping powers in 2021.

cards.s: The Arab Spring began in Tunisia.

cards.p: Turkey spans two continents: a small corner in Europe (Thrace) and the great plateau of Anatolia in Asia, joined at the Bosphorus strait in Istanbul. Whoever held these straits controlled the route between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, which made the city one of the great prizes of history.

Göbekli Tepe, around 9500 BC, is one of the oldest temples ever found. The Hittites ruled an empire here in the Bronze Age; Troy stood on the Aegean coast; Greek cities lined the west, and later it was part of Persia, Alexander's empire and Rome. Many early Christian churches, and the apostle Paul, came from Anatolia.

In 330 Constantine made Byzantium, renamed Constantinople, the capital of the Roman Empire. The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire lasted another thousand years; its great church, Hagia Sophia, built in 537, was the largest building in the world for centuries.

cards.q: Which strait does Istanbul sit on?
cards.why: It links the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara and the Mediterranean.

cards.p: Turkic peoples came from Central Asia. In 1071 the Seljuk Turks crushed the Byzantines at Manzikert and settled Anatolia, which slowly became Turkish-speaking and Muslim.

Around 1300 Osman founded a small state that grew into the Ottoman Empire. In 1453 Mehmed II took Constantinople. Under Suleiman the Magnificent (1520–66) the empire ruled south-east Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, and the sultan was caliph, leader of Sunni Islam. It was a multi-faith empire: Christians and Jews kept their own communities.

After failing to take Vienna in 1683 it slowly declined, 'the sick man of Europe'.

cards.h: World War I and the Armenians
cards.p: The Ottomans joined Germany in World War I. They won at Gallipoli in 1915, where a young officer, Mustafa Kemal, made his name. In 1915–16 the government deported and massacred the Armenians of Anatolia; about a million died. Most historians call it genocide, which Turkey officially rejects.

After defeat, the Allies planned to carve up Anatolia. Mustafa Kemal led a war of independence, drove out Greek and other forces, and in 1923 founded the Republic of Turkey, with Ankara as capital. Greece and Turkey exchanged their minorities, uprooting over a million people.

He took the name Atatürk, 'father of the Turks'.

Atatürk abolished the caliphate, closed religious courts, gave women the vote, replaced Arabic script with the Latin alphabet, banned the fez and made everyone take surnames. Turkey became a strictly secular, Western-facing state; the army saw itself as guardian of his legacy and staged coups in 1960, 1971 and 1980.

Turkey joined NATO in 1952 and applied to join the EU. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, in power since 2003, brought fast growth and a bigger role for Islam in public life. After a failed coup in 2016 he jailed tens of thousands and made the presidency all-powerful. Turkey hosts more refugees than any other country, mostly Syrians, and a conflict with Kurdish militants has run since 1984.

items: Its public role is the great political argument.
Also ties with Russia and the Middle East.
About a fifth of the population
Their rights and a long conflict.

cards.q: What did Atatürk do?
a: Founded a secular republic and modernised Turkey
Led the Ottomans into World War I

cards.p: Tuvalu is nine small coral atolls in the Pacific, one of the smallest countries, with about 11,000 people; its highest point is only about 4.6 m above sea level.

Polynesian navigators, reading stars, waves and birds, settled the remote Pacific in one of humanity's greatest feats of exploration. Britain ruled the islands as the Ellice Islands, together with the Gilbert Islands (now Kiribati), until they separated in 1975.

cards.q: Which internet domain earns Tuvalu money?
cards.why: Popular with TV and streaming sites.

cards.p: Tuvalu became independent in 1978. It earns money from its '.tv' internet domain.
Rising seas threaten to make it uninhabitable. A 2023 treaty lets Tuvaluans move to Australia, and it is creating a digital copy of itself.

cards.s: Tuvalu is threatened by rising sea levels.
cards.why: Its highest point is about 4.6 m.

cards.p: Taiwan is a mountainous island 160 km off China's coast; Portuguese sailors called it Formosa, 'beautiful'. Indigenous Austronesian peoples lived here for thousands of years.

The Dutch held the south from 1624; the Ming loyalist Koxinga drove them out in 1662; the Qing took the island in 1683 and Chinese settlers poured in. Japan ruled it as a colony from 1895 to 1945, building railways and schools.

cards.q: Who ruled Taiwan from 1895 to 1945?

cards.p: After World War II the Republic of China took Taiwan. In 1947 its troops massacred thousands in the '228 Incident'. In 1949, losing China's civil war, Chiang Kai-shek's government fled to Taiwan and ruled under martial law until 1987.

Taiwan grew into an economic powerhouse; TSMC makes most of the world's most advanced chips. It became a vibrant democracy in the 1990s and legalised same-sex marriage first in Asia in 2019. Beijing claims Taiwan and threatens force; few countries recognise it officially, and its future is one of the world's most dangerous questions.

cards.s: Taiwan is a democracy.

cards.p: Tanzania has Africa's highest mountain, Kilimanjaro, the Serengeti plains, the great lakes Victoria and Tanganyika, and the spice island of Zanzibar. Olduvai Gorge holds fossils of human ancestors almost 2 million years old.

Swahili city-states such as Kilwa traded gold and ivory across the Indian Ocean. In the 1800s Zanzibar, ruled by Omani sultans, was the centre of an East African slave trade and of cloves. Germany colonised the mainland (1885), and after World War I Britain ruled it as Tanganyika.

cards.q: What is Africa's highest mountain?

cards.p: Tanganyika became independent in 1961 under Julius Nyerere, 'Mwalimu' (teacher), and united with Zanzibar in 1964 as Tanzania. His socialist 'Ujamaa' villages failed economically, but making Swahili the national language and building a shared identity across 120 ethnic groups gave Tanzania unusual peace.
Tanzania has been peaceful and growing, with tourism, gold and gas. It is dominated by one party, CCM, in power since independence; disputed 2025 elections brought deadly protests.

cards.s: Tanzania was formed by uniting Tanganyika and Zanzibar.

cards.p: Uganda is a green, lake-filled country on the equator; Churchill called it 'the pearl of Africa'. Lake Victoria, Africa's largest lake, is the source of the White Nile. It has mountain gorillas and over 45 million people, one of the youngest populations in the world.
Kingdoms flourished here, above all Buganda, with a sophisticated court under its king, the Kabaka. Britain made Uganda a protectorate in 1894, ruling through Buganda's chiefs.

cards.q: Which great river begins at Lake Victoria in Uganda?

cards.p: Uganda became independent in 1962. In 1971 General Idi Amin seized power; his regime killed perhaps 300,000 people, and he expelled the country's 80,000 Asians in 1972. Tanzania's army overthrew him in 1979.

Yoweri Museveni took power in 1986 after a guerrilla war and has ruled ever since. Uganda fought HIV with frank public campaigns, battled the Lord's Resistance Army in the north, and hosts over 1.5 million refugees, more than any other African country.

cards.s: Idi Amin expelled Uganda’s Asian community in 1972.

cards.p: Ukraine is the largest country entirely in Europe, mostly flat steppe with some of the world's most fertile black soil, which made it a breadbasket and a prize for empires. The Dnipro River runs through its heart past Kyiv.

Kyiv was the capital of Kyivan Rus, the first great East Slavic state, from the 880s. In 988 Prince Volodymyr (Vladimir) adopted Orthodox Christianity. Ukrainians, Russians and Belarusians all trace their roots here, but Ukrainians see Kyiv as theirs; Russia's claim to that heritage is central to today's war.

cards.h: Mongols, Lithuania, Poland and the Cossacks
cards.p: The Mongols destroyed Kyiv in 1240. Western Ukraine then fell under Lithuania and Poland. On the frontier steppe, free Cossack communities grew; in 1648 the Cossack leader Bohdan Khmelnytsky rebelled against Poland and allied with Moscow, which over time absorbed eastern Ukraine.

cards.q: Which city was the capital of Kyivan Rus?

units.title: Russian rule and the Soviet era

cards.p: By the late 1700s most of Ukraine was in the Russian Empire (the far west in Austria). The tsars called Ukrainians 'Little Russians' and banned Ukrainian-language books in 1876, but the poet Taras Shevchenko kept the language and national idea alive.

Ukraine declared independence in 1918 but was conquered by the Bolsheviks and became a Soviet republic. In 1932–33 Stalin's forced collectivisation and grain seizures caused a famine, the Holodomor ('death by hunger'), that killed about 3.5 to 5 million Ukrainians. Ukraine and many countries recognise it as genocide.

World War II devastated Ukraine: about 7 million died, including some 1.5 million Jews, as at Babi Yar. In 1986 a reactor exploded at Chernobyl, the world's worst nuclear disaster, contaminating a vast area.

cards.q: What was the Holodomor?
a: A man-made famine in Soviet Ukraine, 1932–33

cards.p: When the Soviet Union collapsed, 92% of Ukrainians voted for independence in December 1991. Ukraine gave up its Soviet nuclear weapons in 1994 in return for security assurances. In 2004 the Orange Revolution overturned a rigged election.

In 2013–14 protests on Kyiv's Maidan square ousted the pro-Russian president Yanukovych, who had refused an EU deal. Russia then annexed Crimea and backed separatists in the eastern Donbas, starting a war.

On 24 February 2022 Russia launched a full-scale invasion, aiming to take Kyiv; it was driven back. The war, Europe's largest since 1945, has killed hundreds of thousands, displaced millions and devastated cities such as Mariupol. President Volodymyr Zelensky became a symbol of resistance. Ukraine became an EU candidate in 2022.

Kosovo is a small, landlocked Balkan land with an Albanian majority (about 90%), mostly Muslim, and a Serbian minority. It declared independence in 2008; about 100 countries recognise it, but Serbia and others do not.

Kosovo was the heart of medieval Serbia, with famous Orthodox monasteries; the 1389 Battle of Kosovo against the Ottomans is central to Serbian identity. Under Ottoman rule Albanians became the majority.

cards.q: Who opposes Kosovo’s independence?

cards.p: After Serbia took Kosovo in 1912, tensions grew. In 1998–99 Serbian forces drove out about 800,000 Albanians; NATO bombed Serbia and Kosovo came under UN rule.
Kosovo declared independence in 2008. It uses the euro, has a young population and strong diaspora, and tension with the Serb north continues.

cards.s: Most Kosovars are ethnic Albanians.

cards.p: Uruguay lies on the Río de la Plata between Argentina and Brazil, a country of rolling grassland, cattle and beaches. Most of its people are of European, especially Spanish and Italian, descent.
The 'Banda Oriental' was contested between Spain and Portugal. After independence from Spain, Brazil annexed it; with Argentine help, Uruguay won independence in 1828 as a buffer state.

cards.q: What was Uruguay created as?
a: A buffer state between Argentina and Brazil

cards.p: Under President José Batlle (1903–15) Uruguay became one of the world's first welfare states, with divorce, workers' rights and secular schools. It won the first football World Cup in 1930. A military dictatorship ruled from 1973 to 1985.

Uruguay is one of Latin America's most stable, least corrupt democracies. It legalised cannabis in 2013 and same-sex marriage in 2013. The modest ex-guerrilla president José Mujica (2010–15) became world-famous.

cards.s: Uruguay won the first football World Cup.

cards.p: Uzbekistan is a doubly landlocked country in Central Asia, between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers. Its oasis cities, Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva, were among the great stops of the Silk Road. Most Uzbeks are Muslim and speak a Turkic language.

Sogdian merchants dominated Silk Road trade. Arabs brought Islam in the 700s, and Bukhara became a centre of learning, home of scholars such as Avicenna. After Genghis Khan devastated the cities, the conqueror Timur (Tamerlane) built an empire from Samarkand in the 1300s and filled it with turquoise-domed mosques and madrasas, such as the Registan.

cards.q: Who made Samarkand the capital of a great empire in the 1300s?
cards.why: He filled it with grand mosques.

cards.p: Russia conquered the khanates in the 1860s–70s. The Soviets created Uzbekistan in 1924 and turned it into a giant cotton plantation; irrigation drained the Aral Sea, once the world's fourth-largest lake, into a toxic desert.

Uzbekistan became independent in 1991 under Islam Karimov, a harsh dictator until his death in 2016. His successor, Shavkat Mirziyoyev, has opened the economy and ended forced cotton labour, while keeping tight control.

cards.s: The Aral Sea dried up because of Soviet irrigation for cotton.

cards.p: Vatican City, inside Rome, is the smallest country in the world, about 0.5 km², the seat of the Pope and the Catholic Church, leader of about 1.4 billion Catholics.
By tradition, the apostle Peter was buried here; St Peter's Basilica stands over his tomb. Popes once ruled the Papal States across central Italy, until Italy took them in 1860–70.

cards.q: What created Vatican City as a state?

cards.p: The 1929 Lateran Treaty with Mussolini's Italy created Vatican City as an independent state. The Swiss Guard protects the Pope.
It holds the Sistine Chapel, painted by Michelangelo, and the Vatican Museums. Pope Leo XIV, the first American pope, was elected in 2025.

cards.s: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world.

cards.p: St Vincent and the Grenadines is a volcanic island and a chain of small islands in the eastern Caribbean.
Here Caribs and escaped Africans mixed to form the Garifuna, who resisted the British for decades. In 1797 Britain deported them to Central America, where Garifuna communities live today.

cards.q: Who are the Garifuna?
a: Descendants of Caribs and Africans, deported by Britain

cards.p: The country became independent in 1979, the same year La Soufrière volcano erupted.
Bananas, tourism and yachting in the Grenadines support it; La Soufrière erupted again in 2021.

cards.s: St Vincent became independent in 1979.

cards.p: Venezuela lies on South America's Caribbean coast, with the Andes, the Orinoco plains, and Angel Falls, the world's highest waterfall. It has the largest proven oil reserves on Earth.

Spain ruled from the 1500s; the name means 'little Venice', after stilt houses on Lake Maracaibo. Caracas-born Simón Bolívar, 'the Liberator', led the wars that freed Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia from Spain. Venezuela became fully independent in 1830.

cards.q: Who was Simón Bolívar?
a: The Liberator of much of South America

cards.p: Oil was found in 1914, and Venezuela became one of Latin America's richest countries, with a stable democracy from 1958. But wealth was unequal, and the 1980s oil slump brought crisis.

Hugo Chávez, elected in 1998, used oil money for social programmes in his 'Bolivarian revolution' while concentrating power. After his death in 2013, Nicolás Maduro presided over economic collapse: hyperinflation, shortages and repression. About 8 million Venezuelans, a quarter of the population, have fled, the largest exodus in Latin American history.

cards.s: Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves in the world.

units.title: A thousand years under China, a thousand years free

cards.p: Vietnam is a long S-shaped country on the South China Sea, with two great rice deltas, the Red River in the north and the Mekong in the south, linked by a thin coastal strip. Hanoi is the capital, Ho Chi Minh City (Saigon) the biggest city.

China ruled northern Vietnam for about a thousand years (111 BC–AD 938), leaving Confucianism, Buddhism and Chinese characters. The Vietnamese rebelled repeatedly, led by heroes like the Trưng sisters, and finally won independence in 938. They later defeated Mongol invasions three times.

Resisting powerful invaders became the core of Vietnamese identity.
Over centuries Vietnam pushed south, absorbing the Cham kingdom and the Mekong Delta from Cambodia. In 1802 the Nguyễn dynasty united the country, with its capital at Huế.

cards.q: Who ruled northern Vietnam for about a thousand years?

cards.p: France conquered Vietnam from 1858 and ruled it as part of French Indochina, with plantations of rubber and rice worked under harsh conditions. Ho Chi Minh founded the Indochinese Communist Party in 1930; after Japan's defeat he declared independence on 2 September 1945.

France fought to return and was defeated at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. Vietnam was split: a communist North and a US-backed South. The North backed the Viet Cong guerrillas in the South; the US sent over 500,000 troops. The 'American War' killed perhaps two million Vietnamese and 58,000 Americans; US bombing and Agent Orange devastated the land. In 1975 Saigon fell and Vietnam was united.

cards.q: Where were the French decisively defeated in 1954?
cards.why: It ended French rule in Indochina.

cards.p: After 1975 hundreds of thousands were sent to re-education camps and many fled as 'boat people'. Vietnam fought Cambodia's Khmer Rouge and China in 1979. Poverty was severe, until the 1986 Đổi Mới reforms opened the economy to markets while the Communist Party kept power.

Vietnam became one of the world's fastest-growing economies, a manufacturing hub for phones and clothes, and a popular destination. Relations with the US were restored in 1995 and are now close, as both worry about China, with which Vietnam disputes islands in the South China Sea.
Vanuatu is an archipelago of 83 volcanic islands in the South Pacific, with over 100 languages, the most per person of any country.

Lapita people settled about 3,000 years ago. Many islanders were taken as labourers to Australia ('blackbirding') in the 1800s. From 1906 Britain and France ruled it jointly as the New Hebrides Condominium, with two of everything, even police forces.

cards.q: Who ruled Vanuatu jointly?

cards.p: Vanuatu became independent in 1980.
It has frequently been ranked among the happiest countries. Cyclones, earthquakes and rising seas are serious threats; it led a push for climate action at the International Court of Justice.

cards.s: Vanuatu has over 100 languages.
cards.why: The most per person of any country.

cards.p: Samoa is a nation of two main volcanic islands in the South Pacific. Its culture, fa'a Samoa, centres on extended families and chiefs (matai).

Polynesian navigators, reading stars, waves and birds, settled the remote Pacific in one of humanity's greatest feats of exploration. Samoa was settled about 3,000 years ago. In the 1800s Germany, Britain and the US competed for it; Germany took western Samoa in 1899, while the US took the east (American Samoa).

cards.q: Which was the first Pacific nation to become independent?

cards.p: New Zealand seized it in 1914; its mishandled 1918 flu epidemic killed a fifth of Samoans. The non-violent Mau movement campaigned for freedom. In 1962 Samoa became the first Pacific nation to win independence.
Samoa skipped a day in 2011 to move west of the International Date Line, closer to its trading partners.

cards.s: Samoa once skipped a whole day.

cards.p: Yemen, at the south-west tip of Arabia, has mountains green enough that Romans called it 'Arabia Felix', happy Arabia. Its ancient kingdoms, such as Saba (Sheba), grew rich on frankincense and myrrh; the Marib dam was an engineering wonder.

Yemen embraced Islam early. Zaydi Shia imams ruled the northern highlands for about a thousand years. Yemen gave the world coffee: Mocha was the great coffee port. The Ottomans held the north; Britain took Aden in 1839.

cards.q: Which drink was first traded worldwide from the Yemeni port of Mocha?
cards.why: Mocha gave its name to a coffee.

cards.p: North Yemen became a republic after a 1962 revolution; South Yemen, after Britain left Aden in 1967, became the Arab world's only Marxist state. They united in 1990.

After the 2011 Arab Spring the Houthis, a Zaydi movement backed by Iran, seized Sana'a in 2014. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015. The war created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with famine and cholera. The Houthis have also attacked shipping in the Red Sea.

cards.s: North and South Yemen united in 1990.
cards.why: Civil war has divided it again since 2014.

cards.p: South Africa sits at the tip of Africa, between two oceans, rich in gold, diamonds and platinum. It has 12 official languages and is often called the 'rainbow nation'. Some of the oldest evidence of modern human behaviour, such as 70,000-year-old engraved ochre at Blombos Cave, comes from here.
The San and Khoikhoi (Khoisan) were the first inhabitants, hunters and herders. Bantu-speaking farmers, ancestors of the Zulu, Xhosa and Sotho, spread south over many centuries and built kingdoms.

In 1652 the Dutch East India Company founded Cape Town as a supply station. Dutch settlers, later called Boers or Afrikaners, took land and used enslaved people from Asia and Africa. Britain seized the Cape in 1806 and abolished slavery in 1834.

cards.q: Who founded Cape Town in 1652?
cards.why: As a supply station on the route to Asia.

cards.h: The Great Trek and the Zulu
cards.p: From 1835 thousands of Boers left British rule in the Great Trek and founded inland republics, fighting African kingdoms. The Zulu kingdom, built by Shaka in the 1810s, defeated a British army at Isandlwana in 1879 before being conquered.

cards.h: Diamonds, gold and the Boer War
cards.p: Diamonds were found at Kimberley in 1867 and gold at Johannesburg in 1886, the richest goldfield on Earth. Britain wanted control: the Boer War (1899–1902) was brutal; tens of thousands of Boer and African civilians died in British camps. In 1910 the colonies became the Union of South Africa, ruled by whites.

cards.q: What was found at Johannesburg in 1886?

cards.p: In 1948 the National Party began apartheid, 'apartness': everyone was classified by race; mixed marriage was banned; Black South Africans, three-quarters of the population, were pushed into poor 'homelands', needed passes to move and had no vote.

The African National Congress resisted. After police killed 69 protesters at Sharpeville in 1960, it was banned; Nelson Mandela was jailed in 1962 and spent 27 years in prison, much of it on Robben Island. Sanctions, boycotts and uprisings made apartheid unworkable. In 1990 President de Klerk freed Mandela.

In 1994 all South Africans voted for the first time, and Mandela became president, choosing reconciliation and a Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

South Africa has a respected constitution and free elections, but unemployment of around 30%, crime, power cuts and corruption under President Zuma disappointed many. In 2024 the ANC lost its majority for the first time and formed a coalition.

items: Among the most unequal countries on Earth.
Courts and press hold power to account.

cards.p: Zambia is a landlocked plateau in southern Africa, named after the Zambezi River, whose Victoria Falls ('the smoke that thunders') it shares with Zimbabwe. The Copperbelt makes it one of Africa's biggest copper producers.
Bantu kingdoms such as the Lozi and Bemba ruled before Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company took the region in the 1890s. As Northern Rhodesia it supplied copper to the empire.

cards.q: Which famous waterfall does Zambia share with Zimbabwe?

cards.p: Zambia became independent in 1964 under Kenneth Kaunda, who ruled a one-party state for 27 years and supported liberation movements in neighbouring countries. Multi-party democracy returned in 1991.
Zambia has had several peaceful changes of power. Copper prices drive its fortunes; it defaulted on its debts in 2020.

cards.s: Zambia was called Northern Rhodesia.

cards.p: Zimbabwe means 'houses of stone', after the ruins of Great Zimbabwe, a city of fitted stone walls built without mortar around 1100–1450, centre of a kingdom that traded gold to the Swahili coast. It shares Victoria Falls with Zambia.

Cecil Rhodes's company seized the land in the 1890s; it was named Southern Rhodesia. White settlers took the best farmland. In 1965 the white minority government under Ian Smith declared independence to avoid Black majority rule.

cards.q: What does 'Zimbabwe' mean?
cards.why: After the ruins of Great Zimbabwe.

cards.p: A guerrilla war forced majority rule, and Zimbabwe became independent in 1980 under Robert Mugabe. His forces killed about 20,000 in Matabeleland in the 1980s. From 2000 seizures of white-owned farms collapsed agriculture; hyperinflation in 2008 reached billions of percent.
In 2017 the army removed Mugabe; his former deputy Emmerson Mnangagwa has ruled since, and the economy remains troubled.

cards.s: Zimbabwe was formerly called Rhodesia.

IDN.t: Hindu and Buddhist kingdoms such as Srivijaya and Majapahit once ruled these islands, and Islam spread along the trade routes from the 1200s. From the 1600s the Dutch East India Company took control of the spice trade, and the Dutch state later ruled the East Indies as a colony of coffee, sugar and rubber plantations. Japan occupied the islands in World War II, and two days after Japan surrendered, Sukarno declared independence on 17 August 1945. The Dutch fought to return and only recognised independence in 1949, under US pressure. Sukarno led a non-aligned, increasingly left-leaning state until 1965, when a failed coup blamed on the communists gave General Suharto his chance: the army and its allies killed perhaps half a million people. Suharto's 'New Order' brought fast growth, corruption and repression, including a brutal occupation of East Timor from 1975. The 1997 Asian financial crisis brought him down in 1998, Indonesia became a democracy, and East Timor voted for independence in 1999.
IDN.c: Indonesia has more Muslims than any other country, and its 17,000-plus islands stretch about 5,000 km from Sumatra to Papua. Bahasa Indonesia unites hundreds of local languages, while Bali keeps its own Hindu culture. Nasi goreng, satay and rendang are national favourites, batik and gamelan music are famous arts, and badminton is the sport that wins Olympic medals. Motorbikes jam Jakarta's streets.
IDN.p: Prabowo Subianto, a former general once married to Suharto's daughter, became president in October 2024 with the backing of his predecessor, Joko Widodo, and faces little opposition in parliament. His flagship free school meals programme has been costly and hit by food-poisoning cases, and critics worry about the army's growing role in civilian life. In August 2025 protests over lawmakers' perks turned into riots after a police vehicle killed a delivery driver. Floods and landslides killed over 1,000 people in Sumatra in late 2025. In October 2026 the stock market had its worst day since 1998, adding to doubts about the economy.
q: Which country did Sukarno declare independent on 17 August 1945?
Which country did General Suharto rule under his 'New Order' until 1998?
Which country has more Muslims than any other, across 17,000-plus islands?

MYS.t: Malacca was a great trading sultanate in the 1400s until Portugal seized it in 1511, and the Dutch took it in 1641. From 1786 Britain gained Penang, Singapore and Malacca, and then brought the Malay sultanates under its protection. To work the tin mines and rubber plantations it brought in large numbers of Chinese and Indian workers, creating today's multi-ethnic society. Japan occupied Malaya during World War II. Afterwards communist guerrillas, mostly ethnic Chinese, fought the British in the Malayan Emergency from 1948 to 1960. Malaya became independent in 1957 under Tunku Abdul Rahman, and in 1963 it joined Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak to form Malaysia, which Indonesia opposed with an undeclared war. Singapore was expelled in 1965. Riots between Malays and Chinese in 1969 led to policies favouring Malays and other indigenous people, known as bumiputera. Mahathir Mohamad, prime minister from 1981 to 2003, drove industrialisation and built the Petronas Towers.
MYS.c: Malays, Chinese and Indians, plus many indigenous peoples in Sabah and Sarawak, give Malaysia its festivals: Hari Raya, Chinese New Year and Deepavali are all public holidays, and friends visit each other's open houses. Malay is the national language, but most people switch easily to English. Nasi lemak is the national dish, hawker stalls serve roti canai, laksa and satay late into the night, and badminton is the top sport.
MYS.p: Anwar Ibrahim, a reformer once jailed on charges he called political, became prime minister after the 2022 election produced a hung parliament, leading an unlikely coalition of his Pakatan Harapan and the old ruling Barisan Nasional. The main opposition is the Malay-nationalist and Islamist Perikatan Nasional. Race, religion and Malay privileges remain the main fault lines. In December 2025 former prime minister Najib Razak was convicted in the main 1MDB corruption trial. Barisan Nasional won a landslide in the Johor state election in July 2026. The king, Sultan Ibrahim of Johor, has taken an unusually active public role.
q: Which country's Malacca was a great trading sultanate until Portugal seized it in 1511?
Which country expelled Singapore in 1965?
Which country's national dish is nasi lemak, and where Hari Raya, Chinese New Year and Deepavali are all public holidays?

CHL.t: Chile won independence from Spain in 1818 under Bernardo O'Higgins. Squeezed between the Andes and the Pacific, it is about 4,300 km long but on average less than 200 km wide. It won its northern desert from Peru and Bolivia in the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1884), and the nitrates and later the copper found there paid for the state. In the late 1800s it also conquered the Mapuche lands of the south. During the Cold War politics polarised. In 1970 Salvador Allende became the first Marxist elected president in Latin America and nationalised the copper mines. In 1973 General Augusto Pinochet overthrew him with US support, and his dictatorship killed or 'disappeared' more than 3,000 people. Pinochet's free-market reforms made Chile one of the region's most stable economies, and voters ended his rule in a 1988 referendum. Democracy returned in 1990, but anger at inequality and at his constitution boiled over in mass protests in 2019.
CHL.c: Chile's poets Pablo Neruda and Gabriela Mistral both won the Nobel Prize. Chilean wine, empanadas, completo hot dogs piled with avocado, and the Atacama, the driest non-polar desert on Earth, are well known, as are the giant statues of Easter Island. Big international observatories in the Atacama study the sky, and around Independence Day, 18 September, people dance the cueca at festive fairs called fondas.
CHL.p: José Antonio Kast, a hard-right politician who has defended parts of Pinochet's rule, became president in March 2026 after beating the Communist candidate Jeannette Jara with 58% in the December 2025 runoff. He succeeded Gabriel Boric, the leftist president from 2022 to 2026, whose two attempts to replace the Pinochet-era constitution were rejected by voters in 2022 and 2023. Kast campaigned on crime and irregular migration, promising to expel undocumented migrants, and he has suspended dozens of environmental rules to speed up investment. Deadly wildfires and the future of copper and lithium mining are other big issues.
q: Which country elected Salvador Allende, Latin America's first elected Marxist president, in 1970?
Which country was ruled by General Augusto Pinochet from 1973 until a 1988 referendum ended his rule?
Which long, thin country has the Atacama, the driest non-polar desert, and Easter Island?

BOL.t: The silver mountain of Potosí, worked by forced Indigenous labour, funded Spain's empire for two centuries. Bolivia won independence in 1825 and named itself after Simón Bolívar, but it lost its coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1884) and, in the 20th century, most of the Chaco region to Paraguay in the bloody Chaco War of 1932 to 1935. Defeat discredited the old elite of tin barons and landowners. The 1952 revolution nationalised the tin mines, gave land to Indigenous farmers and gave everyone the vote. Military governments ruled for much of the Cold War, and in 1967 the Argentine revolutionary Che Guevara was captured and killed in the Bolivian jungle. Democracy returned in 1982. In 2005 Evo Morales, a leader of coca growers, was elected the first Indigenous president. He took control of the gas industry, and a new constitution in 2009 renamed the country the Plurinational State of Bolivia.
BOL.c: Bolivia is one of the most Indigenous countries in the Americas, with 36 official languages including Quechua and Aymara. Aymara women known as cholitas wear bowler hats, and the navy still trains on Lake Titicaca to keep alive the dream of returning to the sea. Sucre is the official capital, but the government works from La Paz, where cable cars link the city to El Alto.
BOL.p: Rodrigo Paz, a centrist, won the October 2025 runoff, ending almost 20 years of rule by the Movement for Socialism (MAS). The party had split in a bitter feud between Evo Morales and Luis Arce, president from 2020 to 2025, while shortages of dollars and fuel and rising prices wrecked its support. Paz has cut fuel subsidies and taken a $1.9 billion IMF loan. His reforms have met strikes and road blockades, and he declared a state of emergency in June 2026. Morales, who faces an arrest warrant, is shielded by supporters in the Chapare region.
q: Which country lost its coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific?
In which country was Che Guevara captured and killed in 1967?
Which country's navy trains on Lake Titicaca, and whose cholitas wear bowler hats?

PER.t: Peru was the centre of the Inca Empire, conquered by Francisco Pizarro in 1532, and Lima became the capital of Spanish South America. It declared independence in 1821, though Spanish forces held out until 1824. Defeat by Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1884) cost it its southern nitrate lands. For most of the 20th century a small coastal elite ruled over a largely Indigenous highland majority. In 1968 General Juan Velasco seized power and carried out a sweeping land reform. In the 1980s and 1990s the Maoist Shining Path insurgency and the army's response killed about 70,000 people, according to Peru's truth commission. Alberto Fujimori, elected in 1990, crushed hyperinflation and captured Shining Path's leader in 1992, but he also shut down Congress, and he was later convicted of human rights abuses and corruption. He fled to Japan in 2000 and was eventually jailed. Since then mining exports have driven growth, but almost every elected president has faced corruption charges.
PER.c: Machu Picchu is its most famous sight, and Quechua is still spoken by millions. Ceviche and Peruvian cuisine, which blends Inca, Spanish, African, Chinese and Japanese influences, are celebrated worldwide. Pisco sours, thousands of potato varieties, the Inti Raymi sun festival in Cusco and the Nazca Lines draw visitors. Pope Leo XIV, elected in 2025, spent many years as a missionary and bishop in Peru.
PER.p: Keiko Fujimori, Alberto's daughter, became president in July 2026 after narrowly winning the June runoff against the leftist Roberto Sánchez, at her fourth attempt. Peru had been through years of chaos: Congress removed Dina Boluarte, president from 2022 to 2025, in October 2025, then removed her interim successor José Jerí in February 2026. Several former presidents, including Pedro Castillo, Martín Vizcarra and Ollanta Humala, have been jailed, most for corruption and Castillo for his 2022 attempt to dissolve Congress. Extortion by criminal gangs, which target bus drivers and shopkeepers, is the public's biggest worry, along with illegal gold mining.
q: Which country was the centre of the Inca Empire, conquered by Pizarro in 1532?
Which country fought the Maoist Shining Path insurgency, whose leader was captured in 1992?
Which country has Machu Picchu and is celebrated for ceviche?

ARG.t: Argentina declared independence from Spain in 1816, and in the late 1800s its army pushed south into Patagonia, taking land from Indigenous peoples. Millions of Italian and Spanish immigrants arrived around 1900, when beef and wheat exports made it one of the world's richest countries. It stayed neutral in World War I and in World War II until the final weeks, and afterwards some Nazi war criminals, including Adolf Eichmann, hid there. Juan Perón, elected in 1946, and his wife Eva won the loyalty of workers with wage rises and welfare, and Peronism still divides the country. Coups followed one another until a military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983 made about 30,000 people 'disappear', according to human rights groups. In 1982 the junta invaded the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas, and lost a short war with Britain, which brought democracy back. Repeated debt crises and runaway inflation followed, most dramatically in 2001, when the economy collapsed and the country defaulted on its debts.
ARG.c: Tango was born in the port neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires, and football is a passion, with Maradona and Messi as icons; the national team won the 2022 World Cup. Argentines eat some of the most beef per person in the world, grilled at Sunday asados, and drink yerba mate from shared gourds. Dinner often starts after 10 pm, and Pope Francis, the first pope from the Americas, was Argentine.
ARG.p: Javier Milei, a libertarian economist who campaigned with a chainsaw as a symbol of spending cuts, has been president since December 2023. He slashed public spending, balanced the budget and brought inflation down sharply, but wages and pensions lost value and unions held several general strikes. His party won the October 2025 midterm elections, helped by a $20 billion US currency swap. The main divide is between Milei and the Peronists, whose leader Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, president from 2007 to 2015, is under house arrest after a corruption conviction. Cuts to university funding drew big protests in October 2026.
q: Which country did Juan and Eva Perón lead, winning the loyalty of workers?
Which country's junta invaded the Falklands in 1982 and lost a short war with Britain?
Where was tango born, in a country that won the 2022 World Cup?

CYP.t: Britain took over Cyprus from the Ottomans in 1878 as a base guarding the route to the Suez Canal, and made it a colony in 1925. In the 1950s Greek Cypriot fighters of EOKA waged a guerrilla campaign for union with Greece, which alarmed the Turkish Cypriot minority. Cyprus became independent in 1960 with a power-sharing constitution, but it broke down in intercommunal fighting in 1963 and 1964, and UN peacekeepers arrived and have stayed ever since. In 1974 Greece's military junta backed a coup aimed at union, and Turkey invaded, taking about a third of the island. More than 150,000 Greek Cypriots fled south and tens of thousands of Turkish Cypriots moved north. The north declared itself a separate state in 1983, recognised only by Turkey. In 2004 Turkish Cypriots voted for a UN reunification plan and Greek Cypriots rejected it, and a week later the divided island joined the European Union.
CYP.c: Greek and Turkish are official, and English is widely spoken thanks to British rule. Halloumi cheese, long meze dinners and souvla grilled over charcoal are part of island life. Visitors can walk across the UN buffer zone at Ledra Street in Nicosia, the world's last divided capital. Legend says Aphrodite was born from the waves near Paphos, and Britain still keeps two military bases here.
CYP.p: Nikos Christodoulides, an independent, has been president since 2023. Cyprus held the EU Council presidency in the first half of 2026. The centre-right Democratic Rally came first in the May 2026 parliamentary election. In October 2025 Tufan Erhürman, who supports a federal solution, defeated the incumbent in the north's leadership election, raising hopes for UN-led talks, though Turkey backs a two-state solution. When the United States and Israel struck Iran in 2026, missiles and drones were fired towards Cyprus and the British bases, and European navies sent ships to protect the island. Offshore gas finds bring both hope and tension.
q: Which island country was split when Turkey invaded in 1974 after a coup backed by Greece's junta?
Which country joined the European Union in 2004 still divided, a week after rejecting a UN reunification plan?
Which country's capital is the world's last divided capital, with a UN buffer zone at Ledra Street?

IND.t: The Mughal Empire ruled most of the subcontinent from the 1500s, but in the 1700s the British East India Company took control of large areas, and after the rebellion of 1857 Britain ruled India directly as the 'jewel in the crown' of its empire. Millions of Indian soldiers fought for Britain in both world wars. The Indian National Congress, led by Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru, used mass nonviolent protest, such as the 1930 Salt March, to demand independence, while Muhammad Ali Jinnah's Muslim League feared Hindu majority rule and called for a separate state. In 1947 Britain left and partitioned the land into India and Pakistan. About 15 million people crossed the new borders, and up to a million died in the violence. India and Pakistan went to war over Kashmir that year and again in 1965, 1971 and 1999. Nehru built a secular democracy that stayed non-aligned in the Cold War. Reforms in 1991 opened the economy, and India grew into a major exporter of software and services.
IND.c: India has 22 official languages, with Hindi and English most used in government. About four in five people are Hindu, and festivals such as Diwali and Holi light up the year, while India also has one of the world's largest Muslim populations. Cricket is close to a religion, Bollywood and other film industries make more films than any other country, and food ranges from Punjabi tandoori to southern dosas.
IND.p: Narendra Modi of the Hindu nationalist BJP has been prime minister since 2014; in 2024 he won a third term but lost his majority and relies on allies. Critics accuse his government of sidelining Muslims. After gunmen killed 26 people at Pahalgam in Kashmir in April 2025, India and Pakistan fought a four-day air and missile war. A US tariff fight eased in February 2026 with a deal under which, the US said, India would stop buying Russian oil, and India signed a trade deal with the EU. The BJP won West Bengal in 2026, while the opposition has protested against the revision of voter rolls.
q: Which country's independence movement used mass nonviolent protest such as the 1930 Salt March?
Which country was partitioned when Britain left in 1947, with about 15 million people crossing the new borders?
Which country has 22 official languages and celebrates Diwali and Holi?

CHN.t: In the 1800s Britain defeated China in the Opium Wars, and European powers and Japan forced open its ports and seized territory. The Qing, its last imperial dynasty, fell in 1912. The new republic split among warlords until Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists unified much of it in the late 1920s while fighting Mao Zedong's Communists. Japan took Manchuria in 1931 and launched full-scale war in 1937, killing millions of Chinese. After World War II the civil war resumed, and in 1949 the Communists won and founded the People's Republic, while the Nationalists fled to Taiwan. Mao's Great Leap Forward caused a famine that killed tens of millions, and his Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976 brought chaos. After his death Deng Xiaoping opened the economy to markets and foreign investment while keeping one-party rule, and in 1989 the army crushed protests in Tiananmen Square. Fast growth lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty and made China the world's second-largest economy and its biggest manufacturer.
CHN.c: Mandarin is the national language, though Cantonese and many other Chinese languages are spoken at home. Lunar New Year sets off the world's biggest yearly migration as people travel home. Food varies by region, from Sichuan's numbing peppercorns to Cantonese dim sum. Phones run daily life, with payments made through WeChat or Alipay, and Chinese electric cars, drones and short-video apps now sell worldwide.
CHN.p: Xi Jinping has led the Communist Party since 2012 and in 2023 began an unprecedented third term as president, with Li Qiang as premier. He has tightened party control and purged senior generals, including Zhang Youxia, a vice-chair of the Central Military Commission until he was placed under investigation in January 2026. A tariff war with the US under Donald Trump settled into an uneasy truce, and China's trade surplus passed $1 trillion in 2025, while a property slump weighs on growth at home. China held large military drills around Taiwan in December 2025 and is in a bitter dispute with Japan over Taiwan.
q: Which country did Britain defeat in the Opium Wars of the 1800s?
Which country's Great Leap Forward caused a famine that killed tens of millions?
Which country's Lunar New Year sets off the world's biggest yearly migration?

ISR.t: From the late 1800s the Zionist movement encouraged Jews, persecuted in Europe, to settle in Ottoman Palestine, where most people were Arabs. In 1917 Britain's Balfour Declaration backed a 'national home for the Jewish people', and after World War I Britain ruled Palestine as a League of Nations mandate. Jewish immigration grew in the 1930s, Arab revolts followed, and after the Holocaust, in which Nazi Germany murdered six million Jews, pressure for a Jewish state became overwhelming. In 1947 the UN proposed splitting the land into Jewish and Arab states.
