Israel declared independence in 1948 and won the war that followed, during which about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, an event Palestinians call the Nakba. In the 1967 war Israel took the West Bank, Gaza, East Jerusalem, Sinai and the Golan Heights, and began building settlements. It made peace with Egypt in 1979, returning Sinai, and with Jordan in 1994. The 1993 Oslo Accords created the Palestinian Authority, but talks on a Palestinian state collapsed.
ISR.c: Hebrew, revived as an everyday language in the late 1800s, is the main language, and about a fifth of citizens are Arab. Jews whose families came from Europe, the Middle East, Ethiopia and the former Soviet Union shape its food and music. Shabbat slows the country from Friday evening. Military service is compulsory for most young Jews, Tel Aviv is known for tech start-ups and beaches, and Jerusalem is holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims.
ISR.p: Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, returned in 2022 at the head of a right-wing and religious coalition while on trial for corruption. Hamas's attack of 7 October 2023 killed about 1,200 people and set off a war in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians. A US-brokered ceasefire in October 2025 brought the living hostages home. In 2026 Israel and the US went to war with Iran, and Israel invaded Lebanon again to fight Hezbollah. After the coalition split over drafting ultra-Orthodox men, an election on 27 October 2026 gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 of 120 seats and Gadi Eisenkot's 48, leaving neither a majority.
q: Which country declared independence in 1948 and won the war that followed?
Which country took the West Bank, Gaza, Sinai and the Golan Heights in the 1967 war?
Which country revived Hebrew as an everyday language?

PSE.t: For four centuries the land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean was part of the Ottoman Empire, home mostly to Arab Muslims and Christians. Britain captured it in World War I and ruled it under a League of Nations mandate, having promised in the 1917 Balfour Declaration to support a Jewish national home there. Jewish immigration, much of it fleeing persecution in Europe, brought growing conflict. In 1947 the UN proposed splitting the territory, and in the war that followed Israel's founding in 1948 about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, an event Palestinians call the Nakba, or catastrophe. Jordan then held the West Bank and Egypt held Gaza until Israel occupied both in 1967. The Palestine Liberation Organization, led by Yasser Arafat, fought Israel from exile and declared a state in 1988. The Oslo Accords of 1993 created the Palestinian Authority to govern parts of the territories, but final peace talks failed. In 2007 Hamas seized Gaza, splitting Palestinian rule in two.
PSE.c: Most Palestinians are Sunni Muslims, and an old Christian community lives in Bethlehem and Jerusalem. The olive harvest, the black and white keffiyeh, embroidered dresses and dishes such as musakhan and maqluba are proud symbols of identity, and the poet Mahmoud Darwish is widely loved. Millions of descendants of the 1948 refugees live in camps and cities across Jordan, Lebanon and Syria.
PSE.p: Hamas's attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 killed about 1,200 people, and the Gaza war that followed killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and left much of Gaza in ruins. A ceasefire took hold in October 2025, and a Board of Peace chaired by Donald Trump was set up to oversee rebuilding, though Hamas has not disarmed. In 2025 the United Kingdom, France, Canada, Australia and others recognised the State of Palestine, making more than 150 in all; Israel and the US do not. President Mahmoud Abbas and Prime Minister Mohammad Mustafa lead the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank, where Israeli settlements keep expanding.
q: Which country's people call the flight and expulsion of 1948 the Nakba, or catastrophe?
For which country did Yasser Arafat's PLO declare statehood in 1988?
Which country's poet Mahmoud Darwish is widely loved, and whose keffiyeh is a proud symbol?

LBN.t: Mount Lebanon was a refuge for Maronite Christians and Druze, and under the Ottomans it gained self-rule in 1861 after fighting between them. After World War I France took the area and in 1920 created Greater Lebanon, adding Beirut, Tripoli and the Bekaa Valley to the mountain while keeping a slim Christian majority. It became independent in 1943 under an unwritten National Pact: the president is a Maronite Christian, the prime minister a Sunni Muslim and the speaker a Shia Muslim. Beirut boomed as the region's banking and tourism centre. But Palestinian refugees and armed groups arrived after 1948 and 1970, and tensions between communities grew. In 1975 civil war broke out. Syria sent troops in 1976 and Israel invaded in 1982. Hezbollah, a Shia militia backed by Iran, grew by fighting Israel's occupation of the south, which ended in 2000. The 1989 Taif Agreement ended the war, but Syrian troops stayed until 2005, when former prime minister Rafic Hariri was assassinated.
LBN.c: Many Lebanese mix Arabic, French and English in a single sentence. Mezze such as tabbouleh, hummus and kibbeh fill the table, and the cedar tree is on the flag. Christians and Muslims of many sects live side by side, and Beirut's nightlife, music and fashion are famous across the Arab world. A large diaspora, especially in Brazil, Australia and West Africa, sends money home.
LBN.p: Lebanon's economy collapsed in 2019, wiping out savings, and a huge port explosion devastated Beirut in 2020. After a 2024 war with Israel weakened Hezbollah, parliament elected army chief Joseph Aoun president in January 2025, ending a two-year vacancy, and Nawaf Salam, a former judge at the International Court of Justice, became prime minister. When Hezbollah attacked Israel in March 2026 during the Iran war, the government banned its military activity, and Israel launched a ground invasion; Lebanon says the war killed thousands. Lebanon then held its first direct talks with Israel since 1993, and parliament postponed the 2026 election to 2028. Disarming Hezbollah is the central issue.
q: Which country's unwritten National Pact gives the presidency to a Maronite Christian and the premiership to a Sunni Muslim?
Which country's civil war began in 1975 and was ended by the 1989 Taif Agreement?
Which country has a cedar tree on its flag?

ETH.t: Ethiopia is one of the world's oldest states, Christian since the 300s. In 1896 Emperor Menelik II crushed an Italian invasion at the Battle of Adwa, so Ethiopia, with Liberia, escaped colonisation and became a symbol of African freedom. Mussolini's Italy invaded with poison gas and occupied it from 1936 to 1941, and Emperor Haile Selassie's appeal to the League of Nations exposed how powerless the League was. British and Ethiopian forces restored him in 1941. In 1974, amid famine, a Marxist military junta called the Derg overthrew him. Under Mengistu Haile Mariam it killed tens of thousands in the Red Terror, fought rebels in Eritrea and Tigray with Soviet and Cuban support, and presided over the 1984–85 famine that inspired Live Aid. When Soviet support ended, Tigrayan-led rebels took Addis Ababa in 1991, and Eritrea broke away. Their leader, Meles Zenawi, divided the country into ethnic regions, and from the 2000s state-led investment in roads, dams and factories made it one of the world's fastest-growing economies.
ETH.c: Ethiopia has its own alphabet, its own calendar (about seven years behind) and an ancient Orthodox church; Lalibela's churches are carved from solid rock. It is the birthplace of coffee, and the coffee ceremony is a daily ritual. Injera, a spongy sour flatbread, is eaten with spicy stews. Its long-distance runners are world famous, and Ethiopian Airlines is Africa's biggest airline.
ETH.p: Abiy Ahmed, prime minister since 2018, won the Nobel Peace Prize for making peace with Eritrea but then fought a war against Tigray's leaders from 2020 to 2022 that killed hundreds of thousands. Since 2023 Fano militias have fought the army in Amhara, and rebels remain active in Oromia. Abiy's Prosperity Party won a large majority in the June 2026 election. Ethiopia inaugurated its giant Nile dam in 2025, angering Egypt, and Abiy insists the country needs access to the sea. In September 2026 fighting broke out again with the Tigray People's Liberation Front, and Eritrea cut ties with Ethiopia.
q: Which country crushed an Italian invasion at the Battle of Adwa in 1896, becoming a symbol of African freedom?
Which country was ruled by the Derg, whose 1984–85 famine inspired Live Aid?
Which country is the birthplace of coffee, with its own alphabet and a calendar about seven years behind?

SSD.t: The peoples of the south, such as the Dinka, Nuer and Shilluk, were long raided for slaves from the north. Britain ruled Sudan jointly with Egypt from 1899 but ran the south separately, keeping out northern traders and letting Christian missions in. When Sudan became independent in 1956, power went to the Arab Muslim north; southern soldiers had already mutinied in 1955, starting a first civil war that ended in 1972. A second war began in 1983, after the government imposed Islamic law. John Garang's Sudan People's Liberation Army fought for the south, and about two million people died. A 2005 peace deal promised a vote on independence, and in 2011 nearly 99% chose to secede. South Sudan became the world's newest country, but in December 2013 a power struggle between President Salva Kiir, a Dinka, and his vice-president Riek Machar, a Nuer, turned into an ethnic civil war. It killed about 400,000 people before a peace deal in 2018.
SSD.c: English is official, and dozens of peoples live here, the Dinka and Nuer being the largest. Many South Sudanese are cattle herders for whom cows are central to marriage, wealth and identity, and a bride price can run to dozens of cattle. Most people are Christian or follow traditional beliefs. Basketball is a passion: Manute Bol and Luol Deng were born here, and the national team played at the 2024 Olympics.
SSD.p: Salva Kiir has led the country since independence, and elections have been postponed again and again. The 2018 peace deal is close to collapse. In March 2025, after fighting with the Nuer White Army militia, the government arrested Riek Machar, then first vice-president and Kiir's old rival, and later put him on trial for treason; his forces have since seized some towns. Kiir reshuffles officials constantly, fuelling talk about who will succeed him. Most people depend on food aid, and the war in neighbouring Sudan has disrupted oil exports. In September 2026 Kiir dissolved the government ahead of an election planned for December.
q: Which country voted by nearly 99% to secede in 2011, becoming the world's newest country?
Which country fell into civil war in 2013 between President Salva Kiir and his vice-president Riek Machar?
Which country's cattle herders may pay a bride price of dozens of cows, and where Manute Bol and Luol Deng were born?

SOM.t: Somali clans herded camels across the Horn of Africa for centuries, and coastal towns such as Mogadishu traded across the Indian Ocean. In the late 1800s the Somali lands were carved up: Britain took the north, Italy the south and France the area around Djibouti, while Ethiopia took the Ogaden and Britain added Kenya's north. Italy and Britain fought over the region in World War II. In 1960 British Somaliland and Italian Somalia united as one independent country. In 1969 General Siad Barre seized power and allied with the Soviet Union, but when he invaded Ethiopia's Ogaden in 1977 the Soviets backed Ethiopia, and he switched to the United States. His rule turned brutal, and in 1988 he bombed northern cities. When he fell in 1991, Somalia collapsed into clan warfare and famine, and Somaliland declared independence. A US-led intervention ended after the 'Black Hawk Down' battle in Mogadishu in 1993. In 2006 the jihadist group al-Shabaab emerged.
SOM.c: Almost everyone speaks Somali and is a Sunni Muslim, making it one of Africa's most culturally uniform countries, yet loyalty to clan shapes daily life and politics. Somalia is called 'a nation of poets', and oral poetry is still central. Camel milk, spiced rice and goat meat are staples, and an Italian legacy survives in pasta, called baasto, often eaten with a banana. Money sent home by a large diaspora keeps many families going.
SOM.p: Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, president since 2022 after an earlier term from 2012 to 2017, has stayed in office although his four-year mandate expired in May 2026; the opposition and the regional state of Puntland reject his rule, and talks on an election collapsed. Hamza Abdi Barre is prime minister. The president pushed through a new constitution allowing direct elections, which opponents call a power grab. Al-Shabaab still controls much of the countryside and retook several towns in 2025, as a smaller African Union force replaced the old one. In late 2025 Israel became the first country to recognise Somaliland's independence, which Somalia condemned.
q: Which country was formed in 1960 by uniting British and Italian territories?
Which country collapsed into clan warfare after 1991, with the 'Black Hawk Down' battle in its capital in 1993?
Which country is called 'a nation of poets', where pasta is often eaten with a banana?

KEN.t: Arab and Swahili traders ran coastal cities such as Mombasa and Lamu for centuries. Britain built a railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria from 1896, founding Nairobi along the way, and made Kenya a colony in 1920. The fertile highlands were given to white settlers, and Kikuyu and other farmers were pushed onto reserves or became squatters and labourers. The Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s was crushed brutally: tens of thousands were held in detention camps, where many were tortured, and Britain paid compensation to survivors only in 2013. Independence came in 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta, who allied with the West during the Cold War. Under Daniel arap Moi, who ruled from 1978 to 2002, Kenya became a one-party state until pressure forced multiparty elections in 1992. A disputed election in 2007 set off ethnic violence that killed more than 1,000 people, leading to a new constitution in 2010. Kenya also became a target for Somalia's al-Shabaab, which attacked a Nairobi shopping mall in 2013.
KEN.c: Swahili and English are official, along with more than 40 local languages. Kenyan runners dominate world distance running, the Maasai Mara hosts the great wildebeest migration, and Nairobi is East Africa's tech hub, where mobile money (M-Pesa) took off. Ugali, a stiff maize porridge, is eaten with sukuma wiki greens and nyama choma, grilled meat. Matatus, decorated minibuses blasting music, rule the roads.
KEN.p: William Ruto has been president since winning the 2022 election. His tax rises, pushed by debt, set off youth-led 'Gen Z' protests in 2024 in which protesters stormed parliament, and anniversary protests in 2025 left dozens dead, mostly shot by police. In 2025 Ruto made a pact with the opposition leader Raila Odinga, whose death in October 2025 brought huge crowds onto the streets. Debt, the cost of living, abductions of critics and police violence dominate politics ahead of the 2027 election, and Kenya reported its first Ebola case in October 2026.
q: Which country's Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s was crushed brutally by Britain?
Which country did Daniel arap Moi rule from 1978 to 2002?
Which country's runners dominate distance running, and where M-Pesa mobile money took off?

MWI.t: Chewa peoples built the Maravi kingdoms around Lake Malawi from about the 1400s, and in the 1800s the area was raided by Swahili-Arab and Yao slave traders. The Scottish missionary David Livingstone reached the lake in 1859, and his campaign against the slave trade drew Scottish missions and then British rule: a protectorate was declared in 1891, later named Nyasaland. Malawians fought for Britain in both world wars. In 1953 Britain forced Nyasaland into the Central African Federation with the two Rhodesias, dominated by white settlers, which fired up a nationalist movement led by Hastings Kamuzu Banda. The federation broke up, and Malawi became independent in 1964. Banda soon made it a one-party state and named himself president-for-life. During the Cold War he was one of the few African leaders to keep friendly ties with apartheid South Africa. Protests and a 1993 referendum brought back multiparty democracy, and Banda lost the 1994 election. The country is long and narrow because it follows the lake.
MWI.c: English and Chichewa are the main languages, and most people are Christian, with a sizeable Muslim minority. Nsima, a stiff maize porridge, is eaten at almost every meal, often with chambo fish from the lake. Lake Malawi has more fish species than any other lake, many of them colourful cichlids, and Malawi calls itself 'the warm heart of Africa'. Gule Wamkulu masked dancers perform at Chewa ceremonies.
MWI.p: Peter Mutharika won the presidency back in September 2025, beating Lazarus Chakwera, who had defeated him in the court-ordered rerun of 2020. Mutharika, 85 when he returned and the brother of an earlier president, Bingu wa Mutharika, leads the Democratic Progressive Party; Chakwera's Malawi Congress Party is now the main opposition. The vote was driven by economic pain: shortages of fuel and foreign currency, high inflation and food prices. In January 2026 fuel prices rose by more than 40%. Most people farm small plots, and droughts, floods and cholera outbreaks hit often. Mutharika has also ordered a new inquiry into the 2024 plane crash that killed vice-president Saulos Chilima.
q: Which country, once called Nyasaland, was ruled by Hastings Kamuzu Banda as president-for-life?
Which country did the missionary David Livingstone reach the lake of in 1859, drawing Scottish missions?
Which country calls itself 'the warm heart of Africa', with a lake holding more fish species than any other?

TZA.t: Swahili city-states such as Kilwa traded gold and ivory across the Indian Ocean for centuries, and in the 1800s Omani sultans ruled Zanzibar, East Africa's biggest slave market and a great source of cloves. Germany conquered the mainland from the 1880s as German East Africa and crushed the Maji Maji rebellion of 1905 to 1907, in which tens of thousands died, many from famine. In World War I German forces under Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck fought a long bush war against the British. Britain then ruled the territory as Tanganyika. Julius Nyerere led it peacefully to independence in 1961. In 1964 a revolution overthrew Zanzibar's Arab sultan, and the islands merged with the mainland to form Tanzania. Nyerere built a one-party socialist state, moved millions of people into ujamaa villages and promoted Swahili to unite more than 120 ethnic groups. The economy struggled, but Tanzania avoided ethnic conflict, and in 1979 its army invaded Uganda and toppled Idi Amin.
TZA.c: Swahili is the national language, and politeness matters, with elaborate greetings such as 'shikamoo' for elders. Zanzibar's Stone Town blends African, Arab and Indian culture; Freddie Mercury was born there. Bongo Flava music and bright Tingatinga paintings are local styles. Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain, the great migration across the Serengeti and Ngorongoro Crater draw visitors from around the world.
TZA.p: Samia Suluhu Hassan, Tanzania's first woman president, took over when John Magufuli died in office in 2021. She first eased his crackdown, but before the October 2025 election the main opposition party, Chadema, was barred and its leader Tundu Lissu was charged with treason. Official results gave her 98% of the vote. Protests erupted, security forces opened fire, and the opposition says hundreds were killed; she set up an inquiry. Mwigulu Nchemba became prime minister in November 2025. Political rallies were banned in 2026 and planned protests were blocked. The ruling CCM party has governed since independence. Tourism, gold and gas drive growth.
q: Which country was formed in 1964 when Zanzibar merged with Tanganyika?
Which country's founding leader Julius Nyerere moved millions into ujamaa villages and promoted Swahili?
Which country has Kilimanjaro, the Serengeti, and Stone Town, where Freddie Mercury was born?

SYR.t: Damascus and Aleppo are among the world's oldest cities, and Damascus was the capital of the Umayyad caliphate in the 600s and 700s. For four centuries Syria was part of the Ottoman Empire. After World War I drove out the Ottomans, in 1920 Faisal was briefly crowned king in Damascus, but France, given a League of Nations mandate, threw him out and carved Lebanon out of Syria. Independence came in 1946. After a string of coups the Baath Party seized power in 1963, and in 1970 the air force commander Hafez al-Assad took over. Relying on the army, the secret police and his own Alawite minority, and allied with the Soviet Union, he crushed an Islamist uprising in Hama in 1982, killing many thousands. His son Bashar succeeded him in 2000. When peaceful protests began in 2011 the regime fired on them, and the uprising became a civil war that killed about half a million people. Rebels led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham ended the Assad era in December 2024.
SYR.c: Most Syrians are Sunni Arabs, with Alawite, Christian, Druze and Kurdish minorities. The Umayyad Mosque and covered souks of Damascus and the citadel of Aleppo survived the war. Syrian food, from kibbeh and fattoush to Aleppo pepper and syrup-soaked sweets, has spread worldwide with the millions of refugees who fled to Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan and Germany, many of whom are now returning.
SYR.p: Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former jihadist whose Hayat Tahrir al-Sham toppled Assad, was named transitional president in January 2025. The US and the European Union have since lifted most sanctions, and Syria joined the coalition against the Islamic State. Sectarian killings of Alawites on the coast and fighting with Druze militias in Suwayda have killed thousands of people, and Israel holds land in the south. In early 2026 government forces took over most of the Kurdish-led north-east, and the Syrian Democratic Forces agreed to join the army. Rebuilding the economy is the main task.
q: Which country did Hafez al-Assad rule from 1970, crushing an uprising in Hama in 1982?
Which country's Assad era was ended by rebels in December 2024?
Which country's capital was the seat of the Umayyad caliphate, and is home to the Umayyad Mosque?

FRA.t: The French Revolution of 1789 overthrew the monarchy and spread the ideas of citizenship and the nation-state across Europe. In the 1800s France built the world's second-largest colonial empire, across Africa, Indochina and the Pacific. It was a main battlefield of World War I: at Verdun in 1916 hundreds of thousands fell, and about 1.4 million French soldiers died in the war. In 1940 Germany defeated France in six weeks. The Vichy regime under Marshal Pétain collaborated and helped deport about 75,000 Jews, while Charles de Gaulle led the Free French from London. After the 1944 Normandy landings and liberation, France chose reconciliation with Germany and helped found what became the European Union. Losing wars in Indochina in 1954 and Algeria, where independence came in 1962 after a brutal conflict, ended most of the empire. The Algerian crisis brought de Gaulle back in 1958 to found today's Fifth Republic, with its powerful presidency.
FRA.c: French is spoken by about 300 million people worldwide. France is the world's most-visited country, and its cuisine, wine, cheese, fashion and the Eiffel Tower, built in 1889, are global icons. Daily life revolves around the baguette and long lunches. The French take pride in secularism, called laïcité, and in protest: strikes and street marches are part of political life.
FRA.p: Emmanuel Macron, president since 2017, lost his majority in a 2024 snap election that split parliament between the left, his centrists and Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally. Michel Barnier and then François Bayrou fell as prime minister. Sébastien Lecornu, in office since September 2025, pushed the 2026 budget through using special constitutional powers. A court banned Le Pen from office in 2025 for embezzling EU funds, but in July 2026 an appeals court allowed her to run for president while her final appeal is pending. Debt, school funding and living costs drove nationwide protests in October 2026.
q: Which country's Vichy regime under Marshal Pétain collaborated with Nazi Germany?
Which country fought a brutal war in Algeria until 1962, a crisis that founded its Fifth Republic?
Which is the world's most-visited country, home to the Eiffel Tower, built in 1889?

SUR.t: The Dutch took this colony from England in 1667 and, in the same treaty, let England keep New Amsterdam, which became New York. Plantations used enslaved Africans, many of whom escaped into the rainforest and formed Maroon communities that still exist. After slavery ended in 1863, the Dutch brought indentured workers from India and Java. In the 20th century bauxite mining, run by the American firm Alcoa, became the backbone of the economy, and during World War II US troops guarded the mines, which supplied aluminium ore for Allied aircraft. Suriname became independent in 1975, and tens of thousands of people moved to the Netherlands around that time. In 1980 Sergeant-Major Desi Bouterse led a military coup, and in December 1982 his soldiers executed 15 critics. A civil war with Maroon rebels followed from 1986 to 1992. Bouterse later returned as an elected president from 2010 to 2020, but in 2023 he was finally sentenced for the 1982 killings, and he died a fugitive in 2024.
SUR.c: Dutch is the official language, the only place in South America where it is, but most people also speak Sranan Tongo. Its people have African, Indian, Javanese, Chinese and Indigenous roots, and a mosque and synagogue stand side by side in Paramaribo, whose wooden colonial centre is a World Heritage Site. Roti, Javanese bami and pom, a festive oven dish, are favourites, and rainforest covers most of the country.
SUR.p: Jennifer Geerlings-Simons, a doctor and long-time speaker of parliament, became Suriname's first woman president in July 2025. Her National Democratic Party, founded by Desi Bouterse, won the most seats in the May 2025 election and formed a coalition, and parliament then elected her to replace Chan Santokhi, president from 2020 to 2025. She inherited an economy recovering from a debt default and IMF-backed austerity, with high prices still squeezing families. The great hope is offshore oil: TotalEnergies is developing the large GranMorgu field, which could transform public finances. Suriname marked 50 years of independence in November 2025.
q: Which colony did the Dutch keep in 1667 while letting England keep New Amsterdam, which became New York?
Which country's Desi Bouterse led a 1980 coup and was sentenced in 2023 for executing 15 critics?
Which is the only South American country with Dutch as its official language?

GUY.t: The Dutch, and then from 1814 the British, ran sugar plantations on this coast with enslaved Africans. After slavery ended, Britain brought indentured workers from India, whose descendants are now the largest group. That split shaped modern politics. In the 1950s the leftist Cheddi Jagan, of Indian descent, won elections, and Britain, fearing a communist state during the Cold War, suspended the constitution in 1953; with US help it later favoured his rival, Forbes Burnham, of African descent. Racial violence broke out in the early 1960s. British Guiana became independent in 1966 as Guyana, and Burnham held power through rigged elections, declaring a 'Co-operative Republic' in 1970. In 1978 the deaths of more than 900 American followers of the cult leader Jim Jones at Jonestown shocked the world. Free elections returned in 1992. Venezuela claims about two-thirds of the country, the Essequibo region, and huge offshore oil finds since 2015 have made Guyana one of the world's fastest-growing economies.
GUY.c: Guyana is the only South American country where English is official, and it feels more Caribbean than Latin; it plays cricket for the West Indies. Kaieteur Falls is one of the world's tallest single-drop waterfalls. Pepperpot stew at Christmas, curry and roti, the Hindu festivals of Phagwah and Diwali, and Mashramani, the Republic Day carnival, reflect its mix of African, Indian and Indigenous people.
GUY.p: Irfaan Ali of the People's Progressive Party won a second term in September 2025, taking 36 of 65 seats. A new party, We Invest in Nationhood, led by the gold-trading businessman Azruddin Mohamed, came second and replaced the older APNU alliance as the main opposition, even though the United States sanctioned Mohamed in 2024 over alleged corruption and evading taxes on gold exports, and has sought his extradition. Oil money is paying for roads and housing, but critics worry about corruption. Venezuela still claims Essequibo, and Guyanese soldiers were shot at on the border river in 2026. A ferry disaster in July 2026 killed at least 73 people.
q: Where did more than 900 American followers of Jim Jones die in 1978?
Which country, once British Guiana, has two-thirds of its land, the Essequibo, claimed by Venezuela?
Which is the only South American country where English is official, home to Kaieteur Falls?

KOR.t: Korea was a kingdom for centuries before Japan annexed it in 1910. After Japan's defeat in 1945 the peninsula was split at the 38th parallel, and in 1948 the Republic of Korea was founded in the American zone, with Syngman Rhee as president. The North's invasion in 1950 began the Korean War. US-led UN forces saved the South, and the 1953 armistice left a fortified border, the DMZ, that still divides the peninsula. In the 1950s the South was one of the world's poorest countries. Under General Park Chung-hee, who seized power in 1961, the state steered cheap loans to family-run conglomerates such as Samsung and Hyundai, which built ships, steel, cars and later electronics for export. Growth came with repression, including the Gwangju massacre of protesters in 1980. Mass protests in 1987 forced free elections. The 1988 Seoul Olympics showed off the new country, and after the 1997 Asian financial crisis it became one of the world's leading technology economies.
KOR.c: K-pop groups such as BTS and Blackpink, the series Squid Game and the Oscar-winning film Parasite made Korean culture global. Seoul glows late into the night with cafés, PC gaming rooms and barbecue restaurants. Kimchi comes with every meal, the Hangul alphabet was created in the 1400s, and pressure to succeed in school exams is intense. The birth rate is among the lowest in the world.
KOR.p: In December 2024 President Yoon Suk Yeol declared martial law. Parliament overturned it within hours and impeached him, and the Constitutional Court removed him in April 2025. Lee Jae Myung of the liberal Democratic Party won the snap election in June 2025. In 2026 courts sentenced Yoon to life in prison for insurrection, and his former prime minister and his wife were also convicted. Han Seong-sook became prime minister in June 2026. Lee seeks calmer ties with the North, while the 2026 Iran war shook markets and strained the alliance with the US, which cut back joint military exercises.
q: Which country's Gwangju massacre of protesters took place in 1980?
Which country hosted the 1988 Olympics in its capital?
Which country gave the world K-pop, Squid Game and the Oscar-winning film Parasite?

PRK.t: Korea was a kingdom for centuries before Japan annexed it in 1910 and ruled harshly, suppressing the Korean language and drafting labourers for its war. When Japan surrendered in 1945, the US and the Soviet Union divided the peninsula at the 38th parallel. In the Soviet zone Kim Il Sung, a former anti-Japanese guerrilla, founded the Democratic People's Republic of Korea in 1948. In 1950, with Stalin's approval, he invaded the south. The Korean War drew in US-led United Nations forces and millions of Chinese troops, killed millions of people, and ended in 1953 with an armistice but no peace treaty. Kim built a closed state around his own personality cult and the idea of juche, or self-reliance. When the Soviet Union collapsed its aid stopped, and a famine in the 1990s killed hundreds of thousands. His son Kim Jong Il pushed ahead with nuclear weapons, testing the first bomb in 2006, and his grandson Kim Jong Un took over in 2011.
PRK.c: Pyongyang is a showcase capital of wide avenues, monuments and giant portraits of Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il, before which visitors are expected to bow. Most people cannot travel abroad or use the open internet. Kimchi and cold buckwheat noodles, naengmyeon, are favourite foods, and mass games, military parades and patriotic songs fill the calendar. Outside the capital many homes still lack reliable electricity.
PRK.p: Kim Jong Un, the third ruler from the Kim family, holds absolute power. A party congress in February 2026 confirmed him as leader and promoted his sister, Kim Yo Jong. North Korea has drawn close to Russia, sending troops and weapons for its war against Ukraine; in 2026 it opened a museum to the soldiers who fought there and a first road bridge to Russia. Xi Jinping visited Pyongyang in June 2026. Kim now calls South Korea a separate, hostile state rather than a partner for reunification, and missile tests continue despite UN sanctions.
q: Which country did Kim Il Sung found in 1948?
Which country tested its first nuclear bomb in 2006, under Kim Jong Il?
Which country's citizens mostly cannot travel abroad or use the open internet?

MAR.t: Morocco is one of the world's oldest monarchies: the Alaouite dynasty, which still rules, has held the throne since the 1600s, and the country never fell to the Ottoman Empire. European powers competed for it in the early 1900s, and in 1912 France made most of it a protectorate while Spain took the north and the far south. In World War II Allied troops landed at Casablanca in November 1942, and Churchill and Roosevelt met there in January 1943. Sultan Mohammed V became the symbol of the independence movement; France exiled him in 1953 but had to bring him back, and Morocco became independent in 1956. His son Hassan II ruled from 1961 to 1999 with an iron hand, surviving two coup attempts while jailing and 'disappearing' opponents in what Moroccans call the Years of Lead. In 1975 his Green March of 350,000 unarmed Moroccans crossed into Spanish Sahara, starting the long dispute over Western Sahara. Hassan's son Mohammed VI took the throne in 1999.
MAR.c: Arabic and Tamazight (Berber) are official, and many people speak Darija, Moroccan Arabic, mixed with French. Tagine, couscous on Fridays and sweet mint tea are everywhere. The medinas of Fez and Marrakesh, with their souks and riads, and the blue town of Chefchaouen draw millions of tourists. Football is a passion: Morocco reached the World Cup semi-finals in 2022, the first African team to do so, and it is a co-host of the 2030 World Cup.
MAR.p: King Mohammed VI holds the real power, though an elected parliament chooses the government. In the September 2026 election the Authenticity and Modernity Party came first, and the king appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, a former mayor of Marrakesh, as Morocco's first woman prime minister. In 2025 youth-led 'GenZ 212' protests demanded better hospitals and schools instead of spending on stadiums for the World Cup. The Western Sahara claim drives foreign policy, and Morocco has won growing support for its autonomy plan, including a 2025 UN Security Council resolution. Migration to Spain's enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla causes friction, and dozens died in a mass crossing attempt in July 2026.
q: Which country's Alaouite dynasty has held the throne since the 1600s, and never fell to the Ottomans?
Which country's Green March sent 350,000 unarmed civilians into Spanish Sahara in 1975?
Which was the first African team to reach the World Cup semi-finals, in 2022?

ESH.t: For centuries Sahrawi nomads, Arabic-speaking tribes of Arab and Berber descent, herded camels and traded across this stretch of desert on the Atlantic coast. Spain claimed the coast in 1884 and ruled it as Spanish Sahara, taking control of the interior only in the 1930s. Phosphate mining at Bou Craa from the early 1970s raised the stakes. In 1973 Sahrawi nationalists founded the Polisario Front to fight Spanish rule. In 1975, as the dictator Francisco Franco lay dying, Morocco sent about 350,000 unarmed civilians across the border in the Green March. Spain handed the territory to Morocco and Mauritania under the Madrid Accords, although the International Court of Justice had just found that neither had ties amounting to sovereignty over it. In 1976 Polisario proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic and, backed by Algeria, fought a long war. Mauritania withdrew in 1979, and Morocco built a fortified sand wall, the Berm, across the desert. A UN ceasefire in 1991 promised a referendum on independence, but it was never held.
ESH.c: Most Sahrawis speak Hassaniya Arabic, and Spanish is still widely known, especially in the refugee camps near Tindouf in Algeria, where many Sahrawi refugees have lived since the 1970s. Sweet tea served in three glasses, camel meat and the long, colourful melhfa worn by women are part of daily life. El Aaiún, the main city, has grown fast with Moroccan investment, and the lagoon at Dakhla draws kitesurfers.
ESH.p: Morocco controls about three-quarters of the territory and claims all of it. The Polisario Front's Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, based in camps in Algeria and holding the desert east of the Berm, also claims it; it is recognised by some states and belongs to the African Union. The UN lists Western Sahara as a non-self-governing territory. Polisario ended the ceasefire in 2020; low-level fighting continues. In October 2025 UN Security Council Resolution 2797 backed Morocco's autonomy plan as a basis for talks; Polisario still calls for an independence referendum. In April 2026 Mali withdrew its recognition of the SADR.
q: Which territory, once Spanish Sahara, was handed to Morocco and Mauritania under the 1975 Madrid Accords?
Which territory is crossed by the Berm, a fortified sand wall, and still awaits a UN referendum on independence?
Which territory's main city is El Aaiún, with many of its people living in refugee camps near Tindouf?

CRI.t: Spanish settlers found little gold and few people to force into labour on this 'rich coast', so the colony stayed poor and remote, a land of small farmers rather than great estates. It became independent with the rest of Central America in 1821 and went its own way by the 1840s. Coffee, grown from the 1830s, brought wealth to the Central Valley, and bananas spread along a railway to the Caribbean coast, built by Americans whose business became part of the United Fruit Company. After a disputed election in 1948 led to a six-week civil war, the winner, José Figueres, abolished the army and put the money into schools, health care and a welfare state. During the Cold War, while civil wars tore through its neighbours, Costa Rica stayed a democracy, and President Óscar Arias won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1987 for a plan to end the wars in Central America. From the 1990s ecotourism and factories making microchips and medical devices joined coffee and bananas.
CRI.c: 'Pura vida' (pure life) is the national motto, greeting and farewell, and Costa Ricans call themselves Ticos. About a quarter of the land is protected in parks and reserves, home to sloths, toucans and cloud forests, and ecotourism is a big earner. Nearly all electricity comes from renewable sources, mainly hydropower. Gallo pinto, rice and beans, starts the day, usually with a cup of local coffee.
CRI.p: Laura Fernández of the Sovereign People's Party became president in May 2026 after winning the February election outright with about 48% of the vote. She was the chosen successor of Rodrigo Chaves, president from 2022 to 2026, a combative outsider who clashed with the courts, the press and congress and twice survived votes to lift his immunity. Fernández made Chaves her minister of the presidency and of finance. The main issue is crime: gangs moving cocaine to the US and Europe have pushed murders to record levels in recent years. In March 2026 Costa Rica broke off relations with Cuba.
q: Which country abolished its army after a six-week civil war in 1948?
Which country's president Óscar Arias won the 1987 Nobel Peace Prize for a plan to end Central America's wars?
Which country's motto and greeting is 'pura vida'?

NIC.t: Nicaragua became independent from Spain in 1821. In 1856 the American adventurer William Walker seized power and declared himself president before being driven out. Its great lakes made it a possible route for a canal between the oceans, and the US kept a close eye on it, occupying the country from 1912 to 1933. The guerrilla leader Augusto Sandino fought the US Marines and was murdered in 1934 on the orders of Anastasio Somoza García, head of the US-trained National Guard. Somoza and his sons ran Nicaragua like a family business until 1979, when the Sandinista National Liberation Front, named after Sandino, overthrew them. The Sandinistas, led by Daniel Ortega, launched literacy campaigns and land reform and turned to Cuba and the Soviet Union. Ronald Reagan's US armed the Contra rebels, and the war killed tens of thousands. In 1990 voters elected Violeta Chamorro, and the war ended. Ortega returned to power in 2007 and has held it ever since.
NIC.c: Nicaragua is the largest country in Central America, with two huge lakes, a chain of smoking volcanoes and colonial cities such as Granada and León. Gallo pinto, rice and beans fried together, is eaten at almost every meal. Baseball, not football, is the favourite sport, and the poet Rubén Darío is a national hero. Hundreds of thousands of Nicaraguans work in Costa Rica and the US.
NIC.p: Daniel Ortega and his wife Rosario Murillo rule together as co-presidents, a post created by a 2025 constitutional change that also lengthened terms to six years and put the army and police directly under the presidency. Since crushing mass protests in 2018, when more than 300 people were killed, the government has jailed opponents, closed thousands of charities, expelled priests and stripped critics of their citizenship. Several opponents have died in custody or been killed in exile. In 2026 Ortega announced plans to abolish future elections, the US imposed more sanctions, and Nicaragua quit the Central American Parliament.
q: Which country did the American adventurer William Walker seize in 1856?
Which country's Sandinistas overthrew the Somoza family in 1979 and fought US-backed Contras?
Which is Central America's largest country, where baseball beats football and the poet Rubén Darío is a hero?

COG.t: The explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza signed treaties with the Teke king in 1880, and the town named after him, Brazzaville, became the capital of all French Equatorial Africa. Colonial rule was harsh: thousands of forced labourers died building the Congo-Ocean railway to the coast at Pointe-Noire in the 1920s and 1930s. During World War II Brazzaville was the capital of Free France, and in 1944 de Gaulle held a conference there that promised the colonies more rights, an early step towards independence. The country became independent in 1960. After a 1963 uprising it turned left, and from 1970 it was the People's Republic of the Congo, Africa's first Marxist-Leninist state, allied to the Soviet Union. Offshore oil, found in the 1950s and 1970s, became the main source of income. When the Cold War ended, it held multiparty elections in 1992, but a civil war followed in 1997, after which Denis Sassou Nguesso, who had ruled from 1979 to 1992, returned to power.
COG.c: Brazzaville and Kinshasa face each other across the Congo River, the closest pair of capitals in the world after Rome and Vatican City. Its sapeurs, men who dress in extravagant designer suits, have become famous worldwide, and Congolese rumba is the soundtrack of daily life. Saka-saka, pounded cassava leaves, is a staple, and the northern rainforests shelter lowland gorillas.
COG.p: Denis Sassou Nguesso, in power since 1997 and for 13 years before that, won a fifth term in March 2026 with about 95% of the official vote, in an election without serious challengers. Anatole Collinet Makosso has been prime minister since 2021. Oil still pays for most of the state, but the country is weighed down by debt, power cuts and unpaid salaries, and much of the population is poor despite the oil wealth. Foreign courts have investigated the president's family over corruption, which they deny. Opposition figures have been jailed or forced into exile.
q: Which country's capital was the capital of Free France during World War II?
Which country became Africa's first Marxist-Leninist state in 1970?
Which country is famous for its sapeurs, men who dress in extravagant designer suits?

COD.t: At the Berlin Conference of 1884–85, King Leopold II of Belgium won recognition for a Congo Free State that he ran as his personal property. His agents forced villagers to gather wild rubber, cutting off hands and taking hostages to meet quotas, and millions died. An international outcry made Belgium take over the colony in 1908. Belgium mined copper, diamonds and uranium, including the uranium for the first US atomic bombs, but trained almost no Congolese for government. Independence in 1960 came suddenly, and the country fell apart within days as the army mutinied and mineral-rich Katanga broke away. Its first prime minister, Patrice Lumumba, turned to the Soviet Union for help and was killed in 1961 with Belgian and American involvement. Joseph Mobutu, backed by the West as a Cold War ally, ruled from 1965 to 1997, renamed the country Zaire and looted it. After the 1994 Rwandan genocide, Rwanda and its allies invaded and toppled him, and the wars that followed drew in nine countries and killed millions.
COD.c: Lingala, Swahili and French are widely spoken, and Kinshasa is the world's largest French-speaking city. Congolese rumba, born in Kinshasa and Brazzaville in the 1940s, became the sound of African dance floors and is listed as world cultural heritage. The Congo River and rainforest are second only to the Amazon, and in 2026 the national team played at its first World Cup since 1974.
COD.p: Félix Tshisekedi has been president since 2019 and won a disputed second term in 2023. In early 2025 the Rwanda-backed M23 rebels captured Goma and Bukavu in the east. A US-brokered peace deal between Congo and Rwanda, linked to US access to minerals, was signed in December 2025, but fighting continued. Joseph Kabila, president from 2001 to 2019, was sentenced to death in absentia for backing the rebels. In 2026 an Ebola epidemic in Ituri killed more than 2,000 people, and parliament moved towards a referendum that could let Tshisekedi run again.
q: Which country did King Leopold II of Belgium run as his personal property, forcing villagers to gather rubber?
Which country did Joseph Mobutu rule from 1965 to 1997, giving it a new name and looting it?
Which country's capital is the world's largest French-speaking city, and the birthplace of Congolese rumba?

BTN.t: Bhutan was unified in the 1600s by a Tibetan lama, Ngawang Namgyal, who built the great fortress-monasteries called dzongs that still serve as both temples and government offices. After years of civil strife, the Wangchuck family founded the monarchy in 1907 with British approval. Bhutan was never colonised, but treaties in 1910 and 1949 let first Britain and then independent India guide its foreign affairs. China's takeover of Tibet in 1950 closed the northern border and pushed Bhutan closer to India, which built its first roads. It joined the UN in 1971. The fourth king coined the idea of Gross National Happiness and kept the country closed to most outsiders; television and the internet arrived only in 1999. In the early 1990s a campaign to enforce northern Bhutanese dress and culture led about 100,000 Nepali-speaking Lhotshampa to leave or be expelled, many to refugee camps in Nepal. In 2008 the king handed power to an elected parliament, and Bhutan became a constitutional monarchy.
BTN.c: Most people are Vajrayana Buddhists, and prayer flags flutter on every mountain pass. Men wear the knee-length gho and women the kira, required in offices, schools and on official occasions. Ema datshi, chillies in cheese, is the national dish, and archery is the national sport, played with singing and teasing of the other team. Visitors pay a daily sustainable development fee, and forests cover most of the land.
BTN.p: King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck, on the throne since 2006, is widely respected and still guides national policy. Tshering Tobgay's People's Democratic Party won the 2024 election, making him prime minister for a second time. The biggest worry is that young people are leaving in large numbers, many to study and work in Australia. The king's plan for Gelephu Mindfulness City, a special economic zone on the Indian border, is meant to create jobs and keep them at home. Hydropower sold to India is a leading export, and Bhutan has quietly used it to mine bitcoin. Border talks with China continue.
q: Which country's fourth king coined the idea of Gross National Happiness?
Which country only got television and the internet in 1999?
Which country's national sport is archery, and where men wear the knee-length gho?

UKR.t: Kyiv was the centre of Kyivan Rus, the medieval state that Ukrainians, Russians and Belarusians all claim as their origin. For centuries Ukraine's lands were split between Poland-Lithuania, Russia and Austria, and Cossacks on the steppe fought for their freedom. After the Russian Empire collapsed in 1917, Ukrainians declared independence, but the Bolsheviks won the war that followed and made Ukraine a Soviet republic, while its west went to Poland. In 1932–33 Stalin's forced collectivisation caused the Holodomor famine, which killed millions. World War II devastated Ukraine: millions died, including about 1.5 million Jews, as Nazi and Soviet armies fought back and forth across it. In 1986 the Chornobyl nuclear disaster spread radiation across Europe. Ukraine voted overwhelmingly for independence in 1991 and gave up its Soviet nuclear weapons. The Orange Revolution of 2004 and the Maidan protests of 2014 pushed it towards Europe. Russia responded by annexing Crimea and backing separatists in the Donbas, and in 2022 it launched a full-scale invasion.
UKR.c: Ukrainian is the state language, and since 2022 many people who grew up speaking Russian have switched to it. Borscht, varenyky dumplings and salo are national dishes. Embroidered vyshyvanka shirts, painted pysanky eggs and folk songs are symbols of pride. Ukraine is a giant exporter of grain and sunflower oil, and its tech workers, drone makers and Eurovision entries are known worldwide.
UKR.p: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, elected in 2019, has led the country through the full-scale war with Russia, which occupies about a fifth of Ukraine. Elections are suspended under martial law. US-brokered talks in 2025 and 2026 produced only brief ceasefires, and Russian strikes on power plants bring blackouts. A corruption scandal in the energy sector in late 2025 led to arrests and the resignation of Zelenskyy's chief of staff, Andriy Yermak. In July 2026 Zelenskyy reshuffled the government, making former Naftogaz chief Serhii Koretskyi prime minister, and replaced his army commander. Ukraine is an EU candidate, and in 2026 the EU approved a €90 billion loan.
q: Which country was the centre of Kyivan Rus, the medieval state three peoples claim as their origin?
Which country suffered the Holodomor famine of 1932 and 1933 under Stalin?
Which country is a giant exporter of grain and sunflower oil, with borscht and varenyky as national dishes?

BLR.t: Belarusian lands were part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and then Poland-Lithuania before Russia took them in the partitions of the late 1700s. After World War I a short-lived Belarusian republic was declared in 1918, but the country ended up split: the east became a Soviet republic and the west belonged to Poland until the Soviet Union seized it in 1939. During World War II Belarus lost about a quarter of its people, one of the highest shares of any country. The Nazis burned hundreds of villages with their inhabitants, such as Khatyn, and murdered most of its Jews. In 1986 much of the radiation from the Chernobyl disaster in neighbouring Ukraine fell on Belarus. It became independent in 1991. Alexander Lukashenko won the 1994 election and has ruled since, keeping a Soviet-style economy and ever closer ties to Russia. When he claimed victory in 2020, huge peaceful protests were crushed and opposition leaders jailed or forced into exile.
BLR.c: Belarusian and Russian are both official, but Russian dominates daily life. Draniki, crispy potato pancakes with sour cream, are the national dish. Belarus has some of Europe's largest old-growth forest at Białowieża, home to wild bison. Victory Day on 9 May is a major holiday, and Marc Chagall's paintings recall his home town of Vitebsk.
BLR.p: Alexander Lukashenko, president since 1994, was declared winner of a seventh term in January 2025 in an election Western governments called a sham. Alexander Turchin has been prime minister since March 2025. Belarus let Russia use its territory to invade Ukraine in 2022, and Russia says it has stationed nuclear weapons there. Since 2025 it has freed several hundred political prisoners in deals with the United States, which in return eased sanctions, including on its potash industry, though many others remain jailed. Neighbours Lithuania and Poland accuse it of hybrid attacks, including smuggling balloons and migrant crossings.
q: Which country lost about a quarter of its people in World War II, with villages such as Khatyn burned with their inhabitants?
Which country has been ruled by Alexander Lukashenko since 1994?
Which country has some of Europe's largest old-growth forest at Białowieża, home to wild bison?

NAM.t: San and Khoekhoe peoples lived in this dry land for thousands of years before the Herero, Ovambo and others settled it. Germany claimed it in 1884 as German South West Africa. When the Herero and Nama rose up in 1904, German troops drove survivors into the desert and into prison camps, killing tens of thousands in what is often called the first genocide of the 20th century; Germany formally acknowledged it as genocide in 2021. During World War I South Africa seized the colony, and afterwards it ruled it under a League of Nations mandate, later imposing apartheid. From 1966 SWAPO fought a guerrilla war for independence from bases in Angola, where Cuban and South African troops were also fighting. As the Cold War wound down, a 1988 deal linked Cuba's withdrawal from Angola to Namibian independence, which came in 1990 under Sam Nujoma. The odd Caprivi Strip, reaching east to the Zambezi, dates from an 1890 deal between Germany and Britain.
NAM.c: English is official, but Oshiwambo is the most widely spoken home language, and Afrikaans and German are still heard, marks of the colonial past. Windhoek has German bakeries and its own Oktoberfest. Herero women wear Victorian-style long dresses with horn-shaped hats. The red dunes of Sossusvlei in the Namib Desert, the shipwrecks of the Skeleton Coast and Etosha's wildlife draw visitors, and the Himba are known for ochre-covered skin and hair.
NAM.p: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah of SWAPO, the party that has governed since independence, became Namibia's first woman president in March 2025 after winning the November 2024 election with about 57% of the vote. The opposition disputed the poll, which was marred by ballot shortages and extended voting. She took over from Nangolo Mbumba, who had stepped in when Hage Geingob died in office in 2024, and appointed Elijah Ngurare as prime minister. The main issues are unemployment, especially among the young, deep inequality left by apartheid, and land ownership. Big offshore oil finds and plans for green hydrogen could transform the economy, while Germany's offer of reparations for the genocide remains unsettled.
q: Which country saw German troops kill tens of thousands of Herero and Nama, often called the 20th century's first genocide?
Which country won independence from South Africa in 1990 under Sam Nujoma?
Which country has the red dunes of Sossusvlei, the Skeleton Coast and its own Oktoberfest?

ZAF.t: Dutch settlers founded Cape Town in 1652, and Britain took the Cape in 1806. Many Afrikaners trekked inland and set up their own republics, but the discovery of diamonds at Kimberley in 1867 and gold on the Witwatersrand in 1886 drew Britain in. After the brutal Boer War of 1899 to 1902, Britain joined four colonies into the Union of South Africa in 1910, run by and for whites. Black South Africans founded the African National Congress in 1912. South Africa fought for the Allies in both world wars, but in 1948 the National Party won power and built apartheid, which classified everyone by race and pushed Black people into 'homelands' and townships. The Sharpeville massacre of 1960 and the Soweto uprising of 1976 brought world condemnation and sanctions. As the Cold War ended, President F. W. de Klerk freed Nelson Mandela in 1990, and in 1994 Mandela was elected in the first election open to all races. The ANC has led the country ever since.
ZAF.c: There are 12 official languages, including Zulu, Xhosa, Afrikaans and English, and Mandela's 'rainbow nation' remains a powerful idea. Braai (barbecue), boerewors sausage and bunny chow, a curry served in a hollowed-out loaf from Durban, are national favourites. Rugby, cricket and football are passions, and the Springboks have won the Rugby World Cup four times. Amapiano, a house music style born in the townships, has spread worldwide.
ZAF.p: Cyril Ramaphosa, a former trade union leader, has been president since 2018. In the 2024 election the ANC lost its majority for the first time, winning about 40%, and formed a 'government of national unity' with its old rival, the liberal Democratic Alliance, and smaller parties. The partners often clash over land and Black economic empowerment. Jacob Zuma's new MK party is the largest opposition party. Unemployment above 30%, violent crime, failing local services and corruption are the main issues, and anti-immigrant anger erupted in protests in 2026. Relations with the United States have soured over tariffs, Israel and US claims about white farmers.
q: Which country's National Party built apartheid after winning power in 1948?
Which country freed Nelson Mandela in 1990 and elected him president in 1994?
Which country has 12 official languages, and whose Springboks have won the Rugby World Cup four times?

OMN.t: From its ports at Muscat and Sur, Oman built a sea empire after expelling the Portuguese in 1650. By the 1800s its sultans ruled Zanzibar and much of the East African coast, trading in cloves, ivory and slaves and for a time the sultan lived there. After 1856 the realm split into separate Omani and Zanzibari sultanates. Oman was never a colony, but treaties left Britain in charge of its foreign affairs, and under Sultan Said bin Taimur it became one of the most isolated countries on earth, with only a few kilometres of paved road. Oil exports began in 1967, while a rebellion in the southern province of Dhofar, backed by communist South Yemen, spread through the hills. In 1970 Said's son Qaboos overthrew him with British support, defeated the rebels by 1976 with help from Britain, Iran and Jordan, and spent oil money on roads, schools and hospitals. Qaboos ruled for nearly 50 years, kept friendly ties with both Iran and the West, and died in 2020.
OMN.c: Most Omanis are Ibadi Muslims, followers of a branch of Islam distinct from both Sunni and Shia and known for its tolerance. Men wear the white dishdasha with an embroidered cap and, on formal occasions, the curved khanjar dagger shown on the flag. Guests are welcomed with cardamom coffee and dates. Frankincense trees still grow in Dhofar, and mountain forts, desert dunes and turtle beaches draw visitors.
OMN.p: Sultan Haitham bin Tariq, Qaboos's cousin, took the throne in 2020 and rules as an absolute monarch who is also prime minister. He has cut debt and announced plans for the Gulf's first personal income tax, part of an effort to prepare for life after oil. Oman has long been the region's quiet go-between and hosted talks between the US and Iran in 2025. When war broke out in 2026, Iranian strikes hit the port of Duqm and the industrial city of Sohar, and the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, beside Oman's Musandam peninsula, disrupted shipping and trade.
q: Which country's sultans once ruled Zanzibar and much of the East African coast?
Which country did Sultan Qaboos rule for nearly 50 years after overthrowing his father in 1970?
Which country's people are mostly Ibadi Muslims, with a curved khanjar dagger on the flag?

UZB.t: Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva grew rich on the Silk Road, and in the 1300s the conqueror Timur, or Tamerlane, made Samarkand the capital of a vast empire and filled it with blue-domed mosques. Uzbek khanates ruled the region until the Russian Empire conquered them in the 1860s and 1870s. In 1924 the Soviets drew new borders and created the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic, with Tashkent as its capital from 1930. Moscow turned it into a giant cotton farm, draining the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers for irrigation, so the Aral Sea shrank to a fraction of its size. In World War II factories and hundreds of thousands of refugees were evacuated here from the west. A 1966 earthquake flattened much of Tashkent, which was rebuilt as a model Soviet city. Islam Karimov, the Communist Party chief, became president at independence in 1991 and ruled harshly until his death in 2016, using forced labour in the cotton fields and, in 2005, killing hundreds of protesters in Andijan.
UZB.c: Uzbekistan is one of only two doubly landlocked countries, with Liechtenstein. Plov, rice cooked with lamb, carrots and chickpeas, is the national dish and is served at every wedding, and green tea and round flatbreads come with every meal. Samarkand's Registan square and Bukhara's old town are among the finest Islamic architecture anywhere, and the football team played at its first World Cup in 2026.
UZB.p: Shavkat Mirziyoyev, Karimov's long-serving prime minister, became president in 2016 and opened the country up. He freed some political prisoners, ended forced labour in the cotton harvest, let the currency float and welcomed tourists and investors. But no real opposition is allowed. A 2023 constitutional change reset his term limits, which could let him stay in power into the late 2030s, and his daughter Saida became head of the presidential administration in 2025. Abdulla Aripov is prime minister. Protests in Karakalpakstan in 2022 were put down with deadly force, while ties with neighbours have improved, including a 2025 border deal.
q: Which country's Samarkand was made the capital of Timur's vast empire in the 1300s?
Which country's Soviet cotton farms drained the rivers that fed the Aral Sea?
Which country has Samarkand's Registan square and serves plov at every wedding?

KAZ.t: For centuries Kazakh nomads herded horses, sheep and camels across the steppe. The Russian Empire absorbed them during the 1700s and 1800s, and Russian peasants settled the north. Under Stalin, forced collectivisation in the early 1930s seized the nomads' herds, and a famine killed well over a million Kazakhs, around two fifths of the whole people. The Soviets used the vast steppe as a dumping ground: Germans, Chechens, Koreans and others were deported here, many during World War II, and prisoners filled Gulag camps. Semipalatinsk became the main Soviet nuclear test site, with over 450 explosions, and Sputnik and Yuri Gagarin launched from Baikonur. Khrushchev's Virgin Lands campaign of the 1950s ploughed up the north for wheat. By 1991 Kazakhs were barely the largest group in their own country. In December 1991 it was the last republic to leave the Soviet Union. Nursultan Nazarbayev ruled for almost 30 years, moved the capital to Astana in 1997 and built an economy on oil and metals.
KAZ.c: Kazakhstan is the world's largest landlocked country, and most people live in cities such as Almaty and Astana, with its futuristic skyline. Kazakh and Russian are both widely spoken, and Kazakh is switching from Cyrillic to the Latin alphabet. Most people are Muslim, but life is secular. Horse meat, kumis fermented mare's milk and beshbarmak are traditional, and eagle hunting, yurts and horseback games keep nomad culture alive.
KAZ.p: Kassym-Jomart Tokayev became president in 2019, hand-picked by Nursultan Nazarbayev. In January 2022 fuel-price protests turned into deadly riots; Tokayev called in Russian-led troops and then sidelined Nazarbayev's family. He promised a 'New Kazakhstan' with a single seven-year presidential term, but power remains tightly held and critics are jailed. In a March 2026 referendum voters approved a new constitution that replaced the two-chamber parliament with a single chamber, the Kurultai, and restored the office of vice-president; the ruling party won about 70% in the August election. Kazakhstan balances Russia, China and the West, and in 2026 signed a deal for Russia to build its first nuclear power plant.
q: Which country was the last republic to leave the Soviet Union, in December 1991?
Which country's Semipalatinsk was the main Soviet nuclear test site, with over 450 explosions?
Which is the world's largest landlocked country, where eagle hunting and yurts keep nomad culture alive?

TJK.t: Tajiks descend from the Persian-speaking peoples of Central Asia, heirs to cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara that flourished on the Silk Road under the Samanid dynasty in the 800s and 900s. The Russian Empire took the region in the late 1800s. After the 1917 revolution, Muslim fighters known as the Basmachi resisted the Bolsheviks in these mountains for years. In 1929 Tajikistan became a full Soviet republic, but the borders drawn by Soviet planners left Samarkand and Bukhara, with many Tajiks, in Uzbekistan. Soviet rule brought cotton farms, schools and the giant Nurek dam, and also suppressed religion. Independence came unexpectedly in 1991 when the Soviet Union collapsed. Within months a civil war broke out between the old communist elite, backed by Russia and Uzbekistan, and a coalition of Islamists and democrats. It killed tens of thousands and drove hundreds of thousands from their homes before a peace deal in 1997. Emomali Rahmon, who took power in 1992, has ruled ever since.
TJK.c: Tajik is a form of Persian, unlike the Turkic languages of its neighbours, and most people are Sunni Muslims. Mountains cover over 90% of the country, and the Pamir Highway across the 'roof of the world' draws adventurous travellers. Plov, round flatbread called non and green tea fill the table, and Nowruz, the Persian new year, is the biggest festival. Many families depend on relatives working in Russia.
TJK.p: Emomali Rahmon has ruled since 1992 and holds the title 'Leader of the Nation', which lets him run for office without limit; Qohir Rasulzoda is prime minister. His eldest son, Rustam Emomali, is widely seen as his chosen heir. The government jails critics, has banned the main Islamic party and in 2024 restricted the hijab. Money sent home by migrants in Russia props up the economy. In 2025 Tajikistan finally agreed its borders with Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, ending years of deadly clashes, while attacks from Afghanistan have killed Chinese workers near the frontier.
q: Which country fought a civil war from 1992 to 1997 that killed tens of thousands?
Which country has been ruled by Emomali Rahmon since 1992?
Which country speaks a form of Persian, and is crossed by the Pamir Highway over the 'roof of the world'?

LTU.t: Lithuania was the last pagan state in Europe until 1387, and in the late Middle Ages, joined with Poland, it ruled one of Europe's largest states, stretching to the Black Sea. Russia absorbed it in the partitions of the 1790s and later banned books in the Latin alphabet, so smugglers carried them in from Prussia. Lithuania declared independence in 1918, but Poland seized Vilnius, so Kaunas served as the capital between the wars. The Soviet Union annexed the country in 1940. Under German occupation from 1941 more than 90% of its Jews were murdered, destroying Vilnius's famous Jewish community. The Soviets returned in 1944, and partisans called the Forest Brothers fought them into the 1950s. The Sąjūdis movement led the way in 1990, when Lithuania became the first Soviet republic to declare independence. Soviet troops killed 14 people at the Vilnius TV tower in January 1991, but the coup in Moscow that August brought recognition. Lithuania joined NATO and the European Union in 2004.
LTU.c: Lithuanian is one of the oldest living Indo-European languages, close in some ways to ancient Sanskrit. Basketball is almost a religion, and the national team is a source of huge pride. Cepelinai, zeppelin-shaped potato dumplings, are the national dish, and cold pink beetroot soup is a summer favourite. Vilnius has one of Europe's largest baroque old towns.
LTU.p: Gitanas Nausėda has been president since 2019. The Social Democrats won the 2024 election, but their first prime minister, Gintautas Paluckas, resigned in 2025 over his business dealings, and his successor Inga Ruginienė's government fell in June 2026 when the party ended its alliance with the populist Dawn of Nemunas. Mindaugas Sinkevičius became prime minister in July 2026 with a new coalition. Russia and Belarus are the main concern: Lithuania spends heavily on defence, hosts a German army brigade, and has struggled with smuggling balloons from Belarus that disrupted Vilnius airport.
q: Which was the last pagan state in Europe, until 1387?
Which country became in 1990 the first Soviet republic to declare independence?
In which country is basketball almost a religion and zeppelin-shaped potato dumplings the national dish?

BRA.t: Portugal claimed Brazil in 1500, and it received about 40% of all enslaved Africans brought to the Americas, to work sugar plantations and later gold mines and coffee farms. It became independent in 1822 as an empire ruled by a Portuguese prince, and was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888, a year before it became a republic. Getúlio Vargas seized power in 1930 and built a centralised state with labour laws and state-owned industries. Brazil was the only South American country to send troops to fight in World War II, in Italy. In 1960 it moved its capital to Brasília, a planned city built in the empty interior. A military dictatorship ruled from 1964 to 1985, with US backing at the start, and pushed roads and dams deep into the Amazon. After democracy returned, the Real Plan of 1994 tamed hyperinflation, and in the 2000s a commodity boom and welfare programmes lifted millions out of poverty.
BRA.c: Brazil is the largest Portuguese-speaking country. Samba, bossa nova, Carnival in Rio and Salvador, and football (it has won five World Cups) are central to its identity, and about 60% of the Amazon rainforest lies inside Brazil. Weekends mean churrasco barbecue or a plate of feijoada, black beans with pork, and fast-growing evangelical churches now rival the Catholic Church.
BRA.p: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party, who first governed from 2003 to 2011, returned as president in 2023 after narrowly beating Jair Bolsonaro, president from 2019 to 2022. Bolsonaro's supporters stormed government buildings in Brasília in January 2023, and in 2025 the Supreme Court sentenced him to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup; Donald Trump imposed heavy tariffs on Brazilian goods in protest at the trial. In the October 2026 runoff Lula beat Bolsonaro's son Flávio by about 52% to 48% to win a fourth term, though Flávio rejected the result.
q: Which was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888?
Which country moved its capital in 1960 to a planned city built in the empty interior?
Which is the largest Portuguese-speaking country, with five World Cup wins?

URY.t: Brazil and Argentina fought over this territory until Britain helped create Uruguay as a buffer state in 1828. For much of the 1800s two parties, the Blancos and the Colorados, fought civil wars, and both still exist. In the early 1900s President José Batlle y Ordóñez built one of the world's first welfare states, with an eight-hour working day, divorce rights and a strict separation of church and state. Italian and Spanish immigrants helped make it prosperous, earning it the name 'the Switzerland of South America'. Beef and wool exports boomed during World War II and the Korean War, but when prices fell the economy stagnated, and in the 1960s the Tupamaros urban guerrillas rose up. A military dictatorship ruled from 1973 to 1985, jailing more political prisoners per person than almost any country. After democracy returned, the left-wing Broad Front won power in 2004, and its president José Mujica, a former Tupamaro, legalised cannabis and same-sex marriage in 2013.
URY.c: Uruguay hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930, and football is close to a religion. Asado barbecues, the chivito steak sandwich and yerba mate, carried in a thermos under the arm, are daily rituals. Candombe drumming, rooted in African traditions, fills Montevideo's streets during a Carnival that lasts about 40 days. Almost all its electricity comes from renewable sources, mostly wind and hydro.
URY.p: Yamandú Orsi, a former history teacher from the left-wing Broad Front, became president in March 2025 after beating the centre-right Álvaro Delgado in the November 2024 runoff. He succeeded Luis Lacalle Pou, president from 2020 to 2025. Uruguay remains one of Latin America's most stable democracies, with power passing peacefully between left and right. The main issues are rising crime linked to drug trafficking through its ports, slow growth and pension costs. In 2025 parliament legalised euthanasia, and in 2026 the long-awaited EU–Mercosur trade agreement took effect, though the United States imposed a 12.5% tariff on Uruguayan goods.
q: Which country did Britain help create as a buffer state between Brazil and Argentina in 1828?
Which country's president José Mujica, a former guerrilla, legalised cannabis in 2013?
Which country hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930?

MNG.t: In the 1200s Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes, and his successors built the largest land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Hungary. Later the Mongols split, and from the late 1600s China's Qing dynasty ruled them. When the Qing collapsed in 1911, Mongolia declared independence under its Buddhist leader, the Bogd Khan, though China reasserted control for a time. With Soviet help, revolutionaries took power, and in 1924 they created the Mongolian People's Republic, the world's second communist state. In the 1930s purges killed tens of thousands, including many Buddhist monks, and hundreds of monasteries were destroyed. Soviet and Mongolian troops defeated Japan at Khalkhin Gol in 1939. China accepted Mongolian independence after a 1945 referendum, but the country stayed a Soviet satellite through the Cold War. Peaceful protests in 1990 brought multi-party elections and a market economy. Since then the mining of copper, coal and gold has transformed the economy, and Ulaanbaatar has grown fast.
MNG.c: Mongolia is the most thinly populated country on Earth, and many families still herd sheep, goats, horses and camels and live in round felt tents called gers. The Naadam festival every July brings wrestling, archery and horse racing with child jockeys. Genghis Khan is a national hero, Tibetan Buddhism has revived since 1990, buuz dumplings are stuffed with mutton, and throat singing is a famous art.
MNG.p: Mongolia is a democracy squeezed between Russia and China, which buys most of its exports. President Ukhnaagiin Khürelsükh, elected in 2021, is head of state, while the Mongolian People's Party dominates parliament. Governments have been unstable: Prime Minister Luvsannamsrain Oyun-Erdene lost a confidence vote in 2025 after protests over his son's lavish spending, and his successor resigned in March 2026 amid party feuding. Nyam-Osoryn Uchral, a former hip-hop artist and party chairman, then became prime minister. Corruption, how much mining wealth reaches ordinary people, and Ulaanbaatar's winter air pollution are the big issues.
q: Which country became the world's second communist state in 1924?
Which country's tribes Genghis Khan united in the 1200s?
Which country's Naadam festival brings wrestling, archery and horse racing with child jockeys every July?

RUS.t: From Moscow, the tsars built the largest country on Earth, pushing across Siberia to the Pacific and south into the Caucasus and Central Asia. Defeats in World War I brought down the last tsar in 1917, and Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power and won a civil war, founding the Soviet Union in 1922. Under Stalin, forced collectivisation and the purges killed millions, but crash industrialisation helped the country survive Hitler's invasion in 1941. About 27 million Soviet citizens died before the Red Army reached Berlin in 1945. In the Cold War the Soviet Union was a nuclear superpower, the first to put a satellite and a person into space. In 1991 it broke apart into 15 countries. Russia's 1990s brought hyperinflation, the rise of the oligarchs and a brutal war in Chechnya. From 2000 Vladimir Putin restored central control on the back of high oil prices, crushed opposition, fought Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, and in 2022 launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
RUS.c: Russia spans 11 time zones, from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific. Most people are Orthodox Christians, but Tatars, Chechens and other Muslim peoples form a large minority. Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Tchaikovsky and the Bolshoi Ballet are world famous. Families escape to wooden dachas in summer, banya steam baths and tea are rituals, and Victory Day on 9 May, marking the defeat of Nazi Germany, is the biggest national holiday.
RUS.p: Vladimir Putin, in power as president or prime minister since 1999, won a fifth term in 2024 against no serious challenger; Mikhail Mishustin is prime minister. The full-scale war in Ukraine goes on, and US-brokered talks in 2025 and 2026 produced only brief ceasefires. Western sanctions bite, but oil sales to China and India keep money flowing. The opposition leader Alexei Navalny died in an Arctic prison in 2024, and critics of the war get long sentences. In the September 2026 Duma election, with the liberal Yabloko party barred from the party-list vote, United Russia won about three quarters of the seats.
q: Which country's tsars pushed across Siberia to the Pacific, building the largest country on Earth?
Which country annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022?
Which country spans 11 time zones and celebrates Victory Day on 9 May as its biggest holiday?
