CZE.t: Bohemia was a powerful medieval kingdom, and Prague was briefly capital of the Holy Roman Empire. From 1526 the Habsburgs ruled the Czech lands for four centuries. In 1918, as Austria-Hungary collapsed, Tomáš Masaryk founded Czechoslovakia, which stayed a democracy between the wars when most of its neighbours did not. At Munich in 1938 Britain and France let Hitler take the German-speaking border regions, and in March 1939 he seized the rest. After World War II about three million Germans were expelled, and in 1948 the communists took power in a coup. The 1968 Prague Spring tried to build 'socialism with a human face' until Warsaw Pact tanks crushed it. Dissidents such as the playwright Václav Havel kept resistance alive, and the peaceful Velvet Revolution of 1989 made him president. Czechs and Slovaks then split peacefully on 1 January 1993. Czechia joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004.
CZE.c: Czechs drink more beer per person than anyone else, and Pilsner lager was invented in Plzeň in 1842. Pork with dumplings and sauerkraut is a classic meal. Prague's old town, Charles Bridge and astronomical clock draw huge crowds, and Kafka's writing is world famous. Ice hockey is the top sport, and many families spend weekends at country cottages called chaty.
CZE.p: The populist billionaire Andrej Babiš returned as prime minister in December 2025 after his ANO party won the October election with about 35% of the vote. He governs with the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party and the right-wing Motorists. Critics point to his conflicts of interest over his Agrofert business empire and an EU subsidy fraud case. President Petr Pavel, a retired general, often clashes with the government. Plans to change how public television and radio are funded brought around 200,000 people to protest in Prague in March 2026. Support for Ukraine is a main divide.
q: Which country's Prague Spring of 1968 tried to build 'socialism with a human face'?
Which country's Velvet Revolution of 1989 made the playwright Václav Havel president?
In which country was Pilsner lager invented, in 1842?

DEU.t: Germany was a patchwork of kingdoms and duchies until Prussia, led by Otto von Bismarck, united it in 1871 after wars against Austria and France. The new empire quickly became an industrial giant and a rival to Britain. Defeat in World War I brought the harsh Treaty of Versailles, a fragile democratic Weimar Republic, the hyperinflation of 1923 and then the Great Depression. Hitler used the anger and poverty to take power in 1933. His Nazi regime started World War II and murdered six million Jews in the Holocaust. In 1945 Germany lay in ruins, occupied by the four Allies, and in 1949 it split into democratic West Germany and communist East Germany. The West's 'economic miracle' drew millions to flee East until the Berlin Wall went up in 1961. The Wall fell on 9 November 1989, and the country reunited on 3 October 1990. Reunited Germany became the leading power of the European Union, and under Angela Merkel took in about a million refugees in 2015.
DEU.c: Germany is the EU's largest economy, known for car makers such as Volkswagen, BMW and Mercedes, and for engineering firms. Beer gardens, hundreds of kinds of bread, sausages and Christmas markets are part of life, as are Bach and Beethoven. Germans take recycling, punctuality and Sunday rest seriously. Football is the top sport, and Berlin's techno clubs draw visitors from across Europe.
DEU.p: Friedrich Merz of the conservative Christian Democrats became chancellor in May 2025, leading a coalition with the Social Democrats after the February election. The far-right Alternative for Germany came second nationally, and in 2026 it became the largest party in two eastern state elections, Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Merz's government loosened strict debt rules to fund defence and infrastructure, and is rebuilding the army, with plans to bring back conscription sparking school strikes. A stagnant economy, struggling car makers, migration and the threat from Russia dominate politics. Frank-Walter Steinmeier is president.
q: Which country did Otto von Bismarck unite in 1871?
Which country reunited on 3 October 1990, less than a year after its Wall fell?
Which country is the EU's largest economy, home to Volkswagen, BMW and Mercedes?

EST.t: For centuries Estonians were farmers under foreign rule: Danish and German knights, then Sweden, then from 1710 the Russian Empire, while a German nobility owned most of the land. As Russia collapsed in 1918 Estonia declared independence and won a war against the Red Army by 1920. In 1939 the secret deal between Hitler and Stalin placed it in the Soviet sphere, and the Soviet Union annexed it in 1940. Tens of thousands were deported to Siberia in 1941 and 1949, and many others fled west. German occupation came between, and the Soviets returned in 1944. Moscow then moved in Russian-speaking workers, who still make up about a quarter of the population. From 1987 the 'Singing Revolution' of mass song festivals helped Estonia win back independence in August 1991. It joined NATO and the European Union in 2004 and the euro in 2011. In 2007 it suffered one of the first big cyberattacks on a country, blamed on Russia.
EST.c: Estonia is one of the most digital countries in the world: Skype was developed here, almost all public services are online, and citizens can vote over the internet. Its Song and Dance Festival brings tens of thousands of singers together on one stage. Saunas, rye bread, berry picking in the forests and medieval Tallinn are part of life. Estonian is closely related to Finnish.
EST.p: Kristen Michal of the liberal Reform Party has been prime minister since July 2024. In March 2025 he dropped the Social Democrats and governed with the smaller Estonia 200 party, and in 2026 the coalition lost its majority. Tax rises to pay for defence against Russia have made the government unpopular. Parliament elected Ülle Madise, a legal scholar and former Chancellor of Justice, as president in September 2026, and she took office in October, succeeding Alar Karis. Security dominates: Estonia spends heavily on defence, and in March 2026 a Russian drone struck a power plant near Narva.
q: Which country's 'Singing Revolution' of mass song festivals helped it win back independence in 1991?
Which country suffered in 2007 one of the first big cyberattacks on a country, blamed on Russia?
Which country is so digital that Skype was developed there and citizens can vote over the internet?

LVA.t: German crusaders conquered the lands of the Latvians in the 1200s, and German barons owned most of the land for centuries while Poland, Sweden and then Russia ruled. Riga grew rich as a Hanseatic trading port. Latvia declared independence in November 1918 and won it after a war against both Soviet and German forces. The secret Hitler-Stalin pact of 1939 handed it to the Soviet Union, which annexed it in 1940 and deported thousands to Siberia. German occupation followed from 1941 to 1944, and most of Latvia's Jews were murdered. The Soviets returned, deported more people in 1949 and brought in Russian-speaking workers, so that by 1989 Latvians were barely half the population. In August 1989 about two million people from the three Baltic states joined hands in a human chain about 675 km long, the Baltic Way, and Latvia regained independence in 1991. It joined NATO and the European Union in 2004 and the euro in 2014.
LVA.c: Latvians have a tradition of short folk songs, dainas, with over a million collected, and a Song and Dance Festival that brings tens of thousands together. Riga has one of the world's best collections of Art Nouveau buildings. Midsummer, Jāņi, is the biggest holiday, with bonfires, oak-leaf crowns and caraway cheese. Basketball and ice hockey are the top sports.
LVA.p: Edgars Rinkēvičs has been president since 2023, the EU's first openly gay head of state. Prime Minister Evika Siliņa resigned in May 2026 after a coalition partner withdrew support, after a drone from Russia crashed in the town of Rēzekne. Andris Kulbergs of the United List, a businessman, became prime minister later that month, and his party won the most seats, 41 of 100, in the October 2026 election. Security dominates: drones from the Russian side have repeatedly crossed the border, and about a third of the people speak Russian at home. Low growth and emigration also worry voters.
q: Which country declared independence in November 1918 and grew rich through Riga, a Hanseatic trading port?
Which Baltic country was barely half made up of its own people by 1989, after Soviet deportations and Russian-speaking settlers?
Which country has collected over a million short folk songs called dainas and celebrates Midsummer as Jāņi?

NOR.t: Viking chiefs from Norway's fjords raided and settled across the North Atlantic, but from the late 1300s the country was ruled from Copenhagen for over 400 years. In 1814 Denmark had to hand it to Sweden; Norway quickly wrote its own constitution, signed on 17 May, but accepted the Swedish king. A peaceful vote ended the union in 1905, and Norway chose a Danish prince as King Haakon VII. It stayed neutral in World War I, but Germany invaded in April 1940. The king and government fled to London, while Vidkun Quisling's collaborator regime ruled at home; his name became a word for traitor. Scarred by occupation, Norway helped found NATO in 1949. Oil found in the North Sea in 1969 changed everything. Instead of spending the windfall, governments put it into a state fund that grew into the world's largest sovereign wealth fund. Norwegians twice voted against joining the European Union, in 1972 and 1994.
NOR.c: Norwegians love the outdoors: hiking and skiing at weekends, cabins called hytte, and a right to roam on almost anyone's land. On 17 May, Constitution Day, children's parades fill every town and people wear embroidered bunad costumes. Brown cheese, salmon and waffles are staples. Most new cars sold are electric, and the Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo every December. The Sámi people live in the far north.
NOR.p: Jonas Gahr Støre's Labour Party has governed since 2021 and kept power alone after the September 2025 election, with the anti-immigration Progress Party as the largest opposition. In 2025 Støre brought in former NATO chief Jens Stoltenberg as finance minister. In August 2026 King Harald V died after 35 years on the throne, and his son became King Haakon VIII. The oil fund raises hard questions, such as whether to sell shares in companies linked to Israel's occupation of the West Bank. High energy prices from the 2026 Iran war, a new US tariff, pro-Russian cyberattacks and the rape conviction of the crown princess's son have dominated the news.
q: Which country's wartime collaborator gave the world a word for traitor: Quisling?
Which country put its North Sea oil money into what became the world's largest sovereign wealth fund?
In which country is the Nobel Peace Prize awarded every December, and are most new cars sold electric?

SWE.t: In the 1600s Sweden was a great power, ruling Finland and much of the Baltic coast, until Russia defeated Charles XII in 1709. It lost Finland to Russia in 1809 and has not fought a war since 1814. Poverty drove over a million Swedes to emigrate, mostly to the United States, in the decades before 1914. Sweden stayed neutral in World War I. In World War II it was neutral again, but sold iron ore to Germany and let German troops cross by train, while also sheltering refugees, including Danish Jews, and its diplomat Raoul Wallenberg saved thousands of Jews in Budapest. The Social Democrats, in power for most of the 1900s, built a generous welfare state paid for by high taxes. During the Cold War Sweden stayed non-aligned but armed itself heavily. It joined the European Union in 1995 but kept its krona. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it gave up two centuries of neutrality and joined NATO in 2024.
SWE.c: ABBA, IKEA, Volvo, Spotify and the Nobel Prize are Swedish exports. Fika, a coffee break with cinnamon buns, is a daily ritual, and at Midsummer people dance round a maypole and eat pickled herring. Swedes value consensus, equality and long parental leave. The right to roam lets anyone walk and camp in the countryside, and many families have a red-painted summer cottage.
SWE.p: Ulf Kristersson's centre-right government, which relied on the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, ran Sweden from 2022 and toughened migration and crime laws after a wave of gang shootings and bombings. In the September 2026 election the opposition bloc of Social Democrats, Left, Centre and Greens won a narrow majority of 176 of 349 seats. Kristersson resigned and stays on as caretaker. In October parliament voted down the Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson as prime minister, and talks on a new government went on. Gang violence, integration, defence as a new NATO member and Russian threats in the Baltic dominate. King Carl XVI Gustaf is the longest-reigning monarch in Swedish history.
q: Which country has not fought a war since 1814?
Which country's diplomat Raoul Wallenberg saved thousands of Jews in Budapest?
Which country gave the world ABBA, IKEA, Volvo and Spotify?

FIN.t: Finland was part of Sweden for about 600 years, which is why Swedish is still an official language. Russia took it in 1809 and made it a grand duchy with its own laws, and in 1906 Finnish women became the first in Europe to win the vote. Finland declared independence in December 1917, during the Russian Revolution, and a short, bitter civil war between Reds and Whites followed in 1918. In the Winter War of 1939 and 1940 it held off a far larger Soviet invasion, though it lost about a tenth of its land, including Karelia, and over 400,000 people had to move. It then fought alongside Germany against the Soviet Union until 1944, but was never occupied. During the Cold War it stayed neutral and careful not to anger Moscow, a balancing act others called 'Finlandisation'. It joined the European Union in 1995 and the euro in 2002. Russia's full invasion of Ukraine pushed it to join NATO in 2023.
FIN.c: Finland has about three million saunas for 5.6 million people, and many Finns follow a sauna with a plunge into an icy lake. Its schools are admired worldwide, and Finns are known for valuing quiet and personal space. Nokia, Angry Birds, the Moomins and heavy metal bands are Finnish exports. Midsummer at lakeside cottages under the midnight sun is the high point of the year.
FIN.p: Petteri Orpo of the centre-right National Coalition has been prime minister since 2023, leading a coalition that includes the nationalist Finns Party. His government has cut spending and welfare to reduce debt, sparking large strikes, while unemployment rose to the highest in the European Union by mid-2026. Alexander Stubb, a former prime minister, has been president since 2024. Finland closed its border crossings with Russia in late 2023 after accusing Moscow of pushing migrants across, and in 2026 parliament eased long-standing limits on moving nuclear weapons through the country to fit its NATO role.
q: Which country held off a far larger Soviet invasion in the Winter War of 1939 and 1940?
Which country's women became in 1906 the first in Europe to win the vote?
Which country has about three million saunas and gave the world Nokia, Angry Birds and the Moomins?

VNM.t: Vietnam spent about a thousand years under Chinese rule and centuries more resisting it, while expanding south along the coast to the Mekong Delta. France conquered the country between 1858 and 1885 and made it part of French Indochina, with rubber plantations and heavy taxes. Japan occupied it in World War II, and when Japan surrendered in 1945, Ho Chi Minh's communist-led Viet Minh declared independence in Hanoi. France fought to return but lost at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, and a peace conference in Geneva split the country into a communist North and an anti-communist South. Fearing that communism would spread across Asia, the US backed the South and from 1965 sent hundreds of thousands of troops. The Vietnam War killed millions of Vietnamese and about 58,000 Americans. Northern tanks entered Saigon in April 1975, and the country was formally reunited in 1976. After years of poverty, the Doi Moi reforms of 1986 opened it to markets while the Communist Party kept power.
VNM.c: Motorbikes fill the streets of Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, the former Saigon, and people eat pho, banh mi and fresh spring rolls on tiny plastic stools on the pavement. Vietnamese is written in Latin letters with many accents. It is the world's second-largest coffee producer, famous for strong iced coffee with condensed milk, and Tet, the lunar new year, is the biggest holiday.
VNM.p: Vietnam is a one-party communist state. Tô Lâm, a former police minister whose anti-corruption campaign brought down two state presidents, became party leader in 2024. The party congress re-elected him in January 2026, and in April he also became state president, combining the two top jobs as in China. Lê Minh Hưng is prime minister. The government has merged its 63 provinces into 34 and cut the civil service. Factories moving from China have made Vietnam a big exporter to the US, so American tariffs are a major worry, as are typhoons and floods.
q: Which country defeated France at Dien Bien Phu in 1954?
Which country was formally reunited in 1976 after northern tanks entered Saigon?
Which country is the world's second-largest coffee producer, famous for pho and banh mi?

KHM.t: From the 800s to the 1400s the Khmer Empire ruled much of mainland Southeast Asia from Angkor, where it built Angkor Wat in the 1100s. Squeezed for centuries afterwards between Thailand and Vietnam, Cambodia accepted French protection in 1863 and became part of French Indochina. King Norodom Sihanouk won independence in 1953 and tried to keep Cambodia neutral in the Vietnam War, but North Vietnamese supply lines ran through its east, and the US bombed them heavily. In 1970 a US-backed general, Lon Nol, overthrew Sihanouk. Civil war followed, and in 1975 the communist Khmer Rouge under Pol Pot took Phnom Penh. They emptied the cities and forced people into rural labour camps, and from 1975 to 1979 about a quarter of the population died from execution, starvation and disease. Vietnam invaded in 1979, drove them out and occupied the country for a decade. A UN-run election in 1993 restored the monarchy, and Hun Sen, a former Khmer Rouge commander, dominated politics for almost 40 years.
KHM.c: Most Cambodians are Theravada Buddhists, and saffron-robed monks are part of everyday life. Angkor Wat appears on the national flag and draws millions of visitors. Khmer classical dance, almost wiped out under the Khmer Rouge, has been revived. Fish amok, steamed in banana leaves with coconut and spices, is the national dish, and the Water Festival brings long-boat races to Phnom Penh's riverfront.
KHM.p: Hun Sen handed the premiership to his son Hun Manet in 2023, after an election from which the main opposition party was barred, and he remains Senate president and the power behind the ruling Cambodian People's Party. A border dispute with Thailand erupted into fighting in July 2025, killing dozens and forcing hundreds of thousands from their homes; it flared again in December before a new ceasefire, and Cambodia brought in conscription in 2026. The country is also under pressure over huge online scam compounds run by criminal gangs, and in January 2026 Chen Zhi, founder of the Prince Group, was sent to China to face charges.
q: Which country did the Khmer Rouge under Pol Pot rule from 1975 to 1979, when about a quarter of the population died?
Which country's Khmer Empire built Angkor Wat in the 1100s?
Which country has a temple on its national flag?

LUX.t: Luxembourg grew from a castle founded in 963, and its fortress was so strong that it was called the Gibraltar of the North. From 1815 it was a grand duchy ruled by the Dutch king, and it lost its French-speaking western half to Belgium in 1839. In 1867 the great powers guaranteed its neutrality and had the fortress torn down, and in 1890 it got its own ruling family. Germany occupied it in World War I, and in World War II invaded again, annexed it and forced young men into the German army, which led to a general strike in 1942. Grand Duchess Charlotte led resistance from exile in London, and the Battle of the Bulge raged in the north in 1944 and 1945. After the war Luxembourg gave up neutrality, joined NATO in 1949 and helped found the European communities. Steel made it rich, and when that industry declined in the 1970s, banking and investment funds took over.
LUX.c: Luxembourgish, French and German are all official, and almost half the people are foreign nationals, with many Portuguese. Every day about 200,000 workers commute in from France, Belgium and Germany. It has one of the highest incomes in the world and made all public transport free in 2020. The capital's old town perches on cliffs above deep river gorges.
LUX.p: Luc Frieden of the Christian Social People's Party has been prime minister since 2023, in a coalition with the liberal Democratic Party. Guillaume V became Grand Duke in October 2025 when his father, Henri, abdicated after 25 years. A row with the trade unions led the labour minister to resign in December 2025. Luxembourg hosts EU institutions, including the European Court of Justice. Housing costs, among the highest in Europe, and the economy's heavy reliance on finance and cross-border workers are the main concerns.
q: Which country grew from a castle founded in 963, with a fortress called the Gibraltar of the North?
Which country made all public transport free in 2020?
Which country has about 200,000 workers commuting in every day from France, Belgium and Germany?

ARE.t: Bedouin tribes, fishermen and pearl divers lived along this stretch of the Gulf coast for centuries. In the 1800s Britain, wanting to protect its shipping route to India, signed treaties with the local sheikhs, and the area became known as the Trucial States. The collapse of the pearl trade in the 1930s brought hard times. Oil was found in Abu Dhabi in 1958, and exports began in 1962. When Britain announced it would leave the Gulf, Sheikh Zayed of Abu Dhabi and Sheikh Rashid of Dubai led talks on a federation, and six emirates formed the United Arab Emirates in December 1971; Ras al-Khaimah joined early in 1972. Zayed served as president until his death in 2004, sharing oil money across the emirates. Dubai, with little oil, made itself a hub for trade and travel, with free zones, the Emirates airline and, from 2010, the Burj Khalifa. Millions of foreign workers came to build the new cities.
ARE.c: Nearly nine in ten residents are foreigners, especially from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and the Philippines, so English and Hindi are heard as often as Arabic. Dubai's Burj Khalifa is the world's tallest building, and its malls, indoor ski slope and desert safaris draw tourists. Emiratis keep traditions alive with falconry, camel racing, the white kandura robe and Arabic coffee served with dates.
ARE.p: The UAE is a federation of hereditary monarchies. Mohamed bin Zayed of Abu Dhabi has been president since 2022, and Mohammed bin Rashid, ruler of Dubai, is prime minister. The UAE recognised Israel in 2020 and has been accused, including by UN experts and Sudan's army, of arming the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan's war, which it denies. A rift with Saudi Arabia over Yemen led it to announce the withdrawal of its last forces at the end of 2025. In the 2026 Iran war, Iranian missiles and drones hit Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Fujairah, and in May 2026 the UAE left OPEC.
q: Which country was formed by six sheikhdoms in December 1971, led by Sheikh Zayed and Sheikh Rashid?
Which country was known as the Trucial States under its 1800s treaties with Britain?
Which country has the Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building?

BEL.t: Belgium broke away from the Netherlands in 1830, and Britain and the other powers guaranteed its neutrality. Its king Leopold II ran the Congo as a private colony from 1885, where forced labour for rubber killed huge numbers of people. The scandal forced Belgium to take over the Congo in 1908, and it ruled it until 1960. When Germany invaded in 1914 to reach France, Britain went to war to defend Belgian neutrality. The fields of Flanders, around Ypres, saw years of trench warfare, and poison gas was first used on a large scale there in 1915. Germany invaded again in 1940, and the Battle of the Bulge was fought in the Ardennes in 1944. After the war Belgium helped found the European communities, and Brussels became home to the European Union and NATO. Tension between Dutch speakers and French speakers turned it into a federal state in 1993.
BEL.c: Belgium is split between Dutch-speaking Flanders and French-speaking Wallonia, with a small German-speaking area and bilingual Brussels. It is famous for chocolate, waffles, fries with mayonnaise and hundreds of beers, some brewed by monks. Comics such as Tintin and The Smurfs are Belgian, and cycling is a national passion, with cobbled spring races that draw huge crowds.
BEL.p: Bart De Wever, long the leader of a Flemish nationalist party, became prime minister in February 2025 at the head of a five-party coalition. His government is cutting spending and reforming pensions, which has brought repeated national strikes and a union march in Brussels in October 2026. The Brussels region went a record 20 months without a government before one formed in 2026. Belgium also resisted EU plans to use Russian central bank money frozen at the Euroclear clearing house in Brussels, fearing it would be left liable, and in December 2025 EU leaders chose joint borrowing instead. King Philippe is head of state.
q: Which country's king, Leopold II, ran the Congo as a private colony from 1885?
Which country broke away from the Netherlands in 1830?
Which country gave the world Tintin and The Smurfs?

GEO.t: Georgia became Christian in the 4th century, and its medieval kingdom peaked under Queen Tamar around 1200. Squeezed between the Persian and Ottoman empires, it turned to Orthodox Russia, which annexed it in 1801. After the 1917 revolution Georgia set up an independent democratic republic, but the Red Army invaded in 1921. Stalin, the Soviet dictator, was a Georgian from the town of Gori. On 9 April 1989 Soviet troops killed peaceful protesters in Tbilisi, and Georgia declared independence in 1991. Civil war followed, and Abkhazia and South Ossetia broke away with Russian help. The 2003 Rose Revolution brought Mikheil Saakashvili to power; he fought corruption and pushed for NATO membership. In August 2008 Russia fought a five-day war with Georgia and then recognised both breakaway regions as independent; most countries still regard them as part of Georgia. In 2012 the Georgian Dream party of the billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, who made his fortune in Russia, won power.
GEO.c: Georgia may be the birthplace of wine, made here for 8,000 years in clay jars called qvevri, buried in the ground. It has its own alphabet and a deeply Orthodox Christian culture. Supra feasts, led by a toastmaster called the tamada, bring out khachapuri cheese bread and khinkali dumplings. Polyphonic folk singing, rugby and the mountain villages of Svaneti, with their stone towers, are national prides.
GEO.p: Georgian Dream, founded by Bidzina Ivanishvili, has ruled since 2012 and has turned sharply away from the West. It passed a 'foreign agents' law that critics compare to Russia's, won the disputed October 2024 election, and then suspended its bid to join the EU, sparking months of nightly protests. Opposition leaders have been jailed. Mikheil Kavelashvili was chosen president by an electoral college the opposition boycotted, and Irakli Kobakhidze is prime minister. In 2026 the EU suspended visa-free travel for Georgian officials. Georgia and most countries regard Abkhazia and South Ossetia, about a fifth of its territory, as occupied by Russia.
q: Which country's medieval kingdom peaked under Queen Tamar around 1200?
Which country fought a five-day war with Russia in August 2008 over Abkhazia and South Ossetia?
Which country may be the birthplace of wine, made for 8,000 years in clay jars called qvevri?

MKD.t: For five centuries the region was part of the Ottoman Empire, and its mix of Slavs, Albanians, Greeks, Turks, Vlachs and Jews made it a prize every neighbour wanted. The Ilinden Uprising of 1903 against Ottoman rule was crushed. In the Balkan Wars of 1912–13 Greece, Serbia and Bulgaria divided the wider region of Macedonia, and this northern part went to Serbia, then to Yugoslavia. Bulgaria occupied much of it in both world wars, and in 1943 the Jews of Skopje and Bitola were deported to Treblinka. In 1944 Tito's Partisans created a Macedonian republic within Yugoslavia, with its own language. It left peacefully in 1991. Greece, which has its own region called Macedonia, objected to the name, so the country joined the UN as 'the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia'. In 2001 a short Albanian insurgency ended with the Ohrid Agreement, giving Albanians more rights. The 2018 Prespa Agreement with Greece renamed the country North Macedonia in 2019, and it joined NATO in 2020.
MKD.c: Macedonian is a Slavic language written in Cyrillic, close to Bulgarian, and about a quarter of the people are Albanians, most of them Muslim. Lake Ohrid, with its Byzantine churches, is the country's jewel. Skopje is crowded with giant statues and neo-classical buildings put up in the 2010s. Tavče gravče, baked beans, ajvar pepper relish and strong rakija are on most tables. Mother Teresa was born in Skopje.
MKD.p: The nationalist VMRO-DPMNE swept back to power in 2024: Hristijan Mickoski became prime minister, and Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova became the first woman president, pointedly calling the country 'Macedonia' at her swearing-in. EU membership talks are stuck because Bulgaria demands that the constitution recognise a Bulgarian minority, which Mickoski's government has refused to do. In March 2025 a fire at a nightclub in Kočani killed about 60 young people and set off protests over corruption, since the club had been operating without a valid licence. VMRO-DPMNE won most municipalities, including Skopje, in the 2025 local elections.
q: Which country's name was changed by the 2018 Prespa Agreement with Greece?
Which country's 2001 Albanian insurgency ended with the Ohrid Agreement?
Which country was Mother Teresa born in, and has Lake Ohrid with its Byzantine churches?

ALB.t: Albania was ruled by the Ottoman Empire for more than 400 years and declared independence at Vlorë in 1912, during the Balkan Wars that came just before World War I. The great powers drew its borders and left many Albanians outside them, above all in Kosovo. A weak kingdom under King Zog fell to Mussolini's Italy in 1939. Communist partisans led by Enver Hoxha took power in 1944 and built one of the world's harshest dictatorships. Hoxha broke with Yugoslavia in 1948, with the Soviet Union in 1961 and with China in 1978, leaving Albania almost totally isolated. In 1967 he banned religion and declared the first atheist state. When communism fell in 1991, thousands fled on crowded ships to Italy. The collapse of huge pyramid savings schemes in 1997 tipped the country into chaos. Albania joined NATO in 2009 and became a candidate to join the European Union in 2014.
ALB.c: Hoxha built over 170,000 concrete bunkers, and many still dot fields and beaches. Albania is majority Muslim but famously relaxed about religion, and the code of honour called besa led families to shelter Jews during World War II. People nod to mean no and shake their heads to mean yes. The southern coast, with Ksamil's beaches and the ruins of Butrint, now draws millions of tourists.
ALB.p: Edi Rama, a former artist and basketball player, has been prime minister since 2013. His Socialist Party won a fourth straight election in May 2025, and in September 2025 he made headlines by appointing Diella, an AI-generated character, as a 'minister' overseeing public tenders. The opposition Democratic Party of Sali Berisha, himself a former president and prime minister, calls the government corrupt, and its protests in Tirana in early 2026 led to clashes with police. The main issues are corruption, emigration of young people, and the long road to the European Union.
q: Which country declared independence at Vlorë in 1912 after more than 400 years of Ottoman rule?
Which country did Enver Hoxha cut off from almost the whole world, declaring the first atheist state in 1967?
Which country is still dotted with concrete bunkers, over 170,000 of them built under its communist ruler?

AZE.t: Azerbaijanis are a Turkic people, most of them Shia Muslims, whose lands were split between Persia and Russia in 1828; many more Azerbaijanis live in northern Iran today. In the late 1800s Baku became one of the world's first oil boom towns, and the Nobel brothers made fortunes there. In 1918 Azerbaijan declared one of the first democratic republics in the Muslim world, giving women the vote, but the Red Army conquered it in 1920. Baku's oil fuelled the Soviet war effort in World War II, and Hitler's drive into the Caucasus aimed at it. As the Soviet Union weakened, Armenians in Nagorno-Karabakh demanded to join Armenia; in January 1990 Soviet troops killed more than a hundred people in Baku. Azerbaijan became independent in 1991 but lost Karabakh and surrounding districts in a war that displaced hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijanis. Heydar Aliyev took power in 1993 and signed deals with Western oil companies. His son Ilham succeeded him in 2003, and oil money paid for an army that retook the territory in 2020 and 2023.
AZE.c: Baku mixes a walled old city, oil-boom mansions and the glass Flame Towers. The country is officially secular, and its language is close to Turkish. Mugham music, carpet weaving and plov rice dishes are cherished, and Novruz, the spring new year, is the biggest holiday, with bonfires and sweet pastries. Baku also hosts a Formula One race through its streets.
AZE.p: Ilham Aliyev has ruled since 2003, after his father, and won a fifth term in 2024 in an election without real competition; Ali Asadov is prime minister. Since retaking Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023, Azerbaijan has been rebuilding the region and resettling Azerbaijanis displaced in the 1990s. In August 2025 it initialled a peace deal with Armenia at the White House, including a US-backed route to its exclave of Nakhchivan, but it wants Armenia to change its constitution before signing. Relations with Russia soured after Russian air defences shot down an Azerbaijani airliner in 2024. Rights groups say dozens of journalists and activists have been jailed in a broad crackdown.
q: Which country declared in 1918 one of the first democratic republics in the Muslim world, giving women the vote?
Which country's capital became one of the world's first oil boom towns, where the Nobel brothers made fortunes?
Which country celebrates Novruz as its biggest holiday and hosts a Formula One race past its Flame Towers?

UNK.t: For Serbs, Kosovo is holy ground: the site of a famous battle against the Ottomans in 1389 and of medieval Orthodox monasteries. Over the centuries of Ottoman rule, however, Albanians became the majority. Serbia took the region in the Balkan Wars of 1912, and it became part of Yugoslavia. Tito gave it wide autonomy in 1974, but Slobodan Milošević, rising on Serb nationalism, stripped this away in 1989. Albanians then ran a peaceful parallel state under Ibrahim Rugova, until the Kosovo Liberation Army took up arms. In 1998 and 1999 a Serbian crackdown killed thousands and drove hundreds of thousands of Albanians from their homes. NATO bombed Serbia for 78 days in 1999, forcing its forces out, and the UN took over Kosovo's administration with NATO peacekeepers. Kosovo declared independence in 2008. It is recognised by about 100 countries, including the United States and most of the European Union, but not by Serbia, Russia or China. In 2010 the UN's top court said the declaration did not break international law.
UNK.c: Most people are Albanian-speaking Muslims, though religion is worn lightly, and Kosovo has one of Europe's youngest populations. The US is wildly popular here, and Pristina has a statue of Bill Clinton. Macchiato coffee culture fills the cafés. Medieval Serbian Orthodox monasteries such as Dečani are on UNESCO's heritage list, and a Serb minority lives mainly in the north.
UNK.p: Albin Kurti of Vetëvendosje (Self-Determination) has been prime minister since 2021. After a February 2025 election left parliament deadlocked, a repeat vote in December let Kurti form a government in February 2026. Parliament then failed to elect a president, triggering another election in June 2026, and in October 2026, after months with only an acting president, it finally chose the economist Justina Shiroka Pula to succeed Vjosa Osmani. In September 2026 a special court in The Hague sentenced former president Hashim Thaçi to 25 years for war crimes. Tensions with Serbia and the Serb-majority north slow progress towards the EU.
q: Which country declared independence in 2008 after NATO bombed Serbia for 78 days in 1999?
For which country did Ibrahim Rugova run a peaceful parallel state in the 1990s?
Which country has a statue of Bill Clinton in its capital and one of Europe's youngest populations?

TUR.t: From 1453, when it captured Constantinople, the Ottoman Empire ruled the Balkans, the Middle East and North Africa from Istanbul. By the 1800s it was shrinking, and in 1914 it joined World War I on Germany's side. During the war the government deported and killed about a million or more Armenians, in what most historians call a genocide; Turkey rejects the term. Defeat in 1918 left Allied armies occupying Istanbul and Greece invading Anatolia. Mustafa Kemal, later named Atatürk, led a war of independence and founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923, with Ankara as its capital. He abolished the caliphate, gave women the vote, replaced Arabic script with the Latin alphabet and made the state secular. Turkey stayed out of World War II until its final months, joined NATO in 1952 and guarded NATO's south-eastern flank against the Soviet Union. The army staged coups in 1960, 1971 and 1980. In 1974, after a Greek-backed coup in Cyprus, Turkey invaded the island's north. From 2003 Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's AKP gave religious conservatives power.
TUR.c: Istanbul spans Europe and Asia across the Bosphorus, with Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque on its skyline. Most Turks are Muslim, but secular and religious lifestyles sit side by side. Tea is drunk all day from tulip-shaped glasses, and kebabs, meze, baklava and Turkish coffee are famous everywhere. Turkish TV dramas are watched around the world, and Atatürk's portrait still hangs in shops and offices.
TUR.p: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, prime minister from 2003 and president since 2014, won re-election in 2023. His main rival, Istanbul's mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, was arrested in March 2025 on corruption charges that his supporters call political, setting off the biggest protests in a decade. In 2026 a court removed Özgür Özel as leader of the main opposition party, the CHP, by annulling its 2023 congress. A peace process with the Kurdish militant group PKK, which announced its dissolution in 2025, has led to an amnesty law for fighters who give up their weapons. Inflation, which peaked above 80% in 2022, still squeezes families.
q: Which country was founded in 1923 by Mustafa Kemal, later named Atatürk?
Which country replaced Arabic script with the Latin alphabet and abolished the caliphate?
Which country's largest city spans Europe and Asia across the Bosphorus?

ESP.t: Spain was united by the marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella, who completed the conquest of Muslim Granada in 1492, the same year Columbus reached the Americas. Gold and silver from the New World built one of the first global empires, but most of Latin America broke away in the 1820s, and in 1898 the United States took Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines. Spain stayed neutral in World War I. In 1936 General Francisco Franco rose against the elected republic, and the civil war that followed, with Germany and Italy backing Franco and the Soviet Union helping the republic, was a rehearsal for World War II. Franco won in 1939 and ruled as a dictator until his death in 1975, suppressing regional languages. King Juan Carlos then helped lead a peaceful transition to democracy, and a 1981 coup attempt failed. Spain joined NATO in 1982 and the European Community in 1986. The Basque separatist group ETA killed more than 800 people before ending its campaign in 2011.
ESP.c: Spaniards eat late, with lunch around two and dinner after nine, and life spills into streets and bars for tapas. Catalan, Basque and Galician are spoken alongside Spanish, with strong regional identities. Flamenco, paella, jamón, fiestas like Pamplona's running of the bulls and Valencia's Fallas, and the rivalry between Real Madrid and Barcelona are famous worldwide. Spain is one of the world's most visited countries.
ESP.p: Pedro Sánchez of the Socialist Workers' Party has been prime minister since 2018, kept in office after the inconclusive 2023 election by a fragile alliance with left-wing parties and Catalan and Basque nationalists. An amnesty for Catalan separatists and corruption cases touching his party and family fed opposition anger. Spain's economy has been one of Europe's fastest-growing, but a housing crisis has sparked mass protests. In 2026 Sánchez refused to let US forces use Spanish bases against Iran. In October 2026, after Congress rejected his housing legislation, he called a snap general election for 29 November. King Felipe VI is head of state.
q: Which country's monarchs completed the conquest of Granada in 1492, the year Columbus reached the Americas?
Which country was ruled by Francisco Franco as a dictator from 1939 until 1975?
Which country is known for flamenco, paella, tapas and the running of the bulls in Pamplona?

LAO.t: The kingdom of Lan Xang, the 'land of a million elephants', was founded in the 1300s and became a centre of Theravada Buddhism. It later split into rival kingdoms that fell under Thai control. In 1893 France forced Siam to give up the land east of the Mekong and joined Laos to French Indochina, making the river the border with Thailand. Japan occupied it late in World War II, and it gained full independence as a kingdom in 1953. Laos was then pulled into the Vietnam War. The communist Pathet Lao, backed by North Vietnam, fought the royal government, and the Ho Chi Minh Trail ran through the east. From 1964 to 1973 the US secretly bombed the country, dropping more than two million tonnes of bombs and making Laos the most heavily bombed country per person in history. It also armed Hmong fighters. In 1975 the Pathet Lao abolished the monarchy and set up a one-party communist state, and many Hmong fled abroad.
LAO.c: Laos is mostly rural and Buddhist, and at dawn in Luang Prabang lines of saffron-robed monks collect alms of sticky rice, which is eaten with almost every meal. Larb, a minced meat salad with herbs and lime, is the national dish. The Mekong River shapes daily life, and the golden That Luang stupa in Vientiane is the national symbol. Unexploded bombs still kill and injure people in the countryside.
LAO.p: The Lao People's Revolutionary Party has ruled alone since 1975, and there is no legal opposition. Thongloun Sisoulith is party leader and president. After a National Assembly election in February 2026, Saleumxay Kommasith, a former foreign minister, became prime minister in October 2026, taking over from Sonexay Siphandone. The economy is the main worry: Laos borrowed heavily from China for dams and for the railway to Kunming, opened in 2021, and its debts, a weak currency and high inflation have squeezed living standards. Many young people work in Thailand, and scam centres near the Golden Triangle have drawn international criticism.
q: Which country was the 'land of a million elephants', the kingdom of Lan Xang?
Which country did the US secretly bomb from 1964 to 1973, making it the most heavily bombed country per person in history?
In which country's town of Luang Prabang do monks collect alms of sticky rice at dawn?

KGZ.t: Kyrgyz herders lived for centuries in the Tian Shan mountains, on a branch of the Silk Road. In the 1800s the Kokand khanate and then the Russian Empire took control, and Russian settlers moved onto the best land. When the Kyrgyz rose up in 1916 against being drafted for wartime labour, Russian troops crushed the revolt, and tens of thousands fled to China. Under Soviet rule nomads were forced onto collective farms, and in the 1920s and 1930s planners drew borders through the Fergana Valley that left Uzbek and Tajik enclaves inside Kyrgyzstan and Kyrgyz villages in its neighbours. Kyrgyzstan became independent in 1991 when the Soviet Union collapsed. Askar Akayev was at first seen as the most democratic leader in Central Asia, but street protests toppled him in 2005, his successor in 2010 and another president in 2020. In 2010 ethnic clashes around Osh killed hundreds of people, most of them Uzbeks. Rivalry between the north and the south still shapes politics.
KGZ.c: Nomadic traditions live on in yurts on summer pastures, in horse games such as kok-boru, a kind of polo played with a goat carcass, and in the Manas, an epic poem recited by specialist storytellers. Kymyz, fermented mare's milk, and beshbarmak, boiled meat with noodles, are favourites. Russian is still widely spoken, and many young people work in Russia and send money home.
KGZ.p: Sadyr Japarov, freed from prison by protesters in 2020, became president in 2021 and has concentrated power under a new constitution. His long-time ally Kamchybek Tashiev, the security chief who led a hard-line anti-corruption drive, was dismissed in February 2026 and charged in April with plotting to seize power. Independent media such as Kloop and Temirov Live have been banned or prosecuted. A snap parliamentary election was held in November 2025. In 2025 Kyrgyzstan settled its long, sometimes deadly border dispute with Tajikistan. Money sent home from Russia is vital to the economy, and Western governments watch for trade that helps Russia evade sanctions.
q: Which country saw street protests topple presidents in 2005, 2010 and 2020?
Which country saw ethnic clashes around Osh in 2010 that killed hundreds, most of them Uzbeks?
In which country do specialist storytellers recite the Manas, an epic poem?

ARM.t: Armenians have lived around Mount Ararat for nearly 3,000 years, and in 301 AD Armenia became the first kingdom to adopt Christianity as its state religion. For centuries its lands were divided between the Persian and Ottoman empires, and Russia took the eastern part in 1828. During World War I the Ottoman government deported and killed about 1.5 million Armenians, in what Armenia and most historians call a genocide; Turkey rejects the term. A short-lived Armenian republic was absorbed into the Soviet Union in 1920, and Soviet rulers placed Nagorno-Karabakh, an Armenian-majority region, inside Soviet Azerbaijan. As Soviet control weakened in 1988, its Armenians demanded to join Armenia, and the same year an earthquake at Spitak killed at least 25,000 people. Armenia became independent in 1991 and won a war over Karabakh by 1994, also taking surrounding Azerbaijani lands. Azerbaijan, richer from oil, struck back: in 2020 it retook much of the territory, and in 2023 it seized the rest, and nearly all of Karabakh's 100,000 Armenians fled.
ARM.c: Armenia has its own alphabet, created in 405 AD, and its own ancient church. Far more Armenians live abroad than at home, in Russia, the US, France and Lebanon, and celebrities from Charles Aznavour to Kim Kardashian have Armenian roots. Lavash flatbread, apricots, brandy and grilled khorovats are national pride, and Mount Ararat, across the border in Turkey, is the national symbol. Chess is taught in schools.
ARM.p: Nikol Pashinyan, who came to power in the peaceful 'Velvet Revolution' of 2018, has steered Armenia away from Russia, which did not defend it in 2023. In August 2025, at a meeting hosted by Donald Trump, Armenia and Azerbaijan initialled a peace agreement that includes a US-backed transit route across southern Armenia. Pashinyan's Civil Contract won the June 2026 election with about half the vote, ahead of the new Strong Armenia party of the Russian-Armenian billionaire Samvel Karapetyan, who called the vote rigged. Azerbaijan wants Armenia to change its constitution before signing the treaty. A bitter feud with the Armenian Church and moves towards the EU also divide opinion.
q: Which became in 301 AD the first kingdom to adopt Christianity as its state religion?
Which country won a war over Nagorno-Karabakh by 1994, then lost the region in 2020 and 2023?
Which country has its own alphabet created in 405 AD, and far more of its people living abroad than at home?

DNK.t: Denmark is one of the world's oldest kingdoms, and the Vikings sailed from here. It once led a union of all Scandinavia, but lost Norway in 1814 and the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein to Prussia and Austria in 1864, which turned it into a small, cautious nation. It stayed neutral in World War I and won back northern Schleswig in a 1920 vote. Germany occupied it in April 1940 almost without a fight, but resistance grew, and in October 1943 Danes ferried almost all of the country's 7,000 or so Jews to safety in neutral Sweden. Iceland broke away in 1944. After the war Denmark gave up neutrality to help found NATO in 1949, and it joined the European communities in 1973, though voters later refused the euro. It built one of the world's most generous welfare states. Greenland and the Faroe Islands remain part of the kingdom but govern themselves.
DNK.c: Danes rank among the world's happiest people and talk of 'hygge', a cosy sense of togetherness with candles and friends. Copenhagen is full of cyclists, and open sandwiches called smørrebrød are a lunchtime staple. LEGO, Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tales, wind turbines and New Nordic cooking all come from Denmark. Danes pay high taxes and trust their government more than most.
DNK.p: Mette Frederiksen, Social Democrat prime minister since 2019, kept power after the March 2026 election even though her party had its weakest result in over a century. In June 2026 she formed a minority government with the Green Left, the Moderates and the Social Liberals. Frederik X became king in January 2024 after his mother abdicated. The biggest issue has been US President Donald Trump's push to take over Greenland, which drew mass protests and European support for Denmark until the two countries agreed on security guarantees for Greenland in September 2026. Defence, immigration and living costs also matter.
q: Which country ferried almost all of its 7,000 or so Jews to safety in Sweden in October 1943?
Which kingdom still includes Greenland and the Faroe Islands, which govern themselves?
Which country gave the world LEGO and Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tales?

LBY.t: For more than three centuries Libya's coastal towns, Tripoli and Benghazi among them, were part of the Ottoman Empire. Italy invaded in 1911, and its conquest of the interior was brutal: tens of thousands of people died in desert camps in the early 1930s, and the resistance hero Omar Mukhtar was hanged in 1931. In World War II the coast became a battlefield where Rommel's Afrika Korps fought the British around Tobruk. After the war the UN steered Libya to independence in 1951 as a kingdom under King Idris, the first African country to gain independence through the UN. Oil was found in 1959 and made it rich. In 1969 a young officer, Muammar Gaddafi, overthrew the king. He ruled for 42 years, backed militant groups abroad, was blamed for the 1988 Lockerbie bombing and faced years of Western sanctions. In 2011 an uprising, helped by NATO air strikes, toppled and killed him. Militias filled the vacuum, and from 2014 the country split between rival governments in the west and the east.
LBY.c: Arabic is the official language, and Amazigh (Berber) communities live in the western mountains, with Tuareg in the far south. Most people live along the coast, since most of the land is desert. Bazin, a dome of barley dough served with stew, and couscous are favourite dishes, and mint tea is everywhere. Libya has Africa's largest proven oil reserves, and the Roman cities of Leptis Magna and Sabratha are among the best preserved in the Mediterranean.
LBY.p: Libya still has two rival governments. In Tripoli, Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh leads the UN-recognised Government of National Unity, alongside Mohamed al-Menfi, chairman of the Presidential Council; both were chosen through UN-led talks in 2021. The east and much of the south are run by a rival government backed by the military commander Khalifa Haftar. Elections planned for 2021 never happened. Militia clashes shook Tripoli in May 2025, and Saif al-Islam Gaddafi, the old dictator's son, was shot dead in February 2026. Shipwrecks of migrants heading for Europe kill hundreds off its coast every year.
q: Which country did Italy invade in 1911, hanging the resistance hero Omar Mukhtar in 1931?
Which country did Muammar Gaddafi rule for 42 years until he was toppled in 2011?
Which country has Africa's largest proven oil reserves and the Roman city of Leptis Magna?

TUN.t: Phoenicians founded Carthage near today's Tunis, and it rivalled Rome until the Romans destroyed it in 146 BC. Arabs brought Islam in the 600s, and Kairouan became a great religious centre. The Ottomans ruled from the 1500s, and France made Tunisia a protectorate in 1881. In World War II German and Italian forces made their last stand in North Africa here before surrendering in May 1943. Habib Bourguiba's Neo-Destour party led the independence movement, and Tunisia became independent in 1956. As president, Bourguiba banned polygamy, gave women the right to divorce and spread free schooling, making it one of the most secular states in the Arab world. In 1987 Zine El Abidine Ben Ali pushed the ageing Bourguiba aside and ruled through a police state. In December 2010 a street vendor, Mohamed Bouazizi, set himself on fire, and the protests that followed drove Ben Ali out in January 2011, starting the Arab Spring. Tunisia became its only lasting democracy, for a decade.
TUN.c: Arabic is official, Tunisian Arabic is spoken day to day, and French is widely used. Harissa, couscous and brik, a crisp pastry with an egg inside, are staples, and olive oil is a major export. Many Europeans holiday on its beaches and the island of Djerba. The Tunisian desert was the filming location for Luke Skywalker's home planet in Star Wars, and Sidi Bou Said is famous for its white walls and blue doors.
TUN.p: Kais Saied, a law professor elected in 2019, suspended parliament in July 2021, rewrote the constitution and now rules with sweeping powers; opponents call it a coup. He won re-election in 2024 after rivals were jailed or barred. Sara Zaafarani has been prime minister since 2025. Dozens of opposition figures, journalists and lawyers have been jailed, and in 2026 the Islamist leader Rached Ghannouchi was sentenced to life. The economy is weak, with shortages and power cuts, and Saied has rejected IMF loan conditions. Tunisia is a main route for migrants heading to Italy. In October 2026 thousands marched against him, the largest protest in years.
q: Which country's ancient city of Carthage rivalled Rome until it was destroyed in 146 BC?
Which country's street vendor Mohamed Bouazizi set himself on fire in 2010, starting the Arab Spring?
Which country's desert was the filming location for Luke Skywalker's home planet in Star Wars?

ROU.t: Romanian is a Latin language, a legacy of Roman rule, but for centuries Romanians lived divided between Wallachia and Moldavia, under Ottoman overlordship, and Transylvania, under Hungary. The two principalities united in 1859 and won full independence in 1878. Romania joined World War I on the Allied side in 1916 and was largely overrun, but when the empires collapsed in 1918 it gained Transylvania, Bessarabia and Bukovina, doubling in size. In 1940 it lost much of that land, and under the dictator Ion Antonescu it fought alongside Nazi Germany against the Soviet Union; hundreds of thousands of Jews and Roma were killed. Romania switched sides in 1944, and the Soviets installed a communist regime. Nicolae Ceaușescu, in power from 1965, sometimes defied Moscow but impoverished his people to pay off foreign debt. In December 1989 a revolt that began in Timișoara overthrew him, and he was executed. Romania joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007.
ROU.c: Most Romanians are Orthodox Christians, and the painted monasteries of Bucovina and wooden churches of Maramureș are treasures. Sarmale, cabbage rolls, and mămăligă, maize porridge, are comfort food, and țuică plum brandy is offered to guests. Transylvania's castles feed the Dracula legend, inspired by the 15th-century prince Vlad the Impaler. Millions of Romanians work abroad, especially in Italy and Spain, and Bucharest has a booming tech industry.
ROU.p: Romanian politics was shaken when the Constitutional Court annulled the 2024 presidential election over alleged Russian-backed interference in support of the far-right outsider Călin Georgescu. In the 2025 rerun, the pro-European mayor of Bucharest, Nicușor Dan, beat the nationalist George Simion. Dan's prime minister, Ilie Bolojan, cut spending to tame the EU's largest budget deficit but lost a no-confidence vote in May 2026. After months of failed attempts to form a cabinet, the diplomat Luca Niculescu was sworn in as prime minister on 20 October 2026. Romania hosts NATO and US forces near Ukraine, and Russian drones have struck its territory.
q: Which country doubled in size in 1918, gaining Transylvania, Bessarabia and Bukovina?
Which country overthrew and executed Nicolae Ceaușescu in December 1989?
Which country's Transylvanian castles feed the Dracula legend, inspired by Vlad the Impaler?

HUN.t: The Magyars rode in from the east around 895, and Hungary's first king was crowned in 1000. After defeat by the Ottomans in 1526 the country fell under Ottoman and then Habsburg rule, and from 1867 it was the junior half of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Defeat in World War I was a catastrophe: the 1920 Treaty of Trianon cost it about two-thirds of its land, leaving millions of Hungarians in neighbouring countries. Hoping to win that land back, Hungary sided with Germany in World War II. In 1944 Germany occupied it, and about 430,000 Hungarian Jews were deported to Auschwitz in a few weeks. The Soviet army then imposed communism. In 1956 a national uprising was crushed by Soviet tanks and about 200,000 people fled. The softer 'goulash communism' that followed gave Hungarians more freedom than most of the Eastern Bloc, and in 1989 Hungary helped bring down the Iron Curtain by opening its border with Austria. It joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004.
HUN.c: Hungarian is not related to its neighbours' languages, and family names come before first names. Goulash, paprika and lángos fried bread are everyday food, and Budapest's thermal baths, where people play chess in steaming pools, are famous. The Rubik's Cube was invented in Budapest, and Hungarians win an unusual number of Olympic medals in water polo and swimming.
HUN.p: Péter Magyar, a former insider of Viktor Orbán's Fidesz party, ended Orbán's 16 years as prime minister when his Tisza party won a two-thirds majority in April 2026. Since taking office in May he has changed the constitution to remove President Tamás Sulyok, an Orbán ally; parliament elected the jurist András Baka president in August. The new government has agreed anti-corruption reforms with the EU that are releasing billions of euros in frozen funds, abolished Orbán's Sovereignty Protection Office, closed the state media agency and repealed most of his 2021 law restricting LGBTQ content. Fidesz is now the opposition.
q: Which country lost about two-thirds of its land in the 1920 Treaty of Trianon?
Which country's 1956 uprising was crushed by Soviet tanks?
In which country was the Rubik's Cube invented, and where do people play chess in steaming thermal baths?

SVK.t: For about a thousand years the Slovaks lived in the Kingdom of Hungary, and in the late 1800s Budapest tried to make them speak Hungarian. When Austria-Hungary collapsed in 1918, Slovak and Czech leaders founded Czechoslovakia, though many Slovaks felt run from Prague. After Hitler dismembered the country in 1939, a Slovak state under the priest Jozef Tiso became a Nazi ally and deported most of its Jews to death camps. In 1944 the Slovak National Uprising rose against it and was crushed. Czechoslovakia was rebuilt in 1945 and fell to the communists in 1948. Alexander Dubček, a Slovak, led the 1968 Prague Spring, which Soviet tanks ended. After the Velvet Revolution of 1989, politicians agreed a peaceful 'Velvet Divorce', and Slovakia became independent on 1 January 1993. Under Vladimír Mečiar, prime minister for most of the 1990s, it drifted towards isolation, but later reformers took it into NATO and the European Union in 2004, and it adopted the euro in 2009.
SVK.c: Slovakia makes more cars per person than any other country, at Volkswagen, Kia, Stellantis and Jaguar Land Rover plants. The High Tatras offer skiing and hiking, and ruined castles crown many hilltops. Bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep's cheese, is the national dish. Ice hockey is the top sport, and the fujara, a long shepherd's flute, is a UNESCO-listed folk tradition.
SVK.p: Robert Fico, prime minister for a fourth time since 2023, survived an assassination attempt in 2024. He has halted state military aid to Ukraine, kept buying Russian energy, and with Hungary has held up EU sanctions on Russia. His government abolished the special prosecutor's office, and in 2025 parliament changed the constitution to recognise only two sexes and to claim priority over EU law on matters of 'national identity'. Large protests have accused him of steering Slovakia towards Russia. In 2026 a referendum on restoring the special prosecutor failed because turnout was too low. President Peter Pellegrini, elected in 2024, is a Fico ally.
q: Which country became independent on 1 January 1993 after a peaceful 'Velvet Divorce'?
Which country rose against its Nazi-allied state in the National Uprising of 1944?
Which country makes more cars per person than any other?

POL.t: In the 1500s and 1600s Poland and Lithuania together formed one of Europe's largest states. Russia, Prussia and Austria then carved it up in three partitions, and by 1795 it had vanished from the map. It was reborn in 1918 as World War I ended, and in 1920 it beat back Soviet Russia's Red Army outside Warsaw. In September 1939 Germany invaded from the west and the Soviet Union from the east, starting World War II in Europe. About six million Polish citizens died, half of them Jews murdered in the Holocaust, many in death camps the Germans built on Polish soil such as Auschwitz. After the war its borders moved about 200 km west and it became a communist state under Soviet control. The Solidarity trade union, born in the Gdańsk shipyards in 1980, made the first crack in the Iron Curtain: in 1989 Poland held partly free elections and the communists gave up power. It joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004.
POL.c: Poland is one of Europe's most Catholic countries, and John Paul II, the Polish pope, is a national hero. Pierogi dumplings, Chopin, Kraków's medieval old town and the fantasy world of The Witcher are among its best-known exports. Since joining the EU it has been one of Europe's fastest-growing economies, and millions of Poles have worked in Britain, Germany and Ireland.
POL.p: Politics is a duel between Prime Minister Donald Tusk's pro-EU Civic Coalition, in power since late 2023, and the conservative Law and Justice party, which governed from 2015 to 2023. President Karol Nawrocki, backed by Law and Justice, took office in 2025 and has vetoed many government laws, including a 2026 EU defence loan bill. In October 2026 a judge suspended the Constitutional Tribunal's head and police guarded it, deepening the two camps' long fight over the courts. Russian drones straying over the border keep defence on top, and Poland spends a larger share of GDP on its military than any other NATO member.
q: Which country vanished from the map by 1795 after three partitions?
Which country's Solidarity trade union, born in the Gdańsk shipyards in 1980, made the first crack in the Iron Curtain?
Which country's John Paul II, the first pope from there, is a national hero?

IRL.t: England's grip on Ireland began with the Norman invasion of 1169 and tightened as Protestant settlers were planted on Catholic land. In 1801 Ireland was merged into the United Kingdom. The Great Famine of the 1840s, when the potato crop failed while food was still exported, killed about a million people and drove millions abroad, leaving deep bitterness. Britain promised home rule but delayed it during World War I. The 1916 Easter Rising in Dublin failed, yet the execution of its leaders swung opinion behind independence. After a war of independence, a treaty in 1921 created the Irish Free State in 1922, while six northern counties with a Protestant majority stayed British. A short civil war over the treaty followed. Ireland stayed neutral in World War II and became a republic in 1949. It joined the European communities in 1973, and low taxes later drew US tech and drug firms. In Northern Ireland the Troubles killed about 3,500 people before the 1998 Good Friday Agreement.
IRL.c: Around 70 million people worldwide claim Irish descent, and St Patrick's Day is celebrated everywhere. Pubs with live traditional music are the heart of social life. Gaelic football and hurling, amateur sports played in packed stadiums, are hugely popular. Irish literature runs from Joyce to Beckett and Sally Rooney, and Ireland has voted in referendums to allow same-sex marriage and abortion.
IRL.p: Micheál Martin of Fianna Fáil has been Taoiseach since January 2025, leading a coalition with Fine Gael and independents. Catherine Connolly, a left-wing independent backed by Sinn Féin and other opposition parties, won the October 2025 presidential election by a wide margin. Sinn Féin, which wants Irish unity, leads the opposition. The housing shortage is the biggest domestic issue. In 2026 fuel prices driven by the Iran war led farmers to blockade roads and refineries, and in October 2026 more than 300,000 public sector workers struck over pay. Ireland holds the EU Council presidency in the second half of 2026.
q: Which country lost about a million people in the Great Famine of the 1840s, when the potato crop failed?
Which country's 1916 Easter Rising failed, yet swung opinion behind independence?
Which country's people play Gaelic football and hurling, and are celebrated worldwide on St Patrick's Day?

GBR.t: England and Scotland were joined in 1707 to form Great Britain, and Ireland was added in 1801. Britain led the Industrial Revolution, and its navy and trade built the largest empire in history, covering about a quarter of the world's land by the 1920s. In World War I almost a million soldiers from Britain and its empire died. Most of Ireland broke away in 1922, leaving Northern Ireland in the UK. In 1940, under Winston Churchill, Britain fought on against Hitler after France fell, and survived the Blitz. Exhausted and in debt after victory, it built the National Health Service and the welfare state, and let its empire go, starting with India in 1947 and most of Africa in the 1960s. It became a nuclear power and a close US ally, and joined the European Community in 1973. The Troubles in Northern Ireland killed more than 3,500 people before the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. In a 2016 referendum Britain voted to leave the EU, and it left in 2020.
GBR.c: English became the world's common language thanks to Britain's empire and, later, the US. Football, cricket, rugby and tennis were codified here, and the Premier League is watched worldwide. Shakespeare, the Beatles, Harry Potter, the BBC and the royal family are global brands. Pubs, tea, fish and chips and curry are everyday life, and London is one of the world's most diverse cities.
GBR.p: Labour won a landslide in 2024 under Keir Starmer, but slow growth, high living costs and broken promises sent its ratings tumbling, while Nigel Farage's Reform UK surged. In the May 2026 elections Plaid Cymru took power in Wales, with Labour third, and the SNP held on in Scotland. Starmer resigned, and Andy Burnham, the popular mayor of Greater Manchester, won a by-election to return to Parliament and became prime minister in July 2026, unopposed as Labour leader. He promises to move power out of London. Migration, the NHS, energy bills pushed up by the Iran war, and support for Ukraine dominate. King Charles III is head of state.
q: Which country was formed by the 1707 union of two kingdoms, with Ireland added in 1801?
Which country built the National Health Service after World War II and voted to leave the EU in 2016?
Which country codified football, cricket, rugby and tennis and gave the world Shakespeare and the Beatles?

GRC.t: Greece won independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1830 after a long war, the first Balkan nation to do so. Dreaming of uniting all Greeks, it expanded step by step, gaining Crete and Macedonia in the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913. Its invasion of Turkey after World War I ended in disaster in 1922, and in 1923 about 1.2 million Orthodox Christians were moved from Turkey to Greece in a population exchange. In 1940 Greece rejected Mussolini's ultimatum, a 'No' still celebrated every 28 October, and drove back the Italian army, but Germany occupied it in 1941 and a terrible famine followed. A civil war between communists and the US-backed government lasted until 1949. A military junta ruled from 1967 to 1974 and fell after the Cyprus crisis, and Greeks then voted to abolish the monarchy. Greece joined the European communities in 1981 and the euro in 2001, but the debt crisis from 2009 brought three bailouts and shrank the economy by about a quarter.
GRC.c: Ancient Greece gave the world democracy, philosophy and the Olympic Games, and the Acropolis still stands over Athens. Greeks eat late and outdoors: grilled souvlaki, feta, olives and fresh fish by the sea. Orthodox Easter, with midnight candles and roast lamb, is the biggest holiday. Islands such as Santorini and Crete draw huge numbers of tourists every summer.
GRC.p: Kyriakos Mitsotakis of the centre-right New Democracy has been prime minister since 2019 and won a second term in 2023. Konstantinos Tasoulas, a former parliament speaker, became president in 2025. The economy has recovered strongly since the debt crisis, but the government has been hit by scandals: huge protests in 2025 over the cover-up claims around the 2023 Tempi train crash, which killed 57 people, and fraud in EU farm subsidies that forced several ministers out. The opposition is weak and divided. Migration from Libya to Crete, wildfires and tension with Turkey over sea borders remain key issues.
q: Which country celebrates every 28 October its 'No' to Mussolini's ultimatum in 1940?
Which country's debt crisis from 2009 brought three bailouts and shrank its economy by about a quarter?
Which country gave the world democracy, philosophy and the Olympic Games?

ZMB.t: In the 1890s Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company took this land through treaties with local rulers, and it was named Northern Rhodesia after him. Britain took over direct rule in 1924. Huge copper deposits developed in the 1920s turned the Copperbelt into one of the world's leading mining regions, worked by Africans and run by white managers. In 1953 Britain merged it into the Central African Federation with Southern Rhodesia and Nyasaland, which many Africans saw as a way to keep white minority rule. Protests broke the federation, and the country became independent in 1964 as Zambia, after the Zambezi River, under Kenneth Kaunda. Kaunda made it a one-party state, nationalised the mines and gave bases to liberation movements fighting in Rhodesia, South Africa and Angola, which brought raids in return. When copper prices fell in the 1970s, debt and shortages followed. Protests forced multiparty elections in 1991, which Kaunda lost, and power has since changed hands peacefully several times.
ZMB.c: English is official, with Bemba and Nyanja widely spoken among more than 70 ethnic groups. Nshima, a stiff maize porridge, is eaten with relish at almost every meal. Victoria Falls, on the border with Zimbabwe, is known locally as Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the smoke that thunders'. In the Kuomboka ceremony, the Lozi king moves to higher ground in a royal barge as the Zambezi floods rise.
ZMB.p: Hakainde Hichilema, a businessman known as 'HH', won a second term in August 2026 with about 60% of the vote, beating Brian Mundubile of the opposition Tonse Alliance. Hichilema first won in 2021 by defeating Edgar Lungu, president from 2015 to 2021, who died in 2025; a long legal row over his burial followed. EU observers called the vote competitive but uneven, and Mundubile, who was arrested during the count, rejected the result. Zambia has restructured its debts after defaulting in 2020. A severe drought in 2024 drained the Kariba hydropower dam and caused long power cuts, and copper mining is expanding again.
q: Which country, once Northern Rhodesia, became one of the world's leading copper regions?
Which country did Kenneth Kaunda lead from independence in 1964 until losing multiparty elections in 1991?
In which country does the Lozi king move to higher ground in a royal barge as floods rise, in the Kuomboka ceremony?

SLE.t: Portuguese sailors named the mountains here Serra Lyoa, 'lion mountains', in the 1460s. In 1792 British abolitionists founded Freetown as a home for freed slaves, including Black Loyalists who had fought for Britain in the American Revolution and had been resettled in Nova Scotia. After Britain banned the slave trade in 1807, its navy landed tens of thousands of Africans freed from slave ships here, and their descendants, the Krio, became an educated elite; Fourah Bay College, founded in 1827, was West Africa's first Western-style university. Britain declared the interior a protectorate in 1896. Sierra Leone became independent in 1961, and in 1978 Siaka Stevens made it a one-party state while diamond wealth was looted. In 1991 the Revolutionary United Front, backed by Charles Taylor in Liberia, launched a civil war known for amputations and child soldiers, funded partly by 'blood diamonds'. British troops and UN peacekeepers helped end it in 2002. Ebola killed almost 4,000 people in 2014 and 2015.
SLE.c: English is official, but Krio, a creole spoken by almost everyone, is the real shared language. Most people are Muslim and many are Christian, and mixed families and shared holidays are common. Cassava leaf stew with rice is everyday food. Freetown's Cotton Tree was a landmark for freed slaves until it fell in 2023, and the white beaches of the Freetown peninsula are drawing tourists again.
SLE.p: Julius Maada Bio, a former soldier who briefly led a military government in 1996, has been president since 2018. He won a second term in 2023 in an election that the main opposition party, the All People's Congress, rejected and observers said lacked transparency. In November 2023 gunmen attacked the main barracks and prisons in what the government called a coup attempt. David Moinina Sengeh has been chief minister since 2023. Kush, a cheap synthetic drug, has devastated young people, and Bio declared a national emergency over it in 2024. He became chair of ECOWAS in 2025. Poverty and high prices remain the main issues.
q: Which country's capital was founded in 1792 by British abolitionists as a home for freed slaves?
Which country's civil war from 1991 was funded partly by 'blood diamonds'?
Which country's Krio creole is the real shared language, and whose famous Cotton Tree fell in 2023?

GIN.t: Guinea's highlands were part of the medieval Mali empire, and in the 1800s the Muslim leader Samori Touré built a state here that fought French conquest until his capture in 1898. France then ran Guinea as part of French West Africa, exporting rubber and later bananas and bauxite. In 1958 de Gaulle offered France's African colonies a vote on joining a French community. Guinea, led by the trade unionist Ahmed Sékou Touré, was the only one to vote no, saying it preferred 'poverty in freedom to riches in slavery'. It became independent immediately. France pulled out abruptly, taking files, equipment and even light bulbs, and Guinea turned to the Soviet Union for aid. Sékou Touré became a dictator who jailed and killed thousands of suspected opponents at Camp Boiro. After his death in 1984 the army took over under Lansana Conté until 2008. Alpha Condé became the first freely elected president in 2010, but changed the constitution to seek a third term, and was overthrown in a 2021 coup.
GIN.c: French is official, alongside Pular, Maninka and Susu, and most people are Muslim. Guinea holds the largest bauxite reserves in the world, the ore used to make aluminium, and the Simandou mountains hold huge deposits of iron ore. The Fouta Djallon highlands are the source of the Niger, Senegal and Gambia rivers. Guinean dancers and drummers, such as the national ballet, are famous worldwide.
GIN.p: General Mamady Doumbouya, who led the 2021 coup, had a new constitution approved in a 2025 referendum and then won the December 2025 presidential election with about 87% of the vote; the main opposition leaders were absent or in exile. Bah Oury has been prime minister since 2024. In 2026 the government dissolved 40 political parties, including the three main opposition groups, and the African Union lifted its post-coup sanctions. The giant Simandou iron ore mine, developed with Chinese and Anglo-Australian companies, began exporting in late 2025, and the government hopes it will transform the economy.
q: Which was the only French colony to vote no to de Gaulle's French community in 1958, preferring 'poverty in freedom'?
Which country's dictator Ahmed Sékou Touré jailed and killed thousands at Camp Boiro?
Which country holds the world's largest bauxite reserves, and the source of the Niger, Senegal and Gambia rivers?

LBR.t: The American Colonization Society founded Liberia in 1822 as a home for freed African Americans, and it declared independence in 1847, Africa's oldest republic. Americo-Liberian settlers, a small minority, ruled the indigenous majority for over a century through the True Whig Party, and in 1930 a League of Nations inquiry found officials involved in forced labour. The US rubber company Firestone leased a vast plantation in 1926, and Liberia became a close American ally, hosting US bases and relay stations through World War II and the Cold War.
