In 1980 Master Sergeant Samuel Doe, from the Krahn people, killed President William Tolbert and had his ministers shot on a beach, ending settler rule. In 1989 Charles Taylor launched a rebellion that led to two civil wars, lasting until 2003, which killed about 250,000 people and were notorious for child soldiers. Taylor, president from 1997 to 2003, was later convicted of war crimes in Sierra Leone. In 2005 Ellen Johnson Sirleaf became the first woman elected to lead an African country.
LBR.c: English is official, and Liberian English and Kpelle, Bassa and other languages are spoken. Its flag, capital (Monrovia, after US President Monroe) and early laws were modelled on the US, and it still uses the US dollar alongside its own. Rice with palm butter or cassava leaf stew is everyday food, and George Weah, the 1995 world footballer of the year, is a national icon.
LBR.p: Joseph Boakai became president in January 2024 after narrowly defeating George Weah, president from 2018 to 2024. In 2024 he ordered the creation of a war crimes court for the civil-war era, and in 2025 he formally apologised to the wars' victims. Liberia began a seat on the UN Security Council in 2026. Corruption, poverty and drug abuse are major concerns, and the country has become a transit point for cocaine bound for Europe: in August 2026 the former vice-president Jewel Taylor was charged with drug trafficking. Liberia has also agreed to take in migrants deported from the United States.
q: Which country did the American Colonization Society found in 1822 for freed African Americans?
Which country elected Ellen Johnson Sirleaf in 2005, the first woman elected to lead an African country?
Which country's capital is named after US President Monroe, and whose footballer George Weah became a national icon?

CAF.t: For centuries this region was raided for slaves by states to the north and east, which left it thinly populated. France took it in the 1890s and ran it as Ubangi-Shari, handing much of the land to private concession companies that forced people to gather rubber and ivory; thousands died, and the abuses caused a scandal in France in the 1920s. Barthélemy Boganda, a priest turned politician, led the push for independence but died in a plane crash in 1959, a year before it came. The new Central African Republic, named for where it sits, soon fell to coups. Jean-Bédel Bokassa seized power in 1966, crowned himself emperor in 1977 in a ceremony costing about a third of the national budget, and was overthrown with French help in 1979. Coups and mutinies continued. In 2013 the mostly Muslim Séléka rebels took Bangui, and mainly Christian anti-balaka militias struck back, a conflict that killed thousands and split the country along religious lines.
CAF.c: Sango is spoken by almost everyone and is official alongside French. The forests of the southwest are home to the Aka people, whose polyphonic singing is listed as world cultural heritage, and Dzanga-Sangha reserve draws visitors to see forest elephants and gorillas. Cassava and peanuts are staples, and diamonds and gold are dug by hand in small mines.
CAF.p: Faustin-Archange Touadéra, president since 2016, removed term limits in a 2023 referendum and won a third term in December 2025 with about 76% of the official vote; the opposition called it unfair. He relies on Russian mercenaries from the Wagner Group, who guard him and fight rebels in exchange for access to gold and diamond mines, and on a large UN peacekeeping mission. Some rebel groups signed peace deals and disbanded in 2025, but armed groups still control parts of the countryside. Poverty is among the worst in the world.
q: Which country did Jean-Bédel Bokassa rule, crowning himself emperor in 1977 in a ceremony costing about a third of the budget?
Which country's capital, Bangui, was taken in 2013 by the mostly Muslim Séléka rebels?
Which country has Sango as a language spoken by almost everyone, and the Dzanga-Sangha forest reserve?

SDN.t: Northern Sudan was home to ancient Kush, whose kings once ruled Egypt and built pyramids at Meroë. In 1881 a religious leader, the Mahdi, led a revolt against Egyptian rule, and his followers took Khartoum in 1885, killing the British general Charles Gordon. A British and Egyptian army crushed the Mahdist state at Omdurman in 1898, and Britain and Egypt then ruled Sudan jointly, running the Arab Muslim north and the mostly African south separately. Sudan became independent in 1956, and the south soon rose in revolt. Coups followed: Jaafar Nimeiri took power in 1969 and imposed Islamic law in 1983, restarting the southern war. In 1989 Omar al-Bashir seized power with Islamist backing and hosted Osama bin Laden in the 1990s. From 2003 his army and Janjaweed militias crushed a revolt in Darfur, killing an estimated 300,000 people, and the International Criminal Court charged him with genocide. The south broke away in 2011, and protests toppled Bashir in 2019.
SDN.c: Arabic and English are official, and most people are Muslim. Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt, built by Kush at Meroë, and the Blue and White Nile meet at Khartoum. Ful medames, stewed fava beans, is the everyday breakfast, and spiced coffee is poured from a clay pot called a jebena. Sudanese are known for generous hospitality, and henna designs and the colourful toob wrap worn by women are part of daily life.
SDN.p: Since April 2023 Sudan has been torn apart by war between the army, led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary force that grew out of the Janjaweed, led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti. The two had seized power together in 2021. The UN calls it the world's largest humanitarian crisis: more than 12 million people have fled their homes and famine has spread. The army retook Khartoum in 2025, and its government, with Kamil Idris as prime minister, returned there in January 2026. The RSF captured El Fasher in Darfur in October 2025, amid reports of mass killings.
q: Which country's Mahdist forces took Khartoum in 1885, killing the British general Charles Gordon?
Which country's ruler Omar al-Bashir was charged with genocide over Darfur?
Which country has more pyramids than Egypt, and where the Blue and White Nile meet?

DJI.t: France took this patch of desert coast at the mouth of the Red Sea in the 1880s as a coaling station for ships heading through the Suez Canal to Asia, and called it French Somaliland. In 1917 a railway to Addis Ababa was completed, making the port Ethiopia's main outlet to the sea. Two peoples live here: the Afar in the north and the Issa Somalis in the south, and France played them against each other. Fearing that the territory would be absorbed into Somalia, France held referendums in 1958 and 1967 that kept it French, and renamed it the French Territory of the Afars and the Issas. It finally became independent in 1977 as Djibouti, the last French colony on the African mainland. Hassan Gouled Aptidon ruled as president until 1999, facing an Afar rebellion in the 1990s, and handed power to his nephew Ismaïl Omar Guelleh. After the 2001 attacks on the US, Djibouti's position next to Yemen and Somalia made it a magnet for foreign military bases.
DJI.c: Most people are Somali or Afar, and French and Arabic are official, while Somali and Afar are spoken at home. Chewing khat leaves in the afternoon is a daily habit for many men. Lake Assal, about 155 m below sea level, is the lowest point in Africa, and whale sharks gather off the coast in winter. The US, China, France, Japan and Italy all keep military bases here.
DJI.p: Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, president since 1999, won a sixth term in April 2026 with about 98% of the official vote, after the constitution's age limit was removed to let him stand; Abdoulkader Kamil Mohamed has been prime minister since 2013. Opposition parties have little room. The economy depends on the port, the railway to Ethiopia and rent from foreign bases, and attacks on Red Sea shipping by Yemen's Houthis since 2023 have hurt trade. Large Chinese loans have raised worries about debt. Thousands of migrants cross Djibouti each year towards Yemen and the Gulf, and many have died at sea.
q: Which country was renamed the French Territory of the Afars and the Issas?
Which country was the last French colony on the African mainland, independent in 1977?
Which country has Lake Assal, Africa's lowest point, and military bases of the US, China, France, Japan and Italy?

ERI.t: Italy made Eritrea its first colony in 1890, building Asmara into a modern city with railways and factories, and used it as the base for Mussolini's invasion of Ethiopia in 1935. British forces drove the Italians out in 1941 and ran the territory until 1952, when the UN federated it with Ethiopia. Emperor Haile Selassie steadily stripped away its autonomy and annexed it outright in 1962, which set off a 30-year war of independence. The rebels, led from the 1970s by the Eritrean People's Liberation Front, held out in mountain trenches against Ethiopia's Soviet-armed military. When Ethiopia's Marxist regime fell in 1991, the EPLF took Asmara, and in 1993 Eritreans voted almost unanimously for independence, leaving Ethiopia landlocked. A border war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000 killed tens of thousands. Afterwards the government used the threat of Ethiopia to justify shelving the constitution, cancelling elections and keeping young people in national service with no end date, which drove hundreds of thousands to flee abroad.
ERI.c: Asmara's 1930s Italian modernist buildings, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, give the capital the feel of an Italian city, and cappuccino and pasta are local staples alongside injera. Tigrinya and Arabic are the main working languages, and people are roughly half Christian and half Muslim. Cycling, brought by the Italians, is a national passion, and Eritrean riders have raced in the Tour de France.
ERI.p: Isaias Afwerki has ruled since independence in 1993 without ever holding a national election; there is no free press and no opposition. A 2018 peace deal with Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed won Abiy the Nobel Peace Prize, and Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopia in the Tigray war of 2020 to 2022. Relations have since soured badly, as Abiy has spoken of Ethiopia's need for access to the Red Sea, and Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of arming rebels. In October 2026, after fighting returned to Tigray in September, Eritrea cut diplomatic ties with Ethiopia. In September 2026 the United States lifted sanctions on Eritrea's ruling party and forces.
q: Which country did Italy make its first colony in 1890, using it as the base for invading Ethiopia?
Which country voted almost unanimously for independence in 1993, leaving its neighbour landlocked?
Which country's capital, Asmara, is a UNESCO site for its 1930s Italian modernist buildings?

AUT.t: For centuries Vienna was the seat of the Habsburgs, whose Austro-Hungarian Empire ruled much of central Europe. When a Bosnian Serb shot the heir to the throne, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, in 1914, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia and set off World War I. Defeat in 1918 broke the empire into new nations and left Austria as a small, poor German-speaking republic that many doubted could survive. A brief civil war in 1934 brought a dictatorship, and in 1938 Hitler, himself Austrian-born, annexed the country to cheering crowds. After World War II Austria long presented itself as Hitler's first victim, a story only seriously questioned from the 1980s. Occupied by four powers, like Germany, it regained independence in 1955 by promising permanent neutrality. It became a Cold War meeting point, hosting UN agencies and OPEC in Vienna, and joined the European Union in 1995.
AUT.c: Vienna was the city of Mozart, Beethoven, Freud and the waltz, and its coffee houses, where one coffee buys hours at a marble table, are on UNESCO's heritage list. Schnitzel, Sachertorte and apple strudel are staples. Austrians ski from childhood in the Alps, and the Vienna Philharmonic's New Year's Concert is broadcast around the world. Salzburg is the setting of The Sound of Music.
AUT.p: The far-right Freedom Party came first in the 2024 election but could not find partners. Instead the conservative People's Party, the Social Democrats and the liberal NEOS formed a rare three-party coalition, led by Chancellor Christian Stocker since March 2025. Alexander Van der Bellen, a former Green leader, is president. The government is cutting a large budget deficit while the Freedom Party leads opinion polls. Neutrality is under debate: Austria buys air defences with European partners, yet in 2026 it refused US military aircraft the use of its airspace for strikes on Iran.
q: Which country regained independence in 1955 by promising permanent neutrality?
Which country did Hitler annex in 1938, to cheering crowds?
Which country's capital is famous for coffee houses, the waltz and a New Year's Concert broadcast worldwide?

IRQ.t: Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates, saw the first cities and the first writing, and Baghdad later became the capital of the Abbasid caliphate. The Ottoman Empire ruled the area as three provinces: Mosul in the Kurdish north, Baghdad in the Sunni Arab centre and Basra in the Shia south. After World War I Britain joined them into one country under a League of Nations mandate and made Faisal, a Hashemite prince, king. Iraq became independent in 1932, but the monarchy was overthrown in 1958. The Arab nationalist Baath Party seized power in 1968, and Saddam Hussein ruled from 1979. He invaded Iran in 1980, used chemical weapons against the Kurds, and invaded Kuwait in 1990, leading to the Gulf War and years of sanctions. A US-led invasion in 2003 toppled him, but a sectarian civil war followed, and in 2014 the Islamic State group seized Mosul. Iraqi forces, Kurdish fighters and a US-led coalition defeated it by 2017.
IRQ.c: Arabic and Kurdish are both official, and the Kurdistan Region in the north has its own government and armed forces. Most Iraqis are Shia Muslims, and millions of pilgrims walk to Karbala each year for Arbaeen. Masgouf, river carp grilled beside an open fire, is a Baghdad favourite, tea is drunk strong and sweet, and the ruins of Babylon and Ur recall where the first cities began.
IRQ.p: By custom the prime minister is a Shia Arab, the president a Kurd and the speaker a Sunni Arab. After the November 2025 election, months of bargaining ended in May 2026 with Ali al-Zaidi, a banker in his early forties, becoming the youngest prime minister in Iraq's history. Nizar Amidi of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan was elected president in April. The 2026 Iran war spilled into Iraq, with US strikes on Iran-backed militias and attacks on the US embassy. US-led coalition forces completed their withdrawal in September 2026, and the government has given the militias until mid-2027 to disarm. The economy depends almost entirely on oil.
q: Which country did Britain create after World War I by joining the provinces of Mosul, Baghdad and Basra?
Which country was ruled by Saddam Hussein from 1979 until a US-led invasion in 2003?
Which country's millions of pilgrims walk to Karbala each year for Arbaeen?

ITA.t: Italy was divided among many states, some ruled by Austria and the pope, until the Risorgimento movement, with Garibaldi's volunteers and the kingdom of Piedmont, united it in 1861. Rome was added in 1870. Italy joined World War I on the Allied side in 1915, but lost about 650,000 soldiers and felt cheated by the peace. That anger helped Benito Mussolini found Fascism and seize power in 1922. He invaded Ethiopia in 1935 and allied with Hitler in World War II. After the Allies landed in Sicily in 1943, Mussolini was overthrown, Germany occupied the north, and partisans fought on until his capture and execution in 1945. In 1946 Italians voted to replace the king with a republic. Italy helped found the European communities with the Treaty of Rome in 1957, and its postwar economic miracle made it rich. Terrorism in the 1970s and corruption scandals in the 1990s swept away the old parties. The north-south gap in wealth remains wide.
ITA.c: Italy has more UNESCO World Heritage Sites than almost any other country, from Venice to Pompeii. Food is close to sacred: each region has its own pasta, and espresso is drunk standing at the bar. Renaissance art, opera, fashion houses in Milan and Ferrari are world famous. Football is a passion, and the pope lives in Vatican City, inside Rome.
ITA.p: Giorgia Meloni, leader of the right-wing Brothers of Italy, has been prime minister since 2022, heading one of the most stable governments in Italy's postwar history. In March 2026, however, voters rejected her government's reform of the justice system in a referendum, by about 54%. Sergio Mattarella has been president since 2015. Meloni has focused on cutting migration across the Mediterranean, including a disputed plan to hold migrants in centres in Albania, and tightened rules on citizenship. Low growth, high public debt and an ageing, shrinking population are the long-term worries.
q: Which country did Garibaldi and the Risorgimento movement unite in 1861?
In which country did Benito Mussolini found Fascism and seize power in 1922?
Which country has more UNESCO World Heritage Sites than almost any other, from Venice to Pompeii?

CHE.t: Three mountain cantons swore an oath of alliance in 1291, according to tradition, and the Swiss Confederation grew by beating Habsburg and Burgundian armies. After a defeat at Marignano in 1515 it stopped expanding, and Swiss mercenaries fought for others instead. The Congress of Vienna in 1815 fixed its borders and recognised its neutrality. A short civil war in 1847 led to the 1848 constitution, which created today's federal state, with powerful cantons and referendums on almost everything. Geneva became home to the Red Cross in 1863 and later to the League of Nations. Surrounded by fighting, Switzerland stayed neutral in both world wars, mobilising its army in the Alps. Its banks' gold dealings with Nazi Germany and dormant Jewish accounts led to a settlement of over a billion dollars in 1998. Women won the vote nationally only in 1971. Switzerland joined the UN in 2002 and has kept the EU at arm's length, voting against joining the European Economic Area in 1992.
CHE.c: Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. It is known for chocolate, cheese fondue, precise watches, private banks and the pharmaceutical giants of Basel. Voters go to the polls several times a year on national questions. Trains run like clockwork, skiing and hiking are national pastimes, and Geneva hosts the UN's European offices and many international organisations.
CHE.p: Switzerland has no single leader: a seven-member Federal Council, shared by the four main parties, runs the government, and the presidency rotates each year. In 2026 it is held by Guy Parmelin of the Swiss People's Party, the largest party, which campaigns against immigration and closer EU ties. The main debate is a new package of treaties with the European Union. In 2026 voters rejected a cap on the population at 10 million and a stricter definition of neutrality. US tariffs have hit exporters, and a New Year's fire at a bar in Crans-Montana killed about 40 people.
q: Which country, by tradition, began when three mountain cantons swore an oath of alliance in 1291?
Which country only gave women the vote nationally in 1971?
Which country has four national languages, including Romansh, and holds national votes several times a year?

IRN.t: Persia was never colonised, but in 1907 Britain and Russia divided it into spheres of influence, and a British company controlled its oil after oil was found in 1908. An army officer, Reza Khan, took power in 1921, crowned himself Shah and renamed the country Iran in 1935. Britain and the Soviet Union invaded in 1941 and replaced him with his son, Mohammad Reza Shah. When prime minister Mohammad Mosaddegh nationalised the oil industry, a 1953 coup backed by the US and Britain removed him and strengthened the Shah, who became a close Cold War ally of the West. His rapid modernisation, the gap between rich and poor and his secret police fed anger, and in 1979 a revolution led by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini created an Islamic Republic ruled by clerics. Students seized the US embassy and held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days. Iraq invaded in 1980, starting an eight-year war that killed hundreds of thousands. Since then Iran has backed allied militias across the region and expanded its nuclear programme.
IRN.c: Persian, or Farsi, is the official language, and poets such as Hafez and Saadi are quoted in everyday talk; many families consult a book of Hafez's poems for fortune-telling. Nowruz, the Persian new year at the spring equinox, is the biggest celebration. Iran is famous for carpets, saffron, pistachios and rice dishes with a crispy crust called tahdig, and its film-makers win prizes around the world.
IRN.p: Supreme leader Ali Khamenei, who ruled from 1989, was killed in a US and Israeli attack on 28 February 2026, and the Assembly of Experts chose his son Mojtaba Khamenei to succeed him. Masoud Pezeshkian, a reformist, has been president since 2024. The war followed a 12-day conflict with Israel and the US in June 2025. In 2026 Iran fired missiles at Israel and Gulf states and closed the Strait of Hormuz, sending oil prices soaring; a truce in April and a deal in June were followed by more clashes. Mass protests over the collapsing currency were crushed, and a UN mission said the crackdown amounted to crimes against humanity.
q: Which country's prime minister, Mohammad Mosaddegh, was removed in a 1953 coup after nationalising oil?
Which country's 1979 revolution created an Islamic Republic, and whose students held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days?
Which country's people often consult a book of Hafez's poems to tell their fortune?

NLD.t: The Dutch revolted against Spanish rule in 1568, and their republic became the richest trading nation of the 1600s, with colonies from Indonesia to New Amsterdam, later New York. It became a kingdom after Napoleon's defeat, and Belgium broke away in 1830. The Netherlands stayed neutral in World War I, but in May 1940 Germany invaded and bombed Rotterdam. About three quarters of Dutch Jews were murdered in the Holocaust, among them Anne Frank, who had hidden in an Amsterdam canal house. In the 'Hunger Winter' of 1944–45 thousands starved. After the war Indonesia fought for and won its independence in 1949, and Suriname became independent in 1975. The country rebuilt itself as a founding member of NATO and of the European Economic Community. After the 1953 North Sea flood killed about 1,800 people, it built the Delta Works, a chain of giant sea barriers. From the 2000s, debates about immigration and Islam reshaped its politics.
NLD.c: About a quarter of the land lies below sea level, kept dry by dikes and pumps, and there are more bicycles than people. The Dutch are famously direct, and most speak excellent English. King's Day on 27 April turns cities orange, the national colour. Cheese markets, stroopwafels, raw herring, Rembrandt and Van Gogh, tulip fields and the giant port of Rotterdam are all part of the picture.
NLD.p: Dutch politics has fragmented. Geert Wilders' anti-immigration Party for Freedom won the 2023 election, but the government it joined under Dick Schoof collapsed in June 2025 when Wilders pulled out over asylum rules. In the October 2025 election the liberal D66 and the Party for Freedom each won 26 seats. In February 2026 Rob Jetten of D66 became prime minister, leading a minority coalition with the centre-right VVD and the Christian Democrats. Housing shortages, asylum, nitrogen pollution limits that hit farmers, and higher defence spending are the big issues. King Willem-Alexander is head of state.
q: Which country revolted against Spanish rule in 1568 and became the richest trading nation of the 1600s?
Which country built the Delta Works after the 1953 North Sea flood?
In which country does about a quarter of the land lie below sea level, with more bicycles than people?

LIE.t: Liechtenstein became a principality of the Holy Roman Empire in 1719, named after the Austrian noble family that had bought its two lordships, Vaduz and Schellenberg. It became sovereign in 1806 and abolished its tiny army in 1868. For centuries the princes lived in Vienna and the country was poor farmland. After World War I and the fall of Austria-Hungary, it turned from Austria to Switzerland, forming a customs union in 1923 and adopting the Swiss franc. Prince Franz Joseph II moved to Vaduz in 1938, the first ruling prince to live there, and the country stayed neutral through World War II. After the war, low taxes and light regulation drew companies and money, and manufacturers such as the tool maker Hilti grew into global firms. Women won the vote only in 1984. Liechtenstein joined the UN in 1990 and the European Economic Area in 1995. A 2003 referendum gave the prince more powers. It is one of only two doubly landlocked countries.
LIE.c: German is the official language, spoken in an Alemannic dialect. Liechtenstein is one of the richest countries in the world per person, with more registered companies than people and more jobs than residents, filled by commuters from Switzerland and Austria. The prince lives in the castle above Vaduz and invites the whole country to his garden on National Day, 15 August.
LIE.p: Prince Hans-Adam II is head of state, though his son, Hereditary Prince Alois, has handled day-to-day duties since 2004. The prince holds more power than any other European monarch, including a veto over laws. Brigitte Haas became the country's first woman prime minister in 2025. In August 2026 the princely house announced it would change its rules to let women inherit the throne. Liechtenstein relies on exports and finance, so US tariffs and global tax rules matter greatly. It is in Europe's single market through the European Economic Area but is not an EU member.
q: Which country abolished its tiny army in 1868 and later adopted the Swiss franc?
Which country only gave women the vote in 1984?
Which doubly landlocked country has more registered companies than people, with a prince in the castle above Vaduz?

CIV.t: European traders named this coast after the ivory they bought here, and France made it a colony in 1893, building the port and railway that made Abidjan a hub. Its first president, Félix Houphouët-Boigny, had been a cocoa planter and a minister in the French government. After independence in 1960 he kept close ties with France, welcomed farm workers from Burkina Faso and Mali, and made the country the world's biggest cocoa producer and the richest state in French West Africa: the 'Ivorian miracle'. He also made his home village, Yamoussoukro, the capital and built a giant basilica there. When cocoa prices fell in the 1980s the boom ended, and after his death in 1993 politicians played on the idea of 'Ivoirité', questioning who counted as truly Ivorian, which shut out many northerners and migrants. A 1999 coup and a civil war from 2002 split the country in two. When Laurent Gbagbo refused to accept defeat in the 2010 election, a second war ended with his arrest in 2011.
CIV.c: It produces more cocoa than any other country, so a large share of the world's chocolate starts here. Abidjan is a hub of French-language music and pop culture, and coupé-décalé and zouglou dance music spread from here across Africa. Attiéké, a couscous made from cassava, is eaten with grilled fish, and the national football team, the Elephants, won the Africa Cup of Nations at home in 2024.
CIV.p: Alassane Ouattara, president since 2011, won a fourth term in October 2025 with about 90% of the official vote after the two main opposition candidates, Laurent Gbagbo and Tidjane Thiam, were barred from running. Protests were banned and hundreds arrested, and his party then won a large majority in parliament. The economy has grown fast, helped by high cocoa prices, oil and gas finds and big building projects, though many say they have not felt it. French troops left their base near Abidjan in 2025, and who will follow the 84-year-old Ouattara is an open question.
q: Which country's first president, Félix Houphouët-Boigny, built a giant basilica in his home village and made it the capital?
Which country was split by a civil war from 2002, and again after Laurent Gbagbo refused to accept defeat in 2010?
Which country produces more cocoa than any other, and whose football team, the Elephants, won the 2024 Africa Cup of Nations at home?

SRB.t: Serbia's medieval kingdom was crushed by the Ottomans after the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, a defeat still central to Serbian identity. Uprisings from 1804 won self-rule, and full independence came in 1878. In June 1914 Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb, shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo; Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, and World War I began. Serbia lost perhaps a quarter of its people but emerged at the head of a new Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia. In World War II Germany occupied it, and Tito's Partisans fought both the occupiers and the royalist Chetniks. Communist Yugoslavia, run from Belgrade, broke with Stalin in 1948. After Tito died, Slobodan Milošević rose on Serbian nationalism, and the 1990s wars in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo ended with NATO bombing in 1999. Protesters toppled Milošević in 2000. Montenegro left in 2006, and Kosovo declared independence in 2008, which Serbia does not recognise.
SRB.c: Serbian is written in both Cyrillic and Latin letters, and the Serbian Orthodox Church is a pillar of identity: each family celebrates its own patron saint's day, the slava. Grilled meats like ćevapi and pljeskavica, plum rakija and kafana taverns with live music are everywhere. Belgrade's nightlife on river barges, Novak Đoković and the Guča trumpet festival are famous well beyond the Balkans.
SRB.p: Aleksandar Vučić of the Serbian Progressive Party has dominated politics since 2012. In November 2024 a station canopy collapse in Novi Sad killed 16 people, and student-led protests against corruption grew into the largest in Serbia's history, forcing out Prime Minister Miloš Vučević in 2025; Đuro Macut replaced him. In September 2026 parliament was dissolved, and Vučić resigned as president to run for prime minister in a snap election, leaving parliament speaker Ana Brnabić as acting president. In the vote on 25 October the student-led Student List won a majority, and Vučić conceded defeat. Serbia, an EU candidate, keeps close ties with Russia and China and refuses to recognise Kosovo.
q: Which country's defeat at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 is still central to its identity?
Which country's protesters toppled Slobodan Milošević in 2000?
In which country does each family celebrate its own patron saint's day, the slava?

MLI.t: Mali takes its name from the medieval Mali Empire, whose ruler Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 carrying so much gold that he is often called one of the richest people in history. Timbuktu, on the edge of the Sahara, became a centre of trade and Islamic learning. France conquered the region in the late 1800s and ruled it as French Sudan, part of French West Africa. In 1960 it became independent, first in the short-lived Mali Federation with Senegal, then alone under a socialist government that leaned towards the Soviet bloc. A coup in 1968 brought Moussa Traoré's military rule, which ended in 1991 after mass protests and another coup. Mali then became one of West Africa's democracies for two decades. In 2012 Tuareg rebels and jihadists linked to al-Qaeda seized the north, and France sent troops in 2013 to drive them back. The violence spread to the centre of the country, and coups followed in 2012, 2020 and 2021.
MLI.c: Bambara is the most widely spoken language, and most people are Muslim. Timbuktu's mud-brick mosques and manuscripts recall its past as a centre of learning, and the Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest mud-brick building in the world. Griots, hereditary singers and storytellers, keep family histories alive, and musicians such as Ali Farka Touré, Salif Keita and Toumani Diabaté took Malian music worldwide.
MLI.p: General Assimi Goïta has ruled since leading coups in 2020 and 2021. In 2025 his junta dissolved all political parties and gave him a renewable five-year term as president without an election. Mali expelled French troops and a UN peacekeeping mission and turned to Russian forces, first the Wagner Group and then the state-run Africa Corps. With Burkina Faso and Niger, also run by juntas, it left ECOWAS in 2025. The war is going badly: since 2025 the al-Qaeda-linked JNIM has blockaded fuel supplies, and in April 2026 attacks across the country killed the defence minister.
q: Which country is named after a medieval empire whose ruler Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage carrying vast gold?
Which country did France send troops to in 2013 after Tuareg rebels and jihadists seized the north?
Which country has the Great Mosque of Djenné, the largest mud-brick building in the world?

SEN.t: Senegal was France's oldest foothold in West Africa. Saint-Louis was founded as a French trading post in 1659, and the island of Gorée off Dakar became a symbol of the Atlantic slave trade. From 1848 Africans born in the 'Four Communes', the oldest towns, could vote for a member of the French parliament, and in 1914 Blaise Diagne became the first Black African elected to it. Dakar became the capital of French West Africa, and Senegalese riflemen, the tirailleurs, fought for France in both world wars; in 1944 French troops shot dozens of them at Thiaroye when they demanded unpaid wages. Senegal became independent in 1960 under the poet-president Léopold Sédar Senghor, a founder of the Négritude movement. It is one of the few African states never to have had a coup. In 2000 the opposition leader Abdoulaye Wade won the presidency, and in 2012 he lost to Macky Sall, peaceful handovers that cemented Senegal's democratic reputation.
SEN.c: Wolof is spoken by most people and French is official. Most Senegalese are Muslims who belong to Sufi brotherhoods such as the Mourides, whose yearly pilgrimage to Touba draws millions. Teranga, the Wolof word for hospitality, is a point of national pride. Mbalax music, made famous by Youssou N'Dour, Senegalese wrestling and the national dish thieboudienne, fish with rice, are everyday culture.
SEN.p: Bassirou Diomaye Faye won the 2024 presidential election days after leaving prison, standing in for the popular opposition leader Ousmane Sonko, who was barred from running. Faye made Sonko prime minister, and their PASTEF party won a big majority in parliament. The new government found that its predecessor had hidden large debts, which led to a debt crisis and stalled IMF talks. The two men fell out, and in May 2026 Faye sacked Sonko and appointed the economist Ahmadou Al Aminou Lo. Sonko became speaker of parliament, and Faye has launched his own party. Youth unemployment and migration by boat to Europe are big issues.
q: Which country's island of Gorée became a symbol of the Atlantic slave trade?
Which country's first president was the poet Léopold Sédar Senghor, a founder of Négritude?
Which country's Mouride pilgrimage to Touba draws millions, and whose mbalax music was made famous by Youssou N'Dour?

NGA.t: Before colonial rule the land held the Sokoto Caliphate in the Muslim north, Yoruba kingdoms such as Oyo in the southwest, the Benin kingdom, famous for its brass sculptures, and Igbo communities in the southeast. Britain took over step by step in the 1800s and in 1914 merged its northern and southern protectorates into one colony, named after the Niger River. It ruled the north through emirs and the south more directly, leaving very different regions. Nigeria became independent in 1960. Rivalry between regions led to two coups in 1966 and to the civil war of 1967 to 1970, when the Igbo-led southeast tried to break away as Biafra; between half a million and two million people died, many from starvation. Oil from the Niger Delta made the state rich but fed corruption, and military rulers held power for most of the next three decades. Civilian rule returned in 1999. Since 2009 the jihadist group Boko Haram has waged war in the northeast.
NGA.c: With well over 200 million people, Nigeria is Africa's most populous country, home to more than 250 ethnic groups, with English as the shared language and Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo widely spoken. Nollywood makes more films a year than Hollywood, Afrobeats stars like Burna Boy and Wizkid fill stadiums worldwide, and Nigeria and Ghana argue happily over who makes the best jollof rice.
NGA.p: Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress has been president since winning the 2023 election. He scrapped the costly fuel subsidy and let the naira float, which pushed inflation to its highest in decades, though investors welcomed the reforms. Insecurity is the biggest worry: jihadists in the northeast, armed 'bandit' gangs in the northwest and clashes between herders and farmers kill thousands a year, and mass school kidnappings returned in late 2025. That December the United States, which had accused Nigeria of failing to protect Christians, struck Islamic State targets with Nigeria's cooperation. Tinubu seeks a second term in the January 2027 election.
q: Which country's southeast tried to break away as Biafra in a 1967–70 civil war?
Which country did Britain create in 1914 by merging northern and southern protectorates, naming it after a river?
Which is Africa's most populous country, home of Nollywood and Afrobeats stars Burna Boy and Wizkid?

BEN.t: The Kingdom of Dahomey, based at Abomey, grew rich in the 1700s and 1800s by capturing people in war and selling them at the port of Ouidah to European slave traders. Its army included a famous regiment of women soldiers. France conquered it in the 1890s and made it part of French West Africa. Its long, narrow shape comes from colonial borders drawn inland from a short stretch of coast. It became independent as Dahomey in 1960, the Year of Africa, and suffered half a dozen coups in its first twelve years. In 1972 Mathieu Kérékou seized power, declared a Marxist-Leninist state, and in 1975 renamed the country Benin. When the economy collapsed at the end of the Cold War, a national conference in 1990 stripped him of power, and he lost an election the next year, one of the first peaceful handovers in Africa. Benin was long seen as a model West African democracy.
BEN.c: Benin is the birthplace of Vodun, the religion that travelled with enslaved people to become Haitian Vodou, and 10 January is a national Vodun holiday with big celebrations in Ouidah. French is official, alongside Fon, Yoruba and dozens of others. The singer Angélique Kidjo is its best-known star, and the royal palaces of Abomey are a World Heritage Site.
BEN.p: Romuald Wadagni, finance minister for ten years under Patrice Talon, won the April 2026 presidential election with over 94% of the vote and took office in May; Talon, president from 2016 to 2026, stepped down after two terms. Critics say democracy has narrowed sharply since 2016: in January 2026 pro-government parties won every seat in parliament, and terms were extended to seven years. Soldiers tried and failed to overthrow Talon in December 2025. In the north, jihadist fighters spilling over from Burkina Faso and Niger have killed dozens of soldiers, and relations with Niger's military government are tense.
q: Which country was the Kingdom of Dahomey, whose army included a famous regiment of women soldiers?
Which country did Mathieu Kérékou declare a Marxist-Leninist state, and rename in 1975?
Which country is the birthplace of Vodun, celebrated with a national holiday every 10 January?

AGO.t: Portugal held Angola's coast for nearly 400 years and shipped millions of enslaved people from Luanda and Benguela to Brazil. Only in the 20th century did it conquer the interior and send large numbers of settlers to grow coffee and cotton. In 1961 three rival movements, divided largely by region and ethnic group, began a war of independence: the MPLA, UNITA and the FNLA. When Portugal's 1974 Carnation Revolution ended its empire, Angola became independent in 1975 and fell straight into civil war. It became one of the Cold War's biggest proxy fights: the Marxist MPLA government was backed by the Soviet Union and tens of thousands of Cuban troops, while UNITA under Jonas Savimbi had help from the US and apartheid South Africa. The war lasted until Savimbi was killed in 2002. Oil then made Angola one of Africa's biggest producers, but much of the wealth went to a small elite around President José Eduardo dos Santos, who ruled from 1979 to 2017.
AGO.c: Portuguese is the national language, and Luanda is one of the largest Portuguese-speaking cities in the world. Kizomba and semba, Angolan dance music, spread across the Portuguese-speaking world, and the old link to Brazil shows in shared food and rhythms. Angola is Africa's strongest basketball nation, and funje, a cassava porridge, is eaten with fish or chicken stews.
AGO.p: João Lourenço of the MPLA, which has ruled since independence, has been president since 2017 and cannot run again in 2027. He began with an anti-corruption drive against the dos Santos family, but critics say it targeted rivals. Angola left OPEC in 2024 and is trying to rely less on oil, with US and European money going into the Lobito Corridor railway to carry Congolese and Zambian copper to its coast. Cuts to fuel subsidies set off a taxi strike and riots in July 2025 in which 22 people died. Poverty and youth unemployment remain high.
q: Which country's Marxist MPLA government was backed by tens of thousands of Cuban troops against UNITA's Jonas Savimbi?
Which country did José Eduardo dos Santos rule from 1979 to 2017 as oil made it one of Africa's biggest producers?
Which country gave the world kizomba and semba dance music, and is Africa's strongest basketball nation?

HRV.t: Croatia entered a union with the Hungarian crown in 1102 and later became part of the Habsburg lands, defending their border against the Ottomans. When Austria-Hungary collapsed in 1918 it joined the new Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia, where many Croats resented Serbian dominance. In World War II Germany and Italy set up a puppet state run by the fascist Ustaše, which murdered Serbs, Jews and Roma in camps such as Jasenovac. Tito, himself half Croat, led the communist partisans to victory and rebuilt Yugoslavia. As it fell apart, Croatia declared independence in 1991. Local Serbs, backed by the Yugoslav army, rebelled and held about a quarter of the country; Vukovar was flattened and Dubrovnik shelled. In 1995 Operation Storm retook most of that land, and about 200,000 Serbs fled. Croatia joined NATO in 2009 and the European Union in 2013, and adopted the euro in 2023.
HRV.c: The Adriatic coast, Dubrovnik's walls (a Game of Thrones filming location), Split's Roman palace and over 1,000 islands draw millions of tourists, many on sailing holidays. Croats are passionate about football and reached the World Cup final in 2018. The necktie is named after Croatian soldiers' scarves, the cravat. Seafood, truffles from Istria and slow-cooked peka are local favourites.
HRV.p: Andrej Plenković of the conservative Croatian Democratic Union has been prime minister since 2016, and since 2024 has governed with the nationalist Homeland Movement. Zoran Milanović, a former Social Democrat prime minister and now a sharp critic of the government and of arming Ukraine, won a second term as president by a landslide in January 2025. The two men feud openly. Key issues are high inflation and housing costs driven partly by tourism, young people emigrating to richer EU countries, corruption cases in state companies, and summer wildfires such as one that threatened Split in August 2026.
q: Which country retook most of its rebel-held land in Operation Storm in 1995?
Which country entered a union with the Hungarian crown in 1102?
Which country gave the necktie its name, from its soldiers' scarves, the cravat?

SVN.t: Slovenes lived for centuries under the Habsburgs, who ruled from Vienna, and their language survived mainly through priests and poets such as France Prešeren. When Austria-Hungary fell in 1918, Slovenia joined the new kingdom that became Yugoslavia, although Italy took the western lands around Trieste. In World War II Germany, Italy and Hungary carved it up, and Tito's Partisans fought the occupiers while a bitter civil war split Slovenes. After the war Slovenia became the richest of Yugoslavia's six republics, with strong industry and close trade with Austria and Italy. In the 1980s its young people and writers pushed for freedom, and Slovenes grew tired of subsidising the poorer south. It declared independence in June 1991, and the Yugoslav army withdrew after a war of just ten days. Because it was small and almost entirely Slovene, it escaped the wars that followed. It joined NATO and the European Union in 2004 and was the first former communist country to adopt the euro, in 2007.
SVN.c: More than half the country is forest, and brown bears still roam it. Lake Bled with its island church, the Postojna caves and the Julian Alps draw visitors. Beekeeping is a national tradition, with painted beehive panels, and the Carniolan honeybee is native here. Slovenes love skiing and hiking, and basketball star Luka Dončić and cyclists Tadej Pogačar and Primož Roglič are national heroes.
SVN.p: Janez Janša of the conservative Slovenian Democratic Party became prime minister for the fourth time in May 2026, leading a right-wing coalition. In the March election Robert Golob's liberal Freedom Movement, which had governed since 2022, won 29 of 90 seats to Janša's 28, but the right was able to assemble a majority. Janša's government quickly lifted the sanctions that Golob's government had imposed on Israel over the war in Gaza. Nataša Pirc Musar, a liberal, is president. Healthcare waiting lists, housing, media freedom and Janša's past clashes with journalists and the EU shape the debate.
q: Which country won independence in 1991 after a war of just ten days?
Which country was the first former communist country to adopt the euro, in 2007?
Which country has Lake Bled, a beekeeping tradition and basketball star Luka Dončić?

QAT.t: For centuries the people of this small desert peninsula lived from pearl diving, fishing and trade. The Al Thani family emerged as leaders in the mid-1800s, and Qatar spent decades under loose Ottoman control before signing a protection treaty with Britain in 1916. When Japanese cultured pearls and the Great Depression wrecked the pearl trade in the 1930s, many Qataris went hungry or left. Oil was found at Dukhan in 1939, but World War II delayed exports until 1949. When Britain withdrew from the Gulf in 1971, Qatar chose independence rather than join the United Arab Emirates. The real turning point was the North Field, a vast offshore gas field found in 1971 and shared with Iran. Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa, who deposed his father in 1995, invested in exports of liquefied natural gas, launched Al Jazeera in 1996 and hosted the main US air base in the region. Gas wealth made Qatar one of the richest countries per person in the world.
QAT.c: Only about one in ten residents is a Qatari citizen. Most are workers from South Asia, the Philippines and elsewhere, whose treatment drew criticism before the 2022 FIFA World Cup, the first held in the Arab world. Doha has the Museum of Islamic Art, air-conditioned malls and the airline Qatar Airways. Falconry, camel racing and coffee with dates remain part of Qatari life.
QAT.p: Emir Tamim bin Hamad has ruled since his father handed over power in 2013, and there are no political parties; Mohammed bin Abdulrahman is prime minister. Qatar's role as a mediator, including hosting Hamas's political office, drew an Israeli airstrike on Doha in September 2025, and Qatar then helped broker the Gaza ceasefire. In the 2026 Iran war, Iranian missiles and drones hit the US base at Al Udeid and the giant gas plant at Ras Laffan, halting exports. The emir said state revenue fell by more than 40% in the first half of the year.
q: Which country launched Al Jazeera in 1996?
Which country chose independence in 1971 rather than join the United Arab Emirates?
Which country hosted the 2022 FIFA World Cup, the first held in the Arab world?

SAU.t: In 1902 the young Abdulaziz ibn Saud, known as Ibn Saud, recaptured Riyadh for his family, which had ruled central Arabia on and off since the 1700s in alliance with the strict Wahhabi movement of Sunni Islam. During World War I Britain backed both him and his rival, Sharif Hussein of Mecca, against the Ottomans. In 1924 and 1925 Ibn Saud conquered the Hejaz, including Mecca and Medina, and in 1932 he named his united kingdom Saudi Arabia. American geologists struck oil in 1938, and in 1945 Ibn Saud met Franklin Roosevelt aboard a US warship, sealing a partnership of oil for security that lasted through the Cold War. The 1973 oil embargo against Israel's backers made Saudi Arabia hugely rich and powerful. After Islamist militants seized Mecca's Grand Mosque in 1979, the rulers gave clerics more say over daily life. Fifteen of the 19 hijackers of 11 September 2001 were Saudis, which strained ties with the US.
SAU.c: Every year close to two million Muslims perform the Hajj in Mecca, a city non-Muslims may not enter. Saudis drink cardamom-spiced Arabic coffee with dates, eat kabsa, spiced rice with meat, and gather in desert camps in winter. Since 2017 cinemas, concerts and tourist visas have arrived, women have been allowed to drive since 2018, and giant building projects such as NEOM are rising in the desert.
SAU.p: King Salman, now around 90, has reigned since 2015, but day-to-day power lies with his son, Mohammed bin Salman, who is crown prince and prime minister. His Vision 2030 plan aims to end dependence on oil through tourism, entertainment and new industries, while dissent is crushed and executions have reached record numbers. The 2018 murder of the journalist Jamal Khashoggi damaged his reputation in the West. In 2026 Iran struck Saudi oil sites during its war with the US and Israel, and Yemen's Houthis attacked southern cities. Saudi Arabia is now backing a Yemeni government offensive against them.
q: Which country did Ibn Saud name in 1932 after conquering the Hejaz?
Which country's ruler met Franklin Roosevelt aboard a US warship in 1945, sealing a partnership of oil for security?
Which country has allowed women to drive since 2018 and is building NEOM in the desert?

BWA.t: In 1885, Tswana chiefs asked Britain for protection to keep out Boer settlers from the south and Cecil Rhodes's company from the east, and the Bechuanaland Protectorate was largely left alone. Britain even ran it from Mafikeng, a town in South Africa, and spent almost nothing on it. Many expected it to be absorbed into South Africa, but the rise of apartheid made that impossible. When Botswana became independent in 1966 under Seretse Khama, it was one of the poorest countries in the world, with only a few kilometres of paved road. A year later diamonds were discovered. Instead of letting the money vanish, the government formed a 50-50 partnership with De Beers, saved the earnings and spent them on roads, schools and clinics. Botswana became one of the world's fastest-growing economies and one of Africa's most stable democracies, though from the 1990s it was hit hard by HIV/AIDS, which for a time cut life expectancy sharply.
BWA.c: Setswana and English are official, and most people are Tswana. Cattle are a symbol of wealth and status, and seswaa, slow-pounded beef, is the national dish. The Okavango Delta and the Kalahari Desert make it a high-end safari destination, and it has the largest elephant population of any country. Letsile Tebogo won Olympic 200 m gold in 2024, and the country partied.
BWA.p: Duma Boko, a human rights lawyer, became president in November 2024 when his Umbrella for Democratic Change won a landslide, ending 58 years of rule by the Botswana Democratic Party; the handover was peaceful. He inherited a crisis: a global slump in demand for natural diamonds, hit by cheap lab-grown stones, has cut government income. In August 2025 Boko declared a public health emergency over shortages of medicine in hospitals. The government signed a new deal with De Beers giving Botswana a bigger share of diamond sales, and wants local owners to hold stakes in new mines.
q: Which country was so poor at independence in 1966 that it had only a few kilometres of paved road, until diamonds were found a year later?
Which country formed a 50-50 diamond partnership with De Beers and spent the earnings on roads, schools and clinics?
Which country has the largest elephant population of any country, and the Okavango Delta?

ZWE.t: From about the 1100s the Shona built Great Zimbabwe, a stone city that traded gold to the Indian Ocean coast. In 1890 Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company sent settlers north and seized the land; Ndebele and Shona risings in 1896 were crushed, and the colony was named Southern Rhodesia. White settlers, a small minority, took the best farmland and ran the country. In 1965, to avoid majority rule, Ian Smith's government declared independence from Britain. No country recognised it, and a guerrilla war followed against two liberation movements, Robert Mugabe's ZANU and Joshua Nkomo's ZAPU, backed by China and the Soviet Union. A 1979 settlement led to elections, and Mugabe became prime minister of independent Zimbabwe in 1980. In the 1980s his Fifth Brigade killed thousands of Ndebele civilians in the Gukurahundi massacres. From 2000 his seizures of white-owned farms helped cause economic collapse and hyperinflation. Mugabe ruled until the army forced him out in 2017.
ZWE.c: The country takes its name from Great Zimbabwe, and the soapstone Zimbabwe bird is a national emblem. English, Shona and Ndebele are among 16 official languages, and sadza, a maize porridge, is the staple. Mbira (thumb piano) music is central to Shona culture, and Thomas Mapfumo's chimurenga songs fuelled the liberation struggle. Many Zimbabweans work abroad, especially in South Africa and Britain.
ZWE.p: Emmerson Mnangagwa, Mugabe's former deputy, took power with army backing in 2017 and won disputed elections in 2018 and 2023. In 2026 parliament, dominated by his ZANU-PF party, passed a constitutional change that extends presidential and parliamentary terms from five to seven years, letting him stay until 2030 instead of 2028, and replaces direct presidential elections with a vote in parliament. He signed it in July 2026; opposition parties, lawyers and civil society say it needed a referendum. Critics of the government are often arrested. The economy has suffered from repeated currency crises, including the new ZiG currency launched in 2024, and from drought.
q: Which country's white government under Ian Smith declared independence from Britain in 1965?
Which country did Robert Mugabe lead from 1980 until the army forced him out in 2017?
Which country takes its name from a medieval stone city, and has a soapstone bird as its emblem?

PAK.t: Pakistan was born in August 1947, when Britain partitioned India. Muhammad Ali Jinnah's Muslim League argued that Muslims needed their own homeland, and the new state was made of two Muslim-majority regions 1,500 km apart, West and East Pakistan. Partition brought mass killing and one of the largest migrations in history, and war with India over Kashmir began within months. Jinnah died in 1948, and the army soon became the strongest force in the state: generals Ayub Khan, Yahya Khan, Zia ul-Haq and Pervez Musharraf ruled for over 30 years in total. In 1971 the Bengali east rebelled against domination by the west and, with India's help, became Bangladesh. In the Cold War Pakistan sided with the US, and in the 1980s it channelled American and Saudi aid to Afghan fighters resisting the Soviet invasion. It tested nuclear weapons in 1998, weeks after India. After 2001 it was again a US ally, while fighting Taliban militants at home.
PAK.c: Urdu is the national language, though more people speak Punjabi at home, and English is used in government and business. Cricket is a passion: Imran Khan captained the team to the 1992 World Cup. Sufi shrines, qawwali music made famous by Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, biryani, nihari and brightly painted trucks are national trademarks. The Karakoram range holds K2, the world's second-highest mountain.
PAK.p: Shehbaz Sharif has been prime minister since 2024, after an election that the party of former prime minister Imran Khan says was rigged; Asif Ali Zardari is president. Real power lies with army chief Asim Munir, made field marshal after a brief war with India in May 2025 and given command of all the armed forces by a 2025 constitutional amendment. Khan remains in prison on several convictions. Clashes with Afghanistan's Taliban grew into open fighting in 2026, militant attacks continue in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Pakistan tried to broker peace between the US and Iran.
q: Which country was founded in 1947 in two parts 1,500 km apart, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah?
Which country tested nuclear weapons in 1998, weeks after India?
Which country's cricket team Imran Khan captained to the 1992 World Cup?

BGR.t: Medieval Bulgaria's scholars spread the Cyrillic alphabet across the Slavic world. The Ottomans then ruled it for almost 500 years. After a bloody uprising in 1876, Russia went to war with the Ottomans and freed Bulgaria in 1878, which is why many Bulgarians still feel close to Russia. It declared full independence in 1908. Hungry to win back lands with Bulgarian speakers, it fought the Balkan Wars and then joined the losing side in both world wars. In World War II it was allied with Germany but refused to hand over its own Jews, about 48,000 people, though it deported more than 11,000 Jews from Greek and Yugoslav lands it occupied. The Soviet army arrived in 1944, and under Todor Zhivkov, who ruled from 1954 to 1989, Bulgaria became Moscow's most loyal ally. Late in his rule, a campaign to force Turks to take Slavic names drove more than 300,000 to flee to Turkey in 1989. Bulgaria joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007.
BGR.c: Bulgaria uses the Cyrillic alphabet, which is celebrated with a national holiday every 24 May. People nod to mean no and shake their heads to mean yes. It is known for yogurt, rose oil from the Valley of Roses, banitsa pastry and the haunting harmonies of its women's choirs. In March people exchange martenitsi, red and white woven bracelets.
BGR.p: After years of repeated elections, mass anti-corruption protests in December 2025 brought down Rosen Zhelyazkov's government. Rumen Radev, president since 2017, resigned in January 2026 to enter party politics, and his vice-president, Iliana Iotova, became the country's first woman president. Radev's new Progressive Bulgaria alliance won the April 2026 election, and he became prime minister in May. His government stopped supplying weapons to Ukraine. Iotova led the first round of the October 2026 presidential election and faced the pro-Western Andrey Gyurov in a runoff on 1 November. Bulgaria adopted the euro on 1 January 2026; corruption and rising prices remain the main concerns.
q: Which country's medieval scholars spread the Cyrillic alphabet across the Slavic world?
Which country, allied with Germany in World War II, refused to hand over its own 48,000 Jews?
In which country do people exchange red and white martenitsi bracelets in March and make rose oil in the Valley of Roses?

THA.t: The Thai kingdoms of Sukhothai and then Ayutthaya ruled the Chao Phraya valley from the 1200s until Burmese armies sacked Ayutthaya in 1767. The Chakri dynasty, which still reigns, founded Bangkok in 1782. In the age of empire, kings Mongkut and Chulalongkorn modernised the army, schools and railways and gave up border lands to France and Britain, keeping Siam the only Southeast Asian country never colonised. In 1932 officers and officials ended absolute monarchy in a bloodless revolution, and in 1939 the country was renamed Thailand. During World War II it allied with Japan. In the Cold War it became a firm US ally, hosting American air bases during the Vietnam War and fighting a communist insurgency at home. King Bhumibol, who reigned from 1946 to 2016, became a deeply revered figure. Since 1932 the army has staged about a dozen successful coups, most recently in 2006 against Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra and in 2014 against the government of his sister Yingluck.
THA.c: Thai food, from pad thai and green curry to som tam papaya salad, is loved around the world, and Bangkok's street stalls are famous. Most Thais are Theravada Buddhists, many young men spend time as monks, and the royal family is revered and protected by strict laws. Muay Thai boxing, the Songkran water festival in April and beaches such as Phuket draw millions of tourists.
THA.p: For two decades politics pitted parties linked to the former prime minister Thaksin Shinawatra against the army, courts and royalists. In 2024 his daughter Paetongtarn became prime minister, but in 2025 the Constitutional Court removed her over a leaked phone call with Cambodia's Hun Sen during a deadly border dispute. Anutin Charnvirakul of the Bhumjaithai party replaced her and, after a snap election in February 2026, won a full term. Voters also approved drafting a new constitution. Border fighting with Cambodia in 2025, slow growth and household debt dominate. Vajiralongkorn has been king since 2016.
q: Which is the only Southeast Asian country never colonised?
Which country ended absolute monarchy in a bloodless revolution in 1932?
Which country's Songkran water festival and kickboxing are world famous?

SMR.t: San Marino claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic, traditionally founded in 301 AD by Marinus, a Christian stonemason fleeing persecution, on the slopes of Monte Titano. Perched on a mountain and too small to be worth the trouble, it outlasted the city-states around it, and its statutes of 1600 still serve as its constitution. Napoleon offered it more land, which it politely refused. During Italy's unification it sheltered refugees, including Giuseppe Garibaldi in 1849, and Italy recognised its independence by treaty in 1862. In World War I it sided with Italy. A fascist party ran it from the 1920s until 1943, but in World War II it declared neutrality. In 1944 it took in about 100,000 refugees fleeing the fighting on the Gothic Line, and Allied bombers mistakenly hit it. After the war it had one of the world's few elected communist-led governments, from 1945 to 1957. It joined the Council of Europe in 1988 and the United Nations in 1992.
SMR.c: About 34,000 people live inside its 61 km², completely surrounded by Italy, and Italian is spoken. Three medieval towers crown Monte Titano and appear on the flag. Tourists come for the views, tax-free shopping, and the stamps and coins prized by collectors. Torta Tre Monti, a layered wafer cake, is the local treat, and the national football team is famous for almost never winning.
SMR.p: San Marino has no single leader. Two Captains Regent, chosen by parliament every six months, serve together as heads of state; since 1 October 2026 they have been Gerardo Giovagnoli and William Casali. Day-to-day government is run by the Congress of State, a cabinet of secretaries, and since the 2024 election a coalition led by the Christian Democrats has governed. The big long-running question is an association agreement with the European Union, which would give San Marino closer access to the EU single market. Cleaning up its banks after past scandals and the tax and residency rules for foreigners also matter.
q: Which country claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic, traditionally founded in 301 AD?
Which tiny country sheltered Garibaldi in 1849 and took in about 100,000 refugees in 1944?
Which country, completely surrounded by Italy, has three medieval towers on Monte Titano and on its flag?

HTI.t: French Saint-Domingue was the world's richest colony in the 1700s, producing sugar and coffee with the labour of hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans. Their revolt of 1791, led by figures such as Toussaint Louverture, defeated French, Spanish and British armies, and in 1804 Haiti became the first country founded by formerly enslaved people. In 1825 France forced it to pay a huge indemnity in return for recognition, a debt that drained the economy for generations. Worried about German influence during World War I, the US occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934. From 1957 François 'Papa Doc' Duvalier and then his son 'Baby Doc' ruled by terror through the Tonton Macoute militia, tolerated by the US as Cold War anti-communists. After Baby Doc fled in 1986, Jean-Bertrand Aristide became the first freely elected president in 1990, but he was overthrown twice. In January 2010 an earthquake killed well over 100,000 people around Port-au-Prince, and a cholera epidemic brought by UN peacekeepers followed.
HTI.c: Everyone speaks Haitian Creole, while French is the language of school and government. Vodou, which blends West African religion with Catholic saints, shapes art and music. Haiti's bright paintings and sculptures cut from old oil drums are famous, kompa is the dance music, and joumou, a pumpkin soup once denied to slaves, is eaten every 1 January to celebrate independence. Large communities live in Miami, New York and Montreal.
HTI.p: Haiti has no elected officials at national level. After President Jovenel Moïse was assassinated in 2021, a Transitional Presidential Council took charge in 2024, but its mandate ended on 7 February 2026, leaving Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, acting prime minister since 2024, as the sole leader. Gang coalitions such as Viv Ansanm, which the US designated a terrorist group in 2025, control most of Port-au-Prince and more than a million people have been driven from their homes. A UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, replacing a Kenyan-led mission, began arriving in April 2026. Elections set for December 2026 were postponed indefinitely in October.
q: Which became in 1804 the first country founded by formerly enslaved people?
Which country did 'Papa Doc' Duvalier and his son rule through the Tonton Macoute?
In which country is joumou pumpkin soup eaten every 1 January to celebrate independence?

DOM.t: Columbus founded the first lasting European settlements in the Americas on Hispaniola, and Santo Domingo, founded in the 1490s, has the oldest cathedral in the hemisphere. The Taíno who lived there were wiped out within decades. Spain later neglected the eastern part of the island, while France turned the west into Haiti. Haiti ruled the whole island from 1822 to 1844, and Dominicans date their independence from the revolt that ended that rule, which helps explain tense relations between the two countries today. The US occupied the country from 1916 to 1924. Rafael Trujillo, who rose through a US-trained national guard, then ruled as dictator from 1930 until he was assassinated in 1961; in 1937 his troops massacred thousands of Haitians along the border. When a revolt in 1965 seemed to threaten a leftist takeover, the US sent troops. Joaquín Balaguer, Trujillo's former aide, dominated politics for decades afterwards. Since the 1990s tourism, free trade zones and money from emigrants have made it one of Latin America's fastest-growing economies.
DOM.c: Merengue and bachata were born here and play from every car and colmado, the corner shops that double as bars. Baseball is a national obsession, and the country supplies more Major League players than anywhere outside the US. Dominicans eat 'la bandera', rice, beans and meat, at lunch, and mangú, mashed green plantain, at breakfast. Millions of tourists head for the beaches of Punta Cana every year.
DOM.p: Luis Abinader of the Modern Revolutionary Party has been president since 2020 and won a second term in 2024. He backed a 2024 constitutional change that makes it harder to extend presidential term limits, so he cannot run again. His hard line on Haiti, a border wall and mass deportations of Haitians fleeing gang violence, is popular at home, while rights groups criticise the treatment of migrants and of Dominicans of Haitian descent. Other issues are power cuts, including a nationwide blackout in February 2026, corruption and crime. In 2026 the US put a 12.5% tariff on Dominican goods.
q: Which country's capital, founded in the 1490s, has the oldest cathedral in the Americas?
Which country did Rafael Trujillo rule as dictator from 1930 until his assassination in 1961?
Where were merengue and bachata born, in a country that supplies more Major League players than anywhere outside the US?

TCD.t: Around Lake Chad, the Kanem-Bornu empire traded across the Sahara for a thousand years. France conquered the region around 1900 and assembled Chad from a desert, mostly Muslim north and a farming, partly Christian south that it favoured for schools and cotton. In 1940 Chad was the first French colony to side with de Gaulle's Free France in World War II. After independence in 1960, southerners dominated the government, and northern rebels took up arms in 1965, starting decades of civil war. Libya under Muammar Gaddafi occupied the Aouzou Strip in the north from 1973 and intervened in the fighting, while France and the US backed Chadian leaders against him in a Cold War sideshow. In 1987 Chadian troops in pickup trucks routed the Libyan army, and in 1994 the World Court ruled that the strip belongs to Chad. Idriss Déby took power in a 1990 coup and ruled for 30 years with French support, while oil from the south began flowing in 2003.
TCD.c: French and Arabic are official, and more than 100 languages are spoken. Lake Chad, once one of Africa's largest lakes, has shrunk drastically since the 1960s, and herders and farmers often clash over water and land. Zakouma National Park, where elephant numbers have recovered after poaching, and the sandstone arches of the Ennedi Plateau are its natural treasures.
TCD.p: Mahamat Déby took power in 2021 after his father, Idriss Déby, was killed fighting rebels, and was elected president in 2024 in a vote critics called unfair. In 2025 parliament abolished presidential term limits, and Succès Masra, a former prime minister and the main opposition leader, was sentenced to 20 years in prison. Chad ended its defence pact with France, whose last troops left in January 2025. The war in neighbouring Sudan has sent hundreds of thousands of refugees across the border and spilled over in drone strikes and raids, while Boko Haram attacks continue around Lake Chad.
q: Which country was the first French colony to side with de Gaulle's Free France in 1940?
Which country's troops in pickup trucks routed Libya's army in 1987, and won the Aouzou Strip in a 1994 World Court ruling?
Which country's lake, once one of Africa's largest, has shrunk drastically since the 1960s?

KWT.t: The Al Sabah family has ruled Kuwait since the 1700s, when it was a small port living from pearl diving, boat building and trade between India, Arabia and Iraq. Worried about Ottoman ambitions, the ruler signed a treaty with Britain in 1899 that made Kuwait a British protectorate. Oil was found in 1938, and after World War II exports turned it from a poor town into one of the richest places on Earth. Kuwait became independent in 1961, and when Iraq claimed it, British and then Arab League troops deterred an invasion. In 1962 it adopted a constitution with an elected parliament, the first among the Gulf monarchies. Kuwait helped fund Iraq in its war with Iran in the 1980s, but in August 1990 Saddam Hussein invaded, claiming Kuwait as Iraqi territory. A US-led coalition drove Iraq out in the 1991 Gulf War, and retreating Iraqi troops set hundreds of oil wells on fire. Kuwait later served as the main launch pad for the 2003 invasion of Iraq.
KWT.c: Kuwait has some of the world's largest oil reserves, and the Kuwaiti dinar is the world's highest-valued currency unit. Citizens are a minority in their own country: most residents are foreign workers, many from South Asia and Egypt. Men gather in the evening in diwaniyas, reception rooms for talk and politics, machboos is the favourite dish, and the blue-studded Kuwait Towers are its landmark.
KWT.p: Emir Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah, who succeeded his half-brother in December 2023, suspended parliament in May 2024 for up to four years, ending decades of feuding between elected MPs and governments. Sheikh Ahmad Al-Abdullah Al-Sabah has been prime minister since then. The government has since stripped tens of thousands of people of citizenship, many of them women who gained it through marriage. During the 2026 Iran war, Iranian missiles and drones struck the airport, US bases and oil refineries. The state is trying to reduce its dependence on oil and the cost of its huge public payroll.
q: Which country did Saddam Hussein invade in August 1990, leading to the Gulf War?
Which country adopted in 1962 the first constitution with an elected parliament among the Gulf monarchies?
Which country's dinar is the world's highest-valued currency unit?

SLV.t: Spain conquered the Pipil and Lenca peoples here in the 1520s. El Salvador, Central America's smallest country, became independent in 1821. In the late 1800s coffee became king, and a handful of planter families took most of the best land. In 1932 a peasant uprising was crushed in La Matanza, 'the massacre', in which troops killed thousands of mostly Indigenous people, and army officers ruled for much of the next 50 years. In 1980 Archbishop Óscar Romero, who spoke out against army killings, was shot dead while saying Mass, and civil war broke out between the US-backed government and the leftist FMLN guerrillas. About 75,000 people died before UN-brokered peace accords in 1992. Hundreds of thousands fled to the US, where some young refugees in Los Angeles formed gangs such as MS-13. When the US deported gang members in the 1990s, the gangs took root at home, and by the 2010s El Salvador had one of the world's highest murder rates. In 2001 it adopted the US dollar.
SLV.c: Pupusas, thick corn tortillas stuffed with cheese, beans or pork and served with pickled cabbage, are the national dish. El Salvador uses the US dollar, and money sent home by Salvadorans in the US is a big part of the economy. Surfers come for the Pacific breaks around El Tunco. Saint Óscar Romero is revered, and in 2021 the country made Bitcoin legal tender, a policy scaled back in 2025.
SLV.p: Nayib Bukele has been president since 2019. In March 2022 he declared a state of emergency against the gangs and has renewed it again and again; more than 80,000 people have been arrested, murders have fallen sharply, and he is hugely popular. Rights groups report many innocent people detained and hundreds of deaths in custody. He won re-election in 2024 despite a constitutional ban, after judges he had appointed reinterpreted it, and in 2025 his supermajority scrapped term limits and lengthened terms to six years. Supporters see a model for fighting crime; critics see one-man rule.
q: Which country's Archbishop Óscar Romero was shot dead while saying Mass in 1980?
Which country's 1932 uprising was crushed in La Matanza, 'the massacre'?
Which country's national dish is the pupusa, and made Bitcoin legal tender in 2021?

GTM.t: Guatemala was the heart of the Maya world, with great cities such as Tikal at their peak more than 1,000 years ago. Spain conquered it in the 1520s and ruled Central America from here. After independence in 1821, a small elite grew coffee on land taken from Maya communities, and in the early 1900s the American United Fruit Company came to control bananas, railways and ports. In 1944 a revolution brought democracy, and President Jacobo Árbenz began handing unused land, some of it United Fruit's, to peasants. In 1954 a CIA-backed coup overthrew him, an early Cold War intervention in Latin America. A civil war between army governments and leftist guerrillas followed from 1960 to 1996. About 200,000 people died, most of them Maya killed by the army, and a UN-backed truth commission found that the army had committed acts of genocide. After the peace, organised crime and corruption grew. From 2007 a UN-backed commission, CICIG, helped prosecute even a sitting president, until the government shut it down in 2019.
GTM.c: More than 40% of Guatemalans are Indigenous, speaking over 20 Mayan languages, and many women wear hand-woven huipil blouses whose patterns mark their home village. Holy Week in the colonial city of Antigua brings processions over carpets of coloured sawdust and flowers. Black beans, tortillas and pepián stew are staples, coffee from the volcanic highlands is prized, and the temples of Tikal rise above the rainforest.
GTM.p: Bernardo Arévalo, son of Juan José Arévalo, the reforming president of the 1940s, won the 2023 election on an anti-corruption platform. He took office in January 2024 only after the attorney general, Consuelo Porras, tried to suspend his party and challenge the result. Porras, sanctioned by the US and EU as corrupt, kept blocking his reforms until her term ended in May 2026, when Arévalo appointed a replacement. Gangs are the other big issue: after prison escapes, riots and the killing of police officers, he declared a state of siege in January 2026.
q: Which country's president Jacobo Árbenz was overthrown by a CIA-backed coup in 1954?
Which country's civil war from 1960 to 1996 killed about 200,000 people, most of them Maya?
Which country has the temples of Tikal and Holy Week processions over sawdust carpets in its old colonial city?

TLS.t: Portuguese traders came to Timor for sandalwood in the 1500s, and Portugal ruled the eastern half of the island while the Dutch held the west, which later became part of Indonesia. In World War II Australian commandos fought a guerrilla campaign against the Japanese here, and tens of thousands of Timorese died. After Portugal's 1974 revolution its empire unravelled. Fretilin declared independence in November 1975, but nine days later Indonesia invaded, with tacit approval from the US and Australia, who saw Fretilin as leftist. The occupation, through fighting, famine and disease, killed between about 100,000 and 180,000 people. The 1991 Santa Cruz massacre in Dili, filmed by a foreign journalist, drew world attention, and in 1996 Bishop Carlos Belo and José Ramos-Horta won the Nobel Peace Prize. After Suharto fell, Indonesia allowed a UN-run vote in 1999: 78% chose independence, and pro-Indonesian militias then burned much of the country. After a period of UN rule, Timor-Leste became independent in 2002.
TLS.c: Timor-Leste is one of only two Asian countries with a Catholic majority, alongside the Philippines. Tetum and Portuguese are official, and Indonesian and English are widely understood. Coffee from mountain villages is the main export besides oil and gas, and handwoven tais cloth is worn at ceremonies. It is one of the world's youngest countries, with a very young population.
TLS.p: The heroes of the independence struggle still dominate politics.
