José Ramos-Horta was elected president again in 2022, and Xanana Gusmão, the former guerrilla leader, became prime minister again in 2023. In October 2025 the country achieved a long-held goal by joining ASEAN. The oil and gas fields that fund most of the budget are running dry, and the government hopes to develop the Greater Sunrise gas field with Australia. Poverty and youth unemployment are widespread, and in 2025 student protests forced the government to drop plans to buy new cars for MPs.
q: Which country did Indonesia invade nine days after it declared independence in 1975?
Which country's 1991 Santa Cruz massacre, filmed by a foreign journalist, drew world attention?
Which is one of only two Asian countries with a Catholic majority, alongside the Philippines?

BRN.t: In the 1400s and 1500s the sultanate of Brunei was a sea power that controlled much of Borneo's coast and traded as far as the Philippines. It declined, and in the 1800s it lost land to the Brooke family, the British 'White Rajahs' of Sarawak, and to the British North Borneo Company in what is now Sabah. It became a British protectorate in 1888, and in 1890 Sarawak took the Limbang valley, splitting what was left into two small pieces. Oil was found at Seria in 1929 and made it rich. Japan occupied it from 1941 to 1945. In 1962 a revolt by the left-wing Brunei People's Party, which wanted a larger independent state, was crushed by British troops, and the sultan has ruled under emergency powers ever since. Brunei chose not to join Malaysia in 1963, partly over oil revenues and the sultan's status. Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah took the throne in 1967, and Brunei became fully independent in 1984.
BRN.c: Brunei is a strict Muslim monarchy: alcohol is not sold, and the national ideology is Malay Islamic Monarchy. The golden-domed Omar Ali Saifuddien Mosque and the sultan's huge palace dominate the capital, and in the water village of Kampong Ayer people still live in stilt houses over the river. Oil wealth pays for free healthcare and schooling, and there is no personal income tax. Ambuyat, a sticky sago starch, is a local speciality.
BRN.p: Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah, on the throne since 1967, is also prime minister, defence minister and finance minister, and rules as one of the world's few absolute monarchs; there is no elected parliament. In 2019 Brunei brought in the harshest parts of a sharia penal code, including death by stoning, though after protests around the world it extended its moratorium on the death penalty. In June 2026 the sultan brought his sons into the cabinet, making Prince Abdul Mateen foreign minister. The big challenge is life after oil and gas, which still provide most of the state's income and are slowly running down.
q: Which sultanate lost much of its land to the British 'White Rajahs' of Sarawak in the 1800s?
Which country chose not to join Malaysia in 1963 and became fully independent in 1984?
Which oil-rich Muslim monarchy has a water village of stilt houses, Kampong Ayer, and no personal income tax?

MCO.t: In 1297 François Grimaldi and his men, disguised as monks, seized the fortress on the Rock of Monaco, and his family still rules. For centuries the tiny state survived under the protection of Spain, then France, then Sardinia. In 1861 it gave up the towns of Menton and Roquebrune to France, losing most of its land, and needed a new income. Prince Charles III opened a casino on a bare hill that became Monte Carlo, and when the railway arrived from Paris in 1868 the rich came. A 1918 treaty with France said Monaco would become part of France if the Grimaldi line died out. In World War II Italian and then German troops occupied it, and in 1942 its police rounded up dozens of foreign Jews and handed them to the Nazis, for which Prince Albert II apologised in 2015. Prince Rainier III, who reigned from 1949 to 2005, married the Hollywood star Grace Kelly in 1956 and turned Monaco into a hub of banking, property and tourism, even reclaiming land from the sea.
MCO.c: About 38,000 people live here, but only about a quarter are Monégasque citizens; the rest come from France, Italy, Britain and dozens of other countries. French is the official language. Residents pay no income tax, and superyachts fill the harbour. The Formula One Grand Prix races through the streets each spring, and the Monte Carlo casino, the Monte-Carlo Masters tennis and the clifftop Oceanographic Museum draw visitors.
MCO.p: Prince Albert II, who has reigned since 2005, holds real power: he appoints the government, which is led by a minister of state, while the elected National Council has a limited say. Christophe Mirmand, a former French prefect, was appointed minister of state in July 2025 after Didier Guillaume died in office. In June 2025 the EU put Monaco on its list of high-risk countries for money laundering, a blow to a place built on wealth and banking. Monaco recognised the State of Palestine in 2025, and Pope Leo XIV visited in March 2026.
q: Which country's ruling family has held power since François Grimaldi, disguised as a monk, seized its fortress in 1297?
Which country's Prince Rainier III married the Hollywood star Grace Kelly in 1956?
Which country's streets host a Formula One Grand Prix each spring, and whose residents pay no income tax?

DZA.t: France invaded in 1830 and, unlike its other colonies, treated Algeria as part of France itself, splitting it into French departments and settling about a million Europeans on the best farmland. Muslim Algerians had few rights, and France stretched the territory deep into the Sahara, which is why Algeria is now Africa's largest country. The war of independence, launched by the National Liberation Front (FLN) in 1954, was one of the bloodiest of the 20th century, with torture and massacres on both sides. It brought down a French government and returned de Gaulle to power. When Algeria won in 1962, almost all the settlers fled to France. The FLN then ran a one-party socialist state, close to the Soviet Union and funded by oil and gas found in the Sahara. When it cancelled a 1992 election that Islamists were about to win, a civil war killed up to 200,000 people. In 2019 mass street protests, the Hirak, forced President Abdelaziz Bouteflika to resign after 20 years.
DZA.c: Arabic and Berber (Tamazight) are both official, and French is still everywhere, a legacy of 130 years of French rule. Raï music grew up in the port city of Oran, couscous is the national dish, and football is a passion. The ruins of Roman cities such as Timgad, and the Saharan oases and rock art of Tassili n'Ajjer, draw the few tourists who come.
DZA.p: President Abdelmadjid Tebboune, backed by the army, was elected in 2019 and re-elected in 2024, and Sifi Ghrieb has been prime minister since September 2025. Opposition and press freedom remain tightly limited. Relations with France collapsed after Paris backed Morocco's claim to Western Sahara in 2024: the two expelled diplomats, Algeria jailed the French-Algerian writer Boualem Sansal before pardoning him, and parliament passed a law criminalising French colonisation. Algeria also quarrelled with Mali over a downed drone, and in September 2026 cut ties with the United Arab Emirates. Oil and gas still pay for almost everything.
q: Which country did France treat as part of France itself, splitting it into French departments from 1830?
Which country's FLN fought a war of independence from 1954 that brought de Gaulle back to power in France?
Which is Africa's largest country, where raï music grew up in the port city of Oran?

MOZ.t: Arab and Swahili traders ran ports along this coast long before Vasco da Gama arrived in 1498. Portugal set up trading forts from the early 1500s, but it controlled the interior only from the late 1800s, partly through private companies that used forced labour. In 1962 nationalist groups united as FRELIMO, which launched a guerrilla war in 1964. The war ended when Portugal's Carnation Revolution of 1974 brought down its empire, and Mozambique became independent in 1975 under Samora Machel. FRELIMO built a Marxist one-party state allied with the Soviet Union and sheltered guerrillas fighting white rule in Rhodesia and South Africa. In response, Rhodesia and then apartheid South Africa backed the RENAMO rebels. The civil war, along with famine, killed about a million people before a peace deal in 1992. FRELIMO has won every election since multiparty voting began in 1994, while RENAMO became the opposition. In the 2010s huge gas fields were found off the far north coast, promising a boom.
MOZ.c: Portuguese is the official language, though most people first speak an African language such as Emakhuwa or Changana. The flag is the only national flag with a modern rifle on it, an AK-47, a symbol of the independence struggle. Marrabenta music, peri-peri prawns and matapa, cassava leaves cooked with peanuts and coconut, come from here. The Bazaruto islands and the old stone town on Mozambique Island draw visitors.
MOZ.p: Daniel Chapo of FRELIMO became president in January 2025 after an October 2024 election that observers said was flawed. His rival Venâncio Mondlane claimed victory, and months of protests followed in which security forces killed hundreds of people; Mondlane was later charged over the unrest. Chapo appointed Maria Benvinda Levy as prime minister. In the northern province of Cabo Delgado, an insurgency by Islamic State-linked fighters, running since 2017, has killed thousands and driven hundreds of thousands from their homes; Rwandan troops help the army. TotalEnergies restarted its huge liquefied gas project there in January 2026 after a five-year pause. Debt, poverty and cyclones add to the strain.
q: Which country's FRELIMO built a Marxist state, fighting RENAMO rebels backed by Rhodesia and South Africa?
Which country became independent in 1975 under Samora Machel?
Which country's flag is the only national flag with a modern rifle, an AK-47?

SWZ.t: The Swazi kingdom took shape in the early 1800s under kings who united local clans and held off Zulu raids from the south. Later in the century, Boer and British concession hunters persuaded King Mbandzeni to sign away rights to much of the land and minerals. The Boer Transvaal republic ran the territory from 1894, and after Britain won the Boer War it became a British protectorate in 1903. That kept it out of the Union of South Africa formed in 1910, even though it is wedged between South Africa and Mozambique. It became independent in 1968 under King Sobhuza II, who had reigned since 1899. In 1973 he scrapped the constitution and banned political parties, ruling directly until his death in 1982, after one of the longest reigns in recorded history. His son Mswati III was crowned in 1986 at age 18. From the 1990s HIV/AIDS hit Eswatini harder than almost anywhere. In 2018 Mswati renamed the country Eswatini, 'land of the Swazis'.
SWZ.c: SiSwati and English are official, and most people are Swazi. Each year tens of thousands of young women take part in the Umhlanga, the Reed Dance, and the Incwala kingship ceremony is the most sacred event of the year. The king has many wives, and his lavish lifestyle contrasts with widespread poverty. Mbabane and the Ezulwini Valley are surrounded by game reserves.
SWZ.p: King Mswati III, on the throne since 1986, is Africa's last absolute monarch: he appoints the prime minister, now Russell Dlamini, and parties cannot run in elections. Pro-democracy protests in 2021 were crushed, with dozens killed. Eswatini is one of the last countries to recognise Taiwan rather than China, and Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te visited in 2026. It has taken in deportees from the United States in return for payment. With the world's highest HIV rate, it was the first African country to roll out the twice-yearly prevention injection lenacapavir in 2025.
q: Which country's King Sobhuza II reigned from 1899 until 1982, one of the longest reigns in history?
Which country did King Mswati III rename in 2018 as 'land of the Swazis'?
Which kingdom holds the Umhlanga, or Reed Dance, every year?

BDI.t: An old kingdom in the African Great Lakes, ruled by a mwami or king, Burundi became part of German East Africa in the 1890s. After Germany lost World War I, Belgium took it over together with Rwanda as Ruanda-Urundi. The Belgians ruled through the Tutsi elite and issued identity cards marking people as Hutu or Tutsi, hardening a social divide into an ethnic one. Burundi became independent in 1962 as a monarchy, but the army, dominated by Tutsi officers, overthrew the king in 1966. In 1972 the army killed perhaps 100,000 or more Hutu after a rebellion. In 1993 Melchior Ndadaye became the first Hutu president in a free election, and was murdered by soldiers within months. That set off a civil war which killed about 300,000 people before peace deals, brokered with Nelson Mandela's help, shared power between the groups. Pierre Nkurunziza, a former Hutu rebel leader, ruled from 2005 until 2020, and his bid for a third term in 2015 brought protests, a failed coup and a harsh crackdown.
BDI.c: Kirundi, French and English are official, and nearly everyone speaks Kirundi, which is unusual in Africa. The royal drummers of Burundi, who leap and dance around huge drums carried on their heads, are on UNESCO's list of world cultural heritage. Most people farm small plots on steep green hills, and coffee and tea are the main exports.
BDI.p: Évariste Ndayishimiye, a former rebel commander from the ruling CNDD-FDD party, has been president since 2020 and in 2026 also became chairperson of the African Union. In the 2025 parliamentary election his party won every seat, after the main opposition leader, Agathon Rwasa, was removed as head of his party in 2024. Burundi is one of the poorest countries in the world, with chronic fuel and foreign currency shortages. It has sent thousands of troops to fight alongside the Congolese army against the Rwanda-backed M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, and in late 2025 the rebels captured several hundred Burundian soldiers.
q: Which country, ruled by Belgium together with Rwanda, saw its first freely elected Hutu president murdered within months in 1993?
Which country's civil war was ended by peace deals brokered with Nelson Mandela's help, sharing power between Hutu and Tutsi?
Which country's royal drummers, who leap around huge drums carried on their heads, are on UNESCO's heritage list?

RWA.t: For centuries Rwanda was a kingdom ruled by a Tutsi mwami (king), while most people were Hutu farmers; the line between the groups was partly about wealth and cattle and could be crossed. Germany absorbed it into German East Africa in the 1890s, and Belgium took it over after World War I. The Belgians favoured the Tutsi elite and in the 1930s issued identity cards that fixed everyone's ethnic group. In 1959 a Hutu revolution overthrew the monarchy and drove many Tutsi into exile, and Rwanda became independent in 1962 under Hutu-led governments. In 1990 the Rwandan Patriotic Front, a rebel army of Tutsi exiles based in Uganda, invaded. In April 1994, after the president's plane was shot down, Hutu extremists began a genocide in which about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, were killed in 100 days while the world looked away. The RPF, led by Paul Kagame, ended it by seizing the country. Rwanda's invasions of Congo, chasing those who carried out the genocide, helped trigger two wars in which millions died.
RWA.c: Almost everyone speaks Kinyarwanda, and English has replaced French as the main foreign language. On the last Saturday of each month people join umuganda, community work such as cleaning streets, and plastic bags are banned. Intore dancers with long white headdresses perform at celebrations. Mountain gorillas live in Volcanoes National Park, and 'Visit Rwanda' adverts have appeared on the shirts of top European football clubs.
RWA.p: Paul Kagame, Rwanda's leader since the genocide and president since 2000, won a fourth term in 2024 with more than 99% of the vote; critics say real opponents are not allowed to run. Justin Nsengiyumva became prime minister in July 2025. Rwanda is praised for order and growth and criticised for repression. The main issue is eastern Congo: UN experts say Rwanda backs and directs the M23 rebels, who seized Goma and Bukavu in early 2025. Rwanda denies this and points to Hutu militias there. A US-brokered peace deal was signed in 2025, but in 2026 the United States sanctioned Rwanda's army for breaking it.
q: Which country suffered a genocide in 1994 in which about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, were killed in 100 days?
Which country's rebel army, led by Paul Kagame, ended the 1994 genocide by seizing the country?
Which country holds umuganda community work on the last Saturday of each month, and bans plastic bags?

MMR.t: Burmese kings ruled from Bagan from the 1000s, and later dynasties fought wars with Thailand and China. Britain conquered Burma in three wars between 1824 and 1885 and ruled it as a province of British India until 1937. Japan invaded in 1942, and Aung San, a nationalist who first sided with Japan and then switched to the Allies, negotiated independence. He was assassinated in 1947, months before Burma became independent in 1948. Ethnic minorities such as the Karen took up arms almost at once, and some of those wars continue. General Ne Win seized power in 1962 and led the 'Burmese Way to Socialism', isolating and impoverishing the country. In 1988 the army crushed a mass uprising, killing thousands, renamed the country Myanmar in 1989, and in 1990 refused to hand power to Aung San Suu Kyi's party after it won an election. A partial opening from 2011 let Suu Kyi lead the government from 2016, while in 2017 an army campaign drove about 700,000 Rohingya Muslims into Bangladesh.
MMR.c: Myanmar is mostly Theravada Buddhist, with thousands of temples on the plains of Bagan and the golden Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon. Many people wear thanaka, a pale yellow paste made from tree bark, on their faces, and men and women wear the longyi, a wrap-around sarong. Mohinga, fish noodle soup, is the usual breakfast, and tea shops are where people meet and talk.
MMR.p: The army seized power in a coup in February 2021, jailing Aung San Suu Kyi and crushing mass protests. A civil war followed, in which armed ethnic groups and new resistance forces loyal to the opposition National Unity Government took large areas, though the army has since won some back. The junta held an election in stages from December 2025 to January 2026, which critics, including many Western governments, called a sham, and in April 2026 the new parliament made coup leader Min Aung Hlaing president. In 2026 Suu Kyi's sentence was changed to house arrest. An earthquake near Mandalay in March 2025 killed thousands.
q: Which country's army refused to hand power to Aung San Suu Kyi's party after it won the 1990 election?
Which country drove about 700,000 Rohingya Muslims into Bangladesh in 2017?
In which country do many people wear thanaka paste on their faces and have the golden Shwedagon Pagoda?

BGD.t: Bengal, a rich river delta, was the heart of British India, and Calcutta was its capital until 1911. At partition in 1947 the Muslim-majority east became East Pakistan, separated from West Pakistan by more than 1,500 km of India. East Pakistan had more people, but power and money sat in the west. In 1952 students in Dhaka were shot dead while protesting for Bengali to be a national language alongside Urdu. When Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's Awami League won the 1970 election, the army refused to hand over power and in March 1971 launched a brutal crackdown. Hundreds of thousands were killed, perhaps far more, and about 10 million refugees fled to India. India entered the war in December and Pakistan's army surrendered in Dhaka, creating Bangladesh. Mujib was murdered in a 1975 coup, and military rulers followed. From 1991 two women, Sheikh Hasina and Khaleda Zia, took turns in power, while garment factories and microcredit helped lift millions out of poverty.
BGD.c: Almost everyone speaks Bengali, and people are proud that their language movement is honoured worldwide on 21 February, International Mother Language Day. Rice and fish, especially hilsa curry, are the heart of the diet. Cycle rickshaws crowd Dhaka's streets, cricket is a passion, and the country is one of the world's biggest clothing exporters. Rabindranath Tagore wrote the national anthem.
BGD.p: A student-led uprising in July and August 2024 forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to flee to India after 15 years in power, and Muhammad Yunus led an interim government until February 2026. In November 2025 a tribunal sentenced Hasina to death in absentia over the killing of protesters; India has not sent her back. Her Awami League was barred from the February 2026 election, which the Bangladesh Nationalist Party won with a two-thirds majority, and Tarique Rahman became prime minister. Voters also approved the July Charter of reforms in a referendum. Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir became president in August 2026. Energy shortages and jobs are pressing worries.
q: Which country's students were shot dead in 1952 while protesting for their language, now honoured on International Mother Language Day?
Which country was created in 1971 after Pakistan's army surrendered in Dhaka?
Which country, one of the world's biggest clothing exporters, has a national anthem written by Rabindranath Tagore?

AND.t: This small country high in the Pyrenees has been a co-principality since a deal in 1278 that ended a quarrel between the Bishop of Urgell, across the border in Catalonia, and the Count of Foix in France. The count's rights later passed to the kings of France and then to French presidents, so Andorra's joint heads of state are still a Spanish bishop and the President of France. Poor and remote, it stayed neutral through both world wars. During the Spanish Civil War and World War II, refugees, escaped airmen and Jews fleeing Nazi-occupied France crossed its mountain passes, and smugglers did good business. From the 1950s new roads brought skiers and shoppers drawn by low taxes, turning a farming valley into a tourist economy. A constitution in 1993 made it a modern parliamentary democracy, and it joined the United Nations that year. It uses the euro and has slowly given up banking secrecy.
AND.c: Catalan is the official language, though Spanish, French and Portuguese are heard everywhere because most residents were born abroad. Millions of visitors come for tax-free shopping, and skiers fill the slopes of Grandvalira in winter. The capital, Andorra la Vella, sits at about 1,000 metres, one of the highest capitals in Europe. Stone Romanesque churches dot the valleys.
AND.p: The co-princes are Emmanuel Macron, as President of France, and Josep-Lluís Serrano Pentinat, a former Vatican diplomat who became Bishop of Urgell in May 2025 when his predecessor stepped down. Day-to-day power lies with the elected General Council and the government it chooses. The biggest local issue is housing: fast population growth and foreign buyers have pushed rents beyond many workers' reach. Andorra has spent years negotiating a closer association agreement with the European Union, which would open its market but worries businesses that rely on low taxes.
q: Which country's joint heads of state are a Spanish bishop and the President of France?
Which Pyrenean country has been a co-principality since a deal in 1278?
In which country, high in the Pyrenees, is Catalan the official language and tax-free shopping a big draw?

AFG.t: For centuries Afghanistan sat on the trade and invasion routes between Persia, Central Asia and India. In the 1800s it became the buffer in the 'Great Game' between the Russian and British empires. Britain fought three wars there and drew the Durand Line, which still splits the Pashtun people between Afghanistan and Pakistan, and the narrow Wakhan Corridor was added so that Russian and British lands would not touch. Afghanistan won full control of its foreign affairs in 1919. A monarchy ruled until 1973, and a communist coup in 1978 sparked a revolt. The Soviet Union invaded in 1979 to prop up the communists, and the war became a Cold War battleground as the US, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia armed the mujahideen. After Soviet troops left in 1989, rival factions fought a civil war, and the Taliban took Kabul in 1996. They sheltered al-Qaeda, so after the attacks of 11 September 2001 a US-led invasion removed them. Twenty years of war followed, and the Taliban returned to power in 2021 as US forces withdrew.
AFG.c: Pashto and Dari, a form of Persian, are the main languages, and almost everyone is Muslim. Kabuli pulao, rice with lamb, raisins and carrots, is the national dish, and green tea is poured at every meeting. Afghan carpets, Persian poetry and buzkashi, a rough horseback game played with a goat carcass, are part of its heritage, and the national cricket team has become a source of huge pride.
AFG.p: The Taliban's supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, rules by decree from Kandahar, with Hasan Akhund as prime minister. Girls are barred from school after the sixth grade, and women from universities and most jobs; in 2025 the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Akhundzada over the persecution of women. Russia became the first country to formally recognise the Taliban government in 2025. Pakistan accuses the Taliban of sheltering militants, and border clashes in October 2025 grew into repeated Pakistani air strikes in 2026. An earthquake in the east killed over 2,000 people in 2025, and millions of Afghans have been pushed back from Iran and Pakistan.
q: Which country was the buffer between the Russian and British empires in the 'Great Game'?
Which country did the Soviet Union invade in 1979, starting a war that became a Cold War battleground?
Which country is known for buzkashi, a rough horseback game played with a goat carcass?

MNE.t: Montenegro's Orthodox prince-bishops held out in the mountains around Cetinje while the Ottoman Empire ruled most of the Balkans. The Congress of Berlin recognised it as independent in 1878, and in 1910 Nikola I made himself king. Montenegro fought beside Serbia in the Balkan Wars and in World War I, but was occupied by Austria-Hungary. In 1918 an assembly deposed Nikola and joined Serbia, inside the new kingdom that became Yugoslavia; supporters of independence, the Greens, rose in revolt and lost. In World War II Italy occupied it, and Montenegrins fought in large numbers in Tito's Partisans, so it became one of Yugoslavia's six republics in 1945. When Yugoslavia broke up in the 1990s it stayed with Serbia, and its forces joined the 1991 shelling of Dubrovnik. Under Milo Đukanović, who led it for most of the next three decades, it slowly turned away from Belgrade. In a 2006 referendum 55.5% voted to leave, just above the 55% bar the EU had set. It joined NATO in 2017.
MNE.c: Its name means 'black mountain', after the dark forests of Mount Lovćen. About 600,000 people live here, and many identify as Serbs as well as Montenegrins, so language and church are touchy subjects. The fjord-like Bay of Kotor, the walled town of Kotor and the island village of Sveti Stefan draw visitors, and Montenegro uses the euro although it is not in the EU. Basketball and water polo are national passions.
MNE.p: President Jakov Milatović and Prime Minister Milojko Spajić both rose with the Europe Now! movement, which won the 2023 election and ended three decades of dominance by Milo Đukanović's party, though the two men have since fallen out. Spajić governs with a broad coalition that includes pro-Serbian parties. Montenegro is widely seen as the front-runner among EU candidates and has been closing negotiating chapters quickly. The main divides are over national identity and ties with Serbia and the Serbian Orthodox Church, along with organised crime and corruption. A mass shooting in Cetinje on New Year's Day 2025 killed more than ten people and led to tighter gun laws.
q: Which country voted to leave its union with Serbia in 2006 by 55.5%, just above the 55% bar the EU had set?
Which country did Milo Đukanović lead for most of three decades?
Which country's name means 'black mountain' and which uses the euro although it is not in the EU?

BIH.t: The Ottomans ruled Bosnia for four centuries, and many Bosnians became Muslims, while others remained Orthodox Serbs or Catholic Croats. Austria-Hungary took control in 1878 and annexed it in 1908. In 1914 a young Bosnian Serb, Gavrilo Princip, shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, setting off World War I. Bosnia then became part of Yugoslavia. In World War II it was the scene of brutal fighting between fascist Croatian forces, Serb nationalists and Tito's communist partisans. Under Tito the three peoples lived side by side, and Sarajevo hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics. When Yugoslavia broke apart, Bosnia declared independence in 1992 after a referendum most Serbs boycotted. War followed among Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats, with about 100,000 dead. Sarajevo was besieged for nearly four years, and in 1995 Bosnian Serb forces murdered about 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica, a genocide. The US-brokered Dayton agreement ended the war in 1995.
BIH.c: Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats share a language with different names and two alphabets. Ćevapi, small grilled sausages in flatbread, and strong Bosnian coffee are staples. Sarajevo's old Ottoman bazaar, Baščaršija, sits a short walk from Austro-Hungarian streets, and Mostar's rebuilt Old Bridge, where divers leap into the river, is a symbol of reconciliation.
BIH.p: Dayton left a complex state of two entities, the Bosniak-Croat Federation and the Serb-run Republika Srpska, a three-person presidency and an international High Representative. Milorad Dodik, Republika Srpska's long-time leader, was convicted in 2025 of defying the High Representative and removed as its president, but he still dominates Serb politics. The High Representative, Christian Schmidt, announced in May 2026 that he would step down. In the October 2026 general election, according to near-final results, Denis Bećirović and Željka Cvijanović were re-elected to the presidency, and Darijana Filipović won the Croat seat. EU membership talks move slowly.
q: In which country did Gavrilo Princip shoot Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914?
Which country's war of 1992 to 1995 was ended by the US-brokered Dayton agreement?
Which country's town of Mostar has a rebuilt Old Bridge where divers leap into the river?

UGA.t: Several kingdoms, Buganda the strongest, ruled around Lake Victoria before the British arrived. Britain made Uganda a protectorate in 1894, working through Buganda's chiefs, and built a railway from the Kenyan coast that brought Indian workers and traders. Uganda became independent in 1962 with Milton Obote as prime minister and Buganda's king as president, but in 1966 Obote sent the army, led by Idi Amin, to storm the king's palace, and he later abolished the kingdoms. Amin seized power in 1971 and ruled by terror: perhaps 300,000 people were killed, and in 1972 he expelled the country's roughly 80,000 Asians. His attack on Tanzania led Tanzania's army to topple him in 1979. Obote returned, and his second rule was just as bloody. Yoweri Museveni's National Resistance Army won a bush war and took power in 1986. He restored order and the traditional kingdoms, and in the 1990s led a widely praised campaign against HIV and AIDS.
UGA.c: English and Swahili are official, but Luganda is the most widely spoken local language. Matooke, steamed green bananas, is the staple, and the rolex, a chapati rolled around an omelette, is a favourite street snack. Uganda is home to about half of the world's mountain gorillas and to the source of the White Nile at Lake Victoria. Most people are Christian, and the Uganda Martyrs shrine at Namugongo draws huge pilgrimages each June.
UGA.p: Yoweri Museveni, in power since 1986, won a seventh term in January 2026 with about 72% of the vote, according to official results. The pop star turned opposition leader Bobi Wine, who came second, rejected the result, which followed an internet shutdown and the detention of many opposition supporters; several protesters were killed. Museveni's son, army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, is widely seen as a possible successor. Robinah Nabbanja is prime minister. Uganda hosts Africa's largest refugee population, mostly from South Sudan and Congo. Oil fields near Lake Albert, with a pipeline to Tanzania's coast that environmental groups oppose, are central to its economic plans.
q: Which country did Idi Amin rule by terror from 1971, expelling about 80,000 Asians in 1972?
Which country has been led by Yoweri Museveni since his army won a bush war in 1986?
Which country is home to about half the world's mountain gorillas, and the rolex street snack?

CUB.t: Cuba was one of Spain's last colonies in the Americas, a sugar island worked by enslaved Africans until 1886. Cubans fought two long wars for independence, and in 1898 the United States joined in, defeating Spain in the Spanish-American War. Cuba became independent in 1902, but the Platt Amendment let the US intervene and keep a naval base at Guantánamo Bay, and American companies came to own much of the sugar industry. In 1959 Fidel Castro's guerrillas overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista. Castro seized American property and allied with the Soviet Union; the US answered with a trade embargo and the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961. In 1962 the discovery of Soviet nuclear missiles on the island brought the world to the brink of nuclear war. Soviet aid kept Cuba afloat until 1991, when its loss caused years of hunger known as the Special Period. Raúl Castro took over from his ailing brother in 2006 and allowed small private businesses.
CUB.c: Classic 1950s American cars still cruise Havana's streets, kept running for decades because of the US embargo. Son, the ancestor of salsa, and rumba are heard everywhere, and cigars, rum and baseball are national passions. Doctors are a famous export: Cuba sends them to work in dozens of countries. Basic food is rationed through the libreta, a ration book, and long queues are part of daily life.
CUB.p: Miguel Díaz-Canel, the first leader since 1959 not named Castro, heads both the Communist Party and the state, with Manuel Marrero as prime minister. The one-party state faces its worst crisis since the 1990s. After the US captured Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro in January 2026, Washington cut off Venezuelan oil and imposed tariffs on countries selling oil to Cuba. Island-wide blackouts followed, airlines suspended flights, and protesters burned a party office in Morón. Hundreds of thousands of Cubans have emigrated since 2021. In 2026 the government held talks with the US and widened private enterprise.
q: Which country did Fidel Castro's guerrillas take over in 1959?
Which country's Soviet nuclear missiles brought the world to the brink of nuclear war in 1962?
Where do classic 1950s American cars still cruise the streets of the capital, and food is rationed through the libreta?

HND.t: The Maya city of Copán flourished in the west of the country until about 900. Spain conquered the land in the 1520s, and after independence in 1821 Honduras stayed poor, mountainous and often at war with its neighbours. In the early 1900s American fruit companies won huge land grants, built railways and ports, and helped make and unmake governments, which inspired the term 'banana republic'. Military rulers governed for much of the century, and in 1969 a short war with El Salvador, driven by migration and land disputes, became known as the 'Football War' because it followed World Cup qualifying matches. During the Cold War Honduras avoided civil war but became a base for US forces and for the Contras fighting Nicaragua's Sandinista government. Hurricane Mitch killed thousands in 1998. In 2009 the army removed President Manuel Zelaya in a coup after he pushed for a vote on changing the constitution, and gang violence made Honduras one of the world's most violent countries in the 2010s.
HND.c: The carved stone monuments of Copán are its best-known Maya ruins, and the Bay Islands of Roatán and Utila draw divers to the reef. Garifuna communities on the Caribbean coast keep their own language, drumming and punta dance. Baleadas, flour tortillas folded over beans, cream and cheese, are the everyday snack. Football is followed with passion, and many families depend on money sent home from relatives in the US.
HND.p: Nasry Asfura of the conservative National Party, a former mayor of Tegucigalpa, became president in January 2026. He narrowly won the November 2025 election after Donald Trump endorsed him; the count took weeks and the runner-up alleged fraud. Around the time of the vote Trump also pardoned Juan Orlando Hernández, the National Party's president from 2014 to 2022, who was serving 45 years in a US prison for drug trafficking. Asfura replaced Xiomara Castro of the left-wing Libre party, president from 2022 to 2026, and has moved closer to the US and Israel. Gangs, poverty and migration remain the big issues.
q: Which country's American fruit companies inspired the term 'banana republic'?
Which country fought the 'Football War' with El Salvador in 1969?
Which country has the Maya ruins of Copán and the dive islands of Roatán and Utila?

ECU.t: The Andes of Ecuador were part of the Inca Empire before Spain conquered it in the 1530s and ruled it from Quito. It won independence as part of Gran Colombia in 1822, broke away in 1830 and took its name from the Equator. Cocoa exports in the late 1800s and bananas after World War II made Guayaquil, on the coast, the economic rival of highland Quito, a split that still shapes politics. In 1941, while World War II raged elsewhere, Peru invaded and Ecuador was forced to give up much of its Amazon territory; the border was finally settled only in 1998, after another short war in 1995. Oil found in the Amazon in the 1960s funded military governments, which handed back power in 1979. Instability followed, and three elected presidents were forced out between 1997 and 2005. After a banking collapse, Ecuador adopted the US dollar in 2000. Rafael Correa, president from 2007 to 2017, spent oil money on roads and schools but clashed with the press and courts.
ECU.c: Ecuador owns the Galápagos Islands, where Darwin studied evolution. Quito is one of the highest capitals in the world, and the 'Panama hat' is actually woven in Ecuador from toquilla straw. It is one of the world's biggest exporters of bananas and roses. Highland markets such as Otavalo sell Kichwa weaving, and its 2008 constitution was the first to give nature legal rights.
ECU.p: Daniel Noboa, a banana heir, won a 2023 snap election and was re-elected in April 2025 over Luisa González of Rafael Correa's movement. Once one of the region's safest countries, Ecuador has become a cocaine shipping hub, and gang killings soared. Noboa declared an 'internal armed conflict' against the gangs, sent troops into prisons and imposed curfews, yet deadly prison riots continued. In November 2025 voters rejected his proposals to allow foreign military bases and write a new constitution. In 2026 a tariff war with Colombia began, and US forces struck armed groups near the border at Ecuador's request.
q: Which country takes its name from the line it sits on?
Which country adopted the US dollar in 2000 after a banking collapse?
Which country owns the Galápagos Islands?

COL.t: Colombia first declared independence from Spain in 1810 and became the core of Simón Bolívar's Gran Colombia, which won its freedom in 1819 and broke up in 1830. Liberals and Conservatives fought repeated civil wars, the worst being the Thousand Days' War (1899 to 1902), and in 1903 Colombia lost Panama when the United States backed Panamanian independence to build its canal. In 1948 the murder of the popular Liberal leader Jorge Eliécer Gaitán set off La Violencia, a decade of fighting that killed around 200,000 people. Its legacy and deep rural inequality fed Cold War guerrilla groups, above all the FARC, founded in 1964. In the 1980s and 1990s drug cartels led by Pablo Escobar turned cocaine into a vast business and bombed and murdered their way into politics, while right-wing paramilitaries massacred civilians. US aid under Plan Colombia from 2000 strengthened the army, and a 2016 peace deal disarmed most of the FARC, winning President Juan Manuel Santos the Nobel Peace Prize.
COL.c: Colombia is the only South American country with coasts on both the Pacific and the Caribbean. Its coffee, cumbia and vallenato music, singers Shakira, Karol G and Carlos Vives, and writer Gabriel García Márquez are known worldwide. Barranquilla's Carnival is one of the biggest in the Americas, arepas are eaten daily, and cycling and football are national obsessions. Medellín, once Escobar's city, is now known for cable cars.
COL.p: Abelardo de la Espriella, a far-right lawyer and political outsider, became president in August 2026 after narrowly beating the leftist senator Iván Cepeda in the June runoff, by about 50% to 49%. He replaced Gustavo Petro, president from 2022 to 2026 and the country's first left-wing leader, whose 'Total Peace' talks with armed groups failed to stop violence by FARC dissidents, the ELN and drug gangs. De la Espriella formally ended those talks and stepped up military attacks. Relations with the United States, strained under Petro, have warmed, though the US imposed a 12.5% tariff in July 2026.
q: Which country lost Panama in 1903?
Which country's president won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2016 for a deal disarming most of the FARC?
Which is the only South American country with coasts on both the Pacific and the Caribbean?

PRY.t: Paraguay became independent in 1811 and, under the dictator José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, sealed itself off from the world. In the War of the Triple Alliance (1864 to 1870) against Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay, it lost much of its territory and perhaps most of its adult men, a catastrophe that kept it poor for generations. In the 20th century it fought Bolivia in the Chaco War (1932 to 1935) over a dry plain thought to hold oil, and won most of it. General Alfredo Stroessner seized power in 1954 and ruled until 1989, one of the longest dictatorships in the Americas. A firm Cold War ally of the United States, he jailed and tortured opponents and sheltered fugitives, including the Nazi doctor Josef Mengele. With Brazil he built the giant Itaipú dam, which began producing power in 1984 and still makes Paraguay a big exporter of electricity. A coup ended his rule in 1989, but his Colorado Party has stayed in power almost ever since.
PRY.c: Paraguay is the only country in the Americas where most people speak an Indigenous language, Guaraní, alongside Spanish. Tereré, cold yerba mate, is drunk everywhere from big thermos jugs. Chipa cheese bread, sopa paraguaya, which is actually a cornbread, and harp-led polka music are national symbols, and ñandutí lace takes its name from the Guaraní word for a spider's web.
PRY.p: Santiago Peña, an economist from the Colorado Party, has been president since August 2023. His mentor Horacio Cartes, president from 2013 to 2018, leads the party; the United States sanctioned him for corruption in 2022 and 2023 but lifted the sanctions in 2025. Peña has aligned closely with the United States, Argentina's Javier Milei and Israel, and Paraguay is one of the few countries that still recognise Taiwan rather than China. A 2025 spy scandal, in which Brazil admitted spying on Paraguayan officials, soured talks over the price of Itaipú's electricity. The opposition accuses the Colorados of corruption and of ties to organised crime.
q: Which country lost perhaps most of its adult men in the War of the Triple Alliance?
Which country did Alfredo Stroessner rule from 1954 to 1989, sheltering the Nazi doctor Josef Mengele?
Which is the only country in the Americas where most people speak an Indigenous language, Guaraní?

PRT.t: Portugal's borders are among the oldest in Europe, fixed by the 1200s. Its sailors opened the age of sail: Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, and Portugal built an empire stretching from Brazil to Macau. Brazil broke away in 1822, and in 1910 a revolution overthrew the monarchy. The unstable republic ended in a 1926 military coup, and from 1932 António de Oliveira Salazar ran a Catholic, conservative dictatorship called the Estado Novo. Portugal stayed neutral in World War II but joined NATO in 1949. While other European powers let their colonies go, Salazar fought on, and from 1961 wars in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau drained the country, while India seized Goa. On 25 April 1974 army officers overthrew the regime in the bloodless Carnation Revolution, and within two years the African colonies were independent, sending hundreds of thousands of settlers home. Portugal joined the European Community in 1986, adopted the euro, and handed Macau to China in 1999.
PRT.c: Portuguese is spoken by about 260 million people, mostly in Brazil, and links Lisbon to Angola, Mozambique and Cape Verde. Fado songs of longing, blue-and-white azulejo tiles, salt cod cooked in hundreds of ways and custard tarts called pastéis de nata are national icons. Football is close to a religion, and Cristiano Ronaldo is its most famous son. Lisbon has become a magnet for tourists and remote workers.
PRT.p: Luís Montenegro of the centre-right Social Democrats has been prime minister since 2024. His minority government lost a confidence vote in 2025 over his family firm's business dealings, but he won the snap election that May. The bigger story was the rise of André Ventura's hard-right Chega, which became the second-largest party in parliament. In February 2026 the Socialist António José Seguro beat Ventura in the presidential runoff with about two thirds of the vote. Housing costs, immigration and citizenship rules, a contested labour reform that sparked general strikes, and the damage from Storm Kristin in January 2026 dominate debate.
q: Which country's sailor Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498?
Which country's Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 overthrew its dictatorship without bloodshed?
Which country is known for fado songs, azulejo tiles and custard tarts called pastéis de nata?

MDA.t: For centuries the land between the Prut and Dniester rivers belonged to Moldavia, a Romanian-speaking principality. Russia took its eastern half, called Bessarabia, in 1812. When the Russian Empire collapsed in 1918, Bessarabia joined Romania. In 1940, under the secret deal between Stalin and Hitler, the Soviet Union seized it back, and after World War II it became the Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic. Moscow deported tens of thousands of people to Siberia, settled Russian speakers in the towns and insisted that Moldovan was a separate language, written in Cyrillic. In 1989 a national movement restored the Latin alphabet, and in 1991 Moldova declared independence. Russian speakers east of the Dniester feared union with Romania and broke away. A short war in 1992, in which Russian troops sided with the separatists, left Transnistria under its own unrecognised government, and Russian soldiers are still stationed there. Poor and pulled between East and West, Moldova saw hundreds of thousands of its people leave to work abroad.
MDA.c: Most people speak Romanian, and many also speak Russian, especially in Transnistria and in Gagauzia, a southern region of Turkic-speaking Orthodox Christians. Wine is central to life: the Mileștii Mici and Cricova cellars run for tens of kilometres under the ground. Most Moldovans are Orthodox Christians, and plăcinte, stuffed pastries, and mămăligă, a maize porridge, are everyday food. Many families depend on relatives working in the EU.
MDA.p: President Maia Sandu, re-elected in 2024, is pulling Moldova out of Russia's orbit. Moldova became an EU candidate in 2022, and in 2024 voters narrowly backed EU membership in a referendum the authorities said was marred by Russian-funded vote buying. Her Party of Action and Solidarity kept its majority in the September 2025 election. In 2026 Moldova left the Commonwealth of Independent States, and businessman Vasile Tofan became prime minister in July after Alexandru Munteanu resigned. Energy supply is a constant worry, and Russian drones from the war next door have crashed on Moldovan soil.
q: Which country lost Transnistria, where Russian troops are still stationed, after a short war in 1992?
Which country restored the Latin alphabet in 1989 after Moscow had insisted its language be written in Cyrillic?
Which country's Mileștii Mici and Cricova wine cellars run for tens of kilometres underground?

TKM.t: Turkmen tribes were nomadic herders and horse breeders, and their oases, such as Merv, were once great Silk Road cities. Russia conquered them in the 1880s, after storming the fortress of Geok Tepe in a bloody battle in 1881. In 1924 the Soviets created the Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic, forced the nomads onto collective farms and dug the Karakum Canal to carry water from the Amu Darya to cotton fields. When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, the local Communist Party boss, Saparmurat Niyazov, stayed on as president. Calling himself Turkmenbashi, 'leader of the Turkmens', he built golden statues of himself, renamed months after himself and his mother, and made his book, the Ruhnama, required reading. He declared permanent neutrality, recognised by the UN in 1995. Gas exports, increasingly to China, paid for marble buildings in Ashgabat. After Niyazov died in 2006, his dentist and health minister, Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow, took over and built a personality cult of his own.
TKM.c: Most of the country is the Karakum Desert, where the Darvaza gas crater, the 'Door to Hell', has burned since Soviet times. Turkmen carpets, with their deep red patterns, appear on the flag, and the golden Akhal-Teke horse has its own national holiday. Ashgabat is a city of white marble and empty boulevards, and few foreign tourists visit because visas are hard to get.
TKM.p: In 2022 Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow handed the presidency to his son Serdar through an election with no real opposition, but he still wields great power as chairman of the People's Council, the top legislative body. Turkmenistan has no free press, opposition parties or independent courts, and is ranked among the least free countries in the world. Its economy rests on huge gas reserves, sold mostly to China. In 2025 it began issuing electronic visas and in 2026 legalised cryptocurrency mining, but food shortages and emigration remain common.
q: Which country's first president called himself Turkmenbashi and renamed months after himself and his mother?
Which country declared permanent neutrality, recognised by the UN in 1995?
Which country's desert holds the burning Darvaza gas crater, the 'Door to Hell'?

JOR.t: For centuries the land east of the Jordan River was a thinly populated corner of the Ottoman Empire, crossed by Bedouin tribes and by pilgrims heading to Mecca. During World War I the Hashemite family of Mecca led the Arab Revolt against the Ottomans with British support, helped by T. E. Lawrence. Afterwards Britain created Transjordan in 1921 and gave it to the Hashemite prince Abdullah, and it became an independent kingdom in 1946. In the 1948 war Jordan took the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and many Palestinian refugees became citizens. Abdullah was assassinated in Jerusalem in 1951, and his grandson Hussein ruled from 1953 to 1999, steering a small, poor country between larger neighbours. Jordan lost the West Bank to Israel in the 1967 war. In 1970 the army fought and expelled Palestinian guerrilla groups in what became known as Black September. Hussein made peace with Israel in 1994, and his son Abdullah II succeeded him in 1999.
JOR.c: Petra, a city carved into rose-red rock by the Nabataeans, is its most famous sight, and the desert of Wadi Rum has stood in for Mars in films. Mansaf, lamb cooked in fermented dried yogurt and served over rice, is the national dish, eaten at weddings and funerals. Many Jordanians have Palestinian roots, and Bedouin hospitality, with endless cups of cardamom coffee, is a point of pride.
JOR.p: King Abdullah II, on the throne since 1999, holds most power, and in 2024 he made Jafar Hassan, his former chief of staff, prime minister. The Islamic Action Front won the most seats of any party in the 2024 election, but in 2025 the government banned the Muslim Brotherhood after arresting members accused of a weapons plot. Anger over the war in Gaza runs high. During the 2026 Iran war its air defences shot down Iranian missiles and drones, and an Iranian strike hit an air base used by US forces. Unemployment and debt are chronic problems.
q: Which kingdom did Britain create in 1921 for the Hashemite prince Abdullah?
Which country fought and expelled Palestinian guerrilla groups in 1970, an event known as Black September?
Which country's most famous sight is Petra, a city carved into rose-red rock?

NPL.t: For centuries the Kathmandu Valley was home to small Newar kingdoms famous for their temples and pagodas. In 1768 Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha conquered them and founded modern Nepal. It was never colonised, but after losing a war with the British East India Company in 1816 it gave up land and began sending Gurkha soldiers to serve Britain, and they fought in both world wars. From 1846 to 1951 the Rana family ruled as hereditary prime ministers and kept the country sealed off. After their fall Nepal opened to the world, just as Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay made the first ascent of Everest in 1953. Kings ruled with little democracy until protests in 1990. A Maoist insurgency from 1996 to 2006 killed about 17,000 people, and in 2001 the crown prince shot dead King Birendra and much of the royal family. After mass protests in 2006 the Maoists made peace, and in 2008 an elected assembly abolished the monarchy.
NPL.c: Nepal holds eight of the world's fourteen peaks above 8,000 metres, including Everest, and Sherpa guides lead most expeditions. Most people are Hindu, but Lumbini is the Buddha's birthplace, and Buddhist prayer flags flutter across the hills. Dal bhat, lentils with rice, is eaten twice a day, and momo dumplings are everywhere. Its flag is the only national flag that is not a rectangle.
NPL.p: In September 2025 young people angered by corruption and a ban on social media staged the 'Gen Z' protests. More than 70 people were killed, crowds set fire to parliament and politicians' homes, and Prime Minister K. P. Sharma Oli resigned. Sushila Karki, a former chief justice, led an interim government until elections in March 2026, which the Rastriya Swatantra Party won by a landslide. Balen Shah, a former rapper and mayor of Kathmandu in his mid-thirties, became prime minister, and Oli was arrested over the crackdown. Corruption, jobs and the millions of Nepalis working abroad are the big issues.
q: Which country's crown prince shot dead the king and much of the royal family in 2001?
Which country abolished its monarchy in 2008 after a Maoist insurgency?
Which country has the only national flag that is not a rectangle?

LSO.t: King Moshoeshoe I gathered refugees from the wars of the early 1800s into the Basotho nation, using the flat-topped mountain of Thaba Bosiu as a fortress. When Boer settlers seized much of his best farmland, he asked Britain for protection in 1868, and the deal kept his mountain kingdom, then called Basutoland, out of South Africa. Britain ran it cheaply, and generations of Basotho men went to work in South Africa's gold mines. It became independent in 1966, completely surrounded by South Africa. When the ruling party lost the 1970 election, Prime Minister Leabua Jonathan suspended the constitution and ruled until a 1986 military coup backed by apartheid South Africa. Elections returned in 1993, but a disputed 1998 vote led to riots and an intervention by South African and Botswana troops. The whole country lies above 1,400 m, the highest low point of any country. Since 2004 the Lesotho Highlands Water Project has dammed its rivers to sell water to Johannesburg.
LSO.c: Sesotho and English are official, and nearly everyone is Basotho. The Basotho blanket, worn like a cloak against the mountain cold, and the conical mokorotlo hat are national symbols. Herders on sturdy Basotho ponies cross the high passes, and Afriski in the Maluti Mountains is one of Africa's few ski resorts. Lesotho has one of the world's highest HIV rates.
LSO.p: Sam Matekane, a diamond-mining millionaire, became prime minister in 2022 after his new Revolution for Prosperity party won the most seats; King Letsie III has a mostly ceremonial role. Coalition governments in Lesotho often collapse, and efforts to reform the constitution and curb the army's role in politics have dragged on for years. In 2025 the United States announced a 50% tariff on Lesotho's goods, threatening the clothing factories that make jeans for American brands and employ thousands. The government declared a two-year state of disaster over unemployment. Lesotho also depends heavily on water sales and customs payments from South Africa.
q: Which mountain kingdom did Moshoeshoe I build, using the flat-topped Thaba Bosiu as a fortress?
Which country is completely surrounded by South Africa?
Which country lies entirely above 1,400 m, where people wear blankets like cloaks and the conical mokorotlo hat?

CMR.t: Germany claimed Kamerun in 1884. During World War I, British and French troops took it, and afterwards the League of Nations split it between France, which got most of it, and Britain, which got two strips along Nigeria. In the 1950s France fought a brutal, little-known war against the UPC independence movement, which went on after independence; in 2025 France officially acknowledged it as a war. French Cameroon became independent in 1960, and in 1961 the southern British strip voted to join it while the northern strip joined Nigeria. That is why Cameroon is officially bilingual in French and English. The first president, Ahmadou Ahidjo, turned the federation into a one-party unitary state. In 1982 he handed power to his prime minister, Paul Biya, who allowed multiparty elections from 1992 but kept winning them. Oil, timber and cocoa helped make it one of Central Africa's larger economies, but English-speakers increasingly felt sidelined by the French-speaking majority.
CMR.c: With more than 250 languages, Cameroon is often called 'Africa in miniature': it has rainforest, savanna, beaches and Mount Cameroon, an active volcano. Makossa and bikutsi music are famous across Africa, and so is its football team, the Indomitable Lions, with stars such as Roger Milla and Samuel Eto'o. Ndolé, a stew of bitter leaves and peanuts, is a national dish.
CMR.p: Paul Biya, president since 1982 and in his nineties the world's oldest head of state, won an eighth term in October 2025 with 53.7% of the official vote. His former minister Issa Tchiroma claimed he had won; protests followed, several people were killed and Tchiroma fled abroad. In 2026 parliament restored the post of vice president, who would take over if Biya died or left office, and postponed parliamentary elections. The war between the army and English-speaking separatists in the northwest and southwest, which began in 2017, still kills people, and Boko Haram attacks continue in the far north.
q: Which country, once German Kamerun, is officially bilingual because a British strip voted to join the French part in 1961?
Which country has been led by Paul Biya since 1982?
Which country is called 'Africa in miniature', and whose football team is the Indomitable Lions?

GAB.t: Portuguese sailors named the estuary of the Como River 'Gabão' in the 1470s, and the coast became a centre of the slave trade. France founded Libreville in 1849 as a settlement for freed slaves and later made Gabon part of French Equatorial Africa. In 1913 the doctor Albert Schweitzer founded his famous jungle hospital at Lambaréné. Gabon became independent in 1960 under Léon M'ba, and when soldiers overthrew him in 1964, French paratroopers flew in and put him back. His successor Omar Bongo ruled from 1967 until his death in 2009, becoming the symbol of 'Françafrique', the web of personal, business and military ties between France and its former colonies. Oil, manganese and timber made Gabon one of the richest countries in Africa per person, and French troops stayed in Libreville. His son Ali Bongo, president from 2009 to 2023, won disputed elections in 2009 and 2016, and suffered a stroke in 2018. When he was declared the winner of another election in August 2023, army officers seized power within hours.
GAB.c: French is the official language, alongside Fang, Myene and other Bantu languages. About 85% of the country is rainforest, with a network of national parks that are home to forest elephants, gorillas and surfing hippos at Loango. Bwiti, a spiritual tradition using the iboga plant, is part of national identity. Libreville's seafront and nightlife are among the liveliest in Central Africa.
GAB.p: General Brice Oligui Nguema, who led the 2023 coup that ended the Bongo family's 56 years in power, was elected president in April 2025 with about 90% of the vote under a new constitution that abolished the post of prime minister. Ali Bongo's wife and son were released and left the country, then were sentenced in absentia to 20 years for embezzlement. Supporters praise Oligui for building projects; critics say he has kept old networks and is concentrating power. In 2026 the government blocked social media nationwide and asked the IMF for help with its debts.
q: Which country did Omar Bongo rule from 1967 to 2009 as a symbol of 'Françafrique'?
Which country's army seized power within hours of Ali Bongo being declared the winner of the August 2023 election?
Which country is about 85% rainforest, with surfing hippos at Loango?

NER.t: The Niger River crosses only the southwest corner of this huge, mostly desert country. Before colonial rule the area held Hausa city-states, part of the Kanem-Bornu empire and the Tuareg sultanate of Agadez, a hub for caravans crossing the Sahara. France conquered it around 1900 and made it part of French West Africa. It became independent in 1960 under Hamani Diori, who kept close ties with France. Uranium found near Arlit in the north was mined by French-led companies from the early 1970s and fuelled French nuclear power stations. Niger then lived through coups in 1974, 1996, 1999 and 2010, and Tuareg rebellions in the 1990s and 2000s. Droughts in the 1970s and 1980s brought famine. Since the 2010s jihadist groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have attacked from Mali and Burkina Faso in the west, and Boko Haram from around Lake Chad in the southeast. Western countries made Niger a key partner against them, until the army turned on that alliance.
NER.c: Hausa is the most widely spoken language, and most people are Muslim. Niger has one of the highest birth rates in the world, so the population is very young. Tuareg nomads are known for silver jewellery, the Agadez cross and the indigo veils worn by men. Each year Wodaabe herders gather for the Gerewol, where young men paint their faces and dance to be chosen by women. Agadez's mud-brick minaret is a landmark.
NER.p: General Abdourahamane Tiani, head of the presidential guard, seized power in July 2023 and detained the elected president, Mohamed Bazoum. In March 2025 Tiani was sworn in as president for a five-year transition, and political parties were dissolved. Ali Lamine Zeine is prime minister. The junta expelled French and US troops, turned to Russia and, with Mali and Burkina Faso, left ECOWAS to form the Alliance of Sahel States. In 2025 it nationalised the main uranium mine run by France's Orano. Jihadist attacks have grown worse, including two raids on Niamey's airport in 2026, and the junta said it defeated a coup attempt in August 2026.
q: Which country's uranium, mined near Arlit from the 1970s, fuelled French nuclear power stations?
Which country had coups in 1974, 1996, 1999 and 2010, and saw Tuareg rebellions in the 1990s and 2000s?
Which country, with one of the world's highest birth rates, holds the Gerewol, where Wodaabe men dance to be chosen?

BFA.t: The Mossi kingdoms around Ouagadougou were among West Africa's most durable states, resisting Mali and Songhai for centuries before France conquered them in the 1890s. France drew this landlocked colony as Upper Volta, after the Volta rivers, and used it mainly as a reservoir of labour for plantations in Côte d'Ivoire and soldiers for its armies in both world wars. It became independent in 1960 and had its first coup in 1966. In 1983 a 33-year-old captain, Thomas Sankara, took power and the next year renamed it Burkina Faso, 'land of upright people'. He vaccinated children, planted millions of trees, banned forced marriage and rejected foreign aid that came with conditions. In 1987 he was killed in a coup led by his friend Blaise Compaoré, who ruled for 27 years until a popular uprising drove him out in 2014. From 2015 jihadist groups spreading from Mali began attacking the north, and by the 2020s armed groups controlled large parts of the countryside.
BFA.c: Ouagadougou hosts FESPACO, Africa's biggest film festival, every two years, as well as a major crafts fair. French is official, alongside Mooré and dozens of other languages. Faso Dan Fani, a handwoven cotton cloth Sankara made a symbol of self-reliance, is still worn proudly, and Sankara is remembered across Africa as a model of honest leadership.
BFA.p: Captain Ibrahim Traoré has ruled since a September 2022 coup, the country's second that year, and in 2024 extended military rule to 2029. With Mali and Niger he formed the Alliance of Sahel States, expelled French troops, turned to Russia and left the West African bloc ECOWAS in January 2025. Popular online across Africa for his anti-Western message, at home he has dissolved all political parties, shut down hundreds of civic groups, and drafted critics into the army. The jihadist group JNIM still kills soldiers and civilians in large attacks, and the government cut diplomatic ties with France in June 2026.
q: Which country was called Upper Volta under French rule?
Which country's young leader Thomas Sankara planted millions of trees before he was killed in a 1987 coup?
Which country's capital hosts FESPACO, Africa's biggest film festival?

TGO.t: Germany claimed Togoland in 1884 and called it a 'model colony', built on cotton and palm oil plantations and forced labour. In World War I British and French troops seized it within weeks, and afterwards the League of Nations split it: France got the larger eastern part and Britain the west. In 1956 the British part voted to join the Gold Coast, soon to be Ghana, which divided the Ewe people between two countries. French Togo became independent in 1960 under Sylvanus Olympio. In 1963 he was shot dead in one of Africa's first post-independence coups, and in 1967 an army officer, Gnassingbé Eyadéma, took power. He ruled a one-party state for 38 years as a close ally of France during the Cold War, and crushed pro-democracy protests in the early 1990s. When he died in 2005 the army installed his son Faure Gnassingbé, who then won a disputed election marred by violence that killed hundreds. The same family has ruled ever since 1967.
TGO.c: French is official, and Ewe in the south and Kabiyè in the north are widely spoken. Christianity, Islam and Vodun beliefs often mix. Lomé's Akodessewa market sells items for traditional healing, and the Batammariba people in the north build fortress-like clay tower houses, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Fufu, pounded yam, is eaten with spicy sauces, and the footballer Emmanuel Adebayor is a national hero.
TGO.p: Faure Gnassingbé has led Togo since 2005, and in 2025 he kept power under a new constitution that turned the country into a parliamentary system. The presidency became largely ceremonial, now held by Jean-Lucien Savi de Tové, chosen by parliament in 2025, while Gnassingbé took the powerful new post of President of the Council of Ministers, which has no term limits. Critics called it a constitutional coup, and protests in June 2025 were put down, leaving several people dead. Jihadist groups from Burkina Faso have attacked the far north since 2021. The port of Lomé, a regional trade hub, drives the economy.
q: Which country's first president, Sylvanus Olympio, was shot dead in a 1963 coup?
Which country has been ruled by the Gnassingbé family since 1967?
Which country's Batammariba people build fortress-like clay tower houses, a UNESCO site?

GHA.t: The Asante kingdom, based in Kumasi, grew rich on gold and trade and fought the British in a series of wars before Britain annexed it in 1902. On the coast, the British Gold Coast took its name from its gold, and forts such as Cape Coast and Elmina were centres of the slave trade. In the 20th century cocoa farming made it one of Britain's wealthiest African colonies. After World War II, riots in 1948 fuelled demands for self-rule, led by Kwame Nkrumah. In 1957 it became the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence, taking the name of a medieval West African empire, and inspired the wave that swept Africa in 1960. Nkrumah became a leading voice for African unity, but he built a one-party state and was overthrown in 1966 while visiting China. Coups and economic decline followed. Jerry Rawlings, who seized power in 1979 and again in 1981, later oversaw a return to multiparty elections in 1992, and power has since changed hands peacefully several times.
GHA.c: English is official, with Akan (Twi) widely spoken. Kente cloth, highlife music and jollof rice (which Ghana and Nigeria endlessly argue over) are cultural exports, and Afrobeats stars fill stadiums. Funerals are big, colourful events, sometimes with coffins shaped like fish, cars or shoes. Many African Americans visit or settle here, drawn by the history of the slave forts.
GHA.p: John Mahama, president from 2012 to 2017, returned to power in January 2025 after his National Democratic Congress defeated the party of Nana Akufo-Addo, president from 2017 to 2025, in a landslide. He inherited the aftermath of a 2022 debt default and high inflation; with an IMF rescue the economy recovered, and Ghana left the IMF programme in 2026. Illegal gold mining, called galamsey, which poisons rivers and destroys forests, is a major issue. In August 2025 a military helicopter crash killed the defence and environment ministers. In 2026 parliament passed a strict anti-LGBT bill, criticised by human rights groups.
q: Which country, once the Gold Coast, was the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence, in 1957?
Which country's leader Kwame Nkrumah was overthrown in 1966 while visiting China?
Which country is known for kente cloth, highlife music and coffins shaped like fish, cars or shoes?

GNB.t: Portuguese traders arrived in the 1440s, and the coast became a source of captives for the Atlantic slave trade, run from trading posts such as Cacheu. Portugal took full control of the interior only in the early 20th century and invested very little. In 1956 Amílcar Cabral, an agronomist, founded the PAIGC to free Guinea and Cape Verde, and from 1963 it fought one of Africa's most effective guerrilla wars, eventually controlling much of the countryside. Cabral was assassinated in 1973, but the rebels declared independence that year, and Portugal recognised it in 1974 after its own Carnation Revolution. Cabral's half-brother Luís Cabral became president, until a 1980 coup by João Bernardo 'Nino' Vieira ended plans to unite with Cape Verde. A civil war in 1998–99 drove Vieira out; he later returned, and in 2009 he was killed by soldiers. Coups and attempted coups have been frequent since independence, and in the 2000s South American cartels used the country's islands and creeks as a transit point for cocaine heading to Europe.
GNB.c: Portuguese is official, but most people speak Guinea-Bissau Creole. Cashew nuts are the main export and income for many families. Gumbe music and the Bijagós Islands, a World Heritage Site where saltwater hippos and sea turtles live and some islands are run by women, are distinctive. Carnival in Bissau, with huge masks, is the biggest festival.
GNB.p: In November 2025, the day before results of a presidential election were due, the army seized power and removed Umaro Sissoco Embaló, president from 2020 to 2025; both he and his rival Fernando Dias had claimed victory, and armed men destroyed most of the tally sheets. General Horta Inta-A Na Man leads a military transition, with Ilídio Vieira Té as prime minister. West African and African Union bodies suspended the country. Opposition leader Domingos Simões Pereira was jailed. In August 2026 voters approved a new constitution that strengthens the presidency, and new elections were called for December 2026.
q: Which country's PAIGC, founded by Amílcar Cabral, fought one of Africa's most effective guerrilla wars against Portugal?
Which country's president 'Nino' Vieira was killed by soldiers in 2009?
Which country's Bijagós Islands are home to saltwater hippos, and cashew nuts are the main export?

USA.t: Thirteen British colonies declared independence in 1776 and, in the 1800s, pushed west to the Pacific, taking land from Native nations and Mexico. A civil war from 1861 to 1865 ended slavery but not racial segregation in the South. By 1900 the United States had the world's largest economy. It joined World War I late, in 1917, then turned inward until Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941 brought it into World War II. It ended that war by dropping atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and emerged as a superpower, rebuilding Western Europe and Japan and founding NATO. In the Cold War against the Soviet Union it fought in Korea and Vietnam and landed on the Moon in 1969. At home, the civil rights movement led by Martin Luther King Jr won laws in the 1960s that ended legal segregation. After the Soviet Union fell in 1991 it was the only superpower, but the attacks of 11 September 2001 drew it into long wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.
USA.c: American films, music, fast food, sport and technology companies shape culture around the world. People come from every part of the world, and English and Spanish are the most widely spoken languages. Americans are more religious than people in most rich countries, follow American football, baseball and basketball, and gather for Thanksgiving turkey and Fourth of July fireworks. In 2026 the country marked 250 years of independence.
USA.p: Donald Trump, who was president from 2017 to 2021, won back the White House in November 2024, and Republicans control both houses of Congress. His second term has brought sweeping tariffs, partly struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2026, and mass deportation drives that led to deadly shootings by immigration agents. Abroad, US forces captured Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro in January 2026, Trump pressed Denmark to hand over Greenland, and in February the United States and Israel went to war with Iran, pushing up fuel prices.
q: Which country was formed by 13 colonies that declared independence in 1776?
Which country dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and landed on the Moon in 1969?
Which country marked 250 years of independence in 2026?

CAN.t: Canada was formed in 1867 when Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick joined in Confederation, partly from fear of the United States after its Civil War. Railways tied it together, and by 1871 it reached the Pacific, pushing aside First Nations and Métis peoples on the prairies. In World War I about 60,000 Canadians died, and the capture of Vimy Ridge in 1917 became a founding national story. In World War II Canadian troops landed on Juno Beach on D-Day, and the country came out of the war as an industrial power and a founding member of NATO in 1949. Independence from Britain came step by step, from the Statute of Westminster in 1931 to its own constitution and Charter of Rights in 1982. Quebec's Quiet Revolution in the 1960s fed a movement for independence, which lost referendums in 1980 and, by a whisker, in 1995. Free trade with the US from 1989, widened to include Mexico in 1994, tied its economy closely to its neighbour.
CAN.c: Canada is officially bilingual, and French dominates in Quebec, where Montreal is one of the world's largest French-speaking cities. Most Canadians live within a few hundred kilometres of the US border, and Toronto and Vancouver draw immigrants from all over the world. Ice hockey is the national obsession, alongside maple syrup, poutine and Tim Hortons coffee. Indigenous peoples, from the Inuit to the Haida, are reclaiming their languages and land.
CAN.p: Mark Carney, a former governor of the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England, became Liberal leader and prime minister in March 2025 after Justin Trudeau resigned, and won the April 2025 election. MPs crossing the floor from the Conservatives and the NDP gave the Liberals a majority in April 2026, with Pierre Poilievre's Conservatives in opposition. The dominant issue is the United States: Donald Trump's tariffs and talk of making Canada the 51st state rallied Canadians to buy Canadian and pushed the government to seek other partners, including a trade deal with China in January 2026. In October 2026 Albertans voted against moving towards a separation referendum.
q: Which country was formed by Confederation in 1867, partly from fear of its neighbour after the Civil War?
Which country's capture of Vimy Ridge in 1917 became a founding national story?
Which country is officially bilingual, with ice hockey, maple syrup and poutine?

MEX.t: Spain conquered the Aztec Empire in 1521 and built Mexico City on the ruins of its capital, Tenochtitlan. New Spain's silver made the Spanish crown rich, while Indigenous people died in huge numbers from war and new diseases. Mexico won independence in 1821 after a long war, but by 1848 it had lost about half its territory, from Texas to California, to the United States. Under Porfirio Díaz, who ruled for over 30 years, railways and foreign investment grew while peasants lost their land. The Mexican Revolution of 1910 to 1920, with leaders such as Pancho Villa and Emiliano Zapata, killed perhaps a million people and produced a constitution promising land reform. In 1938 President Lázaro Cárdenas nationalised the oil industry. One party, later called the PRI, held power for 71 years until Vicente Fox won in 2000. The NAFTA trade deal of 1994 tied Mexico's economy to the US, and after 2006 a government war on drug cartels unleashed violence that has killed hundreds of thousands.
MEX.c: Mexico has more Spanish speakers than any other country. Its cuisine, from tacos and tamales to mole and pozole, is on UNESCO's heritage list, as is the Day of the Dead, when families build altars to welcome back the dead. Mariachi bands, lucha libre wrestling and football are national passions, and Diego Rivera's murals and Frida Kahlo's paintings are known worldwide. Mexico co-hosted the 2026 World Cup.
MEX.p: Claudia Sheinbaum, a climate scientist and ally of Andrés Manuel López Obrador, president from 2018 to 2024, won the 2024 election by a landslide to become Mexico's first woman president.
