Detroit became the centre of the car industry after Henry Ford's moving assembly line began in 1913, and his $5 daily wage drew workers from the South and from Europe. The United Auto Workers union, which won the 1937 sit-down strike at Flint, helped make car workers middle class. In World War II Detroit's factories built so many tanks, bombers and engines that it was called the 'Arsenal of Democracy'. Later, the 1967 riot, competition from Japanese car makers and white flight to the suburbs hollowed out the city, which shrank from about 1.8 million people in 1950 to under 700,000. In 2013 Detroit became the largest US city to go bankrupt, and from 2014 Flint's water crisis exposed residents to lead.
US-MI.c: Motown Records gave the world the 'Detroit sound' of the 1960s, and Detroit techno followed. Michigan touches four of the five Great Lakes, and people point at their hand as a map because the state is shaped like a mitten. Dearborn has one of America's largest Arab American communities, and coney dogs, pasties and square Detroit-style pizza are local favourites.
US-MI.p: Michigan is a key swing state: it voted for Biden in 2020 and Trump in 2024, and its legislature is split between a Democratic Senate and a Republican House. Gretchen Whitmer, governor since 2019 and serving her final term, has passed gun safety laws and clean energy targets, and has worked with Trump on some local issues. Car makers and their workers have been shaken by Trump's tariffs and by shifting rules on electric vehicles. Detroit's former mayor Mike Duggan has entered the 2026 race for governor as an independent. The cost of living and school results are central issues.
q: Which state's biggest city was called the 'Arsenal of Democracy' in World War II?
Which state's biggest city became the largest US city to go bankrupt, in 2013?
Which state is shaped like a mitten and gave the world Motown?

US-OH.t: Ohio was the first state carved out of the Northwest Territory, joining the Union in 1803 after the Shawnee and other nations were pushed out. Its rivers, canals and railways made it a crossroads, and Underground Railroad routes ran across it towards freedom in Canada. Ohio produced seven presidents, and the Wright brothers of Dayton built the first aeroplane. By 1900 Cleveland, Akron, Toledo and Youngstown were giants of oil refining, rubber, glass and steel; John D. Rockefeller founded Standard Oil in Cleveland. Black families from the South arrived in the Great Migration to work in factories that armed both world wars. In 1969 Ohioan Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon, and in 1970 the National Guard killed four students during a protest against the Vietnam War at Kent State University. From the 1970s many factories closed, and the state became part of the Rust Belt, a bellwether whose vote for president long predicted the winner.
US-OH.c: Ohio State football and its rivalry with Michigan are a passion, and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame stands in Cleveland. Cincinnati chili is served on spaghetti, the Amish community around Holmes County is one of the largest in the US, and Cedar Point's roller coasters draw thrill-seekers. The Wright brothers make it the 'Birthplace of Aviation'.
US-OH.p: Ohio, once the classic swing state, now leans clearly Republican. Republican Mike DeWine has been governor since 2019 and is limited to two terms. Republicans hold large majorities in the legislature, yet voters have broken with them on some issues: in 2023 they wrote abortion rights into the state constitution and legalised recreational marijuana. In 2024 Republican Bernie Moreno unseated Democratic senator Sherrod Brown. A huge Intel chip factory near Columbus has been delayed for years, while rising property taxes, the cost of living and the loss of manufacturing jobs are central issues.
q: Which was the first state carved from the Northwest Territory, and produced seven presidents?
Which state's Kent State University saw the National Guard kill four student protesters in 1970?
Which state calls itself the 'Birthplace of Aviation' and has the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame?

US-PA.t: William Penn, a Quaker, founded Pennsylvania in 1681 as a colony of religious tolerance, and it drew English Quakers, Germans and Scots-Irish settlers. Philadelphia was the cradle of the United States: the Declaration of Independence was signed there in 1776 and the Constitution in 1787. In 1863 the Union victory at Gettysburg turned the Civil War. Coal, oil and iron then made it an industrial giant. Pittsburgh's steel mills, built up by men like Andrew Carnegie, supplied railways, skyscrapers and the ships, tanks and guns of both world wars, and workers from Italy, Poland, Slovakia and the American South poured in. In 1979 a partial meltdown at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant near Harrisburg became America's worst nuclear accident. As the steel industry collapsed in the 1980s, Pittsburgh lost much of its population and reinvented itself around hospitals, universities and technology. On 11 September 2001 a hijacked plane crashed near Shanksville after its passengers fought back.
US-PA.c: The Amish of Lancaster County drive horse-drawn buggies and farm without modern machines. Philadelphia gave the world the cheesesteak, the Liberty Bell and the Rocky steps, while Pittsburgh is known for its bridges, pierogies and fanatical Steelers fans. Hershey is a town built around chocolate, and each February a groundhog in Punxsutawney 'predicts' the end of winter.
US-PA.p: Pennsylvania is the biggest prize among the swing states. Democrat Josh Shapiro, governor since 2023, is one of his party's most popular figures, but Donald Trump carried the state in 2024 and Republican Dave McCormick won a Senate seat. Power in Harrisburg is split: Democrats narrowly control the state House and Republicans the Senate, so budgets are often late; the 2025 budget was more than four months overdue. In April 2025 an arsonist set fire to the governor's residence while Shapiro's family slept inside. Energy and data centres, fracking for natural gas, public transport funding and the cost of living are big issues.
q: Which colony did the Quaker William Penn found in 1681?
Which state saw the Union victory at Gettysburg and the Three Mile Island accident?
Which state has the Liberty Bell, the cheesesteak and the Amish of Lancaster County?

US-NY.t: The Dutch founded New Amsterdam on Manhattan in the 1620s, and the English took it in 1664 and renamed it New York. After the Revolution the city was briefly the first US capital, and George Washington was sworn in there in 1789. The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, linked the Hudson River to the Great Lakes and made New York City the country's leading port. Between 1892 and 1954 about 12 million immigrants passed through Ellis Island, beneath the Statue of Liberty, giving the city its Irish, Italian, Jewish and many other neighbourhoods. By the 1920s it was rivalling London as the world's financial centre, and after World War II the United Nations made its headquarters there. The city nearly went bankrupt in 1975 and suffered high crime in the 1970s and 1980s, then recovered strongly. On 11 September 2001 al-Qaeda terrorists destroyed the World Trade Center, killing nearly 2,800 people. Upstate, the old factory towns along the Erie Canal lost much of their industry.
US-NY.c: New York City is the country's largest city and a world capital of finance, theatre, fashion and media. Broadway shows, bagels, pizza by the slice, the subway and the Statue of Liberty are its icons, and hundreds of languages are spoken in Queens alone. Upstate is a different world of farms, lakes, the Adirondack mountains and Niagara Falls.
US-NY.p: Democrat Kathy Hochul has been governor since 2021, when she replaced Andrew Cuomo after he resigned, and won a full term in 2022. Democrats control the legislature, though Republicans are strong upstate and on Long Island. In 2025 New York City elected Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist who promised free buses and a rent freeze, as mayor, deepening a divide within the Democratic Party. Since January 2025 drivers have paid a congestion charge to enter lower Manhattan, the first in the US, which the Trump administration tried to stop. The cost of living, housing, migrants and federal funding cuts are major issues.
q: Which state's Erie Canal, opened in 1825, linked the Hudson to the Great Lakes?
Through which state's Ellis Island did about 12 million immigrants pass?
Which state has Broadway, the Statue of Liberty and the Adirondacks?

CA-QC.t: Quebec was the heart of New France until Britain won the Battle of the Plains of Abraham in 1759. Britain let the French-speaking Catholics keep their language, religion and civil law, which is why Quebec still feels so different from the rest of Canada. It joined Confederation in 1867, and French Canadians bitterly opposed being conscripted to fight for the British Empire in 1917 and again in 1944, seeing these as Britain's wars, not theirs. Until 1960 the Catholic Church ran schools and hospitals, and English speakers dominated business. The 'Quiet Revolution' of the 1960s changed that: the province took over education, nationalised hydroelectricity and built a modern French-speaking middle class. Nationalism grew, and in 1970 the radical FLQ kidnapped two officials, killing one. The Parti Québécois took power in 1976 and made French the main language of work and schooling. Quebecers voted to stay in Canada in referendums in 1980 and, by just over one percentage point, in 1995.
CA-QC.c: French is the only official language, and Quebec has its own pop stars, films and television that most English Canadians never see. Quebec City's walled old town is the only one north of Mexico. Poutine, bagels from Montreal, spring 'sugar shacks' serving maple syrup, Cirque du Soleil and Céline Dion all come from here, and the Montreal Canadiens are hockey's most successful team.
CA-QC.p: The Coalition Avenir Québec ruled from 2018 under François Legault, who resigned in early 2026 and was succeeded by Christine Fréchette. In the general election on 5 October 2026 the CAQ lost every one of its seats. The Parti Québécois under Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, which wants another referendum on independence, won 59 of 127 seats, just short of a majority, and he was sworn in as premier of a minority government on 21 October. The Liberals came second. Cost of living, housing, US tariffs, health care and protecting the French language dominated the campaign.
q: Which province's 'Quiet Revolution' of the 1960s took schools and hospitals out of Church hands?
Which province voted to stay in Canada by just over one percentage point in 1995?
Which province has French as its only official language, and gave the world poutine and Cirque du Soleil?

US-VT.t: Abenaki people lived in the Green Mountains before French and then English settlers arrived. Both New Hampshire and New York claimed the land, and in 1777 its settlers declared their own republic, whose constitution was the first to ban adult slavery. Ethan Allen's Green Mountain Boys fought the British in the Revolution. Vermont stayed independent until 1791, when it joined as the 14th state. It sent a large share of its young men to fight for the Union in the Civil War. Farms and the granite quarries at Barre and marble quarries at Proctor shaped its economy, and Italian, Scottish and French Canadian workers came to cut stone. The Great Flood of 1927 devastated its valleys. After World War II new highways brought skiers and tourists, and in the 1960s and 1970s back-to-the-land newcomers arrived from the cities. In 2000 Vermont became the first state to create civil unions for same-sex couples.
US-VT.c: Vermont makes the most maple syrup in the US, and its dairy farms supply cheddar cheese and Ben & Jerry's ice cream. Billboards are banned, small towns hold town meetings each March, and covered bridges and white churches dot the hills. Skiing at Stowe and Killington, autumn leaves and a strong do-it-yourself, environmental streak define it. Montpelier is the only state capital without a McDonald's.
US-VT.p: Vermont is one of the most Democratic states, yet Republican Phil Scott, a moderate who often criticises Donald Trump, has been governor since 2017 and won a fifth two-year term in 2024 by a landslide. That year voters, angry about rising property taxes, also ended the Democrats' supermajority in the legislature. In 2025 lawmakers passed a major school funding reform that aims to merge small districts. Severe floods in July 2023, which swamped Montpelier, and again in July 2024 hit many towns, making flood protection a priority. A housing shortage and an ageing population are other worries.
q: Which state was an independent republic until 1791, with a constitution that banned adult slavery?
Which became the first state to create civil unions for same-sex couples, in 2000?
Which state makes the most maple syrup in the US and bans billboards?

US-NH.t: New Hampshire was one of the 13 colonies and, in January 1776, the first to set up its own government, months before the Declaration of Independence. In 1788 it became the ninth state to ratify the Constitution, the one that put it into effect. Through the 1800s its rivers powered textile mills such as the Amoskeag in Manchester, one of the largest in the world, worked by immigrants from Quebec and Ireland. The mills closed in the 1930s, and the state stayed rural and frugal. In July 1944, as World War II neared its end, delegates from 44 Allied nations met at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods and created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, the system that ran the post-war world economy. Since 1920 the state has held the nation's first presidential primary, giving a small state a large voice. After the Cold War, the Boston area's technology boom pushed growth into its southern towns.
US-NH.c: Its motto is 'Live Free or Die', printed on every car number plate, and its distrust of taxes is famous: there is no general sales tax or income tax on wages. The White Mountains draw hikers and skiers, autumn leaves bring crowds, and every four years candidates fill its diners and town halls chasing votes before the first presidential primary.
US-NH.p: Republican Kelly Ayotte, a former US senator, became governor in January 2025, succeeding fellow Republican Chris Sununu. The state is a swing state that Democrats have won in every presidential election since 2004, but Republicans control the governorship and both houses of the legislature. In 2025 Republicans opened the state's education savings accounts, which help pay for private schooling, to all families. Housing shortages and high costs, property taxes that fund schools, energy prices and the opioid crisis top the agenda. The state still guards its first-in-the-nation primary, which national Democrats tried to move in 2024.
q: Which state's Bretton Woods hosted the 1944 meeting that created the IMF and World Bank?
Which state's ratification in 1788 put the US Constitution into effect?
Which state's motto 'Live Free or Die' is on every number plate, and holds the first presidential primary?

US-ME.t: Wabanaki peoples, including the Penobscot and Passamaquoddy, lived along the coast and rivers when English and French settlers arrived in the 1600s, and the region was fought over in a century of colonial wars. Maine was part of Massachusetts until 1820, when it became a free state under the Missouri Compromise, balancing Missouri as a slave state. Its border with British Canada was disputed until the 1842 Webster-Ashburton Treaty. Lumber, shipbuilding, fishing and textile mills built the economy, and French Canadians came south to work in mill towns such as Lewiston. Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote 'Uncle Tom's Cabin' in Brunswick. In both world wars the Bath Iron Works and the naval shipyard at Kittery built warships and submarines, and during the Cold War Loring Air Force Base kept nuclear bombers ready near the shortest route to the Soviet Union. As mills closed in the late 20th century, tourism and second homes grew along the coast. In 1980 the Penobscot and Passamaquoddy won a land claims settlement from the federal government.
US-ME.c: Maine catches most of America's lobster, and lobster rolls, blueberry pie and seaside clam shacks feed summer visitors. Rocky coasts, lighthouses, Acadia National Park and vast northern forests define the state. It is one of the oldest and least diverse states, with French-Canadian roots in the north. Stephen King lives here and sets many of his books in small Maine towns.
US-ME.p: Maine leans Democratic but has an independent streak: it uses ranked-choice voting, splits its electoral votes, and has long re-elected Republican senator Susan Collins. Democrat Janet Mills, governor since 2019 and barred from a third term, launched a campaign in 2025 to challenge Collins for her Senate seat, but suspended it in April 2026. In 2025 she clashed publicly with Trump over transgender athletes in school sports. The 2023 Lewiston shooting, which killed 18 people, led to new gun laws, including a 'red flag' law approved by voters in 2025. Housing costs, an ageing population and the opioid crisis are key issues.
q: Which state split from Massachusetts in 1820 as a free state under the Missouri Compromise?
In which state did Harriet Beecher Stowe write 'Uncle Tom's Cabin'?
Which state catches most of America's lobster and is home to Stephen King?

CA-NB.t: French-speaking Acadians settled the land first, and in 1755 Britain expelled thousands of them because it doubted their loyalty in its wars with France. Some later returned to the north and east coasts. Loyalists fleeing the American Revolution arrived in the 1780s, and Britain created New Brunswick for them in 1784. It was one of the four founders of Confederation in 1867, partly because it wanted a railway link to central Canada. Its forests, shipyards and the port of Saint John supplied the Allies in both world wars, and Camp Gagetown became a major army base during the Cold War. In the 1960s the Acadian premier Louis Robichaud reformed schools, hospitals and taxes so that poorer, mostly French-speaking areas got the same services as English ones. In 1969 New Brunswick became Canada's only officially bilingual province, and language rights remain a sensitive subject between its two communities.
CA-NB.c: About a third of people speak French, and Acadians celebrate their national day on 15 August with the noisy Tintamarre parade. The Bay of Fundy has the highest tides in the world, rising and falling by more than 15 metres. Lobster, fiddleheads and McCain frozen chips, made in Florenceville, are well known, and the Irving family's businesses dominate much of the economy.
CA-NB.p: Susan Holt led the Liberals to a majority in October 2024, defeating the Progressive Conservative premier Blaine Higgs, whose government had clashed with Acadians and teachers over language and school policies. She is the province's first woman premier. Her government has focused on health care, especially access to family doctors, and on the cost of living and housing. US tariffs in 2025 threatened its exports of seafood, lumber and fuel from the Irving refinery in Saint John. Language rights and support for rural hospitals remain sensitive issues.
q: Which province did Britain create in 1784 for Loyalists fleeing the American Revolution?
Which became Canada's only officially bilingual province, in 1969?
Which province's Bay of Fundy has the world's highest tides, and is home to McCain frozen chips?

US-AZ.t: Hohokam farmers dug canals around today's Phoenix centuries ago, and the Navajo, Apache, Hopi and Tohono O'odham still live here. Spain and then Mexico claimed the land, but the US took most of it in the 1848 war with Mexico and bought the southern strip in the 1853 Gadsden Purchase. Apache resistance, led by Geronimo, lasted until 1886. In 1912 Arizona became the last of the 48 contiguous states. Copper, cattle, cotton, citrus and climate were its 'five Cs'. In World War II, Navajo Code Talkers sent messages in their own language that Japan never cracked, while Japanese Americans were held in camps on Arizona reservations. After the war, air conditioning and cheap land drew millions to Phoenix and Tucson, and the Central Arizona Project canal later brought Colorado River water to the desert cities. Barry Goldwater, an Arizona senator, ran for president in 1964 and helped launch modern American conservatism.
US-AZ.c: The Grand Canyon is the icon, and the Navajo Nation, the largest reservation in the US, covers much of the northeast. Sonoran hot dogs, chimichangas and other Mexican-influenced food are everywhere. Saguaro cacti, baseball spring training, retirees escaping cold winters and summer days above 45°C shape life. Most of the state does not use daylight saving time.
US-AZ.p: Arizona is one of the closest swing states: Joe Biden won it in 2020 and Trump in 2024. Democrat Katie Hobbs, governor since 2023, faces a Republican legislature and has vetoed a record number of bills. In 2024 the state Supreme Court revived an 1864 near-total abortion ban; lawmakers repealed it, and voters then wrote abortion rights into the state constitution. Voters also approved a measure letting state police arrest people who cross the border illegally. Water is the long-term worry: drought and a shrinking Colorado River have forced cuts, and groundwater shortages limit new housing around Phoenix.
q: Which was the last of the 48 contiguous states, in 1912, after Geronimo's Apache resistance ended?
Which state's senator Barry Goldwater helped launch modern American conservatism in 1964?
Which state has the Grand Canyon and mostly skips daylight saving time?

US-CA.t: Native peoples lived in hundreds of small nations before Spain built missions along the coast from 1769. Mexico took over in 1821, and the US seized California in the war of 1846 to 1848. Gold was found at Sutter's Mill just before the peace treaty, and the Gold Rush made it a state by 1850. Railways, oranges and oil followed, and in the 1910s film studios moved to Hollywood for its sunshine. World War II transformed it: aircraft factories and shipyards drew millions of workers, including many Black Americans from the South, while Japanese Americans on the West Coast were sent to internment camps. During the Cold War, defence spending built an aerospace industry, and Stanford and military research seeded what became Silicon Valley. Ronald Reagan, governor from 1967 to 1975, later became president. Freeways, suburbs and the 1960s counterculture in San Francisco set trends for the whole country. By 2000 the computer and internet boom had made its economy larger than those of most countries.
US-CA.c: California has more people than any other state, and about 40% are Latino, with large Asian American communities too. Spanish place names, taco trucks, Napa Valley wine, surf culture and In-N-Out burgers are everyday sights. Hollywood films and the phones and apps of Apple, Google and Meta are known worldwide. Freeway traffic, earthquakes and wildfire smoke are part of life.
US-CA.p: California is the biggest Democratic stronghold, and Governor Gavin Newsom, in office since 2019 and serving his final term, has made it the main base of resistance to the Trump administration. In January 2025 wildfires in Los Angeles killed about 30 people and destroyed more than 15,000 buildings. That June, Trump sent the National Guard and Marines into Los Angeles over Newsom's objections after protests against immigration raids. In November 2025 voters approved Proposition 50, redrawing congressional maps to favour Democrats to answer a Republican map in Texas. Housing costs, homelessness, home insurance and budget deficits remain the biggest issues.
q: Which state was made by a gold rush that began at Sutter's Mill in 1848?
Which state's governor from 1967 to 1975, Ronald Reagan, later became president?
Which state has more people than any other, plus Hollywood and Silicon Valley?

US-NM.t: Pueblo peoples have farmed along the Rio Grande for centuries, and Taos Pueblo has been lived in for about 1,000 years. Spanish settlers came north from Mexico in 1598, and Santa Fe became their capital around 1610. In 1680 the Pueblos rose up and drove the Spanish out for twelve years, one of the most successful Native revolts in North America. The US took the region from Mexico in 1848, but New Mexico waited until 1912 for statehood, partly because Congress distrusted its Hispanic and Native majority. World War II changed it overnight. At Los Alamos, a secret laboratory led by J. Robert Oppenheimer designed the atomic bomb, which was tested at Trinity in the southern desert in July 1945. Navajo code talkers served in the Pacific. In the Cold War, Los Alamos, Sandia and the White Sands missile range kept federal science at the heart of the state's economy, while uranium mining left lasting pollution on Navajo land.
US-NM.c: New Mexico has the highest share of Hispanic residents of any state, and Pueblo, Navajo and Apache communities keep their languages and ceremonies alive. The state question is 'Red or green?', about chile, and 'Christmas' means both. Adobe buildings, turquoise jewellery, Albuquerque's hot-air balloon fiesta and the desert light that drew the painter Georgia O'Keeffe define its image.
US-NM.p: Democrat Michelle Lujan Grisham has been governor since 2019 and is limited to two terms. Democrats hold both houses of the legislature, and the state reliably votes Democratic, though by smaller margins than before. Oil from the Permian Basin has made it one of the largest oil producers in the US and filled the state treasury, which helped it become, in 2025, the first state to offer free child care to all families. Yet poverty, crime and some of the weakest school results in the country persist. Wildfires and flash floods, which hit Ruidoso hard in 2024 and 2025, are growing threats.
q: Which state saw the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, which drove the Spanish out for 12 years?
In which state was the atomic bomb designed at Los Alamos and tested at Trinity?
Which state asks 'Red or green?' about chile, and has the highest Hispanic share of any state?

US-TX.t: Comanche, Apache and many other peoples lived in Texas before it became the northern edge of Spain's empire and then of independent Mexico. Mexico invited American settlers in the 1820s, but they rebelled, and after the fall of the Alamo and the victory at San Jacinto in 1836 Texas became the independent Lone Star Republic. The US annexed it in 1845, setting off the Mexican-American War. Texas joined the Confederacy, and its cattle drives and cotton fields fed the cowboy legend. In 1901 the Spindletop gusher near Beaumont began an oil boom that made Texas the centre of the American oil industry. In World War II its refineries, shipyards and air bases fed the war effort. In 1963 President Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, and Texan Lyndon Johnson took over. Houston's Mission Control guided the Apollo Moon landings from 1969. Since the 1980s low taxes and cheap land have drawn companies and millions of newcomers, making Texas the second most populous state.
US-TX.c: Texas is both Mexican and American: Tex-Mex food was born here, cowboy culture grew from Mexican vaqueros, and Spanish is heard everywhere. Brisket barbecue, Friday night high school football, rodeos and country music are shared passions. Houston, Dallas, San Antonio and Austin, known for music festivals and tech firms, each have their own character, and Texans are proud of their size and independence.
US-TX.p: Republicans have won every statewide election since 1994. Greg Abbott, governor since 2015, made border security his signature issue, sending the National Guard and razor wire to the Rio Grande and busing migrants to Democratic cities before Donald Trump returned to power. In 2025 the legislature passed school vouchers and, at Trump's urging, redrew congressional maps to gain up to five Republican seats; Democratic lawmakers left the state for two weeks to delay the vote. In July 2025 flash floods in the Hill Country killed about 135 people, including girls at a summer camp. Water, strain on the power grid and fast growth are big issues.
q: Which state was an independent Lone Star Republic after the Alamo and San Jacinto?
Which state's Spindletop gusher of 1901 began a great oil boom?
Which state gave birth to Tex-Mex food and is the second most populous?

US-AK.t: Iñupiat, Yupik, Aleut, Tlingit, Athabascan and other Native peoples lived here for thousands of years before Russian fur traders arrived in the 1700s. In 1867 the US bought the territory from Russia for $7.2 million, a deal mocked as 'Seward's Folly' until the Klondike and Nome gold rushes of the 1890s brought prospectors north. In 1942 Japan seized the Aleutian islands of Attu and Kiska, the only US soil occupied in World War II, and the Army rushed the Alaska Highway through Canada to supply the territory. Statehood followed in 1959. During the Cold War, Alaska faced the Soviet Union across the Bering Strait, only about 80 km wide, and radar stations and air bases watched for Soviet bombers. The 1964 Good Friday earthquake, the strongest ever recorded in North America, wrecked much of Anchorage. Oil found at Prudhoe Bay in 1968 led to the trans-Alaska pipeline and made the state rich, and in 1989 the Exxon Valdez tanker spilled oil across Prince William Sound.
US-AK.c: About one in seven Alaskans is Alaska Native, and hunting and fishing for caribou, salmon and whales still feed many villages. Every resident gets a yearly cheque from the oil-funded Permanent Fund. The Iditarod sled-dog race, the summer midnight sun, winter northern lights and Denali, North America's highest peak, define the place. Many towns can be reached only by plane or boat.
US-AK.p: Alaska leans Republican but has an independent streak: since 2022 it has used open primaries and ranked-choice voting, which voters narrowly chose to keep in 2024. Republican Mike Dunleavy has been governor since 2018. Politics turns on oil and gas, and the Trump administration has pushed to open more of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and to back a gas pipeline. In August 2025 Anchorage hosted a summit between Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin. Thawing permafrost, eroding coasts and storms, such as the floods that swept western villages in October 2025, threaten Native communities.
q: Which state did the US buy from Russia in 1867, a deal mocked as 'Seward's Folly'?
Which state was hit in 1964 by the strongest earthquake ever recorded in North America?
Which state pays every resident a yearly oil cheque and has Denali, North America's highest peak?

CA-YT.t: The First Nations of the Yukon lived by hunting and trading for thousands of years before outsiders arrived. Then in 1896 gold was found in a creek near the Klondike River, and about 100,000 people set out for the north. Most never reached it or found nothing, but Dawson City briefly grew into one of the largest towns in western Canada. Ottawa made the Yukon a separate territory in 1898 to keep control of the rush and stop American influence. When the gold ran out, the population collapsed. In 1942, during World War II, the US Army built the Alaska Highway through the territory in about eight months, fearing a Japanese attack on Alaska. The road brought new jobs, and the capital moved from Dawson to Whitehorse in 1953. From the 1970s the Yukon's First Nations negotiated land claims, and most now have modern agreements that let them govern themselves.
CA-YT.c: Dawson City still looks like a gold-rush town, with wooden sidewalks and a casino with cancan dancers, and Robert Service's poems about the Klondike are known across Canada. The Yukon Quest sled-dog race, the midnight sun in summer and long dark winters shape life here. About a quarter of people are Indigenous, and most live in Whitehorse.
CA-YT.p: Currie Dixon led the Yukon Party back to power in the November 2025 election, ending years of Liberal government, and he is the first premier born in the territory. Mining is the core of the economy, and the collapse of a heap-leach pad at the Eagle gold mine in 2024 leaked cyanide-contaminated water, pushed the mine's owner into receivership and led to a costly clean-up and debates about how mines are regulated. Housing, the cost of living and health care are other big issues, alongside wildfires and melting permafrost.
q: Which territory saw about 100,000 people set out for the Klondike gold rush in 1896?
Which territory's capital moved from Dawson to Whitehorse in 1953?
Which territory hosts a long-distance sled-dog race from Whitehorse and has a gold-rush town with cancan dancers?

CN-GD.t: For a century Guangzhou, which Europeans called Canton, was the only Chinese port open to Western traders. Britain's opium smuggling there led to the First Opium War of 1839 to 1842, which cost China Hong Kong and opened its ports by force. Guangdong also sent millions of emigrants to Southeast Asia and the Americas, and produced revolutionaries. Sun Yat-sen, born near Macao, plotted against the Qing from abroad, and after 1917 he set up a rival government in Guangzhou. With Soviet help he founded the Whampoa Military Academy in 1924, from which Chiang Kai-shek launched the Northern Expedition to unite China. Japan occupied Guangzhou in 1938. The real transformation came after 1978. In 1980 Deng Xiaoping made Shenzhen, then a small border town opposite Hong Kong, one of China's first special economic zones, and Hong Kong factory owners moved across in droves. Deng's 'southern tour' of 1992 restarted reform after the crackdown of 1989, and the Pearl River Delta became the world's workshop.
CN-GD.c: Cantonese, not Mandarin, is the everyday language of Guangzhou, alongside Hakka and Teochew in other areas. Cantonese cooking is famous for freshness: dim sum, roast pork, wonton noodles and slow-cooked soups, with a saying that people here eat everything with legs except the table. Shenzhen, a city of about 17 million, is a hub of electronics, drones and tech giants such as Huawei, Tencent and BYD.
CN-GD.p: Guangdong has the largest economy and population of any Chinese province. The party secretary, Huang Kunming, a member of the Politburo, outranks Meng Fanli, acting governor. Shenzhen leads China's push in electric cars, batteries and chips, but the province's export factories face US tariffs and firms moving to Vietnam. Guangdong was also at the centre of the property crash: developers Evergrande and Country Garden, both based here, defaulted, and a Hong Kong court ordered Evergrande liquidated in 2024. Beijing is pushing a 'Greater Bay Area' to tie Guangdong to Hong Kong and Macao.
q: Which province's capital, called Canton by Europeans, was the only port open to Western traders before the Opium War?
Which province's Shenzhen was made one of China's first special economic zones in 1980?
Which province speaks Cantonese and is home to Huawei, Tencent and BYD?

CN-HI.t: Hainan, a tropical island the size of Belgium, was for centuries China's place of exile, where disgraced officials such as the poet Su Dongpo were sent to the edge of the known world. Its first people, the Li, lived in the mountainous interior. In the 1920s and 1930s communist guerrillas held out in the hills, and from 1939 to 1945 Japan occupied the island and mined its iron ore. In 1950 the People's Liberation Army crossed the strait in wooden junks and took the island from Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists. For decades it was a poor outpost of Guangdong province, with state rubber farms. In 1988 Hainan became its own province and China's largest special economic zone. A wild property boom followed and crashed in the early 1990s, leaving half-built towers. The island then turned to tourism, and in the 2000s Sanya on the south coast became China's beach resort. In 2001 a US spy plane collided with a Chinese fighter and made an emergency landing there.
CN-HI.c: Hainan is China's tropical island, with palm-lined beaches, coconut and mango orchards, and resorts in Sanya where Russians and northern Chinese escape winter. Hainan chicken rice, with poached chicken and fragrant rice, travelled with emigrants to Singapore. Locals speak Hainanese, a southern Min language, and the Li and Miao minorities live in the hills. Rockets for China's space programme launch from Wenchang on the east coast.
CN-HI.p: The party secretary, Feng Fei, outranks the governor, Liu Xiaoming. Beijing is turning the island into a free trade port: on 18 December 2025 Hainan began operating as a separate customs zone, with most imports tax-free, aiming to attract investment and keep Chinese shoppers spending at home. Duty-free shopping has boomed. Hainan is also the base of China's South China Sea claims, which overlap with those of Vietnam, the Philippines and others, and it hosts naval bases. Typhoons, such as Super Typhoon Yagi in 2024, are a growing threat.
q: Which tropical island was for centuries China's place of exile for disgraced officials?
Where did a US spy plane make an emergency landing after colliding with a Chinese fighter in 2001?
Which province has the beach resorts of Sanya and a space launch site at Wenchang?

CN-FJ.t: Fujian's rugged mountains pushed its people to the sea. Under the Song and Yuan dynasties, Quanzhou was one of the world's great ports, visited by Arab traders and Marco Polo. Fujianese settled Taiwan from the 1600s and spread across Southeast Asia, which is why Hokkien, the local language, is spoken from Singapore to Manila. After the First Opium War, Xiamen and Fuzhou became treaty ports open to foreign trade. In 1949 the Nationalists retreated to Taiwan but kept the islands of Kinmen and Matsu just off the Fujian coast, and communist artillery shelled Kinmen in 1954 and 1958, crises that nearly drew in the United States. For decades Fujian was a frontline zone with little investment. After 1978 that changed: Xiamen became one of the first special economic zones in 1980, and Taiwanese businesses poured in. Xi Jinping spent 17 years in Fujian, from 1985 to 2002, rising to governor, and many of his close allies come from there.
CN-FJ.c: Fujian is known for tea: oolongs such as Tieguanyin and the rock teas of the Wuyi Mountains. The round earthen tulou houses of the Hakka are a World Heritage Site. People speak Min languages, including Hokkien and Fuzhounese, and worship the sea goddess Mazu. Buddha Jumps Over the Wall soup, oyster omelettes and fish balls are favourites. Xiamen, with its colonial-era Gulangyu island, is a popular holiday city.
CN-FJ.p: Zhao Long is the province's party secretary. Fujian sits across the strait from Taiwan, which China claims as its 34th province-level division; Taiwan's government rejects the claim. Beijing calls Fujian a 'demonstration zone' for integration with Taiwan, offering perks to Taiwanese people who move there, while the Chinese military holds large drills nearby. China's third aircraft carrier, named the Fujian, entered service in November 2025. The economy is strong: CATL, the world's biggest maker of electric car batteries, is based in Ningde, and the sportswear makers of Jinjiang, such as Anta, sell worldwide.
q: Which province's port of Quanzhou was one of the world's great ports under the Song and Yuan?
Which province faces Kinmen and Matsu, shelled by communist artillery in 1954 and 1958?
Which province is known for oolong tea and the round earthen tulou houses of the Hakka?

US-LA.t: France claimed the Mississippi valley in 1682 and named it for Louis XIV; New Orleans was founded in 1718. Spain ruled from the 1760s, France briefly took it back, and in 1803 Napoleon sold the whole territory to the US in the Louisiana Purchase, which doubled the country. Louisiana became a state in 1812, and Andrew Jackson defeated the British at New Orleans in 1815. Sugar and cotton plantations made it rich through slavery, and New Orleans had the country's largest slave market. French-speaking Acadians, expelled from Canada, became the Cajuns. In the 1920s and 1930s the populist Huey Long ran the state, building roads and schools until his assassination in 1935. In World War II Andrew Higgins's New Orleans factories built the landing craft that carried troops ashore on D-Day. Oil and gas were found offshore, and petrochemical plants spread along the river. In 2005 Hurricane Katrina broke the levees, flooded most of New Orleans and killed well over a thousand people.
US-LA.c: French heritage survives in Cajun and Creole culture, and Louisiana's law still draws on French civil law; its counties are called parishes. New Orleans gave birth to jazz, and Mardi Gras parades, gumbo, po'boys, beignets and spring crawfish boils are local traditions. Zydeco dance halls, swamp tours and LSU football fill the rest of the state.
US-LA.p: Louisiana is solidly Republican. Jeff Landry, governor since January 2024, has moved the state sharply right. He signed a law, challenged in court, requiring the Ten Commandments in every classroom, toughened criminal sentences and replaced open 'jungle' primaries with party primaries for many races. A fight over the state's congressional map, which added a second mostly Black district, reached the US Supreme Court, which struck it down in April 2026 as a racial gerrymander. Soaring home insurance costs, coastal land loss and pollution along 'Cancer Alley' are pressing issues. On 1 January 2025 a truck attack in New Orleans killed 14 people.
q: Which state is named for Louis XIV, and was sold by Napoleon in a purchase that doubled the country?
Which state was run by the populist Huey Long until his assassination in 1935?
Which state has parishes instead of counties, and gave birth to jazz?

US-MS.t: The Choctaw and Chickasaw nations held most of the land until treaties in the 1830s forced them west. Mississippi became a state in 1817, and its Delta became the richest cotton land in the world, cleared and worked by enslaved people, who made up a majority of the population by 1860. It was the second state to secede in 1861, and Union forces under Grant took Vicksburg in 1863 after a long siege. After Reconstruction, a new constitution in 1890 stripped most Black citizens of the vote, and lynching enforced Jim Crow. Hundreds of thousands of Black Mississippians left for Chicago and other northern cities in the Great Migration, taking the Delta blues with them. In the 1950s and 1960s the state was the hardest battleground of the civil rights movement: Emmett Till was murdered in 1955, Medgar Evers in 1963, and three activists during the 1964 Freedom Summer voter drive. In 2020 the state removed the Confederate battle emblem from its flag.
US-MS.c: The Mississippi Delta is the birthplace of the blues, and Elvis Presley was born in Tupelo. William Faulkner and Eudora Welty set their stories here. Fried catfish, Delta hot tamales, church life and college football fill the week, and casinos line the Gulf Coast and the river at Tunica.
US-MS.p: Mississippi is solidly Republican. Tate Reeves, governor since 2020, won re-election in 2023 against Brandon Presley, a distant cousin of Elvis. In 2025 he signed a law to phase out the state income tax over many years. Mississippi remains one of the poorest states, with among the lowest life expectancy, and it has not expanded Medicaid even as rural hospitals struggle. Big gains in children's reading scores, called the 'Mississippi miracle', have drawn national attention. Jackson, the mostly Black capital, has suffered repeated water system failures, and a scandal over misspent welfare money has dragged on for years.
q: Which state's city of Vicksburg fell to Grant after a long siege in 1863?
Which state was the hardest battleground of the civil rights movement, where Emmett Till was murdered in 1955?
Which state's Delta is the birthplace of the blues, and Elvis Presley's birthplace?

US-AL.t: Alabama became a state in 1819 on land taken from the Creek and other Native nations, who were forced west in the 1830s. Cotton grown by enslaved people on the dark soil of the Black Belt made planters wealthy, and in 1861 Montgomery became the first capital of the Confederacy. After the Civil War, Jim Crow laws kept Black Alabamians segregated and stopped most of them from voting. In the 20th century the state became the heart of the civil rights movement. Rosa Parks's arrest sparked the 1955 Montgomery bus boycott, led by a young Martin Luther King Jr. In 1963 police turned fire hoses and dogs on children marching in Birmingham, and a church bombing there killed four girls. The 1965 Selma to Montgomery marches pushed Congress to pass the Voting Rights Act. World War II and the Cold War brought new industry: from 1960 NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville developed the Saturn V rocket that carried astronauts to the Moon.
US-AL.c: College football is close to a religion, and the Alabama–Auburn 'Iron Bowl' splits families every November. Visitors notice barbecue with tangy white sauce, sweet tea, gospel music and a church in every small town. Huntsville, the 'Rocket City', is still full of engineers, and Mobile claims America's oldest Mardi Gras. Car plants built by Mercedes, Honda, Hyundai and Toyota now dot the state.
US-AL.p: Republicans control every statewide office and both houses of the legislature. Kay Ivey has been governor since 2017. In 2023 the US Supreme Court ruled that Alabama's congressional map weakened Black votes, and judges imposed a map with a second district where Black voters can choose their representative. In 2024 the state Supreme Court ruled that frozen embryos count as children, briefly halting IVF until lawmakers passed a shield law. Alabama also became the first state to execute prisoners with nitrogen gas. In 2025 President Trump announced that US Space Command would move to Huntsville from Colorado.
q: Which state's capital was the first capital of the Confederacy, and saw the 1955 bus boycott sparked by Rosa Parks?
Which state's Huntsville developed the Saturn V rocket that carried astronauts to the Moon?
Which state is split every November by the 'Iron Bowl' football game?

US-FL.t: Spain founded St. Augustine in 1565, the oldest continuously settled European city in the US. Florida passed between Spain and Britain, and Spain agreed in 1819 to hand it to the US. Wars in the 1830s pushed most Seminole people west, though some held out in the Everglades. Florida became a state in 1845 and joined the Confederacy in 1861. For decades it stayed poor and thinly settled, until railways opened the coast to tourists around 1900. After World War II, air conditioning, mosquito control and highways made it a magnet for retirees from the North. The Cold War shaped it deeply: after Fidel Castro took power in Cuba in 1959, hundreds of thousands of Cubans fled to Miami, and in 1962 the Cuban Missile Crisis put Soviet missiles about 150 km from Key West. Apollo rockets left for the Moon from Cape Canaveral, and Walt Disney World opened near Orlando in 1971. In 2000 the presidential election was decided by 537 votes in Florida.
US-FL.c: Miami is a bilingual city where Cuban coffee, Venezuelan arepas and Spanish-language radio are part of daily life. Theme parks around Orlando, the Everglades and their alligators, spring-break beaches, retirement communities and orange groves are known worldwide. Floridians live with hurricane season every summer and autumn, and rocket launches from Cape Canaveral still draw crowds to the beach.
US-FL.p: Florida has moved from swing state to Republican stronghold, with large Republican majorities in the legislature. Ron DeSantis, governor since 2019 and serving his final term, has pushed laws limiting what schools teach about race and gender, a six-week abortion ban and tough immigration measures, including a migrant detention centre in the Everglades nicknamed 'Alligator Alcatraz', opened in 2025 and closed in 2026. In 2024 most voters backed an abortion rights amendment, but it fell short of the 60% needed. Hurricanes such as Ian, Helene and Milton have pushed home insurance costs sharply up, and housing and condo costs squeeze residents.
q: Which state has the oldest continuously settled European city in the US, founded by Spain in 1565?
Which state decided the 2000 presidential election by 537 votes?
Which state has Walt Disney World, the Everglades and rocket launches from Cape Canaveral?

US-GA.t: Founded in 1733 as a buffer between British South Carolina and Spanish Florida, Georgia was the last of the 13 colonies and joined the Union in 1788. Cotton and slavery spread across the state, and in the 1830s the Cherokee were forced out on the Trail of Tears after gold was found on their land. In 1864 General Sherman burned Atlanta and marched to the sea. After the Civil War, Atlanta rebuilt as the railway hub of the 'New South', but Jim Crow laws and lynching drove many Black Georgians north in the Great Migration. Atlanta was the home of Martin Luther King Jr., and its Black colleges and churches made it a centre of the civil rights movement. Jimmy Carter, a peanut farmer from Plains, became president in 1977. Its airport, Coca-Cola, Delta and CNN made Atlanta a global city, and it hosted the 1996 Olympics. Since 2000, fast growth, immigration and a large Black middle class have turned a solidly Republican state into a fierce battleground.
US-GA.c: Atlanta is home to Coca-Cola, Delta and one of the world's busiest airports, and its hip-hop and trap artists lead the American charts. Peaches, peanuts, Vidalia onions, sweet tea and Sunday church suppers mark the countryside. Savannah's oak-shaded squares draw tourists, the Masters golf tournament is played at Augusta, and film studios have made the state a rival to Hollywood.
US-GA.p: Georgia is a top swing state: Joe Biden won it in 2020 and Trump in 2024, while both its US senators are Democrats. Republicans run state government, and Governor Brian Kemp, in office since 2019, is serving his final term. He signed a six-week abortion ban and courted electric-vehicle and battery plants, including Hyundai's factory near Savannah, where a 2025 immigration raid detained hundreds of workers, most of them South Korean. The Fulton County criminal case against Trump over the 2020 election was dropped in 2025. Hurricane Helene ravaged farms in 2024, and voting rules remain fiercely contested.
q: Which was the last of the 13 colonies, founded in 1733 as a buffer against Spanish Florida?
Which state's capital was burned by General Sherman in 1864 before his march to the sea?
Which state is home to Coca-Cola and Delta, and hosts the Masters at Augusta?

US-SC.t: English planters from Barbados founded Charles Town, now Charleston, in 1670. Rice, indigo and later cotton plantations were worked by enslaved Africans, who made up most of the population, and Charleston was the main port where captives arrived. Fearing that Abraham Lincoln's election threatened slavery, South Carolina was the first state to secede, in December 1860, and the Civil War began when Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour in April 1861. Defeat left it poor for generations, and Jim Crow laws kept Black citizens from voting until the civil rights era; a case from Clarendon County was one of those decided in Brown v. Board of Education in 1954. Fort Jackson and Parris Island trained soldiers and marines for both world wars, and the Savannah River Site made material for nuclear weapons in the Cold War. Since the 1990s, foreign carmakers such as BMW and a booming coast have transformed its economy.
US-SC.c: Gullah Geechee culture, kept alive by descendants of enslaved West Africans on the Sea Islands, shapes its food, crafts such as sweetgrass baskets, and speech. Charleston's pastel houses and church steeples, shrimp and grits, Lowcountry boils and mustard-based barbecue define the coast. Myrtle Beach draws huge summer crowds, and football at Clemson and the University of South Carolina divides families.
US-SC.p: Republicans dominate South Carolina. Henry McMaster, governor since 2017, is serving his last term. Republicans hold large majorities in the legislature, and in 2023 the state supreme court upheld a ban on most abortions after about six weeks of pregnancy. Rapid growth along the coast and around Greenville and Charleston has strained roads, schools and housing, while hurricanes and rising seas threaten the Lowcountry. The state has drawn big car and battery factories, from BMW and Volvo to Scout Motors, and power supply for new industry and data centres is a growing debate.
q: Which was the first state to secede, in December 1860?
In which state's harbour did the Civil War begin, at Fort Sumter?
Which state's Sea Islands keep Gullah Geechee culture alive?

US-NC.t: North Carolina was one of the 13 colonies and ratified the Constitution in 1789, once a Bill of Rights was promised. Tobacco, cotton and the labour of enslaved people built its economy, and it joined the Confederacy in 1861. After the Civil War, tobacco and textile mills, from Durham's cigarettes to the mill towns of the Piedmont, became its industry. On 17 December 1903 the Wright brothers made the first powered aeroplane flights at Kitty Hawk on the Outer Banks. The world wars brought huge army and marine bases, Fort Bragg and Camp Lejeune, that still shape the state. In 1960 four Black students sat at a whites-only Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro; their sit-in spread across the South and pushed the civil rights movement forward. From the 1950s Research Triangle Park, between Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill, helped turn a farm state into a centre for universities and technology, while Charlotte grew into a major banking city.
US-NC.c: College basketball rivalries between Duke, UNC and NC State are close to a religion, and Charlotte is the heart of NASCAR racing. Barbecue divides the state: vinegar-based in the east, tomato-tinged in the west. The Blue Ridge Mountains and Outer Banks beaches draw visitors, and fast-growing Charlotte and Raleigh attract newcomers from across the country.
US-NC.p: North Carolina is a swing state that leans Republican in presidential races. Democrat Josh Stein became governor in January 2025, succeeding fellow Democrat Roy Cooper, but Republicans control the legislature and often override his vetoes. Just before he took office, they moved some of the governor's powers to other officials. A 2024 state supreme court race was disputed for six months before the Democrat was confirmed as the winner, and in 2025 Republicans redrew the congressional map to gain a seat. Rebuilding western mountain towns devastated by Hurricane Helene in September 2024, fast population growth and housing costs are major issues.
q: Where did the Wright brothers make the first powered flights, at Kitty Hawk in 1903?
Which state's Greensboro lunch-counter sit-in of 1960 spread across the South?
Which state has Research Triangle Park and the Duke–UNC basketball rivalry?

US-VA.t: Jamestown, founded in 1607, was the first permanent English settlement in the Americas, and in 1619 the first enslaved Africans recorded in the English colonies arrived there. Tobacco plantations built on slavery made Virginia the richest and most populous colony. Virginians such as George Washington, Thomas Jefferson and James Madison led the American Revolution, which ended with the British surrender at Yorktown in 1781. In the Civil War Richmond was the Confederate capital, Virginia was the main battlefield, its western counties broke away, and the war ended at Appomattox in 1865. Segregation was strict, and in the late 1950s some counties closed their public schools rather than admit Black students. World War II and the Cold War transformed the state: the Pentagon was built in Arlington in 1943, the Norfolk naval base became the world's largest, and the CIA settled at Langley. Northern Virginia's suburbs grew rapidly on defence contracts and technology firms.
US-VA.c: Eight presidents were born in Virginia, more than any other state. Colonial Williamsburg, Monticello and Civil War battlefields draw history lovers, while the Blue Ridge Parkway, Shenandoah National Park and Virginia Beach draw everyone else. Smithfield ham, Chesapeake Bay oysters and a fast-growing wine industry feed it, and Northern Virginia holds the world's largest cluster of data centres.
US-VA.p: Democrat Abigail Spanberger, a former CIA officer and congresswoman, became Virginia's first woman governor in January 2026 after winning by a wide margin in November 2025, succeeding Republican Glenn Youngkin. Democrats also won the other statewide offices and expanded their majority in the House of Delegates, helped by anger at Trump's cuts to the federal workforce, which hit Northern Virginia hard. In April 2026 voters narrowly approved a Democratic plan to redraw congressional districts, but the state supreme court struck it down in May. Electricity demand from data centres, the cost of living and housing are central issues.
q: Which state was home to Jamestown, the first permanent English settlement in the Americas?
Which state's capital was the Confederate capital, and where did the war end at Appomattox?
Which state was the birthplace of eight presidents and has the Pentagon?

US-DC.t: In 1790 Congress chose a site on the Potomac River for a capital that belonged to no state, on land given by Maryland and Virginia. Pierre L'Enfant laid out its wide avenues. British troops burned the White House and the Capitol in 1814. Slavery was abolished here in 1862, and freed people made the city a centre of Black American life, with Howard University founded in 1867. The New Deal and World War II swelled the federal workforce, and during the Cold War Washington became the command centre of the Western alliance. It was also the nation's stage for protest: in 1963 Martin Luther King Jr. gave his 'I Have a Dream' speech at the Lincoln Memorial. Residents won a vote for president in 1961 and an elected mayor and council in 1973, but Congress can still overrule local laws. Riots in 1968 and the crack epidemic of the 1980s left deep scars; since the 2000s the city has grown richer and gentrified.
US-DC.c: Washington is not a state, and its licence plates protest 'Taxation Without Representation'. The Smithsonian museums on the National Mall are free. Its long Black majority gave it go-go music, the half-smoke sausage and a strong civil rights tradition, and today those neighbourhoods mix with young professionals, students and diplomats from embassies around the world. Cherry blossoms around the Tidal Basin draw crowds every spring.
US-DC.p: Washington votes overwhelmingly Democratic and elects a mayor and council, but Congress has the final say over its laws and budget, and its residents have only a non-voting delegate in Congress. Muriel Bowser, mayor since 2015, decided not to seek a fourth term in 2026. In August 2025 President Trump took temporary control of the city's police and sent the National Guard onto the streets, citing crime, over local objections. In November 2025 two Guard soldiers were shot near the White House, and one died. Federal job cuts in 2025 hit the local economy and housing market.
q: Which capital was burned by British troops in 1814?
Where did Martin Luther King Jr. give his 'I Have a Dream' speech in 1963?
Which place's licence plates protest 'Taxation Without Representation'?

US-MD.t: Maryland was founded in 1634 as a refuge for English Catholics, and its 1649 Toleration Act was an early law protecting freedom of worship. Tobacco plantations relied on enslaved Africans. Maryland joined the Union in 1788 and gave land for Washington, D.C. In 1814 the defence of Fort McHenry in Baltimore inspired 'The Star-Spangled Banner'. A slave state that stayed in the Union during the Civil War, it saw the war's bloodiest single day at Antietam in 1862, and both Frederick Douglass and Harriet Tubman escaped slavery from here. Baltimore's port, railways and the huge Sparrows Point steelworks made it an industrial city, which built Liberty ships in World War II. In the Cold War the federal government spread into the suburbs: the NSA settled at Fort Meade, and NASA's Goddard centre and the National Institutes of Health grew nearby. Baltimore lost factories and people after the 1968 riots, while the suburbs grew rich. In 2015 the death of Freddie Gray in police custody led to protests in Baltimore.
US-MD.c: Blue crabs from Chesapeake Bay, steamed and dusted with Old Bay seasoning, are the signature meal, cracked with mallets on newspaper-covered tables. The US Naval Academy is in Annapolis, sailing fills the bay and lacrosse is unusually popular. Baltimore offers Ravens football, row houses with marble steps, Edgar Allan Poe's grave and the setting of the TV series 'The Wire'.
US-MD.p: Maryland is firmly Democratic. Wes Moore, an Army veteran and author, became governor in 2023 as the state's first Black governor. A large budget gap led to tax rises in 2025, and federal job cuts under Trump hit Maryland harder than most states because so many residents work for the government. In March 2024 a container ship knocked down Baltimore's Francis Scott Key Bridge, killing six road workers, and rebuilding will take years. In 2025 Moore vetoed a bill to study reparations for slavery, and he has backed redrawing congressional maps in answer to Republican states.
q: Which colony was founded in 1634 as a refuge for English Catholics?
Which state's Fort McHenry inspired 'The Star-Spangled Banner' in 1814?
Which state is famous for blue crabs with Old Bay, and is the setting of 'The Wire'?

US-DE.t: Swedish and Dutch settlers came first, before England took over. On 7 December 1787 Delaware became the first state to ratify the US Constitution, so it calls itself 'the First State'. It was a slave state that stayed in the Union during the Civil War. In 1802 the French immigrant É. I. du Pont built a gunpowder mill on the Brandywine River, and DuPont grew into one of the world's biggest chemical companies. It supplied explosives in World War I, and in the 1930s its labs invented nylon, later used for parachutes in World War II. In 1899 the state passed a flexible corporation law, and its Court of Chancery, where expert judges decide business disputes without juries, made it the favourite legal home of American companies. In the 1980s loose limits on interest rates drew credit card banks to Wilmington. Joe Biden represented Delaware in the US Senate for 36 years before becoming vice president in 2009.
US-DE.c: Most big American companies are legally registered here, many at a single office address in Wilmington, though few have staff in the state. With no sales tax, shoppers from nearby states flock to its outlet malls. Beach towns such as Rehoboth fill up in summer, scrapple is a breakfast staple, and Joe Biden, president from 2021 to 2025, still lives near Wilmington.
US-DE.p: Delaware is solidly Democratic. Matt Meyer, a former county executive, became governor in January 2025. The state's biggest worry is its business franchise, which pays a large share of the budget. After a Delaware judge struck down Elon Musk's huge Tesla pay package in 2024, Tesla and other firms moved their legal homes to Texas or Nevada, and in 2025 lawmakers rushed through changes to make corporate law friendlier to controlling shareholders. Rising electricity bills, property taxes and school funding are also big issues.
q: Which state was first to ratify the US Constitution, on 7 December 1787?
Which state's DuPont labs invented nylon in the 1930s?
Which state is the legal home of most big American companies, and has no sales tax?

US-NJ.t: New Jersey saw some of the hardest fighting of the American Revolution: George Washington crossed the Delaware to win at Trenton on Christmas night 1776 and again at Princeton days later. It was the third state to ratify the Constitution, in 1787. Wedged between New York and Philadelphia, it industrialised early. Paterson's mills, Newark's factories and Thomas Edison's laboratory at Menlo Park, where he developed the phonograph and the electric light bulb, made it an engine of invention. Millions of immigrants from Italy, Ireland, Poland and elsewhere arrived to work there. In both world wars its shipyards and chemical works ran flat out, and in 1937 the airship Hindenburg burst into flames at Lakehurst. Albert Einstein, a refugee from Nazi Germany, lived and worked in Princeton from 1933. After 1945 highways like the Turnpike and the Garden State Parkway made it a model of American suburbia, and old industries gave way to pharmaceuticals and offices.
US-NJ.c: It is the most densely populated state, and its diners, boardwalks and the Jersey Shore are part of American pop culture. Bruce Springsteen and Frank Sinatra are its musical heroes. Pizza and bagels rival New York's, pork roll sandwiches start the day, and a large share of residents were born abroad, from India, the Dominican Republic and many other countries.
US-NJ.p: Democrat Mikie Sherrill, a former Navy helicopter pilot and congresswoman, became governor in January 2026 after a clear win in November 2025, succeeding fellow Democrat Phil Murphy. Democrats control the legislature, but the state had swung towards Donald Trump in 2024, so her result was watched as a test of his popularity. She campaigned mainly on the cost of living, promising to freeze electricity bills, which soared in 2025 as demand from data centres pushed up power prices. Property taxes, among the highest in the US, housing costs and New Jersey Transit's troubled trains are other big issues.
q: In which state did Washington win at Trenton after crossing the Delaware in 1776?
In which state did Thomas Edison develop the light bulb, and did the Hindenburg burn in 1937?
Which is the most densely populated state, home of Bruce Springsteen and the Jersey Shore?

US-CT.t: Puritans from Massachusetts settled the Connecticut River valley in the 1630s, and the 1639 Fundamental Orders are often called one of the first written constitutions, hence 'the Constitution State'. Connecticut joined the Union in 1788. In the 1800s its inventors and factories in Hartford, New Haven and Waterbury made clocks, brass, rubber goods and Colt revolvers, and immigrants from Ireland, Italy and Poland filled the mills. In both world wars its factories made guns, aircraft engines and submarines, earning it the name 'Arsenal of the Nation'. During the Cold War the Electric Boat yard in Groton built the Nautilus, the first nuclear-powered submarine, launched in 1954, and Pratt & Whitney built jet engines. Hartford became known as the insurance capital of the world. Wealthy New York commuters settled in Fairfield County, while old factory cities such as Bridgeport lost jobs and people. In 2012 a gunman killed 20 children and six adults at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown.
US-CT.c: Yale University dominates New Haven, where coal-fired 'apizza' from old pizzerias draws long queues. Mark Twain wrote Tom Sawyer while living in Hartford. The state mixes wealthy suburbs with yacht clubs, quiet colonial villages with white churches, the UConn basketball teams that fans follow fiercely, and two huge casinos run by Native nations, Foxwoods and Mohegan Sun.
US-CT.p: Connecticut is firmly Democratic. Ned Lamont, a businessman who has been governor since 2019, has kept a tight budget, built large reserves and paid down pension debt. Housing costs and the shortage of new homes in wealthy suburbs dominate debate: in 2025 Lamont vetoed a major housing bill, saying it went too far, then signed a revised version passed in a special session. Electricity bills are among the highest in the country. Federal cuts to Medicaid and research worry hospitals and universities, while Electric Boat is hiring thousands of workers to build submarines.
q: Which state is called 'the Constitution State' after its 1639 Fundamental Orders?
Which state's Groton shipyard built the Nautilus, the first nuclear-powered submarine?
Which state is home to Yale, and whose capital is known as the insurance capital of the world?

US-RI.t: Roger Williams, banished from Massachusetts for his religious views, founded Providence in 1636 as a refuge where church and state were kept apart. Rhode Island's merchants later grew rich from shipping, including a large part of the American slave trade. It was the first colony to renounce allegiance to Britain, in May 1776, but it feared a strong central government and was the last of the 13 to ratify the Constitution, in 1790. Around the same time Samuel Slater's mills in Pawtucket started America's industrial revolution, and textile and jewellery factories drew immigrants from Ireland, Italy, Portugal and French Canada. In the Gilded Age the richest families built summer mansions in Newport. Both world wars made Narragansett Bay a naval hub: the Newport torpedo station turned out torpedoes for the fleet, and the Naval War College still trains officers there. After World War II the mills closed, and Providence became known for political corruption before reviving its downtown from the 1990s.
US-RI.c: It is the smallest state, and nowhere is far from the sea. Rhode Islanders drink coffee milk, eat clam chowder, stuffed quahogs and 'hot wieners', and many have Italian, Portuguese or Irish roots. Newport hosts famous jazz and folk festivals and sailing races, and Providence's WaterFire lights bonfires on its rivers on summer evenings.
US-RI.p: Rhode Island is solidly Democratic, and politics is personal. Democrat Dan McKee became governor in 2021 when Gina Raimondo left to join President Biden's cabinet, and won a full term in 2022. His approval ratings have been low, partly because of the Washington Bridge, a main route into Providence that was suddenly closed to westbound traffic in December 2023 because of structural failures and had to be rebuilt. In September 2026 he lost the Democratic primary to Helena Foulkes. Housing costs, among the fastest rising in New England, offshore wind projects that the Trump administration tried to halt in 2025, and the state's finances are key issues.
q: Which colony did Roger Williams found at Providence in 1636, keeping church and state apart?
Which was the last of the 13 colonies to ratify the Constitution, in 1790?
Which is the smallest state, where people drink coffee milk?

US-MA.t: The Pilgrims landed at Plymouth in 1620 with help from the Wampanoag people, and Puritans founded Boston in 1630 and Harvard in 1636. Boston led the resistance to Britain: the Boston Tea Party of 1773 and the first battles at Lexington and Concord in 1775 began the Revolution. Massachusetts joined the Union in 1788 and became a centre of the movement to abolish slavery. In the 1800s textile mills at Lowell and Lawrence drew Irish, Italian and French-Canadian workers, and Irish Americans came to dominate Boston politics. In World War II and the Cold War, radar and computer labs at MIT and military contracts built a high-tech industry along Route 128. In 1960 John F. Kennedy of Massachusetts became the first Catholic president. Boston's fights over school busing in the 1970s exposed deep racial divisions. Since then universities, hospitals and biotechnology have made Greater Boston one of the world's great research centres, and in 2004 Massachusetts became the first state to allow same-sex marriage.
US-MA.c: Harvard and MIT draw students and scientists from around the world. Bostonians are known for their accent, the Red Sox and Fenway Park, and the Boston Marathon every April. Clam chowder, lobster rolls and Dunkin' coffee are local staples. Cape Cod's beaches, Plymouth's Pilgrim story and the autumn leaves of the Berkshires draw visitors.
US-MA.p: Massachusetts is among the most Democratic states. Maura Healey, governor since 2023, is the first woman elected to the job. Housing costs, among the highest in the country, are the main issue, and Healey has pushed laws to build more homes. In 2023 and 2024 a surge of migrant families overwhelmed the emergency shelter system, leading to limits on stays. In 2025 Harvard took the Trump administration to court after it froze billions of dollars in research grants, and federal cuts threaten the state's universities and hospitals. High energy costs are another worry.
q: Which state saw the Boston Tea Party and the first battles of the Revolution?
Which became in 2004 the first state to allow same-sex marriage?
Which state is home to Harvard, MIT and the Red Sox?

CN-ZJ.t: Zhejiang has been one of China's richest regions for a thousand years. Hangzhou was the capital of the Southern Song dynasty in the 1100s and 1200s, and Marco Polo called it the finest city in the world. The Grand Canal carried its rice and silk north. After the First Opium War, Ningbo became a treaty port, and Ningbo merchants went on to dominate business in nearby Shanghai. Chiang Kai-shek was born in Fenghua in Zhejiang, and many of his Nationalist leaders were from the province. Japan occupied much of it from 1937, and in 1942 its troops used germ weapons in Zhejiang. After 1978 Zhejiang pioneered private business: Wenzhou's family workshops making shoes, lighters and buttons became the model of bottom-up capitalism, and Yiwu grew into the world's largest market for small goods. In 1999 Jack Ma founded Alibaba in Hangzhou. Xi Jinping was the province's party secretary from 2002 to 2007, and several of his trusted officials came from his time there.
CN-ZJ.c: Hangzhou's West Lake, ringed by willows, pagodas and tea hills, is one of China's classic views, and its Longjing green tea is prized. Shaoxing makes yellow rice wine, and canal towns like Wuzhen draw crowds. The local Wu dialects are very different from Mandarin. Food is light and slightly sweet: Dongpo pork, West Lake fish in vinegar sauce and Ningbo rice cakes. Hangzhou hosted the 2023 Asian Games.
CN-ZJ.p: The party secretary, Wang Hao, outranks the governor, Liu Jie. Zhejiang is China's private-sector heartland, and Beijing named it a demonstration zone for Xi Jinping's 'common prosperity' drive to narrow wealth gaps. Hangzhou became the symbol of China's tech revival in 2025, when local start-up DeepSeek released a low-cost AI model that shook global markets, and robot makers like Unitree drew attention. Alibaba recovered after a government crackdown on tech giants from 2020. Exporters in Yiwu and Ningbo, one of the world's busiest ports, face the strain of US tariffs.
q: Which province's capital was the Southern Song capital, called by Marco Polo the finest city in the world?
Which province's Wenzhou and Yiwu became models of bottom-up capitalism after 1978?
Which province's capital has the West Lake and Longjing tea, and is the home of Alibaba?

CN-SH.t: Shanghai was a modest county town until the First Opium War. In 1842 the Treaty of Nanking opened it to foreign trade, and the British, French and Americans carved out settlements that they ran themselves, outside Chinese law. By the 1920s it was Asia's most cosmopolitan city, with banks along the riverfront Bund, factories, gangsters and jazz. The Chinese Communist Party held its first congress here in 1921. In 1927 Chiang Kai-shek massacred communists and unionists in the city. Japan fought a brutal battle for Shanghai in 1937 and occupied it, and some 20,000 Jewish refugees from Europe found shelter in the Hongkou district. After 1949 foreigners left and Shanghai became a state-run industrial city; it was also the base of the radical 'Gang of Four' during the Cultural Revolution. In 1990 Beijing opened Pudong, the farmland across the river, as a new financial zone, and its skyline of skyscrapers now faces the Bund. Shanghai hosted the 2010 World Expo.
CN-SH.c: China's biggest city, with about 25 million people, Shanghai is its financial capital and most international place. The Bund, the Pudong skyline and the old alleyway lilong houses sit side by side. People speak Shanghainese at home and Mandarin at work. Xiaolongbao soup dumplings, shengjian fried buns and sweet braised pork are local classics. Tesla's first factory outside the United States opened here in 2019.
CN-SH.p: The party secretary, Chen Jining, a member of the Politburo, outranks the mayor, Zhu Zhongming. Shanghai's party chief is usually a rising national figure: Li Qiang, its party secretary during the harsh two-month Covid lockdown of 2022, became China's premier in 2023. The city is a centre of carmaking, chips, finance and biotech, and it is building up its stock exchange's tech board. Its challenges are a fast-ageing population, falling house prices and foreign firms scaling back as tensions with the United States grow.
q: Where did the Chinese Communist Party hold its first congress, in 1921?
Which city sheltered some 20,000 Jewish refugees from Europe in its Hongkou district?
Which is China's biggest city, with the Bund and the Pudong skyline?

CN-JS.t: Jiangsu, on the lower Yangtze, has been rich since the Grand Canal connected it to Beijing. Suzhou's silk and gardens and Yangzhou's salt merchants made the region famous. Nanjing, 'southern capital', was the capital of the early Ming dynasty and later of the Taiping rebels, whose defeat in 1864 left the city wrecked. In 1842 the treaty that ended the First Opium War was signed at Nanjing. Sun Yat-sen was sworn in there as first president of the Republic of China in 1912, and Chiang Kai-shek made it his capital from 1927. In December 1937 Japanese troops captured Nanjing and murdered and raped on a huge scale in the Nanjing Massacre; China puts the death toll at 300,000. After 1949 Jiangsu was split in two, then reunited in 1952. From the 1980s rural township enterprises boomed, and Suzhou's industrial parks, built with Singapore, drew foreign factories, making Jiangsu one of the richest provinces.
CN-JS.c: Suzhou's classical gardens and canals and Nanjing's city walls and Purple Mountain are top sights. Jiangsu's Huaiyang cuisine is delicate and slightly sweet: lion's head meatballs, salted duck from Nanjing and Yangzhou fried rice. People here speak Wu dialects in the south and Mandarin in the north. In 2025 an amateur football league between Jiangsu's cities, the 'Su Super League', became a national craze with packed stadiums and fierce banter.
CN-JS.p: The party secretary, Xin Changxing, outranks the governor, Liu Xiaotao. Jiangsu has the second-largest economy among China's provinces, with industries from solar panels and chemicals to chips and biomedicine. It is a manufacturing base for foreign companies, which makes it exposed to US tariffs and supply chains moving elsewhere. Like other provinces it faces a property slump, local-government debts and a rapidly ageing population. Pollution in Lake Tai and the Yangtze has improved after closures of chemical plants.
q: Which province's capital was the scene of a massacre by Japanese troops in December 1937?
In which province was the treaty ending the First Opium War signed, in 1842?
Which province has Suzhou's classical gardens and gave its name to Yangzhou fried rice?

US-OR.t: Chinook, Klamath, Nez Perce and many other peoples lived in what is now Oregon before fur traders came. In the 1840s thousands of American families followed the Oregon Trail to the Willamette Valley, and the 1846 Oregon Treaty with Britain set the border at the 49th parallel.
